questions.question: A payment service at mcnz.com uses a Cloud Firestore transaction to decrease a user's wallet balance and to add a ledger entry. If one of the operations inside this transaction fails, what will Cloud Firestore do?

options.text: Firestore converts the attempt into a batch write and keeps the successful writes
Firestore commits the successful changes and skips only the failing step
The transaction is aborted and none of the operations are committed
The failed step is placed on Cloud Tasks for a later retry

questions.correct_text: The transaction is aborted and none of the operations are committed
questions.explanation:
The correct option is The transaction is aborted and none of the operations are committed.

Cloud Firestore transactions are atomic, meaning either every operation in the transaction succeeds and the commit applies or any failure causes a full rollback. Nothing is partially written, and changes are only made visible if the entire transaction function completes successfully. The client SDK may retry the whole transaction when there are contention or transient errors, but if it ultimately fails then nothing is committed.

Firestore converts the attempt into a batch write and keeps the successful writes is wrong because transactions and batched writes are different APIs and Firestore does not convert one into the other. A failed transaction never keeps partial results and there is no automatic fallback to a batched write.

Firestore commits the successful changes and skips only the failing step is wrong because that would violate the all or nothing guarantee of transactions. If one operation fails, the entire set of operations is rolled back.

The failed step is placed on Cloud Tasks for a later retry is wrong because Firestore does not enqueue failed operations into Cloud Tasks. Any retry behavior is handled by the SDK retrying the whole transaction or by your application logic.

questions.explanation_pt:
A opção correta é: A transação é abortada e nenhuma das operações é confirmada (committed).

As transações do Cloud Firestore são atômicas, o que significa que ou todas as operações da transação são bem-sucedidas e o commit é aplicado, ou qualquer falha causa um rollback completo. Nada é gravado parcialmente, e as alterações só se tornam visíveis se toda a função da transação for concluída com sucesso. O SDK do cliente pode tentar novamente a transação inteira quando há contenção ou erros transitórios, mas se ela falhar definitivamente, nada é confirmado.

O Firestore converte a tentativa em uma gravação em lote (batch write) e mantém as gravações bem-sucedidas está incorreto porque transações e gravações em lote são APIs diferentes, e o Firestore não converte uma na outra. Uma transação que falha nunca mantém resultados parciais e não há fallback automático para uma batched write.

O Firestore confirma as alterações bem-sucedidas e pula apenas a etapa que falhou está incorreto porque isso violaria a garantia de tudo ou nada das transações. Se uma operação falha, todo o conjunto de operações sofre rollback.

A etapa que falhou é colocada no Cloud Tasks para uma nova tentativa posterior está incorreto porque o Firestore não enfileira operações que falharam no Cloud Tasks. Qualquer comportamento de nova tentativa é tratado pelo SDK, que repete a transação inteira, ou pela lógica da sua aplicação.

questions.question: Your team at Lakeshore Artworks is building a Cloud Function that responds to Cloud Storage object finalize events for a bucket that receives uploads from sample-shop.io. You want to cut the development feedback loop to under five minutes while following Google recommended practices so developers can test quickly and iterate safely. What should you do?

options.text: Configure Cloud Audit Logs to trigger a new Cloud Function when the original function source changes and test the new function with synthetic requests
Edit a duplicate of the function in the console editor and route the production web application to it to validate changes live
Refactor the function into an HTTP triggered variant and test it by calling the endpoint with mock payloads during development
Run the storage triggered function locally using Functions Framework and emulate Cloud Storage events with curl to localhost

questions.correct_text: Run the storage triggered function locally using Functions Framework and emulate Cloud Storage events with curl to localhost
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Refactor the function into an HTTP triggered variant and test it by calling the endpoint with mock payloads during development.

This approach shortens the feedback loop because an HTTP function can be invoked instantly with representative request bodies that mirror Cloud Storage event payloads. Google recommends separating business logic from the trigger and exercising that logic through fast, repeatable calls, which an HTTP entry point enables during development and CI. Developers can validate parsing and error paths quickly without waiting for real object finalize events and without touching production buckets.

Configure Cloud Audit Logs to trigger a new Cloud Function when the original function source changes and test the new function with synthetic requests is not appropriate because Audit Logs are not designed to react to source edits in order to spin up test functions. Source changes should flow through a proper build and deploy pipeline, and this method would not deliver fast or reliable iteration on event handling.

Edit a duplicate of the function in the console editor and route the production web application to it to validate changes live is risky and not recommended. Editing in the console bypasses version control and code review, and sending production traffic to validate changes endangers reliability and user experience.

Run the storage triggered function locally using Functions Framework and emulate Cloud Storage events with curl to localhost is not the recommended fastest path. While you can run HTTP functions locally with the Functions Framework, accurately producing Cloud Storage CloudEvents requires extra tooling. Simply curling localhost doesn't faithfully emulate storage event metadata and envelopes, so this won't provide reliable or streamlined feedback for development.

A opção correta é: Refatorar a função para uma variante acionada por HTTP e testá-la chamando o endpoint com payloads simulados (mock) durante o desenvolvimento.

Essa abordagem encurta o ciclo de feedback porque uma função HTTP pode ser invocada instantaneamente com corpos de requisição representativos que espelham os payloads de eventos do Cloud Storage. O Google recomenda separar a lógica de negócio do gatilho (trigger) e exercitar essa lógica por meio de chamadas rápidas e repetíveis, o que um ponto de entrada HTTP permite durante o desenvolvimento e a CI. Configurar o Cloud Audit Logs para acionar uma nova Cloud Function quando o código-fonte da função original mudar e testar a nova função com requisições sintéticas não é apropriado, porque os Audit Logs não foram projetados para reagir a edições de código-fonte com o objetivo de criar funções de teste. Mudanças no código-fonte devem fluir por um pipeline adequado de build e deploy, e esse método não entregaria iteração rápida ou confiável no tratamento de eventos.

Editar uma duplicata da função no editor do console e direcionar a aplicação web de produção para ela para validar mudanças ao vivo é arriscado e não recomendado. Editar no console contorna o controle de versão e a revisão de código, e enviar tráfego de produção para validar mudanças coloca em risco a confiabilidade e a experiência do usuário.

Executar a função acionada por storage localmente usando o Functions Framework e emular eventos do Cloud Storage com curl para localhost não é o caminho mais rápido recomendado. Embora você possa executar funções HTTP localmente com o Functions Framework, produzir com precisão CloudEvents do Cloud Storage exige ferramentas adicionais. Simplesmente usar curl no localhost não emula fielmente os metadados e envelopes dos eventos de storage, então isso não fornecerá um feedback confiável ou otimizado para o desenvolvimento.

questions.question: Birchwood Logistics runs ten containerized microservices on Compute Engine virtual machines. Traffic surges by roughly 15 times during a 90 minute marketing window and then drops to near idle levels for about 10 hours overnight. The team wants to redesign the system to improve elasticity and performance while minimizing cost when demand is low, and they prefer a managed approach to cut operational burden. Which platform should they adopt?

options.text: Replatform to App Engine standard environment
Increase the fixed pool of Compute Engine instances
Migrate the services to Cloud Run
Deploy on GKE Autopilot with Horizontal Pod Autoscaler

questions.correct_text: Migrate the services to Cloud Run
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Migrate the services to Cloud Run.

This service runs container images without requiring you to manage servers, and it automatically scales up quickly to absorb brief marketing surges. It can also scale to zero when idle, which minimizes cost during the long overnight lull. It bills on actual usage rather than provisioned capacity and it lowers operational burden while delivering strong elasticity and performance for HTTP driven microservices.

Replatform to App Engine standard environment is not a great fit for arbitrary containerized workloads because standard relies on specific language runtimes rather than custom containers. It would likely require code and deployment changes to fit the sandbox constraints and offers less flexibility for existing container images.

Increase the fixed pool of Compute Engine instances wouldn't be elastic and would force you to overprovision for the 15 times peak, which wastes money during the long idle period. It also leaves you with ongoing instance and configuration management that the team wants to avoid.

Deploy on GKE Autopilot with Horizontal Pod Autoscaler reduces some node management but still requires Kubernetes expertise and ongoing tuning. It commonly keeps baseline capacity running and introduces extra operational complexity compared with a fully managed request driven platform, so it is usually less cost efficient than a scale to zero service for spiky traffic.

A opção correta é: Migrar os serviços para o Cloud Run.

Esse serviço executa imagens de contêiner sem exigir que você gerencie servidores, e ele escala automaticamente e rapidamente para absorver picos breves de marketing. Ele também pode escalar até zero quando ocioso, o que minimiza custos durante a longa calmaria da madrugada. A cobrança é baseada no uso real, em vez de capacidade provisionada, reduzindo a carga operacional ao mesmo tempo em que entrega forte elasticidade e desempenho para microsserviços orientados a HTTP.

Replataformar para o App Engine standard environment não é uma ótima opção para workloads arbitrárias em contêiner, porque o standard depende de runtimes de linguagem específicos em vez de contêineres customizados. Isso provavelmente exigiria mudanças de código e de deploy para se adequar às restrições do sandbox e oferece menos flexibilidade para imagens de contêiner existentes.

Aumentar o pool fixo de instâncias do Compute Engine não seria elástico e forçaria você a superprovisionar para o pico de 15 vezes, o que desperdiça dinheiro durante o longo período ocioso. Também deixaria você com o gerenciamento contínuo de instâncias e configuração que a equipe quer evitar.

Fazer deploy no GKE Autopilot com Horizontal Pod Autoscaler reduz parte do gerenciamento de nós, mas ainda exige expertise em Kubernetes e ajustes contínuos. Ele comumente mantém uma capacidade base em execução e introduz complexidade operacional extra em comparação com uma plataforma totalmente gerenciada e orientada a requisições, então geralmente é menos eficiente em custo do que um serviço que escala até zero para tráfego com picos.

questions.question: PineMutual Media runs its mobile API on App Engine Standard, and the growth team wants to run an A and B experiment on a new recommendation feature to measure user engagement. The platform must serve two live API versions with a 70 to 30 traffic split and capture request metrics, and the team cannot modify application code. What should you do?

options.text: Migrate the backend to Cloud Run and deploy two revisions with percent based traffic splitting
Deploy two versions on App Engine and configure built in traffic splitting for the desired percentages
Recreate the service on Compute Engine and place an NGINX reverse proxy in front to route users by cookie
Place an External HTTP(S) Load Balancer in front and use URL maps to distribute 70 and 30 percent to two backends

questions.correct_text: Deploy two versions on App Engine and configure built in traffic splitting for the desired percentages
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Deploy two versions on App Engine and configure built in traffic splitting for the desired percentages.

With App Engine traffic splitting you can run two live versions and route seventy percent to one and thirty percent to the other without touching application code. The platform supports random, cookie, or IP based splits, which enables clean A and B experiments. Request logs and metrics are captured per version in Cloud Monitoring and Cloud Logging so you can measure engagement without any code changes.

Migrate the backend to Cloud Run and deploy two revisions with percent based traffic splitting is unnecessary for an app already on App Engine Standard and likely requires containerization and operational changes that conflict with the constraint to avoid modifying the application. Although Cloud Run supports percent based traffic splitting, migrating offers no benefit over the native capability already available.

Recreate the service on Compute Engine and place an NGINX reverse proxy in front to route users by cookie introduces heavy operational overhead and complexity when the platform already provides built in percentage based routing. Cookie management, proxy configuration, and metrics correlation would all become custom work and none of it is required to meet the stated needs.

Place an External HTTP(S) Load Balancer in front and use URL maps to distribute 70 and 30 percent to two backends does not meet the requirement because URL maps route by host or path rather than by percentage. It also adds an extra layer that does not improve on the native version level splitting available in the service.

A plataforma suporta divisões baseadas em random, cookie ou IP, o que permite experimentos A/B limpos. Os logs de requisição e métricas são capturados por versão no Cloud Monitoring e Cloud Logging, então você pode medir o engajamento sem nenhuma alteração de código.

Migrar o backend para o Cloud Run e fazer deploy de duas revisões com divisão de tráfego baseada em porcentagem é desnecessário para uma aplicação que já está no App Engine Standard e provavelmente exige containerização e mudanças operacionais que conflitam com a restrição de evitar modificar a aplicação. Embora o Cloud Run suporte divisão de tráfego baseada em porcentagem, migrar não oferece benefício sobre a capacidade nativa já disponível.

Recriar o serviço no Compute Engine e colocar um proxy reverso NGINX na frente para rotear usuários por cookie introduz uma sobrecarga operacional e complexidade pesadas, quando a plataforma já fornece roteamento integrado baseado em porcentagem. Gerenciamento de cookies, configuração de proxy e correlação de métricas se tornariam todos trabalho customizado, e nada disso é necessário para atender às necessidades informadas.

Colocar um External HTTP(S) Load Balancer na frente e usar URL maps para distribuir 70 e 30 por cento para dois backends não atende ao requisito, porque os URL maps roteiam por host ou path em vez de por porcentagem. Isso também adiciona uma camada extra que não melhora a divisão nativa em nível de versão disponível no serviço.

questions.question: A regional credit union must keep application audit logs for 7 years to satisfy regulatory controls. The logs are seldom accessed during normal operations, yet auditors may request them on short notice and the team must retrieve them quickly. Which Google Cloud service is the most appropriate for storing these logs?

options.text: Cloud Firestore
Cloud Storage Coldline storage class
Cloud Storage Standard storage class
Cloud Bigtable

questions.correct_text: Cloud Storage Coldline storage class
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Cloud Storage Coldline storage class because it provides low cost long term storage for data that is rarely accessed while still offering fast retrieval when auditors request it.

This storage class is designed for multi year retention and provides immediate access with high availability, satisfying the need to retrieve logs quickly. It minimizes ongoing storage costs and applies retrieval and early deletion charges only when you access the data, which aligns with seldom read audit logs. You can also enforce compliance with retention policies and bucket lock, so the seven year requirement can be met reliably.

The Cloud Storage Standard storage class is optimized for frequently accessed data and would be unnecessarily expensive for storing rarely accessed logs for seven years even though it delivers fast retrieval.

Cloud Firestore is a transactional document database for application data and is not intended for bulk log archiving. It lacks the cost profile and lifecycle controls that make object storage suitable for long term compliance retention.

Cloud Bigtable is a managed NoSQL database for high throughput and low latency workloads such as time series processing and is not an archival storage solution. Keeping inactive logs there for seven years would be costly and operationally unnecessary.

questions.explanation_pt:
A opção correta é: A classe de armazenamento Cloud Storage Coldline, porque oferece armazenamento de longo prazo a baixo custo para dados que raramente são acessados, ao mesmo tempo em que ainda oferece recuperação rápida quando os auditores solicitam.

Essa classe de armazenamento foi projetada para retenção de múltiplos anos e oferece acesso imediato com alta disponibilidade, atendendo à necessidade de recuperar logs rapidamente. Ela minimiza os custos contínuos de armazenamento e aplica cobranças de recuperação e exclusão antecipada apenas quando você acessa os dados, o que se alinha a logs de auditoria raramente lidos. Você também pode impor conformidade com políticas de retenção e bucket lock, de modo que o requisito de sete anos possa ser atendido de forma confiável.

A classe de armazenamento Cloud Storage Standard é otimizada para dados acessados com frequência e seria desnecessariamente cara para armazenar logs raramente acessados por sete anos, mesmo entregando recuperação rápida.

O Cloud Firestore é um banco de dados de documentos transacional para dados de aplicação e não se destina ao arquivamento em massa de logs. Ele não possui o perfil de custo e os controles de ciclo de vida que tornam o armazenamento de objetos adequado para retenção de conformidade de longo prazo.

O Cloud Bigtable é um banco de dados NoSQL gerenciado para workloads de alta vazão e baixa latência, como processamento de séries temporais, e não é uma solução de armazenamento de arquivamento. Manter logs inativos lá por sete anos seria caro e operacionalmente desnecessário.

questions.question: Sagebrush Logistics runs several containerized microservices on Google Kubernetes Engine. The security team requires every container image in use to be scanned for known vulnerabilities with as little operational overhead as possible, and they prefer a solution that integrates natively with Google Cloud and runs automatically when images are pushed. What should you implement?

options.text: Configure Web Security Scanner to scan your GKE services for container image vulnerabilities
Run a scheduled GKE CronJob that pulls images in use and scans them with open source tools like Trivy or Clair
Turn on vulnerability scanning in Artifact Registry and enable the Container Analysis API so images are scanned automatically on push
Rely on a Binary Authorization policy to block images and use it as your only control for vulnerability checks

questions.correct_text: Turn on vulnerability scanning in Artifact Registry and enable the Container Analysis API so images are scanned automatically on push
questions.explanation:
The right answer is Turn on vulnerability scanning in Artifact Registry and enable the Container Analysis API so images are scanned automatically on push.

Artifact Registry vulnerability scanning combined with the Container Analysis API is a native Google Cloud capability that automatically analyzes container images on push. It requires very little management effort, stores findings centrally, and integrates well with GKE workflows. You can view results in Cloud Console and automate policy gates by combining the scan results with deployment controls if needed.

Configure Web Security Scanner to scan your GKE services for container image vulnerabilities is not appropriate because Web Security Scanner performs dynamic testing of running web applications. It does not scan container images in a registry and does not trigger on image push events.

Run a scheduled GKE CronJob that pulls images in use and scans them with open source tools like Trivy or Clair adds significant operational overhead and maintenance. It is not a native push triggered workflow and you would need to build scheduling, permissions, result storage, and alerting yourself.

Rely on a Binary Authorization policy to block images and use it as your only control for vulnerability checks is insufficient because Binary Authorization enforces deploy time policy and does not perform vulnerability scanning. It works best when it uses attestations from a scanner such as Container Analysis rather than replacing scanning.

questions.question: Your team is building a SaaS platform for BirchValley Creative that needs to send email from each user's Gmail account. The application must authenticate each individual user and request only the least privilege needed to send messages without reading or managing drafts or inboxes. Which approach should you implement for authentication and authorization?

options.text: Create an OAuth client ID and request the https://www.googleapis.com/auth/gmail.compose scope to obtain a per user access token
Create an OAuth client ID and request only the https://www.googleapis.com/auth/gmail.send scope to acquire an access token per user
Configure a service account with domain wide delegation and the https://www.googleapis.com/auth/gmail.compose scope
Use an API key with HTTP referrer restrictions to call the Gmail API

questions.correct_text: Create an OAuth client ID and request only the https://www.googleapis.com/auth/gmail.send scope to acquire an access token per user
questions.explanation:
The correct approach is Create an OAuth client ID and request only the https://www.googleapis.com/auth/gmail.send scope to acquire an access token per user.

This approach respects least privilege because the gmail.send scope allows only sending messages. It does not permit reading messages or managing drafts and labels. It also ensures each user explicitly consents and receives their own access token, which fits a multi-tenant SaaS pattern where users authenticate individually.

Create an OAuth client ID and request the https://www.googleapis.com/auth/gmail.compose scope to obtain a per user access token is too permissive because the compose scope grants permission to manage drafts in addition to sending. That exceeds the requirement to send email without reading or managing inboxes or drafts.

Configure a service account with domain wide delegation and the https://www.googleapis.com/auth/gmail.compose scope is not appropriate for a SaaS app that must authenticate each individual user because domain wide delegation relies on an administrator granting organization wide impersonation. It also requests a broader compose scope than needed.

Use an API key with HTTP referrer restrictions to call the Gmail API does not work because Gmail requires user authorization with OAuth and API keys cannot access user data or send mail as a user.

questions.explanation_pt:
A abordagem correta é criar um OAuth client ID e solicitar apenas o escopo https://www.googleapis.com/auth/gmail.send para adquirir um access token por usuário.

Essa abordagem respeita o privilégio mínimo, porque o escopo gmail.send permite apenas o envio de mensagens. Ele não permite ler mensagens nem gerenciar rascunhos e labels. Também garante que cada usuário consinta explicitamente e receba seu próprio access token, o que se encaixa em um padrão SaaS multi-tenant em que os usuários se autenticam individualmente.

Criar um OAuth client ID e solicitar o escopo https://www.googleapis.com/auth/gmail.compose para obter um access token por usuário é permissivo demais, porque o escopo compose concede permissão para gerenciar rascunhos além de enviar. Isso excede o requisito de enviar e-mail sem ler ou gerenciar caixas de entrada ou rascunhos.

Configurar uma service account com delegação em todo o domínio (domain-wide delegation) e o escopo https://www.googleapis.com/auth/gmail.compose não é apropriado para um app SaaS que precisa autenticar cada usuário individualmente, porque a domain-wide delegation depende de um administrador conceder personificação em toda a organização. Além disso, solicita um escopo compose mais amplo do que o necessário.

Usar uma API key com restrições de HTTP referrer para chamar a Gmail API não funciona, porque o Gmail exige autorização do usuário com OAuth, e API keys não conseguem acessar dados do usuário nem enviar e-mail como um usuário.

questions.question: OvertureLive operates an online box office for a chain of concert halls, and demand spikes sharply the moment a popular show goes on sale. As soon as a particular seat is locked in, the customer's browser should receive an instant confirmation, and the platform has to absorb those peaks gracefully. How would you architect the booking flow to satisfy both goals?

options.text: Persist each booking as an object in Cloud Storage and use an object finalize trigger to fire a Cloud Run service that finalizes the order
Publish each booking as a message onto a Pub/Sub topic and wire Eventarc to invoke a GKE service that handles the booking
Enqueue the booking in Cloud Tasks, which kicks off a Workflows orchestration to carry out the booking
POST the booking over HTTP to an external Application Load Balancer that hands it to a Compute Engine managed instance group for handling

questions.correct_text: Publish each booking as a message onto a Pub/Sub topic and wire Eventarc to invoke a GKE service that handles the booking
questions.explanation:
The best fit is to publish each booking as a message onto a Pub/Sub topic and wire Eventarc to invoke a GKE service that handles the booking.

Decoupling the web tier from the booking processor through a message broker keeps the front end responsive and lets the system push very high volume. During an on-sale rush the broker absorbs the burst so that stateless workers can fan out horizontally and clear the backlog quickly. A worker claims the seat with a transactional write, emits the result, and the browser surfaces an immediate confirmation, whether by briefly awaiting the outcome or receiving a push over a web socket. Pairing an ordering key per seat with idempotent handlers guarantees a single winner and prevents retries from double booking.

Persisting each booking as a Cloud Storage object and reacting to a finalize trigger is a poor fit, because object storage is not a transactional booking queue. Writing one file per request adds latency and offers no clean per-seat ordering or contention-safe way to stop double bookings.

Enqueuing in Cloud Tasks to drive a Workflows orchestration layers on orchestration latency and suits rate-limited background jobs more than a very high fan-in event stream. It lacks native per-key ordering and does not handle the bursty streaming throughput an on-sale event generates.

POSTing directly to an external Application Load Balancer fronting a Compute Engine managed instance group couples synchronous processing to VMs and depends on instance autoscaling that can lag a sudden surge. With no buffering layer, overload and contention become likely and safe seat locking is harder to build at scale.

questions.explanation_pt:
A melhor opção é publicar cada reserva como uma mensagem em um tópico do Pub/Sub e conectar o Eventarc para invocar um serviço do GKE que processa a reserva.

Desacoplar a camada web do processador de reservas por meio de um message broker mantém o front end responsivo e permite que o sistema sustente um volume muito alto. Durante um pico de vendas, o broker absorve a rajada para que workers stateless possam escalar horizontalmente e limpar a fila rapidamente. Um worker reivindica o assento com uma escrita transacional, emite o resultado, e o navegador apresenta uma confirmação imediata, seja aguardando brevemente o desfecho ou recebendo um push por um web socket. Combinar uma ordering key por assento com handlers idempotentes garante um único vencedor e impede que retentativas causem reservas duplicadas.

Persistir cada reserva como um objeto no Cloud Storage e reagir a um trigger de finalização é uma escolha ruim, porque armazenamento de objetos não é uma fila de reservas transacional. Escrever um arquivo por requisição adiciona latência e não oferece uma ordenação por assento limpa nem uma forma segura contra contenção para impedir reservas duplicadas.

Enfileirar no Cloud Tasks para acionar uma orquestração com Workflows adiciona latência de orquestração e é mais adequado para jobs em segundo plano com limite de taxa do que para um fluxo de eventos com fan-in muito alto. Falta-lhe ordenação nativa por chave e ele não lida com a vazão de streaming em rajadas que um evento de venda gera.

Fazer POST diretamente para um external Application Load Balancer na frente de um managed instance group do Compute Engine acopla o processamento síncrono a VMs e depende do autoscaling de instâncias, que pode ficar atrás de um pico repentino. Sem uma camada de buffer, sobrecarga e contenção tornam-se prováveis, e o bloqueio seguro de assentos fica mais difícil de construir em escala.

questions.question: Which gcloud command should you run first to authenticate and set the default project and compute zone after installing the Google Cloud SDK?

options.text: gcloud auth login
gcloud init
gcloud config set project

questions.correct_text: gcloud init
questions.explanation:
The correct option is gcloud init.

This command launches an interactive setup that authenticates your account and configures your active gcloud settings. It guides you to choose the default project and to set the default compute region and zone, so it is the right first command after installing the SDK.

The option gcloud auth login only authenticates you with your Google account. It does not configure the default project or compute zone, so it does not meet the requirement to both authenticate and set defaults.

questions.question: Brookline Hub is a digital platform for coordinating volunteer projects, scheduling fitness classes, and connecting neighborhood businesses with residents. The startup is expanding to new continents and needs enhanced capabilities so customers in those markets have a reliable experience. Brookline Hub will hire and train regional support teams that operate in local time zones. Its environment combines an on premises data center with Google Cloud services, and they must scale seamlessly while providing transparent uptime insights and fast incident investigation. Investors require the application to launch in more regions, support 15 times as many concurrent users, deliver a consistent experience for users who travel between regions, collect user activity metrics to inform monetization, ensure compliance with regional rules such as GDPR, reduce infrastructure management effort and cost, and adopt Google recommended practices for standardized release workflows along with clearly defined service level indicators and service level objectives. Technical needs include secure connectivity between the on premises network and cloud workloads, faster and more reliable validation of new features, and actionable logging and performance telemetry that enable debugging and alerting as demand grows. Which Google Cloud product best satisfies the need to define and track service level indicators and service level objectives across these services?

options.text: Cloud Trace
Cloud Monitoring
Cloud Logging
Cloud Profiler

questions.correct_text: Cloud Monitoring
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Cloud Monitoring.

Cloud Monitoring provides built in capabilities to define services, choose appropriate SLIs such as availability and latency, create SLOs with error budgets, visualize conformance on dashboards, and configure alerts including burn rate alerts. It also offers uptime checks and multi region visibility, which together deliver the transparent reliability insights and standardized SRE workflows the scenario requires.

It ingests metrics from Google Cloud and from on premises systems through agents and custom metrics. This lets teams track user experience and reliability as demand grows and as users move between regions. It also accelerates incident investigation by correlating SLO breaches with telemetry, while the SLO management features remain within Cloud Monitoring.

Cloud Trace focuses on distributed tracing and latency analysis for requests and microservices. It helps diagnose performance issues but does not provide a way to define or track SLIs and SLOs.

Cloud Logging centralizes and analyzes logs and can create log based metrics and alerts. It does not offer SLO objects or error budget tracking, so it cannot directly manage SLIs and SLOs.

Cloud Profiler continuously profiles resource usage such as CPU and memory to optimize code performance. It is not used to define or monitor service level indicators or objectives.

questions.question: Cypress Retail is creating a new Google Cloud project and the platform lead wants to understand why they would assign predefined roles to developers. What is the primary goal of predefined roles in Google Cloud IAM?

options.text: To enforce explicit deny rules on targeted resources
To enable a rapid start by granting broad permissions across a project
To define custom role bundles unique to an organization
To provide narrowly scoped permissions for specific services and tasks

questions.correct_text: To provide narrowly scoped permissions for specific services and tasks
questions.explanation:
The correct option is To enable a rapid start by granting broad permissions across a project. Predefined roles package commonly needed permissions and can be granted at the project level so developers can start working quickly without waiting for custom roles to be designed and reviewed.

Predefined roles are maintained by Google, which reduces administrative overhead and speeds onboarding. By assigning these curated permission sets at the appropriate scope, teams can move forward while still avoiding the overexposure that comes from using basic roles.

To enforce explicit deny rules on targeted resources is wrong because explicit denies are configured with IAM Deny policies and not with roles. Predefined roles only grant permissions and do not enforce deny behavior.

To define custom role bundles unique to an organization is wrong because that describes custom roles, which are created and managed by the organization. Predefined roles are created and maintained by Google.

To provide narrowly scoped permissions for specific services and tasks is wrong in this context because the question asks for the primary goal for assigning these roles to developers when starting a new project, which is to accelerate onboarding and productivity rather than to emphasize narrow scoping as the main objective.

Fornecer permissões com escopo restrito para serviços e tarefas específicos está errado neste contexto porque a questão pede o objetivo principal de atribuir esses papéis aos desenvolvedores ao iniciar um novo projeto, que é acelerar a integração e a produtividade, em vez de enfatizar o escopo restrito como objetivo principal.

questions.question: At Hawthorn Retail a team built a Google Cloud Functions service that calls Pub/Sub, Cloud Storage, and Secret Manager for a new order processing workflow, and they want to keep deployment responsibilities separate from runtime permissions while following least privilege. How should they configure identities and access for the function?

options.text: Use the default Compute Engine service account and grant it the Project Owner role
Create a new service account and assign the Editor role, and allow the deployer to act as that service account
Create a new service account with a custom IAM role limited to required permissions and allow the deployer to act as that service account
Create a new service account with a custom IAM role and grant the deployer permission to generate access tokens for that service account

questions.correct_text: Create a new service account with a custom IAM role limited to required permissions and allow the deployer to act as that service account
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Create a new service account with a custom IAM role limited to required permissions and allow the deployer to act as that service account.

This approach gives the function its own runtime identity with only the permissions it needs for Pub/Sub, Cloud Storage, and Secret Manager. You can include just the necessary actions such as publishing or subscribing to topics, accessing required storage objects, and reading secrets. The deployer retains deployment responsibilities by having permission to deploy the function and to act as the runtime service account through the Service Account User capability. This cleanly separates deployment from runtime and enforces least privilege.

Use the default Compute Engine service account and grant it the Project Owner role violates least privilege because Owner is unrestricted across the project and the default service account is shared. This expands blast radius and does not separate deployment from runtime permissions.

Create a new service account and assign the Editor role, and allow the deployer to act as that service account is still overly broad. Editor grants many permissions unrelated to Pub/Sub, Cloud Storage, and Secret Manager, so it does not meet least privilege.

Create a new service account with a custom IAM role and grant the deployer permission to generate access tokens for that service account gives the deployer token minting ability that allows impersonation of the service account outside deployment workflows. Deployment only requires the ability to act as the service account rather than to generate access tokens, so this grants more access than necessary.

Essa abordagem dá à função sua própria identidade de execução (runtime) com apenas as permissões de que ela precisa para Pub/Sub, Cloud Storage e Secret Manager. Você pode incluir apenas as ações necessárias, como publicar ou se inscrever em tópicos, acessar os objetos de armazenamento exigidos e ler secrets. O implantador mantém as responsabilidades de implantação tendo permissão para implantar a função e para atuar como a service account de runtime por meio da capacidade Service Account User. Isso separa de forma clara a implantação da execução e aplica o privilégio mínimo (least privilege).

Usar a service account padrão do Compute Engine e conceder a ela o papel Project Owner viola o privilégio mínimo porque Owner é irrestrito em todo o projeto e a service account padrão é compartilhada. Isso amplia o raio de impacto (blast radius) e não separa as permissões de implantação das de execução.

Criar uma nova service account e atribuir o papel Editor, permitindo que o implantador atue como essa service account, ainda é excessivamente amplo. Editor concede muitas permissões não relacionadas a Pub/Sub, Cloud Storage e Secret Manager, portanto não atende ao privilégio mínimo.

Criar uma nova service account com um papel IAM personalizado e conceder ao implantador permissão para gerar tokens de acesso para essa service account dá ao implantador a capacidade de cunhar tokens, o que permite a impersonação da service account fora dos fluxos de trabalho de implantação. A implantação requer apenas a capacidade de atuar como a service account, e não de gerar tokens de acesso, portanto isso concede mais acesso do que o necessário.

questions.question: WestBridge Tickets is preparing to roll out a new revision of its service to a production Google Kubernetes Engine cluster. You expect that some containers might fail on startup and you want to reduce customer impact while following Google's recommended rollout practices. What should you do?

options.text: Convert the Deployment to a StatefulSet and run a rolling update while setting the HorizontalPodAutoscaler scale down behavior to 0
Perform a rolling update and apply a PodDisruptionBudget that ensures at least 80% of pods remain available
Perform a rolling update and configure the HorizontalPodAutoscaler scale down behavior to 0 to block scale in during the release
Convert the Deployment to a StatefulSet and perform a rolling update with a PodDisruptionBudget that keeps at least 80% of pods available

questions.correct_text: Perform a rolling update and apply a PodDisruptionBudget that ensures at least 80% of pods remain available
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Perform a rolling update and apply a PodDisruptionBudget that ensures at least 80% of pods remain available.

Rolling updates are the recommended way to release changes for a Deployment in GKE because they keep traffic flowing while new pods come up and pass readiness checks. A PodDisruptionBudget enforces a minimum level of availability during voluntary disruptions and upgrades, so at least 80 percent of replicas remain serving while the rollout progresses. This rolling update with a PDB combination reduces customer impact if some new containers fail to start because healthy pods continue to handle requests until replacements are ready.

Convert the Deployment to a StatefulSet and run a rolling update while setting the HorizontalPodAutoscaler scale down behavior to 0 is not appropriate because StatefulSet is intended for workloads that need stable identities or persistent storage. Switching controllers adds complexity without helping with startup failures, and the HPA scale down behavior does not ensure availability during a rollout.

Perform a rolling update and configure the HorizontalPodAutoscaler scale down behavior to 0 to block scale in during the release focuses on autoscaling behavior rather than rollout safety. HPA behavior affects how quickly replicas are reduced under low load and does not guarantee a minimum number of ready pods during updates, which is what a PodDisruptionBudget and the Deployment strategy provide.

Convert the Deployment to a StatefulSet and perform a rolling update with a PodDisruptionBudget that keeps at least 80% of pods available still makes the unnecessary switch to StatefulSet. If the application does not need stable network identity or ordered updates, a Deployment with a rolling update and a PDB is the recommended pattern.

Realizar um rolling update e configurar o comportamento de scale down do HorizontalPodAutoscaler para 0 para bloquear a redução durante o lançamento foca no comportamento de autoscaling em vez da segurança da implantação. O comportamento do HPA afeta a rapidez com que as réplicas são reduzidas sob baixa carga e não garante um número mínimo de pods prontos durante as atualizações, que é o que um PodDisruptionBudget e a estratégia do Deployment fornecem.

Se a aplicação não precisa de identidade de rede estável ou atualizações ordenadas, um Deployment com um rolling update e um PDB é o padrão recomendado.

questions.question: How can you enable time limited per object access to Cloud Storage with a 45 minute default expiry while letting senders set custom expirations and without granting standing permissions?

options.text: Object ACLs per recipient
Signed URLs with per object custom expiry
IAM Conditions time bound role on bucket
Cloud CDN signed cookies

questions.correct_text: Signed URLs with per object custom expiry
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Signed URLs with per object custom expiry. It delivers time limited access to an individual object and you can set a 45 minute expiration by default while still letting the sender choose a different expiration when creating the URL. It does not require granting any standing IAM or ACL permissions to the recipient.

With Signed URLs you sign a URL for a specific object using a service account or an HMAC key and include an expiration timestamp. Anyone with that link can read or write as allowed until it expires. Your implementation can default the expiration to 45 minutes and let callers override the value per object, which satisfies both the default and customization requirements.

Object ACLs per recipient would require granting each recipient an access entry that persists until you remove it, which violates the requirement to avoid standing permissions. ACLs are also a legacy mechanism and are often disabled by uniform bucket level access, so they are not a good fit for new designs.

IAM Conditions time bound role on bucket applies a temporary role to a principal at the bucket scope, so it is not per object and still grants the principal permissions for a period of time. This does not create a shareable time limited link and does not let senders set different expirations for each object.

Cloud CDN signed cookies are used to control access to content served through Cloud CDN and an HTTP load balancer. They do not apply to direct Cloud Storage API access and are typically scoped to a domain or path rather than a single object, so they do not meet the requirement here.

ACLs também são um mecanismo legado e frequentemente ficam desativadas pelo acesso uniforme no nível do bucket (uniform bucket level access), portanto não são adequadas para novos designs.

O papel temporal com IAM Conditions limitado por tempo no bucket aplica um papel temporário a um principal no escopo do bucket, portanto não é por objeto e ainda concede ao principal permissões por um período. Isso não cria um link compartilhável por tempo limitado e não permite que os remetentes definam expirações diferentes para cada objeto.

questions.question: A Cloud Storage bucket is the destination for Cloud Logging audit logs that are exported and held for 90 days. What is the reason for assigning the Coldline storage class to that bucket?

options.text: It boosts how available the bucket is across regions
It cuts the cost of storing logs that are seldom read
It shortens the network latency between Cloud Logging and Cloud Storage
It makes BigQuery log analytics run faster

questions.correct_text: It cuts the cost of storing logs that are seldom read
questions.explanation:
The right reason is that it cuts the cost of storing logs that are seldom read.

Coldline targets data touched only occasionally, which describes exported audit logs that simply need to sit for 90 days. Its 90-day minimum storage duration lines up precisely with the retention window in this case. Picking Coldline over Standard or Nearline lowers what you pay to keep the data, and you can still pull logs back when required, keeping in mind that retrievals carry a charge.

Boosting availability across regions is not what the class does, because cross-regional availability comes from the bucket's location type such as region, dual-region, or multi-region rather than from the storage class. Coldline adds no geographic reach and in fact carries a lower availability SLA than Standard.

Shortening network latency is unrelated, since latency is driven by the locations you pick and the export pipeline, not the storage class. The class has no bearing on the network path or the speed of delivering exports.

Making BigQuery analytics faster is incorrect, because analytics speed depends on BigQuery configuration, the data format, and where the data lives. The storage class does nothing to accelerate analysis, and Coldline can even tack on retrieval costs when you read.

questions.question: At MarinerMedia, a BigQuery dataset named "CoreLedger" stores employee travel and expense records and each row has a department code. There are ten departments, and you want a simple setup that prevents staff from seeing data outside their own department while keeping all data in a single place. What should you do?

options.text: Create a separate dataset for each department and build a Dataflow or scheduled query pipeline that copies only that department's rows from the "CoreLedger" tables, then grant users access to their department dataset
Keep a single dataset and create one authorized view per department in the "CoreLedger" dataset where each view filters by department, then grant users access only to their department's view
In the "CoreLedger" dataset create a distinct physical table for each department and give employees permissions to query only their department table

Create a dataset for each department and in each one define a view that selects just that department's rows from the "CoreLedger" tables and authorize the view to read the source dataset, then grant access to the per department dataset

questions.correct_text: Keep a single dataset and create one authorized view per department in the "CoreLedger" dataset where each view filters by department, then grant users access only to their department's view
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Keep a single dataset and create one authorized view per department in the "CoreLedger" dataset where each view filters by department, then grant users access only to their department's view.

This approach satisfies the requirement to keep all data in one place while enforcing row level restrictions through query filtering. It avoids copying or reshaping data and relies on logical definitions that return only the rows a user should see. Administration is simpler because the underlying tables remain centralized and unchanged while you only manage access to the filtered objects that users query. This keeps costs lower, reduces the chance of data drift, and makes governance and auditing easier.

Create a separate dataset for each department and build a Dataflow or scheduled query pipeline that copies only that department's rows from the "CoreLedger" tables, then grant users access to their department dataset is wrong because it duplicates data, adds pipeline complexity, and introduces latency and inconsistency risks while also violating the goal of a simple setup that keeps everything in one place.

In the "CoreLedger" dataset create a distinct physical table for each department and give employees permissions to query only their department table is wrong because it fragments the schema and increases maintenance overhead. It also leads to data duplication and brittle queries and it scales poorly as departments or reporting needs change.

Create a dataset for each department and in each one define a view that selects just that department's rows from the "CoreLedger" tables and authorize the view to read the source dataset, then grant access to the per department dataset is wrong because it multiplies datasets and access policies, making administration more complex. The question emphasizes a simple setup with a single place for data, and this approach moves away from that.

questions.question: On Google Kubernetes Engine, which autoscaling mechanism should you use to automatically tune pod replicas as load shifts so response times stay steady?

options.text: Node Auto Provisioning
Horizontal Pod Autoscaler driven by average CPU utilization
Vertical Pod Autoscaler

questions.correct_text: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler driven by average CPU utilization
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Horizontal Pod Autoscaler driven by average CPU utilization. It scales the replica count of a deployment based on observed CPU load, so response times remain steady as traffic varies.

It uses a target average CPU utilization percentage to add or remove replicas. This matches the goal of keeping latency stable because additional replicas come online when CPU climbs and replicas are removed when demand falls. It integrates with the Kubernetes Metrics Server in GKE and reacts quickly under load.

Node Auto Provisioning is wrong because it focuses on adding or resizing nodes by extending the cluster autoscaler. It does not modify the pod replica count and does not directly manage application latency.

Vertical Pod Autoscaler is wrong because it adjusts CPU and memory requests for pods rather than scaling replica counts. It can trigger pod restarts and is geared toward right sizing resources rather than maintaining steady response times as traffic changes.

Ele se integra com o Kubernetes Metrics Server no GKE e reage rapidamente sob carga.

questions.question: A research startup named Cascade Metrics is building microservices on Google Cloud that communicate through Pub/Sub topics, and the team wants to run integration tests on laptops without sending requests to the managed service. What should they use to emulate Pub/Sub locally?

options.text: Create a separate Google Cloud project and use the actual Pub/Sub service
Pub/Sub Lite
Cloud Pub/Sub emulator
Implement a custom mock messaging layer

questions.correct_text: Cloud Pub/Sub emulator
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Cloud Pub/Sub emulator.

This emulator runs a local in memory Pub/Sub service so your microservices can publish and subscribe on laptops without sending traffic to the managed service. It supports the standard client libraries when you point them to the local endpoint and enables realistic integration tests while avoiding network dependencies and billing.

Create a separate Google Cloud project and use the actual Pub/Sub service is wrong because it still calls the managed service over the network and can incur costs. It does not allow fully local and offline testing on developer machines.

Pub/Sub Lite is wrong because it is a different managed product with distinct semantics and capacity provisioning. It is not an emulator and does not provide a local developer runtime.

Implement a custom mock messaging layer is wrong because custom mocks rarely match real Pub/Sub behavior, which can lead to gaps in ordering, delivery semantics, flow control, and error handling. This increases maintenance effort and reduces test fidelity compared with using the official emulator.

questions.question: You need a Google Cloud combination for a stateless REST API that sees brief bursts of roughly 2,200 requests per second lasting about 12 minutes, must drop to zero instances while idle, and must sit on a serverless datastore. Which pairing fits best?

options.text: A Compute Engine managed instance group together with Cloud Bigtable
App Engine flexible together with Firestore in Native mode
Cloud Functions together with Firestore in Native mode
Cloud Run together with Firestore Datastore mode

questions.correct_text: Cloud Run together with Firestore Datastore mode
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Cloud Run together with Firestore Datastore mode, because it covers a stateless REST API that has to scale to zero when idle, ride out short bursts near 2,200 requests per second, and sit on a serverless datastore.

Cloud Run is a fully managed container runtime that drops to zero while idle and scales out fast on request concurrency, which is exactly what sudden bursts demand. Raising concurrency lets a single instance field many requests at once, trimming cold starts and sustaining thousands of requests per second through a brief surge. Firestore Datastore mode is a serverless NoSQL store that scales on its own with no capacity to plan, matching the need for a low-overhead managed backend.

A Compute Engine managed instance group with Cloud Bigtable does not fit. The instance group means managing VMs and is not serverless, and Bigtable needs provisioned nodes and ongoing capacity work, so it never reaches zero and is not serverless.

App Engine flexible with Firestore in Native mode falls short because the flexible environment will not scale to zero and is slow to spin up instances, driving idle cost up and reaction to short bursts down. Firestore Native is serverless, but the compute layer breaks the scale-to-zero requirement.

Cloud Functions with Firestore in Native mode is weaker for a high-throughput REST API. Functions is serverless and scales fast, but its model centers on event-driven single-purpose handlers and can hit heavier cold-start or concurrency limits depending on generation and settings. Cloud Run gives tighter control over concurrency and container resources, a better match for sustained HTTP bursts.

Aumentar a concorrência permite que uma única instância atenda muitas requisições ao mesmo tempo, reduzindo cold starts e sustentando milhares de requisições por segundo durante uma rajada breve. O Firestore no modo Datastore é um armazenamento NoSQL serverless que escala por conta própria, sem capacidade a planejar, atendendo à necessidade de um backend gerenciado de baixo overhead.

Cloud Functions com Firestore no modo Native é mais fraco para uma API REST de alta vazão. As Functions são serverless e escalam rapidamente, mas seu modelo é centrado em handlers de propósito único orientados a eventos e pode esbarrar em limites maiores de cold start ou concorrência, dependendo da geração e das configurações. questions.question: You need to process new Cloud Storage objects within 25 seconds and you want an event driven, auto scaling solution that incurs compute cost only when files arrive. What should you use?

options.text: Dataflow streaming with Pub/Sub notifications
Cloud Functions with Storage finalize trigger
App Engine with Cron Service
Cloud Run with Cloud Scheduler

questions.correct_text: Cloud Functions with Storage finalize trigger
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Cloud Functions with Storage finalize trigger.

It runs automatically when a new object is successfully created in Cloud Storage and begins processing immediately. It scales up on demand and scales to zero when idle, so you pay only while the function is executing. Typical cold starts and invocation times make processing within 25 seconds realistic for most workloads.

Dataflow streaming with Pub/Sub notifications isn't the best fit because a streaming pipeline runs continuously and keeps workers active. This incurs ongoing compute cost even when no new files arrive, which breaks the pay only on arrival requirement.

App Engine with Cron Service is schedule based rather than event driven. It would require polling on a schedule, which can delay processing and does not guarantee action within 25 seconds of object creation. It can also waste compute between checks.

Cloud Run with Cloud Scheduler is also timer based. This pair would invoke on a schedule rather than on storage events, which introduces polling delay and unnecessary cost. While Cloud Run can be event driven with the right trigger, that is not what this option proposes.

questions.question: Your team at sample-shop.io is preparing a staged rollout of a new build of a web service. You want only users whose browsers present a specific User Agent header to reach the new build for a limited pilot, and if there are problems you must be able to send all requests back to the prior release within about 60 seconds without another deployment. How should you set up the release so it meets these requirements?

options.text: Deploy on Cloud Run and use percentage based traffic splitting to send a small share of requests to the new revision
Use GKE with Istio Service Mesh and define a VirtualService that routes requests matching a User Agent header to the new version, and update routing to revert instantly if needed
Deploy on App Engine and configure traffic splitting so that the new version receives requests based on the User Agent header
Publish the app as multiple Cloud Functions and create distinct HTTP triggers for each browser type

questions.correct_text: Use GKE with Istio Service Mesh and define a VirtualService that routes requests matching a User Agent header to the new version, and update routing to revert instantly if needed
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Use GKE with Istio Service Mesh and define a VirtualService that routes requests matching a User Agent header to the new version, and update routing to revert instantly if needed.

This approach satisfies the requirement to send only browsers with a specific User Agent header to the new build because an Istio VirtualService can match on HTTP headers and route only those requests to the pilot revision. It also enables a quick rollback because you only change routing configuration without redeploying, so traffic can be shifted back to the prior release within seconds, satisfying the 60 second target.

Deploy on Cloud Run and use percentage based traffic splitting to send a small share of requests to the new revision is wrong because percentage based splitting cannot target requests by User Agent header. It can gradually shift traffic but it cannot confine the pilot to only the specified browsers.

Deploy on App Engine and configure traffic splitting so that the new version receives requests based on the User Agent header is wrong because App Engine traffic splitting supports random, cookie based, or IP based splits rather than routing by arbitrary headers like User Agent. It therefore cannot meet the selective header based pilot requirement.

Publish the app as multiple Cloud Functions and create distinct HTTP triggers for each browser type is wrong because it forces an unnecessary architectural split and does not provide centralized header based routing. It also complicates rollback and would likely require redeployment or client changes rather than a quick configuration switch.

Portanto, ela não consegue atender ao requisito de piloto seletivo baseado em header.

Publicar a aplicação como múltiplas Cloud Functions e criar gatilhos HTTP distintos para cada tipo de navegador está errado, porque força uma divisão arquitetural desnecessária e não fornece roteamento centralizado baseado em header. questions.question: scrumtuous.com runs a serverless REST API on Cloud Run. The engineering group wants to compare response latency for several runtime configurations using real production traffic over the next 21 days. The API must stay fully available and the application code cannot be modified. What should you do?

options.text: Migrate the API to Compute Engine and place a global HTTP load balancer in front to spread requests across VM templates with different settings
Deploy the API to App Engine as multiple versions and send a percentage of traffic to each version
Use Cloud Run revisions and split traffic between revisions that are configured differently
Use Cloud Functions with one function per configuration and route traffic among them

questions.correct_text: Use Cloud Run revisions and split traffic between revisions that are configured differently
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Use Cloud Run revisions and split traffic between revisions that are configured differently. This lets you test multiple runtime configurations with real production requests while keeping the API fully available and without changing the application code.

Cloud Run creates a new revision for each deployment, and each revision can carry different configuration settings such as CPU, memory, concurrency, and autoscaling limits. You can then split incoming traffic by percentage across those revisions to run an A or B or multivariant comparison using real users. You can keep this split in place for 21 days and observe response latency through Cloud Run metrics and logs, and you can instantly shift all traffic back to the best performing revision without any code change.

Migrate the API to Compute Engine and place a global HTTP load balancer in front to spread requests across VM templates with different settings is not appropriate because this moves away from a serverless platform, adds operational overhead, and requires a migration that risks availability. It also conflicts with the constraint to avoid code changes when a native capability already exists on the current service.

Deploy the API to App Engine as multiple versions and send a percentage of traffic to each version is unnecessary and risky because it requires moving the workload to a different platform, which likely needs packaging or configuration changes and introduces migration effort. Cloud Run already provides revisions and traffic splitting that meet the requirement without moving services.

Use Cloud Functions with one function per configuration and route traffic among them would require restructuring the API into multiple functions and changing code, and functions are better suited to single purpose handlers rather than a full REST service. This violates the requirement to make no application changes and does not match the current architecture.

questions.question: A Cloud Run workload in your project must create and modify Firestore documents but should not hold any administrative rights. Following least privilege, which IAM role do you bind to the service's service account so it can write to Firestore?

options.text: roles/firestore.user
roles/firestore.databaseViewer
roles/firestore.databaseUser
roles/firestore.admin

questions.correct_text: roles/firestore.user
questions.explanation:
The correct role is roles/firestore.databaseUser. It lets the service account write documents to Firestore without granting any administrative power, which is exactly what least privilege calls for.

This role covers creating and updating documents along with running queries and transactions. It deliberately leaves out heavyweight admin abilities such as managing indexes, importing or exporting data, or changing database configuration, so the access stays confined to application-level data operations.

roles/firestore.user is not the right pick for granting document write access against Firestore database resources, because it does not carry the database-scoped permissions that the database user role is built to provide.

roles/firestore.databaseViewer permits only viewing database data and metadata. It cannot create or update documents, so it fails the requirement to write.

roles/firestore.admin hands over sweeping administrative control of Firestore, far more than plain document writes need, which breaks least privilege.

roles/firestore.user não é a escolha certa para conceder acesso de escrita de documentos aos recursos do banco de dados Firestore, porque não carrega as permissões com escopo de banco de dados que o papel database user foi feito para fornecer.

roles/firestore.databaseViewer permite apenas visualizar os dados e metadados do banco de dados. Ele não consegue criar ou atualizar documentos, então falha no requisito de escrita.

roles/firestore.admin entrega amplo controle administrativo do Firestore, muito mais do que simples escritas de documentos exigem, o que quebra o princípio de menor privilégio.

questions.question: ElmRiver Media runs an analytics platform on a zonal managed instance group with 20 Compute Engine virtual machines and needs to share a 900 GB static read only dataset with all instances so the application can read it from a normal filesystem path with very low latency and fast instance initialization while keeping costs low. Which approach should you use?

options.text: Store the dataset in Cloud Storage and use a startup script to copy the data to each VM boot disk during initialization
Place the data on a Compute Engine persistent disk, create a snapshot, then create one disk per VM from the snapshot and attach it to each VM
Put the dataset on a zonal Compute Engine persistent disk and attach the disk in read only mode to all instances in the managed instance group
Move the data to a Cloud Storage bucket and mount it on each VM using Cloud Storage FUSE

questions.correct_text: Put the dataset on a zonal Compute Engine persistent disk and attach the disk in read only mode to all instances in the managed instance group
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Put the dataset on a zonal Compute Engine persistent disk and attach the disk in read only mode to all instances in the managed instance group.

This approach gives every VM a normal filesystem path with block storage performance and very low latency. It avoids per instance data copy so instances start quickly. It also keeps costs low because you maintain a single copy of the 900 GB dataset on one persistent disk while safely sharing it read only across all VMs in the same zone.

Store the dataset in Cloud Storage and use a startup script to copy the data to each VM boot disk during initialization causes long boot times because each VM must copy 900 GB before the application can run, and it multiplies storage costs across all instances.

Place the data on a Compute Engine persistent disk, create a snapshot, then create one disk per VM from the snapshot and attach it to each VM provides a normal filesystem path but creates 20 full copies, which greatly increases storage costs and slows provisioning compared with sharing a single read only disk.

Move the data to a Cloud Storage bucket and mount it on each VM using Cloud Storage FUSE does not meet very low latency requirements because user space FUSE access introduces higher latency and lower throughput than persistent disks and can slow application startup when reading many objects.

Mover os dados para um bucket do Cloud Storage e montá-lo em cada VM usando Cloud Storage FUSE não atende aos requisitos de latência muito baixa, porque o acesso FUSE em espaço de usuário introduz maior latência e menor throughput do que os persistent disks e pode tornar a inicialização da aplicação mais lenta ao ler muitos objetos.

questions.question: On GKE, how can you use the Google Cloud HTTP(S) Load Balancer to serve two distinct hostnames on a single static external IP and route each one to its own Service?

options.text: Create a Service of type LoadBalancer and set loadBalancerIP to the existing address
Extend the current Ingress with a host rule for the new hostname
Use Cloud DNS CNAME records to point both hostnames at the same IP and depend on backend routing
Create a new Ingress and set the kubernetes.io/ingress.global-static-ip-name annotation to reuse the same static IP

questions.correct_text: Extend the current Ingress with a host rule for the new hostname
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Extend the current Ingress with a host rule for the new hostname.

This approach uses a single global HTTP load balancer with a URL map that supports multiple host rules on one static external IP. Adding another host entry and path mapping to the existing Ingress causes the controller to update the same load balancer so each hostname is routed to its own Kubernetes Service.

Create a Service of type LoadBalancer and set loadBalancerIP to the existing address is wrong because a Service of type LoadBalancer provisions an L4 load balancer and does not provide host based HTTP routing. It would also try to allocate its own forwarding rule rather than reuse the existing HTTP load balancer configuration.

Use Cloud DNS CNAME records to point both hostnames at the same IP and depend on backend routing is wrong because DNS only resolves names to an IP. The routing decision happens on the load balancer, and without Ingress host rules all traffic would go to the default backend rather than being separated by hostname.

Create a new Ingress and set the kubernetes.io/ingress.global-static-ip-name annotation to reuse the same static IP is wrong because GKE creates one external HTTP load balancer per Ingress and a single IP and port cannot be bound by two separate forwarding rules. The supported way to share one IP across multiple hostnames is to define multiple host rules in a single Ingress.

A decisão de roteamento acontece no load balancer, e sem as regras de host do Ingress todo o tráfego iria para o backend padrão, em vez de ser separado por hostname.

Criar um novo Ingress e definir a anotação kubernetes.io/ingress.global-static-ip-name para reutilizar o mesmo IP estático está errado, porque o GKE cria um external HTTP load balancer por Ingress e um único IP e porta não podem ser vinculados por duas forwarding rules separadas. A forma suportada de compartilhar um IP entre múltiplos hostnames é definir múltiplas regras de host em um único Ingress.

questions.question: The online marketplace mcnz.com operates in multiple countries and must comply with strict rules for data retention and residency. Regulations require order event data to be preserved for 7 years and each object must remain stored within the same country where the purchase occurred. You plan to use Google Cloud Storage for this archival design. How should you structure storage and retention to meet these requirements?

options.text: Place all objects in a dual region bucket and enable Object Lifecycle Management to delete data after 7 years
Use a multi region bucket with a 7 year Bucket Lock retention policy
Store data in country specific regional buckets and configure Object Lifecycle Management to purge objects after 7 years
Place all objects in a single region bucket and script deletions of records older than 7 years

questions.correct_text: Store data in country specific regional buckets and configure Object Lifecycle Management to purge objects after 7 years
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is Store data in country specific regional buckets and configure Object Lifecycle Management to purge objects after 7 years. This approach keeps every object in the country where the purchase occurred and schedules deletion after the seven year retention period.

Using country specific regional buckets ensures residency because Cloud Storage keeps objects only in the location of the bucket. Creating a separate regional bucket per country lets you route and store each order event in the correct country. Object Lifecycle Management provides a policy driven way to automatically delete objects after seven years, meeting the stated preservation and purge requirement.

Place all objects in a dual region bucket and enable Object Lifecycle Management to delete data after 7 years is not acceptable because placing all countries' data into one dual region bucket does not keep each object within its country of purchase. A dual region also spans two regions and would not satisfy per country residency across multiple markets.

Use a multi region bucket with a 7 year Bucket Lock retention policy fails the residency requirement because multi region locations span many regions and often multiple countries. While a retention policy with Bucket Lock enforces immutability, the multi region scope violates the need to keep each object in the same country where it was created.

Place all objects in a single region bucket and script deletions of records older than 7 years centralizes data in one country and therefore breaks per country residency. Relying on ad hoc scripts is also less reliable than using built in policy based lifecycle management.

Um dual-region também abrange duas regiões e não satisfaria a residência por país em vários mercados.

Usar um bucket multi-region com uma política de retenção Bucket Lock de 7 anos falha no requisito de residência porque locais multi-region abrangem muitas regiões e frequentemente vários países. Embora uma política de retenção com Bucket Lock imponha imutabilidade, o escopo multi-region viola a necessidade de manter cada objeto no mesmo país onde foi criado.

Colocar todos os objetos em um bucket de uma única região e criar scripts para excluir registros com mais de 7 anos centraliza os dados em um país e, portanto, quebra a residência por país. questions.question: FrostHaul Freight gathers structured telemetry from a large fleet of refrigerated trucks that continuously push temperature and location readings into Google Cloud for real-time dashboards. Volume runs near 2.2 million sensor rows per minute, the workload is extremely write-heavy, and reads of the freshest data must return with very low latency. Which Google Cloud storage service should the team pick?

options.text: BigQuery
Cloud Bigtable
Cloud Firestore
Cloud Spanner

questions.correct_text: Cloud Bigtable
questions.explanation:
The right answer is Cloud Bigtable.

Bigtable is engineered for extremely high write throughput paired with low-latency reads, which is precisely what a relentless telemetry feed of millions of rows per minute requires. When you key rows by device and timestamp it stores time series compactly, scales out horizontally to millions of operations per second, and serves recent readings in single-digit millisecond latency.

BigQuery is tuned for analytical queries and large scans, not ultra-low-latency point reads of the hottest data. It can ingest streams, but its query latency and cost profile make it a weak match for the immediate operational lookups described here.

Cloud Firestore is a document database that shines for hierarchical application data organized as documents and collections. It carries practical write and hot-document ceilings and was not built for sustained, massive time series ingestion with subsecond lookups at this scale.

Cloud Spanner delivers globally consistent relational transactions and scales well for OLTP. It is generally not the pick for raw time series telemetry, where a wide-column NoSQL store offers better write throughput and access patterns for the most recent readings.
