O Bigtable foi projetado para throughput de gravação extremamente alto combinado com leituras de baixa latência, que é exatamente o que um fluxo incessante de telemetria com milhões de linhas por minuto exige. Quando você usa device e timestamp como chave das linhas, ele armazena séries temporais de forma compacta, escala horizontalmente para milhões de operações por segundo e entrega as leituras recentes com latência de poucos milissegundos.

O BigQuery é otimizado para consultas analíticas e grandes varreduras, não para leituras pontuais de latência ultrabaixa dos dados mais quentes. Ele pode ingerir streams, mas sua latência de consulta e seu perfil de custo o tornam pouco adequado para as consultas operacionais imediatas descritas aqui.

O Cloud Firestore é um banco de dados de documentos que se destaca para dados de aplicação hierárquicos organizados como documentos e coleções. Ele tem limites práticos de gravação e de documentos quentes (hot documents) e não foi construído para ingestão massiva e sustentada de séries temporais com consultas em menos de um segundo nessa escala.

O Cloud Spanner oferece transações relacionais globalmente consistentes e escala bem para OLTP. Geralmente não é a escolha para telemetria bruta de séries temporais, onde um armazenamento NoSQL wide-column oferece melhor throughput de gravação e padrões de acesso para as leituras mais recentes.

questions.question: Which API protocol on Google Cloud best supports legacy browsers and mobile clients and enables easy request inspection and replay?

options.text: GraphQL
REST with XML
REST over HTTP with JSON
gRPC with Protocol Buffers

questions.correct_text: REST over HTTP with JSON
questions.explanation:
The correct option is REST over HTTP with JSON because it is widely compatible with legacy browsers and mobile clients and makes requests easy to inspect and replay.

This approach uses standard HTTP methods and straightforward headers that work across virtually all browsers and mobile stacks. JSON payloads are human readable, which makes them simple to debug with common tools such as curl or Postman. Stateless requests over HTTP make it easy to capture and resend the same call for troubleshooting or testing.

GraphQL is powerful for aggregating data but typically funnels operations through a single endpoint and often relies on POST, which makes caching and simple URL based replay less straightforward. It also benefits most from dedicated tooling rather than the ubiquitous HTTP tooling that teams already use.

REST with XML is broadly supported, but XML is more verbose and heavier to parse on mobile clients and isn't as easy to read and manually craft as JSON. Modern Google Cloud APIs generally favor JSON for simplicity and efficiency.

gRPC with Protocol Buffers offers high performance and strong contracts, but it uses HTTP/2 and binary payloads that are not natively supported by legacy browsers and are harder to inspect without specialized tools. Browser clients typically require a translation layer such as gRPC Web, which reduces the simplicity and replay advantages sought in this scenario.

Os payloads JSON são legíveis por humanos, o que os torna simples de depurar com ferramentas comuns como curl ou Postman. Requisições stateless sobre HTTP facilitam capturar e reenviar a mesma chamada para troubleshooting ou testes.

O GraphQL é poderoso para agregar dados, mas normalmente canaliza as operações por meio de um único endpoint e frequentemente depende de POST, o que torna o cache e a reexecução simples baseada em URL menos diretos. Ele também se beneficia mais de ferramentas dedicadas do que das ferramentas HTTP onipresentes que as equipes já usam.

REST com XML é amplamente suportado, mas o XML é mais verboso e mais pesado de parsear em clientes móveis e não é tão fácil de ler e construir manualmente quanto o JSON. As APIs modernas do Google Cloud geralmente favorecem o JSON pela simplicidade e eficiência.

O gRPC com Protocol Buffers oferece alto desempenho e contratos fortes, mas usa HTTP/2 e payloads binários que não são suportados nativamente por navegadores legados e são mais difíceis de inspecionar sem ferramentas especializadas. Clientes de navegador normalmente exigem uma camada de tradução como o gRPC Web, o que reduz as vantagens de simplicidade e reexecução buscadas neste cenário.

questions.question: Larkfield Retail is moving its microservices to Google Kubernetes Engine and wants to balance performance and spending by letting the platform automatically increase or decrease both pods and nodes as CPU usage rises and falls during daily traffic peaks while targeting roughly 65 percent CPU across pods. Which configuration should they implement to meet this goal with native capabilities and low operational overhead?

options.text: Enable autoscaling on the managed instance group for the node pool and use Vertical Pod Autoscaler to change CPU requests based on load
Turn on Cluster Autoscaler for the cluster and configure Horizontal Pod Autoscaler to scale Deployments using a custom metric from Cloud Monitoring
Enable Cluster Autoscaler on the node pool and set a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler to scale pods based on average CPU utilization
Migrate the cluster to GKE Autopilot and depend on Autopilot to scale both pods and nodes when CPU usage changes

questions.correct_text: Enable Cluster Autoscaler on the node pool and set a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler to scale pods based on average CPU utilization
questions.explanation:
The correct choice is Enable Cluster Autoscaler on the node pool and set a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler to scale pods based on average CPU utilization.

This configuration uses native GKE features to handle both layers of elasticity. Cluster Autoscaler grows and shrinks the node pool when pods cannot be scheduled or when nodes are underutilized. The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler adjusts the number of replicas to maintain a target average CPU utilization, which directly aligns with the requirement to hold around 65 percent CPU across pods. This avoids extra setup because CPU is a built in resource metric that HPA can use without custom integrations, and it provides low operational overhead while balancing performance and cost.

Enable autoscaling on the managed instance group for the node pool and use Vertical Pod Autoscaler to change CPU requests based on load is not appropriate because GKE node pools should be scaled by Cluster Autoscaler rather than enabling the Compute Engine managed instance group autoscaler directly. Vertical Pod Autoscaler changes resource requests for pods and can conflict with replica based scaling, and it does not adjust the number of pod replicas to track a 65 percent CPU target across pods.

Turn on Cluster Autoscaler for the cluster and configure Horizontal Pod Autoscaler to scale Deployments using a custom metric from Cloud Monitoring adds unnecessary complexity for this use case. CPU is already a standard resource metric supported by HPA, so introducing custom metrics increases setup and operational overhead without providing benefit for a simple CPU utilization target.

Migrate the cluster to GKE Autopilot and depend on Autopilot to scale both pods and nodes when CPU usage changes is not the best fit because Autopilot manages the infrastructure but doesn't automatically change Deployment replica counts based on CPU without an HPA. A migration also adds effort that isn't required to meet the requirement with Standard mode using the built in autoscalers.

O Cluster Autoscaler aumenta e reduz o node pool quando os pods não podem ser agendados ou quando os nós estão subutilizados. O Horizontal Pod Autoscaler ajusta o número de réplicas para manter uma utilização média de CPU alvo, o que se alinha diretamente com o requisito de manter cerca de 65 por cento de CPU entre os pods. Isso evita configuração extra porque CPU é uma métrica de recurso integrada que o HPA pode usar sem integrações personalizadas, e oferece baixa sobrecarga operacional ao equilibrar desempenho e custo.

Habilitar o autoscaling no managed instance group do node pool e usar o Vertical Pod Autoscaler para alterar as requisições de CPU com base na carga não é apropriado porque os node pools do GKE devem ser escalados pelo Cluster Autoscaler em vez de habilitar diretamente o autoscaler do managed instance group do Compute Engine. O Vertical Pod Autoscaler altera as requisições de recursos dos pods e pode entrar em conflito com o escalonamento baseado em réplicas, além de não ajustar o número de réplicas de pods para acompanhar uma meta de 65 por cento de CPU entre os pods.

Ativar o Cluster Autoscaler para o cluster e configurar o Horizontal Pod Autoscaler para escalar os Deployments usando uma métrica personalizada do Cloud Monitoring adiciona complexidade desnecessária para este caso de uso. A CPU já é uma métrica de recurso padrão suportada pelo HPA, então introduzir métricas personalizadas aumenta a configuração e a sobrecarga operacional sem trazer benefício para uma simples meta de utilização de CPU.

questions.question: ZenithKnit Outfitters is rolling out about 18 microservices on Google Cloud and needs to publish them as APIs for partner apps and internal web clients while enforcing authentication and quotas and gathering request analytics and latency telemetry. Which Google Cloud product should they choose?

options.text: Anthos Service Mesh
Cloud Endpoints
Cloud Functions
Google API Gateway

questions.correct_text: Cloud Endpoints
questions.explanation:
The correct choice is Cloud Endpoints.

This service lets you publish multiple microservices as APIs for external partners and internal clients while enforcing API keys or JWT based authentication, configurable quotas, and request analytics. It integrates with Cloud Logging, Cloud Monitoring, and Cloud Trace to surface latency telemetry and operational dashboards. It also supports backends on Cloud Run, App Engine, Google Kubernetes Engine, and Compute Engine, which aligns well with a microservices rollout on Google Cloud.

Anthos Service Mesh focuses on service to service security, traffic management, and observability within a mesh. It is not an external API management product and does not directly provide API key management, consumer facing authentication, usage quotas, or turnkey API publishing for partner developers.

Cloud Functions is a serverless compute platform to run code in response to events or HTTP requests. It can host backend logic but is not an API management layer that enforces cross service quotas, API consumer authentication, and consolidated request analytics.

Google API Gateway is designed primarily for serverless backends on Cloud Run and App Engine. The scenario does not specify serverless backends and involves microservices that may run on Google Kubernetes Engine or Compute Engine, so Cloud Endpoints is the better fit because it supports a wider range of backends while providing the required authentication, quota enforcement, and telemetry.

questions.correct_text: Cloud SQL Client
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Cloud SQL Client because it provides the minimal IAM permissions a Compute Engine VM needs to establish a connection to a Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instance, while query execution is governed by database user credentials.

This role allows a VM to connect to Cloud SQL instances and to obtain the necessary ephemeral certificates when using the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy or connectors. It avoids broad administrative capabilities, keeping access aligned with the principle of least privilege. SQL statements are authorized by PostgreSQL users and not by IAM, so IAM only needs to permit the connection path and not data manipulation inside the database.

Cloud SQL Admin grants full administrative control over Cloud SQL resources, including creating, modifying, or deleting instances and users. This is far more access than is needed for simply connecting and running queries, so it isn't the least privilege choice.

Project Editor is a primitive project wide role that grants broad permissions across many services and is not specific to Cloud SQL connectivity. It is excessive for a VM that only needs to connect and query a database.

Cloud SQL Viewer provides read only access to instance metadata and monitoring information but does not include the permissions to connect to an instance or create ephemeral certificates. It therefore cannot enable a VM to establish a database connection.

questions.question: Your team runs a web application on Compute Engine virtual machine instances in a managed instance group. Over the past few days the service has started crashing at unpredictable times with no clear pattern. As the cloud developer, what is the first action you should take to diagnose the problem using Cloud Monitoring?

options.text: Examine CPU utilization metrics for the virtual machine instances
Review the crash details in Cloud Logging
Monitor persistent disk read and write throughput for the instances
Set up Error Reporting to aggregate and surface uncaught exceptions

questions.correct_text: Review the crash details in Cloud Logging
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Review the crash details in Cloud Logging.

Logs are the quickest way to pinpoint the exact time and cause of failures because they capture stack traces, exit codes, and system or application messages. Cloud Logging automatically collects logs from Compute Engine and your managed instance group, which lets you correlate crash events with instance restarts, recent deploys, or configuration changes so you can form a clear hypothesis before diving into metrics.

Examine CPU utilization metrics for the virtual machine instances is not the best first step because CPU charts may show saturation or idleness but they rarely explain why a process crashed. You should confirm the error and context in logs first, then use CPU metrics to validate whether resource pressure contributed to the issue.

Monitor persistent disk read and write throughput for the instances focuses on storage performance and can be useful later to confirm I/O bottlenecks. It is not the first action for unexplained crashes since it does not provide error details or stack traces that identify the failing component.

Set up Error Reporting to aggregate and surface uncaught exceptions can help with ongoing visibility into application exceptions. However, it is not the first move for active crashes because it may miss system level failures or process terminations, and it requires setup that won't immediately reveal the current crash details already available in the logs.

O Cloud Logging coleta automaticamente os logs do Compute Engine e do seu managed instance group, o que permite correlacionar eventos de falha com reinicializações de instâncias, deploys recentes ou alterações de configuração, de modo que você possa formar uma hipótese clara antes de mergulhar nas métricas.

Examinar as métricas de utilização de CPU das instâncias de máquina virtual não é o melhor primeiro passo, pois os gráficos de CPU podem mostrar saturação ou ociosidade, mas raramente explicam por que um processo falhou. Você deve primeiro confirmar o erro e o contexto nos logs e, em seguida, usar as métricas de CPU para validar se a pressão de recursos contribuiu para o problema.

Monitorar a taxa de transferência de leitura e escrita do persistent disk das instâncias foca no desempenho de armazenamento e pode ser útil mais tarde para confirmar gargalos de I/O. Não é a primeira ação para falhas inexplicadas, pois não fornece detalhes de erro ou stack traces que identifiquem o componente que está falhando.

Configurar o Error Reporting para agregar e expor exceções não tratadas pode ajudar na visibilidade contínua das exceções da aplicação. No entanto, não é a primeira medida para falhas ativas, pois pode deixar passar falhas em nível de sistema ou encerramentos de processo, e requer uma configuração que não revelará imediatamente os detalhes da falha atual já disponíveis nos logs.

questions.question: A developer at NimbusCircuit Labs is building services on Cloud Run and GKE that need to call Google Cloud APIs, and the team wants the most secure and maintainable way to handle authentication without distributing long lived secrets. What should they use?

options.text: Configure a project wide API key for every call
Store a service account key file in Secret Manager and load it at startup
Use Application Default Credentials for Google Cloud
Embed a service account JSON key inside the application code

questions.correct_text: Use Application Default Credentials for Google Cloud
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Use Application Default Credentials for Google Cloud.

Application Default Credentials let Cloud Run and GKE workloads automatically obtain short lived tokens from the attached service account so you do not need to distribute or rotate secrets. On Cloud Run you assign a service account to the service and the Google authentication libraries use the runtime identity to call Google Cloud APIs. On GKE you enable Workload Identity and map a Kubernetes service account to a Google service account so pods can acquire tokens without keys. This is secure and maintainable and it is the recommended pattern for server to server access to Google Cloud.

Configure a project wide API key for every call is not appropriate because this mechanism does not convey identity or IAM permissions and many Google Cloud APIs do not accept it. This approach is less secure and offers no fine grained access control, which makes it unsuitable for backend services.

Store a service account key file in Secret Manager and load it at startup still relies on a long lived user managed key and adds rotation and leakage risk. Cloud Run and GKE provide keyless authentication through Application Default Credentials, so managing keys is unnecessary and discouraged.

Embed a service account JSON key inside the application code is a serious anti pattern because the key can leak through source control or logs and is hard to rotate. Google recommends avoiding user managed keys when first party identity is available, which is the case on Cloud Run and GKE.

A opção correta é Usar Application Default Credentials para o Google Cloud.

No Cloud Run, você atribui uma service account ao serviço e as bibliotecas de autenticação do Google usam a identidade de runtime para chamar as APIs do Google Cloud. No GKE, você habilita o Workload Identity e mapeia uma service account do Kubernetes para uma service account do Google, de modo que os pods possam adquirir tokens sem chaves. Isso é seguro e sustentável e é o padrão recomendado para acesso server-to-server ao Google Cloud.

Configurar uma API key de abrangência por projeto para cada chamada não é apropriado, pois esse mecanismo não transmite identidade nem permissões IAM e muitas APIs do Google Cloud não a aceitam. Essa abordagem é menos segura e não oferece controle de acesso granular, o que a torna inadequada para serviços de backend.

Armazenar um arquivo de chave de service account no Secret Manager e carregá-lo na inicialização ainda depende de uma chave gerenciada pelo usuário e de longa duração, além de adicionar risco de rotação e vazamento. O Cloud Run e o GKE fornecem autenticação sem chaves por meio das Application Default Credentials, portanto gerenciar chaves é desnecessário e desencorajado.

Embutir uma chave JSON de service account dentro do código da aplicação é um sério antipadrão, pois a chave pode vazar pelo controle de versão ou pelos logs e é difícil de rotacionar. O Google recomenda evitar chaves gerenciadas pelo usuário quando a identidade nativa está disponível, o que é o caso do Cloud Run e do GKE.

questions.question: AstralPay is preparing to launch a microservices platform on Google Kubernetes Engine and expects to ship new releases every 18 hours. The workload uses many distinct Linux based container images and the team wants to be promptly informed about known operating system vulnerabilities as new images are introduced. Following Google's recommended practices, what should the team do?

options.text: Enable Security Command Center and use its dashboards to watch for container vulnerability findings across projects
Call the Container Analysis REST API to start scans for each new image and examine the results before each rollout
Turn on Container Analysis, push new container images to Artifact Registry, and review the vulnerability findings prior to each rollout
Enable Container Analysis, store images in Artifact Registry, and check only critical vulnerabilities before deploying

questions.correct_text: Turn on Container Analysis, push new container images to Artifact Registry, and review the vulnerability findings prior to each rollout
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Turn on Container Analysis, push new container images to Artifact Registry, and review the vulnerability findings prior to each rollout.

This approach enables native vulnerability scanning that runs automatically when images are pushed to Artifact Registry. Container Analysis records the results so the team can quickly review operating system vulnerability findings before each frequent release. This aligns with recommended practices because it integrates scanning into the image lifecycle and removes the need for manual triggers while providing timely and centralized results.

Enable Security Command Center and use its dashboards to watch for container vulnerability findings across projects is not the best primary action. Security Command Center aggregates findings from other services and provides organization level visibility, yet it does not perform image scans itself nor does it replace enabling scanning in Artifact Registry for immediate feedback on each new image.

Call the Container Analysis REST API to start scans for each new image and examine the results before each rollout is unnecessary for images stored in Artifact Registry. When scanning is enabled, images are scanned automatically on push. Manually invoking scans adds overhead and slows a rapid release cadence without providing additional value for this workflow.

Enable Container Analysis, store images in Artifact Registry, and check only critical vulnerabilities before deploying is not recommended because it ignores high severity issues and other relevant findings that can still pose significant risk. Best practice is to review the vulnerability findings as a whole and apply policy driven gates as needed rather than limiting reviews to only the most severe category.

A opção correta é Ativar o Container Analysis, enviar novas imagens de contêiner para o Artifact Registry e revisar as descobertas de vulnerabilidades antes de cada rollout.

Essa abordagem habilita o escaneamento nativo de vulnerabilidades que é executado automaticamente quando as imagens são enviadas para o Artifact Registry. O Container Analysis registra os resultados para que a equipe possa revisar rapidamente as descobertas de vulnerabilidades do sistema operacional antes de cada lançamento frequente. Isso está alinhado às práticas recomendadas, pois integra o escaneamento ao ciclo de vida da imagem e elimina a necessidade de acionamentos manuais, ao mesmo tempo em que fornece resultados oportunos e centralizados.

Ativar o Security Command Center e usar seus dashboards para observar descobertas de vulnerabilidades de contêineres em vários projetos não é a melhor ação primária. O Security Command Center agrega descobertas de outros serviços e fornece visibilidade em nível de organização, porém ele não realiza os escaneamentos de imagens por si só nem substitui a habilitação do escaneamento no Artifact Registry para feedback imediato sobre cada nova imagem.

Chamar a API REST do Container Analysis para iniciar escaneamentos de cada nova imagem e examinar os resultados antes de cada rollout é desnecessário para imagens armazenadas no Artifact Registry. Quando o escaneamento está habilitado, as imagens são escaneadas automaticamente no push. Acionar os escaneamentos manualmente adiciona sobrecarga e desacelera uma cadência de lançamento rápida sem fornecer valor adicional para esse fluxo de trabalho.

Ativar o Container Analysis, armazenar imagens no Artifact Registry e verificar apenas vulnerabilidades críticas antes de implantar não é recomendado, pois ignora problemas de alta severidade e outras descobertas relevantes que ainda podem representar risco significativo. A prática recomendada é revisar as descobertas de vulnerabilidades como um todo e aplicar gates orientados por políticas conforme necessário, em vez de limitar as revisões apenas à categoria mais severa.

questions.question: Lyric Daily runs live polls in a mobile and web app for a worldwide audience and expects heavy spikes in submissions during each 60 minute window for each question. They need to ingest every vote, compute counts within the active window, and retain raw events for long term analytics and dashboarding. What solution should they implement?

options.text: Use Firebase Authentication and write votes directly to Firestore, then export to CSV and load into Google Sheets for reporting
Buffer votes in Memorystore and invoke Cloud Functions to periodically push aggregates into BigQuery while relying on the cache for raw data
Send votes to Pub/Sub and run a Dataflow pipeline that computes windowed aggregates and writes both counts and raw events into BigQuery, then visualize in Looker Studio
Publish votes to Pub/Sub and stream them into Cloud Bigtable, then schedule a nightly Dataflow job to copy data to BigQuery for reporting

questions.correct_text: Send votes to Pub/Sub and run a Dataflow pipeline that computes windowed aggregates and writes both counts and raw events into BigQuery, then visualize in Looker Studio
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Send votes to Pub/Sub and run a Dataflow pipeline that computes windowed aggregates and writes both counts and raw events into BigQuery, then visualize in Looker Studio.

This approach ingests every vote at global scale through Pub/Sub, which smooths bursty traffic and provides durable buffering. Dataflow can apply fixed 60 minute windows and appropriate triggers to compute near real time counts, then write those aggregates to BigQuery for low latency dashboards. The pipeline can also write the full raw event stream into a separate BigQuery table for long term analytics and replay. Looker Studio connects directly to BigQuery so teams can visualize both current window counts and historical trends without additional export steps.

Use Firebase Authentication and write votes directly to Firestore, then export to CSV and load into Google Sheets for reporting is wrong because this is a manual batch process and does not provide real time windowed counting, and Firestore plus Sheets is not designed for high volume streaming analytics at worldwide scale.

Buffer votes in Memorystore and invoke Cloud Functions to periodically push aggregates into BigQuery while relying on the cache for raw data is wrong because Memorystore is an in memory cache and not durable storage, so raw events can be lost during failures, and periodic function runs do not provide continuous reliable windowed computation under heavy spikes.

Publish votes to Pub/Sub and stream them into Cloud Bigtable, then schedule a nightly Dataflow job to copy data to BigQuery for reporting is wrong because nightly copying delays results and fails the requirement for counts within the active window, and Bigtable is not a natural fit for analytical aggregations and ad hoc SQL reporting.

questions.question: A retail analytics startup is deploying a Cloud Run service that must call the Cloud Storage JSON API over HTTP because its runtime does not include Google Cloud Client Libraries. They want authentication to happen automatically by using the service account attached to the Cloud Run service and they do not want to handle long lived secrets. What should they do?

options.text: Implement a three legged OAuth flow with a user consent screen to acquire an access token when the service starts
Use an API key and send it in the Authorization header for every HTTP request
Request a short lived OAuth 2 access token from the metadata server during each run and include it as a Bearer token in the Authorization header
Store a service account key in Secret Manager and have the service sign a JWT to exchange for an access token

questions.correct_text: Request a short lived OAuth 2 access token from the metadata server during each run and include it as a Bearer token in the Authorization header
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Request a short lived OAuth 2 access token from the metadata server during each run and include it as a Bearer token in the Authorization header. This satisfies the requirement to use the Cloud Run service account automatically and avoids handling long lived secrets while enabling authenticated HTTP calls to the Cloud Storage JSON API.

On Cloud Run the metadata server can issue a short lived OAuth 2 access token that represents the attached service account. You retrieve the token from the metadata server and include it in the Authorization header as a Bearer token when calling the Cloud Storage JSON API. The token is short lived and IAM on the service account governs access to buckets and objects, which aligns with least privilege and removes key management tasks.

Implement a three legged OAuth flow with a user consent screen to acquire an access token when the service starts is wrong because this is an end user flow that requires interactive consent and typically involves refresh tokens. The scenario is server to server and should rely on the service account identity without user interaction.

Use an API key and send it in the Authorization header for every HTTP request is wrong because API keys do not provide identity and do not authorize access to private Cloud Storage data. API keys are not used in the Authorization header and the JSON API requires OAuth 2 access tokens for authenticated access.

Store a service account key in Secret Manager and have the service sign a JWT to exchange for an access token is wrong because it introduces a long lived secret and adds key lifecycle risk and operational overhead. The platform can provide short lived tokens through the metadata server, which eliminates the need to manage keys.

questions.question: A data processing service at a logistics firm named CrestPort runs on a Compute Engine virtual machine in europe-west1 that has no external IP. It must call the Cloud Storage JSON API to read and write objects, and the security team wants traffic to stay on Google's network rather than traverse the public internet. What should you configure so the VM can reach Google APIs using only its private address?

options.text: Configure Cloud NAT
Use Shared VPC
Enable Private Google Access
Set up VPC Network Peering

questions.correct_text: Enable Private Google Access
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Enable Private Google Access.

This setting is applied on the subnet that hosts the VM and allows instances without external IP addresses to reach Google APIs and services using only their internal addresses. Traffic stays on Google's network rather than traversing the public internet, which meets the security team's requirement.

Configure Cloud NAT would allow egress to the internet without an external IP, but traffic to Google APIs would still use public internet paths rather than staying entirely on Google's private network.

Use Shared VPC centralizes network administration across projects and allows service projects to use a host project's VPC. It does not provide private access to Google APIs for VMs without external IPs.

Set up VPC Network Peering connects two VPC networks so they can exchange private traffic. It does not enable access to Google APIs and services from instances without external IPs.

questions.question: Which Cache-Control header should you use in Cloud CDN to prevent caching of API and dynamic responses in shared caches while still letting only end clients cache them?

options.text: Set Cache-Control to "public, max-age=900"
Set Cache-Control to "private"
Set Cache-Control to "no-cache"
Set Cache-Control to "max-age=0"

questions.correct_text: Set Cache-Control to "private"
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Set Cache-Control to "private".

This directive tells shared caches such as Cloud CDN not to store the response. It still permits user agent private caches to store it, which allows only end clients to cache API or dynamic responses while keeping them out of CDN and other intermediary caches.

Set Cache-Control to "public, max-age=900" is wrong because public explicitly allows shared caches to store the response and the max age of 900 seconds would keep it in Cloud CDN for that duration.

Set Cache-Control to "no-cache" is wrong because no-cache allows caches to store the response but requires revalidation before reuse. Cloud CDN could still store it, which does not prevent caching in shared caches.

Set Cache-Control to "max-age=0" is wrong because this makes the response immediately stale but still cacheable. Shared caches can store it and revalidate on each request, which does not prevent storage in Cloud CDN.

questions.question: How should your deployment pipeline reliably determine the environment for Compute Engine instances across seven projects with minimal maintenance?

options.text: Instance labels read by the pipeline via the API
Bake per environment images and templates
Project metadata "environment" read via the metadata server
Per VM custom metadata "stage" at creation time

questions.correct_text: Project metadata "environment" read via the metadata server
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Project metadata "environment" read via the metadata server.

This approach sets a single environment attribute at the project level that every instance in that project automatically inherits. Instances can read it from the metadata server at runtime, making the signal consistent and eliminating per instance configuration. It scales cleanly across seven projects because you set one value per project, and the deployment pipeline can rely on a single source of truth with very little ongoing maintenance.

Instance labels read by the pipeline via the API is less reliable because it depends on every instance being labeled correctly and kept up to date. Labels are easy to omit or change, and the pipeline must query each resource, which increases operational overhead and risk of drift.

Bake per environment images and templates increases image and template sprawl and creates unnecessary rebuild work whenever the environment indicator changes. It encodes environment into artifacts rather than discovering it at runtime, which raises maintenance effort and slows iteration.

Per VM custom metadata "stage" at creation time requires setting a value on every instance, which is error prone and hard to enforce across autoscaled or frequently recreated VMs. It is not centralized and therefore does not minimize maintenance compared with a project level setting.

questions.question: Which Google Cloud service offers a fully managed relational database supporting MySQL, PostgreSQL, and SQL Server with automated backups along with read replicas?

options.text: Cloud Spanner
Cloud SQL
Cloud Storage

questions.correct_text: Cloud SQL
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Cloud SQL.

It is a fully managed relational database service that supports MySQL, PostgreSQL, and SQL Server. It provides automated backups for protection and supports read replicas to offload reads and improve scalability. It also handles patching and maintenance so teams can focus on their applications.

Cloud Spanner is a fully managed relational database that is globally distributed and horizontally scalable. It does not provide managed MySQL, PostgreSQL, or SQL Server instances and uses its own SQL dialect, so it does not meet the requirement in the question.

Cloud Storage is an object storage service rather than a database. It does not run relational database engines and does not offer automated backups and read replicas in the sense required by the question.

questions.question: On GKE, which technology delivers fine grained pod to pod traffic control and deep visibility into service traffic and metrics?

options.text: Kubernetes Network Policies
Google Anthos Service Mesh
Cloud Monitoring
Traffic Director

questions.correct_text: Google Anthos Service Mesh
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Google Anthos Service Mesh.

This managed service mesh on GKE provides fine grained service to service controls such as routing, retries, circuit breaking, and mTLS between workloads. It also generates rich telemetry for requests and services, which feeds dashboards, metrics, and traces for deep visibility into traffic behavior and health.

Kubernetes Network Policies control connectivity at the IP and port level between pods and namespaces, which is useful for allow and deny lists. This option does not provide application layer traffic management, resilience features, or deep service level metrics and tracing.

Cloud Monitoring offers observability for resources and workloads and can display metrics and dashboards. It does not enforce or configure pod to pod traffic behavior and depends on sources such as a service mesh or exporters to supply service traffic metrics.

Traffic Director is a global control plane for proxy based traffic management. In GKE you use the service mesh to get per workload policy and integrated telemetry, and this option by itself does not deliver fine grained pod to pod traffic control or deep service metrics.

questions.question: MeadowCity Threads migrated its primary PostgreSQL database from a self managed server to Cloud SQL three days ago, and now some API calls that query the database are noticeably slower. You want to find which SQL statements consume the most resources in the managed environment and understand how they execute so you can optimize them. What should you do?

options.text: Enable Cloud Monitoring dashboards and alerts to track query latency trends
Turn on Cloud SQL Query Insights and use it to profile statements and examine execution details
Increase the Cloud SQL instance tier to a larger machine type to add more vCPUs and memory
Instrument the application with Cloud Trace to analyze end to end request timing

questions.correct_text: Turn on Cloud SQL Query Insights and use it to profile statements and examine execution details
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Turn on Cloud SQL Query Insights and use it to profile statements and examine execution details. This directly identifies the most resource consuming SQL and reveals how they execute in the managed database, so you can focus your tuning efforts where they matter most.

Once enabled, this feature aggregates query statistics by normalized pattern and highlights top statements by CPU time, IO wait, lock time, and latency. You can drill into a statement to view execution details and wait events, and for PostgreSQL you can capture and view execution plans to understand plan shape and row estimates. It works without application changes and is available in the Cloud SQL console, which makes it especially useful right after a migration. With Query Insights you can also filter by database or user and correlate spikes with specific statements to quickly find root causes.

Enable Cloud Monitoring dashboards and alerts to track query latency trends is not sufficient because it shows instance and high level metrics and trends but does not attribute resource usage to specific SQL statements or surface execution plans.

Increase the Cloud SQL instance tier to a larger machine type to add more vCPUs and memory might mask symptoms but it does not tell you which queries are inefficient or why they are slow, and it offers no insight into execution details needed for optimization.

Instrument the application with Cloud Trace to analyze end to end request timing helps with distributed tracing in the application but does not profile SQL inside Cloud SQL or expose query plans, so it will not show which statements consume the most database resources.

questions.question: Your team is building a stateful payments API for a fintech startup that needs to keep a long lived TCP session open to a managed database while running on a fully managed serverless platform on Google Cloud. Which service should you use?

options.text: Cloud Run fully managed
App Engine flexible environment
Google Kubernetes Engine
App Engine standard environment

questions.correct_text: App Engine flexible environment
questions.explanation:
The correct option is App Engine flexible environment because it lets your payments API maintain a long lived TCP session to a managed database while running on a fully managed serverless platform.

It runs your application in long running instances that can keep background processes and persistent network connections active across requests. The platform is fully managed by Google, scales automatically, and offers robust networking and database connectivity, which fits a stateful payments API that must hold a continuous session.

Cloud Run fully managed is optimized for stateless request driven HTTP workloads and does not support long running background work or maintaining an open TCP session independent of active requests, so it does not satisfy the requirement.

Google Kubernetes Engine can support long lived connections, but it is not a fully managed serverless platform because you are responsible for clusters and Kubernetes resources, which doesn't satisfy the fully managed serverless constraint.

App Engine standard environment imposes strict request and instance constraints and discourages background threads and persistent connections, and instances may be frequently restarted, which makes long lived TCP sessions unreliable.

questions.question: NorthGate Commerce runs a backend made of many microservices on Google Kubernetes Engine. The team does not need to support legacy browsers or older client stacks, and it cares most about low latency and lean resource use for around 1,100 internal service-to-service calls per second. Which protocol should they pick?

options.text: REST carried over HTTP/2
gRPC carried over HTTP/1.1
gRPC over HTTP/2
REST carried over HTTP/1.1

questions.correct_text: gRPC over HTTP/2
questions.explanation:
The right answer is gRPC over HTTP/2.

This option serializes messages compactly with Protocol Buffers and leans on HTTP/2 capabilities like multiplexing and header compression, which together trim latency and CPU. It also offers bidirectional streaming and efficient request handling, a good match for high-volume internal calls between services on GKE. Since browser compatibility is off the table, gRPC is a sound, performant default for internal microservices.

REST carried over HTTP/2 upgrades the transport but still ships JSON text and bulkier messages, which usually burn more bandwidth and CPU than gRPC with Protocol Buffers. It also misses the strong schema and code-generation advantages that gRPC gives tight service contracts.

gRPC carried over HTTP/1.1 is not a workable pairing for server-to-server traffic, because gRPC relies on HTTP/2 for framing, flow control, and multiplexing. gRPC-Web can cross HTTP/1.1 through a proxy for browsers, but that is irrelevant for internal microservices on GKE.

REST carried over HTTP/1.1 is widely compatible yet adds latency from head-of-line blocking and lacks multiplexing. Its text format and larger payloads make it less efficient against the stated performance goals.

questions.question: An engineering team at Sunpoint Outfitters is deploying a retail ordering microservice on Google Kubernetes Engine that must read from and write to a regional Cloud Spanner instance with minimal latency. They want to cut connection overhead and rely on built in session and channel pooling from the client side. What is the recommended way for the service to connect to Cloud Spanner?

options.text: Set up Dedicated Interconnect to reach Cloud Spanner from the cluster
Configure VPC Network Peering to the Cloud Spanner service network
Use the official Cloud Spanner client library in the GKE service so it manages sessions and gRPC channels
Run the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy as a sidecar and connect through it

questions.correct_text: Use the official Cloud Spanner client library in the GKE service so it manages sessions and gRPC channels
questions.explanation:
The correct choice is Use the official Cloud Spanner client library in the GKE service so it manages sessions and gRPC channels.

This approach delivers built in session pooling and efficient gRPC channel reuse, which directly addresses the need to reduce connection overhead and minimize latency. The libraries create and manage a session pool for you and multiplex requests across a small number of channels, improving throughput and tail latency. Placing the GKE workloads in the same region as the Cloud Spanner instance further reduces network round trips and helps meet the low latency requirement.

Set up Dedicated Interconnect to reach Cloud Spanner from the cluster is not appropriate because Interconnect is designed for private connectivity from on premises networks to a VPC. It does not change how a GKE workload reaches a Google managed API like Cloud Spanner, and it does not provide client side session or channel pooling.

Configure VPC Network Peering to the Cloud Spanner service network is not supported because VPC Network Peering cannot be used to reach Google APIs and services. Cloud Spanner is accessed through its public endpoint or through Private Service Connect rather than through VPC peering.

Run the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy as a sidecar and connect through it is wrong because that proxy is only for Cloud SQL and is not used with Cloud Spanner. Spanner does not require or support the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy, and the recommended method is to use the client libraries that implement session and channel pooling.

questions.question: On a GKE cluster, you want releases that never drop traffic while you funnel about one-fifth of live requests onto a candidate build so you can vet it. Which release technique fits?

options.text: A blue-green release that switches all traffic at once
A Deployment rolling update
An Anthos Service Mesh weighted canary set to 20 percent

questions.correct_text: An Anthos Service Mesh weighted canary set to 20 percent
questions.explanation:
The right answer is an Anthos Service Mesh weighted canary set to 20 percent, because it can split traffic precisely so that about 20 percent of requests hit the new version while the rest stay on the stable one, enabling zero-downtime validation.

With weighted routing both versions run simultaneously and only a defined slice of traffic reaches the new release. You can watch its metrics and logs during the canary window and then raise the weight or roll back fast, all without disrupting users.

A blue-green release that switches all traffic at once is wrong because it cuts everything from blue to green in a single move. It can be built for zero downtime, but it does not route just 20 percent of traffic to the new version for incremental checking.

A Deployment rolling update is wrong because it replaces pods gradually rather than weighting traffic at the request level. Service load balancing distributes across available pods, which cannot guarantee a precise 20 percent of user requests land on the new version.

Com o roteamento ponderado, ambas as versões rodam simultaneamente e apenas uma fatia definida do tráfego chega à nova release. Você pode observar suas métricas e logs durante a janela do canary e então aumentar o peso ou fazer rollback rapidamente, tudo sem afetar os usuários.

Uma release blue-green que troca todo o tráfego de uma só vez está errada porque move tudo de blue para green em um único passo. Ela pode ser construída para zero downtime, mas não roteia apenas 20 por cento do tráfego para a nova versão para uma verificação incremental.

Um rolling update de Deployment está errado porque substitui os pods gradualmente em vez de ponderar o tráfego no nível da requisição. O load balancing de Service distribui entre os pods disponíveis, o que não pode garantir que exatos 20 por cento das requisições dos usuários cheguem à nova versão.

questions.question: An engineering group at Crestlake Analytics has moved a microservices platform to Google Kubernetes Engine to speed up delivery, yet they have noticed that releases are taking longer to reach production over the past 75 days. Which trade off of adopting a managed Kubernetes platform like GKE might be contributing to the slower rollout cadence?

options.text: Limited support for multi region deployment patterns in GKE
Inflexible container resource assignments that prevent dynamic adjustment
Additional operational overhead to administer clusters and orchestrate releases
GKE imposes strict limits that block workloads from scaling beyond a small pod count

questions.correct_text: Additional operational overhead to administer clusters and orchestrate releases
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Additional operational overhead to administer clusters and orchestrate releases.

GKE eases the burden of provisioning and maintaining the control plane, yet teams still own release engineering. You must design and operate CI and CD pipelines, manage deployment strategies such as canary or blue green, enforce policies and approvals, and coordinate with cluster maintenance windows. These added steps can increase lead time and reduce deployment frequency until processes and automation mature.

Limited support for multi region deployment patterns in GKE is wrong because GKE supports regional clusters and multi cluster patterns and provides features that enable highly available and distributed deployments. This capability does not inherently slow rollouts.

Inflexible container resource assignments that prevent dynamic adjustment is wrong because Kubernetes on GKE supports resource requests and limits and offers autoscaling features such as horizontal and vertical pod autoscaling. These capabilities enable dynamic adjustment rather than preventing it.

GKE imposes strict limits that block workloads from scaling beyond a small pod count is wrong because GKE supports large scale clusters with cluster and pod autoscaling. While quotas and limits exist, they are designed for safety and can be tuned, and they don't cap workloads at a small pod count.

Atribuições inflexíveis de recursos de container que impedem ajuste dinâmico está errado porque o Kubernetes no GKE oferece suporte a requests e limits de recursos e disponibiliza recursos de autoscaling como horizontal e vertical pod autoscaling. Essas capacidades viabilizam o ajuste dinâmico em vez de impedi-lo.

O GKE impõe limites rígidos que impedem as cargas de trabalho de escalar além de uma pequena contagem de pods está errado porque o GKE oferece suporte a clusters de larga escala com autoscaling de cluster e de pods. Embora existam cotas e limites, eles são projetados para segurança e podem ser ajustados, e não limitam as cargas de trabalho a uma pequena contagem de pods.

questions.question: A stateless service on GKE chews through memory and is hit by load bursts lasting roughly four minutes that recur a few times every hour; it has to add capacity quickly so latency stays flat. Which autoscaling method is the right pick?

options.text: Cluster Autoscaler reacting to memory pressure
HPA driven by CPU utilization
HPA driven by average memory utilization
Vertical Pod Autoscaler in automatic mode

questions.correct_text: HPA driven by average memory utilization
questions.explanation:
The right answer is HPA driven by average memory utilization.

Scaling pods on the memory metric maps directly to a memory-bound workload. It responds quickly as memory climbs and adds replicas fast enough to ride out short four-minute bursts that recur several times an hour. Because the service is stateless, spinning up replicas during peaks holds performance steady with no complex coordination.

Cluster Autoscaler reacting to memory pressure is not a fit, since it changes the node count rather than the pod count and chiefly reacts to unschedulable pods. Bringing nodes online usually takes minutes, too slow for brief surges, and memory pressure is not a direct scaling signal for it.

HPA driven by CPU utilization is a weak match because CPU is not the bottleneck for a memory-bound service. CPU can stay moderate while memory saturates, so scaling would not trigger when it matters most.

Vertical Pod Autoscaler in automatic mode focuses on right-sizing requests and limits over time and may evict pods to apply changes. It does not react quickly to short spikes and can cause disruption, making it unsuitable for rapid surges.

A resposta correta é HPA orientado pela utilização média de memória.

Escalar os pods pela métrica de memória se mapeia diretamente a uma carga de trabalho limitada por memória. Ele responde rapidamente conforme a memória sobe e adiciona réplicas rápido o suficiente para absorver picos curtos de quatro minutos que se repetem várias vezes por hora. Como o serviço é stateless, subir réplicas durante os picos mantém o desempenho estável sem coordenação complexa.

O Cluster Autoscaler reagindo à pressão de memória não é adequado, pois ele altera a contagem de nodes em vez da contagem de pods e reage principalmente a pods não agendáveis. Colocar nodes online geralmente leva minutos, lento demais para surtos breves, e a pressão de memória não é um sinal de escalonamento direto para ele.

HPA orientado pela utilização de CPU é uma correspondência fraca porque a CPU não é o gargalo de um serviço limitado por memória. A CPU pode permanecer moderada enquanto a memória satura, então o escalonamento não seria acionado quando mais importa.

O Vertical Pod Autoscaler em modo automático foca em dimensionar corretamente requests e limits ao longo do tempo e pode despejar (evict) pods para aplicar as mudanças. Ele não reage rapidamente a picos curtos e pode causar interrupção, o que o torna inadequado para surtos rápidos.

questions.question: Larkfield Data is assembling an event-driven pipeline on Google Cloud where files land in Cloud Storage, notifications flow over Pub/Sub, and Cloud Functions process about 60 thousand events per hour. Before promoting to production you must be confident that these services talk to one another correctly from end to end. Which testing strategy validates the integrations across them?

options.text: Lean on Cloud Monitoring dashboards and alerts to confirm every service is reporting healthy metrics
Run everything locally with the Pub/Sub emulator and the Functions Framework, swapping Cloud Storage for an in-memory mock
Build a staging environment that mirrors production and run end-to-end integration tests against Cloud Storage, Pub/Sub, and Cloud Functions
Write isolated unit tests for each component and assert that the function handlers behave as expected

questions.correct_text: Build a staging environment that mirrors production and run end-to-end integration tests against Cloud Storage, Pub/Sub, and Cloud Functions
questions.explanation:
The right answer is to build a staging environment that mirrors production and run end-to-end integration tests against Cloud Storage, Pub/Sub, and Cloud Functions.

Only a staging environment that closely matches production exercises the real integrations among these services with the same triggers, service accounts, permissions, and quotas. You can drive realistic traffic near sixty thousand events per hour to verify delivery, retries, ordering, idempotency, and error handling, which builds genuine confidence before promotion.

Leaning on Cloud Monitoring dashboards and alerts is wrong because observability reports system health and latency but never proves that events flow correctly or that payloads are processed as intended. It is valuable after deployment yet does not validate integration behavior beforehand.

Running everything locally with the Pub/Sub emulator, the Functions Framework, and an in-memory Cloud Storage mock is wrong because local emulation and mocks do not exercise managed triggers, IAM, event formats, or production-scale behavior. The Pub/Sub emulator does not cover Cloud Storage notifications, and local execution cannot fully reproduce the Cloud Functions environment.

Writing isolated unit tests for each component is wrong because unit tests confirm logic in isolation but do not verify cross-service wiring, authentication, retries, backoff, or end-to-end delivery. They are necessary but not sufficient for integration confidence.

Apoiar-se em dashboards e alertas do Cloud Monitoring está errado porque a observabilidade reporta a saúde do sistema e a latência, mas nunca prova que os eventos fluem corretamente ou que os payloads são processados como pretendido. É valiosa após o deployment, mas não valida o comportamento de integração de antemão.

Rodar tudo localmente com o emulador do Pub/Sub, o Functions Framework e um mock in-memory do Cloud Storage está errado porque emulação e mocks locais não exercitam triggers gerenciados, IAM, formatos de evento ou comportamento em escala de produção. O emulador do Pub/Sub não cobre notificações do Cloud Storage, e a execução local não consegue reproduzir totalmente o ambiente do Cloud Functions.

Escrever testes unitários isolados para cada componente está errado porque testes unitários confirmam a lógica de forma isolada, mas não verificam a integração entre serviços, autenticação, retries, backoff ou entrega end-to-end. Eles são necessários, mas não suficientes para a confiança de integração.

questions.question: A connected-vehicle startup at example.com is standing up a telemetry ingestion service that must sustain roughly 220,000 writes per second and serve recent data with read latency in the single-digit to low-tens-of-milliseconds range. Eventual consistency on reads is acceptable, and there is no need for cross-region transactions. Which Google Cloud storage option fits?

options.text: Cloud Firestore
AlloyDB for PostgreSQL
Cloud Bigtable
Cloud Spanner

questions.correct_text: Cloud Bigtable
questions.explanation:
The right answer is Cloud Bigtable.

Bigtable is purpose-built for large-scale time series and telemetry. It returns single-digit millisecond reads at scale and scales linearly to hundreds of thousands of writes per second as you add nodes. With multi-cluster replication it supports eventual consistency and offers no cross-region transactions, which lines up exactly with the stated tolerance for eventual reads and the absence of any need for distributed transactions.

Cloud Firestore is a document database tuned for application data rather than high-volume telemetry. Its write-throughput limits and hot-spot risk make sustaining around 220,000 writes per second impractical, and workarounds would add complexity without reliably hitting the latency and scale targets.

AlloyDB for PostgreSQL is relational and concentrates write capacity on a single primary while scaling reads with replicas. At this volume the sustained write rate would outstrip typical single-primary capacity, and the advanced SQL and transactional guarantees are unnecessary for this telemetry use case.

Cloud Spanner can deliver low latency at scale plus global transactions, but those capabilities are not needed here. Since the workload accepts eventual consistency and skips cross-region transactions, Spanner would only add cost and complexity over Bigtable.

Ele retorna leituras com latência de milissegundos de um dígito em escala e escala linearmente para centenas de milhares de gravações por segundo conforme você adiciona nodes. Com replicação multi-cluster, ele oferece suporte a consistência eventual e não oferece transações entre regiões, o que se alinha exatamente à tolerância declarada para leituras eventuais e à ausência de qualquer necessidade de transações distribuídas.

O Cloud Firestore é um banco de dados de documentos ajustado para dados de aplicação em vez de telemetria de alto volume. Seus limites de throughput de gravação e o risco de hot-spot tornam impraticável sustentar cerca de 220.000 gravações por segundo, e contornar isso adicionaria complexidade sem atingir de forma confiável as metas de latência e escala.

O AlloyDB for PostgreSQL é relacional e concentra a capacidade de gravação em um único primary, escalando as leituras com réplicas. Nesse volume, a taxa sustentada de gravação ultrapassaria a capacidade típica de um único primary, e as garantias avançadas de SQL e transacionais são desnecessárias para este caso de uso de telemetria.

O Cloud Spanner pode entregar baixa latência em escala além de transações globais, mas essas capacidades não são necessárias aqui. Como a carga de trabalho aceita consistência eventual e dispensa transações entre regiões, o Spanner apenas adicionaria custo e complexidade em relação ao Bigtable.

questions.question: Summit Tutoring runs a Go service on Cloud Run that has to read from and write to a Cloud Storage bucket named learning-media inside the same project, and you want the workload's identity to follow least privilege. How should you grant the access?

options.text: Bind the predefined Storage Admin role to a service account at the project level
Give the service account that Cloud Run uses the Project Editor role
Set up a user-managed service account for the Cloud Run service and grant it a custom IAM role on the specific bucket carrying only the Cloud Storage permissions it needs
Leave the default Cloud Run service account in place for the production revision and add no extra role bindings

questions.correct_text: Set up a user-managed service account for the Cloud Run service and grant it a custom IAM role on the specific bucket carrying only the Cloud Storage permissions it needs
questions.explanation:
The right answer is to set up a user-managed service account for the Cloud Run service and grant it a custom IAM role on the specific bucket carrying only the Cloud Storage permissions it needs.

Cloud Run runs under a service identity, and the least-privilege path is a dedicated user-managed service account holding just the minimal Cloud Storage permissions on the single learning-media bucket. You create a custom role in the project containing only the required storage.objects permissions, bind that role on the bucket to the service account, and configure the Cloud Run service to run as that account. Access stays tightly scoped to the bucket and avoids unnecessary privileges elsewhere in the project.

Binding the predefined Storage Admin role at the project level is far too broad, granting administrative control over every bucket and object in the project. That breaks least privilege and is not confined to the learning-media bucket.

Giving the service account the Project Editor role uses a legacy primitive role with sweeping permissions across many services. It is discouraged and does not represent least privilege for accessing one bucket.

Leaving the default Cloud Run service account with no extra bindings will not supply the needed read and write access, since that account lacks the necessary Cloud Storage permissions by default, and using it unscoped is not a production best practice.

Você cria um custom role no projeto contendo apenas as permissões storage.objects necessárias, vincula esse role no bucket à service account e configura o serviço do Cloud Run para ser executado como essa conta. O acesso permanece estritamente restrito ao bucket e evita privilégios desnecessários em outras partes do projeto.

Vincular o role predefinido Storage Admin no nível do projeto é amplo demais, concedendo controle administrativo sobre todos os buckets e objetos do projeto. Isso quebra o least privilege e não fica confinado ao bucket de learning-media.

Conceder à service account o role Project Editor usa um primitive role legado com permissões abrangentes em muitos serviços. É desencorajado e não representa o menor privilégio para acessar um único bucket.

Deixar a service account padrão do Cloud Run sem vinculações adicionais não fornecerá o acesso de leitura e escrita necessário, pois essa conta não possui as permissões necessárias do Cloud Storage por padrão, e usá-la sem escopo definido não é uma boa prática de produção.

questions.question: ClearFolio Studios is launching a public portal that serves only static assets such as images, CSS, and JavaScript to users around the world. They want the simplest architecture with minimal operational work, and they also need very low latency and high reliability for global visitors. Which approach should they choose?

options.text: Deploy a Cloud Run service that serves the static files, create an external HTTP(S) load balancer with a serverless network endpoint group, and enable Cloud CDN

Create a multi regional Cloud Storage bucket with the Standard storage class, store the static assets there, reserve a global external IP address and set up an external HTTP(S) load balancer, then enable Cloud CDN and route traffic to a backend bucket
Create a regional Cloud Storage bucket with the Standard storage class for the files, configure an external HTTP(S) load balancer with a backend bucket, and enable Cloud CDN
Create a managed instance group and replicate the static content across the VMs, set up an external HTTP(S) load balancer, and enable Cloud CDN to send traffic to the group

questions.correct_text: Create a multi regional Cloud Storage bucket with the Standard storage class, store the static assets there, reserve a global external IP address and set up an external HTTP(S) load balancer, then enable Cloud CDN and route traffic to a backend bucket
questions.explanation:
The correct choice is Create a multi regional Cloud Storage bucket with the Standard storage class, store the static assets there, reserve a global external IP address and set up an external HTTP(S) load balancer, then enable Cloud CDN and route traffic to a backend bucket.

This architecture gives globally distributed storage with high availability and durability while requiring almost no operational work. The external HTTP(S) load balancer with a backend bucket integrates natively with Cloud CDN, so content is cached at edge locations close to users which delivers very low latency and high reliability. There are no servers to manage and no application runtime to patch, which keeps the solution simple. A global static IP helps with DNS and custom domain mapping while the load balancer handles TLS and routing cleanly.

Deploy a Cloud Run service that serves the static files, create an external HTTP(S) load balancer with a serverless network endpoint group, and enable Cloud CDN adds an unnecessary compute layer for a static site. While it can work, it introduces cold starts and higher operational complexity and cost than using a Cloud Storage origin with a backend bucket.

Create a regional Cloud Storage bucket with the Standard storage class for the files, configure an external HTTP(S) load balancer with a backend bucket, and enable Cloud CDN doesn't meet the global reliability requirement because the data resides in a single region. It can also increase latency for users far from that region, whereas a multi regional bucket improves availability and better serves a worldwide audience.

Create a managed instance group and replicate the static content across the VMs, set up an external HTTP(S) load balancer, and enable Cloud CDN to send traffic to the group requires VM management, image updates, and scaling operations. This is not the simplest approach for static files and creates avoidable operational overhead compared with using Cloud Storage and a backend bucket.

Também pode aumentar a latência para usuários distantes dessa região, ao passo que um bucket multirregional melhora a disponibilidade e atende melhor a um público mundial.

Criar um managed instance group e replicar o conteúdo estático entre as VMs, configurar um external HTTP(S) load balancer e habilitar o Cloud CDN para enviar tráfego ao grupo exige gerenciamento de VMs, atualizações de imagens e operações de escalonamento. questions.question: A teammate at MeadowCom Retail is using the BigQuery Java client to stream about 1 million tiny records into dataset analytics_dw and table clickstream_logs. The code currently builds an InsertAllRequest for each individual row and calls insertAll inside the loop, which results in one request per row. You are asked to suggest a change that will boost throughput and cut per request overhead while keeping the same approach. What should you recommend?

options.text: Publish rows to Pub/Sub and use a Dataflow pipeline to write to BigQuery
Use multiple threads that each call insertAll for a single row
Group many rows into each InsertAllRequest and send them in a single call
Write each row as its own object to Cloud Storage then run BigQuery load jobs

questions.correct_text: Group many rows into each InsertAllRequest and send them in a single call
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Group many rows into each InsertAllRequest and send them in a single call. This keeps the existing BigQuery streaming workflow with the Java client while cutting per request overhead and improving throughput.

The Java client allows you to build a single InsertAllRequest that contains many rows and then call insertAll once. This reduces the number of network round trips and server side processing compared with issuing one request for each tiny record. It also makes retries more efficient because you can handle partial failures at the row level without repeating thousands of separate calls.

Publish rows to Pub/Sub and use a Dataflow pipeline to write to BigQuery is wrong because it changes the architecture rather than keeping the same approach. While Pub/Sub and Dataflow are excellent for scalable pipelines, they add components and latency that are unnecessary for simply optimizing the current insertAll usage.

Use multiple threads that each call insertAll for a single row is wrong because it still sends one request per row. This preserves the same per request overhead and can increase pressure on streaming quotas. Batching rows into fewer requests is a more efficient way to raise throughput.

Write each row as its own object to Cloud Storage then run BigQuery load jobs is wrong because load jobs are designed for batching larger files rather than millions of tiny objects. This would add substantial overhead and would not preserve the low latency streaming behavior.

A opção correta é: agrupar muitas linhas em cada InsertAllRequest e enviá-las em uma única chamada. Isso mantém o fluxo de trabalho existente de streaming do BigQuery com o cliente Java, ao mesmo tempo em que reduz a sobrecarga por requisição e melhora a vazão (throughput).

O cliente Java permite que você construa um único InsertAllRequest que contenha muitas linhas e então chame insertAll uma vez. Isso reduz o número de idas e voltas pela rede (round trips) e o processamento do lado do servidor em comparação com emitir uma requisição para cada registro minúsculo. Também torna as repetições (retries) mais eficientes, pois você pode tratar falhas parciais no nível da linha sem repetir milhares de chamadas separadas.

Publicar as linhas no Pub/Sub e usar uma pipeline do Dataflow para escrever no BigQuery está errado porque muda a arquitetura em vez de manter a mesma abordagem. Embora Pub/Sub e Dataflow sejam excelentes para pipelines escaláveis, eles adicionam componentes e latência desnecessários para simplesmente otimizar o uso atual do insertAll.

Usar múltiplas threads, cada uma chamando insertAll para uma única linha, está errado porque ainda envia uma requisição por linha. Isso preserva a mesma sobrecarga por requisição e pode aumentar a pressão sobre as cotas de streaming. Agrupar linhas em menos requisições é uma forma mais eficiente de elevar a vazão.

Escrever cada linha como seu próprio objeto no Cloud Storage e então executar load jobs do BigQuery está errado porque os load jobs são projetados para agrupar arquivos maiores em vez de milhões de objetos minúsculos. Isso adicionaria uma sobrecarga substancial e não preservaria o comportamento de streaming de baixa latência.

questions.question: Your team at a logistics startup called HaulPoint is shipping a containerized service to Google Kubernetes Engine. The service relies on API keys and database passwords that must stay secret yet be surfaced to the running pods as environment variables. How should these values be delivered to the workload securely?

options.text: Keep the sensitive values in a ConfigMap and reference them as environment variables
Drop the sensitive values into a publicly readable Cloud Storage bucket and have the app pull them at startup
Create a Kubernetes Secret and surface the values to pods as environment variables or mounted files
Encrypt a secrets file with Cloud KMS, bake it into the image, and decrypt it at container start with a bootstrap script

questions.correct_text: Create a Kubernetes Secret and surface the values to pods as environment variables or mounted files
questions.explanation:
The right answer is to create a Kubernetes Secret and surface the values to pods as environment variables or mounted files.

A Kubernetes Secret exists specifically to hold credentials and other confidential data. In GKE you can expose its values to containers either as environment variables or as mounted files, which satisfies the requirement. You can lock down access with Kubernetes RBAC, and the data sits in etcd with support for encryption at rest.

Keeping the sensitive values in a ConfigMap is wrong because ConfigMaps are meant for non-sensitive configuration. Their contents are only base64 encoded and are not treated as confidential, so anyone with enough access to the namespace can read them.

Dropping the values into a publicly readable Cloud Storage bucket is insecure because it exposes the credentials to anyone who can reach the bucket, violating least privilege and offering no protection at all.

Encrypting a secrets file with Cloud KMS, baking it into the image, and decrypting it at start is not advisable here because secrets should never be embedded in images, and custom decryption logic adds complexity and risk. Images are widely distributed and long-lived, which magnifies the impact if keys or processes are exposed, and Kubernetes already provides secure delivery through Secret resources.

questions.question: TideCart Retail runs a set of microservices on Google Kubernetes Engine in us-central1 that must publish messages to a Pub/Sub topic named "ship-events" for order processing, and you are asked to implement authentication that follows least privilege and avoids storing long lived keys in pods. What should you do?

options.text: Use a user managed service account for the GKE nodes and grant it the Pub/Sub Editor role at the project level
Create a Kubernetes Service Account per workload and mount a JSON key for a Google service account that has Pub/Sub Publisher
Grant the Pub/Sub Publisher role to allUsers at the project scope
Enable Workload Identity and bind a Kubernetes Service Account to a Google service account that has Pub/Sub Publisher on the "ship-events" topic

questions.correct_text: Enable Workload Identity and bind a Kubernetes Service Account to a Google service account that has Pub/Sub Publisher on the "ship-events" topic
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Enable Workload Identity and bind a Kubernetes Service Account to a Google service account that has Pub/Sub Publisher on the "ship-events" topic.

Workload Identity lets pods authenticate to Google APIs without storing long lived keys in containers because the Kubernetes service account is federated to a Google service account and tokens are issued dynamically. Granting the publisher role directly on the specific Pub/Sub topic matches least privilege because only publish on the required resource is allowed and no broader project level access is given.

With Workload Identity each microservice can use its own Kubernetes service account that is bound to a distinct Google service account, giving fine grained control. You can then grant Pub/Sub Publisher only on the ship-events topic so the microservices can publish messages while being unable to subscribe or modify other resources.

Use a user managed service account for the GKE nodes and grant it the Pub/Sub Editor role at the project level is wrong because the node service account would be shared by all pods and project level Editor is overly broad. This violates least privilege and increases blast radius if a pod is compromised.

Create a Kubernetes Service Account per workload and mount a JSON key for a Google service account that has Pub/Sub Publisher is wrong because mounting JSON keys introduces long lived credentials in pods and creates operational burden for rotation and revocation. The question asks to avoid storing such keys, which Workload Identity solves.

Grant the Pub/Sub Publisher role to allUsers at the project scope is wrong because it allows anyone on the internet to publish messages to your project, which is not authenticated and is the opposite of least privilege.

Usar uma service account gerenciada pelo usuário para os nós do GKE e conceder a ela o role Pub/Sub Editor no nível do projeto está errado porque a service account do nó seria compartilhada por todos os pods, e o Editor no nível do projeto é amplo demais.
