questions.question: Sailwind Insights runs a data transformation service on a GKE cluster, and the service performs heavy batch computations from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. on weekdays, which causes sharp spikes in CPU and memory usage while demand is low at night and on weekends. You want to cut costs by automatically reducing unused capacity during quiet times. What should you configure to meet these goals?

options.text: Enable autoscaling on the node pool's underlying managed instance group so node counts change with CPU and memory metrics
Build a custom controller that watches traffic and adjusts node counts through the API at the start and end of shifts
Turn on Cluster Autoscaler for the node pool and use a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler that scales pods on CPU consumption
Configure Vertical Pod Autoscaler to adjust container requests automatically and enable Cluster Autoscaler for the cluster

questions.correct_text: Turn on Cluster Autoscaler for the node pool and use a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler that scales pods on CPU consumption
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Turn on Cluster Autoscaler for the node pool and use a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler that scales pods on CPU consumption. This combination scales pods up to handle the weekday spikes and removes unused nodes when demand is low at night and on weekends, which cuts cost without sacrificing performance.

The Cluster Autoscaler reacts to unschedulable pods by adding nodes and evicts underutilized nodes when workloads can be rescheduled, capturing savings during quiet periods. The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler adjusts replica counts based on CPU so batch jobs can absorb sharp load spikes during business hours without permanent overprovisioning.

Enable autoscaling on the node pool's underlying managed instance group so node counts change with CPU and memory metrics is not suitable because GKE manages the instance groups and the instance group autoscaler does not act on Kubernetes pod scheduling signals. This can conflict with Kubernetes decisions and fails to rightsize capacity based on pending pods.

Build a custom controller that watches traffic and adjusts node counts through the API at the start and end of shifts adds unnecessary complexity and operational risk. It reimplements mature platform features and is less responsive and reliable than the native autoscalers.

Configure Vertical Pod Autoscaler to adjust container requests automatically and enable Cluster Autoscaler for the cluster focuses on retuning resource requests rather than scaling replicas to meet rapid demand. It can cause restarts and may lag behind sudden spikes, which makes it a poor fit for sharp daytime bursts without a pod autoscaler.

O Cluster Autoscaler reage a pods que não podem ser agendados adicionando nós e despeja nós subutilizados quando as cargas de trabalho podem ser reagendadas, capturando economias durante os períodos de baixa atividade. O Horizontal Pod Autoscaler ajusta a contagem de réplicas com base na CPU, de modo que os jobs em lote possam absorver picos acentuados de carga durante o horário comercial sem provisionamento excessivo permanente.

Habilitar o autoscaling no managed instance group subjacente do node pool para que a contagem de nós mude conforme as métricas de CPU e memória não é adequado, porque o GKE gerencia os instance groups e o autoscaler do instance group não atua sobre os sinais de agendamento de pods do Kubernetes. Isso pode entrar em conflito com as decisões do Kubernetes e não dimensiona corretamente a capacidade com base em pods pendentes.

Construir um controlador personalizado que observa o tráfego e ajusta a contagem de nós por meio da API no início e no fim dos turnos adiciona complexidade desnecessária e risco operacional. Ele reimplementa recursos maduros da plataforma e é menos responsivo e confiável do que os autoscalers nativos.

Configurar o Vertical Pod Autoscaler para ajustar automaticamente as requests dos contêineres e habilitar o Cluster Autoscaler para o cluster concentra-se em reajustar as requests de recursos em vez de escalar réplicas para atender à demanda rápida. Isso pode causar reinicializações e pode ficar atrás de picos repentinos, o que o torna inadequado para rajadas acentuadas durante o dia sem um pod autoscaler.

questions.question: You are designing the data platform for Wrenwick Metrics where multiple services emit structured and semi structured events at about 22 TB per day. The data must be readily consumable by analytics and machine learning tools across Google Cloud, and you require a fully managed repository that provides high performance SQL querying. Which service should you choose?

options.text: Cloud Spanner
Adopt BigQuery for a serverless analytics warehouse
Cloud SQL
Cloud Bigtable

questions.correct_text: Adopt BigQuery for a serverless analytics warehouse
questions.explanation:
The correct choice is Adopt BigQuery for a serverless analytics warehouse because it is a fully managed analytics repository that supports high performance SQL and integrates broadly with Google Cloud analytics and machine learning tools.

It handles tens of terabytes per day with elastic scaling and separates storage from compute, which keeps performance high while controlling cost. It supports structured and semi structured data using nested and array types and a native JSON data type, which allows flexible ingestion of diverse event payloads. It offers partitioning and clustering that improve query performance and integrates with Dataflow and Pub/Sub for ingestion and with Vertex AI and its native ML features for modeling and prediction.

Cloud Spanner is designed for globally distributed relational transactions with strong consistency, which makes it excellent for OLTP systems but it is not an analytics data warehouse and is not optimized for large scale SQL analytics over columnar storage.

Cloud SQL is a managed relational database service for transactional workloads and smaller scale reporting that does not scale to petabyte level analytics and does not provide the columnar storage and serverless query engine expected in a data warehouse.

Cloud Bigtable is a wide column NoSQL database for low latency key value and time series access. It is ideal for operational workloads and real time serving but does not provide native SQL analytics or warehouse features.

O Cloud SQL é um serviço de banco de dados relacional gerenciado para cargas de trabalho transacionais e relatórios de menor escala, que não escala para análises em nível de petabyte e não fornece o armazenamento colunar e o mecanismo de consulta serverless esperados em um data warehouse.

O Cloud Bigtable é um banco de dados NoSQL wide column para acesso de baixa latência a key value e séries temporais. Ele é ideal para cargas de trabalho operacionais e serviço em tempo real, mas não fornece análises SQL nativas ou recursos de data warehouse.

questions.question: Borealis Metrics is building an ingestion pipeline that writes about 4 million telemetry events per minute into Cloud Bigtable, and the team wants a row key design that sustains high write throughput while avoiding hotspots that occur with sequential identifiers. Which row key strategy should the team use?

options.text: Use the event timestamp as the entire row key
Apply a hashed or salted prefix to the row key so writes spread across tablets
Choose a row key that increases monotonically with the event identifier
Write all events under a single constant row key

questions.correct_text: Apply a hashed or salted prefix to the row key so writes spread across tablets
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Apply a hashed or salted prefix to the row key so writes spread across tablets. This strategy randomizes the leading bytes of each key, which spreads write traffic across many tablets and nodes, so it sustains very high ingestion rates without hotspots.

Bigtable stores rows in lexicographic order, so inserts that cluster near each other are handled by the same tablet. This approach distributes keys evenly which enables automatic splitting and balanced load across the cluster. You can keep query locality by appending an event identifier or timestamp after the prefix so related data remains logically grouped while writes remain well distributed.

Use the event timestamp as the entire row key concentrates all recent writes at the end of the keyspace, which targets a small number of tablets and creates hotspots during heavy ingestion.

Choose a row key that increases monotonically with the event identifier also funnels writes into an ever advancing tail of the table, which overloads a single tablet until a split occurs and then repeats the pattern.

Write all events under a single constant row key is the worst pattern because every write hits the same row, which prevents parallelism and immediately creates a severe hotspot.

questions.explanation_pt:
A opção correta é aplicar um prefixo com hash ou salt à row key para que as gravações se espalhem pelos tablets. Essa estratégia aleatoriza os bytes iniciais de cada chave, o que distribui o tráfego de gravação por muitos tablets e nós, sustentando taxas de ingestão muito altas sem hotspots.

O Bigtable armazena as linhas em ordem lexicográfica, de modo que inserções agrupadas próximas umas das outras são tratadas pelo mesmo tablet. Essa abordagem distribui as chaves de maneira uniforme, o que permite a divisão automática e o balanceamento de carga no cluster. Você pode manter a localidade de consulta anexando um identificador de evento ou timestamp após o prefixo, de modo que os dados relacionados permaneçam logicamente agrupados enquanto as gravações continuam bem distribuídas.

Usar o timestamp do evento como a row key inteira concentra todas as gravações recentes no final do keyspace, o que atinge um pequeno número de tablets e cria hotspots durante a ingestão intensa.

Escolher uma row key que aumenta monotonicamente com o identificador do evento também canaliza as gravações para uma cauda sempre crescente da tabela, o que sobrecarrega um único tablet até que ocorra uma divisão e então repete o padrão.

Gravar todos os eventos sob uma única row key constante é o pior padrão, porque cada gravação atinge a mesma linha, o que impede o paralelismo e cria imediatamente um hotspot severo.

questions.question: Skywood Media hosts its customer portal on App Engine. You need to measure realistic latency and throughput by simulating 3,200 concurrent users who access the site from at least eight different geographic regions. Which approach will yield the most accurate performance test results?

options.text: Use Cloud Monitoring dashboards to observe response time trends during a small internal test
Use Network Intelligence Center to evaluate end to end network performance for your service
Run a geographically distributed load test that sends traffic from several regions using a load generating tool on Compute Engine or Cloud Run
Turn on Cloud CDN and estimate user experience by reviewing cache metrics and request logs

questions.correct_text: Run a geographically distributed load test that sends traffic from several regions using a load generating tool on Compute Engine or Cloud Run
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Run a geographically distributed load test that sends traffic from several regions using a load generating tool on Compute Engine or Cloud Run. This approach most closely mirrors real user behavior by originating traffic from at least eight regions while controlling 3,200 concurrent sessions, so you can measure true end user latency and throughput.

This method sends synthetic requests from multiple locations, which captures DNS resolution, TLS negotiation, and network path variability that real users experience. You can scale the generators to hold target concurrency and shape the workload to include ramp up and steady state. You also collect both client side timings and server side metrics, which gives the most accurate view of application performance.

Use Cloud Monitoring dashboards to observe response time trends during a small internal test is wrong. This only visualizes metrics from a limited internal exercise and does not generate the required multi region load, so results will not reflect realistic latency or throughput.

Use Network Intelligence Center to evaluate end to end network performance for your service is wrong. This evaluates paths and connectivity quality but does not drive application layer traffic or simulate thousands of concurrent users across regions.

Turn on Cloud CDN and estimate user experience by reviewing cache metrics and request logs is wrong. Cache metrics and logs help you understand hit ratios and request patterns but do not replace controlled distributed load generation, and they can mask performance of uncached dynamic content.

questions.question: Your team at Lumen Analytics pushes well over 400 container images each week into Artifact Registry and wants CVEs in those images detected automatically, all while preserving developer speed and sticking to managed Google Cloud services. What should you put in place?

Turn on Security Command Center Premium to watch projects and surface security issues
Enable the Container Analysis API so images in Artifact Registry are scanned for vulnerabilities
Set up Cloud Monitoring to observe Cloud Build results and flag builds that reference known vulnerable versions

questions.correct_text: Enable the Container Analysis API so images in Artifact Registry are scanned for vulnerabilities
questions.explanation:
The right answer is to enable the Container Analysis API so images in Artifact Registry are scanned for vulnerabilities.

This API performs managed, automatic vulnerability scanning of container images held in Artifact Registry. Scans run after a push, which keeps developer velocity intact, and findings are recorded as vulnerability occurrences that you can view in Artifact Registry or query programmatically. It directly satisfies the requirement to detect CVEs through a managed Google Cloud capability.

Requiring only organization-approved base images strengthens supply-chain hygiene but does not automatically detect CVEs in images that get pushed. It is a preventive control, not a scanning solution.

Turning on Security Command Center Premium aggregates and displays findings, yet it does not by itself perform the image vulnerability scans for Artifact Registry. You still need the scanning service to generate those findings.

Setting up Cloud Monitoring to watch Cloud Build results relies on monitoring and custom logic rather than a vulnerability analysis engine. It will not automatically scan pushed images for CVEs and adds operational overhead that can slow the team.

questions.question: QuantaPay is constructing a microservices platform whose services call one another constantly within a single VPC. Traffic is projected near 90,000 requests per minute, with payloads almost always smaller than 1 KB. Which communication protocol best optimizes throughput and efficiency for these interactions?

options.text: REST over HTTP using JSON
gRPC using Protocol Buffers
GraphQL over HTTP
gRPC using JSON

questions.correct_text: gRPC using Protocol Buffers
questions.explanation:
The right answer is gRPC using Protocol Buffers, because it pairs compact binary serialization with HTTP/2 to maximize throughput and efficiency for many small requests inside the same VPC.

This gives you multiplexed streams on one connection, header compression, and persistent connections, all of which cut latency and CPU overhead. Protocol Buffers produce far smaller payloads than JSON, which helps even more when messages stay under 1 KB. Built-in streaming and flow control add further benefit for high-rate service-to-service traffic.

REST over HTTP using JSON is approachable and interoperable, but its text-based encoding and larger headers raise bandwidth and parsing costs, lowering throughput for many small calls. Even on HTTP/2 it stays less efficient for this internal microservice case.

GraphQL over HTTP excels at client-driven data shaping but adds query parsing and resolver overhead and typically rides on JSON. That overhead is unnecessary for internal point-to-point calls with small messages at high rates.

gRPC using JSON strips away the main efficiency win, since JSON is larger and slower to parse than Protocol Buffers. You keep gRPC's transport features but lose the compact binary serialization that drives the best throughput and CPU efficiency.

A resposta certa é gRPC usando Protocol Buffers, porque combina serialização binária compacta com HTTP/2 para maximizar a taxa de transferência e a eficiência de muitas requisições pequenas dentro da mesma VPC.

Isso oferece streams multiplexados em uma única conexão, compressão de cabeçalhos e conexões persistentes, tudo isso reduzindo a latência e a sobrecarga de CPU. O Protocol Buffers produz payloads muito menores que JSON, o que ajuda ainda mais quando as mensagens ficam abaixo de 1 KB. O streaming e o controle de fluxo embutidos trazem benefícios adicionais para tráfego serviço-a-serviço de alta frequência.

REST sobre HTTP usando JSON é acessível e interoperável, mas sua codificação baseada em texto e cabeçalhos maiores elevam os custos de largura de banda e parsing, reduzindo a taxa de transferência para muitas chamadas pequenas. Mesmo sobre HTTP/2 ele permanece menos eficiente para esse caso de microsserviço interno.

GraphQL sobre HTTP se destaca na modelagem de dados orientada pelo cliente, mas adiciona sobrecarga de parsing de queries e de resolvers e normalmente trafega sobre JSON. Essa sobrecarga é desnecessária para chamadas internas ponto a ponto com mensagens pequenas em alta frequência.

gRPC usando JSON elimina o principal ganho de eficiência, já que JSON é maior e mais lento de parsear que Protocol Buffers. Você mantém os recursos de transporte do gRPC, mas perde a serialização binária compacta que proporciona a melhor taxa de transferência e eficiência de CPU.

questions.question: ArcadiaPay is launching an internet facing analytics API on Google Kubernetes Engine that ingests user events in real time. The engineering team must ship updates without downtime, and they want to try a new release on a small fraction of live traffic before a full rollout. They also require an easy way to revert if a problem is found. Your rollout should ensure uninterrupted updates, minimize impact to the majority of users during testing, and provide quick rollback. What should you implement?

options.text: Use a Kubernetes Deployment with a rolling update and manually change the container image then monitor metrics and roll back by reverting the Deployment if needed
Create two GKE clusters for version isolation and use a self managed reverse proxy on Compute Engine to direct 25% of requests to the new cluster then retire the old cluster after validation

Enable Anthos Service Mesh on the GKE cluster and deploy "v1" and "v2" in separate namespaces then configure a VirtualService and DestinationRule to send 20% of traffic to "v2" and ramp up or roll back by editing the route
Deploy the new version in the same namespace and rely on the default Service to balance requests during a rolling update without additional configuration

questions.correct_text: Enable Anthos Service Mesh on the GKE cluster and deploy "v1" and "v2" in separate namespaces then configure a VirtualService and DestinationRule to send 20% of traffic to "v2" and ramp up or roll back by editing the route
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Enable Anthos Service Mesh on the GKE cluster and deploy "v1" and "v2" in separate namespaces then configure a VirtualService and DestinationRule to send 20% of traffic to "v2" and ramp up or roll back by editing the route.

This approach supports true canary releases because it lets you shift a precise percentage of live traffic to the new version while keeping the majority on the stable version. You can start small to minimize user impact and increase gradually as confidence grows. Rollback is quick because you only update routing configuration to return traffic to the stable version, with no need to redeploy or restart workloads, which keeps updates uninterrupted.

VirtualService rules provide weighted request routing and DestinationRule defines versioned subsets, commonly via labels, which together enable controlled traffic splitting. Editing these resources is fast and safe, and they integrate cleanly with GKE ingress so you can observe metrics and adjust or revert in place.

Use a Kubernetes Deployment with a rolling update and manually change the container image then monitor metrics and roll back by reverting the Deployment if needed is wrong because a rolling update replaces pods over time rather than holding two versions and directing a fixed percentage of traffic to the new one. It does not provide precise percentage based routing for a live canary and rollback requires another rollout rather than an immediate traffic shift.

Create two GKE clusters for version isolation and use a self managed reverse proxy on Compute Engine to direct 25% of requests to the new cluster then retire the old cluster after validation is wrong because it adds significant operational complexity and cost without improving the canary mechanics. Managing your own proxy across clusters is slower to change and harder to observe, and it is unnecessary when traffic splitting can be handled natively at the service layer.

Deploy the new version in the same namespace and rely on the default Service to balance requests during a rolling update without additional configuration is wrong because the default Service balances across ready endpoints but does not support weighted routing between versions. You cannot hold a steady 20 percent of traffic on the new version for evaluation with this setup.

questions.explanation_pt:
A opção correta é habilitar o Anthos Service Mesh no cluster GKE e implantar "v1" e "v2" em namespaces separados, depois configurar um VirtualService e um DestinationRule para enviar 20% do tráfego para "v2" e aumentar gradualmente ou reverter editando a rota.

Essa abordagem oferece suporte a verdadeiros lançamentos canário porque permite direcionar uma porcentagem precisa do tráfego ao vivo para a nova versão, mantendo a maioria na versão estável. Você pode começar com pouco para minimizar o impacto nos usuários e aumentar gradualmente conforme a confiança cresce. O rollback é rápido porque você apenas atualiza a configuração de roteamento para devolver o tráfego à versão estável, sem necessidade de reimplantar ou reiniciar as cargas de trabalho, o que mantém as atualizações ininterruptas.

As regras do VirtualService fornecem roteamento de requisições ponderado e o DestinationRule define subconjuntos versionados, comumente por meio de labels, que juntos permitem a divisão controlada de tráfego. Editar esses recursos é rápido e seguro, e eles se integram de forma limpa com o ingress do GKE, para que você possa observar as métricas e ajustar ou reverter no local.

Usar um Deployment do Kubernetes com rolling update e alterar manualmente a imagem do contêiner, depois monitorar métricas e reverter o Deployment se necessário está errado porque um rolling update substitui pods ao longo do tempo em vez de manter duas versões e direcionar uma porcentagem fixa de tráfego para a nova. Ele não fornece roteamento preciso baseado em porcentagem para um canário ao vivo, e o rollback exige outro lançamento em vez de uma mudança imediata de tráfego.

Criar dois clusters GKE para isolamento de versão e usar um reverse proxy autogerenciado no Compute Engine para direcionar 25% das requisições para o novo cluster, depois aposentar o cluster antigo após a validação está errado porque adiciona complexidade operacional e custo significativos sem melhorar a mecânica do canário. Gerenciar seu próprio proxy entre clusters é mais lento de alterar e mais difícil de observar, e é desnecessário quando a divisão de tráfego pode ser tratada nativamente na camada de serviço.

Implantar a nova versão no mesmo namespace e confiar no Service padrão para balancear as requisições durante um rolling update sem configuração adicional está errado porque o Service padrão balanceia entre endpoints prontos, mas não oferece suporte a roteamento ponderado entre versões. Você não consegue manter 20 por cento constante do tráfego na nova versão para avaliação com essa configuração.

questions.question: CivicCircles is a neighborhood meetup app connecting nearby residents to plan events and helping local shops reach customers. Following a launch across six districts in Toronto, adoption has accelerated as the company goes international, rolling out features in new regions and hiring support staff in local time zones. They need dependable horizontal scaling and accurate uptime visibility. Their stack straddles on-premises systems and Google Cloud, and although they know their app well, they have little experience operating globally. Today the APIs run on Compute Engine VMs and state lives in a single-node MySQL 8.0 instance on Google Cloud, with data exported to on-premises Teradata and Vertica warehouses and analysts using an on-premises Hadoop cluster. Logging is thin and only basic availability is tracked. Investors expect wider regional coverage, more concurrent users, a consistent traveler experience, richer activity metrics for monetization, regulatory compliance such as GDPR, lower operational overhead, and adoption of Google best practices. The platform must expose metrics and monitoring, enforce strong authentication and authorization, improve logging, and keep analytics data in a cloud-native platform; it should move to serverless for elastic scale and secure internal tooling. The data science team intends to run text analytics over user reviews. How should the team prepare the review data so it can be analyzed while protecting sensitive information?

options.text: Apply BigQuery policy tags and dynamic data masking to conceal sensitive content within the free-form review text
Run the review text through the Cloud Data Loss Prevention API to redact it before analysis
Run the review text through the Cloud Data Loss Prevention API to de-identify it before analysis
Use the Cloud Natural Language API to de-identify names and addresses inside the review text

questions.correct_text: Run the review text through the Cloud Data Loss Prevention API to de-identify it before analysis
questions.explanation:
The right answer is to run the review text through the Cloud Data Loss Prevention API to de-identify it before analysis.

De-identification with the Cloud Data Loss Prevention API spots common sensitive data such as names, addresses, emails, phone numbers, and many other infoTypes, then swaps those spans for consistent tokens or generalized values. Grammar and context survive, so downstream work like sentiment analysis and topic modeling still functions while the risk of re-identification drops. You can choose irreversible transformations for stronger protection or reversible keyed cryptography when you need to join across datasets, which supports privacy obligations like GDPR.

Applying BigQuery policy tags and dynamic data masking is not appropriate, because those controls govern what query results expose inside BigQuery rather than transforming the data itself. They do not automatically detect sensitive entities in unstructured text and offer no protection once data leaves BigQuery for other services.

Redacting the review text with the Cloud Data Loss Prevention API would strip or obscure content and often destroys the linguistic signal that accurate text analytics depends on. De-identification keeps utility by substituting sensitive spans with consistent surrogates instead of simply deleting them.

Using the Cloud Natural Language API to de-identify names and addresses is incorrect because that service does entity and sentiment analysis and provides no de-identification transformations or broad PII workflow. It is not meant to enforce data protection or emit consistent privacy-preserving tokens.

A resposta certa é processar o texto da avaliação pela Cloud Data Loss Prevention API para desidentificá-lo antes da análise.

A desidentificação com a Cloud Data Loss Prevention API detecta dados sensíveis comuns, como nomes, endereços, e-mails, números de telefone e muitos outros infoTypes, e então substitui esses trechos por tokens consistentes ou valores generalizados. A gramática e o contexto são preservados, então trabalhos posteriores como análise de sentimento e modelagem de tópicos ainda funcionam, enquanto o risco de reidentificação diminui. Você pode escolher transformações irreversíveis para proteção mais forte ou criptografia reversível com chave quando precisar fazer joins entre conjuntos de dados, o que dá suporte a obrigações de privacidade como o GDPR.

Aplicar policy tags do BigQuery e dynamic data masking não é apropriado, porque esses controles regem o que os resultados de consultas expõem dentro do BigQuery em vez de transformar os dados em si. Eles não detectam automaticamente entidades sensíveis em texto não estruturado e não oferecem proteção depois que os dados saem do BigQuery para outros serviços.

Redigir o texto da avaliação com a Cloud Data Loss Prevention API removeria ou ocultaria conteúdo e frequentemente destrói o sinal linguístico do qual uma análise de texto precisa depende. A desidentificação mantém a utilidade substituindo trechos sensíveis por substitutos consistentes em vez de simplesmente apagá-los.

Usar a Cloud Natural Language API para desidentificar nomes e endereços está incorreto porque esse serviço faz análise de entidades e de sentimento e não fornece transformações de desidentificação nem um fluxo amplo de tratamento de PII. Ele não foi feito para impor proteção de dados ou emitir tokens consistentes que preservem a privacidade.

questions.question: When a GKE node is drained, what mechanism lets a stateful service wrap up its outstanding requests and exit gracefully inside a 30-second budget?

options.text: Configure a readiness probe
Add a preStop lifecycle hook
Set terminationGracePeriodSeconds to 30

questions.correct_text: Add a preStop lifecycle hook
questions.explanation:
The right answer is to add a preStop lifecycle hook.

A preStop hook fires just before the container is sent the termination signal, giving the application a chance to stop taking new work and finish what is in flight. In GKE, draining a node evicts pods and begins graceful termination, and the preStop hook is the natural place to drain connections or sleep briefly while upstream traffic is pulled away. That is what lets the service exit cleanly inside the allotted window.

Configuring a readiness probe only governs when a pod is considered ready to receive traffic; it carries no shutdown logic. During termination Kubernetes already removes the pod from Service endpoints, so a readiness probe does nothing to finish ongoing work.

Setting terminationGracePeriodSeconds to 30 merely defines how long the kubelet waits before sending the kill signal, and 30 seconds is already the default. Without actual shutdown logic such as a preStop hook or proper signal handling, the pod can still abandon in-flight work even with the grace period set.

A resposta certa é adicionar um preStop lifecycle hook.

Um preStop hook é disparado logo antes de o contêiner receber o sinal de término, dando à aplicação a chance de parar de aceitar novo trabalho e finalizar o que está em andamento. No GKE, drenar um nó despeja os pods e inicia o término gracioso, e o preStop hook é o lugar natural para drenar conexões ou aguardar brevemente enquanto o tráfego upstream é removido. É isso que permite ao serviço sair de forma limpa dentro da janela alocada.

Configurar um readiness probe apenas determina quando um pod é considerado pronto para receber tráfego; ele não contém nenhuma lógica de desligamento. Durante o término, o Kubernetes já remove o pod dos endpoints do Service, então um readiness probe não faz nada para concluir o trabalho em andamento.

Definir terminationGracePeriodSeconds como 30 apenas determina quanto tempo o kubelet espera antes de enviar o sinal de kill, e 30 segundos já é o padrão. Sem uma lógica real de desligamento, como um preStop hook ou o tratamento adequado de sinais, o pod ainda pode abandonar o trabalho em andamento mesmo com o grace period definido.

questions.question: At Helios Systems, several product teams intend to use Cloud Build to compile and publish Docker images to Container Registry. The platform operations group requires that every image be pushed into one registry they administer, so access control and auditing stay centralized. How do you implement this while letting teams build inside their own projects without storing long-lived secrets in source code?

options.text: Stand up an operations project with Container Registry, mint a unique service account key per team, and commit those key files into each team's repository for Docker authentication
Place a separate Container Registry in each development project and give the operations team admin access to every registry
Provision an operations-owned project with Container Registry and grant each project's Cloud Build service account permission to push images into that central registry
Run an open source Docker Registry on a Compute Engine VM in a dedicated project and hand each team a username and password kept in their repositories

questions.correct_text: Provision an operations-owned project with Container Registry and grant each project's Cloud Build service account permission to push images into that central registry
questions.explanation:
The right answer is to provision an operations-owned project with Container Registry and grant each project's Cloud Build service account permission to push images into that central registry.

This meets the goal of centralizing access control and auditing, because every image lands in a single registry the operations team owns and runs. Teams can still build in their own projects, since Cloud Build uses a project-specific service account by default, and you only need to authorize that identity to push to the registry in the operations project.

It also keeps long-lived secrets out of source code. Cloud Build authenticates with its service account, and you authorize cross-project pushes through IAM, so there are no static keys or passwords to create or store in repositories. The implementation is simple: find each project's Cloud Build service account and grant it the permissions it needs in the operations project to push images to Container Registry.

Container Registry is being superseded by Artifact Registry, so newer exams may favor the same pattern built on a central Artifact Registry repository, with each Cloud Build service account granted the required permissions. The principle of centralized control via IAM with no embedded secrets is unchanged.

Standing up an operations project and committing per-team service account keys into repositories is wrong because it depends on long-lived keys in source control, which is insecure and unnecessary when Cloud Build already supplies a managed service account.

Placing a separate registry in each development project breaks the requirement for one centralized registry and increases the operational burden of access control and auditing.

Running an open source Docker Registry on a VM with shared usernames and passwords introduces credentials that must be stored and rotated, and it swaps a managed, integrated service for a self-managed system that adds complexity without meeting the security goals.

A resposta certa é provisionar um projeto de propriedade da equipe de operações com o Container Registry e conceder à service account do Cloud Build de cada projeto permissão para enviar imagens (push) para esse registry central.

Isso atende ao objetivo de centralizar o controle de acesso e a auditoria, porque cada imagem chega a um único registry que a equipe de operações possui e opera. As equipes ainda podem fazer build em seus próprios projetos, já que o Cloud Build usa uma service account específica do projeto por padrão, e você só precisa autorizar essa identidade a fazer push para o registry no projeto de operações.

Isso também mantém segredos de longa duração fora do código-fonte. O Cloud Build se autentica com sua service account, e você autoriza pushes entre projetos por meio do IAM, então não há chaves estáticas ou senhas para criar ou armazenar em repositórios. A implementação é simples: encontre a service account do Cloud Build de cada projeto e conceda a ela as permissões necessárias no projeto de operações para fazer push de imagens para o Container Registry.

O Container Registry está sendo substituído pelo Artifact Registry, então exames mais recentes podem favorecer o mesmo padrão construído sobre um repositório central do Artifact Registry, com cada service account do Cloud Build recebendo as permissões necessárias. O princípio de controle centralizado via IAM sem segredos embutidos permanece inalterado.

Criar um projeto de operações e fazer commit de chaves de service account por equipe nos repositórios está errado porque depende de chaves de longa duração no controle de versão, o que é inseguro e desnecessário quando o Cloud Build já fornece uma service account gerenciada.

Colocar um registry separado em cada projeto de desenvolvimento quebra o requisito de um único registry centralizado e aumenta a carga operacional de controle de acesso e auditoria.

Executar um Docker Registry open source em uma VM com nomes de usuário e senhas compartilhados introduz credenciais que precisam ser armazenadas e rotacionadas, e troca um serviço gerenciado e integrado por um sistema autogerenciado que adiciona complexidade sem atender aos objetivos de segurança.

questions.question: A retail analytics startup named NovaCart runs workloads on Google Kubernetes Engine in us-central1 and needs its Pods to access Google Cloud managed services using least privilege. The team wants a one time configuration that avoids distributing long lived keys and relies on automatic credential rotation while keeping secrets encrypted at rest. You have already created a Google Cloud service account with the needed roles. What should you do next?

options.text: Export the service account key and create a Kubernetes Secret to mount it into the Pod
Configure Workload Identity and bind a Kubernetes service account to the Google Cloud service account
Store the service account JSON key in Secret Manager and mount it with the Secrets Store CSI Driver
Embed the service account key file into the application container image at build time

questions.correct_text: Configure Workload Identity and bind a Kubernetes service account to the Google Cloud service account
questions.explanation:
The correct choice is Configure Workload Identity and bind a Kubernetes service account to the Google Cloud service account.

With Workload Identity you perform a one time cluster and account binding so Pods assume the Google Cloud service account through federated credentials. Workload Identity removes the need for distributing JSON keys and provides short lived tokens that Google rotates automatically. Permissions are managed on the Google Cloud service account with IAM, which supports least privilege, and there are no long lived secrets stored in the cluster, so the requirement for encryption at rest is satisfied because there is nothing sensitive to persist.

Export the service account key and create a Kubernetes Secret to mount it into the Pod is not appropriate because it introduces a long lived private key that must be distributed and rotated manually. Even if the Secret is encrypted at rest, the risk of leakage and the operational burden remain.

Store the service account JSON key in Secret Manager and mount it with the Secrets Store CSI Driver still relies on a user managed key. This approach adds complexity and does not provide automatic rotation to running Pods, which violates the goal to avoid long lived keys.

Embed the service account key file into the application container image at build time is the least secure option because the secret becomes part of the image and is difficult to rotate or revoke, and it can be exposed wherever the image is stored or pulled.

O Workload Identity elimina a necessidade de distribuir chaves JSON e fornece tokens de curta duração que o Google rotaciona automaticamente. As permissões são gerenciadas na conta de serviço do Google Cloud com o IAM, que oferece suporte ao princípio do menor privilégio, e não há segredos de longa duração armazenados no cluster, então o requisito de criptografia em repouso é atendido porque não há nada sensível a ser persistido.

Exportar a chave da conta de serviço e criar um Secret do Kubernetes para montá-la no Pod não é apropriado porque introduz uma chave privada de longa duração que precisa ser distribuída e rotacionada manualmente. Armazenar a chave JSON da conta de serviço no Secret Manager e montá-la com o Secrets Store CSI Driver ainda depende de uma chave gerenciada pelo usuário. Essa abordagem adiciona complexidade e não fornece rotação automática para os Pods em execução, o que viola o objetivo de evitar chaves de longa duração.

questions.question: An online learning cooperative running on Google Cloud stores user submitted files in a Cloud Storage bucket. To satisfy a new compliance requirement, you must automatically delete any files older than 7 years while keeping custom code to a minimum. What should you implement?

options.text: Publish a Pub/Sub message on a seven year schedule to start a workflow that deletes outdated files
Create a Cloud Function that runs daily to scan the bucket and remove objects older than seven years
Configure Object Lifecycle Management on the Cloud Storage bucket to delete objects when they reach seven years of age
Enable a bucket retention policy with Bucket Lock set to seven years so objects are removed automatically at the end of the period

questions.correct_text: Configure Object Lifecycle Management on the Cloud Storage bucket to delete objects when they reach seven years of age
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Configure Object Lifecycle Management on the Cloud Storage bucket to delete objects when they reach seven years of age.

Object Lifecycle Management is a native Cloud Storage feature that enforces data lifecycle rules on the server side. You can define a Delete action that evaluates the age of objects and removes them once they reach seven years. This meets the requirement for automatic deletion while keeping custom code to a minimum because the platform handles listing and deletion without any user managed scripts or services.

Publish a Pub/Sub message on a seven year schedule to start a workflow that deletes outdated files is wrong because it introduces multiple moving parts and custom orchestration. You would still need additional services to schedule and run deletion logic, and this is unnecessary when a built in lifecycle policy can delete the objects automatically.

Create a Cloud Function that runs daily to scan the bucket and remove objects older than seven years is wrong because it relies on custom code to list and filter objects, which increases operational overhead and cost. A daily scan is inefficient and error prone when Object Lifecycle Management can perform the deletion natively.

Enable a bucket retention policy with Bucket Lock set to seven years so objects are removed automatically at the end of the period is wrong because retention policies prevent deletion before the period ends and do not delete data automatically when the period expires. Bucket Lock makes the policy immutable, which is unnecessary here and can block future changes. Automatic deletion with minimal code is best achieved with Object Lifecycle Management.

questions.explanation_pt:
A opção correta é configurar o Object Lifecycle Management no bucket do Cloud Storage para excluir objetos quando atingirem sete anos de idade.

O Object Lifecycle Management é um recurso nativo do Cloud Storage que aplica regras de ciclo de vida dos dados no lado do servidor. Você pode definir uma ação Delete que avalia a idade dos objetos e os remove assim que atingem sete anos. Isso atende ao requisito de exclusão automática mantendo o código personalizado ao mínimo, pois a plataforma cuida da listagem e da exclusão sem nenhum script ou serviço gerenciado pelo usuário.

Publicar uma mensagem do Pub/Sub em um cronograma de sete anos para iniciar um fluxo de trabalho que exclui arquivos desatualizados está errado porque introduz várias partes móveis e orquestração personalizada. Você ainda precisaria de serviços adicionais para agendar e executar a lógica de exclusão, e isso é desnecessário quando uma política de ciclo de vida integrada pode excluir os objetos automaticamente.

Criar uma Cloud Function que roda diariamente para varrer o bucket e remover objetos com mais de sete anos está errado porque depende de código personalizado para listar e filtrar objetos, o que aumenta a sobrecarga operacional e o custo. Uma varredura diária é ineficiente e propensa a erros quando o Object Lifecycle Management pode realizar a exclusão de forma nativa.

Habilitar uma política de retenção do bucket com Bucket Lock definido para sete anos para que os objetos sejam removidos automaticamente ao final do período está errado porque políticas de retenção impedem a exclusão antes do término do período e não excluem dados automaticamente quando o período expira. O Bucket Lock torna a política imutável, o que é desnecessário aqui e pode bloquear mudanças futuras. A exclusão automática com código mínimo é melhor alcançada com o Object Lifecycle Management.

questions.question: You require an HTTPS ingestion API that scales automatically to roughly 70 thousand requests per minute, falls to zero when idle, keeps operations minimal, and bills only for what you actually use. Which Google Cloud service should you choose?

options.text: Cloud Functions
App Engine standard
Cloud Run fully managed
GKE Autopilot

questions.correct_text: Cloud Run fully managed
questions.explanation:
The right answer is Cloud Run fully managed, because it exposes an HTTPS endpoint, autoscales to very high request rates such as seventy thousand per minute, drops to zero while idle, and bills only for actual usage, all of which minimizes operations.

Cloud Run runs your container as a fully managed service with built-in HTTPS, request-driven autoscaling, and per-request billing for CPU, memory, and requests. It launches new instances quickly when traffic spikes and scales back to zero with no traffic, so you pay nothing while idle and manage no servers.

Cloud Functions also autoscales with a pay-per-use model, but it is geared toward single-purpose functions rather than a containerized HTTP ingestion API and gives less control over concurrency, routing, and runtime dependencies. For a high-throughput web API, Cloud Run is the recommended fit.

App Engine standard can autoscale and may reach zero depending on configuration, yet it relies on instance-based scaling and billing and imposes runtime restrictions. It is less aligned with a container-based API needing fast scale-out and precise pay-only-for-use economics, so Cloud Run is the stronger match.

GKE Autopilot trims cluster management, but you still operate Kubernetes resources and pay for provisioned pod resources even when idle. It does not give true scale-to-zero for HTTP services by default and is not a pay-per-request service, which makes Cloud Run more appropriate here.

questions.question: A product team at Tessera Books built an event-driven backend on Google Cloud Functions, and although the system stays stable, the pace of shipping new features has dropped over recent sprints. Which inherent trade-off of a serverless Function as a Service platform could plausibly be dragging down that feature velocity?

options.text: Thin native support for CI or CD pipelines
The risk of vendor lock-in
Limited control over the execution environment
Trouble scaling for sudden traffic spikes

questions.correct_text: Limited control over the execution environment
questions.explanation:
The right answer is limited control over the execution environment. Function as a Service platforms restrict what developers can control in the runtime and operating system, which often forces design changes and extra engineering. Teams may have to fit fixed language runtimes and timeouts, work around ephemeral filesystems, package native dependencies differently, or rework features that assume background jobs or long-lived processes. Those constraints can slow coding, testing, and troubleshooting, dragging down feature velocity even on a stable system.

The same constraint complicates tooling and debugging. Developers spend more time reproducing the managed runtime locally, stubbing cloud services, and confirming that packaged dependencies and configuration behave identically in the managed environment. Those extra steps add delivery latency compared with full control over the environment.

Thin native support for CI or CD pipelines is not the main issue, because Cloud Functions integrates well with Cloud Build and Cloud Deploy and supports automated deployments from repositories and triggers. GCP's pipeline tooling is mature and generally speeds delivery rather than slowing it.

The risk of vendor lock-in is a strategic portability concern rather than a day-to-day sprint blocker. The Functions Framework aids portability across environments, and lock-in rarely explains a sudden slowdown on an already stable system.

Trouble scaling for sudden traffic spikes does not fit, because Cloud Functions is built to autoscale quickly in response to events and request volume. Rapid scaling is a core strength, not a limitation that would impede feature delivery.

questions.question: Cypress Mobility runs its services on Google Cloud and aggregates about 220 thousand log entries per minute in Cloud Logging. The team must deliver these logs to a third party analytics platform at sample-shop.io for immediate processing with minimal delay. Which approach should you implement?

options.text: Export Cloud Logging to BigQuery and let the third party query the dataset
Use a Cloud Function that calls the Logging API and forwards entries to the vendor endpoint
Create a Cloud Logging sink that streams to Pub/Sub for the third party to consume
Export Cloud Logging to Cloud Storage and have the third party fetch new files

questions.correct_text: Create a Cloud Logging sink that streams to Pub/Sub for the third party to consume
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Create a Cloud Logging sink that streams to Pub/Sub for the third party to consume.

This approach uses the Logs Router to continuously stream entries with very low latency, satisfying the need for immediate processing. It scales easily to the stated volume and you can add a Pub/Sub push subscription that delivers messages directly to the vendor HTTPS endpoint at sample-shop.io. This keeps delivery near real time and provides reliability features such as retries and dead letter queues.

Export Cloud Logging to BigQuery and let the third party query the dataset is not suitable because it does not stream entries to an external endpoint and there is ingestion latency before data becomes available. It supports analytics rather than immediate delivery to a vendor system.

Use a Cloud Function that calls the Logging API and forwards entries to the vendor endpoint is not the recommended pattern for sustained high throughput and low latency. Polling or pulling logs introduces delays, and scaling a function to reliably handle this volume is more complex than using the native streaming path through the Logs Router and Pub/Sub.

Export Cloud Logging to Cloud Storage and have the third party fetch new files is batch oriented because logs are written to objects over time. This requires the third party to poll or react to file notifications and does not meet the requirement for minimal delay.

Fazer polling ou pull dos logs introduz atrasos, e escalar uma função para lidar de forma confiável com esse volume é mais complexo do que usar o caminho de streaming nativo através do Logs Router e do Pub/Sub.

questions.question: Greenwood Apparel split a legacy monolith into microservices on Google Kubernetes Engine. For compliance, the company keeps its CRM platform and a MySQL database holding PII inside its on-premises data center. A Cloud VPN already links the VPC to that data center, yet services time out and occasionally crash whenever round-trip latency leaps from roughly 30 ms to more than 300 ms because of fluctuating bandwidth. What should you do to ease these latency problems?

options.text: Stand up Istio to build a service mesh stretching across the GKE cluster and the on-premises services
Insert Cloud Pub/Sub between GKE and the on-premises CRM so calls are queued and handled asynchronously
Add more Cloud VPN tunnels between Google Cloud and the on-premises network to raise throughput and resiliency
Drop the Cloud VPN MTU below the default to shrink packet size on the network

questions.correct_text: Add more Cloud VPN tunnels between Google Cloud and the on-premises network to raise throughput and resiliency
questions.explanation:
The right answer is to add more Cloud VPN tunnels between Google Cloud and the on-premises network to raise throughput and resiliency.

Adding tunnels increases aggregate bandwidth and lets you use equal-cost multipath routing to spread traffic across them. That improves throughput and adds redundancy when a single tunnel is congested or unstable. Provisioning more tunnels is a direct way to blunt latency spikes caused by fluctuating bandwidth on the existing path, and it hardens resiliency without touching the application architecture.

Standing up Istio does not address the root cause, because a mesh cannot lower round-trip time across a congested WAN link. It can add retries and policy, but it does not increase network throughput between the cluster and the data center.

Inserting Cloud Pub/Sub shifts the model to asynchronous messaging, which does not suit synchronous CRM and database calls that need immediate responses. It adds complexity and leaves the underlying network latency on the required request-response paths unresolved.

Dropping the Cloud VPN MTU below the default does not fix latency spikes from bandwidth variability. Smaller packets raise per-packet overhead and guarantee no improvement in round-trip time, and Cloud VPN already recommends MTU settings that avoid fragmentation.

questions.question: At Brookmont Analytics you need to allow a Google group to send messages to Pub/Sub topics across a project while ensuring they cannot create or modify subscriptions. Which IAM role should you grant to that group?

options.text: roles/pubsub.admin
roles/pubsub.publisher
roles/pubsub.subscriber
roles/pubsub.editor

questions.correct_text: roles/pubsub.publisher
questions.explanation:
The correct option is roles/pubsub.publisher. This lets the Google group publish messages to topics across the project while ensuring they cannot create or modify subscriptions.

This Publisher predefined role grants the ability to send messages to topics through the publish permission. It does not include permissions to create, update, or delete subscriptions, so it meets the requirement to send but not manage subscriptions. You can grant it at the project level so the group can publish to all topics in that project without gaining subscription management capabilities.

roles/pubsub.admin is wrong because it provides full administrative control over Pub/Sub, which includes creating and modifying subscriptions, and that violates the requirement.

roles/pubsub.subscriber is wrong because it allows receiving messages from subscriptions and does not allow publishing to topics, so it fails to meet the need to send messages.

roles/pubsub.editor is wrong because it is not a valid Pub/Sub predefined role and would not represent least privilege. The broad Editor capability in IAM would allow changing Pub/Sub resources, including subscriptions, which is not allowed here.

questions.question: At Cobalt Freight you run a Python-based microservices platform on a production Google Kubernetes Engine cluster. One service has to upload files to Cloud Storage, and you want to grant it the permissions it needs using the method that matches Google's recommended practices for GKE workloads. What should you do?

options.text: Save a service account key in Secret Manager and inject it into the pod for the client library to use
Create a Google service account and a Kubernetes service account, turn on Workload Identity for the cluster, and bind the Kubernetes account to the Google account
Enable the Cloud Storage API and let the pods reach the bucket through the default Compute Engine service account
Configure the node pool to run under a Google service account that has Cloud Storage permissions so any pod on those nodes can write to the bucket

questions.correct_text: Create a Google service account and a Kubernetes service account, turn on Workload Identity for the cluster, and bind the Kubernetes account to the Google account
questions.explanation:
The right answer is to create a Google service account and a Kubernetes service account, turn on Workload Identity for the cluster, and bind the Kubernetes account to the Google account.

This matches Google's GKE guidance because it gives the pod a scoped identity without storing any long-lived credentials. The Kubernetes service account maps to a Google service account that holds only the required Cloud Storage IAM roles, and the workload picks up short-lived tokens through the GKE metadata integration, so no keys are distributed to pods and least privilege holds.

Python client libraries use application default credentials, so once this is wired up the application calls Cloud Storage with no code changes and authenticates automatically through the mapped identity. That lowers operational overhead and risk while following best practices.

Saving a service account key in Secret Manager and injecting it is discouraged, because service account keys are long-lived and must be rotated and guarded. Even inside Secret Manager they can leak, and Google advises avoiding keys on GKE when Workload Identity is available.

Letting pods reach the bucket through the default Compute Engine service account is ill-advised, because it relies on a node-scoped identity that can grant broad permissions to many pods. The default account is often overly permissive or disabled and does not provide least privilege per workload.

Configuring the node pool to run under a Google service account grants those permissions to every pod on the nodes, which breaks least privilege and widens the blast radius. It does not deliver the per-workload identity Google recommends for GKE.

Permitir que os pods acessem o bucket por meio da service account padrão do Compute Engine é desaconselhável, porque depende de uma identidade com escopo de nó que pode conceder permissões amplas a muitos pods. questions.question: In GKE, how should you configure an internal only service that must scale quickly for spikes up to 40 times?

options.text: Cluster Autoscaler with a ClusterIP Service
Internal HTTP(S) Load Balancer with NEG and backend autoscaling
Horizontal Pod Autoscaler with a ClusterIP Service
Horizontal Pod Autoscaler with a NodePort Service

questions.correct_text: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler with a ClusterIP Service
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Horizontal Pod Autoscaler with a ClusterIP Service.

This pairing keeps the service reachable only inside the cluster while the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler adjusts pod replicas based on metrics. Because it scales pods directly, it can respond quickly to sudden spikes such as 40 times traffic if there is enough node capacity.

Using the internal service type also avoids exposing node ports or creating a VPC level load balancer when only in cluster access is required. This keeps the path simple and efficient for internal consumers.

Cluster Autoscaler with a ClusterIP Service is not suitable because cluster autoscaling changes the number of nodes rather than the number of pods, and adding nodes takes longer which makes it slower to absorb sharp spikes.

Internal HTTP(S) Load Balancer with NEG and backend autoscaling adds a VPC level layer 7 load balancer that is unnecessary for an in cluster only service, and backend autoscaling targets instance groups rather than pods so it would not scale your application replicas.

Horizontal Pod Autoscaler with a NodePort Service exposes a port on every node which is not needed for an internal only service, and it does not improve scaling behavior while increasing exposure and operational overhead.

questions.question: How can you expose you expose a web app on Compute Engine so users can authenticate with Google Workspace from anywhere without a VPN?

options.text: TCP proxy load balancer with Identity Aware Proxy
External HTTP(S) Load Balancer with Cloud Armor and corporate IP allowlist
External HTTP(S) Load Balancer with Identity Aware Proxy and Workspace access
Cloud VPN between the office and the VPC

questions.correct_text: External HTTP(S) Load Balancer with Identity Aware Proxy and Workspace access
questions.explanation:
The right answer is External HTTP(S) Load Balancer with Identity Aware Proxy and Workspace access.

This setup places the app behind a global web load balancer and requires Google identity at the edge before any request reaches the VM. Identity Aware Proxy verifies the user with Google Workspace and only then forwards traffic through the External HTTP(S) Load Balancer to the backend. Users can reach the app from anywhere on the internet and no VPN is needed while access can be limited to specific Workspace users or groups.

TCP proxy load balancer with Identity Aware Proxy is not viable because IAP protects HTTP and HTTPS based web apps at the edge and does not integrate with the TCP proxy load balancer for browser based access.

External HTTP(S) Load Balancer with Cloud Armor and corporate IP allowlist does not meet the requirement because IP allowlists do not authenticate users and they prevent access from anywhere by restricting to corporate networks.

Cloud VPN between the office and the VPC contradicts the requirement since it depends on a VPN and it does not provide Google Workspace based user authentication to the web app.

questions.question: You must pick a GCP host for a stateless web app that has to ramp up almost instantly for traffic surges north of 150x and then drop back to zero between surges to hold costs down. Which option fits?

options.text: GKE Autopilot with HPA
App Engine standard
Cloud Run with Firestore
Cloud Functions

questions.correct_text: Cloud Run with Firestore
questions.explanation:
The right answer is Cloud Run with Firestore.

Cloud Run is a fully managed serverless container platform that scales automatically on incoming requests and can absorb very large bursts such as 150x spikes. It scales back to zero while idle to minimize cost, is built for stateless HTTP services, and supports high concurrency, delivering quick cold starts with little operational overhead.

Firestore rounds this out as a serverless, highly scalable database that needs no capacity planning. It scales transparently through traffic surges and incurs no cost when unused, which aligns with a scale-to-zero architecture.

GKE Autopilot with HPA can autoscale pods on load but is not the best fit when you want a serverless experience that reaches zero and minimizes operational complexity. Cluster-based platforms react more slowly to sudden surges and still leave you with more infrastructure to consider than Cloud Run.

App Engine standard supports automatic scaling, but it can hold idle instances for responsiveness and is less flexible than container deployments. For rapid burst scaling with predictable scale-to-zero behavior, Cloud Run is the better choice.

Cloud Functions is tuned for single-purpose event-driven functions rather than hosting a complete stateless web application with many routes. It scales quickly, but running a full web app container on Cloud Run gives better control over routing, concurrency, and service configuration.

questions.question: At Sentinel Trust you are deploying a compliance microservice on Google Kubernetes Engine that processes confidential customer data. You must tightly govern which workloads are allowed to reach it while keeping ongoing policy upkeep to a minimum. Which approach should you take?

options.text: Put Google Cloud Armor policies in front of the HTTP load balancer
Use VPC Service Controls to draw a secure perimeter around the Google APIs the service calls
Write Kubernetes Network Policies that constrain pod-to-pod and namespace traffic inside the cluster
Insert a Cloud Function into the request path to evaluate access on each call before the service runs

questions.correct_text: Write Kubernetes Network Policies that constrain pod-to-pod and namespace traffic inside the cluster
questions.explanation:
The right answer is to write Kubernetes Network Policies that constrain pod-to-pod and namespace traffic inside the cluster. This directly governs which workloads may talk to the microservice and limits policy churn, because the rules use labels and namespace scoping that apply automatically as pods scale and roll.

Network policies let you adopt a default-deny posture and then permit only the specific pods and namespaces that should reach the service. In Google Kubernetes Engine you enable network policy and use selectors to target workloads, keeping the rules concise and durable as deployments change. This controls workload-to-workload traffic, which is exactly what a confidential service inside the cluster needs.

Putting Google Cloud Armor policies in front of the HTTP load balancer is not suitable, because Cloud Armor protects applications at the edge and filters external traffic at the load balancer. It does not govern pod-to-pod communication within a cluster.

Using VPC Service Controls is not appropriate, because they aim to reduce data exfiltration to and from Google APIs. They do not control intra-cluster communication between Kubernetes workloads.

Inserting a Cloud Function into the request path adds latency and complexity and provides no network-level isolation between pods. It raises maintenance rather than lowering it and is not a native mechanism for Kubernetes traffic control.

questions.question: An engineering team at mcnz.com rebuilt a customer facing API on Google Compute Engine so they could fine tune the operating system and network settings and scale virtual machines horizontally. After adopting this IaaS approach, their release cadence slipped from every 5 days to roughly every 18 days. Which factor most plausibly explains this trade off in delivery speed?

options.text: Limited autoscaling and horizontal scale on Google Compute Engine
Engineering effort spent provisioning, patching, and operating VM infrastructure
No ability to customize the OS image or runtime stack
Cloud Build pipelines slowed by lower parallelism quotas

questions.correct_text: Engineering effort spent provisioning, patching, and operating VM infrastructure
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Engineering effort spent provisioning, patching, and operating VM infrastructure. When teams adopt an IaaS model on Compute Engine, they take on more platform responsibilities, which commonly slows release cadence as engineering time shifts from feature delivery to infrastructure operations.

With Compute Engine you must provision and configure instances and images, apply operating system patches, harden the runtime, manage instance groups and autoscaling settings, handle network and security policies, and troubleshoot environment drift. That additional work increases lead time for changes and reduces the frequency of deployments, which makes this the most plausible explanation for going from five to eighteen day releases.

Limited autoscaling and horizontal scale on Google Compute Engine is not accurate because Compute Engine supports horizontal scaling using managed instance groups with built in autoscaling, so scaling limits are unlikely to be the reason releases slowed.

No ability to customize the OS image or runtime stack is incorrect since Compute Engine lets you choose and customize operating system images and even create your own, so flexibility was not reduced by the move.

Cloud Build pipelines slowed by lower parallelism quotas is not a likely root cause because Cloud Build concurrency is separate from the choice to run on Compute Engine, and quotas can be adjusted, so adopting IaaS does not inherently slow pipelines.

questions.question: RidgePay is moving a containerized payments service to Cloud Run with builds created by Cloud Build and images stored in Artifact Registry. You plan to use Cloud Deploy to promote releases through three stages named test, preprod, and production. How can you ensure that only trusted images are allowed into production?

options.text: Use Cloud Armor in front of Cloud Run to inspect and block malicious requests
Enable Artifact Analysis scanning and encrypt images with Cloud Key Management Service before promotion
Enable Binary Authorization and require attestations signed by a trusted key before Cloud Deploy promotes the image to production
Store the container image as a secret in Secret Manager and pull it during deployment

questions.correct_text: Enable Binary Authorization and require attestations signed by a trusted key before Cloud Deploy promotes the image to production
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Enable Binary Authorization and require attestations signed by a trusted key before Cloud Deploy promotes the image to production.

Binary Authorization enforces deploy time controls by verifying that a container image carries the required attestations from trusted signers. With Cloud Run and Cloud Deploy you can gate promotions so that only images signed with approved keys are allowed to reach the production target, and any image without the necessary attestations is blocked.

You can configure Cloud Deploy to check Binary Authorization policy between test, preprod, and production. This creates a consistent release flow in which trust in the image is verified automatically before every promotion.

Use Cloud Armor in front of Cloud Run to inspect and block malicious requests is wrong because a web application firewall protects services at request time and does not verify the trust or provenance of container images before deployment.

Enable Artifact Analysis scanning and encrypt images with Cloud Key Management Service before promotion is wrong because vulnerability scanning and encryption improve security posture but do not enforce a deployment gate that blocks untrusted images from being promoted.

Store the container image as a secret in Secret Manager and pull it during deployment is wrong because Secret Manager is not designed to store or serve container images, and Cloud Run deployments pull images from registries such as Artifact Registry.

questions.question: You want to expose an internal web app for secure remote use, touching as little application code as possible and keeping the design lean. Which Google Cloud approach delivers that?

options.text: Cloud Endpoints
Identity-Aware Proxy fronted by an external HTTPS load balancer
Cloud VPN

questions.correct_text: Identity-Aware Proxy fronted by an external HTTPS load balancer
questions.explanation:
The right answer is Identity-Aware Proxy fronted by an external HTTPS load balancer, because it puts user-based access control in front of your web app, keeps the app private, demands little or no code change, and stays architecturally simple.

With this design you place the application behind a managed external HTTPS load balancer and enforce access using Google identities and IAM. Authentication happens at the edge, so the app usually needs no modification, and when it does need the user identity it can read the headers the service injects. Enabling it is straightforward: you turn it on for the backend service and grant access to particular users or groups, keeping the deployment clean.

Cloud Endpoints is aimed at API management rather than user-facing web access and typically requires adding a proxy or libraries, which means configuration and code changes. It is also deprecated, making it a less likely pick on newer exams.

Cloud VPN provides network-level connectivity between environments but adds no per-user authentication or application-aware access. Publishing a single internal web app securely with it would require extra components, raising complexity and failing the minimal-code-change goal.

questions.question: FieldLink Robotics runs its application on Google Cloud against a MySQL relational schema with heavy read and write traffic. The team wants automated backups and guidance for growing capacity, and while they can handle light maintenance, they do not want to operate the database from top to bottom. How should they deploy the database?

options.text: Spin up MySQL from Google Cloud Marketplace on Compute Engine and import the schema
Stand up Cloud Spanner and load the relational schema
Run MySQL on Cloud SQL and import the schema
Move the data into Firestore and host it there
Provision Bigtable and load the data into a new table

questions.correct_text: Run MySQL on Cloud SQL and import the schema
questions.explanation:
The right answer is to run MySQL on Cloud SQL and import the schema.

Cloud SQL is a fully managed MySQL service with automated backups and point-in-time recovery, high-availability configurations, read replicas to scale reads, and automatic storage growth. It surfaces performance metrics and Query Insights that aid capacity planning and right-sizing, and you can set maintenance windows and rely on automatic patching, which trims operational effort while still letting the team handle light maintenance.

Spinning up MySQL on Compute Engine leaves you running MySQL on VMs, meaning you own backups, replication, failover, patching, and capacity planning. That clashes with the requirement to avoid operating the database end to end.

Standing up Cloud Spanner brings in a different distributed relational service that is not MySQL compatible. It excels at global scale but would demand significant schema and application changes the scenario never asks for.

Moving the data into Firestore switches to a document store rather than a relational engine. It does not match a MySQL relational schema or support joins the same way and would require a major redesign.

Provisioning Bigtable uses a wide-column NoSQL database built for very low-latency key-value and time series workloads. It offers no relational SQL features or transactional behavior that MySQL applications expect.

questions.question: PineLoop is a neighborhood engagement app that helps residents coordinate meetups and lets small businesses reach nearby customers. The company plans to open service in additional continents, and investors expect a surge in traffic with a similar experience whether members are 25 or 14,000 miles away. PineLoop's stack combines an on premises data center with Google Cloud where APIs run on Compute Engine and a single instance MySQL database stores state. Releases currently require manual evening deployments, there is no centralized logging, and uptime signals are minimal which causes frequent alerts when APIs go silent. Leadership wants to shorten release cycles, adopt Google recommended SRE practices, and comply with regional regulations while scaling to support 15x more concurrent users. As the team prepares new regions, they need to increase API development velocity while keeping the QA environment stable and aligned with the QA team's feature acceptance criteria. Which approach should they take?

options.text: Require unit test coverage in every change and stop QA deployments unless all unit tests pass
Migrate the APIs to Cloud Run and use traffic splitting for QA to hold back traffic from new revisions when errors are detected
Integrate automated performance tests into the CI pipeline and block promotion to QA until all performance checks meet defined thresholds
Configure HTTP health checks for the QA environment and redeploy the APIs later if the environment is reported as unhealthy

questions.correct_text: Integrate automated performance tests into the CI pipeline and block promotion to QA until all performance checks meet defined thresholds
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Integrate automated performance tests into the CI pipeline and block promotion to QA until all performance checks meet defined thresholds.

This approach enforces performance gates before any build reaches QA, which keeps the QA environment stable and aligned with acceptance criteria. It catches latency and throughput regressions early, supporting the goal to scale for much higher concurrency while maintaining a consistent experience across regions. It also advances SRE practices by turning performance expectations into automated checks tied to promotion, which shortens release cycles and reduces noisy alerts later.

Require unit test coverage in every change and stop QA deployments unless all unit tests pass is insufficient because unit tests validate functional correctness rather than capacity, latency, or resource efficiency. Relying on unit tests alone will not protect QA from performance regressions and will not ensure readiness for the expected traffic surge.

Migrate the APIs to Cloud Run and use traffic splitting for QA to hold back traffic from new revisions when errors are detected addresses runtime platform and production canary techniques rather than stabilizing QA. Traffic splitting is designed for progressive delivery in production and does not create a deterministic QA gate that validates performance before promotion.

Configure HTTP health checks for the QA environment and redeploy the APIs later if the environment is reported as unhealthy is reactive and focuses on liveness checks rather than enforcing performance thresholds. This would allow problematic builds into QA and increase toil because redeploying after failures slows releases and does not prevent regressions upfront.
