questions.explanation_pt:
Otimizar o acesso aos dados e usar retentativas com exponential backoff e jitter está correto.

Um HTTP 429 RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED significa que o Firestore está limitando (throttling) as requisições durante picos. Adicionar jitter ao exponential backoff escalona as retentativas para que os clientes não as repitam todos em sincronia. Isso quebra o efeito de thundering herd, dá ao serviço espaço para se recuperar e ainda permite que as operações pendentes avancem.

Refinar seus padrões de acesso então reduz as chances de documentos quentes (hot documents) e atualizações de índice concentradas. Você pode distribuir leituras e escritas por meio de sharding de contadores, distribuição de chaves entre prefixos, agrupamento em lotes (batching) onde ajudar e remoção de índices desnecessários. Tais decisões de design reduzem a contenção e suavizam o tráfego, o que diminui diretamente a ocorrência de erros 429 durante picos.

Introduzir cache com Memorystore mantendo a política de retentativas atual é uma solução parcial: um cache pode aliviar parte da pressão de leitura, mas não faz nada pela vazão de escrita nem pelas retentativas sincronizadas. O comportamento de retentativa inalterado ainda pode produzir tempestades de retentativas alinhadas que disparam mais erros 429.

Solicitar um aumento de cota do Firestore e depender do exponential backoff padrão ignora a causa real dos erros 429 provocados por picos. Alguns limites não mudam com aumentos de cota, e o backoff sem jitter ainda pode sincronizar as retentativas dos clientes e prolongar o throttling.

Otimizar o acesso aos dados e usar retentativas com intervalo fixo mantém uma estratégia de retentativa ruim. Intervalos fixos tendem a alinhar os clientes, sobrecarregando repetidamente o Firestore durante as ondas de tráfego e produzindo respostas 429 contínuas.

questions.question: A Node.js web app your team is developing has to reach Google Cloud APIs while acting for users who have logged in with their Google Accounts. To obtain the tokens needed for those API requests, which authentication and authorization flow is the one to build?

options.text: Gather each user's Google username and password and forward the credentials to Google over HTTPS to obtain an access token
Put the app behind Identity-Aware Proxy and depend on IAP headers to call Google Cloud APIs as the signed in user
Use the OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow by redirecting to the Google consent screen then exchange the returned code on the server for access tokens used to call Google Cloud APIs
Save the short lived authorization code in a browser cookie and pass that code directly when calling Google Cloud APIs

questions.correct_text: Use the OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow by redirecting to the Google consent screen then exchange the returned code on the server for access tokens used to call Google Cloud APIs
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is Use the OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow by redirecting to the Google consent screen then exchange the returned code on the server for access tokens used to call Google Cloud APIs.

This is the standard web server flow for a Node.js backend that must act for signed in users. The app sends the user to the consent screen and gets back a one time authorization code, which the server exchanges for access and refresh tokens. Keeping that exchange on the server limits credential exposure and lets you refresh tokens later without prompting the user again, all while calling Google Cloud APIs with the scopes the user approved.

Gathering each user's Google username and password and forwarding the credentials to Google is wrong because Google prohibits third party apps from collecting Google Account passwords, and doing so violates security best practices. OAuth exists precisely to grant delegated access without sharing passwords.

Putting the app behind Identity-Aware Proxy and depending on IAP headers is wrong because IAP gates access to your app and can assert user identity to your backend, but it does not mint OAuth tokens for Google Cloud APIs. You still need a user OAuth flow to obtain those tokens for delegated calls.

Saving the short lived authorization code in a browser cookie and passing it directly is wrong because authorization codes are single use and short lived and must be exchanged on the server for tokens. They are not valid bearer credentials, and storing them in cookies raises the risk of interception.

Esse é o fluxo padrão de servidor web para um backend Node.js que precisa agir em nome de usuários autenticados. A aplicação envia o usuário para a tela de consentimento e recebe de volta um authorization code de uso único, que o servidor troca por access tokens e refresh tokens. Manter essa troca no servidor limita a exposição de credenciais e permite renovar os tokens depois sem pedir nova autorização ao usuário, tudo isso chamando as APIs do Google Cloud com os escopos que o usuário aprovou.

Coletar o nome de usuário e a senha do Google de cada usuário e encaminhar as credenciais ao Google está errado porque o Google proíbe que aplicativos de terceiros coletem senhas de Contas Google, e fazer isso viola as práticas recomendadas de segurança. O OAuth existe justamente para conceder acesso delegado sem compartilhar senhas.

Colocar a aplicação atrás do Identity-Aware Proxy e depender dos cabeçalhos do IAP está errado porque o IAP controla o acesso à sua aplicação e pode afirmar a identidade do usuário ao seu backend, mas não emite tokens OAuth para as APIs do Google Cloud. Você ainda precisa de um fluxo OAuth do usuário para obter esses tokens para chamadas delegadas.

Salvar o authorization code de curta duração em um cookie do navegador e passá-lo diretamente está errado porque os authorization codes são de uso único e de curta duração e devem ser trocados no servidor por tokens. Eles não são credenciais bearer válidas, e armazená-los em cookies aumenta o risco de interceptação.

questions.question: SummitPay runs a regional Google Kubernetes Engine cluster spanning three zones. You need to deploy a payment validation microservice that retains roughly 100 GiB of persistent data, survives individual pod restarts, and scales automatically with load without anyone intervening. How should you deploy it?

options.text: Run it as a DaemonSet with a Compute Engine persistent disk attached so each node hosts one pod
Create a Deployment that mounts a PersistentVolumeClaim and configure a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler to scale replicas based on metrics
Use a StatefulSet with hostPath volumes and depend on a Vertical Pod Autoscaler to adjust CPU and memory for pods
Deploy a Deployment backed by an emptyDir volume and attach a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler to absorb traffic spikes

questions.correct_text: Create a Deployment that mounts a PersistentVolumeClaim and configure a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler to scale replicas based on metrics
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Create a Deployment that mounts a PersistentVolumeClaim and configure a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler to scale replicas based on metrics. It is the only choice that delivers both durable storage across pod restarts and automatic, metric driven horizontal scaling.

A Deployment suits a microservice, and a PersistentVolumeClaim keeps the 100 GiB of data intact when individual pods restart. On GKE the claim can be backed by a Compute Engine persistent disk, and in a multi zone cluster a regional persistent disk raises availability while still attaching to one node at a time. The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler then adjusts replica count from CPU or custom metrics, so the service scales on its own with no manual steps.

Running it as a DaemonSet with a Compute Engine persistent disk so each node hosts one pod is wrong because a DaemonSet places one pod on every node, which suits node level agents rather than a demand driven microservice. It cannot autoscale replica count, and a single persistent disk cannot attach to many nodes at once.

Using a StatefulSet with hostPath volumes and a Vertical Pod Autoscaler does not meet the requirements because hostPath stores data on the node filesystem, so the data is lost if the pod reschedules elsewhere. VPA only tunes resource requests and limits and does not scale the number of replicas.

Deploying a Deployment backed by an emptyDir volume fails the persistence requirement because emptyDir is wiped when the pod restarts or moves. Even though HPA would scale replicas, the service would lose its 100 GiB of data on restart.

É a única escolha que entrega tanto armazenamento durável entre reinícios de pods quanto escalonamento horizontal automático e orientado por métricas.

Um Deployment se adequa a um microsserviço, e um PersistentVolumeClaim mantém os 100 GiB de dados intactos quando pods individuais reiniciam. No GKE, o claim pode ser respaldado por um persistent disk do Compute Engine, e em um cluster multizona um persistent disk regional aumenta a disponibilidade enquanto ainda se anexa a um nó por vez. O Horizontal Pod Autoscaler então ajusta a contagem de réplicas a partir de CPU ou métricas personalizadas, de modo que o serviço escala por conta própria, sem etapas manuais.

Executá-lo como um DaemonSet com um persistent disk do Compute Engine para que cada nó hospede um pod está errado porque um DaemonSet coloca um pod em cada nó, o que se adequa a agentes de nível de nó em vez de a um microsserviço orientado por demanda. Ele não pode autoescalar a contagem de réplicas, e um único persistent disk não pode se anexar a vários nós ao mesmo tempo.

Usar um StatefulSet com volumes hostPath e um Vertical Pod Autoscaler não atende aos requisitos porque o hostPath armazena dados no sistema de arquivos do nó, de modo que os dados são perdidos se o pod for reagendado em outro lugar. O VPA apenas ajusta as solicitações e limites de recursos e não escala o número de réplicas.

Implantar um Deployment respaldado por um volume emptyDir falha no requisito de persistência porque o emptyDir é apagado quando o pod reinicia ou é movido. Mesmo que o HPA escalasse as réplicas, o serviço perderia seus 100 GiB de dados ao reiniciar.

questions.question: Your team is relocating several backend services to Google Cloud. One of them runs today on a virtual machine and has no special operating system requirements. You authored a Dockerfile, built the container, and pushed the image to Artifact Registry. You want the simplest way to serve HTTP requests while cutting infrastructure and operational effort to a minimum. Which platform should you choose?

options.text: Compute Engine
Cloud Run
GKE Autopilot
App Engine flexible environment

questions.correct_text: Cloud Run
questions.explanation:
Cloud Run is the correct option.

Cloud Run is a fully managed platform for stateless containers that scales automatically with incoming HTTP traffic and hides servers and clusters entirely. It deploys straight from Artifact Registry with little configuration and hands you a secure HTTPS endpoint by default. That matches the goal of the simplest path that minimizes infrastructure and operations while serving HTTP requests.

Compute Engine would make you provision and manage virtual machines, set up instance groups and load balancing, and own patching and autoscaling. That is far more operational work than Cloud Run for a simple containerized service.

GKE Autopilot removes node management, yet you still manage Kubernetes objects such as Deployments and Services and must reason about cluster and networking concepts. For a straightforward HTTP container that is more complex than Cloud Run.

App Engine flexible environment can run containers but carries longer startup times and instance lifecycle management and is less streamlined for generic containers. For new container based HTTP workloads, Cloud Run is the simpler and more modern choice.

questions.question: An events company called EventBridge runs its API on Cloud Run, and that API must read from a relational database. The workload is read dominant at about 95% reads and can spike to roughly 18,000 requests per second. You want the lowest possible latency and solid throughput with the least operational overhead for the connection. Which Google Cloud data store should you pick, and how should Cloud Run connect to it?

options.text: Cloud SQL, connecting through the instance public IP with the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy
Cloud Bigtable, connecting with the Bigtable client libraries
Cloud SQL and connect over private IP using the Cloud SQL connector
Cloud Spanner, connecting with the Spanner client libraries

questions.correct_text: Cloud SQL and connect over private IP using the Cloud SQL connector
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Cloud SQL and connect over private IP using the Cloud SQL connector.

The workload needs a relational database, and Cloud SQL offers managed MySQL or PostgreSQL with minimal operational effort. A private IP keeps traffic on your VPC, avoiding public egress and typically trimming latency. The Cloud SQL connectors handle secure connections with IAM and TLS and simplify configuration on Cloud Run; from Cloud Run you attach a Serverless VPC Access connector to keep that path private and simple.

A read heavy profile at this request rate can be served by Cloud SQL when you right size the instance, manage connections in the application, and optionally add read replicas for extra read throughput. That meets the throughput goal while keeping the connection method simple and dependable.

Connecting Cloud SQL through the instance public IP with the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy does work, but it runs an extra process inside your container and depends on public IP networking. That adds overhead under heavy traffic and can raise latency compared with a private IP path managed by the connector.

Cloud Bigtable with the Bigtable client libraries does not fit because Bigtable is a NoSQL wide column store while the requirement calls for a relational database.

Cloud Spanner with the Spanner client libraries is a powerful relational service for large global workloads, but it is unnecessary here and brings higher cost and adoption complexity. Cloud SQL fits the latency and throughput needs with lower operational complexity.

A carga de trabalho precisa de um banco de dados relacional, e o Cloud SQL oferece MySQL ou PostgreSQL gerenciado com esforço operacional mínimo. Os Cloud SQL connectors lidam com conexões seguras usando IAM e TLS e simplificam a configuração no Cloud Run; a partir do Cloud Run, você anexa um conector de Serverless VPC Access para manter esse caminho privado e simples.

Conectar o Cloud SQL pelo public IP da instância com o Cloud SQL Auth Proxy funciona, mas executa um processo adicional dentro do seu contêiner e depende de rede com public IP. Isso adiciona sobrecarga sob tráfego intenso e pode aumentar a latência em comparação com um caminho de private IP gerenciado pelo connector.

Cloud Bigtable com as bibliotecas de cliente do Bigtable não se encaixa porque o Bigtable é um armazenamento NoSQL wide-column, enquanto o requisito pede um banco de dados relacional.

Cloud Spanner com as bibliotecas de cliente do Spanner é um serviço relacional poderoso para grandes cargas de trabalho globais, mas é desnecessário aqui e traz custo mais alto e complexidade de adoção. O Cloud SQL atende às necessidades de latência e vazão com menor complexidade operacional.

questions.question: InkBoard, a design studio, is launching a collaborative whiteboard service on Google Kubernetes Engine. It must hold user session state only while a session is active and drop it when the session ends, and that state must stay available even if application pods restart. Which storage approach should you choose?

options.text: Bigtable
Run Redis as an in-memory store in the GKE cluster
Cloud Firestore in Native mode
A Kubernetes emptyDir volume per pod

questions.correct_text: Run Redis as an in-memory store in the GKE cluster
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Run Redis as an in-memory store in the GKE cluster. It covers the need for short lived session data that can expire or be deleted at session end while staying reachable by new or restarted application pods, because the store lives outside the app pod lifecycle.

Running Redis in the cluster gives very low latency access and supports key expirations, so the application can set a TTL or explicitly delete keys when a session finishes. Because Redis runs as a shared service behind a Kubernetes Service, multiple pods read and write the same session data, and a restarted application pod simply reconnects to Redis and continues using the active session keys.

Bigtable is a durable wide column database for large analytical or time series workloads, not for ephemeral session data that should vanish at session end. It would keep data longer than needed and add needless operational and cost overhead.

Cloud Firestore in Native mode is a durable document database optimized for persistent data and offline synchronization. It does not offer the in memory semantics and simple key expiration model typically wanted for transient session state.

A Kubernetes emptyDir volume per pod holds data only for the pod's lifetime and is not shared across pods. The data is removed when the pod is deleted or rescheduled, which contradicts the requirement that session data survive pod restarts.

questions.explanation_pt:
A opção correta é executar o Redis como um armazenamento em memória (in-memory store) no cluster GKE. Ela atende à necessidade de dados de sessão de curta duração que podem expirar ou ser excluídos ao final da sessão, ao mesmo tempo em que permanecem acessíveis por pods da aplicação novos ou reiniciados, porque o armazenamento existe fora do ciclo de vida do pod da aplicação.

Executar o Redis no cluster oferece acesso de latência muito baixa e suporta expiração de chaves, de modo que a aplicação pode definir um TTL ou excluir chaves explicitamente quando uma sessão termina. Como o Redis roda como um serviço compartilhado por trás de um Kubernetes Service, múltiplos pods leem e gravam os mesmos dados de sessão, e um pod da aplicação reiniciado simplesmente se reconecta ao Redis e continua usando as chaves de sessão ativas.

O Bigtable é um banco de dados durável de colunas largas (wide column) para grandes cargas analíticas ou de séries temporais, e não para dados de sessão efêmeros que devem desaparecer ao final da sessão. Ele manteria os dados por mais tempo do que o necessário e adicionaria sobrecarga operacional e de custo desnecessária.

O Cloud Firestore no modo Native é um banco de dados de documentos durável otimizado para dados persistentes e sincronização offline. Ele não oferece a semântica em memória nem o modelo simples de expiração de chaves normalmente desejado para estado de sessão transitório.

Um volume emptyDir do Kubernetes por pod mantém dados apenas durante o tempo de vida do pod e não é compartilhado entre pods. Os dados são removidos quando o pod é excluído ou reagendado, o que contradiz o requisito de que os dados de sessão sobrevivam a reinícios de pods.

questions.question: Cobalt Imaging Labs is building a photo analysis workflow on Cloud Functions second generation. Because the chosen language has no Google Cloud client libraries, the code calls the Cloud Vision API directly over REST. The team wants those HTTP calls to authenticate as the function's attached service account and wants to avoid managing long lived keys. What is the correct way to authenticate these requests?

options.text: Create an API key for the Cloud Vision API and place it in the Authorization header
Request an OAuth 2.0 access token from the metadata server for the function's service account and include it as a Bearer token in the Authorization header
Store a service account JSON key file in Cloud Storage and load it at runtime to sign the REST requests
Obtain an identity token from the metadata server with the Vision API as the audience and place it in the Authorization header

questions.correct_text: Request an OAuth 2.0 access token from the metadata server for the function's service account and include it as a Bearer token in the Authorization header
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Request an OAuth 2.0 access token from the metadata server for the function's service account and include it as a Bearer token in the Authorization header.

This relies on the runtime's attached service account and the metadata server to mint short lived OAuth 2.0 access tokens, so rotation is automatic and you never handle long lived secrets. The token goes into the Authorization header as a Bearer token, and Google Cloud APIs such as Vision validate it against the service account's IAM permissions. It works even with no client library available, since you only need an HTTP call to the metadata server followed by the API call.

Creating an API key for the Cloud Vision API and placing it in the Authorization header is wrong because API keys are long lived and carry neither the function's identity nor its IAM permissions. API keys are not used in the Authorization header, and this would not meet the requirement to avoid managing long lived keys.

Storing a service account JSON key file in Cloud Storage and loading it at runtime is wrong because it requires creating and managing a long lived service account key. That raises risk and is unnecessary when the platform can supply short lived tokens through the metadata server.

Obtaining an identity token from the metadata server with the Vision API as the audience is wrong because identity tokens are for authenticating to services that accept OpenID Connect tokens, such as Cloud Run services and HTTP endpoints. Google APIs like Vision expect OAuth 2.0 access tokens, not identity tokens.

API keys não são usadas no cabeçalho Authorization, e isso não atenderia ao requisito de evitar o gerenciamento de chaves de longa duração.

Armazenar um arquivo de chave JSON de service account no Cloud Storage e carregá-lo em tempo de execução está errado porque exige criar e gerenciar uma chave de service account de longa duração. Isso aumenta o risco e é desnecessário quando a plataforma pode fornecer tokens de curta duração por meio do metadata server.

Obter um identity token do metadata server tendo a Vision API como audience está errado porque identity tokens servem para autenticar em serviços que aceitam tokens OpenID Connect, como serviços do Cloud Run e endpoints HTTP. APIs do Google como a Vision esperam tokens de acesso OAuth 2.0, não identity tokens.

questions.question: A media company keeps its asset files in a Cloud Storage bucket and applies two lifecycle rules to them. The first removes any object once it reaches 150 days, while the second shifts objects into Coldline at the 120 day mark. Suppose an object has now reached 160 days, making both rules eligible during the very same evaluation pass. Which action does Cloud Storage carry out?

options.text: The storage class is switched to Coldline first, and deletion is handled on a later run
The delete action is applied to the object
The most recently created rule takes precedence
The action producing the lowest monthly cost is chosen

questions.correct_text: The delete action is applied to the object
questions.explanation:
The correct option is The delete action is applied to the object.

Cloud Storage lifecycle management evaluates every matching rule for an object and, when several actions are eligible at once, applies the one with the highest precedence. Deletion holds the highest precedence, so when an object qualifies for both deletion and a storage class transition on the same run, the object is deleted and no transition happens. At 160 days both rules qualify, so the object is removed.

The storage class is switched to Coldline first with deletion on a later run is wrong because Cloud Storage does not transition the class when deletion is also eligible. The object is removed rather than transitioned.

The most recently created rule takes precedence is wrong because creation time does not factor into lifecycle evaluation. Precedence comes from the action type, not from rule order or recency.

The action producing the lowest monthly cost is wrong because lifecycle decisions are deterministic and are not cost driven. The platform applies the predefined precedence of actions rather than computing costs.

questions.explanation_pt:
A opção correta é que a ação de exclusão (delete) é aplicada ao objeto.

O gerenciamento de ciclo de vida (lifecycle management) do Cloud Storage avalia cada regra correspondente a um objeto e, quando várias ações estão elegíveis ao mesmo tempo, aplica aquela com a maior precedência. A exclusão tem a maior precedência, então quando um objeto se qualifica tanto para exclusão quanto para uma transição de storage class na mesma execução, o objeto é excluído e nenhuma transição ocorre. Aos 160 dias, ambas as regras se qualificam, portanto o objeto é removido.

A opção de que a storage class é alterada para Coldline primeiro, com a exclusão em uma execução posterior, está errada porque o Cloud Storage não faz a transição da class quando a exclusão também está elegível. O objeto é removido em vez de transicionado.

A opção de que a regra criada mais recentemente tem precedência está errada porque o momento de criação não influencia a avaliação do ciclo de vida. A precedência vem do tipo de ação, não da ordem ou da recência das regras.

A opção da ação que produz o menor custo mensal está errada porque as decisões de ciclo de vida são determinísticas e não são guiadas por custo. A plataforma aplica a precedência predefinida das ações em vez de calcular custos.

questions.question: At Lumina Broadcasting your team uses Cloud Build to build, test, and deploy a microservices application whose code lives in several repositories split between Cloud Source Repositories and GitHub. You need every push in any repository to kick off an automated build while leaving the multi repository layout intact. What should you configure?

options.text: Set Cloud Scheduler to invoke Cloud Build on a frequent schedule
Define a single Cloud Build trigger that uses a wildcard pattern spanning all repositories
Create a separate Cloud Build trigger for each repository
Use Pub/Sub to capture repository change events and route them to one trigger

questions.correct_text: Create a separate Cloud Build trigger for each repository
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Create a separate Cloud Build trigger for each repository.

A Cloud Build trigger is bound to a single repository and listens for events such as pushes or pull requests there. When the codebase spans many repositories, you create one trigger per repository so each push starts its own automated build without disturbing the multi repository layout. This works for both Cloud Source Repositories and GitHub and lets you keep branch or tag filters and build configurations tailored to each service.

Setting Cloud Scheduler to invoke Cloud Build on a frequent schedule is wrong because a scheduler fires on time based intervals rather than on push events, so it would miss commits and could launch needless builds when nothing changed.

Defining a single Cloud Build trigger with a wildcard spanning all repositories is wrong because wildcards in triggers filter branches or tags within one repository, and a trigger cannot span multiple repositories.

Using Pub/Sub to capture repository change events and route them to one trigger is wrong because this is not the native integration for source pushes from Cloud Source Repositories or GitHub. It would require custom eventing that alters the architecture and adds complexity without meeting the requirement as cleanly as per repository triggers.

Configurar o Cloud Scheduler para invocar o Cloud Build em um cronograma frequente está errado porque um scheduler dispara em intervalos baseados em tempo em vez de em eventos de push, então ele perderia commits e poderia lançar builds desnecessárias quando nada mudou.

Definir um único trigger do Cloud Build com um wildcard abrangendo todos os repositórios está errado porque wildcards em triggers filtram branches ou tags dentro de um repositório, e um trigger não pode abranger múltiplos repositórios.

Usar o Pub/Sub para capturar eventos de mudança de repositório e roteá-los para um único trigger está errado porque essa não é a integração nativa para pushes de código do Cloud Source Repositories ou do GitHub. questions.question: You are a backend developer at a ticketing platform that records purchases in Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL. The analytics team's heavy reporting queries are slowing the live checkout path. You must give analysts fresh order data without hurting production performance. What should you do?

options.text: Change the application to write each transaction to both Cloud SQL and Bigtable, and give the analytics team access to Bigtable
Spin up a cloned Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instance for analytics and run a job every 20 minutes to sync recent changes
Create a BigQuery dataset and use Datastream to continuously replicate selected Cloud SQL tables into BigQuery
Have Cloud Scheduler invoke a Cloud Function every 2 hours to export order data as CSV files to a Cloud Storage bucket

questions.correct_text: Create a BigQuery dataset and use Datastream to continuously replicate selected Cloud SQL tables into BigQuery
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Create a BigQuery dataset and use Datastream to continuously replicate selected Cloud SQL tables into BigQuery. It supplies fresh data for analytics while isolating production traffic, so reporting no longer slows checkouts.

This uses change data capture from Cloud SQL, streaming only inserts, updates, and deletes with low latency. Analysts then query a serverless warehouse that scales for heavy scans and joins, decoupling reporting compute from the transactional database. You get near real time updates without custom sync scripts and avoid contention on production tables.

Changing the application to write each transaction to both Cloud SQL and Bigtable is unsuitable because dual writes add complexity and risk to transactional integrity. Bigtable targets large scale key value and wide column workloads rather than interactive SQL analytics and ad hoc joins.

Spinning up a cloned Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instance with a 20 minute sync job is brittle and lagging. A clone is a point in time copy, and scheduled syncs add delay and operational overhead. Even kept current, it keeps analytics on a relational instance that does not scale like a warehouse and can still be resource intensive.

Having Cloud Scheduler invoke a Cloud Function every 2 hours to export CSV files yields data that is too stale, and CSV files have no query engine. This adds batch latency and forces extra pipelines before analysts can run efficient SQL.

Provisionar uma instância clonada do Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL com um job de sincronização de 20 minutos é frágil e atrasado. Um clone é uma cópia em um ponto no tempo, e sincronizações agendadas adicionam atraso e sobrecarga operacional. Mesmo mantido atualizado, ele mantém a análise em uma instância relacional que não escala como um warehouse e ainda pode consumir muitos recursos.

Fazer o Cloud Scheduler invocar uma Cloud Function a cada 2 horas para exportar arquivos CSV produz dados desatualizados demais, e arquivos CSV não têm um mecanismo de consulta (query engine). questions.question: Granite Insights hosts workloads on Google Cloud for one of its domains and needs centralized control over customer managed encryption keys for data at rest across multiple projects. The team requires key lifecycle management with automatic rotation every 90 days, and the keys must work with Cloud Storage, BigQuery, and Compute Engine disks. Which Google Cloud service should they adopt?

options.text: Cloud Storage
Cloud Key Management Service
Cloud HSM
Secret Manager

questions.correct_text: Cloud Key Management Service
questions.explanation:
Cloud Key Management Service is the correct answer.

Cloud Key Management Service centralizes the creation and governance of customer managed encryption keys across many projects. It handles key lifecycle management, including automatic rotation on a schedule you can set to 90 days, and it integrates directly with Cloud Storage, BigQuery, and Compute Engine disks so you can enforce CMEK consistently for data at rest across those services.

Cloud Storage is a storage service that can consume customer managed keys, but it is not the service that centrally creates, rotates, and manages keys across projects. It depends on an external key management system for CMEK, so on its own it cannot meet the centralized key control requirement.

Cloud HSM provides hardware security modules for hardware backed keys and acts as a protection level within KMS. By itself it does not deliver broad lifecycle management, rotation policies, or the seamless integrations across Cloud Storage, BigQuery, and Compute Engine; you still use KMS to manage and rotate keys.

Secret Manager stores application secrets such as API keys and passwords and is not used to manage CMEK for data at rest in storage systems or disks. It lacks the required integrations and automated key rotation for those services.

questions.question: Which Google Cloud logging storage approach satisfies a 6 month internal retention plus a 5 year compliance retention, keeps logs easy to search right after ingestion, and demands the least operational work?

options.text: A BigQuery export with a 5 year expiration
Cloud Logging custom bucket with 5 year retention
Cloud Storage with Bucket Lock
A Cloud Logging sink to Cloud Storage with lifecycle rules

questions.correct_text: Cloud Logging custom bucket with 5 year retention
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is Cloud Logging custom bucket with 5 year retention, because it keeps logs immediately searchable in Logs Explorer and lets you set a five year retention that covers compliance while still allowing easy search of the most recent six months with almost no operational effort.

With a custom log bucket set to five year retention, you configure retention on the managed bucket and continue using Logs Explorer for fast searches right after ingestion. This avoids export pipelines and extra storage systems, and you can shape access with log views to highlight the most recent six months for internal users while retaining the full five years for compliance.

A BigQuery export with a 5 year expiration is not ideal because it adds operational overhead to manage sinks, datasets, schemas, and cost, and it pulls routine searches out of Logs Explorer, which contradicts the easy search with minimal operations requirement.

Cloud Storage with Bucket Lock provides WORM retention but has no native log query capability. You would need extra tooling to search, increasing complexity and missing the easy search requirement.

A Cloud Logging sink to Cloud Storage with lifecycle rules can enforce deletion timing, but Cloud Storage offers no native log search. You would still load the data into another system to query it, raising operations and defeating the minimal operations goal.

O Cloud Storage com Bucket Lock fornece retenção WORM, mas não tem capacidade nativa de consulta de logs. Você precisaria de ferramentas adicionais para pesquisar, aumentando a complexidade e não atendendo ao requisito de pesquisa fácil.

Um sink do Cloud Logging para o Cloud Storage com regras de ciclo de vida pode impor o momento da exclusão, mas o Cloud Storage não oferece pesquisa nativa de logs. questions.question: An online ticketing platform runs its backend on Cloud Run, and a major release introduces a redesigned checkout that you worry may contain hidden defects. You want to direct only a small slice of live users to the new build at first while everyone else stays on the stable version, the rollout must avoid noticeable disruption, and you need to watch latency and error metrics for the new code during the trial. Which approach meets these goals?

options.text: Stand up an external HTTP load balancer with two serverless network endpoint groups pointing at separate Cloud Run services and weight a small slice of traffic to the service running the new build
Use Cloud Run revision traffic splitting to route about 10% of requests to the new revision and then raise the share as metrics remain healthy
Push the new build straight to production and keep watching logs for errors
Create a separate Cloud Run service for the new version and switch the domain mapping to it after testing

questions.correct_text: Use Cloud Run revision traffic splitting to route about 10% of requests to the new revision and then raise the share as metrics remain healthy
questions.explanation:
The correct approach is Use Cloud Run revision traffic splitting to route about 10% of requests to the new revision and then raise the share as metrics remain healthy.

Cloud Run can send a controlled percentage of requests to a new revision while the rest stay on the stable one. The service URL stays the same, so users notice no change and disruption is avoided. You can start at ten percent and ramp up gradually as latency and error rates stay healthy. Cloud Monitoring provides per revision metrics, so you can observe the canary's latency and error ratios independently before promoting it.

Standing up an external HTTP load balancer with two serverless network endpoint groups pointing at separate Cloud Run services is unnecessary and adds operational complexity. It splits traffic across different services rather than revisions, making it harder to attribute and compare metrics for a single code revision. Cloud Run already supports percentage based rollouts within one service, which better fits a low disruption canary.

Pushing the new build straight to production and watching logs does not satisfy sending only a fraction of users first and risks broad impact if defects exist. Logs alone do not give the clear per revision performance view needed for a safe trial.

Creating a separate Cloud Run service and switching the domain mapping after testing is a hard cutover rather than a gradual rollout. It can cause noticeable disruption at switchover and prevents side by side comparison of latency and errors between new and stable versions.

questions.explanation_pt:
A abordagem correta é usar a divisão de tráfego por revisão (revision traffic splitting) do Cloud Run para rotear cerca de 10% das solicitações para a nova revisão e, em seguida, aumentar a proporção conforme as métricas permanecerem saudáveis.

O Cloud Run pode enviar uma porcentagem controlada das solicitações para uma nova revisão enquanto o restante permanece na revisão estável. A URL do serviço permanece a mesma, então os usuários não percebem nenhuma mudança e a interrupção é evitada. Você pode começar com dez por cento e aumentar gradualmente conforme a latência e as taxas de erro se mantiverem saudáveis. O Cloud Monitoring fornece métricas por revisão, então você pode observar a latência e as proporções de erro do canary de forma independente antes de promovê-lo.

Montar um external HTTP load balancer com dois serverless network endpoint groups apontando para serviços separados do Cloud Run é desnecessário e adiciona complexidade operacional. Isso divide o tráfego entre serviços diferentes em vez de revisões, dificultando a atribuição e a comparação de métricas para uma única revisão de código. O Cloud Run já oferece suporte a lançamentos baseados em porcentagem dentro de um único serviço, o que se adapta melhor a um canary de baixa interrupção.

Enviar o novo build diretamente para produção e observar os logs não satisfaz o requisito de enviar apenas uma fração dos usuários primeiro e arrisca um impacto amplo se houver defeitos. Os logs por si só não fornecem a visão clara de desempenho por revisão necessária para um teste seguro.

Criar um serviço separado do Cloud Run e trocar o domain mapping após os testes é uma transição abrupta em vez de um lançamento gradual. Isso pode causar interrupção perceptível na troca e impede a comparação lado a lado de latência e erros entre as versões nova e estável.

questions.question: You run the subscription billing platform at Vellum Media on Google Cloud. Legal policy requires that certain application access logs be kept 9 months for internal reviews while a different set must be kept 4 years for regulatory audits. You want to reduce on-premises storage and keep the logs easy to search while minimizing operational effort. How should you store incoming logs on Google Cloud?

options.text: Place logs in a Cloud Storage bucket with a 4 year retention policy
Write logs to Cloud Storage with 9 month retention, then schedule transfers to a second bucket that retains them for another 3 years and 3 months
Use Cloud Logging with two log buckets that have custom retention settings and configure a sink to route the relevant logs to each bucket
Export all logs to BigQuery with partitioned tables and set a default table expiration of 4 years

questions.correct_text: Use Cloud Logging with two log buckets that have custom retention settings and configure a sink to route the relevant logs to each bucket
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is Use Cloud Logging with two log buckets that have custom retention settings and configure a sink to route the relevant logs to each bucket.

This lets you give one log bucket a retention of roughly nine months and a second bucket a retention of four years. Inclusion filters on sinks route only the required log streams to each destination, so each policy is enforced automatically. The logs stay in Cloud Logging, remaining indexed and searchable in Logs Explorer with minimal operational effort.

Placing logs in a single Cloud Storage bucket with a 4 year retention policy cannot satisfy two distinct retention requirements with one bucket, and Cloud Storage lacks the integrated search and querying experience for logs without extra tooling.

Writing logs to Cloud Storage with 9 month retention then transferring to a second bucket for another 3 years and 3 months adds needless complexity and does not keep logs easy to search. Scheduled transfers create copies and do not turn object storage into a log search solution, and managing two retention phases in object storage is operationally heavier and error prone.

Exporting all logs to BigQuery with partitioned tables and a single 4 year default expiration does not meet the nine month requirement because it assigns one four year expiration to everything. BigQuery is searchable, but you would need separate tables or datasets with different expirations, which is not what this option proposes.

questions.explanation_pt:
A resposta correta é usar o Cloud Logging com dois log buckets que têm configurações de retenção personalizadas e configurar um sink para rotear os logs relevantes para cada bucket.

Isso permite que você dê a um log bucket uma retenção de aproximadamente nove meses e a um segundo bucket uma retenção de quatro anos. Filtros de inclusão nos sinks roteiam apenas os fluxos de log necessários para cada destino, de modo que cada política é aplicada automaticamente. Os logs permanecem no Cloud Logging, continuando indexados e pesquisáveis no Logs Explorer com esforço operacional mínimo.

Colocar os logs em um único bucket do Cloud Storage com uma política de retenção de 4 anos não consegue satisfazer dois requisitos distintos de retenção com um único bucket, e o Cloud Storage carece da experiência integrada de pesquisa e consulta de logs sem ferramentas adicionais.

Gravar logs no Cloud Storage com retenção de 9 meses e depois transferir para um segundo bucket por mais 3 anos e 3 meses adiciona complexidade desnecessária e não mantém os logs fáceis de pesquisar. Transferências agendadas criam cópias e não transformam o armazenamento de objetos em uma solução de pesquisa de logs, e gerenciar duas fases de retenção no armazenamento de objetos é operacionalmente mais pesado e propenso a erros.

Exportar todos os logs para o BigQuery com tabelas particionadas e uma única expiração padrão de 4 anos não atende ao requisito de nove meses porque atribui uma expiração de quatro anos a tudo. O BigQuery é pesquisável, mas você precisaria de tabelas ou datasets separados com expirações diferentes, o que não é o que essa opção propõe.

questions.question: At a fintech startup named Tidelock Pay you run many microservices on Google Kubernetes Engine, each exposing a REST API through its own Kubernetes Service. You must ship new API versions without breaking current consumers and without disrupting third party integrations on your domain. You also want one managed entry point that routes to the right backend by versioned URL paths such as /v1 and /v2, following Google's recommended approach. How should you set up the client connection?

options.text: Adopt a Service Discovery system so clients pick the backend matching the requested version
Configure an Ingress with path rules that direct /v1 and /v2 traffic to their corresponding Services
Run a separate GKE cluster per API version and use DNS records to steer traffic to each versioned backend
Publish multiple API versions behind one Service and require the POST body to carry the version

questions.correct_text: Configure an Ingress with path rules that direct /v1 and /v2 traffic to their corresponding Services
questions.explanation:
The correct choice is Configure an Ingress with path rules that direct /v1 and /v2 traffic to their corresponding Services. This gives one managed entry point on your domain and routes each request to the right backend by versioned path.

On GKE an Ingress provisions a Google Cloud HTTP(S) Load Balancer that terminates TLS and supports path based routing. URL maps that match /v1 and /v2 forward traffic to the appropriate Kubernetes Services while clients keep using a single hostname. This follows Google guidance to version APIs in the URI and lets you introduce new versions without breaking existing consumers or changing client integrations.

Adopting a Service Discovery system so clients pick the backend is unsuitable because it pushes version selection to clients, increasing coupling and removing the single managed entry point on your domain.

Running a separate GKE cluster per API version with DNS steering adds needless complexity and cost, and DNS cannot route by URL path. It also brings propagation delays and makes controlled cutovers harder than edge path routing.

Publishing multiple API versions behind one Service and requiring the POST body to carry the version is wrong because load balancers match on host, path, and headers rather than request bodies. Versioning in the URI is the recommended approach, and body based routing would not work at the edge.

No GKE, um Ingress provisiona um Google Cloud HTTP(S) Load Balancer que termina TLS e oferece suporte a roteamento baseado em caminho. URL maps que correspondem a /v1 e /v2 encaminham o tráfego para os Services do Kubernetes apropriados enquanto os clientes continuam usando um único hostname. Isso segue a orientação do Google de versionar APIs na URI e permite introduzir novas versões sem quebrar os consumidores existentes ou alterar as integrações dos clientes.

Adotar um sistema de Service Discovery para que os clientes escolham o backend é inadequado porque transfere a seleção de versão para os clientes, aumentando o acoplamento e removendo o único ponto de entrada gerenciado no seu domínio.

Executar um cluster GKE separado por versão de API com direcionamento via DNS adiciona complexidade e custo desnecessários, e o DNS não consegue rotear por caminho de URL. Isso também traz atrasos de propagação e torna as transições controladas mais difíceis do que o roteamento de caminho na borda.

Publicar várias versões de API atrás de um único Service e exigir que o corpo do POST carregue a versão está errado porque os load balancers correspondem por host, caminho e cabeçalhos, e não por corpos de solicitação. Versionar na URI é a abordagem recomendada, e o roteamento baseado no corpo não funcionaria na borda.

questions.question: An internal background job hosted on Compute Engine produces events and sends them to Cloud Pub/Sub topics, but it has no reason to ever pull or read messages back. To keep the job's service account scoped to the bare minimum it requires for sending, which single predefined IAM role is the right one to bind to it?

options.text: Pub/Sub Viewer
Pub/Sub Subscriber
Pub/Sub Publisher
Pub/Sub Editor

questions.correct_text: Pub/Sub Publisher
questions.explanation:
Pub/Sub Publisher is the correct option.

This role grants exactly the permissions required to send messages to Pub/Sub topics and nothing more. Assigning it to the service account enforces least privilege because it includes publish permission to topics while withholding the ability to subscribe or to perform administrative actions such as creating or deleting topics and subscriptions.

Pub/Sub Viewer is read only and cannot publish to topics, so it does not meet the requirement.

Pub/Sub Subscriber is meant for pulling and acknowledging messages from subscriptions and does not allow publishing to topics.

Pub/Sub Editor is broader than necessary and bundles many management permissions, which breaks the least privilege goal.

questions.question: A retail analytics team needs to invoke external partner APIs that require mutual TLS on outbound calls, and it must also validate API keys and enforce request rate limits. The traffic path runs Web application, then Cloud Load Balancing, then a managed component, then the partner APIs. Which Google Cloud component belongs in that managed position to satisfy these needs?

options.text: Anthos Service Mesh
Cloud Armor
Cloud Endpoints
Cloud VPN

questions.correct_text: Cloud Endpoints
questions.explanation:
Cloud Endpoints is the correct choice for the managed component between Cloud Load Balancing and the partner APIs.

Cloud Endpoints validates API keys and enforces quota based rate limiting through Google Service Control, which covers the key validation and rate limiting needs. With ESPv2, Cloud Endpoints can also establish mutual TLS toward upstream services, so it can securely call external partner APIs that demand client certificates. It sits naturally behind Cloud Load Balancing and acts as a managed API proxy for outbound calls.

Anthos Service Mesh centers on service to service communication inside a mesh and is mainly for east west traffic within clusters or across services. It is not the right managed edge component to validate API keys for a web application or to front outbound calls to external partner APIs.

Cloud Armor is a web application firewall and DDoS protection service for inbound requests to your load balancer. It neither validates API keys for applications nor performs mutual TLS as a client to external partner APIs.

Cloud VPN provides network layer site to site connectivity. It offers no application level features such as API key validation, request rate limiting, or mutual TLS to specific external APIs.

questions.explanation_pt:
Cloud Endpoints é a escolha correta para o componente gerenciado entre o Cloud Load Balancing e as APIs do parceiro.

O Cloud Endpoints valida API keys e aplica rate limiting baseado em quotas por meio do Google Service Control, o que cobre as necessidades de validação de chaves e de rate limiting. Com o ESPv2, o Cloud Endpoints também pode estabelecer mutual TLS em direção a serviços upstream, então ele pode chamar com segurança APIs externas de parceiros que exigem certificados de cliente. Ele se posiciona naturalmente atrás do Cloud Load Balancing e atua como um proxy de API gerenciado para chamadas de saída.

O Anthos Service Mesh é centrado na comunicação service-to-service dentro de uma mesh e é voltado principalmente para tráfego east-west dentro de clusters ou entre serviços. Não é o componente de borda gerenciado adequado para validar API keys de uma aplicação web ou para fazer front de chamadas de saída a APIs externas de parceiros.

O Cloud Armor é um web application firewall e serviço de proteção contra DDoS para requisições de entrada ao seu load balancer. Ele não valida API keys de aplicações nem realiza mutual TLS como cliente para APIs externas de parceiros.

O Cloud VPN fornece conectividade site-to-site na camada de rede. Ele não oferece recursos no nível da aplicação, como validação de API keys, rate limiting de requisições ou mutual TLS para APIs externas específicas.

questions.question: Larkspur Robotics is unifying its build pipeline on Google Cloud and you must add an automated vulnerability scan for container images produced by Cloud Build. The findings need to integrate smoothly into the existing Google Cloud deployment workflow so other teams are not affected. Which approach should you take?

options.text: Connect your Aqua Security deployment with Artifact Registry to perform image scans
Turn on the Container Scanning capability in Artifact Registry and scan the images that Cloud Build pushes
Activate Binary Authorization and require an attestor that certifies the image has no vulnerabilities
Push the built images to Docker Hub and execute vulnerability scans there

questions.correct_text: Turn on the Container Scanning capability in Artifact Registry and scan the images that Cloud Build pushes
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Turn on the Container Scanning capability in Artifact Registry and scan the images that Cloud Build pushes.

This option leverages the native vulnerability scanning that triggers automatically when Cloud Build pushes images. Findings are stored within Google Cloud, surface in the console and APIs, and can be consumed by existing pipelines. It demands minimal pipeline changes and keeps artifacts in the same registry that teams already use, which avoids disruption.

The option Connect your Aqua Security deployment with Artifact Registry to perform image scans introduces a third party dependency and additional setup. It raises cost and operational burden and is not as seamless as the native scanner for teams already operating in Google Cloud.

The option Activate Binary Authorization and require an attestor that certifies the image has no vulnerabilities is not a scanner. It is a deploy time policy control that requires a separate scanning system to generate attestations, and it can prevent deployments when attestations are absent which risks disrupting teams.

The option Push the built images to Docker Hub and execute vulnerability scans there relocates artifacts outside Google Cloud and modifies existing workflows. It adds permission and egress concerns and does not blend cleanly with native deployment phases in Google Cloud.

questions.question: How should a web application whose users do not have Google accounts grant temporary read access to a single Cloud Storage object without exposing the bucket publicly?

options.text: Cloud CDN signed cookies
Assign allUsers the Storage Object Viewer role
Signed URL for Cloud Storage
Cloud Storage signed policy document

questions.correct_text: Signed URL for Cloud Storage
questions.explanation:
The right answer is Signed URL for Cloud Storage.

A Signed URL grants time bounded read access to a particular Cloud Storage object, and it works even when users have no Google accounts. You produce it from a service account or HMAC key and set an expiration so the link offers temporary access without making the bucket public.

The choice Cloud CDN signed cookies secures content delivered via Cloud CDN, and it does not grant direct access to a single Cloud Storage object unless you place a CDN in front of it, which is unnecessary here.

The choice Assign allUsers the Storage Object Viewer role would expose the object publicly to everyone and the access would not be temporary, so it does not satisfy the requirement.

The choice Cloud Storage signed policy document is intended for browser based uploads with HTML forms and it does not grant temporary read access to existing objects.

questions.question: Cedarcliff Analytics is implementing CI and CD on Google Cloud with Cloud Build and Artifact Registry. They want a build trigger that fires whenever a commit is pushed to the main branch of their repository. When you define this Cloud Build trigger, which field must be supplied for it to be created?

Source
Service account

questions.correct_text: Source

The Service account is optional at trigger creation because Cloud Build can use its default service account, and you can configure a specific one later.

The Substitution variables are optional values used in the build configuration, and they are not required to define a trigger.

questions.question: At Cascade Courier, a microservice on Google Kubernetes Engine reads from a Pub/Sub subscription and processes messages. The publish rate is very uneven, and roughly every 30 minutes there are brief surges where up to 65,000 messages arrive at once. You need to keep processing latency low by automatically adjusting the number of pods based on the backlog rather than CPU. Which GKE feature should you configure to adapt the workload automatically?

options.text: Vertical Pod Autoscaler in Auto mode
Horizontal Pod Autoscaler with an external metric from Cloud Monitoring
Cluster Autoscaler on the node pool
Horizontal Pod Autoscaler based on average CPU utilization

questions.correct_text: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler with an external metric from Cloud Monitoring
questions.explanation:
The right pick is Horizontal Pod Autoscaler with an external metric from Cloud Monitoring.

With the Cloud Monitoring adapter, the HPA can use the Pub/Sub subscription backlog metric to drive replica counts. You configure a target such as undelivered messages per pod, and the HPA rapidly increases pods during the 65,000 message bursts and scales them back down once the queue drains. This keeps processing latency low because scaling decisions are tied directly to backlog instead of resource usage.

Vertical Pod Autoscaler in Auto mode tunes CPU and memory requests for existing pods and may restart them to apply changes. It does not change the number of pods and cannot react to a Pub/Sub backlog metric, so it will not satisfy the requirement.

Cluster Autoscaler on the node pool only adds or removes nodes when pods are pending due to insufficient capacity. It does not determine how many replicas of your workload should run, and it cannot scale based on a queue backlog on its own.

Horizontal Pod Autoscaler based on average CPU utilization reacts to CPU rather than message backlog. A pull based Pub/Sub consumer can show low CPU while a sizable queue builds up, which would fail to keep latency low.

Você configura um alvo, como mensagens não entregues por pod, e o HPA aumenta rapidamente os pods durante os picos de 65.000 mensagens e os reduz novamente assim que a fila é esvaziada. Isso mantém a latência de processamento baixa porque as decisões de escalonamento estão diretamente ligadas ao backlog, e não ao uso de recursos.

questions.question: BrightTrail Apps is launching a public REST API on Google Cloud for its Android and iOS clients. Around 250 external developers at brighttrail-dev.io are expected to integrate within the first 75 days, and you must provide usage metrics while blocking any unauthorized calls. Which Google Cloud service configuration should you choose?

options.text: Cloud Endpoints with Identity and Access Management (IAM)
API Gateway integrated with Identity and Access Management (IAM)
API Gateway only
API Gateway with Cloud Logging

questions.correct_text: API Gateway integrated with Identity and Access Management (IAM)
questions.explanation:
The right pick is API Gateway integrated with Identity and Access Management (IAM). This combination delivers built in authentication and authorization to stop unauthorized calls, and it provides out of the box usage metrics through Cloud Monitoring and logs through Cloud Logging, which fits a public mobile API consumed by hundreds of external developers.

With API Gateway integrated with Identity and Access Management (IAM), you can require Google signed tokens and grant invoke permission only to the identities or groups you allow, such as a group containing developers from brighttrail-dev.io. This ensures only authenticated and authorized callers reach your backend, while the gateway automatically emits request counts, latency, and error metrics to Cloud Monitoring along with detailed request logs to Cloud Logging. The combination satisfies both the need for usage visibility and strong access control for a public API.

Cloud Endpoints with Identity and Access Management (IAM) is not the preferred option for new designs. Google recommends moving to API Gateway, and there is dedicated guidance to migrate. While it can enforce auth and provide metrics, it is an older solution and is less likely to be the best answer on current exams.

API Gateway only does not satisfy the need to prevent unauthorized calls because it lacks an authentication and authorization layer in this configuration. You must pair the gateway with IAM or another supported auth method to restrict access.

API Gateway with Cloud Logging emphasizes collecting logs, which helps troubleshooting, but logging by itself does not block unauthorized requests and is not a replacement for authentication and authorization. You still need IAM or another auth control to secure the API, and metrics need Cloud Monitoring rather than logs alone.

questions.question: harborbay.io is preparing to launch a new checkout service on Google Kubernetes Engine ahead of a holiday promotion and expects up to 65,000 concurrent sessions, and the team wants to tune autoscaling and verify stability under expected demand; what is the primary purpose of running load tests in this situation?

options.text: Assess the visual layout and branding of the site across devices
Spend more on cloud services to qualify for higher committed use discounts
Verify that the application can sustain heavy concurrent traffic without failures or unacceptable latency
Cloud Profiler

questions.correct_text: Verify that the application can sustain heavy concurrent traffic without failures or unacceptable latency
questions.explanation:
The right answer is Verify that the application can sustain heavy concurrent traffic without failures or unacceptable latency.

Load testing confirms the service can meet expected concurrency and latency goals at peak demand and that autoscaling on Google Kubernetes Engine scales pods and nodes quickly enough to maintain service level objectives. It validates that error rates remain low and response times stay acceptable through scale up and scale down events.

These tests also surface bottlenecks in CPU, memory, I/O, database connections, or network limits so the team can right size container resources and tune the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler and Cluster Autoscaler accordingly. This reduces the chance of instability during the holiday promotion.

The option Assess the visual layout and branding of the site across devices is unrelated because visual and cross device checks examine presentation and rendering rather than system behavior under heavy concurrent load.

The option Spend more on cloud services to qualify for higher committed use discounts is a purchasing concern and not a technical objective of performance testing.

The option Cloud Profiler is a continuous profiling service that helps analyze CPU and memory usage in running applications. It does not generate traffic or validate scalability, which means it is not the primary purpose of running load tests.

questions.question: Your public application for brightorbit.io runs on Google Cloud. options.text: Firebase Authentication
Identity-Aware Proxy
Identity Platform
Identity and Access Management

questions.correct_text: Identity Platform
questions.explanation:

This service is a fully managed customer identity and access management product on Google Cloud that supports multifactor authentication for end users. It lets you add sign in and MFA to a public app without building and operating a custom identity stack. It also offers enterprise capabilities such as standards based federation, risk controls, and support that help meet compliance and business policy requirements on a tight timeline.

Firebase Authentication targets app developer use cases, and while it can handle end user authentication, it is not the enterprise CIAM service on Google Cloud designed for compliance driven customer identity scenarios with the operational guarantees many organizations require.

Identity-Aware Proxy protects access to applications for your workforce and depends on user identities to gate access to internal or controlled apps. It is not intended to be the customer identity solution for public user sign in or MFA for your external users.

Identity and Access Management controls permissions to Google Cloud resources for project members and service accounts. It does not provide customer authentication or multifactor sign in flows for a public application.

questions.question: Brookdale Outfitters is rolling out a checkout service on Google Kubernetes Engine and needs each pod that is being terminated during a rolling update to stop receiving new traffic and finish any in flight work before it is removed. Which practice should they adopt to ensure a graceful shutdown of each pod?

options.text: Define a Pod Disruption Budget for the Deployment
Set terminationGracePeriodSeconds to allow sufficient time for graceful shutdown
Use a liveness probe
Add a readiness probe

questions.correct_text: Set terminationGracePeriodSeconds to allow sufficient time for graceful shutdown
questions.explanation:
The right answer is Set terminationGracePeriodSeconds to allow sufficient time for graceful shutdown.

When a Pod is terminated, Kubernetes sends SIGTERM to the containers and waits for the duration you set in terminationGracePeriodSeconds before sending SIGKILL. This grace period lets the application stop accepting new work and finish any in flight requests during a rolling update. You can also pair this with a preStop hook or signal handling so the service drains cleanly while terminationGracePeriodSeconds guarantees there is enough time to complete the shutdown.

Define a Pod Disruption Budget for the Deployment is not correct because a disruption budget only limits how many Pods can be voluntarily disrupted at one time and it does not control the shutdown behavior of an individual Pod or grant time to finish in flight work.

Use a liveness probe is not correct because liveness triggers restarts when a container is unhealthy and it does not manage graceful termination or traffic draining during updates.

Add a readiness probe alone is not correct because that probe only controls whether new traffic is sent to a Pod and it does not ensure the Pod gets enough time to finish existing requests without terminationGracePeriodSeconds.

Você também pode combinar isso com um hook preStop ou tratamento de sinais, para que o serviço seja drenado de forma limpa, enquanto o terminationGracePeriodSeconds garante que haja tempo suficiente para concluir o encerramento.

questions.question: Marlowe Logistics is migrating its event tracking workload to Cloud Bigtable, and the team needs row keys that operators can easily read while also spreading traffic evenly across the cluster to prevent hotspots, so which row key strategy should they choose?

options.text: Use a truncated SHA256 of the full row contents as the row key
Build row keys by joining several human readable attributes and place the most high cardinality attribute first
Use a Unix epoch timestamp in microseconds as the entire row key
Use monotonically increasing integers as the primary key for each new row

questions.correct_text: Build row keys by joining several human readable attributes and place the most high cardinality attribute first
questions.explanation:
The right answer is Build row keys by joining several human readable attributes and place the most high cardinality attribute first.

This approach matches how Cloud Bigtable stores data because rows are sorted lexicographically by the key. Placing a high cardinality attribute first spreads keys across tablets, which evens out write and read traffic and reduces hotspots. Joining human readable attributes keeps the key understandable for operators while still letting you order the fields to support common range scans and locality.

Use a truncated SHA256 of the full row contents as the row key would distribute keys well, but it fails the human readable requirement and removes the ability to perform natural range scans. Tying the key to the entire row contents is also risky because any change to the data would change the key.

Use a Unix epoch timestamp in microseconds as the entire row key produces a strictly increasing key that concentrates writes on the most recent tablet and causes hotspots. It also does not naturally group related entities for efficient scans.

Use monotonically increasing integers as the primary key for each new row has the same hotspot problem because inserts always land at the end of the keyspace.

Juntar atributos legíveis por humanos mantém a chave compreensível para operadores, ao mesmo tempo em que permite ordenar os campos para apoiar range scans comuns e localidade.

Usar um timestamp Unix epoch em microssegundos como a row key inteira produz uma chave estritamente crescente que concentra as escritas no tablet mais recente e causa hotspots. Além disso, não agrupa naturalmente entidades relacionadas para scans eficientes.

Usar inteiros monotonicamente crescentes como chave primária para cada nova linha tem o mesmo problema de hotspot, porque as inserções sempre caem no final do keyspace.

questions.question: Crestline Analytics is moving its microservices onto Google Kubernetes Engine with container images in Artifact Registry, and a Cloud Build pipeline pushes about 25 images per day. The security team requires that workloads with known critical CVEs never reach any cluster. What should you implement in the build workflow and at deployment time to enforce this?

options.text: Run Web Security Scanner against the staging service URL and block the release if critical issues appear while using Binary Authorization to gate the rollout

Turn on Artifact Analysis scanning in Artifact Registry, then have Cloud Build query the Container Analysis API for critical findings and create an attestation that is required by a Binary Authorization policy before GKE deployment
Review vulnerability reports for images in the Cloud Console and have a release engineer manually create an attestation that Binary Authorization will require before deployment
Deploy an OPA Gatekeeper admission policy in the clusters that denies images unless they carry a specific label indicating no critical CVEs

questions.correct_text: Turn on Artifact Analysis scanning in Artifact Registry, then have Cloud Build query the Container Analysis API for critical findings and create an attestation that is required by a Binary Authorization policy before GKE deployment
questions.explanation:
The right pick is Turn on Artifact Analysis scanning in Artifact Registry, then have Cloud Build query the Container Analysis API for critical findings and create an attestation that is required by a Binary Authorization policy before GKE deployment.

This approach automates vulnerability detection during the build stage and enforces admission control at deploy time. Artifact Registry vulnerability scanning produces findings in Container Analysis that include severity and package details. A build step can query for critical issues and fail early or move on to create a signed attestation only when the image is clean. A Binary Authorization policy on the clusters requires that attestation, which prevents images with critical CVEs from being admitted. This forms a reliable and scalable gate that fits a pipeline that pushes dozens of images daily.

Run Web Security Scanner against the staging service URL and block the release if critical issues appear while using Binary Authorization to gate the rollout is wrong because Web Security Scanner tests web application endpoints after deployment rather than image CVEs before deployment. It does not provide the authoritative image vulnerability metadata needed for admission control, and it does not integrate to create attestations bound to container images.

Review vulnerability reports for images in the Cloud Console and have a release engineer manually create an attestation that Binary Authorization will require before deployment is wrong because a manual process is error prone and does not scale to frequent image pushes. The requirement demands a reliable automated gate, so human review could let vulnerable images slip through.

Deploy an OPA Gatekeeper admission policy in the clusters that denies images unless they carry a specific label indicating no critical CVEs is wrong because labels can be forged or omitted and do not represent verified vulnerability status. Gatekeeper rules on labels alone cannot authoritatively evaluate CVE findings. Binary Authorization with attestations based on Container Analysis data offers a stronger integration purpose built for this control.

Essa abordagem automatiza a detecção de vulnerabilidades durante a etapa de build e impõe controle de admissão no momento da implantação. Uma etapa de build pode consultar problemas críticos e falhar cedo, ou prosseguir para criar uma attestation assinada apenas quando a imagem estiver limpa. Ele não fornece os metadados autoritativos de vulnerabilidade de imagem necessários para o controle de admissão e não se integra para criar attestations vinculadas às imagens de contêiner.

Revisar relatórios de vulnerabilidade de imagens no Cloud Console e fazer um release engineer criar manualmente uma attestation que o Binary Authorization exigirá antes da implantação está errado, porque um processo manual é propenso a erros e não escala para envios frequentes de imagens. O Binary Authorization com attestations baseadas em dados do Container Analysis oferece uma integração mais forte, criada especificamente para esse controle.

questions.question: A team at Larkspur Analytics is building an internal reporting dashboard for roughly 800 employees, and the organization manages identities in Google Workspace. You want to deploy the application on Google Cloud with minimal operations overhead and restrict access to people signed in with their company Google accounts, and you prefer a serverless platform that integrates with Google identity. Which actions should you take to meet these requirements?

options.text: Provision a managed instance group on Compute Engine and run the web app behind an HTTP load balancer
Package the application into a container image and run it on Cloud Run
Configure Identity Aware Proxy and grant roles/iap.tunnelResourceAccessor to the employee group
Protect the service with Identity Aware Proxy and grant roles/iap.httpsResourceAccessor to the workforce group
Build a custom sign in flow using a Cloud SQL table of users and password hashes

questions.correct_text: Package the application into a container image and run it on Cloud Run | Protect the service with Identity Aware Proxy and grant roles/iap.httpsResourceAccessor to the workforce group
questions.explanation:
The correct actions are Package the application into a container image and run it on Cloud Run and Protect the service with Identity Aware Proxy and grant roles/iap.httpsResourceAccessor to the workforce group.

Packaging the application into a container image and running it on Cloud Run meets the serverless and minimal operations requirement, since the platform handles scaling, patching, and availability for you. It comfortably serves an internal audience of this size and integrates cleanly with Google identity controls for secure access.

Protecting the service with Identity Aware Proxy and granting roles/iap.httpsResourceAccessor to the workforce group ensures only users signed in with company Google accounts can reach the app. IAP enforces Google identity in front of HTTPS resources, and assigning the workforce group the HTTPS IAP access role provides the intended gated access for employees.

Provisioning a managed instance group on Compute Engine behind an HTTP load balancer is a poor fit because it is not serverless and adds operational work to manage instances, images, autoscaling, and patching. It also does not by itself integrate with Google identity for per user access control.

Configuring Identity Aware Proxy and granting roles/iap.tunnelResourceAccessor to the employee group is wrong because that role applies to IAP TCP forwarding rather than to web applications over HTTPS, so it would not grant access to an IAP protected HTTPS endpoint.

Building a custom sign in flow with a Cloud SQL table of users and password hashes contradicts the requirement to integrate with Google identity and increases operational and security burden. It needlessly duplicates identity management already provided by Google Workspace and IAP.

Provisionar um managed instance group no Compute Engine atrás de um HTTP load balancer é uma escolha ruim, porque não é serverless e adiciona trabalho operacional para gerenciar instâncias, imagens, autoscaling e patching. Além disso, por si só, não se integra com a identidade Google para controle de acesso por usuário.
