A integração certa é usar as bibliotecas oficiais de cliente do Cloud Pub/Sub do Google Cloud.

Elas proporcionam o comportamento de ponta a ponta mais rápido porque, internamente, dependem de streaming gRPC eficiente e mantêm conexões de longa duração. Elas tratam de batching automático e controle de fluxo, publishers e subscribers assíncronos, pré-busca de mensagens e retentativas inteligentes com backoff. Em conjunto, isso reduz a sobrecarga por mensagem e as idas e voltas, diminuindo a latência tanto no envio quanto no recebimento.

Acessar os endpoints REST diretamente a cada chamada está errado, porque o HTTP síncrono adiciona sobrecarga de conexão e serialização e o modelo de pull REST aumenta a latência, e você abre mão do batching e do streaming do lado do cliente que mantêm o throughput alto e a latência baixa.

Invocar o gcloud a partir da aplicação está errado, porque o gcloud é uma ferramenta de administração e scripting. Iniciar um processo por operação é pesado e inadequado para um caminho de baixa latência ou alto throughput.

Gerar e usar stubs gRPC brutos está errado, porque, embora stubs brutos possam ser rápidos, você teria que reimplementar batching, controle de fluxo, concorrência de streaming-pull, lógica de retentativas e gerenciamento de conexões. As bibliotecas oficiais já implementam e ajustam tudo isso.

options.text: Have the service call the Cloud Logging API and stuff cluster and node values into each JSON record
Hand-install Fluent Bit as a DaemonSet that tails /var/log/containers and forwards entries to Cloud Logging
Enable Cloud Operations for GKE so its built-in collector forwards stdout logs to Cloud Logging with Kubernetes metadata
Attach a persistent disk to every node, write logs there, and upload the files to Cloud Logging with a custom script

questions.question: Cinder Outfitters runs a Kotlin service on a GKE Standard cluster, and it writes structured JSON to standard output. You need those logs in Cloud Logging carrying Kubernetes metadata such as cluster name and node name, and you must achieve it without editing the application code. What should you do?
questions.correct_text: Enable Cloud Operations for GKE so its built-in collector forwards stdout logs to Cloud Logging with Kubernetes metadata
questions.explanation:
You should enable Cloud Operations for GKE so its built-in collector forwards stdout logs to Cloud Logging with Kubernetes metadata.

Enabling it activates the managed logging pipeline on the cluster. The collector tails container standard output from the node file system and delivers entries to Cloud Logging, enriching each one with Kubernetes resource metadata such as cluster name, node name, namespace, pod, and container, meeting the requirement with no application code change.

When the service writes structured JSON to standard output, Cloud Operations for GKE forwards those lines to Cloud Logging, which parses them as structured logs. The JSON becomes the jsonPayload while the Kubernetes metadata remains available as resource labels and fields, keeping queries and filters simple.

Having the service call the Cloud Logging API and embed cluster and node values is wrong, because it requires code changes and duplicates metadata the platform already supplies, risking inconsistent or missing labels next to the automatic enrichment.

Hand-installing Fluent Bit as a DaemonSet is unnecessary on GKE, since the managed collector ships when you enable Cloud Operations for GKE; running your own adds overhead and configuration to map metadata the managed solution already handles.

Attaching a persistent disk per node and uploading files with a custom script ignores container logging best practices, adding complexity and cost, risking data loss on node changes, omitting Kubernetes metadata, and shifting log shipping into custom scripts instead of the supported managed pipeline.

O coletor lê a saída padrão (standard output) dos contêineres a partir do sistema de arquivos do nó e entrega as entradas ao Cloud Logging, enriquecendo cada uma com metadados de recursos do Kubernetes, como nome do cluster, nome do nó, namespace, pod e contêiner, atendendo ao requisito sem nenhuma alteração no código da aplicação.

Quando o serviço escreve JSON estruturado na saída padrão, o Cloud Operations for GKE encaminha essas linhas para o Cloud Logging, que as interpreta como logs estruturados. O JSON se torna o jsonPayload, enquanto os metadados do Kubernetes permanecem disponíveis como labels e campos de recurso, mantendo consultas e filtros simples.

Fazer o serviço chamar a API do Cloud Logging e incorporar os valores de cluster e nó está errado, porque exige alterações de código e duplica metadados que a plataforma já fornece, arriscando labels inconsistentes ou ausentes ao lado do enriquecimento automático.

Instalar manualmente o Fluent Bit como um DaemonSet é desnecessário no GKE, já que o coletor gerenciado vem incluído quando você habilita o Cloud Operations for GKE; executar o seu próprio adiciona sobrecarga e configuração para mapear metadados que a solução gerenciada já trata.

Anexar um disco persistente por nó e enviar arquivos com um script personalizado ignora as melhores práticas de logging de contêineres, adicionando complexidade e custo, arriscando perda de dados em mudanças de nó, omitindo metadados do Kubernetes e transferindo o envio de logs para scripts personalizados em vez do pipeline gerenciado suportado.

options.text: Pub/Sub as primary store

questions.question: For real-time collaborative editing that must propagate updates to all clients quickly and scale to about twenty thousand simultaneous editors, which Google Cloud data store should you choose?
questions.correct_text: Firestore Native with snapshot listeners
questions.explanation:
Choose Firestore Native with snapshot listeners.

Firestore ships built-in real-time change streams through snapshot listeners that push updates to clients the moment data changes. As a fully managed document database it scales horizontally by itself and sustains large numbers of concurrent connections, which suits collaborative editing where many editors need low-latency updates and consistent document state.

Pub/Sub as a primary store is wrong, because it is messaging rather than a database, offering no queries and no persistent document model for collaborative editing, and it is not meant to be the system of record.

Cloud SQL with polling is wrong, because polling injects latency and load and never delivers instant push updates, and handling many connections with frequent polls at this scale is inefficient and falls short of strict real-time collaboration.

Memorystore for Redis as a primary store is wrong, because Redis in Memorystore is an in-memory cache rather than a durable primary store, lacking the native real-time document synchronization model and durability guarantees these workloads usually need.

Usar o Pub/Sub como armazenamento primário está errado, porque ele é mensageria e não um banco de dados, não oferecendo consultas nem um modelo de documento persistente para edição colaborativa, e não foi feito para ser o sistema de registro.

Memorystore for Redis como armazenamento primário está errado, porque o Redis no Memorystore é um cache em memória e não um armazenamento primário durável, faltando o modelo nativo de sincronização de documentos em tempo real e as garantias de durabilidade que essas cargas de trabalho normalmente precisam.

options.text: Prefix the key with a two-byte hash of cust_id and then append event_time
Build a composite row key of cust_id followed by event_time
Build a composite row key of event_time followed by cust_id
Use cust_id as the only row key component

questions.question: Migrating a payments ledger from MySQL to Cloud Bigtable, your team at Vellum Payments must settle on an effective row key. In MySQL the table is Customer_Transactions, with columns cust_id INT, event_time DATETIME, txn_type STRING, and amount DECIMAL(19,2), and the composite primary key is cust_id then event_time. You want a Bigtable row key that preserves each customer's activity in chronological order while reducing the risk of hot spotting. Which row key should you choose?
questions.correct_text: Build a composite row key of cust_id followed by event_time
questions.explanation:
The row key to choose is a composite of cust_id followed by event_time.

This aligns with Bigtable row-key best practices. Because Bigtable stores rows in lexicographic order, leading with the customer identifier keeps all of a customer's transactions together, and appending the event time orders them within that customer, making scans by customer and by time efficient. Since customers have different leading keys, write load spreads across tablets, which lowers hot-spotting risk compared with a design that starts with a globally increasing value.

Prefixing with a two-byte hash of cust_id and appending event_time is unsuitable, because it removes the real customer identifier from the key space, interleaving customers under the same short hash, blocking efficient single-customer range scans, and not guaranteeing per-customer time order.

Leading with event_time then cust_id will likely hot spot, because new events share a monotonically increasing leading key, and it scatters a customer's transactions across many ranges rather than keeping them contiguous.

Using cust_id alone collapses a customer's transactions into one very large row, a poor fit for per-event access and time-range scans, with no natural ordering of individual events and a risk of uneven load on large rows.

questions.explanation_pt:
A row key a escolher é uma composição de cust_id seguido de event_time.

Isso está alinhado com as melhores práticas de row-key do Bigtable. Como o Bigtable armazena as linhas em ordem lexicográfica, iniciar com o identificador do cliente mantém todas as transações de um cliente juntas, e anexar o tempo do evento as ordena dentro daquele cliente, tornando eficientes as varreduras por cliente e por tempo. Como clientes têm chaves iniciais diferentes, a carga de escrita se espalha entre os tablets, o que reduz o risco de hot-spotting em comparação com um design que começa com um valor globalmente crescente.

Prefixar com um hash de dois bytes do cust_id e anexar event_time é inadequado, porque remove o identificador real do cliente do espaço de chaves, intercalando clientes sob o mesmo hash curto, bloqueando varreduras de intervalo eficientes para um único cliente e não garantindo a ordem temporal por cliente.

Iniciar com event_time e depois cust_id provavelmente causará hot spot, porque novos eventos compartilham uma chave inicial monotonicamente crescente, e isso espalha as transações de um cliente por muitos intervalos em vez de mantê-las contíguas.

Usar cust_id sozinho colapsa as transações de um cliente em uma única linha muito grande, uma má opção para acesso por evento e varreduras por intervalo de tempo, sem ordenação natural dos eventos individuais e com risco de carga desigual em linhas grandes.

options.text: Cloud SQL
Cloud Bigtable

questions.question: Northwind Athletics is launching a social feed service with intense reads and writes on user profiles and posts, peaking near 50,000 writes per second across two regions. Whichever region serves a request, users must immediately see the latest committed change right after it is made. Which Google Cloud storage service meets these consistency and scale demands?
questions.correct_text: Cloud Spanner
questions.explanation:
Cloud Spanner is the choice, since it provides global external strong consistency together with horizontally scalable throughput, so users read the latest committed update from any region even at peaks near 50,000 writes per second.

Spanner replicates synchronously across multi-region configurations and uses a globally synchronized clock to guarantee read-after-write consistency from any region, and it scales linearly as you add processing units or nodes, sustaining very high read and write rates with transactional guarantees intact.

Cloud SQL uses a single primary with asynchronous replicas for cross-region reads, so a user elsewhere may not see a fresh write right away, and it does not scale to sustained tens of thousands of writes per second without heavy sharding and complexity.

Cloud Bigtable handles enormous throughput, but its multi-cluster replication is eventually consistent across regions, so it cannot guarantee immediate cross-region read-after-write, and it lacks the multi-row transactions strongly consistent profile and feed updates often need.

Cloud Firestore offers strong consistency for single-document reads and queries but is not intended for very high sustained multi-region write rates at this scale, and its index and hot-spot limits can constrain it, while it also lacks global relational transactions for cross-document consistency a feed often requires.

O Spanner replica de forma síncrona entre configurações multi-região e usa um relógio sincronizado globalmente para garantir consistência de leitura após escrita (read-after-write) de qualquer região, e escala linearmente conforme você adiciona processing units ou nós, sustentando taxas de leitura e escrita muito altas com as garantias transacionais intactas.

Cloud SQL usa um único primário com réplicas assíncronas para leituras entre regiões, então um usuário em outro lugar pode não ver uma escrita recente imediatamente, e ele não escala para dezenas de milhares de escritas por segundo de forma sustentada sem sharding pesado e complexidade.

Cloud Bigtable lida com throughput enorme, mas sua replicação multi-cluster é eventualmente consistente entre regiões, então não pode garantir leitura após escrita imediata entre regiões, e lhe falta o perfil de transações multi-linha fortemente consistentes que atualizações de feed costumam exigir.

Cloud Firestore oferece consistência forte para leituras e consultas de documento único, mas não foi feito para taxas de escrita multi-região muito altas e sustentadas nessa escala, e seus limites de índice e hot-spot podem restringi-lo, além de lhe faltarem transações relacionais globais para consistência entre documentos que um feed frequentemente requer.

questions.question: Your team at a logistics startup runs production workloads on Google Kubernetes Engine, and you must prevent any deployment unless the container image originates from your approved registry and meets your organization's vulnerability policy. Which Google Cloud service can enforce an admission policy so only trusted images are allowed to run in the cluster?

options.text: Artifact Registry vulnerability scanning
Cloud Identity-Aware Proxy
Binary Authorization
Cloud Audit Logs

questions.correct_text: Binary Authorization
questions.explanation:
The right pick is Binary Authorization because it provides an admission controller for Google Kubernetes Engine that enforces policies so only trusted images from approved registries and with required attestations are allowed to deploy.

Binary Authorization lets you define a policy that restricts images to specific registries and requires attestations such as vulnerability checks before admission. It evaluates each deployment request at admission time and blocks any image that does not meet your organization's requirements. It integrates with scanning results so you can enforce vulnerability thresholds rather than only detecting issues.

Artifact Registry vulnerability scanning identifies vulnerabilities in images stored in the registry, yet it does not act as an admission controller in the cluster. On its own it cannot block pods from being deployed.

Cloud Identity-Aware Proxy controls access to web applications and resources behind HTTPS. It does not evaluate container images or enforce Kubernetes admission policies.

Cloud Audit Logs records administrative and data access events for auditing. It provides visibility but cannot prevent deployments or enforce policy at admission time.

Ele avalia cada solicitação de implantação no momento da admissão e bloqueia qualquer imagem que não atenda aos requisitos da sua organização. Ele se integra aos resultados de varredura para que você possa impor limites de vulnerabilidade em vez de apenas detectar problemas.

A varredura de vulnerabilidades do Artifact Registry identifica vulnerabilidades em imagens armazenadas no registry, mas não atua como um admission controller no cluster. Por si só, não consegue bloquear a implantação de pods.

O Cloud Identity-Aware Proxy controla o acesso a aplicações e recursos web por trás de HTTPS. Ele não avalia imagens de contêiner nem aplica políticas de admissão do Kubernetes.

Os Cloud Audit Logs registram eventos administrativos e de acesso a dados para auditoria. Eles fornecem visibilidade, mas não conseguem impedir implantações nem aplicar políticas no momento da admissão.

options.text: Enable GKE application-layer secrets encryption with a Cloud KMS key so Kubernetes Secret objects are encrypted at rest

Keep the secret in Secret Manager, grant a Google service account access, and use Workload Identity so a Kubernetes service account impersonates it, letting Pods retrieve the secret without going through the Kubernetes Secrets API
Use the Secret Manager CSI driver, authenticating by mounting a service account JSON key held in a Kubernetes Secret
Store the secret in Cloud KMS and mount a Google service account JSON key into the Pod through a ConfigMap so the app calls KMS directly

questions.question: Riverton Media runs roughly 24 microservices across two regional Google Kubernetes Engine clusters. A database password must never be obtainable by reading Kubernetes API objects, and the team also wants to steer clear of distributing long-lived service account keys. Which approach best meets both constraints?
questions.correct_text: Keep the secret in Secret Manager, grant a Google service account access, and use Workload Identity so a Kubernetes service account impersonates it, letting Pods retrieve the secret without going through the Kubernetes Secrets API
questions.explanation:
The best approach is to keep the secret in Secret Manager, grant a Google service account access, and use Workload Identity so a Kubernetes service account impersonates it, letting Pods retrieve the secret without going through the Kubernetes Secrets API. That both blocks retrieval via Kubernetes API object reads and avoids handing out long-lived service account keys.

Workload Identity ties a Kubernetes service account to a Google service account, so Pods automatically obtain short-lived credentials. The application reads the password from Secret Manager at runtime, meaning there is no Kubernetes Secret object anyone could read. IAM governs the access, and you pick up Secret Manager features like versioning and audit logging that work uniformly across clusters.

Enabling GKE application-layer secrets encryption with a Cloud KMS key only encrypts Secret resources at rest and does nothing to stop authorized API clients from reading those Secret objects, so the password stays retrievable through Kubernetes API reads, violating the constraint.

Using the Secret Manager CSI driver with a mounted JSON key in a Kubernetes Secret relies on a long-lived key stored inside a readable Kubernetes Secret. The CSI driver can be secure with Workload Identity, but this option specifically uses a JSON key, failing the key-management constraint.

Storing the secret in Cloud KMS and mounting a JSON key via a ConfigMap uses a long-lived key and puts sensitive material in a ConfigMap, which is not for secrets. Cloud KMS manages keys rather than storing secrets, so the app would handle ciphertext storage and decryption, adding complexity and missing the constraints.

Isso bloqueia a recuperação por meio de leituras de objetos da Kubernetes API e evita distribuir chaves de service account de longa duração.

O Workload Identity vincula uma Kubernetes service account a uma Google service account, de modo que os Pods obtêm automaticamente credenciais de curta duração. A aplicação lê a senha do Secret Manager em tempo de execução, o que significa que não existe nenhum objeto Kubernetes Secret que alguém possa ler. O IAM controla o acesso, e você ganha recursos do Secret Manager como versionamento e audit logging, que funcionam de forma uniforme entre clusters.

Habilitar a criptografia de segredos na camada de aplicação do GKE (application-layer secrets encryption) com uma chave do Cloud KMS apenas criptografa os recursos Secret em repouso e não faz nada para impedir que clientes autorizados da API leiam esses objetos Secret, então a senha continua recuperável por meio de leituras da Kubernetes API, violando a restrição.

Usar o Secret Manager CSI driver com uma chave JSON montada em um Kubernetes Secret depende de uma chave de longa duração armazenada dentro de um Kubernetes Secret legível. O CSI driver pode ser seguro com Workload Identity, mas essa opção usa especificamente uma chave JSON, falhando na restrição de gerenciamento de chaves.

Armazenar o segredo no Cloud KMS e montar uma chave JSON via ConfigMap usa uma chave de longa duração e coloca material sensível em um ConfigMap, que não serve para segredos. O Cloud KMS gerencia chaves em vez de armazenar segredos, então a aplicação teria que lidar com o armazenamento de texto cifrado e a descriptografia, adicionando complexidade e descumprindo as restrições.

questions.question: A team at Brookbend Analytics plans to launch a new service on Cloud Run without providing a Dockerfile, and company policy requires every container image to be stored in a centrally managed Artifact Registry repository. Which actions will let you build the container image without a Dockerfile and ensure it is stored in the central registry?

options.text: Set up a Cloud Deploy pipeline to build and push an image to Artifact Registry
Run gcloud run deploy with the --source flag so Cloud Build uses buildpacks and stores the image in Artifact Registry
Use the pack CLI to run pack build and push the resulting image to Artifact Registry
Upload your application source tree to Artifact Registry and let Cloud Run build from there
Add the --platform=kubernetes option to gcloud run deploy and rely on that to create the image

questions.correct_text: Run gcloud run deploy with the --source flag so Cloud Build uses buildpacks and stores the image in Artifact Registry
questions.explanation:
The right picks are Run gcloud run deploy with the --source flag so Cloud Build uses buildpacks and stores the image in Artifact Registry and Use the pack CLI to run pack build and push the resulting image to Artifact Registry.

Using gcloud run deploy with the --source flag lets Cloud Build invoke Google Cloud Buildpacks to detect your application and build a container image without a Dockerfile. The resulting image is automatically pushed to Artifact Registry which satisfies a policy that images must be stored in a centrally managed registry. This path also streamlines source to service deployment for Cloud Run.

Using the pack CLI with Google Cloud Buildpacks also builds a container image from source without a Dockerfile. You can configure the image name to point to your centrally managed Artifact Registry repository and push the built image there, which fulfills the storage requirement before deploying the image to Cloud Run.

Set up a Cloud Deploy pipeline to build and push an image to Artifact Registry is incorrect because Cloud Deploy is for continuous delivery and release orchestration, and it expects artifacts such as container images to be built by another system like Cloud Build or pack.

Upload your application source tree to Artifact Registry and let Cloud Run build from there is incorrect because Artifact Registry stores built artifacts such as container images and language packages, and it does not store raw source trees or perform builds. Cloud Run does not build directly from a source tree stored in Artifact Registry.

Add the --platform=kubernetes option to gcloud run deploy and rely on that to create the image is incorrect because that option targets the Kubernetes based variant and it still requires a prebuilt container image and does not create one from source. This variant has also been de emphasized in favor of fully managed Cloud Run on newer exams.

Usar gcloud run deploy com a flag --source permite que o Cloud Build invoque os Google Cloud Buildpacks para detectar sua aplicação e construir uma imagem de contêiner sem um Dockerfile. A imagem resultante é automaticamente enviada (push) para o Artifact Registry, o que satisfaz uma política de que as imagens devem ser armazenadas em um registro gerenciado centralmente. Esse caminho também simplifica a implantação de código-fonte para serviço no Cloud Run.

Usar a CLI pack com os Google Cloud Buildpacks também constrói uma imagem de contêiner a partir do código-fonte sem um Dockerfile. Você pode configurar o nome da imagem para apontar para seu repositório Artifact Registry gerenciado centralmente e enviar a imagem construída para lá, o que cumpre o requisito de armazenamento antes de implantar a imagem no Cloud Run.

Configurar um pipeline do Cloud Deploy para construir e enviar uma imagem para o Artifact Registry está incorreto, porque o Cloud Deploy é para entrega contínua e orquestração de releases, e ele espera que artefatos como imagens de contêiner sejam construídos por outro sistema como Cloud Build ou pack.

Enviar (upload) a árvore de código-fonte da sua aplicação para o Artifact Registry e deixar o Cloud Run construir a partir dali está incorreto, porque o Artifact Registry armazena artefatos construídos, como imagens de contêiner e pacotes de linguagem, e não armazena árvores de código-fonte brutas nem realiza builds. O Cloud Run não constrói diretamente a partir de uma árvore de código-fonte armazenada no Artifact Registry.

Configure Firebase Authentication with local persistence so the sign in state is stored in the browser's local storage

questions.correct_text: Configure Firebase Authentication with local persistence so the sign in state is stored in the browser's local storage
questions.explanation:
The right pick is Configure Firebase Authentication with local persistence so the sign in state is stored in the browser's local storage.

This configuration uses Firebase on the web to store the authentication state in the browser's local storage, which survives tab opens and browser restarts. When you enable local persistence, Firebase saves the credentials in a storage area that is shared across tabs for the same origin, so users remain signed in when they open a new tab and when they return later.

Manage sessions using HTTP cookies that you create and set from the application server is not appropriate because Firebase Authentication already manages client side session persistence and token refresh, and custom cookies add unnecessary complexity and security risk for a web client flow.

Use Cloud Memorystore to keep user session tokens and retrieve them when the user returns is incorrect because Memorystore is a server side cache and does not maintain client side sign in state. Storing tokens there would not automatically restore a user session in the browser and would complicate security.

Save session information in Firebase Realtime Database and load it on every request is not advisable because authentication secrets should not be stored in a database, and this approach bypasses the built in, secure persistence provided by Firebase Authentication on the client.

Gerenciar sessões usando HTTP cookies que você cria e define a partir do servidor da aplicação não é apropriado, porque o Firebase Authentication já gerencia a persistência de sessão no lado do cliente e a renovação de tokens, e cookies personalizados adicionam complexidade desnecessária e risco de segurança para um fluxo de cliente web.

options.text: Configure a Cloud Function that runs your code on Cloud Storage object change events
Create an Eventarc trigger on the bucket with attribute filters for an exact object name and route the events to Cloud Run
Have Cloud Scheduler hit a Cloud Run endpoint on a fixed interval and let the service check whether the file changed
Forward Cloud Storage notifications to Pub/Sub and launch a Cloud Build job to run the application on each message

questions.question: A service at Zephyr Retail should fire only on updates to one specific Cloud Storage object, reports/daily.csv. Across the coming 120 days the team expects to flip among various object event types and may layer on a metadata-based filter as well. The arrangement needs to be simple and declarative so that multiple engineers can revise or swap out these triggers without ever redeploying the app. Which approach fits?
questions.correct_text: Create an Eventarc trigger on the bucket with attribute filters for an exact object name and route the events to Cloud Run
questions.explanation:
The approach to use is to create an Eventarc trigger on the bucket with attribute filters for an exact object name and route the events to Cloud Run. Eventarc can target only reports/daily.csv by filtering on the CloudEvents subject, and it can switch between object finalized and metadata updated events when you edit the trigger. Teammates manage those filters declaratively and apart from the service, so the Cloud Run deployment never needs to be redeployed.

Because Eventarc triggers are resources separate from the application, you can add or change attribute filters such as bucket and subject to match a single object path, and you can update the event type as needs shift. That leaves the application immutable while the trigger configuration evolves across the 120 days.

Configuring a Cloud Function on object change events is not the best fit, because its trigger is bound to the function deployment. Changing event types or adding an exact object filter usually forces a redeploy or filtering logic in code, which works against simple declarative updates by several teammates.

Having Cloud Scheduler hit a Cloud Run endpoint on an interval is polling rather than event driven. It fires needless runs when nothing changed, adds latency, and offers no trigger-level filters for event types or an exact object name.

Forwarding Cloud Storage notifications to Pub/Sub to launch a Cloud Build job is heavy and operationally complex. Cloud Build is built for builds and CI, not for repeatedly running application code, and this path lacks straightforward attribute filters and easy updates without retooling the pipeline.

The entire effort is creating a bucket, uploading the HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and images, setting an index and error page, and granting public access. No servers need patching or scaling, capacity adjusts itself, cost stays low for about 110 pages, and operational burden is minimal.

Creating a Compute Engine VM with Nginx is unnecessary for a static site, since it brings VM provisioning, OS and web-server patching, firewall configuration, and availability concerns that raise setup and maintenance.

Building a minimal container for Cloud Run adds container build and service configuration for something that needs no runtime, layering on features simple file serving does not require.

options.text: Create a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler driven by a custom application metric

questions.question: A stateless API for scrumtuous.com runs on Google Kubernetes Engine with a handful of replicas in one deployment. You have 14 days to deliver automatic scaling, you want to touch the manifests as little as possible, and you would rather use default metrics than wire up custom integrations. Which approach should you take?
questions.correct_text: Create a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler that targets average CPU utilization
questions.explanation:
The approach to take is to create a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler that targets average CPU utilization.

It rides on the built-in CPU utilization metric that Kubernetes already exposes for Pods through the metrics server and Cloud Monitoring. All it takes is a small HorizontalPodAutoscaler manifest, with no custom metric adapters and no code changes. It scales the replica count horizontally, which suits a stateless API and can be stood up quickly.

Creating an HPA driven by a custom application metric is not ideal, because it means publishing custom metrics into Cloud Monitoring and configuring the custom or external metrics pipeline, adding integration effort and time the team wants to avoid.

Switching on the cluster autoscaler while holding the Pod count fixed is wrong, because the cluster autoscaler scales nodes, not Pods. Fixing the Pods provides no automatic scaling of the application replicas.

Adding a Vertical Pod Autoscaler does not meet the goal, because VPA adjusts CPU and memory requests rather than the replica count. It can also restart Pods, and while it complements horizontal scaling it does not deliver the replica scaling required.

questions.question: You have a Java service running on a Linux VM and need it containerized with as little code change as possible so it can land on GKE in a simple deployment inside 45 days. Which Google Cloud approach fits?
questions.correct_text: Migrate to Containers
questions.explanation:
The approach that fits is Migrate to Containers.

It automates turning existing Linux VM workloads, including Java services, into containers. It inspects the application's artifacts and runtime dependencies on the VM, emits both a container image and a deployment configuration, and aims that output at GKE. That holds code changes to a minimum and comfortably supports a short timeline such as wrapping up within forty-five days.

Jib produces Java container images straight from source using Maven or Gradle. It does not lift an existing VM into a container or pick up the OS-level dependencies that reside on that VM.

Cloud Buildpacks convert source code into container images with no Dockerfile, which assumes you build from source rather than migrating a running VM environment.

A Compute Engine custom image yields a reusable VM image for spinning up more virtual machines. It produces neither a container nor any GKE deployment artifacts.

questions.question: A Cloud Run service needs to fetch objects from a Cloud Storage bucket that must stay completely private. You want to honor least privilege and rule out any public access. What is the right configuration?
questions.correct_text: Switch on public access prevention and have Cloud Run run under a dedicated user-managed service account granted Storage Object Viewer on just that bucket
questions.explanation:
The right configuration is to switch on public access prevention and have Cloud Run run under a dedicated user-managed service account granted Storage Object Viewer on just that bucket.

With its own dedicated identity carrying only the read-only role on the one bucket, Cloud Run authenticates to Cloud Storage under exactly the access it requires and nothing more. The role grants object reads alone and is scoped to a single bucket, which is least privilege in practice, and a dedicated user-managed service account keeps these permissions separate from any other workload.

Public access prevention on the bucket guarantees that no public principal can reach the objects, closing off accidental exposure via IAM or legacy ACLs. The service reads objects with its service account credentials while the bucket remains private.

Handing out signed URLs with the default service account misses the mark, because signed URLs grant anonymous bearer access to whoever holds the link, which contradicts blocking public-style access, and the default service account is shared across services rather than scoped per workload.

Granting project-level Storage Admin breaks least privilege, since Storage Admin confers full control, including writes and deletes, over every bucket in the project. That is vastly more than reading from a single bucket needs.

Using public access prevention but granting Storage Object Viewer to the default compute service account gets the bucket setting right yet leans on the default compute service account that other resources share. That broadens the blast radius and ignores the practice of giving the Cloud Run service its own dedicated user-managed identity.

O papel concede apenas leitura de objetos e está limitado a um único bucket, o que é o privilégio mínimo na prática, e uma service account dedicada gerenciada pelo usuário mantém essas permissões separadas de qualquer outro workload.

O public access prevention no bucket garante que nenhum principal público possa alcançar os objetos, eliminando a exposição acidental via IAM ou ACLs legadas. O serviço lê os objetos com as credenciais de sua service account enquanto o bucket permanece privado.

Conceder Storage Admin no nível do projeto quebra o privilégio mínimo, pois o Storage Admin confere controle total, incluindo escritas e exclusões, sobre todos os buckets do projeto. Isso é muito mais do que a leitura de um único bucket exige.

Usar public access prevention mas conceder Storage Object Viewer à service account padrão do Compute acerta a configuração do bucket, porém se apoia na service account padrão do Compute que outros recursos compartilham. Isso amplia o raio de impacto e ignora a prática de dar ao serviço do Cloud Run sua própria identidade dedicada gerenciada pelo usuário.

questions.question: Three weeks after moving its inventory API to Google Kubernetes Engine, Sparrow Retail is hit with intermittent outages during busy checkout windows that never occurred in the old data center. Engineers suspect the pods are starved of CPU and memory and want to examine utilization across clusters, namespaces, and workloads to prevent further incidents. Which tool should you use to analyze and diagnose resource utilization so you can stop the outages?
questions.correct_text: Cloud Monitoring with GKE dashboards and Metrics Explorer
questions.explanation:
Use Cloud Monitoring with GKE dashboards and Metrics Explorer, because it consolidates CPU and memory visibility across clusters, namespaces, and workloads and lets you drill into pods and containers to find constraints and prevent outages.

The built-in GKE dashboards let you compare requested versus actual resources, catch pod restarts and saturation, and watch trends during busy checkout windows, while Metrics Explorer filters by cluster, namespace, and workload to chart CPU and memory utilization, and alerts can fire as usage nears limits so you act before outages.

Cloud Trace centers on distributed tracing and latency for requests and spans, not cluster-wide CPU and memory across Kubernetes resources.

Expanding the cluster before investigating is not diagnostic; it can mask the real bottleneck, raise cost, and never reveal which pods are constrained.

Cloud Profiler samples application CPU and heap to find hot code paths, aimed at code-level analysis rather than fleet-wide Kubernetes resource monitoring across clusters and namespaces.

questions.question: Aurora Fitness intends to open a set of REST APIs to outside mobile developers, and it wants those developers to integrate easily through a client SDK, it wants API key checks to be compulsory, and it wants deep usage analytics. Incoming mobile calls travel through Cloud Load Balancing, then into the service that manages these APIs, and on to the internal services. Which Google Cloud service should run API management here?
questions.correct_text: Apigee Edge
questions.explanation:
Apigee Edge is the service to use, since it brings full-lifecycle API management that lines up with SDK-based integration, compulsory API key checks, and deep analytics, and it sits comfortably behind Cloud Load Balancing before traffic reaches the internal services.

For third-party developers, Apigee Edge offers genuine API productization: it issues and verifies API keys, manages quotas and traffic, and adds advanced threat protection. Its analytics are extensive, with dashboards and detailed reports that reveal usage and developer behavior, and it provides developer portals where you publish docs, samples, and SDKs to smooth onboarding. That combination suits an external mobile-developer ecosystem where onboarding and observability are first-class concerns.

Be aware that Apigee Edge is the legacy generation of the platform, and newer exams may stress the current generation. Even so, of the choices here it is the only one that fully covers SDK enablement, API key validation, and advanced analytics together.

API Gateway is a lighter gateway focused on exposing services on Google Cloud. It does support API keys and basic monitoring, but it lacks the comprehensive analytics, monetization, and mature developer-portal features expected of a third-party SDK program.

Cloud Endpoints validates API keys, works with OpenAPI or gRPC, and integrates with Cloud Logging and Cloud Monitoring, yet it falls short on deep analytics, a full developer portal, and the enterprise API-product capabilities a broad external program requires.

Cloud Identity-Aware Proxy protects access to applications by checking user identity and context. It offers no API productization, no third-party API key management, and no API analytics, so it does not fit.

O Apigee Edge é o serviço a ser usado, já que oferece gerenciamento de API de ciclo de vida completo, que se alinha à integração baseada em SDK, à verificação obrigatória de API keys e a analytics aprofundadas, além de se encaixar confortavelmente atrás do Cloud Load Balancing antes que o tráfego chegue aos serviços internos.

Para desenvolvedores terceiros, o Apigee Edge oferece uma verdadeira produtização de APIs: ele emite e verifica API keys, gerencia cotas e tráfego, e adiciona proteção avançada contra ameaças. Suas analytics são extensas, com dashboards e relatórios detalhados que revelam o uso e o comportamento dos desenvolvedores, e ele fornece developer portals onde você publica documentação, exemplos e SDKs para facilitar o onboarding. Essa combinação atende a um ecossistema externo de desenvolvedores mobile, onde onboarding e observabilidade são preocupações de primeira ordem.

Esteja ciente de que o Apigee Edge é a geração legada da plataforma, e provas mais novas podem enfatizar a geração atual. Ainda assim, dentre as opções aqui, ele é o único que cobre completamente a habilitação de SDK, a validação de API keys e analytics avançadas em conjunto.

O API Gateway é um gateway mais leve, focado em expor serviços no Google Cloud. Ele suporta API keys e monitoramento básico, mas carece das analytics abrangentes, da monetização e dos recursos maduros de developer portal esperados de um programa de SDK para terceiros.

O Cloud Endpoints valida API keys, funciona com OpenAPI ou gRPC e integra-se com Cloud Logging e Cloud Monitoring, mas fica aquém em analytics aprofundadas, em um developer portal completo e nas capacidades de produto de API empresarial que um programa externo amplo exige.

O Cloud Identity-Aware Proxy protege o acesso a aplicações verificando a identidade e o contexto do usuário. Ele não oferece produtização de API, nem gerenciamento de API keys de terceiros, nem analytics de API, portanto não se encaixa.

options.text: Run a Blue Green deployment and move all traffic to the new feature at once
Run an A/B test that sends a randomized subset of users to the new feature while everyone else stays on the current one
Perform a rolling update in GKE that gradually swaps the existing pods for ones running the new feature
Use a canary release in GKE with traffic splitting to send a small percentage of requests to the new feature

questions.question: CoastalCart runs its recommendation service on Google Kubernetes Engine, and the team has built a new widget it wants to measure against the existing one using live user traffic while disturbing as few shoppers as possible. Which approach should they use to compare the new widget with the current widget?
questions.correct_text: Run an A/B test that sends a randomized subset of users to the new feature while everyone else stays on the current one
questions.explanation:
The right approach is to run an A/B test that sends a randomized subset of users to the new feature while everyone else stays on the current one.

An A/B test compares two experiences simultaneously with real users, assigning them to buckets in a controlled, randomized way so you can measure impact on conversion, engagement, or latency while most shoppers keep the current widget. In GKE you implement it by routing on a stable user attribute through your ingress or a service mesh, so each user consistently sees one version, yielding clean experiment data with minimal disruption.

A Blue Green deployment that moves all traffic at once switches everyone's experience in a single cutover. It reduces release downtime rather than running a controlled comparison, so it cannot evaluate both widgets with real user cohorts at once.

A rolling update gradually updates workloads for reliability and offers neither consistent user assignment nor randomized cohorts for experiment analysis, so it is unsuited to this comparison.

A canary release with traffic splitting focuses on risk mitigation and early issue detection by routing a small slice of traffic to a new version. It uses real traffic but is not built for randomized, persistent cohorts with experiment metrics, so it is weaker for a rigorous head-to-head than an A/B test.

questions.explanation_pt:
A abordagem correta é executar um teste A/B que envia um subconjunto aleatório de usuários para a nova funcionalidade, enquanto todos os demais permanecem na funcionalidade atual.

Um teste A/B compara duas experiências simultaneamente com usuários reais, atribuindo-os a grupos de forma controlada e aleatória, para que você possa medir o impacto em conversão, engajamento ou latência, enquanto a maioria dos compradores continua com o widget atual. No GKE, você o implementa roteando com base em um atributo estável do usuário por meio do seu ingress ou de um service mesh, de modo que cada usuário veja consistentemente uma versão, gerando dados de experimento limpos com mínima disrupção.

Um deployment Blue Green, que move todo o tráfego de uma vez, troca a experiência de todos em um único cutover. Ele reduz o downtime de release em vez de executar uma comparação controlada, portanto não consegue avaliar ambos os widgets com coortes de usuários reais ao mesmo tempo.

Um rolling update atualiza gradualmente as workloads por questões de confiabilidade e não oferece nem atribuição consistente de usuários nem coortes aleatórias para análise de experimento, sendo, portanto, inadequado para essa comparação.

Um canary release com divisão de tráfego foca na mitigação de risco e na detecção precoce de problemas, roteando uma pequena fatia de tráfego para uma nova versão. Ele usa tráfego real, mas não foi feito para coortes aleatórias e persistentes com métricas de experimento, sendo, portanto, mais fraco para uma comparação rigorosa direta do que um teste A/B.

options.text: Use Identity-Aware Proxy to gate access to the Cloud Storage endpoints
Enable server-side encryption for Cloud Storage using customer-managed keys in Cloud KMS
Wrap the project holding the buckets in a VPC Service Controls perimeter
Apply Cloud Armor policies to protect the storage buckets

questions.question: Your team at a fintech startup serving scrumtuous.com clients is building a Google Cloud service that keeps sensitive customer profiles and monthly transaction statements in Cloud Storage for 240 days. Strict compliance means you must maximize protection of the data at rest while retaining control over the encryption keys. What should you implement?
questions.correct_text: Enable server-side encryption for Cloud Storage using customer-managed keys in Cloud KMS
questions.explanation:
You should enable server-side encryption for Cloud Storage using customer-managed keys in Cloud KMS.

This applies Cloud Storage server-side encryption with keys you own in Cloud KMS. You can schedule rotation, restrict who may use the key through IAM, audit every cryptographic operation, and disable or destroy the key to make data unreadable. Cloud Storage encrypts at rest by default, and supplying your own managed key raises the control and attestation strict compliance demands, all while fitting the 240-day retention.

Using Identity-Aware Proxy to gate the Cloud Storage endpoints is incorrect, because IAP guards web applications behind Google Cloud load balancers and provides neither at-rest encryption nor customer key control.

Wrapping the project in a VPC Service Controls perimeter is incorrect, because it lowers data exfiltration risk for supported services but does not encrypt data at rest or grant you key control.

Applying Cloud Armor policies is incorrect, because Cloud Armor defends application traffic in front of load-balanced endpoints and addresses neither object encryption nor key management for data at rest.

O Cloud Storage criptografa em repouso por padrão, e fornecer sua própria chave gerenciada eleva o controle e a atestação que requisitos de conformidade rigorosos exigem, tudo isso enquanto se encaixa na retenção de 240 dias.

Usar o Identity-Aware Proxy para controlar os endpoints do Cloud Storage está incorreto, porque o IAP protege aplicações web atrás dos load balancers do Google Cloud e não fornece nem criptografia em repouso nem controle de chave pelo cliente.

Envolver o projeto em um perímetro do VPC Service Controls está incorreto, porque isso reduz o risco de exfiltração de dados para serviços suportados, mas não criptografa dados em repouso nem concede a você controle sobre a chave.

Aplicar políticas do Cloud Armor está incorreto, porque o Cloud Armor defende o tráfego de aplicações na frente de endpoints com balanceamento de carga e não aborda nem a criptografia de objetos nem o gerenciamento de chaves para dados em repouso.

questions.question: You are setting up IAM for a data processing service account in the staging environment at Heron Retail, and it must be able to read tables and views in a specific BigQuery dataset while it must not change data or schemas. Which role should you grant on that dataset?

options.text: roles/bigquery.jobUser
roles/bigquery.dataEditor
roles/bigquery.dataViewer
roles/bigquery.dataOwner

questions.correct_text: roles/bigquery.dataViewer
questions.explanation:
The right pick is roles/bigquery.dataViewer because it grants read only access to tables and views within a specific dataset and it does not permit any changes to data or schemas.

The dataViewer role lets an identity read table data and view metadata for tables and views in the dataset. It does not allow inserting, updating, or deleting data and it does not allow creating, altering, or dropping tables, views, or schemas. This aligns exactly with the requirement to read without making changes.

The roles/bigquery.jobUser role is intended to allow creating and running BigQuery jobs at the project level, and by itself it does not grant access to read dataset data or metadata. Granting jobUser on a dataset would not meet the read requirement and it would not provide the necessary dataset permissions.

The roles/bigquery.dataEditor role includes permissions to modify data and schemas which violates the requirement that the service account must not change data or schemas.

The roles/bigquery.dataOwner role grants full control over the dataset including permission to change data and manage access, which is far beyond what is needed for read only access.

O papel dataViewer permite que uma identidade leia dados de tabelas e visualize metadados de tabelas e views no dataset. Ele não permite inserir, atualizar ou excluir dados e não permite criar, alterar ou remover tabelas, views ou schemas. Isso se alinha exatamente ao requisito de ler sem fazer alterações.

O papel roles/bigquery.jobUser destina-se a permitir a criação e a execução de jobs do BigQuery no nível do projeto e, por si só, não concede acesso para ler dados ou metadados do dataset. O papel roles/bigquery.dataEditor inclui permissões para modificar dados e schemas, o que viola o requisito de que a service account não deve alterar dados ou schemas.

O papel roles/bigquery.dataOwner concede controle total sobre o dataset, incluindo permissão para alterar dados e gerenciar o acesso, o que vai muito além do necessário para acesso somente leitura.

options.text: Bump the liveness probe initialDelaySeconds up to 70 seconds
Add a readiness probe with a larger failureThreshold
Add a Kubernetes startupProbe to suspend liveness checks until the service has initialized
Raise the container CPU limit from 500m to 1000m

questions.question: Riverton Media runs a video transcoding microservice on Google Kubernetes Engine Autopilot in us-central1. On some cold starts the container takes as much as 65 seconds to initialize, while the liveness probe begins at 12 seconds and runs every 7 seconds, prompting unwanted restarts. You want to keep liveness checks for catching real hangs while avoiding false failures during startup. What should you do?
questions.correct_text: Add a Kubernetes startupProbe to suspend liveness checks until the service has initialized
questions.explanation:
The right step is to add a Kubernetes startupProbe to suspend liveness checks until the service has initialized.

A startupProbe disables liveness and readiness checks until the container has started successfully, preventing premature restarts during slow initialization, yet it still catches real hangs because repeated startupProbe failures up to the configured threshold trigger a restart. This directly handles cold starts of up to 65 seconds while keeping liveness for genuine failures, and Autopilot supports startupProbe, the Kubernetes-recommended pattern for long or variable startup times.

Bumping initialDelaySeconds to 70 seconds only delays the first liveness check and postpones detection of genuine early hangs, forces you to guess a worst-case startup time, and grows brittle as the app changes; Kubernetes guidance favors a startupProbe here.

Adding a readiness probe with a larger failureThreshold does not fix it, because readiness only governs whether the Pod receives traffic and does nothing to stop liveness from failing during startup, so the Pod could still be restarted while initializing.

Raising the CPU limit from 500m to 1000m might speed some starts but does not guarantee initialization finishes before liveness begins, and it changes cost and scheduling without addressing the real need to gate liveness during startup.

questions.explanation_pt:
O passo correto é adicionar um startupProbe do Kubernetes para suspender as verificações de liveness até que o serviço tenha sido inicializado.

Um startupProbe desativa as verificações de liveness e readiness até que o contêiner tenha iniciado com sucesso, evitando reinícios prematuros durante uma inicialização lenta, mas ainda assim captura travamentos reais, porque falhas repetidas do startupProbe até o limite configurado disparam um reinício. Isso lida diretamente com cold starts de até 65 segundos, mantendo o liveness para falhas genuínas, e o Autopilot suporta o startupProbe, o padrão recomendado pelo Kubernetes para tempos de inicialização longos ou variáveis.

Aumentar o initialDelaySeconds para 70 segundos apenas atrasa a primeira verificação de liveness e adia a detecção de travamentos genuínos no início, força você a adivinhar um tempo de inicialização de pior caso e se torna frágil à medida que a aplicação muda; a orientação do Kubernetes favorece um startupProbe aqui.

Adicionar uma readiness probe com um failureThreshold maior não resolve o problema, porque a readiness apenas controla se o Pod recebe tráfego e não faz nada para impedir que o liveness falhe durante a inicialização, de modo que o Pod ainda poderia ser reiniciado enquanto inicializa.

Aumentar o limite de CPU de 500m para 1000m pode acelerar algumas inicializações, mas não garante que a inicialização termine antes que o liveness comece, e altera custo e agendamento sem abordar a real necessidade de controlar o liveness durante a inicialização.

questions.question: Beacon Freight is building a cloud native service that ingests and stores video clips from depot cameras. Security staff review the clips every week during the first 60 days, and afterward the footage is rarely accessed except during incident reviews. Regulations require the footage to be retained for at least eight years. You want to keep storage spend as low as possible while staying compliant. What should you implement?

options.text: Set a lifecycle rule to move objects to Coldline storage after 60 days
Define an eight year bucket retention policy and lock it using Bucket Lock
Store all footage in Standard storage
Enable Autoclass on the bucket to manage transitions automatically
Set a lifecycle rule to move objects to Archive storage after 60 days

questions.correct_text: Set a lifecycle rule to move objects to Archive storage after 60 days
questions.explanation:
The right picks are Define an eight year bucket retention policy and lock it using Bucket Lock and Set a lifecycle rule to move objects to Archive storage after 60 days.

Define an eight year bucket retention policy and lock it using Bucket Lock ensures regulatory compliance because it enforces a minimum retention period and prevents users from deleting objects or shortening the policy. Locking the policy makes it tamper resistant, which is required when regulations mandate a fixed retention term.

Set a lifecycle rule to move objects to Archive storage after 60 days minimizes cost because the footage is reviewed only during the first 60 days and is rarely accessed afterward. Archive provides the lowest storage cost for long term retention, and the occasional retrieval cost is acceptable for rare incident reviews.

Set a lifecycle rule to move objects to Coldline storage after 60 days is not the lowest cost approach for multi year retention when access is rare after the first two months and Archive is cheaper than Coldline for long term storage, which makes Coldline less optimal for keeping spend as low as possible.

Store all footage in Standard storage would significantly increase costs over eight years because Standard is optimized for frequent access rather than long term archival needs.

Enable Autoclass on the bucket to manage transitions automatically does not guarantee a timely move to the lowest cost class that matches the known 60 day access window, and it does not itself satisfy the compliance requirement to lock an eight year retention policy. An explicit retention lock and a defined lifecycle to Archive are more predictable and cost efficient for this pattern.

questions.explanation_pt:
As escolhas corretas são Definir uma política de retenção de oito anos no bucket e bloqueá-la usando Bucket Lock e Definir uma regra de ciclo de vida (lifecycle) para mover objetos para o armazenamento Archive após 60 dias.

Definir uma política de retenção de oito anos no bucket e bloqueá-la usando Bucket Lock garante a conformidade regulatória, porque impõe um período mínimo de retenção e impede que os usuários excluam objetos ou encurtem a política. Bloquear a política a torna resistente a adulterações, o que é exigido quando as regulamentações determinam um prazo de retenção fixo.

Definir uma regra de ciclo de vida (lifecycle) para mover objetos para o armazenamento Archive após 60 dias minimiza o custo, porque as gravações são revisadas apenas durante os primeiros 60 dias e raramente são acessadas depois disso. O Archive oferece o menor custo de armazenamento para retenção de longo prazo, e o custo ocasional de recuperação é aceitável para revisões raras de incidentes.

Definir uma regra de ciclo de vida para mover objetos para o armazenamento Coldline após 60 dias não é a abordagem de menor custo para retenção de vários anos quando o acesso é raro após os dois primeiros meses, e o Archive é mais barato que o Coldline para armazenamento de longo prazo, o que torna o Coldline menos ideal para manter os gastos o mais baixos possível.

Armazenar todas as gravações no armazenamento Standard aumentaria significativamente os custos ao longo de oito anos, porque o Standard é otimizado para acesso frequente, e não para necessidades de arquivamento de longo prazo.

Habilitar o Autoclass no bucket para gerenciar as transições automaticamente não garante uma movimentação oportuna para a classe de menor custo que corresponda à janela de acesso conhecida de 60 dias, e por si só não satisfaz o requisito de conformidade de bloquear uma política de retenção de oito anos. Um bloqueio de retenção explícito e um ciclo de vida definido para o Archive são mais previsíveis e econômicos para esse padrão.

questions.question: Orchard Analytics is assembling a CI/CD pipeline on Google Cloud using Cloud Build, Artifact Registry, and Google Kubernetes Engine. Builds must run in a containerized environment with no Docker daemon present and no elevated privileges permitted, and the team plans to reference the kaniko builder in cloudbuild.yaml to create images. Here, what does kaniko primarily do?
questions.correct_text: Build container images in Cloud Build without needing a Docker daemon or root access
questions.explanation:
Kaniko's primary job here is to build container images in Cloud Build without needing a Docker daemon or root access.

Kaniko builds images from a Dockerfile inside a container or Kubernetes cluster where no Docker daemon is available and privileged mode is disallowed. That lines up with Cloud Build's default unprivileged environment, so you can run the kaniko executor as a build step to create images and push them to Artifact Registry without root.

Providing application health monitoring and alerting is wrong, because that belongs to Cloud Monitoring and related services, not an image builder. Kaniko offers no observability.

Cloud Deploy is wrong, because it orchestrates releases and progressive delivery to targets such as GKE. It does not build images and usually runs after images already exist.

Running the repository's unit tests is wrong, because although Cloud Build can run test steps, kaniko's focus is building images from Dockerfiles rather than executing tests.

questions.question: Brookbend Retail operates a Google Kubernetes Engine cluster that autoscales between 5 and 15 nodes across three zones in one region, and you need to deploy a third party log collector so one instance runs on every node now and on any new nodes that appear during scaling while you investigate sporadic CPU throttling and disk latency during traffic spikes. Which deployment method should you choose to meet these requirements?

options.text: Use Terraform to deploy a standard Kubernetes Deployment for the logging agent
Deploy the third party logging agent as a Kubernetes DaemonSet
Connect with SSH to each Google Kubernetes Engine node and install the agent by hand
Embed the log collector inside every workload container image

questions.correct_text: Deploy the third party logging agent as a Kubernetes DaemonSet
questions.explanation:
The right pick is Deploy the third party logging agent as a Kubernetes DaemonSet.

A DaemonSet is designed to run exactly one pod on every node, and it automatically creates pods on any new nodes that join the cluster during autoscaling. This matches the requirement to collect logs on all current nodes and all future nodes across the three zones. It also continues to work when nodes are replaced or rescheduled during traffic spikes, which keeps your investigation consistent.

Use Terraform to deploy a standard Kubernetes Deployment for the logging agent is not appropriate because a Deployment manages a desired number of replicas rather than one replica per node. You would have to constantly adjust the replica count to match the changing node count and even with affinity rules this does not guarantee exactly one pod per node on a rapidly scaling cluster.

Connect with SSH to each Google Kubernetes Engine node and install the agent by hand is operationally fragile because GKE nodes are managed and ephemeral. Manually installed software will not survive node replacement or autoscaling events and it violates recommended practices for managing workloads in Kubernetes.

Embed the log collector inside every workload container image adds unnecessary overhead and does not ensure node level coverage. It forces image rebuilds for every workload and still may miss system or node level logs, whereas a single node scoped agent is the intended pattern for this use case.

Um DaemonSet é projetado para executar exatamente um pod em cada nó (node) e cria pods automaticamente em quaisquer novos nós que entrem no cluster durante o autoscaling. Isso atende ao requisito de coletar logs em todos os nós atuais e em todos os nós futuros nas três zonas. Ele também continua funcionando quando os nós são substituídos ou reagendados durante picos de tráfego, o que mantém sua investigação consistente.

Usar Terraform para implantar um Deployment padrão do Kubernetes para o agente de logging não é apropriado, porque um Deployment gerencia um número desejado de réplicas, em vez de uma réplica por nó. Você teria que ajustar constantemente a contagem de réplicas para acompanhar a contagem variável de nós, e mesmo com regras de afinidade isso não garante exatamente um pod por nó em um cluster que escala rapidamente.

Conectar via SSH a cada nó do Google Kubernetes Engine e instalar o agente manualmente é operacionalmente frágil, porque os nós do GKE são gerenciados e efêmeros. Software instalado manualmente não sobreviverá à substituição de nós ou a eventos de autoscaling, e isso viola as práticas recomendadas para gerenciar workloads no Kubernetes.

Embutir o coletor de logs dentro da imagem de contêiner de cada workload adiciona sobrecarga desnecessária e não garante cobertura no nível do nó. Isso força a reconstrução das imagens para cada workload e ainda pode perder logs de sistema ou no nível do nó, enquanto um único agente com escopo de nó é o padrão pretendido para esse caso de uso.

questions.question: AltaMart's backend service runs on Compute Engine virtual machines, and you are using Cloud Profiler to chase down sustained CPU saturation during peak hours. You want to find which functions are burning processor time so your optimizations land where they matter. Which profiler type should you pick?
questions.correct_text: CPU time profiler
questions.explanation:
Pick the CPU time profiler. It tracks the time the processor spends actively executing your code and attributes it to individual functions, which is precisely what locating hotspots during sustained CPU saturation requires.

It samples stack traces statistically while the CPU is busy and tallies the samples by function. You can then direct your effort at the functions truly consuming processor time rather than time spent waiting.

The Wall time profiler measures total elapsed time, including time blocked on I/O or locks, so it suits latency that involves blocking rather than pure CPU saturation.

The Heap profiler concentrates on memory allocation and usage and is meant for memory leaks or high allocation rates, not CPU-bound functions.

The Thread state profiler reports time threads spend running, runnable, waiting, or sleeping, aiding contention analysis but not attributing processor time to specific functions.

options.text: Add a startup script on each GKE node that mounts the NFS export, copies the configuration into the container, and starts the service from an ENTRYPOINT script
Bake the configuration in with a Dockerfile COPY step and start the process from an ENTRYPOINT script
Define a PersistentVolume and PersistentVolumeClaim for the NFS export, mount it into the pod, and use an ENTRYPOINT script that only starts once the configuration is present
Run gsutil inside the container at startup to pull the configuration from Cloud Storage, then start the service from an ENTRYPOINT script

questions.question: A legacy billing service that Ridgefield Analytics is moving onto Google Kubernetes Engine reads its configuration off an existing NFS export. The pod must not start handling requests until those config files have appeared inside the container during startup. How should you accomplish that?
questions.correct_text: Define a PersistentVolume and PersistentVolumeClaim for the NFS export, mount it into the pod, and use an ENTRYPOINT script that only starts once the configuration is present
questions.explanation:
What you should do is define a PersistentVolume and PersistentVolumeClaim for the NFS export, mount it into the pod, and use an ENTRYPOINT script that only starts once the configuration is present.

With an NFS-backed PersistentVolume and its matching PersistentVolumeClaim, the kubelet mounts the export into the pod before the container process begins. The entrypoint can then check for the required files and launch the billing service only after they exist. Pairing this with a readiness probe further ensures the pod takes no traffic until the configuration is confirmed available.

A startup script on each node is unreliable, because pods can land on any node and be rescheduled at any time. Node-level scripts harm portability and do not guarantee the configuration is inside the container at the right moment, and copying files into running containers violates immutability and is fragile to operate.

Baking the configuration in via a Dockerfile COPY step fails the requirement to read from an existing NFS export and instead embeds configuration in the image, blocking dynamic updates and forcing rebuilds whenever the configuration changes.

Running gsutil at startup to pull from Cloud Storage swaps the source from NFS to Cloud Storage and introduces an extra dependency and credentials, so it does not satisfy the requirement to read from the existing NFS export.

options.text: Add a Cloud NAT gateway to the VPC so the nodes can reach the API via egress to the internet

questions.question: NorthWind Metrics operates a private Google Kubernetes Engine cluster whose nodes carry only internal IP addresses for security, yet the cluster's services have to call the Cloud Bigtable API from inside the VPC. What is the best way to allow that without giving the nodes public IP addresses?
questions.correct_text: Enable Private Google Access on the subnet hosting the GKE nodes
questions.explanation:
The best approach is to enable Private Google Access on the subnet hosting the GKE nodes. That lets nodes with only internal IPs reach Google APIs such as Cloud Bigtable without crossing the public internet and without external IPs.

The setting permits instances in a subnet to use their internal addresses to reach Google APIs and services, keeping traffic on Google's network. That satisfies a private GKE cluster whose nodes must call the Bigtable API from within the VPC with no public exposure, and it is the simplest fitting control.

Adding a Cloud NAT gateway is not appropriate, because it routes traffic to public endpoints over the internet even though the nodes need no external IPs. The aim is private access to Google APIs, not internet egress.

Putting Cloud Endpoints in front of the Cloud Bigtable API is not feasible, because you cannot slot a third-party proxy ahead of a first-party Google-managed API in a way that reroutes the network path from clients to the service, and it does nothing for private access from internal IPs. Cloud Endpoints is also deprecated, making it less likely on newer exams.

Briefly attaching external IPs to the nodes violates the security requirement and adds needless exposure and risk. There is no reason to assign public IPs when a native private-access mechanism exists.

Adicionar um gateway Cloud NAT não é apropriado, porque ele roteia o tráfego para endpoints públicos pela internet mesmo que os nós não precisem de IPs externos. O objetivo é o acesso privado às APIs do Google, não a saída para a internet.

O Cloud Endpoints também está descontinuado, tornando-o menos provável em provas mais recentes.

options.text: Have the Cloud Run service account mint a signed JWT carrying the "https://www.googleapis.com/auth/drive.file" scope and call the Drive API with it
Register an OAuth 2.0 Client ID and request the "https://www.googleapis.com/auth/drive.file" scope so the app gets a user-consented access token each session
Configure an OAuth 2.0 Client ID with Google Workspace domain-wide delegation so the app can impersonate any user in the organization
Use a service account with domain-wide delegation across the Workspace domain to drop files into user Drives without asking each user

questions.question: A customer portal you are launching on Cloud Run has to write the reports it generates into the Google Drive of whichever user is signed in. The integration with the Google Drive API must be secure, authorize each user individually, and request the fewest permissions possible. What should you do?
questions.correct_text: Register an OAuth 2.0 Client ID and request the "https://www.googleapis.com/auth/drive.file" scope so the app gets a user-consented access token each session
questions.explanation:
The right approach is to register an OAuth 2.0 Client ID and request the "https://www.googleapis.com/auth/drive.file" scope so the app gets a user-consented access token each session.

This follows the standard OAuth 2.0 web application flow, in which the portal obtains an access token on behalf of the signed-in user. It authorizes per user and respects least privilege, because the drive.file scope confines access to files the app created or files the user explicitly opened with the app. Cloud Run can then call the Drive API with the user's consent while access stays narrow. You exchange an authorization code for tokens and can keep a refresh token to maintain the session securely.

Having the Cloud Run service account mint a signed JWT is wrong, because a service account represents the application, not the user. A signed JWT by itself does not unlock a user's Drive and would operate on the service account's own resources unless domain-wide delegation is set up. It provides neither per-user consent nor minimal per-user permissions.

Configuring an OAuth 2.0 Client ID with domain-wide delegation is inappropriate, because that allows admin-sanctioned impersonation of any user with no individual consent, which contradicts the per-user authorization requirement and is broader than necessary.

Using a service account with domain-wide delegation to write into user Drives without asking is wrong, because it skips user consent and grants organization-wide reach. That is meant for administrative automation, not a customer portal that must honor per-user authorization and least privilege.

questions.explanation_pt:

Isso segue o fluxo padrão de aplicação web do OAuth 2.0, no qual o portal obtém um access token em nome do usuário autenticado. Ele autoriza por usuário e respeita o privilégio mínimo, porque o escopo drive.file restringe o acesso aos arquivos que o app criou ou aos arquivos que o usuário abriu explicitamente com o app. O Cloud Run pode então chamar a Drive API com o consentimento do usuário enquanto o acesso permanece restrito. Você troca um authorization code por tokens e pode manter um refresh token para manter a sessão de forma segura.

Fazer a service account do Cloud Run gerar um JWT assinado está errado, porque uma service account representa a aplicação, não o usuário. Um JWT assinado por si só não desbloqueia o Drive de um usuário e operaria nos próprios recursos da service account, a menos que a delegação em todo o domínio (domain-wide delegation) esteja configurada. Ele não fornece nem consentimento por usuário nem permissões mínimas por usuário.

Configurar um OAuth 2.0 Client ID com domain-wide delegation é inadequado, porque isso permite a personificação de qualquer usuário sancionada por administrador, sem consentimento individual, o que contradiz o requisito de autorização por usuário e é mais amplo do que o necessário.

Usar uma service account com domain-wide delegation para gravar nos Drives dos usuários sem pedir está errado, porque pula o consentimento do usuário e concede alcance em toda a organização. Isso é destinado à automação administrativa, não a um portal de clientes que deve respeitar a autorização por usuário e o privilégio mínimo.

options.text: Front the VM with a regional internal HTTP(S) Load Balancer on a reserved internal IP and add a private Cloud DNS A record for clients
Lean on Compute Engine internal DNS and let clients reach the VM via its internal FQDN "https://[INSTANCE_NAME].[ZONE].c.[PROJECT_ID].internal/"
Expose the API through API Gateway on an external endpoint and attach a DNS name to it
Register the VM in Service Directory and make clients resolve the endpoint through the Service Directory API

questions.question: Quasar Pixel, a media-analytics startup, is rolling out a REST API on one Compute Engine VM in zone us-east5-b, reachable only by workloads inside the same VPC. You would like other client services in that network to find the VM by name and resolve to its internal IP, with nothing exposed externally and no extra infrastructure introduced. What do you recommend?
questions.correct_text: Lean on Compute Engine internal DNS and let clients reach the VM via its internal FQDN "https://[INSTANCE_NAME].[ZONE].c.[PROJECT_ID].internal/"
questions.explanation:
The recommendation is to lean on Compute Engine internal DNS and let clients reach the VM via its internal FQDN "https://[INSTANCE_NAME].[ZONE].c.[PROJECT_ID].internal/".

Every VM is automatically given this hostname, and it resolves to the instance's internal IP inside the VPC. Nothing extra is deployed, and the service stays private because the name resolves only within the project's network context and the connected networks that are permitted. That delivers name-based access with no external exposure and no new infrastructure, exactly as required.

Fronting the VM with a regional internal HTTP(S) Load Balancer on a reserved internal IP plus a private Cloud DNS A record is overkill for a single backend VM and introduces the very components the scenario rules out. The automatic instance hostname already provides internal name resolution.

Exposing the API through API Gateway on an external endpoint breaks the no-external-exposure rule, because that endpoint is external by design even if the callers all sit inside the same VPC.

Registering the VM in Service Directory and resolving through its API adds a registry and forces clients to change how they discover endpoints. That is new infrastructure you do not need when the instance hostname already resolves inside the VPC.
