A escolha correta é autenticar os usuários com Google OAuth e fazer o backend gerar uma V4 signed URL de curta duração para o objeto de destino, para que o navegador possa fazer o upload diretamente para o Cloud Storage.

Essa abordagem primeiro autentica o usuário com Google OAuth, o que satisfaz o requisito de login com Google. Depois que o usuário é autenticado, o backend autoriza a requisição e emite uma V4 signed URL de curta duração que é limitada ao objeto de destino e ao método HTTP pretendido. O navegador então faz o upload diretamente para o Cloud Storage usando essa signed URL, o que remove os servidores da aplicação do caminho dos dados e permite que a solução escale para arquivos grandes. Expirações curtas e escopo específico do objeto impedem uploads anônimos ou arbitrários, porque apenas usuários autenticados recebem uma signed URL nova do backend.

Para arquivos grandes, como 20 GB, a equipe pode usar um resumable upload iniciado com uma V4 signed URL, e deve configurar CORS no bucket para que o navegador possa chamar o endpoint do Cloud Storage a partir do domínio da aplicação.

Fazer a aplicação solicitar aos usuários o nome de usuário e a senha do Google e trocar as credenciais por um access token, e então fazer o upload do arquivo para o bucket, é inseguro e não tem suporte. As aplicações não devem coletar senhas do Google e devem usar OAuth para login. Isso também corre o risco de forçar os servidores a fazer proxy dos uploads, o que falha no requisito de escalabilidade.

Proteger o bucket com o Cloud Identity Aware Proxy e exigir login com Google antes de permitir que os usuários façam upload para o endpoint de armazenamento não é viável, porque o Identity Aware Proxy protege apps por trás do HTTP load balancing do Google Cloud e não fica na frente das APIs do Cloud Storage. Ele não forneceria acesso controlado a uploads diretos do navegador para o endpoint de armazenamento.

Usar o Firebase Authentication e deixar o cliente apresentar o token do Firebase ao Cloud Storage para realizar o upload não funciona com as APIs JSON ou XML brutas do Cloud Storage. Os ID tokens do Firebase são avaliados pelo Cloud Storage for Firebase por meio do Firebase SDK e suas Security Rules, e não são aceitos diretamente pelos endpoints padrão do Cloud Storage.

questions.question: A subscription platform called Marigold Cart runs its checkout API on Cloud Run, and customers report slow responses during an evening traffic surge that lasts about 60 minutes. As you use Cloud Monitoring to determine whether resource saturation is causing the slowdown, which metric should you look at first?

options.text: Count of active instances for the Cloud Run service
Container startup latency for new Cloud Run instances
CPU and memory utilization of the Cloud Run service
Distribution of HTTP response status codes for the service

questions.correct_text: CPU and memory utilization of the Cloud Run service
questions.explanation:
The right answer is CPU and memory utilization of the Cloud Run service.

The count of active instances shows scaling behavior but not whether each instance is saturated. You could have many lightly loaded instances or a few heavily loaded ones, so it is not the first metric for diagnosing saturation.

Container startup latency for new instances helps diagnose cold starts, but a sustained 60 minute slowdown points to steady state load rather than one time startup delays. Startup latency is transient and would not explain continued slowness throughout the surge.

The distribution of HTTP response status codes can reveal errors or client impact but does not identify the resource bottleneck. Status codes are a symptom view and do not show whether CPU or memory limits are being hit.

questions.question: The team at mcnz.com launched a service on App Engine that behaves correctly, yet over the past 48 hours customers have reported occasional response time spikes during normal traffic. You want to find the root cause of these intermittent delays while changing as little code as possible. What should you do?

options.text: Start Cloud Profiler to sample CPU and heap usage in the service
Enable verbose application logging and review per request entries in Cloud Logging
Turn on Cloud Trace and review distributed traces to find the slowest spans and endpoints
Redeploy the application to a different App Engine region to lower latency

questions.correct_text: Turn on Cloud Trace and review distributed traces to find the slowest spans and endpoints
questions.explanation:
The only correct choice is to turn on Cloud Trace and review distributed traces to find the slowest spans and endpoints.

Cloud Trace provides request level latency data with spans across services, so you can see exactly where time is spent on the slow requests. On App Engine, basic tracing can often be enabled with little or no code change, which matches the goal of minimizing changes while investigating recent spikes. You can filter traces by latency, compare normal and slow requests, and pinpoint slow endpoints or downstream calls.

By reviewing spans in Cloud Trace you can tell whether latency comes from application code, RPCs, database queries, or external calls. You can also visualize percentile distributions over the last 48 hours to focus on intermittent tail latency rather than average behavior.

Starting Cloud Profiler to sample CPU and heap usage is better for finding ongoing CPU or memory hotspots and samples rather than tracing individual requests. It does not give end to end request timing with spans, so it is weaker for diagnosing intermittent latency spikes across dependencies.

Enabling verbose application logging and reviewing per request entries can create noise and overhead, and logs alone lack automatic end to end timing and cross service correlation. Without distributed spans you may miss where time is actually spent on a slow request.

Redeploying to a different App Engine region changes geographic latency but does not explain or diagnose intermittent spikes during normal traffic. You should identify the cause with traces before considering a regional move.

questions.explanation_pt:
A única escolha correta é ativar o Cloud Trace e revisar os traces distribuídos para encontrar os spans e endpoints mais lentos.

O Cloud Trace fornece dados de latência em nível de requisição com spans entre serviços, então você pode ver exatamente onde o tempo é gasto nas requisições lentas. No App Engine, o rastreamento básico muitas vezes pode ser ativado com pouca ou nenhuma alteração de código, o que combina com o objetivo de minimizar mudanças enquanto se investigam picos recentes. Você pode filtrar os traces por latência, comparar requisições normais e lentas e identificar endpoints lentos ou chamadas downstream.

Ao revisar os spans no Cloud Trace você pode dizer se a latência vem do código da aplicação, de RPCs, de consultas a banco de dados ou de chamadas externas. Você também pode visualizar distribuições por percentil ao longo das últimas 48 horas para focar na latência de cauda intermitente, em vez do comportamento médio.

Iniciar o Cloud Profiler para amostrar o uso de CPU e heap é melhor para encontrar hotspots contínuos de CPU ou memória e faz amostragem em vez de rastrear requisições individuais. Ele não fornece o tempo de requisição de ponta a ponta com spans, então é mais fraco para diagnosticar picos intermitentes de latência entre dependências.

Ativar logging detalhado da aplicação e revisar as entradas por requisição pode criar ruído e sobrecarga, e os logs sozinhos não têm tempo automático de ponta a ponta nem correlação entre serviços. Sem spans distribuídos você pode não perceber onde o tempo é realmente gasto em uma requisição lenta.

Reimplantar em uma região diferente do App Engine muda a latência geográfica, mas não explica nem diagnostica picos intermitentes durante tráfego normal. Você deve identificar a causa com os traces antes de considerar uma mudança de região.

questions.question: Crestpoint Insurance is building the backend for a claims-portal IVR. One persistent gRPC connection backs each caller's distinct session, and a dropped connection forces a reconnect that briefly delays the caller. Calls run 2 to 45 minutes, concentrate in business hours, and spike sharply at open enrollment and major policy releases. Aiming to keep cost, effort, and operational overhead low, where should the backend run?

options.text: Cloud Functions
Google Kubernetes Engine Standard mode
Cloud Run
App Engine flexible environment

questions.correct_text: Cloud Run
questions.explanation:
The right answer is Cloud Run.

Cloud Run is a fully managed, container based service that supports HTTP and gRPC over HTTP 2, so it can hold a persistent gRPC connection for the length of each IVR session. Typical call lengths of 2 to 45 minutes fit within the configurable request timeout, and it scales automatically to absorb sharp spikes during open enrollment or policy updates while scaling to zero outside business hours to save cost. You can also set minimum instances to keep a few containers warm during peaks to reduce reconnect delays, which keeps effort and operational overhead low.

Cloud Functions is a poor fit because it is built for short lived stateless invocations and HTTP style requests rather than hosting client facing persistent gRPC services. Maintaining long lived bidirectional streams to individual callers is not what functions are designed for, and the platform lacks the gRPC server capabilities Cloud Run provides.

Google Kubernetes Engine Standard mode could host gRPC services and long connections, but it requires managing clusters, node pools, upgrades, and scaling policies. That operational burden and baseline cost run against the goal of minimizing cost, effort, and overhead, while Cloud Run removes most of that management.

App Engine flexible environment can handle longer requests but keeps instances running, raising baseline cost, and it scales more slowly for spiky workloads. It is also less straightforward for modern gRPC serving than Cloud Run, so it is not the most cost effective or low effort choice here.

Também é menos direto para servir gRPC moderno do que o Cloud Run, então não é a escolha mais econômica ou de menor esforço aqui.

questions.question: Nexus Pharma runs a group of microservices on Google Kubernetes Engine that need to pull a private container image hosted in Artifact Registry, and you must allow the pods to retrieve the image securely without distributing long lived credentials inside the cluster, so which step should you take?

options.text: Configure the node pool to use the default Compute Engine service account with broad cloud platform scope so the kubelet can pull the image
Create a Kubernetes Secret of type docker registry that holds a service account key and reference it with imagePullSecrets in the pod manifest
Enable Workload Identity and map a Kubernetes service account to a Google service account that has read access to the Artifact Registry repository
Grant allAuthenticatedUsers the reader role on the Artifact Registry repository

questions.correct_text: Enable Workload Identity and map a Kubernetes service account to a Google service account that has read access to the Artifact Registry repository
questions.explanation:
The best answer is Enable Workload Identity and map a Kubernetes service account to a Google service account that has read access to the Artifact Registry repository.

With Workload Identity, pods use a Kubernetes service account that is bound to a Google service account, which allows short lived federated credentials to be issued automatically. The Google service account needs only the minimum permissions including reader access on the Artifact Registry repository, so the pods can pull private images without embedding secrets or keys.

Configure the node pool to use the default Compute Engine service account with broad cloud platform scope so the kubelet can pull the image is one poor match since it relies on broad and node scoped credentials, which violates minimal privilege and exposes more permissions than needed. It also does not supply pod level identity.

Create a Kubernetes Secret of type docker registry that holds a service account key and reference it with imagePullSecrets in the pod manifest is insecure because it relies on long lived service account keys persisted in the cluster. The scenario explicitly asks to stop distributing long lived credentials.

Grant allAuthenticatedUsers the reader role on the Artifact Registry repository would in practice make the repository accessible to anyone with a Google account, which removes proper access control and is not secure for private images.

questions.question: Within loomwright.io the engineering team adopted Google App Engine as a managed PaaS to accelerate releases. During the last 53 days they observed that getting new features into production takes longer even though build durations remain unchanged. Which inherent trade-off of App Engine could be contributing to the slower rollout?

options.text: Limited ability to handle high traffic loads
Inadequate support for CI or CD
Less control over the underlying runtime and system configuration
No support for traffic splitting or canary strategies

questions.correct_text: Less control over the underlying runtime and system configuration
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Less control over the underlying runtime and system configuration. This managed PaaS abstraction can slow the path to production when features require system level changes or custom runtime tweaks that the platform does not expose.

App Engine owns the operating system and language runtimes, which means teams cannot install arbitrary system packages or run custom daemons or pin unsupported runtime versions. When a new feature needs a specific native library, kernel capability, custom networking, or startup configuration, engineers must rework the design to fit the platform or move to a different environment. That extra adaptation increases release lead time even though the build itself has not changed.

Limited ability to handle high traffic loads is not an inherent issue for App Engine. The service is built to autoscale and absorb bursts, so traffic capacity would not explain a slower rollout of features.

Inadequate support for CI or CD is incorrect. App Engine integrates well with Cloud Build, Cloud Deploy, and common Git based pipelines, so automated delivery is supported.

No support for traffic splitting or canary strategies is wrong. App Engine offers built in versioning and traffic splitting which allows gradual rollouts and canary releases.

Quando um novo recurso precisa de uma biblioteca nativa específica, capacidade de kernel, rede personalizada ou configuração de inicialização, os engenheiros precisam reformular o design para se ajustar à plataforma ou migrar para um ambiente diferente. questions.question: Elderbrook Studios is building a public API for order processing that must store data in a relational schema and will encounter very high write throughput near 102,000 inserts per second during sales campaigns. The team needs low-latency writes with strong consistency and the ability to scale horizontally without managing replicas. Which GCP service should they select?

options.text: Bigtable
Cloud SQL
Cloud Spanner
Firestore in Datastore mode

questions.correct_text: Cloud Spanner
questions.explanation:
The proper option is Cloud Spanner since it offers a relational schema with SQL support, strongly consistent low latency writes, and automatic horizontal scaling without replica management, which matches the 100,000 inserts per second requirement.

With Cloud Spanner you get a fully managed relational database that on its own shards data and uses synchronous replication to preserve strong consistency while delivering high availability. It scales write throughput by adding nodes so it can handle very high sustained insert rates during sales campaigns while keeping latency low. The service distributes writes across partitions on its own so there is no need to create or manage replicas to scale writes.

Although Bigtable can provide massive throughput and low latency, it is a wide column NoSQL database and does not support a relational schema, joins, or multi row transactions. Since the service needs a relational model, it is not a fit.

Cloud SQL is relational and strongly consistent but it primarily scales vertically and read replicas do not increase write capacity. At 105,000 inserts per second the single primary would become a bottleneck and you would still need to manage replicas, which does not satisfy the requirement for horizontal write scaling without replica management.

Firestore in Datastore mode is a document database and not relational. It lacks joins and traditional relational constraints, and its transactional model focuses on entity groups that limit relational patterns, so it does not meet the need for a high throughput relational store.

questions.explanation_pt:
A opção apropriada é o Cloud Spanner, pois ele oferece um esquema relacional com suporte a SQL, gravações de baixa latência fortemente consistentes e escalabilidade horizontal automática sem gerenciamento de réplicas, o que atende ao requisito de 100.000 inserções por segundo.

Com o Cloud Spanner você obtém um banco de dados relacional totalmente gerenciado que, por conta própria, faz o sharding dos dados e usa replicação síncrona para preservar a consistência forte ao mesmo tempo em que entrega alta disponibilidade. Ele escala a taxa de transferência de gravação adicionando nós, de modo que pode lidar com taxas de inserção sustentadas muito altas durante campanhas de vendas, mantendo a latência baixa. O serviço distribui as gravações entre as partições por conta própria, então não há necessidade de criar ou gerenciar réplicas para escalar as gravações.

Embora o Bigtable possa fornecer enorme taxa de transferência e baixa latência, ele é um banco de dados NoSQL wide column e não suporta esquema relacional, joins ou transações multi-linha. Como o serviço precisa de um modelo relacional, ele não é adequado.

O Cloud SQL é relacional e fortemente consistente, mas escala principalmente de forma vertical, e as réplicas de leitura não aumentam a capacidade de gravação. Com 105.000 inserções por segundo, o primário único se tornaria um gargalo e você ainda precisaria gerenciar réplicas, o que não satisfaz o requisito de escalabilidade horizontal de gravação sem gerenciamento de réplicas.

O Firestore em modo Datastore é um banco de dados de documentos e não relacional. Ele não tem joins nem restrições relacionais tradicionais, e seu modelo transacional foca em grupos de entidades que limitam padrões relacionais, de modo que não atende à necessidade de um armazenamento relacional de alta taxa de transferência.

questions.question: Catalyst Health uses a BigQuery analytics workspace to deliver insights to more than 100 employees. A data scientist wants to run queries that must not disrupt critical reporting workloads, and they do not care if their queries complete much later. You want to meet this request with the least cost and minimal administrative effort. Which approach should you take?

options.text: Purchase a small dedicated BigQuery Reservations slot commitment for the analyst and assign their jobs to that reservation
Submit the queries as BigQuery batch jobs so they are queued and executed only when idle capacity is available
Move the analyst to a separate Google Cloud project and have them run all work there to isolate impact
Allow the analyst to run jobs only during off peak hours by agreeing on a manual schedule

questions.correct_text: Submit the queries as BigQuery batch jobs so they are queued and executed only when idle capacity is available
questions.explanation:
The proper option is Submit the queries as BigQuery batch jobs so they are queued and executed only when idle capacity is available.

This strategy aligns with the requirement to stop disrupting critical workloads since it queues the scientists queries and runs them when resources are not in use by higher priority work. It also involves almost no administration since it is a per job setting and it avoids extra infrastructure or configuration. It meets the least cost requirement because it does not require purchasing dedicated capacity or building and managing new projects.

Purchase a small dedicated BigQuery Reservations slot commitment for the analyst and assign their jobs to that reservation is not the least cost option because it introduces ongoing flat rate spend and added administrative work to size, manage, and monitor a separate reservation. It is unnecessary when the scientist is comfortable with delayed completion.

Move the analyst to a separate Google Cloud project and have them run all work there to isolate impact adds overhead for IAM, billing, and dataset sharing while it still does not guarantee isolation from shared capacity contention. It also does not meet the minimal effort requirement compared to just changing query priority.

Allow the analyst to run jobs only during off peak hours by agreeing on a manual schedule relies on manual coordination and offers no enforcement or guarantee that capacity will be idle. It increases operational burden and is less dependable than letting the service queue and start work when resources are available.

questions.question: Lighthouse Realty wants to validate a new production release with a small cohort of real users and they need to target the rollout by operating system using request metadata while maintaining the ability to revert instantly if problems occur and they plan to start with roughly 24% of eligible traffic going to the new build. What should they implement to meet these requirements?

options.text: Compute Engine with Traffic Director and configure weighted routing to send a small portion to a canary Managed Instance Group
Cloud Run with traffic splitting by revision tag and send about 20% to the new revision
Google Kubernetes Engine with Anthos Service Mesh and use user agent header based routing to direct about 20% of the selected operating system traffic to the canary
App Engine with traffic splitting based on client IP address ranges

questions.correct_text: Google Kubernetes Engine with Anthos Service Mesh and use user agent header based routing to direct about 20% of the selected operating system traffic to the canary
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Google Kubernetes Engine with Anthos Service Mesh and use user agent header based routing to direct about 16% of the picked operating system traffic to the canary.

This selection accommodates matching on request headers including the User-Agent so developers can pick only traffic from specific operating systems. It also handles weighted routing so you can send roughly 25 percent to the new revision while the rest continues to the stable version. Developers can revert instantly by updating the routing weights back to the stable version which does not require a redeploy and takes effect quickly.

Compute Engine with Traffic Director and configure weighted routing to send a small portion to a canary Managed Instance Group is suboptimal because while Traffic Director can distribute traffic, achieving header based targeting by operating system for end user HTTP traffic needs deploying and managing Envoy proxies in front of the instances. This adds significant complexity compared to a service mesh on GKE that already offers header matches and percentage based canary rules.

Cloud Run with traffic splitting by revision tag and send about 25% to the new revision does not meet the requirement because Cloud Run traffic splitting is percentage based only and does not natively route to revisions based on request headers such as user agent. You cannot target specific operating systems without custom routing outside the platform or application level logic.

App Engine with traffic splitting based on client IP address ranges fails the requirement because IP based splitting does not align with targeting by operating system and it does not supply header based matching to select only the desired cohort.

questions.question: Within TerraNova Studios you are building an app that stores user files in Cloud Storage under a per user folder including customers 55000 followed by a trailing slash. When a new account is provisioned you want an empty folder to appear in listings so that web consoles and client libraries show it as a directory. Which approach should you take?

options.text: Grant the user the Storage Object Creator role on the bucket so the folder is created automatically on first access
Set the object metadata Content-Type to application x directory and upload a zero byte placeholder
Create a zero byte object whose name ends with a trailing slash for the per user path
Create an object for the user path and immediately delete it so an empty directory remains

questions.correct_text: Create a zero byte object whose name ends with a trailing slash for the per user path
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Create a zero byte object whose name ends with a trailing slash for the per user path.

Cloud Storage uses a flat namespace and folder views are a convenience that come from object name prefixes. Creating a zero byte object whose name ends with a trailing slash acts as a placeholder so consoles and many client SDK libraries display that prefix as an empty directory.

Grant the client the Storage Object Creator role on the bucket so the folder is created on its own on first access is wrong because permissions do not create objects and folder like entries only appear when an object actually exists with that prefix.

Set the object metadata Content-Type to application x directory and send a zero byte placeholder is wrong because Cloud Storage does not infer folder behavior from Content Type and the special type application x directory is not used for directories in this service. Only object names with prefixes and trailing slashes influence folder like listings.

Create an object for the user path and immediately delete it so an empty directory remains is wrong because there is no directory metadata in Cloud Storage and deleting the only object at that prefix leaves nothing to display.

questions.question: The engineering team at Cascade Analytics manages two Google Cloud projects named Project Sable and Project Marble. You must deploy a Cloud Function in Project Sable that writes its results to a Cloud Storage bucket called marble-output-vault in Project Marble. You want to follow the principle of least privilege and keep control of the function's identity within Project Sable. Which approach should you take?

options.text: Deploy the Cloud Function in Project Sable to run as the default App Engine service account in that project and grant roles/storage.objectAdmin on the marble-output-vault bucket in Project Marble
Create a service account in Project Marble and have the Cloud Function in Project Sable run as that identity and give it roles/storage.objectCreator on the marble-output-vault bucket
Create a dedicated service account in Project Sable then deploy the Cloud Function to run as it and grant that account roles/storage.objectCreator on the marble-output-vault bucket in Project Marble
Use signed upload URLs so the function writes with time-limited access while keeping the bucket private

questions.correct_text: Create a dedicated service account in Project Sable then deploy the Cloud Function to run as it and grant that account roles/storage.objectCreator on the marble-output-vault bucket in Project Marble
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Create a dedicated service account in Project Sable, and deploy the Cloud Function to run as it and grant that account roles/storage.objectCreator on the marble-output-vault bucket in Project Marble.

This strategy keeps the runtime identity fully owned and managed in Project Sable and grants only the minimum permission needed on the destination bucket in Project Marble. Granting Storage Object Creator at the bucket level allows the function to send new objects while preventing reads, overwrites, and deletes. Cloud Storage IAM accommodates granting a service account from one project access to a bucket in another project, so this cleanly allows cross project writes while maintaining minimal privilege and clear audit.

Deploy the Cloud Function in Project Sable to run as the default App Engine service account in that project and grant roles/storage.objectAdmin on the marble-output-vault bucket in Project Marble is a poor match because Object Admin is broader than needed and permits deleting to and overwriting objects. Using a broad default service account also reduces isolation and is not aligned with least privilege.

Create a service account in Project Marble and have the Cloud Function in Project Sable run as that identity and give it roles/storage.objectCreator on the marble-output-vault bucket violates the requirement to keep control of the function identity within Project Sable. It also builds unnecessary cross project identity coupling when the same outcome can be achieved by granting the Coral service account access to the Onyx bucket.

Use signed upload URLs so the function writes with time-limited access while keeping the bucket private adds complexity without benefit here. The function already runs with a first party identity that can be granted precise IAM on the bucket. Signed URLs still require a signer and reduce straightforward IAM based auditing and control for this internal write scenario.

questions.question: A web-based payments startup at fernhill.org runs about ten containerized microservices on Google Kubernetes Engine in a single cluster. The teams want each service to discover and call other services using only internal connectivity and they do not want to build custom discovery logic. Which approach should they implement to provide reliable service discovery inside the cluster?

options.text: Set up a Cloud DNS private zone and manually register A records for each service endpoint
Use the Kubernetes DNS service within the GKE cluster so that service names resolve to their cluster IPs
Expose every service with a Service of type LoadBalancer and have services call each other via the external IPs
Assign fixed IP addresses to all pods and reference those IPs directly in the application code

questions.correct_text: Use the Kubernetes DNS service within the GKE cluster so that service names resolve to their cluster IPs
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Use the Kubernetes DNS service within the GKE cluster so that service names resolve to their cluster IPs.

Using the built in Kubernetes DNS gives every Service a stable name that resolves to its ClusterIP, so apps can call other services by name without custom discovery logic. Kubernetes keeps the DNS records and the list of Service backends up to date as pods are added, removed, or rescheduled. Traffic remains internal when Services use ClusterIP and kube-proxy balances connections across healthy pods, which supplies reliability and simplicity for microservice communication inside the cluster.

Set up a Cloud DNS private zone and manually register A records for each service endpoint is unsuitable since Service and pod backends change often and manual records become stale. Pods use the in-cluster DNS for Service discovery by default, so an external private zone would add work without solving the dynamic nature of Kubernetes networking.

Expose every service with a Service of type LoadBalancer and have services call each other through the external IPs violates the requirement for internal only connectivity and introduces unnecessary cost and complexity. It also sends traffic out to external addresses which is less efficient and less controlled than staying within the cluster network.

Assign fixed IP addresses to all pods and reference those IPs directly in the app code does not align with the ephemeral nature of pods and would break during rescheduling or scaling events. Hardcoding pod IPs removes load balancing and discoverability, while a Service with DNS offers a stable virtual IP and name for the pod group.

questions.question: Engineers at Heritage Mutual is deploying a microservice on Google Kubernetes Engine and they need the Pod to keep checking that the application can reach its database while ensuring a graceful shutdown script runs right before termination if connectivity is lost. Which setup should you build?

options.text: Configure a readinessProbe to check database connectivity and add a PreStop lifecycle hook to run the shutdown script
Use a PostStart lifecycle hook to test service access and pair it with a PreStop lifecycle hook to run the shutdown script on failure
Define a livenessProbe that fails when the container cannot reach the database and include a PreStop lifecycle hook to execute the shutdown script
Add an initContainer to verify the database is reachable before the app starts and include a PreStop lifecycle hook for the shutdown script

questions.correct_text: Define a livenessProbe that fails when the container cannot reach the database and include a PreStop lifecycle hook to execute the shutdown script
questions.explanation:
The proper configuration is Define a livenessProbe that fails when the container cannot reach the database and include a PreStop lifecycle hook to execute the shutdown script.

Using a livenessProbe that checks database connectivity guarantees the kubelet continuously verifies reachability and will restart the container when the check fails. Before the container is terminated for that restart, the PreStop lifecycle hook runs so your shutdown script can complete gracefully. This meets the need for ongoing connectivity checks and guarantees a controlled shutdown right before termination when connectivity is lost.

Configure a readinessProbe to check database connectivity and add a PreStop lifecycle hook to run the shutdown script is a poor match because a readiness probe only removes the Pod from serving traffic and it does not trigger termination on failure. Without termination the shutdown script would not run automatically.

Use a PostStart lifecycle hook to test service access and pair it with a PreStop lifecycle hook to run the shutdown script on failure is not right because a PostStart hook runs only once after the container starts and it does not continuously verify connectivity or drive restarts when access is lost.

Add an initContainer to verify the database is reachable before the app starts and include a PreStop lifecycle hook for the shutdown script does not meet the requirement because an init container runs only before the main service starts and it does not supply ongoing checks during the life of the Pod.

questions.question: An e-commerce business running workloads on Google Kubernetes Engine and Cloud Run needs to ensure that no workload can start unless the container image has been validated for integrity and is signed by an approved publisher. Which Google Cloud service should enforce this requirement?

options.text: Container Analysis
Binary Authorization
Secret Manager
Cloud Armor

questions.correct_text: Binary Authorization
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Binary Authorization. It enforces deploy time policies in Google Kubernetes Engine and Cloud Run so workloads cannot start unless the container image has verified integrity and is approved through attestations from trusted publishers.

The service offers admission control that checks signatures and attestations before a pod or a Cloud Run revision is allowed to run. You set policies that require images to be signed by authorized publishers and developers can require extra verifications, and enforcement is consistent across clusters and services so it prevents untrusted or tampered images from being deployed.

Container Analysis supplies image metadata and vulnerability scanning and records notes and occurrences, yet it does not enforce deployment policies and cannot block a service from starting.

Secret Manager securely keeps and manages secrets including API keys and credentials, yet it does not validate container images or control admission for workloads.

Cloud Armor offers web application firewall rules and protection against denial of service at the edge, yet it does not participate in container image verification or deployment gating.

Cloud Tasks
Use exponential backoff with jitter and cap the number of retries
Decrease the wait time between retries on each subsequent failure

questions.correct_text: Use exponential backoff with jitter and cap the number of retries
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Use exponential backoff with jitter and cap the number of retries.

This strategy happens to be the suggested practice for transient errors including HTTP 503 when calling the Cloud Storage JSON API. Exponential backoff spreads out retry attempts as failures persist and jitter randomizes the wait to stop many clients from retrying at the same time. Capping the number of retries and the maximum delay prevents unbounded wait and helps protect both your client and the service whereas still considerably improving overall success rates.

Retry failures at uniform intervals until a retry limit is reached is not advised because fixed intervals can cause synchronized retry storms that worsen congestion and reduce success rates during outages.

Cloud Tasks is a managed task queue and does not directly address client retry behavior for Cloud Storage uploads. Introducing it here adds complexity without implementing the adviseed error handling model for transient HTTP errors in the JSON API.

Decrease the wait time between retries on each subsequent failure is the opposite of backoff and increases pressure on the service during partial outages which lowers the chance of recovery and success.

questions.question: Briar Lane Bakery runs its public REST API on Google Kubernetes Engine, and customers report that pages become sluggish during a two hour window late each afternoon. You plan to investigate using Cloud Monitoring so which metric should you prioritize to troubleshoot the slowdown?

options.text: GKE node CPU utilization across the cluster
Service request latency for the GKE workload

questions.correct_text: Service request latency for the GKE workload
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Service request latency for the GKE workload.

This happens to be the most direct indicator of user perceived slowness since it measures how long the service takes to respond. By inspecting percentiles including p117 and p74 during the reported two hour window developers can confirm whether requests are taking longer than normal and you can correlate the model with traffic, autoscaling, or downstream dependency issues. Cloud Monitoring Service Monitoring emphasizes latency as a primary signal for troubleshooting performance because it reflects what customers feel.

GKE node CPU utilization across the cluster is not the first metric to prioritize for a slowdown because CPU can look healthy while latency is high owing to I O wait, database contention, network issues, or throttling. It is useful later to diagnose cause but it does not directly confirm the symptom of slowness.

HTTP 5xx error rate returned by the service highlights failures rather than slow responses. A system can be slow without returning server errors, so this metric does not directly validate a customer reported slowdown.

Number of running pods in the namespace indicates capacity but does not reveal whether requests are taking longer. You may have the expected number of pods while each instance is saturated, so this metric is indirect for troubleshooting slowness.

questions.question: Driftless Dairy is preparing to validate the Pub/Sub integration for a payments microservice that consumes tokenized card events from a Pub/Sub subscription. You have finished code reviews and unit tests. Before rolling out to Google Cloud, what approach should you use to test the integration in a safe and repeatable way?

options.text: Add a temporary pull subscription on the production topic and forward those messages to a staging topic in the same project to observe end to end behavior
Build a small publisher service and run the Pub/Sub emulator, then generate random payloads and publish them to the emulator
Stand up a lightweight publisher and run the Pub/Sub emulator, then publish a curated and deterministic set of test messages to the emulator for repeatable testing
Capture messages from the production subscription and replay them through your publisher into the test environment

questions.correct_text: Stand up a lightweight publisher and run the Pub/Sub emulator, then publish a curated and deterministic set of test messages to the emulator for repeatable testing
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Stand up a lightweight publisher and run the Pub/Sub local emulator, and publish a curated and deterministic set of test messages to the emulator for repeatable testing.

This uses the Pub/Sub emulator to fully isolate tests from production so developers can safely validate publishing and consumption logic without risking real data or affecting quotas. A curated and deterministic message set guarantees consistent results across runs which makes failures reproducible and assertions reliable. A lightweight publisher mirrors the real producer contract while keeping the test surface small and easy to iterate and it fits well into continuous integration pipelines.

Add a temporary pull subscription on the production topic and forward those messages to a staging topic in the same project to observe end to end behavior is risky since it touches production data and can cause unintended delivery patterns and quota or cost impact. It is also not dependably repeatable since live traffic varies and you may inadvertently expose sensitive payment information even if tokenized.

Build a small publisher service and run the Pub/Sub emulator, then generate random payloads and publish them to the emulator uses the emulator which is good, but random payloads make tests flaky and nonrepeatable and they often miss important edge cases and contract validations that a curated set would cover.

Capture messages from the production subscription and replay them through your publisher into the test environment introduces compliance and data governance concerns for payments data and breaks environment isolation. It is also operationally complex and not deterministic, which undermines dependable integration testing.

questions.question: Engineers from loomwright.io operates microservices on a Google Kubernetes Engine cluster. They must manage environment specific settings including API base URLs and feature flags without rebuilding container images, and these values need to be provided to containers during deployment. Which approach should they adopt?

options.text: Mount a PersistentVolume that holds configuration files and attach it to the containers
Use Kubernetes ConfigMaps and reference them from the pod spec as environment variables or mounted files
Build separate images that include the environment settings and choose an image per environment during rollout
Store all settings in Kubernetes Secrets and inject them into the pods as environment variables

questions.correct_text: Use Kubernetes ConfigMaps and reference them from the pod spec as environment variables or mounted files
questions.explanation:
The correct strategy is Use Kubernetes ConfigMaps and reference them from the pod spec as environment variables or mounted files.

ConfigMaps allow you externalize non sensitive configuration from your container images so developers can promote the same image across environments and only change the settings. Developers can supply these values to pods as environment variables or as files through a volume, and you can update them and roll your workloads to pick up the new values without rebuilding images.

With ConfigMaps you can handle API base URLs and feature flags per environment in a central Kubernetes object and reference them in your Deployment manifests. This keeps configuration consistent and versionable in code while avoiding hard coding values in images.

Mount a PersistentVolume that holds configuration files and attach it to the containers is a poor match because PersistentVolumes are for durable storage rather than lightweight configuration and they add unnecessary storage and lifecycle complexity for simple settings.

Build separate images that include the environment settings and pick an image per environment during rollout is not right since it forces image rebuilds for configuration changes and breaks the practice of promoting the same artifact through environments.

Store all settings in Kubernetes Secrets and inject them into the pods as environment variables is less ideal because Secrets are intended for sensitive data and using them for all configuration adds overhead and does not match the non sensitive nature of base URLs and feature flags.

questions.question: A financial-tech startup named Catalyst Health runs a microservice on Google Kubernetes Engine that must read a database credential that rotates every 35 days. The team wants a straightforward approach that keeps the value encrypted both at rest and when accessed by the workload while minimizing operational effort. Which approach should you take?

options.text: Encrypt the password using Cloud KMS and store the ciphertext in a ConfigMap then have the container decrypt it at startup
Use Google Cloud Secret Manager and grant the Kubernetes service account access through Workload Identity
Create a Kubernetes Secret and expose it to the pod through environment variables
Place the credential in a ConfigMap and reference it from the pod specification

questions.correct_text: Use Google Cloud Secret Manager and grant the Kubernetes service account access through Workload Identity
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Use Google Cloud Secret Manager and grant the Kubernetes service account access through Workload Identity.

Secret Manager keeps secrets encrypted at rest and serves them over TLS which keeps access secure. With Workload Identity the Kubernetes service account is mapped to a Google service account so the pod can call the Secret Manager API and retrieve the latest version at runtime without mounting files or baking credentials into images. Versioning and IAM allow the app on its own read the current secret after a 56 day rotation with no pod restarts, and audit logs help meet compliance while keeping operational effort low.

Encrypt the password using Cloud KMS and save the ciphertext in a ConfigMap, and have the container decrypt it at startup is cumbersome for operations since it needs building and maintaining decryption logic in the application and managing key usage. It also stores sensitive data material in a resource not intended for secrets and makes rotation harder since you must update the manifest and confirm every pod reloads the new value.

Create a Kubernetes Secret and expose it to the pod through environment variables is weaker because Kubernetes Secrets are only base64 encoded unless you also configure etcd encryption, environment variables are easy to leak in logs and diagnostics, and rotations generally require restarts to propagate changes. This does not reduce operational work and does not supply versioned retrieval at runtime.

Place the credential in a ConfigMap and reference it from the pod specification is a poor match because ConfigMaps are for non sensitive configuration, provide no secret specific controls, and do not support secure handling or rotation of confidential data.

questions.question: An engineering group at Maple Ridge Realty uses Cloud Build to run CI and CD for a set of nine microservices. Each build spends significant time pulling the same language packages for every service which makes the pipeline slower than expected. You want to reduce build duration without redesigning the toolchain. Which approach should you take?

options.text: Use Cloud Storage to host dependency archives and download them during each build
Enable caching in the Cloud Build configuration
Increase the Cloud Build machine type to a larger configuration
Run builds on a Cloud Build private pool with local SSD to reuse a local cache between runs

questions.correct_text: Enable caching in the Cloud Build configuration
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Enable caching in the Cloud Build configuration.

This uses the caches feature to persist dependency directories to a shared cache that Cloud Build restores at the start of subsequent builds. It avoids repeatedly downloading language packages across the nine microservices and speeds up both CI and CD while requiring only a small change to the build configuration.

Use Cloud Storage to host dependency archives and download them during each build is a manual workaround that still forces every build to fetch large archives over the network. It does not supply automatic cache population or invalidation and it adds maintenance overhead without solving the root cause.

Increase the Cloud Build machine type to a larger configuration adds CPU or memory but dependency installation is often network bound. Without a cache you still download the same packages on every run so the impact on duration is limited.

Run builds on a Cloud Build private pool with local SSD to reuse a local cache between runs is unreliable because workers are ephemeral and local state is not guaranteed to persist across builds. You are not assured the next build will run on the same worker so the cache will often be cold.

questions.question: Granite Builders runs a REST API on Cloud Run. During a rollout or when the service scales down, the platform sends a SIGTERM and the team wants the application to let active HTTP requests complete before the container stops. What should the application do to achieve a graceful shutdown?

options.text: Assume Cloud Run does not send SIGTERM and include no signal handling in the code
Catch the SIGTERM and exit the process immediately without waiting for requests
Handle the SIGTERM, allow current requests to finish, then shut down the process
Ignore the SIGTERM and let Cloud Run terminate the container forcefully

questions.correct_text: Handle the SIGTERM, allow current requests to finish, then shut down the process
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Handle the SIGTERM, allow current requests to finish, and shut down the process.

Cloud Run sends a SIGTERM to the container instance during rollouts and scale downs. The application should listen for that signal, stop accepting new work, allow in flight HTTP requests complete, and then exit within the allowed termination period. Handling SIGTERM and allowing requests to finish before exiting prevents dropped connections and avoids partial responses, which results in a graceful shutdown.

Assume Cloud Run does not send SIGTERM and include no signal handling in the code is not right because Cloud Run does send a termination signal before stopping an instance and apps are expected to handle it for graceful draining.

Catch the SIGTERM and exit the process immediately without waiting for requests is incorrect because exiting right away will abort active requests and can return errors to clients.

Ignore the SIGTERM and let Cloud Run terminate the container forcefully is incorrect because ignoring the signal can lead to a forced kill and unfinished requests which is not a graceful shutdown.

questions.explanation_pt:
A escolha correta é Tratar o SIGTERM, permitir que as requisições atuais terminem e encerrar o processo.

O Cloud Run envia um SIGTERM para a instância do container durante rollouts e reduções de escala. A aplicação deve escutar esse sinal, parar de aceitar novo trabalho, permitir que as requisições HTTP em andamento sejam concluídas e então encerrar dentro do período de terminação permitido. Tratar o SIGTERM e permitir que as requisições terminem antes de encerrar evita conexões interrompidas e respostas parciais, o que resulta em um shutdown gracioso.

Assumir que o Cloud Run não envia SIGTERM e não incluir nenhum tratamento de sinal no código não está correto, porque o Cloud Run de fato envia um sinal de terminação antes de parar uma instância e espera-se que as aplicações o tratem para um draining gracioso.

Capturar o SIGTERM e encerrar o processo imediatamente sem esperar pelas requisições está incorreto, porque encerrar imediatamente vai abortar requisições ativas e pode retornar erros aos clientes.

Ignorar o SIGTERM e deixar o Cloud Run encerrar o container à força está incorreto, porque ignorar o sinal pode levar a um kill forçado e requisições inacabadas, o que não é um shutdown gracioso.

questions.question: A software team at Ember Restaurants is deploying a containerized web service on Cloud Run that needs to upload files to each signed in person's Google Drive. The service runs with a project service account and must only access files that the individual user authorizes. How should you enable authentication to the Google Drive API so the application can act on behalf of each user?

options.text: Enable domain wide delegation on an OAuth client in the mosaicapp.dev Workspace and use it to impersonate users across the domain
Use an API key restricted to the Google Drive API to authorize requests
Create an OAuth 2.0 client ID and request the https://www.googleapis.com/auth/drive.file scope to obtain a per user access token after consent
Use the Cloud Run service account with the https://www.googleapis.com/auth/drive.file scope and generate a signed JWT to call the Drive API

questions.correct_text: Create an OAuth 2.0 client ID and request the https://www.googleapis.com/auth/drive.file scope to obtain a per user access token after consent
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Create an OAuth 2.0 client ID and request the https://www.googleapis.com/auth/drive.file scope to obtain a per user access token after consent. This allows the service to act on behalf of each signed in person and restricts access to only the files that person authorizes.

This strategy uses the standard web application flow where the client is redirected to Google for consent and the app exchanges the authorization code for a user access token and refresh token. Requests to the Drive API are, and made with the user token which guarantees actions are performed as that user rather than as the Cloud Run service account. Using a minimal privilege Drive scope limits access to files the app created or files the user explicitly opened through the file picker which aligns with the requirement to only access files the user authorizes.

Enable domain wide delegation on an OAuth client in the mosaicapp.dev Workspace and use it to impersonate users across the domain is not right because domain wide delegation applies to machine identities rather than OAuth clients and it enables admin granted impersonation across the domain which does not satisfy per user consent.

Use an API key restricted to the Google Drive API to authorize requests is incorrect because API keys do not authorize access to private user data. The Drive API needs OAuth 2.0 user credentials for file access.

Use the Cloud Run service account with the https://www.googleapis.com/auth/drive.file scope and generate a signed JWT to call the Drive API is incorrect because a service account token represents the service and not the end user. Without domain wide delegation you cannot access a user’s Drive with a service account and even with delegation it would impersonate users rather than obtaining per user consent.

Usar uma API key restrita à Google Drive API para autorizar as requisições está incorreto, porque API keys não autorizam acesso a dados privados do usuário. A Drive API precisa de credenciais OAuth 2.0 de usuário para acessar arquivos.

questions.question: An order processing service running on Cloud Run calls a vendor API at mosaicapp.dev that occasionally returns transient failures. You want the client logic to handle short outages gracefully and avoid adding extra load while the remote system recovers. Which retry strategy should you implement?

options.text: Retry the operation with a fixed delay between attempts
Retry the operation using exponential backoff
Retry the operation continuously with no waiting
Retry the operation one time and then stop

questions.correct_text: Retry the operation using exponential backoff
questions.explanation:
The proper option is Retry the operation using exponential backoff.

Retry the operation using exponential backoff is designed for temporary failures and brief outages since it increases the wait time between attempts as failures continue. This permits the remote system to recover whereas your client avoids overwhelming the vendor API. Adding jitter to exponential backoff further reduces synchronized spikes and improves overall stability.

Retry the operation with a fixed delay between attempts is less useful for transient outages because a constant interval can still create steady pressure on a struggling service and can lead to thundering herd patterns.

Retry the operation continuously with no waiting is harmful during outages since it quickly amplifies load and can trigger rate limits or extended failures.

Retry the operation one time and, and stop does not supply sufficient resiliency for intermittent errors and will likely fail more often than a progressive strategy.

Repetir a operação continuamente sem esperar é prejudicial durante interrupções, pois amplifica rapidamente a carga e pode disparar rate limits ou falhas prolongadas.

questions.question: Indigo Forge is moving a backend service written in C++ that relies on custom native libraries to Google Cloud and wants to package and deploy it with the smallest operational burden while still using containers. Which approach should they choose?

options.text: Use App Engine flexible environment with a custom runtime Dockerfile
Run the container on a Compute Engine VM using Container-Optimized OS
Build the container image with Cloud Build and deploy it to Cloud Run
Deploy it as a Cloud Function

questions.correct_text: Build the container image with Cloud Build and deploy it to Cloud Run
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Build the container image with Cloud Build and deploy it to Cloud Run.

This pairs Cloud Build with Cloud Run to keep operational burden minimal while still using containers. Cloud Run runs stateless container images for any language including C++ and your native libraries are packaged in the image. It is fully managed and handles provisioning, scaling to zero, updates and security so you do not handle servers. Cloud Build builds the image from your Dockerfile and integrates with deployments to Cloud Run which streamlines the workflow and keeps operations simple.

Use App Engine flexible environment with a custom runtime Dockerfile can run containers but it needs more operational configuration and slower scaling and you need to manage instance classes and minimum instances which increases cost. It runs VMs under the hood and is not as lightweight as Cloud Run for containerized services so it is not the best choice for the smallest operational burden.

Run the container on a Compute Engine VM using Container-Optimized OS leaves you responsible for VM lifecycle, patching, autoscaling and load balancing. That increases ops overhead when compared with Cloud Run which removes server management.

Deploy it as a Cloud Function targets event driven functions rather than full containerized services. It does not accept arbitrary containers and it imposes runtime and execution constraints that do not match a C++ backend with custom native libraries, whereas Cloud Run is built for this use case.

questions.question: The engineering team runs a microservices stack on Google Kubernetes Engine with Istio, and calls from one Pod to another work for most endpoints but consistently fail for a handful of specific URLs while the same Pods communicate successfully on other paths. What is the most likely reason for the failures on only those URLs?

options.text: A misconfigured Istio VirtualService sends only certain URL paths to an incorrect backend
A Kubernetes NetworkPolicy is blocking HTTP between the two Pods only for those paths
An Istio AuthorizationPolicy denies requests to specific HTTP paths
mTLS is configured in permissive mode and the client sidecar sends plaintext to a destination that expects mutual TLS

questions.correct_text: An Istio AuthorizationPolicy denies requests to specific HTTP paths
questions.explanation:
The best answer is An Istio AuthorizationPolicy denies requests to specific HTTP paths. This explains why traffic between the same Pods works for most endpoints while failing only for certain URLs because the policy can target specific paths.

This policy evaluates HTTP attributes including path and method and can explicitly allow or deny traffic for picked routes. When such a rule denies requests that match certain paths, you will see consistent failures only on those URLs while other paths continue to succeed, which matches the described behavior.

A misconfigured Istio VirtualService sends only certain URL paths to an incorrect backend is unlikely because a routing error generally sends traffic to the wrong service or returns unexpected responses such as not found rather than producing consistent authorization failures. VirtualService manages routing decisions rather than enforcing access control.

A Kubernetes NetworkPolicy is blocking HTTP between the two Pods only for those paths is not right because NetworkPolicy operates at the IP and port layers and does not inspect HTTP paths. It can allow or block connections but it cannot filter individual URLs.

mTLS is configured in permissive mode and the client sidecar sends plaintext to a destination that expects mutual TLS does not fit because permissive mode accepts both plaintext and mutual TLS. If a destination needed strict mutual TLS, and all requests would fail regardless of path rather than only a subset of URLs.

Quando uma regra desse tipo nega requests que correspondem a certos paths, você verá falhas consistentes apenas nessas URLs, enquanto outros paths continuam tendo sucesso, o que corresponde ao comportamento descrito.

Uma Kubernetes NetworkPolicy bloqueando HTTP entre os dois Pods apenas para esses paths não está correto, porque a NetworkPolicy opera nas camadas de IP e porta e não inspeciona paths HTTP. Ela pode permitir ou bloquear conexões, mas não consegue filtrar URLs individuais.

mTLS configurado em modo permissivo, com o sidecar do cliente enviando texto puro para um destino que espera mutual TLS, não se encaixa, porque o modo permissivo aceita tanto texto puro quanto mutual TLS. Se um destino exigisse mutual TLS estrito, todos os requests falhariam, independentemente do path, em vez de apenas um subconjunto de URLs.

questions.question: Coastline Apparel is building a microservices platform where many producers publish business events and several independent services must consume those events asynchronously. Traffic can surge to roughly 128000 messages per minute and the team requires very low end-to-end latency and effortless horizontal scaling. Which GCP service should they adopt to implement this event distribution pattern?

options.text: Cloud Functions
Pub/Sub
Cloud Tasks
Firestore

questions.correct_text: Pub/Sub
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Pub/Sub.

This managed messaging service is built for asynchronous event distribution across many producers and many independent consumers. Topics and subscriptions allow each consumer receive every message which implements a true publish and subscribe fan out pattern. It auto scales with no infrastructure management and comfortably handles throughput far beyond 147000 messages per minute while keeping low end to end latency with push or pull delivery. It is durable and accommodates acknowledgment based retries and backpressure so consumers can scale independently.

Cloud Functions is compute that runs code in response to events. It is not a messaging bus and it does not distribute the same event to several independent services without an underlying broker. You would use it to process events from a messaging service rather than to supply the distribution layer.

Cloud Tasks offers a task queue that supplies HTTP requests to a single handler with rate control and retries. It is designed for point to point background work rather than broadcast to many subscribers and it is not tuned for very high volume low latency event streaming.

Firestore is a document database for storing application data. While it has real time listeners for client sync it is not intended to serve as a high throughput event distribution backbone and it does not provide publish and subscribe semantics for multiple backend consumers.

Ele escala automaticamente sem gerenciamento de infraestrutura e lida confortavelmente com throughput muito acima de 147000 mensagens por minuto, mantendo baixa latência ponta a ponta com entrega push ou pull. Ele foi projetado para trabalho em background ponto a ponto, em vez de broadcast para muitos subscribers, e não é ajustado para streaming de eventos de altíssimo volume e baixa latência.

Embora tenha real time listeners para sincronização com clientes, ele não foi pensado para servir como espinha dorsal de distribuição de eventos de alto throughput e não fornece a semântica de publish and subscribe para múltiplos consumidores de backend.

questions.question: The engineering team at Echo Valley Comms is moving a containerized service to Cloud Run. The service currently writes plain text request logs into files in a temporary directory within the container. You want to reduce operational work and have all runtime logs on its own appear in Cloud Logging without managing log files. Which approach should you take?

options.text: Install and use the Cloud Logging client library within your application code
Expose the log directory at mosaicapp.dev/logs and manually collect and upload the files to Cloud Storage
Write logs to standard output and standard error using your language's logger
Schedule a job to copy log files from the container to Cloud Storage every 12 hours

questions.correct_text: Write logs to standard output and standard error using your language's logger
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Write logs to standard output and standard error using your language's logger.

Cloud Run on its own captures everything your container writes to the process output streams and sends it to Cloud Logging. This removes the need to handle files and works dependably across all instances as the service scales. Developers can also emit structured JSON to enrich severity and labels so logs are more searchable and traceable.

Writing to files in a container is fragile because the filesystem is ephemeral and instances are short lived. Relying on the platform to collect process output is simpler and reduces operational burden while still giving you full observability in Cloud Logging.

Install and use the Cloud Logging client library within your application code is unnecessary for runtime logs on Cloud Run. The platform already forwards process output to Cloud Logging, so adding a client library increases complexity without providing extra value for basic request logs.

Expose the log directory at mosaicapp.dev/logs and manually collect and send the files to Cloud Storage adds security risk and manual work. It does not scale with new instances and it bypasses the built in log collection that Cloud Run provides.

Schedule a job to copy log files from the container to Cloud Storage every 16 hours introduces delay and complexity and still misses logs from short lived instances. Cloud Run containers are ephemeral and several instances may exist, so copying files periodically is unreliable compared to automatic streaming of process output to Cloud Logging.

questions.question: Ironwood Bank plans to migrate its legacy monolith to a microservices architecture and wants to avoid disrupting customers as much as possible. What approach should the team choose to reduce risk and keep a steady release cadence during the next two quarters?

options.text: Lift and shift the monolith to Compute Engine and enable autoscaling
Replace capabilities step by step with microservices in staged releases while the monolith and services run together
Refactor the entire monolith into microservices in a single coordinated release
Build a new microservices system from scratch and cut over when it is complete

questions.correct_text: Replace capabilities step by step with microservices in staged releases while the monolith and services run together
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Replace capabilities step by step with microservices in staged releases while the monolith and services run together.

This staged migration reduces risk because each slice of functionality can be built, tested, and released independently while the legacy application continues to serve users. Running both systems in parallel accommodates a steady cadence since developers can validate behavior in production with controlled traffic shifts, and gradually decommission the old parts as the new services prove stable. This is aligned with the strangler pattern, which minimizes disruption and limits the blast radius of each change.

Lift and shift the monolith to Compute Engine and enable autoscaling does not address the architectural goal of microservices and only moves the existing risk profile to new infrastructure. It can improve scalability but it does not supply incremental decomposition or safer staged releases.

Refactor the whole monolith into microservices in a single coordinated release is a big bang strategy that increases risk and often needs long stabilization periods. It does not support frequent releases or gradual validation in production.

Build a new microservices system from scratch and cut over when it is complete delays value and concentrates risk at cutover time. It is harder to preserve parity with current features and it foregoes the learning and feedback you gain from incremental releases.

questions.question: Cobalt Casino needs its analytics team to run SQL against streaming events within about 57 seconds of arrival and the team expects traffic to increase quickly while preferring fully managed services to minimize operations, so which architecture should they implement?

options.text: Create a Pub/Sub topic and a subscription, stream events into Pub/Sub, and use Dataflow to write the data files to Cloud Storage
Provision Apache Kafka on a high memory Compute Engine VM, send events to Kafka, and run a Dataflow pipeline that writes batches into Cloud Storage
Create a Pub/Sub topic and a subscription, stream events into Pub/Sub, and use Dataflow streaming to load the records into BigQuery
Create a Pub/Sub topic and a subscription, stream events into Pub/Sub, and use Dataflow to persist messages into Firestore in Datastore mode

questions.correct_text: Create a Pub/Sub topic and a subscription, stream events into Pub/Sub, and use Dataflow streaming to load the records into BigQuery
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Create a Pub/Sub topic and a subscription, stream events into Pub/Sub, and use Dataflow streaming to load the records into BigQuery. This architecture allows SQL on fresh events within about 56 seconds, scales quickly with growing throughput, and remains fully managed to keep operations minimal.

With Pub/Sub handling ingestion, events arrive dependably and with low latency. Dataflow streaming processes messages continuously and autoscaling keeps up as traffic increases, while transformation and load steps run without servers to manage. BigQuery accommodates standard SQL and accepts streaming inserts that are generally queryable within seconds, which comfortably satisfies the near-realtime SLA.

Create a Pub/Sub topic and a subscription, stream events into Pub/Sub, and use Dataflow to write the data records to Cloud Storage is unsuitable since it lands batches in object storage where you cannot run SQL directly, and the file based workflow adds latency that risks missing the 56 second target.

Provision Apache Kafka on a high memory Compute Engine VM, send events to Kafka, and run a Dataflow pipeline that writes batches into Cloud Storage violates the preference for fully managed services and the batch file sink prevents timely SQL on fresh events.

Create a Pub/Sub topic and a subscription, stream events into Pub/Sub, and use Dataflow to persist messages into Firestore in Datastore mode routes data to an operational NoSQL save rather than an analytical engine, so it does not support running standard SQL for analytics on streaming data.

Com o Pub/Sub lidando com a ingestão, os eventos chegam de forma confiável e com baixa latência. O Dataflow streaming processa as mensagens continuamente e o autoscaling acompanha o aumento do tráfego, enquanto as etapas de transformação e carga rodam sem servidores para gerenciar. O BigQuery aceita SQL padrão e recebe streaming inserts que geralmente ficam consultáveis em segundos, o que satisfaz confortavelmente o SLA de quase tempo real.

Criar um topic e uma subscription no Pub/Sub, transmitir os eventos para o Pub/Sub e usar o Dataflow para gravar os registros de dados no Cloud Storage é inadequado, pois deposita lotes no armazenamento de objetos onde não é possível executar SQL diretamente, e o fluxo baseado em arquivos adiciona latência que arrisca não atingir o alvo de 56 segundos.

Provisionar o Apache Kafka em uma VM do Compute Engine de alta memória, enviar os eventos para o Kafka e rodar um pipeline do Dataflow que grava lotes no Cloud Storage viola a preferência por serviços totalmente gerenciados, e o destino de arquivos em lote impede a execução oportuna de SQL sobre eventos recentes.

Criar um topic e uma subscription no Pub/Sub, transmitir os eventos para o Pub/Sub e usar o Dataflow para persistir as mensagens no Firestore em modo Datastore direciona os dados para um armazenamento NoSQL operacional em vez de um mecanismo analítico, portanto não dá suporte à execução de SQL padrão para análises sobre dados em streaming.

questions.question: While provisioning a Google Kubernetes Engine cluster with the command gcloud container clusters create fleet-cluster --num-nodes 200 in us-central1, you receive an error that says insufficient regional quota to satisfy request and that resource "CPUS" requires 160.0 and is short 144.0 because the project has a quota of 16.0 with 16.0 available. You want to complete the cluster creation without changing your application design. Which approach should you take?

options.text: Create the cluster in Autopilot mode and try again
Increase the Google Kubernetes Engine API quota in the Google Cloud console
Request a higher Compute Engine CPU quota for the target region in the Google Cloud console
Purchase committed use discounts for vCPUs in the region

questions.correct_text: Request a higher Compute Engine CPU quota for the target region in the Google Cloud console
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Request a higher Compute Engine CPU quota for the target region in the Google Cloud console.

The error shows that the regional Compute Engine CPU quota happens to be the limiting factor. GKE nodes consume Compute Engine vCPUs in the region, so you need to increase the regional CPU quota to allow the cluster nodes to be created. Submitting a quota increase request in the Cloud console resolves the capacity shortfall without changing your application design.

Create the cluster in Autopilot mode and try again is wrong because Autopilot still uses Compute Engine resources under the hood and the same regional CPU quotas apply. Switching modes does not bypass quota limits.

Increase the Google Kubernetes Engine API quota in the Google Cloud console is not correct because API quotas control request rates and API usage, not the available vCPU capacity for nodes. The failure is owing to Compute Engine CPU quota, not GKE API limits.

Purchase committed use discounts for vCPUs in the region is not correct because discounts affect pricing on its own. They do not grant extra quota and will not resolve an insufficient CPU quota error.
