questions.question: Vanguard Couriers is building a community chat service on Google Cloud and plans to use Cloud Firestore. The app will support dozens of chat channels and it must keep each channel's messages for 72 days for search and moderation. How should you model the data in Firestore to keep reads and writes efficient as channels grow?

options.text: Create a top level collection named messages with one document per message and include a channelId field then keep a separate channels collection only for channel metadata
Create one collection named rooms containing a document per room and store an array field that holds the full text of the last 90 days of messages in each room document
Create a collection named channels where each channel document contains a messages subcollection and store each message as its own document with a timestamp
Create a separate top level collection for each channel and place one document per message in that collection with no parent channel document

questions.correct_text: Create a collection named channels where each channel document contains a messages subcollection and store each message as its own document with a timestamp
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Create a collection named channels where each channel document contains a messages subcollection and save each message as its own document with a timestamp.

This hierarchical model mirrors how the app will access data and it keeps each channel’s traffic isolated. Each message is a small document that can be written and read independently which accommodates high write throughput and efficient pagination with queries that filter by the channel and order by timestamp. The timestamp also allows range queries to fetch recent history and it handles automatic cleanup using a time to live policy to meet the 110 day retention requirement.

This structure simplifies security rules and lifecycle operations. Developers can secure and handle a channel at its document and subcollection boundary and developers can delete or archive a channel by targeting its subcollection. If you ever need cross channel analytics you can still use collection group queries over the messages subcollections without changing the data model.

Create a top level collection named messages with one document per message and include a channelId field, and keep a separate channels collection only for channel metadata is less optimal since it mixes all channels in one large collection which makes per channel access rely on filtering rather than natural hierarchy. It complicates targeted lifecycle actions like deleting a single channel’s data and makes rule scoping and organization harder as the dataset grows.

Create one collection named rooms containing a document per room and store an array field that holds the full text of the last 112 days of messages in each room document is not scalable. Arrays that grow to hold many messages risk hitting document size limits and every new message writes the whole document which increases contention and cost. It also prevents efficient indexing and pagination of individual messages.

Create a separate top level collection for each channel and place one document per message in that collection with no parent channel document scatters data across many uniquely named collections which makes discovery and management difficult. It prevents simple collection group queries across all channels and removes a natural place to store channel metadata and enforce channel level permissions.

A escolha correta é criar uma collection chamada channels onde cada documento de channel contém uma subcollection messages e salvar cada mensagem como seu próprio documento com um timestamp.

Esse modelo hierárquico espelha a forma como o app acessará os dados e mantém o tráfego de cada channel isolado. Cada mensagem é um documento pequeno que pode ser escrito e lido de forma independente, o que acomoda alta vazão de escrita e paginação eficiente com queries que filtram pelo channel e ordenam por timestamp. O timestamp também permite range queries para buscar o histórico recente e lida com a limpeza automática usando uma política de time to live para atender ao requisito de retenção de 110 dias.

Essa estrutura simplifica as regras de segurança e as operações de ciclo de vida. Os desenvolvedores podem proteger e tratar um channel no limite de seu documento e subcollection, e podem excluir ou arquivar um channel direcionando sua subcollection. Se algum dia você precisar de análises entre channels, ainda pode usar collection group queries sobre as subcollections messages sem alterar o modelo de dados.

Criar uma collection de nível superior chamada messages com um documento por mensagem e incluir um campo channelId, mantendo uma collection channels separada apenas para os metadados do channel, é menos ótimo, pois mistura todos os channels em uma única collection grande, o que faz o acesso por channel depender de filtragem em vez da hierarquia natural. Isso complica ações de ciclo de vida direcionadas, como excluir os dados de um único channel, e dificulta o escopo das regras e a organização conforme o conjunto de dados cresce.

Criar uma collection chamada rooms contendo um documento por room e armazenar um campo array que guarda o texto completo dos últimos 112 dias de mensagens em cada documento de room não é escalável. Arrays que crescem para conter muitas mensagens arriscam atingir os limites de tamanho de documento, e cada nova mensagem reescreve o documento inteiro, o que aumenta a contenção e o custo. Isso também impede a indexação e a paginação eficientes de mensagens individuais.

Criar uma collection de nível superior separada para cada channel e colocar um documento por mensagem nessa collection sem um documento de channel pai espalha os dados por muitas collections com nomes únicos, o que dificulta a descoberta e o gerenciamento. Isso impede collection group queries simples entre todos os channels e elimina um lugar natural para armazenar os metadados do channel e impor permissões em nível de channel.

questions.question: A digital media analytics service at mosaicapp.dev runs on Google Kubernetes Engine and users have reported sporadic increases in response time over the past 55 minutes. As the developer on call, what is the first action you should take to begin diagnosing the latency?

options.text: Increase CPU and memory requests and limits for the pods in the cluster
Use Cloud Profiler to collect runtime CPU and heap profiles from the service
Open Cloud Logging and inspect recent application logs for errors and latency details
Examine Cloud Trace to view distributed request latency across services

questions.correct_text: Open Cloud Logging and inspect recent application logs for errors and latency details
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Open Cloud Logging and inspect recent application logs for errors and latency details. This happens to be the best first step since it gives immediate visibility into errors and request timings during the exact window when users reported issues.

Logs are aggregated from pods and services, which permits you to quickly check for spikes in error rates, slow handler durations, timeouts, or resource warnings over the past 34 minutes. Developers can filter by service, namespace, severity, and known error strings to narrow the problem and correlate with recent deploys or autoscaling events. This fast feedback helps you decide what to investigate next and whether the issue is code, dependency, or infrastructure related.

Increase CPU and memory requests and limits for the pods in the cluster is a remediation step rather than an initial diagnostic step. Changing resource settings without evidence could worsen scheduling or cause unnecessary restarts. You should gather data first to confirm resource pressure.

Use Cloud Profiler to collect runtime CPU and heap profiles from the service is powerful for code level performance analysis, yet it is not the first move for a sudden or intermittent latency report. Profiler data is sampled over time and best used after you confirm a CPU bound or memory related bottleneck from logs and metrics.

Examine Cloud Trace to view distributed request latency across services is helpful when tracing is enabled and you need end to end latency breakdowns, but it is not as immediate as logs for catching errors, timeouts, or configuration issues. Use tracing after the initial log review to follow specific slow requests across services.

Os logs são agregados a partir dos pods e services, o que permite verificar rapidamente picos nas taxas de erro, durações lentas de handlers, timeouts ou avisos de recursos nos últimos 34 minutos. Os desenvolvedores podem filtrar por service, namespace, severidade e strings de erro conhecidas para delimitar o problema e correlacioná-lo com deploys recentes ou eventos de autoscaling. Esse feedback rápido ajuda a decidir o que investigar em seguida e se o problema está relacionado ao código, a uma dependência ou à infraestrutura.

Alterar as configurações de recursos sem evidências poderia piorar o agendamento ou causar reinícios desnecessários. Você deve coletar dados primeiro para confirmar a pressão de recursos.

Usar o Cloud Profiler para coletar profiles de CPU e heap em tempo de execução do service é poderoso para análise de desempenho em nível de código, mas não é o primeiro movimento para um relato de latência súbita ou intermitente. Os dados do Profiler são amostrados ao longo do tempo e melhor usados depois que você confirma, a partir de logs e métricas, um gargalo limitado por CPU ou relacionado à memória.

Examinar o Cloud Trace para visualizar a latência distribuída das requisições entre services é útil quando o tracing está habilitado e você precisa de detalhamentos de latência de ponta a ponta, mas não é tão imediato quanto os logs para capturar erros, timeouts ou problemas de configuração. Use o tracing depois da revisão inicial dos logs para acompanhar requisições lentas específicas entre os services.

questions.question: A logistics company named Saffron Spices is releasing a major redesign of a payments microservice that runs on Google Kubernetes Engine, and the change alters request flows and adds new service dependencies. You want to keep the blast radius small while you watch error rates and latency before rolling out to everyone, so which rollout approach should you choose?

options.text: Use the default rolling update strategy in the GKE Deployment so new pods gradually replace old pods across the cluster
Gate the feature behind a feature flag and enable it for every user at the same time once the build passes tests
Use a canary rollout that sends a small portion of traffic to the new version and expand gradually when telemetry shows no regressions
Perform a Blue and Green deployment and switch all traffic to the new release after a final smoke test

questions.correct_text: Use a canary rollout that sends a small portion of traffic to the new version and expand gradually when telemetry shows no regressions
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Use a canary rollout that sends a small portion of traffic to the new version and expand gradually when telemetry shows no regressions. This strategy keeps the blast radius small and permits you to watch error rates and latency before expanding to more users.

A canary rollout aligns with progressive delivery on GKE. You send a small percentage of production traffic to the new version and use monitoring to confirm no regressions. If metrics look good, and you incrementally increase traffic until all users receive the new release. This method directly addresses the goal of limiting impact while you observe real telemetry.

Use the default rolling update strategy in the GKE Deployment so new pods gradually replace old pods across the cluster is not sufficient because a rolling update focuses on replacing pods and not on controlling the share of user traffic. Once new pods are ready the Service sends normal load balanced traffic to them which can expose many users at once and that does not keep the blast radius small.

Gate the feature behind a feature flag and enable it for every user at the same time once the build passes tests does not meet the requirement because turning it on for everyone at once is onen all at once exposure. While feature flags are useful for quick disable they do not supply gradual traffic ramping in this scenario.

Perform a Blue and Green deployment and switch all traffic to the new release after a final smoke test allows fast rollback yet it moves all traffic in one step. That does not allow you observe live metrics with a small subset of users before expanding the rollout.

questions.explanation_pt:
A escolha correta é usar um canary rollout que envia uma pequena parcela do tráfego para a nova versão e expande gradualmente quando a telemetria mostra que não há regressões. Essa estratégia mantém o raio de impacto pequeno e permite observar as taxas de erro e a latência antes de expandir para mais usuários.

Um canary rollout está alinhado com a entrega progressiva no GKE. Você envia uma pequena porcentagem do tráfego de produção para a nova versão e usa o monitoramento para confirmar que não há regressões. Se as métricas parecerem boas, você aumenta o tráfego de forma incremental até que todos os usuários recebam o novo release. Esse método aborda diretamente o objetivo de limitar o impacto enquanto você observa a telemetria real.

Usar a estratégia padrão de rolling update no Deployment do GKE para que os novos pods substituam gradualmente os pods antigos pelo cluster não é suficiente, porque um rolling update foca em substituir pods e não em controlar a parcela do tráfego de usuários. Assim que os novos pods estiverem prontos, o Service envia o tráfego normal com balanceamento de carga para eles, o que pode expor muitos usuários de uma vez e não mantém o raio de impacto pequeno.

Proteger o recurso atrás de um feature flag e habilitá-lo para todos os usuários ao mesmo tempo quando o build passar nos testes não atende ao requisito, porque ativá-lo para todos de uma só vez é uma exposição total simultânea. Embora feature flags sejam úteis para desativar rapidamente, eles não fornecem o aumento gradual de tráfego neste cenário.

Realizar um Blue and Green deployment e alternar todo o tráfego para o novo release após um smoke test final permite rollback rápido, mas move todo o tráfego em uma única etapa. Isso não permite observar as métricas ao vivo com um pequeno subconjunto de usuários antes de expandir o rollout.

questions.question: The engineering team at loomwright.io operates a Google Kubernetes Engine cluster for a billing service, and a new Deployment keeps restarting because the application starts before a setup script creates a configuration file and warms a cache, and you need the setup to finish before the primary container launches. Which Kubernetes feature should you use to enforce this startup ordering so the Pods stabilize?

options.text: Readiness probes
Persistent Volumes
Init Containers
DaemonSet

questions.correct_text: Init Containers
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Init Containers.

Init Containers run and complete before any app containers start, which permits you to run your setup script to create the configuration file and warm the cache. By placing the initialization logic in an init container, the primary container will only launch after the setup has finished, which prevents repeated restarts and allows the Pods to stabilize.

Readiness probes only control when a Pod is considered ready to receive traffic. They do not delay the start of the main container, so they will not enforce the needed startup ordering.

Persistent Volumes supply durable storage for Pods. They do not provide a mechanism to orchestrate execution order between containers in a Pod.

DaemonSet guarantees that a Pod runs on each node in the cluster. It does not handle intra Pod startup sequencing or gate the app container on a setup step.

Readiness probes apenas controlam quando um Pod e considerado pronto para receber trafego. Elas nao atrasam o inicio do container principal, portanto nao garantem a ordem de inicializacao necessaria.

questions.question: Umbra Security runs a customer API backed by Cloud Bigtable as the primary database. The current Bigtable app profile uses single cluster routing and the operations team performs a manual failover if the us-central1 cluster is unavailable. You plan to add a second cluster in europe-west1 and you want client traffic to remain efficient and highly available without manual intervention. What should you change to achieve this?

options.text: Deploy Memorystore for Memcached to cache reads in front of Bigtable
Update the app profile to use multi cluster routing so requests can go to any healthy cluster automatically
Increase the Bigtable client connection pool to allow more simultaneous RPCs
Create a second replicated cluster and keep the app profile configured for single cluster routing

questions.correct_text: Update the app profile to use multi cluster routing so requests can go to any healthy cluster automatically
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Update the app profile to use multi cluster routing so requests can go to any healthy cluster automatically.

This change shifts the Bigtable app profile from routing to a single target to a policy that permits the client send to reads and writes to any healthy replicated cluster. The client will on its own fail over if one cluster becomes unavailable and will resume using the closest healthy cluster when it recovers. With a second cluster in europe-west1, this routing also helps users in that region access a nearby cluster for lower latency while retaining high availability without manual action.

Deploy Memorystore for Memcached to cache reads in front of Bigtable does not supply automatic cross cluster failover. A cache can reduce read latency for hot keys but it does not route requests to a different Bigtable cluster and it does not help with writes or cache misses.

Increase the Bigtable client connection pool to allow more simultaneous RPCs can improve throughput and concurrency against the current target but it does not change routing behavior or provide automatic failover between clusters.

Create a second replicated cluster and keep the app profile configured for single cluster routing still pins requests to one cluster and would continue to require manual failover, which does not meet the requirement for automatic high availability.

O cliente fara o failover por conta propria se um cluster ficar indisponivel e voltara a usar o cluster saudavel mais proximo quando ele se recuperar. Com um segundo cluster em europe-west1, esse roteamento tambem ajuda os usuarios dessa regiao a acessar um cluster proximo para menor latencia, mantendo alta disponibilidade sem acao manual.

Implantar Memorystore for Memcached para fazer cache de leituras na frente do Bigtable nao fornece failover automatico entre clusters. Um cache pode reduzir a latencia de leitura para hot keys, mas nao roteia requisicoes para um cluster diferente do Bigtable e nao ajuda com gravacoes ou cache misses.

Aumentar o connection pool do cliente Bigtable para permitir mais RPCs simultaneos pode melhorar a throughput e a concorrencia em relacao ao destino atual, mas nao altera o comportamento de roteamento nem fornece failover automatico entre clusters.

Criar um segundo cluster replicado e manter o app profile configurado para single cluster routing ainda fixa as requisicoes em um unico cluster e continuaria exigindo failover manual, o que nao atende ao requisito de alta disponibilidade automatica.

questions.question: Beacon Press is decomposing a legacy shipment tracker into GKE microservices. A legacy component still reads and writes a single 80 KB configuration file and up to twelve replicas may run on different nodes and must share the same file. You want to keep operations simple and you cannot change the application code. How should you provide a shared file system for these pods?

options.text: Create a new persistent disk and back a Kubernetes PersistentVolume that all replicas mount as a shared volume
Move the configuration into Cloud SQL and have the service read and write the settings using SQL queries
Provision Cloud Filestore and mount it to the pods through an NFS PersistentVolume with ReadWriteMany access
Mount a Cloud Storage bucket into each container by using gcsfuse

questions.correct_text: Provision Cloud Filestore and mount it to the pods through an NFS PersistentVolume with ReadWriteMany access
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Provision Cloud Filestore and mount it to the pods through an NFS PersistentVolume with ReadWriteMany access.

Filestore gives you a managed NFS file system that developers can present to pods as a NFS PersistentVolume with ReadWriteMany so several replicas on different nodes can read and write the same file at the same time. This preserves POSIX behavior and file locking and it needs no code changes, which matches the legacy component that expects a shared configuration file. It also keeps operations simple because Filestore is a managed service with native GKE integration.

Create a new persistent disk and back a Kubernetes PersistentVolume that all replicas mount as a shared volume. On GKE a persistent disk can only be mounted read write by one node at a time, and when attached to multiple nodes it is read only, so it cannot supply concurrent writers to the same file across replicas.

Move the configuration into Cloud SQL and have the service read and write the settings using SQL queries. This would require application changes and it does not provide a file system interface with POSIX semantics, so it does not meet the requirement to keep the code unchanged.

Mount a Cloud Storage bucket into each container by using gcsfuse. Cloud Storage FUSE does not offer full POSIX compatibility or robust file locking for multiple writers, so it is not suggested for a shared writable mount for apps that expect a real file system.

Mover a configuracao para o Cloud SQL e fazer o servico ler e gravar as configuracoes usando consultas SQL. Isso exigiria alteracoes na aplicacao e nao fornece uma interface de sistema de arquivos com semantica POSIX, portanto nao atende ao requisito de manter o codigo inalterado.

Montar um bucket do Cloud Storage em cada container usando gcsfuse. questions.question: Driftwood Outfitters runs microservices on a private Google Kubernetes Engine cluster in us-central1, and each Pod must call Google Cloud APIs including Pub/Sub and Secret Manager that reside in three different projects within the same organization while avoiding long-lived credentials and following least privilege; what should you do?

options.text: Use Kubernetes RBAC with a Google service account to grant access to Google Cloud APIs
Store a Google service account JSON key in a Kubernetes Secret and mount it into the Pod
Enable Workload Identity on the cluster and map a Kubernetes service account to a Google service account that has only the needed IAM roles
Attach a single Google service account to the GKE node pool and allow all Pods to use it

questions.correct_text: Enable Workload Identity on the cluster and map a Kubernetes service account to a Google service account that has only the needed IAM roles
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Enable Workload Identity on the cluster and map a Kubernetes service account to a Google service account that has only the needed IAM roles.

Workload Identity permits Pods to authenticate to Google Cloud without storing keys. You bind a Kubernetes service account to a Google service account and Google issues short lived tokens to the Pod. You, and grant only the needed IAM roles on Pub/Sub and Secret Manager to that Google service account in the appropriate projects which satisfies minimal privilege and accommodates access across several projects in the same organization. Workload Identity works on private GKE clusters and offers automatic credential rotation and isolation at the Pod level.

Use Kubernetes RBAC with a Google service account to grant access to Google Cloud APIs is not right because Kubernetes RBAC governs access to the Kubernetes API server and it does not grant permissions to Google Cloud APIs. You must use IAM for Google Cloud services and RBAC cannot replace that.

Store a Google service account JSON key in a Kubernetes Secret and mount it into the Pod is incorrect since it uses long lived credentials and increases the risk of key leakage. Google suggests avoiding service account keys when running on GKE and to use Workload Identity instead.

Attach a single Google service account to the GKE node pool and allow all Pods to use it is incorrect because all Pods on the node would inherit broad permissions which violates least privilege. It also makes it hard to scope access per service whereas Workload Identity allows fine grained Pod level identities.

questions.question: Stratus Cloudworks is launching an inventory processing service on Google Cloud that must call both the Pub/Sub API and the Cloud Storage API to publish events and store files. Which is the best way to enable these services for the project so the application works across all environments?

options.text: Run gcloud commands on your workstation each time to enable the APIs before you start the app
Add logic to the application to programmatically enable both APIs during startup
Turn on the needed APIs in Google Cloud Console for the project
Grant the service account Storage Admin and Pub/Sub Admin roles without changing API settings

questions.correct_text: Turn on the needed APIs in Google Cloud Console for the project
questions.explanation:
The best answer is Turn on the needed APIs in Google Cloud web console for the project. This guarantees the Pub/Sub API and the Cloud Storage API are enabled at the project level so the app can call both services consistently in development, testing, and production.

Enabling needed services in the project through the Cloud Console is a one time administrative action that persists and applies to all environments and identities within that project. It separates service activation from application logic and keeps permission management clean because you, and grant only the needed IAM roles to the service account while relying on the project level API enablement to allow requests to reach the services.

Run gcloud commands on your workstation each time to enable the APIs before you start the app is not right because API enablement is not something you should repeat before every run. It is a persistent project setting and relying on local commands does not guarantee that CI or production environments will have the APIs enabled.

Add logic to the application to programmatically enable both APIs during startup is incorrect because API activation is an administrative concern that generally needs elevated permissions and must not be done by the application at runtime. This strategy is fragile since it can fail if the identity lacks permission and it couples environment setup with business logic.

Grant the service account Storage Admin and Pub/Sub Admin roles without changing API settings is incorrect because IAM roles do not enable disabled services. The APIs must be enabled for the project additionally to granting only the minimum needed permissions.

questions.question: A dev team at Cobalt Casino is standardizing container builds for services that will run on Cloud Run and Google Kubernetes Engine. To reduce the attack surface and lower the chance of bundling vulnerable components, what type of operating system base image should they select when creating their container images?

options.text: Pick a community image that is not validated by a trusted publisher
Use a fully loaded image that includes many common libraries and utilities
Choose a minimal base image that contains only the libraries that the service requires
Ubuntu LTS base image

questions.correct_text: Choose a minimal base image that contains only the libraries that the service requires
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Choose a minimal base image that contains only the libraries that the service requires.

This selection reduces the attack surface since it removes packages that your service does not need. Fewer components mean fewer potential vulnerabilities and a smaller image that pulls faster and starts more quickly on Cloud Run and Google Kubernetes Engine. This strategy aligns with Google guidance to keep images small and to prefer hardened runtimes including distroless that omit shells and package managers.

Google kept distroless images are a strong example of this strategy since they include only the language runtime and essential system libraries. They help limit exposure, improve startup performance, and simplify vulnerability management.

Pick a community image that is not validated by a trusted publisher is not right because unverified images carry supply chain risk and may include hidden malware or outdated components. Using trusted and maintained images helps confirm provenance and better security posture.

Use a fully loaded image that includes many common libraries and utilities is incorrect because bundling extra tools increases the number of packages and potential vulnerabilities and it also increases image size which can slow deployments and cold starts.

Ubuntu LTS base image is not the best choice for this goal because it is one general purpose distribution that includes many packages your service does not need. While stable and well supported it builds a larger attack surface compared with a minimal or distroless base.

questions.question: You manage a payments API at Ridgeline Mortgage that runs in a production Google Kubernetes Engine cluster and you release updates with Cloud Deploy. Engineers push frequent small changes each day, and you want a local workflow that on its own rebuilds and redeploys on edits and that uses a lightweight Kubernetes environment on a laptop so it closely mirrors production. Which tools should you choose to build images and run containers locally while keeping resource usage low?

options.text: kaniko and Tekton
Minikube and Skaffold
Docker Compose and dockerd
Terraform and kubeadm

questions.correct_text: Minikube and Skaffold
questions.explanation:
The best answer is Minikube and Skaffold.

Skaffold offers a developer friendly loop that watches your source files, rebuilds images, and redeploys to Kubernetes on its own when you edit code. It accommodates rapid local iteration and integrates with Kubernetes manifests or Helm charts so your workflow matches how you deploy to production.

Minikube runs a lightweight single node Kubernetes cluster on a laptop which keeps resource usage low while still giving you real Kubernetes APIs and behavior. Using Skaffold with Minikube closely mirrors a GKE based production environment since you are developing and testing on Kubernetes rather than on a different container orchestrator.

kaniko and Tekton target container builds and CI pipelines in a cluster environment and they are great for build systems but they are not tuned for a fast local inner development loop on a laptop. This pair would add unnecessary complexity for automatic rebuild and redeploy on local edits.

Docker Compose and dockerd run containers with Docker rather than Kubernetes which means the local environment does not match Kubernetes primitives or behavior. This makes it a poor fit when you want a development setup that mirrors GKE.

Terraform and kubeadm focus on provisioning and bootstrapping infrastructure rather than providing a lightweight local Kubernetes cluster with an automatic build and deploy loop. They do not address rapid local iteration on code changes.

questions.question: How can you best enable a user to download a large Cloud Storage object for 24 minutes while keeping the application stateless and scalable?

options.text: Cloud CDN signed cookies for 30 minutes
Cloud Storage signed URL with 30 minute expiry
Temporary bucket with lifecycle and object copy
Cloud Function streams file to client

questions.correct_text: Cloud Storage signed URL with 30 minute expiry
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Cloud Storage signed URL with 38 minute expiry.

A signed URL grants time bound access to a specific object without needing the caller to authenticate through your application. You generate the URL with a 38 minute expiration and the client downloads directly from Cloud Storage. This keeps your service stateless and it scales well because your servers do not proxy the file transfer.

Cloud CDN signed cookies for 22 minutes is one poor match because signed cookies are intended for use with Cloud CDN behind a load balancer to control access to cached content across many resources. It adds unnecessary infrastructure when you only need a single object download from Cloud Storage.

Temporary bucket with lifecycle and object copy is not right because copying objects per request adds cost and latency and builds state to handle deletions. It is much more complex than issuing a signed URL and it does not scale as cleanly.

Cloud Function streams file to client is not suggested for large files since it forces all bytes through your function which increases cost and risks timeout or memory limits. It also couples delivery to your compute path instead of letting Cloud Storage serve the object directly with a signed URL.

questions.question: Engineers at Bramble Coffee uses Cloud Build to produce Docker images for a backend service and they want to run unit tests and integration tests during the build while making it easy to see in the build history which test stage failed if one does. Which approach should they take?

options.text: Add RUN instructions in the Dockerfile to execute unit and integration tests during image build
Have the cloudbuild.yaml trigger a separate Cloud Build pipeline dedicated to running unit and integration tests
Define distinct steps in cloudbuild.yaml to compile then run unit tests and in a separate step to run integration tests
Use a single Cloud Build step that invokes a test script which runs both unit and integration tests

questions.correct_text: Define distinct steps in cloudbuild.yaml to compile then run unit tests and in a separate step to run integration tests
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Define distinct steps in cloudbuild.yaml to compile, and run unit tests and in a separate step to run integration tests.

Using separate Cloud Build steps gives clear isolation for compile, unit tests, and integration tests. Cloud Build records each step with its own status and logs so the build history immediately shows which step failed and developers can jump straight to the failing step output. This also allows fast feedback because unit tests can fail the build before integration tests run and it keeps test execution concerns in the pipeline rather than inside the image build.

Add RUN instructions in the Dockerfile to execute unit and integration tests during image build is less ideal because all testing would be hidden inside the docker build step in Cloud Build so the build history would only show the image build failed rather than which test stage failed. This also couples tests to image layers which slows caching and often conflicts with integration test needs that rely on external services.

Have the cloudbuild.yaml trigger a separate Cloud Build pipeline dedicated to running unit and integration tests adds unnecessary complexity and splits visibility across builds. You lose a single build timeline that pinpoints which stage failed and you increase maintenance with extra triggers and permissions.

Use a single Cloud Build step that invokes a test script which runs both unit and integration tests offers poor granularity. If the step fails you must sift through one large log to infer whether the unit or integration tests failed and the build history will not show the failure per stage.

questions.question: Your Linux service on Compute Engine consumes messages from a single Google Cloud Pub/Sub topic and persists records to a transactional database, and the service runs on preemptible instances to control cost. You want the application to shut down gracefully when the VM is terminated so that connections and in flight processing are handled cleanly. Which implementation should you choose?

options.text: Configure the application as a systemd service and rely on systemd to stop it automatically during OS shutdown without adding a shutdown script
Create a shutdown script that writes a marker file to a known path and have the application poll for that file every four minutes before disconnecting from the database
Implement a Compute Engine shutdown script that sends a termination signal to the application process so it can close database connections and stop cleanly
Publish a message to the same Pub/Sub topic during shutdown that announces the instance is terminating and have the application react by closing the database connection

questions.correct_text: Implement a Compute Engine shutdown script that sends a termination signal to the application process so it can close database connections and stop cleanly
questions.explanation:
The best answer is Implement a Compute Engine shutdown script that sends a termination signal to the app process so it can close database connections and stop cleanly.

A shutdown script that signals the application aligns with how Compute Engine handles termination and preemption events. When a preemptible VM is about to stop, Compute Engine issues a shutdown signal and runs shutdown scripts so your script can immediately send a termination signal to the service. This allows the Pub/Sub consumer to stop pulling, acknowledge processed messages, and close transactional database connections within the short preemption window, which leads to a clean and consistent shutdown.

Configure the application as a systemd service and rely on systemd to stop it on its own during OS shutdown without adding a shutdown script is not sufficient since it does not integrate with Compute Engine lifecycle hooks. Default systemd behavior might not give the service enough time within the brief preemption window and it does not confirm your process stops pulling messages and finishes in flight work in a controlled way.

Create a shutdown script that writes a marker file to a known path and have the application poll for that file every four minutes before disconnecting from the database is unreliable because polling on a multi minute interval can miss the short preemption notice. The instance can be terminated before the application notices the marker, which risks lost work and unclosed connections.

Publish a message to the same Pub/Sub topic during shutdown that announces the instance is terminating and have the application react by closing the database connection is a poor control model because the message may not be delivered or processed before the VM stops. It also mixes control and business data on the same topic and does not actually stop message consumption on the instance.

questions.explanation_pt:
A melhor resposta é Implementar um shutdown script no Compute Engine que envie um sinal de término ao processo da aplicação para que ela possa fechar as conexões com o banco de dados e parar de forma limpa.

Um shutdown script que sinaliza a aplicação está alinhado com a forma como o Compute Engine lida com eventos de término e preempção. Quando uma VM preemptível está prestes a ser interrompida, o Compute Engine emite um sinal de shutdown e executa os shutdown scripts, de modo que seu script pode imediatamente enviar um sinal de término ao serviço. Isso permite que o consumidor do Pub/Sub pare de fazer pull, confirme (ack) as mensagens já processadas e feche as conexões transacionais com o banco de dados dentro da curta janela de preempção, o que leva a um desligamento limpo e consistente.

Configurar a aplicação como um serviço systemd e confiar que o systemd a pare por conta própria durante o desligamento do SO sem adicionar um shutdown script não é suficiente, pois não se integra aos lifecycle hooks do Compute Engine. O comportamento padrão do systemd pode não dar tempo suficiente ao serviço dentro da breve janela de preempção e não garante que seu processo pare de fazer pull de mensagens e finalize o trabalho em andamento de forma controlada.

Criar um shutdown script que escreva um arquivo de marcação em um caminho conhecido e fazer a aplicação verificar esse arquivo a cada quatro minutos antes de se desconectar do banco de dados é pouco confiável porque a verificação em um intervalo de vários minutos pode perder o curto aviso de preempção. A instância pode ser encerrada antes de a aplicação notar a marcação, o que arrisca perda de trabalho e conexões não fechadas.

Publicar uma mensagem no mesmo tópico do Pub/Sub durante o desligamento anunciando que a instância está sendo encerrada e fazer a aplicação reagir fechando a conexão com o banco de dados é um modelo de controle ruim porque a mensagem pode não ser entregue ou processada antes de a VM parar. Isso também mistura dados de controle e de negócio no mesmo tópico e, na prática, não interrompe o consumo de mensagens na instância.

questions.question: You are upgrading eight stateful services that run on Google Kubernetes Engine and they must keep data on durable volumes and allow rolling updates without any service interruption. Which configuration meets these goals?

options.text: Run each service as a single Pod that uses a PersistentVolumeClaim and switch traffic with a blue green strategy by updating the Service selector
Deploy each service as a Deployment that mounts a Compute Engine persistent disk and choose a Recreate update strategy to prevent downtime
Use StatefulSets with PersistentVolumeClaims for storage and configure the updateStrategy as RollingUpdate
Create a DaemonSet for each service that mounts local SSD and manage upgrades by hand during planned windows

questions.correct_text: Use StatefulSets with PersistentVolumeClaims for storage and configure the updateStrategy as RollingUpdate
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Use StatefulSets with PersistentVolumeClaims for storage and configure the updateStrategy as RollingUpdate.

This strategy is designed for stateful workloads that need stable identities and durable storage. PersistentVolumeClaims give each replica its own persistent disk so data survives restarts and rescheduling. The RollingUpdate strategy updates pods in a controlled and ordered way which permits traffic to continue to flow as new versions become ready. With proper readiness probes and at least two replicas per service developers can accomplish rolling updates without interruption while keeping data on persistent disks.

The option Run each service as a single Pod that uses a PersistentVolumeClaim and switch traffic with a blue green strategy by updating the Service selector is not right because a single pod builds a single point of failure and cannot supply zero downtime during updates. Blue green with a ReadWriteOnce persistent disk is also problematic since the same volume cannot be attached to two pods on different nodes at the same time which complicates any cutover and risks interruption.

The option Deploy each service as a Deployment that mounts a Compute Engine persistent disk and pick a Recreate update strategy to stop downtime is incorrect because Deployments target stateless workloads and Recreate deliberately stops all old pods before starting new ones which causes downtime. It also does not provide the stable identity and per replica storage guarantees that stateful workloads require.

The option Create a DaemonSet for each service that mounts local SSD and handle upgrades by hand during planned windows is incorrect because DaemonSets run one pod per node which does not match typical stateful service patterns and local SSD is ephemeral rather than durable so data is lost on node failure. Manual upgrade windows contradict the requirement for rolling updates without interruption.

questions.explanation_pt:
A escolha correta é Usar StatefulSets com PersistentVolumeClaims para armazenamento e configurar a updateStrategy como RollingUpdate.

Essa estratégia foi projetada para cargas de trabalho stateful que precisam de identidades estáveis e armazenamento durável. Os PersistentVolumeClaims dão a cada réplica seu próprio disco persistente, de forma que os dados sobrevivem a reinicializações e reagendamentos. A estratégia RollingUpdate atualiza os pods de maneira controlada e ordenada, o que permite que o tráfego continue fluindo à medida que novas versões ficam prontas. Com readiness probes adequados e ao menos duas réplicas por serviço, os desenvolvedores conseguem realizar rolling updates sem interrupção, mantendo os dados em discos persistentes.

A opção Executar cada serviço como um único Pod que usa um PersistentVolumeClaim e alternar o tráfego com uma estratégia blue green atualizando o selector do Service não está correta porque um único pod cria um ponto único de falha e não consegue fornecer zero downtime durante as atualizações. Blue green com um disco persistente ReadWriteOnce também é problemático, já que o mesmo volume não pode ser anexado a dois pods em nós diferentes ao mesmo tempo, o que complica qualquer cutover e arrisca interrupção.

A opção Implantar cada serviço como um Deployment que monta um disco persistente do Compute Engine e escolher a estratégia de atualização Recreate para impedir downtime está incorreta porque Deployments são voltados para cargas de trabalho stateless e a estratégia Recreate deliberadamente encerra todos os pods antigos antes de iniciar os novos, o que causa downtime. Ela também não fornece a identidade estável nem as garantias de armazenamento por réplica que as cargas de trabalho stateful exigem.

A opção Criar um DaemonSet para cada serviço que monta um SSD local e tratar os upgrades manualmente durante janelas planejadas está incorreta porque DaemonSets executam um pod por nó, o que não corresponde aos padrões típicos de serviços stateful, e o SSD local é efêmero em vez de durável, de modo que os dados são perdidos em caso de falha do nó. Janelas de upgrade manuais contradizem o requisito de rolling updates sem interrupção.

questions.question: Within Opalwood Furniture, an HTTP-triggered Cloud Function receives POST requests that contain a flat JSON payload with numeric and string fields. After the function completes, analysts across several teams need to run complex queries on the ingested records and they require the data to be queryable within 3 seconds of receipt. How should you persist the incoming data to meet these requirements?

options.text: Transform the JSON and insert the records into a regional Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instance
Normalize the incoming JSON and write the rows into BigQuery using the streaming interface
Store each request body as a document in Cloud Firestore
Write each payload to a Cloud Storage object and query via a BigQuery external table

questions.correct_text: Normalize the incoming JSON and write the rows into BigQuery using the streaming interface
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Normalize the incoming JSON and write the rows into BigQuery using the streaming interface. It offers near-realtime availability for queries and accommodates complex analytics for many concurrent users.

Streaming inserts make newly ingested rows queryable within seconds in most cases, which satisfies the requirement to be queryable within three seconds. This strategy is one good fit for flat JSON with numeric and string fields because the records map cleanly to a defined table schema. It also permits several teams run advanced SQL without managing infrastructure or indexes, and a Cloud Function can invoke the client library to stream each record as it arrives.

Transform the JSON and insert the records into a regional Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instance is a poor match since it targets transactional workloads and does not scale well for heavy analytic queries across large datasets and many users. Meeting near real time analytical freshness and concurrency would be difficult and would require significant tuning.

Store each request body as a document in Cloud Firestore is unsuitable because its query model is limited and does not support complex ad hoc analytics. Organizations often export this data to a warehouse for analysis, which introduces extra steps and latency that would not meet the three second target.

Write each payload to a Cloud Storage object and query through a BigQuery external table will not meet the freshness requirement because external tables over objects are not designed for low latency discovery of new files. Query performance on many small files is also poor compared with native tables.

questions.explanation_pt:
A escolha correta é Normalizar o JSON recebido e gravar as linhas no BigQuery usando a interface de streaming. Ela oferece disponibilidade quase em tempo real para consultas e acomoda análises complexas para muitos usuários simultâneos.

Os streaming inserts tornam as linhas recém-ingeridas consultáveis em segundos na maioria dos casos, o que satisfaz o requisito de estarem disponíveis para consulta em três segundos. Essa estratégia é uma boa opção para JSON plano com campos numéricos e de string, porque os registros se mapeiam de forma limpa para um schema de tabela definido. Ela também permite que várias equipes executem SQL avançado sem gerenciar infraestrutura ou índices, e uma Cloud Function pode invocar a client library para fazer streaming de cada registro à medida que chega.

Transformar o JSON e inserir os registros em uma instância regional do Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL é uma escolha ruim, pois ele é voltado para cargas de trabalho transacionais e não escala bem para consultas analíticas pesadas sobre grandes conjuntos de dados e muitos usuários. Atender à atualização analítica quase em tempo real e à concorrência seria difícil e exigiria ajustes significativos.

Armazenar cada corpo de requisição como um documento no Cloud Firestore é inadequado porque seu modelo de consulta é limitado e não suporta análises ad hoc complexas. As organizações frequentemente exportam esses dados para um data warehouse para análise, o que introduz etapas extras e latência que não atenderiam à meta de três segundos.

Gravar cada payload em um objeto do Cloud Storage e consultar por meio de uma external table do BigQuery não atenderá ao requisito de atualização, porque external tables sobre objetos não são projetadas para descoberta de baixa latência de novos arquivos. O desempenho das consultas sobre muitos arquivos pequenos também é ruim em comparação com tabelas nativas.

questions.question: A hosted analytics platform at api.loomwright.io has operated for eight years and serves about 3.2 million users. Your team plans to introduce a major API redesign, yet many partner integrations still call the existing endpoints. What should you do to roll out the new API while protecting current partner integrations from breaking?

options.text: Replace the existing API with the new API and share updated docs for partners to change quickly
Use App Engine traffic splitting to send some requests to a new deployment while the rest go to the current one
Publish the new API under a new version and keep the current API running as a legacy version until partners migrate
Place an Apigee proxy in front and rewrite old requests so they hit the new API then turn off the old backend

questions.correct_text: Publish the new API under a new version and keep the current API running as a legacy version until partners migrate
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Publish the new API under a new version and keep the current API running as a legacy version until partners migrate.

This versioning strategy permits you to introduce breaking changes safely while preserving backward compatibility. Developers can expose the new surface on a clearly versioned endpoint while leaving the legacy endpoint in place so partners can migrate on their own schedule. This reduces risk, allows staged adoption, and aligns with widely suggested API design practices for managing change.

Replace the existing API with the new API and share updated docs for partners to change quickly is risky since it forces immediate partner changes and will likely break existing integrations. Documentation alone does not stop outages when clients depend on the old contract.

Use App Engine traffic splitting to send some requests to a new deployment while the rest go to the current one does not solve compatibility issues because traffic splitting is for gradual rollout of compatible versions. If the new API is not backward compatible, and splitting requests will create inconsistent behavior and still break clients.

Place an Apigee proxy in front and rewrite old requests so they hit the new API then turn off the old backend is fragile for a major redesign because proxies can map simple changes but cannot dependably translate deeper semantic or behavioral differences. Turning off the old backend removes a stable contract that partners rely on and increases the chance of breakage.

questions.explanation_pt:
A escolha correta é Publicar a nova API sob uma nova versão e manter a API atual em execução como uma versão legada até que os parceiros migrem.

Essa estratégia de versionamento permite que você introduza breaking changes de forma segura, preservando a compatibilidade retroativa. Os desenvolvedores podem expor a nova superfície em um endpoint claramente versionado, mantendo o endpoint legado no lugar para que os parceiros migrem no próprio cronograma. Isso reduz o risco, permite adoção em etapas e está alinhado às práticas de design de API amplamente recomendadas para gerenciar mudanças.

Substituir a API existente pela nova API e compartilhar documentação atualizada para que os parceiros mudem rapidamente é arriscado, pois força mudanças imediatas nos parceiros e provavelmente quebrará integrações existentes. Documentação sozinha não impede interrupções quando os clientes dependem do contrato antigo.

Usar o traffic splitting do App Engine para enviar algumas requisições a um novo deployment enquanto o restante vai para o atual não resolve problemas de compatibilidade, porque o traffic splitting serve para rollout gradual de versões compatíveis. Se a nova API não for retrocompatível, dividir as requisições criará comportamento inconsistente e ainda assim quebrará os clientes.

Colocar um proxy do Apigee na frente e reescrever as requisições antigas para que atinjam a nova API, e então desligar o backend antigo, é frágil para um redesign de grande porte, porque proxies conseguem mapear mudanças simples, mas não conseguem traduzir de forma confiável diferenças semânticas ou comportamentais mais profundas. Desligar o backend antigo remove um contrato estável do qual os parceiros dependem e aumenta a chance de quebra.

questions.question: Within Aether Networks your platform team is rolling out a containerized HTTP service on Google Kubernetes Engine. Traffic fluctuates with user actions and CPU and memory remain low even when requests spike to about 640 requests per second in the evening. You want the workload to scale based on incoming request rate instead of CPU or memory utilization. Which implementation should you choose?

options.text: Enable the Cluster Autoscaler to grow the node pool when request volume increases
Configure a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler that uses a custom request rate metric from Cloud Monitoring to adjust replica count
Cloud Run
Deploy a Vertical Pod Autoscaler and scale from the CPU utilization of each pod

questions.correct_text: Configure a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler that uses a custom request rate metric from Cloud Monitoring to adjust replica count
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Configure a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler that uses a custom request rate metric from Cloud Monitoring to adjust replica count.

Horizontal Pod Autoscaler is designed to change replica counts based on metrics that reflect service demand. When CPU and memory are low yet request traffic varies, using a request rate metric from Cloud Monitoring allows the HPA to scale pods in response to incoming traffic rather than resource utilization. This aligns with the requirement to scale by requests per second so that the workload can add replicas during evening spikes and reduce them when traffic subsides.

Enable the Cluster Autoscaler to grow the node pool when request volume increases is one poor match because the Cluster Autoscaler only adds or removes nodes when pods are pending owing to insufficient capacity. It does not change the number of pods and it does not react to request rate.

Cloud Run does scale on its own with request load, though it would require moving the service to a different platform and it does not meet the requirement to scale an existing workload on GKE. The question asks for scaling the current Kubernetes deployment rather than migrating it.

Deploy a Vertical Pod Autoscaler and scale from the CPU utilization of each pod is not right because VPA adjusts resource requests for pods and it is driven by CPU and memory usage. It does not scale replica count and it does not use request rate.

questions.explanation_pt:
A escolha correta é Configurar um Horizontal Pod Autoscaler que use uma métrica customizada de taxa de requisições do Cloud Monitoring para ajustar a contagem de réplicas.

O Horizontal Pod Autoscaler foi projetado para alterar a contagem de réplicas com base em métricas que refletem a demanda do serviço. Quando CPU e memória estão baixas, mas o tráfego de requisições varia, usar uma métrica de taxa de requisições do Cloud Monitoring permite que o HPA escale os pods em resposta ao tráfego de entrada, em vez de à utilização de recursos. Isso está alinhado ao requisito de escalar por requisições por segundo, de modo que a carga de trabalho possa adicionar réplicas durante os picos noturnos e reduzi-las quando o tráfego diminui.

Habilitar o Cluster Autoscaler para aumentar o node pool quando o volume de requisições cresce é uma escolha ruim, porque o Cluster Autoscaler apenas adiciona ou remove nós quando há pods pendentes devido a capacidade insuficiente. Ele não altera o número de pods e não reage à taxa de requisições.

O Cloud Run de fato escala por conta própria com a carga de requisições, porém exigiria mover o serviço para uma plataforma diferente e não atende ao requisito de escalar uma carga de trabalho existente no GKE. A questão pede para escalar o deployment atual do Kubernetes em vez de migrá-lo.

Implantar um Vertical Pod Autoscaler e escalar a partir da utilização de CPU de cada pod não está correto, porque o VPA ajusta os resource requests dos pods e é orientado pelo uso de CPU e memória. Ele não escala a contagem de réplicas e não usa a taxa de requisições.

questions.question: You are building a module at Carbon Forge Steel that records hourly shift submissions in an internal workforce system and needs to notify several independent payroll, compliance, and analytics services. The design must keep producers and consumers loosely coupled and should allow new processing steps to be added next quarter while handling about 380 submissions per minute. What approach will provide reliable communication with downstream services and keep future additions simple?

options.text: Use Cloud Tasks with a queue for each step to push HTTP requests to every downstream system
Create a separate Pub/Sub topic for every step and have each team subscribe only to its own step
Build a microservice on Google Kubernetes Engine that invokes downstream steps in sequence and waits for each response
Publish a shift.submitted event to a single Pub/Sub topic and let each downstream team create and manage its own subscription

questions.correct_text: Publish a shift.submitted event to a single Pub/Sub topic and let each downstream team create and manage its own subscription
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Publish a shift.submitted event to a single Pub/Sub topic and allow each downstream team create and handle its own subscription.

This strategy implements an event driven fan out model that keeps producers and consumers loosely coupled. The producer emits a single event and each downstream service owns its subscription which permits teams scale independently, set their own acknowledgement and retry behavior, and use dead letter handling without coordinating changes with the producer. Adding a new processing step next quarter stays simple because a new subscription can be created without modifying the publisher.

This architecture easily handles 360 submissions per minute because the service is built for high throughput and offers durable at least once delivery. Independent subscriptions stop one slow or failing consumer from blocking others and backlogs can accumulate per consumer until it catches up.

Use Cloud Tasks with a queue for each step to push HTTP requests to every downstream system is one poor match because that service is tuned for targeted task delivery to a specific handler and rate control rather than broadcast to many independent consumers. Managing many queues also couples the producer to every step and increases operational overhead.

Create a separate Pub/Sub topic for every step and have each team subscribe only to its own step increases coupling because the producer must know every step and publish to several topics. It complicates future additions since new steps require publisher changes, whereas a single topic with multiple subscriptions keeps the producer unaware of consumers.

Build a microservice on Google Kubernetes Engine that invokes downstream steps in sequence and waits for each response introduces tight coupling and synchronous dependencies. It builds a single point of failure, increases latency, and makes adding new steps require code changes and redeployments instead of just attaching another subscription.

questions.explanation_pt:
A escolha correta é publicar um evento shift.submitted em um único tópico do Pub/Sub e permitir que cada equipe downstream crie e gerencie sua própria subscription.

Essa estratégia implementa um modelo de fan-out orientado a eventos que mantém produtores e consumidores fracamente acoplados (loosely coupled). O produtor emite um único evento e cada serviço downstream é dono de sua subscription, o que permite que as equipes escalem de forma independente, definam seu próprio comportamento de acknowledgement e retry, e usem dead letter handling sem coordenar alterações com o produtor. Adicionar uma nova etapa de processamento no próximo trimestre permanece simples, porque uma nova subscription pode ser criada sem modificar o publisher.

Essa arquitetura lida facilmente com 360 submissões por minuto, pois o serviço foi construído para alta vazão (throughput) e oferece entrega durável at-least-once. Subscriptions independentes impedem que um consumidor lento ou com falha bloqueie os demais, e os backlogs podem se acumular por consumidor até que ele se recupere.

Usar Cloud Tasks com uma fila para cada etapa para enviar requisições HTTP a cada sistema downstream é uma escolha ruim, porque esse serviço é otimizado para entrega direcionada de tarefas a um handler específico e para controle de taxa, e não para broadcast a muitos consumidores independentes. Gerenciar muitas filas também acopla o produtor a cada etapa e aumenta a sobrecarga operacional.

Criar um tópico separado do Pub/Sub para cada etapa e fazer cada equipe assinar apenas a sua própria etapa aumenta o acoplamento, porque o produtor precisa conhecer todas as etapas e publicar em vários tópicos. Isso complica adições futuras, já que novas etapas exigem alterações no publisher, enquanto um único tópico com múltiplas subscriptions mantém o produtor alheio aos consumidores.

Construir um microsserviço no Google Kubernetes Engine que invoca as etapas downstream em sequência e aguarda cada resposta introduz acoplamento forte e dependências síncronas. Isso cria um ponto único de falha, aumenta a latência e faz com que adicionar novas etapas exija mudanças de código e re-deploys, em vez de apenas anexar outra subscription.

questions.question: Westgate Hospitals is preparing to run a payment microservice on Google Kubernetes Engine that must scale out to as many as 17 pods during busy periods, and each instance needs a consistent network identity for peer discovery and it also requires its own persistent disk that remains available after rescheduling. Which GKE workload resource should you use?

options.text: Deployment
StatefulSet
ReplicationController
ReplicaSet

questions.correct_text: StatefulSet
questions.explanation:
The right choice is StatefulSet since it offers stable network identities for each Pod and gives every replica its own persistent volume that persists across rescheduling while still allowing you to scale to the needed number of replicas during busy periods.

This resource assigns stable Pod names and works with a headless Service so each instance has a predictable DNS name for peer discovery. It also uses a volume claim template to create a unique PersistentVolumeClaim per replica so the same disk stays associated with the same logical instance after rescheduling, which satisfies the requirement for storage that remains available.

Deployment manages interchangeable stateless replicas and does not guarantee a stable identity for each replica. It also does not supply automatic per replica persistent volumes through volume claim templates, which makes it unsuitable for this stateful requirement.

ReplicationController is a legacy controller that has largely been replaced by ReplicaSet and Deployment and it shares the same limitations for stateful needs. It is less likely to appear on newer exams because it is rarely used in modern clusters.

ReplicaSet is a lower level controller focused on maintaining a desired number of replicas and it does not assign stable identities or create unique persistent volumes for each replica, so it does not meet the requirements.

A escolha correta é StatefulSet, pois ele oferece identidades de rede estáveis para cada Pod e dá a cada réplica seu próprio volume persistente que sobrevive ao reagendamento (rescheduling), ao mesmo tempo em que ainda permite escalar até o número necessário de réplicas durante períodos de pico.

Esse recurso atribui nomes estáveis aos Pods e funciona com um headless Service, de modo que cada instância tem um nome DNS previsível para descoberta de peers. Ele também usa um volume claim template para criar um PersistentVolumeClaim único por réplica, de forma que o mesmo disco permaneça associado à mesma instância lógica após o reagendamento, o que satisfaz o requisito de armazenamento que permanece disponível.

O Deployment gerencia réplicas stateless intercambiáveis e não garante uma identidade estável para cada réplica. Ele também não fornece volumes persistentes automáticos por réplica via volume claim templates, o que o torna inadequado para esse requisito stateful.

O ReplicationController é um controlador legado que foi em grande parte substituído por ReplicaSet e Deployment, e compartilha as mesmas limitações para necessidades stateful. É menos provável que apareça em provas mais recentes, pois raramente é usado em clusters modernos.

O ReplicaSet é um controlador de nível mais baixo focado em manter um número desejado de réplicas, e não atribui identidades estáveis nem cria volumes persistentes únicos para cada réplica, portanto não atende aos requisitos.

questions.question: A media insights platform runs on Google Kubernetes Engine in europe-west1 and must submit queries to BigQuery. You want to grant the GKE service account only the minimal permissions so that workloads can start and manage BigQuery jobs without broad dataset privileges. Which IAM role should you assign to the GKE service account to follow least privilege?

options.text: roles/bigquery.dataOwner
roles/bigquery.user
roles/bigquery.jobUser
roles/bigquery.dataViewer

questions.correct_text: roles/bigquery.jobUser
questions.explanation:
The right choice is roles/bigquery.jobUser.

This role permits the service account create and handle its own BigQuery jobs which includes submitting queries, loads, exports and copies. It grants bigquery.jobs.create and related permissions to get, list and cancel only the caller’s jobs. It does not grant dataset level read or write permissions, which means developers can keep data access separate and only grant dataset roles where they are truly required. This satisfies the requirement to start and manage tasks without broad dataset privileges.

roles/bigquery.dataOwner is overly permissive since it grants full control over datasets and their tables, including the ability to create, update and delete them. This violates minimal privilege when the need is only to run jobs.

roles/bigquery.user is broader than necessary because it allows building datasets and discovering metadata across the project additionally to running jobs. It exceeds the minimal scope needed to only start and manage jobs.

roles/bigquery.dataViewer offers read access to dataset contents but does not allow creating or managing jobs. It would not allow workloads submit queries.

questions.question: A subscription news site at fernhill.org has an application that is stable in staging but defects only appear under real customer traffic after a release. The team wants to ship new versions while limiting the blast radius and reducing how many users are affected if issues slip through. Which deployment approach should they choose?

options.text: Rolling update
Blue green deployment
Canary rollout
Shadow launch

questions.correct_text: Canary rollout
questions.explanation:
The proper option is Canary rollout since it permits you to release a new version to a small percentage of real users first, observe behavior under production traffic, and safely ramp up if metrics look healthy which directly limits blast radius.

A canary rollout starts by sending only a small slice of production traffic to the new version whereas most users continue using the stable version. You monitor key indicators including error rates, latency, and business metrics, and if issues appear developers can immediately halt or roll back so only a small cohort is affected. If results are good, you gradually increase traffic until the new version serves everyone, which matches the need to ship while minimizing how many customers are impacted by defects that only surface under real load.

Rolling update replaces old instances with new ones in batches to preserve availability, yet traffic steadily shifts to the new version as the rollout proceeds and there is no fixed small audience for validation, so a defect can quickly reach many users during the progression.

Blue green deployment keeps two production environments and switches all traffic at once after validation, which allows fast rollback but does not expose only a small percentage of users first, so the blast radius at cutover is all users.

Shadow launch mirrors real traffic to a new version but discards its responses, which is useful for testing under production patterns without user impact. It does not actually serve real users, so it does not meet the goal of shipping new versions while limiting the number of customers who could be affected.

A opção adequada é o Canary rollout, pois ele permite liberar uma nova versão primeiro para uma pequena porcentagem de usuários reais, observar o comportamento sob tráfego de produção e aumentar a adoção com segurança se as métricas parecerem saudáveis, o que limita diretamente o raio de impacto (blast radius).

Um canary rollout começa enviando apenas uma pequena fração do tráfego de produção para a nova versão, enquanto a maioria dos usuários continua usando a versão estável. Você monitora indicadores-chave, incluindo taxas de erro, latência e métricas de negócio, e, se surgirem problemas, os desenvolvedores podem imediatamente interromper ou fazer rollback, de modo que apenas um pequeno grupo seja afetado. Se os resultados forem bons, você aumenta gradualmente o tráfego até que a nova versão atenda a todos, o que corresponde à necessidade de entregar minimizando quantos clientes são impactados por defeitos que só aparecem sob carga real.

O Rolling update substitui instâncias antigas por novas em lotes para preservar a disponibilidade, porém o tráfego se desloca continuamente para a nova versão à medida que o rollout avança, e não há um público pequeno e fixo para validação, de modo que um defeito pode alcançar rapidamente muitos usuários durante a progressão.

O Blue green deployment mantém dois ambientes de produção e alterna todo o tráfego de uma só vez após a validação, o que permite rollback rápido, mas não expõe primeiro apenas uma pequena porcentagem de usuários, de modo que o raio de impacto no momento da troca (cutover) é todos os usuários.

O Shadow launch espelha o tráfego real para uma nova versão, mas descarta suas respostas, o que é útil para testar sob padrões de produção sem impacto para o usuário. Ele não atende usuários reais de fato, portanto não cumpre o objetivo de entregar novas versões limitando o número de clientes que poderiam ser afetados.

questions.question: Which GCP service centrally manages internal service to service traffic with retries, timeouts and telemetry for HTTP and gRPC without changing application code?

options.text: Apigee X
Traffic Director
Cloud Load Balancing
Service Directory

questions.correct_text: Traffic Director
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Traffic Director.

Traffic Director is Google Clouds managed service mesh control plane that centrally configures service to service traffic across HTTP and gRPC. It accommodates policy driven retries and timeouts and offers rich telemetry through Cloud Monitoring and Cloud Logging. Because it programs data planes including Envoy or uses proxyless gRPC, you gain these behaviors without changing application code.

Apigee X focuses on API management for publishing and securing external and partner facing APIs with features like developer portals and monetization. It is not designed to handle internal east west service traffic or to centrally apply retries, timeouts, and mesh telemetry without code changes.

Cloud Load Balancing distributes incoming client traffic to backends and is tuned for north south traffic. It does not act as a service mesh control plane and it does not supply centrally managed client side retries and timeouts for service to service HTTP or gRPC calls.

Service Directory is one managed registry for service names and endpoints that helps with discovery. It does not manage traffic behavior and does not provide retries, timeouts, or telemetry for service communication.

O Traffic Director é o control plane gerenciado de service mesh do Google Cloud, que configura centralmente o tráfego serviço-a-serviço em HTTP e gRPC. Ele suporta retries e timeouts orientados por políticas e oferece telemetria rica por meio do Cloud Monitoring e do Cloud Logging. Como ele programa os data planes, incluindo o Envoy, ou usa gRPC proxyless, você obtém esses comportamentos sem alterar o código da aplicação.

O Apigee X foca em gerenciamento de APIs para publicar e proteger APIs externas e voltadas a parceiros, com recursos como portais para desenvolvedores e monetização. Ele não foi projetado para lidar com tráfego interno leste-oeste entre serviços nem para aplicar centralmente retries, timeouts e telemetria de mesh sem alterações de código.

O Cloud Load Balancing distribui o tráfego de clientes que chega para os backends e é otimizado para tráfego norte-sul. Ele não atua como control plane de service mesh e não fornece retries e timeouts gerenciados centralmente no lado do cliente para chamadas HTTP ou gRPC entre serviços.

O Service Directory é um registro gerenciado de nomes e endpoints de serviços que ajuda na descoberta. Ele não gerencia o comportamento do tráfego e não fornece retries, timeouts ou telemetria para a comunicação entre serviços.

questions.question: You operate a ride sharing platform on Google Cloud where an HTTP-triggered Cloud Function calls an external SMS gateway to send trip completion texts. Following a large referral campaign, some riders report missing texts and your logs show intermittent HTTP 500 errors from the function during spikes in traffic. How should you redesign the system so that outbound messages are durably queued and processed even when there are transient failures in the function or the SMS provider?

options.text: Increase the Cloud Function memory to 3 GB and implement local retries for failed SMS HTTP requests
Publish every SMS request to a Pub/Sub topic and have a subscriber Cloud Function send messages to the SMS API with retries and a dead-letter topic
Use Memorystore for Redis as a queue for pending SMS and have the function pop entries and call the provider
Add exponential backoff in the mobile app and retry the function invocation up to 12 times on failure

questions.correct_text: Publish every SMS request to a Pub/Sub topic and have a subscriber Cloud Function send messages to the SMS API with retries and a dead-letter topic
questions.explanation:
The best answer is Publish every SMS request to a Pub/Sub topic and have a subscriber Cloud Function send messages to the SMS API with retries and a dead-letter topic.

This architecture decouples message production from delivery and offers a durable queue. Messages are persisted in the topic and are redelivered until acknowledged. A subscriber function processes messages and handles transient errors by letting the message be retried automatically. A dead letter topic safely captures messages that repeatedly fail so operators can inspect and replay them.

This strategy absorbs traffic spikes because producers only publish to the topic quickly while workers scale out to process at a sustainable rate. It also contains failures. If the SMS API or the function has a transient error, and the message remains in the subscription and is retried with backoff. The dead letter topic prevents infinite retries and supplies a clear path for alerting and manual remediation. Ensure the message processing is idempotent so that retried deliveries do not send duplicate SMS.

Increase the Cloud Function memory to 3 GB and implement local retries for failed SMS HTTP requests is not sufficient because more memory does not add durability. Local retries vanish when an instance restarts and they can still lose requests during crashes or timeouts.

Use Memorystore for Redis as a queue for pending SMS and have the function pop entries and call the provider is a poor match because Memorystore is an in memory cache and is not a managed durable message queue. You would need to build your own acknowledgement, retry, and dead letter handling and you still risk data loss and operational complexity.

Add exponential backoff in the mobile app and retry the function invocation up to 9 times on failure pushes reliability to clients and does not supply durable queuing. If the backend or the SMS provider is unavailable then requests are not persisted and traffic bursts can be amplified by client retries.
