questions.explanation_pt:
A escolha correta é O IAM role binding da service account foi alterado e ele não concede mais as permissões necessárias do Cloud Storage.

Um HTTP 403 Permission denied do Cloud Storage significa que o chamador está autenticado, mas não está autorizado. Quando uma carga de trabalho do GKE que usa uma service account dedicada perde repentinamente o acesso de leitura sem nenhuma mudança nos nomes dos objetos ou na localização do bucket, a causa mais plausível é uma mudança nos role bindings dessa conta. Remover ou alterar roles que contêm permissões como storage.objects.get fará com que as leituras falhem com 403.

Uma regra de Object Lifecycle Management ter arquivado ou excluído alguns objetos após 59 dias é improvável porque transições ou exclusões de lifecycle resultariam em objetos ausentes e geralmente levariam a 404 Not Found para solicitações de objetos que não existem mais. Mudar a storage class não remove a autorização de leitura e não retornaria, por si só, um 403.

A chave da service account ter sido rotacionada recentemente e o processo do app não ter sido atualizado com a nova chave não se alinha com o sintoma, pois uma chave inválida ou ausente costuma causar falhas de autenticação, que geralmente são erros 401 em vez de falhas de autorização. No GKE, muitas cargas de trabalho usam Workload Identity em vez de chaves gerenciadas pelo usuário, e um problema de chave não explicaria um 403 consistente após uma autenticação bem-sucedida.

Os objetos terem sido reorganizados sob um prefixo diferente dentro do bucket, o que mudou seus caminhos, na prática mudaria os nomes dos objetos e se apresentaria como 404 Not Found para os caminhos antigos. O cenário estabelece que não houve mudanças recentes nos nomes dos objetos, então essa explicação conflita com a informação fornecida.

questions.question: A small team at fernhill.org is creating an MVP that uses a microservices design on Cloud Run with data stored in Bigtable and event messaging through Pub/Sub. They want to finish debugging within 17 days and keep costs as low as possible whereas iterating quickly. Which approach should they take?

options.text: Use Cloud Code to develop and iterate, deploy each service to Cloud Run for end to end tests, and review telemetry in Cloud Logging and Cloud Trace
Provision a separate staging project that mirrors production, configure Cloud Deploy with manual approval gates, and run end to end validation of the Cloud Run services
Run the Bigtable and Pub/Sub emulators locally to test integrations on a developer machine, then deploy the services to the Google Cloud project
Create a Cloud Build pipeline that runs unit and integration tests and includes a manual approval step before promoting the deployment

questions.correct_text: Run the Bigtable and Pub/Sub emulators locally to test integrations on a developer machine, then deploy the services to the Google Cloud project
questions.explanation:
The correct strategy is Run the Bigtable and Pub/Sub local emulators locally to test integrations on a developer machine, and deploy the services to the Google Cloud project.

This strategy permits the team perform to realistic integration testing without incurring managed service costs during rapid iteration. The Bigtable and Pub/Sub emulators run on a developer machine which shortens feedback loops, avoids per message and storage charges, and keeps the team focused on debugging within the 10 day window. Once core issues are resolved, the services can be deployed to the project for limited end to end verification.

Use Cloud Code to develop and iterate, deploy each service to Cloud Run for end to end tests, and review telemetry in Cloud Logging and Cloud Trace is workable but it needs frequent remote deployments and use of managed telemetry for each cycle which increases cost and slows iteration compared to using local emulators for integration tests.

Provision a separate staging project that mirrors production, configure Cloud Deploy with manual approval gates, and run end to end validation of the Cloud Run services adds significant setup and operational overhead. It is a strong production practice, yet it is not the fastest or cheapest path for a small team trying to debug an MVP within two weeks.

Create a Cloud Build pipeline that runs unit and integration tests and includes a manual approval step before promoting the deployment introduces manual gates and pipeline complexity that slow down rapid iteration. It also tends to validate against managed services rather than local emulators, which increases cost during frequent test cycles.

questions.question: Lyric Music is migrating an internal file upload service to App Engine. The current API permits files up to 560 MB and stakeholders want to retain that limit whereas ensuring secure and scalable ingestion. What should you implement on Google Cloud to satisfy these requirements?

options.text: Enable multipart uploads handled entirely by the App Engine service
Set up an SFTP endpoint on a Compute Engine VM and direct clients to upload there
Issue V4 signed URLs and use Cloud Storage resumable uploads from the client
Use Cloud Pub or Sub to stream file chunks and reassemble them in a worker

questions.correct_text: Issue V4 signed URLs and use Cloud Storage resumable uploads from the client
questions.explanation:
The only correct choice is Issue V4 signed link URLs and use Cloud Storage resumable uploads from the client.

This strategy permits your App Engine service mint V4 signed URLs so clients send directly to the object save using resumable uploads. Direct to storage uploads bypass App Engine request size and instance constraints, support large files and unreliable networks, and scale because your service performs only lightweight URL signing while storage handles the data path. Security is preserved because the signed URL is time bound and scoped to specific objects and methods, and developers can enforce content type and other conditions.

Enable multipart uploads handled completely by the App Engine service is not viable for 920 MB files because App Engine has strict HTTP request size limits, and proxying large bodies through the service would be resource intensive and scale poorly.

Set up an SFTP endpoint on a Compute Engine VM and direct clients to upload there needs you to handle servers, capacity, and credentials. It is not serverless or autoscaling, and it still leaves you moving data into Cloud Storage after the fact which adds cost and operational risk.

Use Cloud Pub or Sub to stream file chunks and reassemble them in a worker misuses the messaging service. Pub/Sub messages have a small size limit and are not intended for bulk file transfer, so chunking and reassembly would be complex, inefficient, and unreliable for hundreds of megabytes.

Não é serverless nem com autoescalonamento, e ainda deixa você movendo dados para o Cloud Storage depois, o que adiciona custo e risco operacional.

Usar o Cloud Pub/Sub para transmitir pedaços do arquivo e remontá-los em um worker faz uso indevido do serviço de mensageria. questions.question: Which GCP service should you use to run a Python 3.12 web API with request based autoscaling, fast rollouts several times per day, and low operational cost?

options.text: GKE Autopilot
Cloud Run
App Engine flexible

questions.correct_text: Cloud Run
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Cloud Run. It runs a Python 3.12 web API with request based autoscaling, accommodates fast rollouts several times per day, and keeps operational cost low.

Cloud Run is a fully managed request driven container service that on its own scales instances based on concurrent requests and can scale to zero when idle, which minimizes cost. It handles quick deployments, revisions, traffic splitting, and instant rollbacks so developers can release many times per day with minimal risk. Because you supply a container image you may use Python 3.12 without extra runtime setup and you stop server management.

GKE Autopilot still needs Kubernetes manifests and ops overhead and generally uses metric based pod autoscaling rather than simple request based scaling. It does not scale to zero as seamlessly and there is a baseline cost for the cluster resources, so it does not meet the low operational cost and simplicity needed here.

App Engine flexible has slower deployments and longer instance startup times and often keeps at least one instance running, which increases cost. It lacks the rapid rollouts and scale to zero behavior desired for a request driven web API, so it is suboptimal.

questions.question: A travel booking platform for Skylark Trips runs on Google Kubernetes Engine and the team sees that certain defects only appear after a new release begins handling real customer traffic. You need to reduce the scope of impact and limit how many users are touched whereas still validating the new build under production load. Which deployment approach should you choose?

options.text: Rolling update
Canary deployment
Recreate deployment
Blue green deployment

questions.correct_text: Canary deployment
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Canary deployment.

This strategy sends a small and controlled portion of active traffic to the new version whereas the majority continues to use the stable version. The team can observe error rates, latency, and business metrics and, and either increase the traffic share or quickly roll back. This limits how many users are affected while still testing under real load, which directly satisfies the goal of validating the new build with minimal impact.

Rolling update replaces pods gradually, yet each new pod immediately receives normal production traffic behind the Service. This does not supply precise control over a small test cohort and defects can affect users throughout the rollout.

Recreate deployment stops the old version before starting the new one, which causes downtime and then exposes all users to the new version at once. This does not reduce the scope of impact.

Blue green deployment runs two environments and switches traffic between them, generally moving all users to the new version in one step. While rollback is fast, it does not limit exposure to a small subset of users for incremental validation unless you add traffic splitting, which aligns more with a canary strategy.

questions.question: A logistics company named Nightingale Health is deploying a payments microservice on Google Kubernetes Engine that must store data in a Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instance. The security team requires the most secure connection pattern that avoids using the public internet. Which connection approach should you implement?

options.text: Connect using Cloud SQL public IP and enforce SSL/TLS from the application
Expose the database through a Cloud VPN tunnel and use the public IP with mutual TLS from the pods
Configure private IP on the instance and run the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy as a sidecar in each GKE pod
Configure private IP on the instance and connect directly from the application without the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy

questions.correct_text: Configure private IP on the instance and run the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy as a sidecar in each GKE pod
questions.explanation:
The proper option is Configure private IP on the instance and run the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy as a sidecar in each GKE pod. This strategy keeps database traffic on your VPC and adds strong authentication and encryption that satisfies the need to stop the public internet.

Private IP guarantees the instance has no public endpoint and traffic flows only over Google Cloud's private network. Running the proxy as a sidecar means each pod authenticates to Cloud SQL with its service account and the proxy negotiates TLS to the database automatically. The proxy also accommodates IAM database authentication and short lived certificates which reduces credential exposure and aligns with minimal privilege on GKE.

Connect using Cloud SQL public IP and enforce SSL/TLS from the app is not acceptable since it still uses the public internet which violates the requirement even though encryption in transit is present. It also increases exposure and network controls are weaker than a private path.

Expose the database through a Cloud VPN tunnel and use the public IP with mutual TLS from the pods is not viable because Cloud SQL is a managed service that is not reachable over your VPN and the public IP remains an internet endpoint. This does not provide the most secure private path.

Configure private IP on the instance and connect directly from the application without the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy avoids the public internet, yet it lacks the proxy features that harden access including automatic TLS, IAM database authentication, and centralized connection handling. It often relies on static database passwords and manual certificate management which is less secure than the proxy sidecar pattern.

questions.question: Lumen Media runs integration tests in Cloud Build for mosaicapp.dev and each build deploys a temporary Cloud Function named audit-check-fn for validation. You must ensure the function is always removed even if the tests fail and the build should still fail when assertions do not pass. How should you structure the Cloud Build steps to achieve this?

options.text: Reorder the steps so the build deletes the Cloud Function before any tests run
Configure the deletion step with waitFor on the test step so the function is deleted only when the test step succeeds

Write the test outcome to a file in a shared location and have the test step exit with code 0 so the build continues then delete the Cloud Function and run a final step that reads the file and fails the build if the expected result is not present
Store the test result in an environment variable named "RESULT" then delete the function and have a later step read that variable to decide whether to fail the build

questions.correct_text: Write the test outcome to a file in a shared location and have the test step exit with code 0 so the build continues then delete the Cloud Function and run a final step that reads the file and fails the build if the expected result is not present
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Write the test outcome to a file in a shared location and have the test step exit with code 0 so the build continues, and delete the Cloud Function and run a final step that reads the file and fails the build if the expected result is not present.

This strategy works because Cloud Build stops running steps when a step exits with a nonzero code. By having the test step record its result to a file in a shared path including the workspace and exit with code 0, the cleanup step will always run and remove the Cloud Function. A final step can then read the recorded result and exit with a failing code when assertions did not pass so the overall build still fails whereas ensuring the function is deleted.

Reorder the steps so the build deletes the Cloud Function before any tests run is not right since it removes the function before validation and does not meet the requirement to validate with the deployed function. It also does not confirm cleanup after tests.

Configure the deletion step with waitFor on the test step so the function is deleted only when the test step succeeds is incorrect because waitFor controls ordering on its own. If the test step fails, Cloud Build stops the build and the deletion step will not run, which risks leaving the function undeleted.

Store the test result in an environment variable named "RESULT" then delete the function and have a later step read that variable to decide whether to fail the build is incorrect because each step runs in its own collection and runtime environment variables do not persist between steps. To share state across steps you should use files in the workspace or a shared volume.

Essa estratégia funciona porque o Cloud Build para de executar as etapas quando uma etapa sai com um código diferente de zero. Ao fazer a etapa de teste registrar seu resultado em um arquivo em um caminho compartilhado, incluindo o workspace, e sair com código 0, a etapa de limpeza sempre será executada e removerá a Cloud Function. Uma etapa final pode então ler o resultado registrado e sair com um código de falha quando as asserções não passaram, de modo que o build geral ainda falhe, ao mesmo tempo em que garante que a function seja excluída.

Reordenar as etapas para que o build exclua a Cloud Function antes de quaisquer testes serem executados não está correto, pois remove a function antes da validação e não atende ao requisito de validar com a function implantada. Também não confirma a limpeza após os testes.

Configurar a etapa de exclusão com waitFor na etapa de teste para que a function seja excluída somente quando a etapa de teste tiver sucesso está incorreto porque o waitFor controla apenas a ordenação. Se a etapa de teste falhar, o Cloud Build para o build e a etapa de exclusão não será executada, o que corre o risco de deixar a function não excluída.

Armazenar o resultado do teste em uma variável de ambiente chamada "RESULT", então excluir a function e fazer uma etapa posterior ler essa variável para decidir se falha o build está incorreto porque cada etapa é executada em sua própria coleção e as variáveis de ambiente de runtime não persistem entre as etapas. Para compartilhar estado entre etapas, você deve usar arquivos no workspace ou um volume compartilhado.

questions.question: A regional retailer named Riverstone Bank operates an on-premises Hadoop platform that holds roughly 200 TB of data and expects steady growth over the next year. Rising HDFS storage costs and maintenance are driving a move to Google Cloud whereas leadership insists on keeping existing Spark and Hive jobs with as few changes as possible. Which migration approach should the team implement to meet these goals?

options.text: Load the Hadoop data into BigQuery and modify analytics so all workloads run as SQL queries in BigQuery
Run your existing Hadoop stack on Cloud Dataproc and place all datasets in Cloud Storage and use the Dataproc GCS connector so jobs read and write directly to Cloud Storage
Rebuild your pipelines on Cloud Dataflow reading from Cloud Storage and convert current MapReduce and Spark code to Apache Beam
Provision Cloud Dataproc and keep data in HDFS on larger standard persistent disks to reduce storage cost

questions.correct_text: Run your existing Hadoop stack on Cloud Dataproc and place all datasets in Cloud Storage and use the Dataproc GCS connector so jobs read and write directly to Cloud Storage
questions.explanation:
The proper option is Run your existing Hadoop stack on Cloud Dataproc and place all datasets in Cloud Storage and use the Dataproc GCS connector so jobs read and write directly to Cloud Storage.

This strategy preserves your existing Spark and Hive workloads with very few or no code changes because the managed service runs the same Hadoop ecosystem and jobs can transparently read and write gs paths. Moving data to Cloud Storage lowers storage cost and removes HDFS operational burdens including NameNode management while providing durable regional storage that scales easily for a 200 TB environment with expected growth. Developers can scale compute and storage independently which reduces cluster bloat that is caused by storing data on cluster disks.

You can also run short lived clusters for processing while keeping all data in object storage which improves reliability and simplifies operations. Jobs access buckets directly so you stop rebalancing HDFS and you gain straightforward data lifecycle and security controls.

Load the Hadoop data into BigQuery and modify analytics so all workloads run as SQL queries in BigQuery is a poor match since it would require significant rewrites of Spark and Hive logic into SQL and would change the execution model. The requirement is to keep existing jobs with minimal changes.

Rebuild your pipelines on Cloud Dataflow reading from Cloud Storage and convert current MapReduce and Spark code to Apache Beam is unsuitable since it forces a migration to a different programming model which needs extensive refactoring and validation. This fails the minimal change requirement.

Provision Cloud Dataproc and keep data in HDFS on larger standard persistent disks to reduce storage cost does not meet the cost and maintenance goals because you would still pay for large persistent disks at this scale and continue to operate HDFS and NameNode services. Using object storage removes this overhead and is generally more economical for large datasets.

Essa estratégia preserva suas cargas de trabalho Spark e Hive existentes com pouquíssimas ou nenhuma alteração de código, porque o serviço gerenciado executa o mesmo ecossistema Hadoop e os jobs podem ler e gravar caminhos gs de forma transparente. Mover os dados para o Cloud Storage reduz o custo de armazenamento e elimina os encargos operacionais do HDFS, incluindo o gerenciamento do NameNode, ao mesmo tempo que oferece armazenamento regional durável que escala facilmente para um ambiente de 200 TB com crescimento esperado. Os desenvolvedores podem escalar computação e armazenamento de forma independente, o que reduz o inchaço do cluster causado por armazenar dados nos discos do cluster.

Você também pode executar clusters de curta duração para processamento mantendo todos os dados em armazenamento de objetos, o que melhora a confiabilidade e simplifica as operações. Os jobs acessam os buckets diretamente, então você deixa de rebalancear o HDFS e ganha controles simples de ciclo de vida e segurança dos dados.

Carregar os dados do Hadoop no BigQuery e modificar a análise para que todas as cargas de trabalho rodem como consultas SQL no BigQuery é uma escolha ruim, pois exigiria reescritas significativas da lógica Spark e Hive em SQL e mudaria o modelo de execução. O requisito é manter os jobs existentes com mudanças mínimas.

Reconstruir seus pipelines no Cloud Dataflow lendo do Cloud Storage e converter o código atual de MapReduce e Spark para Apache Beam é inadequado, pois força uma migração para um modelo de programação diferente que exige refatoração e validação extensas. Isso não atende ao requisito de mudança mínima.

Provisionar o Cloud Dataproc e manter os dados no HDFS em discos persistentes standard maiores para reduzir o custo de armazenamento não atende às metas de custo e manutenção, porque você ainda pagaria por discos persistentes grandes nessa escala e continuaria a operar os serviços HDFS e NameNode. Usar armazenamento de objetos elimina essa sobrecarga e geralmente é mais econômico para datasets grandes.

questions.question: Kestrel Aerospace plans to deploy a new service to Cloud Run and the team prefers not to maintain a Dockerfile, whereas corporate policy requires every built image to live in a centrally managed Artifact Registry repository in the platform project. How should you build the container from source with Google Cloud so that the image is published to the central repository?

options.text: Push your source code to Artifact Registry
Include the --source flag with the gcloud run deploy CLI command
Run gcloud builds submit with no configuration and expect an image to be created
Use the pack build command with the pack CLI
Use Cloud Deploy to build and publish the image to Artifact Registry

questions.correct_text: Use the pack build command with the pack CLI
questions.explanation:
The correct options are Include the --source flag with the gcloud run deploy CLI command and Use the pack build command with the pack CLI.

Include the --source flag with the gcloud run deploy CLI command builds directly from your local source using Cloud Buildpacks, so you do not need a Dockerfile. Developers can direct the resulting image to the centrally managed Artifact Registry repository by specifying the full Artifact Registry image path with the image flag during deployment, which guarantees the build pushes to the repository in the platform project and, and deploys that image to Cloud Run.

Use the pack build command with the pack CLI also builds from source without a Dockerfile by using Cloud Native Buildpacks. You can tag the produced image with the full Artifact Registry path for the central repository and push it after authenticating with Artifact Registry, which satisfies the requirement to publish into the platform project’s repository.

Push your source code to Artifact Registry is not right because Artifact Registry keeps built artifacts including container images and it does not host raw source code.

Run gcloud builds submit with no configuration and expect an image to be created is incorrect because without a Dockerfile, a buildpacks flag, or a Cloud Build configuration file, Cloud Build has no instructions to build an image from source.

Use Cloud Deploy to build and publish the image to Artifact Registry is incorrect because Cloud Deploy orchestrates delivery of already built artifacts and it does not build container images.

questions.question: Tidewater Shipping is building a serverless processor that must react only when objects are added under the folder prefix /ingest/photos/ in a Cloud Storage bucket. The service must scale with bursts of uploads and you want to keep operations minimal. You also need to be able to change the folder prefix later without redeploying the service code. Which approach should you take?

options.text: Create a Cloud Function that triggers on Cloud Storage finalize events for objects with the /ingest/photos/ prefix and runs the processing logic
Enable Firebase Functions to listen for uploads with the /ingest/photos/ prefix in the bucket and invoke the processing logic
Deploy the processor to Cloud Run and use Eventarc to add a Cloud Storage trigger that filters by the /ingest/photos/ object name prefix
Run a Compute Engine instance that polls the bucket for new objects under /ingest/photos/ and processes them as they arrive

questions.correct_text: Deploy the processor to Cloud Run and use Eventarc to add a Cloud Storage trigger that filters by the /ingest/photos/ object name prefix
questions.explanation:
The best answer is Deploy the processor to Cloud Run and use Eventarc to add a Cloud Storage trigger that filters by the /ingest/photos/ object name prefix.

This strategy offers an event trigger that natively filters by the object name prefix so the processor runs only for files under the specified path. It is fully serverless and scales rapidly with bursts of uploads while keeping operations minimal. Because the trigger is a separate resource from the service, developers can change the folder prefix later by updating or recreating the trigger configuration without redeploying the service code.

Event routing is handled by the managed trigger so the service receives only the relevant events. This keeps invocation costs and noise low and permits you to evolve the filter independently of the app container.

Create a Cloud Function that triggers on Cloud Storage finalize events for objects with the /ingest/photos/ prefix and runs the processing logic is less ideal because the trigger is tightly coupled to the function deployment. Changing the prefix generally needs redeploying the function and earlier generations did not support trigger level prefix filtering which often forced filtering in code and unnecessary invocations.

Enable Firebase Functions to listen for uploads with the /ingest/photos/ prefix in the bucket and invoke the processing logic targets Firebase centric workloads and Firebase Storage integrations rather than general Cloud Storage in GCP projects. It adds unnecessary platform coupling and you would still need to redeploy to change the prefix, which does not meet the operational goal.

Run a Compute Engine instance that polls the bucket for new objects under /ingest/photos/ and processes them as they arrive is not serverless and introduces management overhead and cost. Polling is inefficient and does not scale on its own to handle bursts of uploads.

Como o gatilho é um recurso separado do serviço, os desenvolvedores podem alterar o prefixo da pasta posteriormente atualizando ou recriando a configuração do gatilho sem reimplantar o código do serviço.

O roteamento de eventos é tratado pelo gatilho gerenciado, então o serviço recebe apenas os eventos relevantes. Isso mantém os custos de invocação e o ruído baixos e permite que você evolua o filtro de forma independente do contêiner da aplicação.

Criar uma Cloud Function que dispara em eventos finalize do Cloud Storage para objetos com o prefixo /ingest/photos/ e executa a lógica de processamento é menos ideal porque o gatilho está fortemente acoplado à implantação da função. Alterar o prefixo geralmente exige reimplantar a função, e gerações anteriores não suportavam filtragem por prefixo no nível do gatilho, o que muitas vezes forçava a filtragem no código e invocações desnecessárias.

Habilitar o Firebase Functions para escutar uploads com o prefixo /ingest/photos/ no bucket e invocar a lógica de processamento é voltado para cargas de trabalho centradas no Firebase e integrações com o Firebase Storage, em vez do Cloud Storage geral em projetos GCP. Isso adiciona acoplamento de plataforma desnecessário e você ainda precisaria reimplantar para alterar o prefixo, o que não atende à meta operacional.

Executar uma instância do Compute Engine que faz polling no bucket por novos objetos sob /ingest/photos/ e os processa à medida que chegam não é serverless e introduz sobrecarga de gerenciamento e custo. O polling é ineficiente e não escala por conta própria para lidar com picos de uploads.

questions.question: Northwind Couriers runs a CI pipeline for a service that uses Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL. Each test execution must have a fresh database with a defined schema and seeded test data, and up to 9 executions can occur at the same time. The team wants strong isolation and fast setup whereas keeping costs manageable. How should the pipeline provision database environments to achieve these goals?

options.text: Build a read replica from a baseline Cloud SQL primary for each test run then run tests against the replica and discard the replica when done
Use a single database on one Cloud SQL instance for all runs and rely on transaction isolation to avoid interference
Use one Cloud SQL instance and create a uniquely named database for each run then drop that database after the run completes
Create a dedicated Cloud SQL instance for every test run then install the schema and sample data and delete the instance when the test finishes

questions.correct_text: Use one Cloud SQL instance and create a uniquely named database for each run then drop that database after the run completes
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Use one Cloud SQL instance and create a uniquely named database for each run, and drop that database after the run completes. This offers strong isolation because each run has its own database while keeping setup fast and costs low by reusing a single instance.

Creating a separate database per run isolates test data and schema changes so runs do not interfere with each other. Setup can be very quick by running migrations and seed scripts into each new database or by using a template database model in PostgreSQL. A single instance easily accommodates a dozen concurrent databases and you pay for one instance rather than many.

Build a read replica from a baseline Cloud SQL primary for each test run then run tests against the replica and discard the replica when done is unsuitable since Cloud SQL read replicas are read only. Most tests need to perform writes and schema initialization and replica creation is slower and more expensive than building a new database on an existing instance.

Use a single database on one Cloud SQL instance for all runs and rely on transaction isolation to stop interference does not meet the strong isolation requirement. Parallel tests can still conflict through shared objects including sequences or locks and one run can affect performance or state for another run.

Create a dedicated Cloud SQL instance for every test run then install the schema and sample data and delete the instance when the test finishes supplies isolation but it is slow to provision and tear down and is expensive at scale. It can also run into instance quotas which makes it impractical for up to twelve concurrent runs.

questions.explanation_pt:

Isso oferece forte isolamento, porque cada execução tem seu próprio banco de dados, mantendo a configuração rápida e os custos baixos ao reutilizar uma única instância.

Criar um banco de dados separado por execução isola os dados de teste e as mudanças de esquema, de modo que as execuções não interferem umas nas outras. A configuração pode ser muito rápida executando migrações e scripts de seed em cada novo banco de dados ou usando um modelo de banco de dados template no PostgreSQL. Uma única instância acomoda facilmente uma dúzia de bancos de dados simultâneos e você paga por uma instância em vez de muitas.

Construir uma read replica a partir de um Cloud SQL primário de baseline para cada execução de teste, executar os testes contra a réplica e descartar a réplica ao terminar é inadequado, pois as read replicas do Cloud SQL são somente leitura. A maioria dos testes precisa realizar gravações e inicialização de esquema, e a criação de réplicas é mais lenta e cara do que construir um novo banco de dados em uma instância existente.

Usar um único banco de dados em uma instância do Cloud SQL para todas as execuções e contar com o isolamento de transações para impedir interferências não atende ao requisito de forte isolamento. Testes paralelos ainda podem entrar em conflito por meio de objetos compartilhados, incluindo sequências ou locks, e uma execução pode afetar o desempenho ou o estado de outra.

Criar uma instância dedicada do Cloud SQL para cada execução de teste, instalar o esquema e os dados de amostra e excluir a instância quando o teste terminar fornece isolamento, mas é lento para provisionar e desmontar e é caro em escala. Também pode esbarrar em cotas de instâncias, o que o torna impraticável para até doze execuções simultâneas.

questions.question: An e-commerce startup at fernhill.org uploads product images to Cloud Storage through the Cloud Client Libraries and sometimes the upload requests return HTTP 504 Gateway Timeout. You need to improve reliability for these uploads without asking users to take action and without changing the storage service design. Which approach should you take?

options.text: Publish failed uploads to a Pub/Sub topic and notify customers that the system will retry them after 12 minutes
Add automatic retries around the Cloud Storage upload that use exponential backoff and follow the client library's retry policy
Sleep for two seconds between retries around the upload and continue retrying with no limit
Place Cloud Load Balancing in front of Cloud Storage to eliminate gateway timeouts

questions.correct_text: Add automatic retries around the Cloud Storage upload that use exponential backoff and follow the client library's retry policy
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Add automatic retries around the Cloud Storage send that use exponential backoff and follow the client library's retry policy.

HTTP 504 errors are generally transient and the Cloud Client Libraries for Cloud Storage are designed to handle such conditions with built in retry semantics. Implementing automatic retries that respect the library's policy uses exponential backoff with appropriate limits and jitter, and it aligns with how the service expects clients to recover from temporary failures. This strategy needs no user interaction and does not change the storage service design. Using resumable uploads further improves reliability since only the missing chunks are retried rather than the whole object.

Publish failed uploads to a Pub/Sub topic and notify customers that the system will retry them after 8 minutes adds unnecessary delay and complexity and it shifts the workflow to asynchronous processing. It does not directly address temporary failures at the client and it introduces user notifications that are not needed for this scenario.

Sleep for two seconds between retries around the upload and continue retrying with no limit uses a fixed delay and unbounded retries, which is not a best practice. It ignores exponential backoff and jitter and it can cause runaway retry behavior, waste resources, and hide persistent errors.

Place Cloud Load Balancing in front of Cloud Storage to eliminate gateway timeouts is not applicable because Cloud Storage is already fronted by Google's global infrastructure and you cannot place your own load balancer in front of the service to change its error behavior. This would not resolve transient 504 responses and would add unnecessary complexity.

questions.explanation_pt:
A escolha certa é adicionar novas tentativas automáticas em torno do envio para o Cloud Storage que usem exponential backoff e sigam a política de retry da biblioteca cliente.

Erros HTTP 504 geralmente são transitórios e as Cloud Client Libraries para Cloud Storage são projetadas para lidar com tais condições com semântica de retry integrada. Implementar novas tentativas automáticas que respeitem a política da biblioteca usa exponential backoff com limites apropriados e jitter, e se alinha com a forma como o serviço espera que os clientes se recuperem de falhas temporárias. Essa estratégia não precisa de interação do usuário e não altera o design do serviço de armazenamento. Usar uploads resumable melhora ainda mais a confiabilidade, pois apenas os chunks ausentes são reenviados, em vez do objeto inteiro.

Publicar uploads com falha em um tópico do Pub/Sub e notificar os clientes de que o sistema os reenviará após 8 minutos adiciona atraso e complexidade desnecessários e desloca o fluxo de trabalho para processamento assíncrono. Não aborda diretamente as falhas temporárias no cliente e introduz notificações ao usuário que não são necessárias para este cenário.

Dormir por dois segundos entre as tentativas em torno do upload e continuar tentando sem limite usa um atraso fixo e tentativas ilimitadas, o que não é uma boa prática. Ignora o exponential backoff e o jitter e pode causar comportamento de retry descontrolado, desperdiçar recursos e ocultar erros persistentes.

Colocar o Cloud Load Balancing na frente do Cloud Storage para eliminar timeouts de gateway não é aplicável, porque o Cloud Storage já está fronteado pela infraestrutura global do Google e você não pode colocar seu próprio load balancer na frente do serviço para alterar seu comportamento de erro. Isso não resolveria respostas 504 transitórias e adicionaria complexidade desnecessária.

questions.question: Coastline Apparel, a logistics startup, is rolling out a Cloud Run service that must connect to PostgreSQL whereas keeping all communication on Google Cloud's private network. To follow Google's recommendations and rely on managed services with low operational overhead, what should the team implement?

options.text: Host PostgreSQL on a Compute Engine VM in the same project as Cloud Run, assign a private IP, enable private services access, create a Serverless VPC Access connector, and configure Cloud Run to reach the VM through the connector
Keep Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL on a public IP and require Cloud Run to use the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy or the Cloud SQL connectors over the public endpoint

Use Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL and Cloud Run in the same project, give Cloud SQL a private IP, enable private services access, create a Serverless VPC Access connector, and have Cloud Run connect to Cloud SQL through that connector

Use Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL in a different project from Cloud Run, configure a private IP and private services access, create a Serverless VPC Access connector, and establish a VPN between the projects so Cloud Run can reach Cloud SQL via the connector

questions.correct_text: Use Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL and Cloud Run in the same project, give Cloud SQL a private IP, enable private services access, create a Serverless VPC Access connector, and have Cloud Run connect to Cloud SQL through that connector
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Use Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL and Cloud Run in the same project, give Cloud SQL a private IP, enable private services access, create a Serverless VPC Access connector, and have Cloud Run connect to Cloud SQL through that connector.

This strategy keeps traffic on Google Cloud's private network because Cloud SQL uses a private IP that is reachable only within your VPC through private services access. Cloud Run gains access to that VPC through a Serverless VPC Access connector which permits the service initiate to connections to the database over private RFC 1918 addresses. It aligns with Google guidance to use managed services and it minimizes operational work since Cloud SQL handles maintenance, high availability, and backups while Cloud Run is fully managed.

Keeping both resources in the same project simplifies identity and access management and networking. There is no need for public egress, IP allowlists, or manual tunneling, and the design remains private, simple, and low overhead.

Host PostgreSQL on a Compute Engine VM in the same project as Cloud Run, assign a private IP, enable private services access, create a Serverless VPC Access connector, and configure Cloud Run to reach the VM through the connector is less ideal since it places the database on a self-managed VM. That increases operational burden for patching, backups, replication, and failover which goes against the requirement to rely on managed services with low overhead.

Keep Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL on a public IP and require Cloud Run to use the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy or the Cloud SQL connectors over the public endpoint does not meet the requirement to keep all communication on the private network. Even though connections are encrypted and authenticated, traffic reaches a public endpoint which violates the private networking constraint.

Use Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL in a different project from Cloud Run, configure a private IP and private services access, create a Serverless VPC Access connector, and establish a VPN between the projects so Cloud Run can reach Cloud SQL through the connector adds unnecessary complexity and operational overhead. Cross project private access to Cloud SQL does not require a VPN and is better handled with Shared VPC or appropriate VPC peering, so introducing a VPN is not suggested here.

O Cloud Run obtém acesso a essa VPC através de um conector Serverless VPC Access, que permite ao serviço iniciar conexões com o banco de dados sobre endereços privados RFC 1918. Isso está alinhado com a orientação do Google de usar serviços gerenciados e minimiza o trabalho operacional, já que o Cloud SQL cuida da manutenção, alta disponibilidade e backups, enquanto o Cloud Run é totalmente gerenciado.

Manter ambos os recursos no mesmo projeto simplifica o gerenciamento de identidade e acesso e a rede. Não há necessidade de egress público, listas de permissão de IP ou tunneling manual, e o design permanece privado, simples e de baixo overhead.

Hospedar o PostgreSQL em uma VM do Compute Engine no mesmo projeto que o Cloud Run, atribuir um IP privado, habilitar o private services access, criar um conector Serverless VPC Access e configurar o Cloud Run para alcançar a VM através do conector é menos ideal, pois coloca o banco de dados em uma VM autogerenciada. Isso aumenta a carga operacional para patching, backups, replicação e failover, o que vai contra o requisito de depender de serviços gerenciados com baixo overhead.

Manter o Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL em um IP público e exigir que o Cloud Run use o Cloud SQL Auth Proxy ou os Cloud SQL connectors sobre o endpoint público não atende ao requisito de manter toda a comunicação na rede privada. Mesmo que as conexões sejam criptografadas e autenticadas, o tráfego alcança um endpoint público, o que viola a restrição de rede privada.

Usar o Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL em um projeto diferente do Cloud Run, configurar um IP privado e o private services access, criar um conector Serverless VPC Access e estabelecer uma VPN entre os projetos para que o Cloud Run possa alcançar o Cloud SQL através do conector adiciona complexidade e overhead operacional desnecessários. O acesso privado entre projetos ao Cloud SQL não requer uma VPN e é melhor tratado com Shared VPC ou VPC peering apropriado, portanto introduzir uma VPN não é recomendado aqui.

questions.question: You manage a GKE Standard cluster that powers a real time event processing service for loomwright.io. Traffic during promotions is unpredictable and can triple for about 26 minutes several times each week, and you must keep availability high whereas using resources efficiently. How should you configure autoscaling to handle these bursts reliably?

options.text: Run Spot VMs in the node pool and change the node count by hand during spikes
Set the managed instance groups that back the cluster to scale on traffic patterns and also use a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler for replicas
Enable Cluster Autoscaler for the cluster and configure a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler that scales replicas based on average CPU utilization
Enable Cluster Autoscaler and use Vertical Pod Autoscaler in auto mode to tune pod resource requests as traffic changes

questions.correct_text: Enable Cluster Autoscaler for the cluster and configure a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler that scales replicas based on average CPU utilization
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Enable Cluster Autoscaler for the cluster and configure a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler that scales replicas based on average CPU utilization.

This pairing addresses both dimensions of autoscaling. Horizontal Pod Autoscaler reacts to increased CPU load by adding replicas so the service can absorb unpredictable bursts within the existing nodes. When the replica count cannot fit on current nodes, Cluster Autoscaler adds nodes to the node pool so pending pods can be scheduled, and removes excess nodes after the surge ends. CPU is a common and useful signal for real time processing throughput, and this strategy keeps availability high while using resources efficiently for short spikes that last about twenty minutes.

Run Spot VMs in the node pool and change the node count by hand during spikes is unreliable for high availability because Spot VMs can be reclaimed at any time and manual scaling is slow and error prone for sudden bursts.

Set the managed instance groups that back the cluster to scale on traffic patterns and also use a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler for replicas is not suggested because GKE expects node pool sizes to be managed by the cluster autoscaler rather than by directly autoscaling the backing managed instance groups. External MIG policies can conflict with Kubernetes scheduling signals and lead to instability.

Enable Cluster Autoscaler and use Vertical Pod Autoscaler in auto mode to tune pod resource requests as traffic changes is a poor match for rapid bursts because Vertical Pod Autoscaler in Auto mode may evict pods to apply new adviseations and it converges over longer windows. It also conflicts with HPA when scaling on CPU or memory, so it is not preferred for quick traffic spikes.

questions.explanation_pt:
A escolha correta é habilitar o Cluster Autoscaler para o cluster e configurar um Horizontal Pod Autoscaler que escala réplicas com base na utilização média de CPU.

Essa combinação aborda ambas as dimensões do autoscaling. O Horizontal Pod Autoscaler reage ao aumento da carga de CPU adicionando réplicas, para que o serviço possa absorver picos imprevisíveis dentro dos nós existentes. Quando a contagem de réplicas não cabe nos nós atuais, o Cluster Autoscaler adiciona nós ao node pool para que os pods pendentes possam ser agendados, e remove os nós em excesso após o fim do pico. CPU é um sinal comum e útil para throughput de processamento em tempo real, e essa estratégia mantém a disponibilidade alta enquanto usa os recursos de forma eficiente para picos curtos que duram cerca de vinte minutos.

Executar Spot VMs no node pool e alterar a contagem de nós manualmente durante os picos é não confiável para alta disponibilidade, porque as Spot VMs podem ser recuperadas a qualquer momento e o escalonamento manual é lento e propenso a erros para picos repentinos.

Configurar os managed instance groups que dão suporte ao cluster para escalar com base em padrões de tráfego e também usar um Horizontal Pod Autoscaler para réplicas não é recomendado, porque o GKE espera que os tamanhos do node pool sejam gerenciados pelo cluster autoscaler, em vez de fazer autoscaling diretamente nos managed instance groups de suporte. Políticas externas de MIG podem entrar em conflito com os sinais de agendamento do Kubernetes e levar à instabilidade.

Habilitar o Cluster Autoscaler e usar o Vertical Pod Autoscaler em modo auto para ajustar as solicitações de recursos dos pods conforme o tráfego muda é uma escolha ruim para picos rápidos, porque o Vertical Pod Autoscaler em modo Auto pode despejar pods para aplicar novas recomendações e converge ao longo de janelas mais longas. Ele também entra em conflito com o HPA ao escalar por CPU ou memória, portanto não é preferível para picos rápidos de tráfego.

questions.question: Within Silvercrest Logistics you run multiple microservices on Google Kubernetes Engine with Istio. Your team rolled out a mesh wide PeerAuthentication in STRICT mode to require mutual TLS for all service to service calls. Soon after the rollout some internal calls begin to fail sporadically whereas other calls continue to work. Which underlying cause best explains the intermittent reachability?

options.text: A misconfigured Gateway resource is sporadically blocking inbound traffic to the internal services
Client traffic lacks a matching DestinationRule to originate mutual TLS to services that now enforce STRICT
Some workloads do not have the Envoy sidecar injected so they make plaintext calls that are rejected under STRICT
A custom EnvoyFilter is altering clusters or routes which leads to intermittent routing issues

questions.correct_text: Some workloads do not have the Envoy sidecar injected so they make plaintext calls that are rejected under STRICT
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Client traffic lacks a matching DestinationRule to originate mutual TLS to services that now enforce STRICT.

With a mesh wide PeerAuthentication set to STRICT, all servers require mutual TLS. Clients must originate mTLS, which is generally configured through a matching DestinationRule that sets the TLS mode to ISTIO_MUTUAL. Without that client side configuration, calls may be sent in plaintext and are rejected by servers that now require mTLS.

The behavior often looks intermittent because some traffic flows match an existing DestinationRule or benefit from automatic mTLS while other flows do not. Differences including namespace scoping, hostnames that are short versus fully qualified, subsets, or conflicting rules can cause some requests to originate mTLS correctly while others do not, which leads to sporadic reachability.

A misconfigured Gateway resource is sporadically blocking inbound traffic to the internal services is not the best explanation because Gateways control edge or egress traffic and are not in the path for typical in mesh service to service calls. Internal calls failing right after enforcing STRICT point to mTLS policy and client origination rather than a Gateway issue.

Some workloads do not have the Envoy sidecar injected so they make plaintext calls that are rejected under STRICT would cause consistent failures for those specific callers rather than sporadic successes and failures for the same call pattern. Lack of a sidecar is a clear on or off condition and does not often manifest as intermittent reachability.

A custom EnvoyFilter is altering clusters or routes which leads to intermittent routing issues could explain routing anomalies, yet the timing with a mesh wide STRICT rollout and the specific symptom of mTLS related rejections make this a less likely root cause than missing client side TLS origination.

questions.explanation_pt:
A escolha correta é que o tráfego do cliente não tem uma DestinationRule correspondente para originar mutual TLS para serviços que agora aplicam STRICT.

Com uma PeerAuthentication em nível de mesh definida como STRICT, todos os servidores exigem mutual TLS. Os clientes devem originar mTLS, o que geralmente é configurado por meio de uma DestinationRule correspondente que define o modo TLS como ISTIO_MUTUAL. Sem essa configuração do lado do cliente, as chamadas podem ser enviadas em texto puro e são rejeitadas por servidores que agora exigem mTLS.

O comportamento muitas vezes parece intermitente porque alguns fluxos de tráfego correspondem a uma DestinationRule existente ou se beneficiam do mTLS automático, enquanto outros fluxos não. Diferenças, incluindo escopo de namespace, hostnames curtos versus totalmente qualificados, subsets ou regras conflitantes, podem fazer com que algumas solicitações originem mTLS corretamente enquanto outras não, o que leva a acessibilidade esporádica.

Um recurso Gateway mal configurado bloqueando esporadicamente o tráfego de entrada para os serviços internos não é a melhor explicação, porque os Gateways controlam o tráfego de borda ou egress e não estão no caminho das chamadas típicas de serviço a serviço dentro do mesh. Chamadas internas falhando logo após a aplicação de STRICT apontam para a política de mTLS e a originação no cliente, em vez de um problema de Gateway.

Alguns workloads não têm o sidecar Envoy injetado, então fazem chamadas em texto puro que são rejeitadas sob STRICT causaria falhas consistentes para esses chamadores específicos, em vez de sucessos e falhas esporádicos para o mesmo padrão de chamada. A ausência de um sidecar é uma condição clara de ligado ou desligado e não costuma se manifestar como acessibilidade intermitente.

Um EnvoyFilter personalizado alterando clusters ou rotas, o que leva a problemas intermitentes de roteamento, poderia explicar anomalias de roteamento, mas o momento da implantação do STRICT em nível de mesh e o sintoma específico de rejeições relacionadas ao mTLS tornam isso uma causa raiz menos provável do que a falta de originação de TLS do lado do cliente.

questions.question: In Cloud Build a step generates a 16 KB config file that later steps must read without external services. Where should it be stored so all subsequent steps can access it?

options.text: Secret Manager
Write to /workspace
Create a named volume
Cloud Storage

questions.correct_text: Write to /workspace
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Write to /workspace.

In Cloud Build the working directory at /workspace is automatically mounted into every step within the same build and files written there persist for the duration of the build so later steps can read them. Writing the 15 KB config file to /workspace keeps it inside the build environment and avoids any external services.

Secret Manager is wrong since it is designed for secrets rather than arbitrary build outputs and it relies on an external service which the question forbids.

Create a named volume is unnecessary for this scenario. Although volumes can share data across steps when mounted in each step they add configuration overhead and /workspace already offers a shared directory available to all steps.

Cloud Storage would place the file outside the build environment and would require network access and credentials which violates the requirement to stop external services.

Criar um volume nomeado é desnecessário para este cenário. Embora os volumes possam compartilhar dados entre steps quando montados em cada step, eles adicionam overhead de configuração e o /workspace já oferece um diretório compartilhado disponível para todos os steps.

questions.question: The engineering team at Petalstone Cosmetics Data is delivering a public streaming API that runs on GKE. The API has two subscription levels named "starter" and "pro", and each level must limit how many requests a single client application can make in any rolling 24 hour window. You want an architecture that follows Google guidance for external APIs and allows you to enforce these per client daily limits without duplicating clusters. Which implementation should you choose?

options.text: Deploy the API behind an external HTTP load balancer and apply Cloud Armor rate limiting policies that vary by URL path for the "starter" and "pro" tiers
Place the GKE service behind an Apigee proxy and provide API keys to consumers then configure a SpikeArrest policy based on the tier of each key
Expose the service through Apigee as the gateway and issue API keys for each client then apply an Apigee Quota policy that enforces a daily cap per tier for each key
Run separate GKE clusters for the "starter" and "pro" plans with distinct Ingress resources and connect each cluster to its own Apigee proxy with different rate settings

questions.correct_text: Expose the service through Apigee as the gateway and issue API keys for each client then apply an Apigee Quota policy that enforces a daily cap per tier for each key
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Expose the service through Apigee as the gateway and issue API keys for each client, and apply an Apigee Quota policy that enforces a daily cap per tier for each key.

This strategy aligns with Google guidance for external APIs because Apigee happens to be the managed API gateway for enterprise use cases. By issuing API keys to identify each client and configuring a Quota policy with a one day time unit, developers can enforce a per client daily allowance and assign different limits for the starter and pro plans. The quota enforcement happens at the gateway independently of which GKE pod or cluster node serves the traffic, so you do not need to duplicate clusters to keep counts accurate.

Deploy the API behind an external HTTP load balancer and apply Cloud Armor rate limiting policies that vary by URL path for the "starter" and "pro" tiers is unsuitable since Cloud Armor rate limiting is designed for edge protection and burst control rather than per consumer daily quotas. It does not handle per API key subscription plans and is not a replacement for an API management layer that tracks client entitlements.

Place the GKE service behind an Apigee proxy and supply API keys to consumers then configure a SpikeArrest policy based on the tier of each key is not right because SpikeArrest smooths traffic by limiting requests per second or per minute. It does not enforce a fixed daily allowance per client, which is needed for the rolling 24 hour limits.

Run separate GKE clusters for the "starter" and "pro" plans with distinct Ingress resources and connect each cluster to its own Apigee proxy with different rate settings is unnecessary and violates the requirement to stop duplicating clusters. Per tier and per client limits can be applied centrally at the gateway using quotas without changing the cluster topology.

questions.explanation_pt:
A escolha correta é expor o serviço através do Apigee como gateway e emitir API keys para cada cliente, e aplicar uma Apigee Quota policy que imponha um limite diário por tier para cada chave.

Essa estratégia está alinhada com a orientação do Google para APIs externas, porque o Apigee é o API gateway gerenciado para casos de uso empresariais. Ao emitir API keys para identificar cada cliente e configurar uma Quota policy com uma unidade de tempo de um dia, os desenvolvedores podem impor uma cota diária por cliente e atribuir limites diferentes para os planos starter e pro. A aplicação da cota acontece no gateway, independentemente de qual pod ou nó de cluster do GKE atende ao tráfego, portanto você não precisa duplicar clusters para manter as contagens precisas.

Implantar a API atrás de um external HTTP load balancer e aplicar políticas de rate limiting do Cloud Armor que variam por caminho de URL para os tiers "starter" e "pro" é inadequado, pois o rate limiting do Cloud Armor é projetado para proteção de borda e controle de picos, em vez de cotas diárias por consumidor. Ele não lida com planos de assinatura por API key e não substitui uma camada de gerenciamento de API que rastreia os direitos do cliente.

Colocar o serviço GKE atrás de um proxy Apigee e fornecer API keys aos consumidores, então configurar uma SpikeArrest policy baseada no tier de cada chave não está correto, porque o SpikeArrest suaviza o tráfego limitando solicitações por segundo ou por minuto. Ele não impõe uma cota diária fixa por cliente, que é necessária para os limites contínuos de 24 horas.

Executar clusters GKE separados para os planos "starter" e "pro" com recursos Ingress distintos e conectar cada cluster ao seu próprio proxy Apigee com configurações de rate diferentes é desnecessário e viola o requisito de parar de duplicar clusters. Limites por tier e por cliente podem ser aplicados centralmente no gateway usando cotas, sem alterar a topologia do cluster.

questions.question: Within Cedarpoint Hotels you operate about 23 RESTful microservices that expose public APIs. Several services run on Google Kubernetes Engine and others run on Compute Engine. You need a managed solution that applies authentication and quotas, offers request analytics in Cloud Monitoring, and lets partner developers receive API keys without migrating the workloads to a different runtime. Which GCP service should you choose?

options.text: Cloud Run
Cloud Endpoints
API Gateway
Cloud Functions

questions.correct_text: Cloud Endpoints
questions.explanation:
The proper option is Cloud Endpoints since it permits you to enforce authentication and API key based quotas, offers request analytics through Cloud Monitoring, and sits in front of services already running on Google Kubernetes Engine and Compute Engine so there is no need to move them to a different runtime.

The service deploys a proxy to your existing backends and uses Google Service Infrastructure to validate API keys and JWTs while enforcing quotas. It exports latency, traffic, and error metrics to Cloud Monitoring and Cloud Logging which gives you request analytics and dashboards. Partner developers can obtain and use API keys tied to your published API while you keep the workloads where they are.

Cloud Run is a serverless compute platform rather than an API management layer. Selecting it would require moving services to that runtime and it does not supply centralized API key issuance and quotas for existing backends across GKE and Compute Engine.

API Gateway can secure and route to existing backends and it integrates with Cloud Monitoring. However it does not include a built in developer portal for partner self service API key registration and its built in capabilities for analytics and key distribution are more limited for this scenario, which weakens its fit for the requirement to allow partner developers receive keys.

Cloud Functions is an event driven compute product and using it would mean replatforming code. It does not address centralized API authentication, quotas, and request analytics for several microservices already hosted on GKE and Compute Engine.

No entanto, ele não inclui um portal de desenvolvedores embutido para autosserviço de registro de API key por parceiros, e suas capacidades internas de análise e distribuição de chaves são mais limitadas para este cenário, o que enfraquece sua adequação ao requisito de permitir que desenvolvedores parceiros recebam chaves.

questions.question: The engineering team at Lantern Theatres Market will move its on-premises online store to Google Cloud in stages and adopt microservices over the next 72 days. Most revenue comes from digital sales so you must reduce risk during the first migration. You need to decide which business capability to migrate first and define its initial integrations so that you can validate the platform with the smallest blast radius. Which capability should you choose to move first?

options.text: Move order fulfillment and connect it to the orders database, the warehouse inventory service, and the external shipping partner
Shift payment processing and tie it into the checkout interface, the orders database, and the third party payment gateway
Migrate the product catalog and integrate it with the web frontend and the catalog database
Migrate the shopping cart and integrate it with the web frontend, the cart data store, the inventory service, and the payment system

questions.correct_text: Migrate the product catalog and integrate it with the web frontend and the catalog database
questions.explanation:
The proper option is Migrate the product catalog and integrate it with the web frontend and the catalog database. This capability is largely read heavy and has limited side effects which makes it ideal for validating the new platform with minimal risk and minimal dependencies.

The catalog permits you to exercise core cloud concerns including networking, identity and access, CI and CD, observability, scaling, and caching while keeping the blast radius small. It generally does not handle payments or sensitive customer data and it can often be migrated with simple database replication or bulk loads and with straightforward integration to the web frontend. If issues occur the impact is often limited to product display rather than critical order flows.

Move order fulfillment and connect it to the orders database, the warehouse inventory service, and the external shipping partner is risky for a first step. It spans several internal systems and an external partner and introduces asynchronous processes and side effects on inventory and shipments which increases the blast radius.

Shift payment processing and tie it into the checkout interface, the orders database, and the third party payment gateway touches the money path and needs strict compliance controls and robust integration with a gateway. Any defect here directly affects revenue and customer trust which makes it a poor first workload.

Migrate the shopping cart and integrate it with the web frontend, the cart data store, the inventory service, and the payment system is highly coupled and stateful. It brings concurrency, session management, and consistency challenges and it also intersects with inventory and payment which raises risk during an initial migration.

Em geral, ele não lida com pagamentos ou dados sensíveis de clientes e muitas vezes pode ser migrado com replicação simples de banco de dados ou cargas em massa, e com integração direta ao web frontend. questions.question: Argentum Mining plans to publish a REST API that exposes three paths which are /orders, /customers, and /catalog, and each path must trigger a separate function in your code. How should you deploy this on Google Cloud so that each request is routed to the correct function?

options.text: Use API Gateway with a single backend Cloud Function that inspects the path and dispatches to the appropriate logic

Provision three Cloud Functions and register each as a separate backend service on an HTTPS load balancer then configure path rules so /orders, /customers, and /catalog route to their respective functions
Create three Cloud Functions and expose each one directly with its own HTTPS trigger for /orders, /customers, and /catalog
Deploy a single Cloud Function as a backend of an HTTPS load balancer to handle requests for /orders, /customers, and /catalog

questions.correct_text: Provision three Cloud Functions and register each as a separate backend service on an HTTPS load balancer then configure path rules so /orders, /customers, and /catalog route to their respective functions
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Provision three serverless functions and register each as a separate backend service on an HTTPS load balancer, and configure path rules so /orders, /customers, and /catalog route to their respective functions.

This architecture uses an external HTTPS load balancer with a URL map and path matchers so that each path is mapped to its own Cloud Function through serverless network endpoint groups. Each request to the three paths is routed directly to the appropriate function which satisfies the requirement that each path triggers a separate function and it avoids custom routing code inside the function.

Use API Gateway with a single backend Cloud Function that inspects the path and dispatches to the appropriate logic is not right since it funnels all requests into one function and relies on code to dispatch. The requirement is that each path triggers a separate function which this option does not meet.

Create three Cloud Functions and expose each one directly with its own HTTPS trigger for /orders, /customers, and /catalog is incorrect because each function gets its own unique URL. You cannot present a single API host with clean path routing without a gateway or load balancer so you would not publish a unified REST API with the three specified paths.

Deploy a single Cloud Function as a backend of an HTTPS load balancer to handle requests for /orders, /customers, and /catalog is incorrect because it still uses one function. A load balancer in front does not satisfy the requirement that each path invokes a distinct function.

questions.question: A retail brand named Concord Aerospace runs a promotional landing site on Cloud Run and during sudden surges of traffic new instances spin up and users experience slow first requests because startup work reads external configuration and reference files. What change should you make to improve the experience during these spikes?

options.text: Defer noncritical processing to background tasks after sending the response
Load configuration and static lookup data from the database when each instance starts
Bake configuration and immutable static data into the container image at build time
Retrieve configuration from Secret Manager every time a new instance initializes

questions.correct_text: Bake configuration and immutable static data into the container image at build time
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Bake configuration and immutable static data into the container image at build time.

This change removes network calls and disk reads from instance initialization because the needed configuration and lookup files are already present in the container filesystem when a new instance starts. It shortens first request latency during traffic spikes since each instance can begin serving immediately without fetching external data. It also scales predictably because every instance is self contained.

Defer noncritical processing to background tasks after sending the response does not address slow first requests because the delay occurs before the first response is sent. Cloud Run is request driven and work done after sending the response is not a dependable way to speed up initialization.

Load configuration and static lookup data from the database when each instance starts still introduces startup overhead from network calls and I O which is exactly what causes cold start slowness during surges.

Retrieve configuration from Secret Manager every time a new instance initializes is appropriate for sensitive and dynamic values but it adds latency on each cold start and can increase load on Secret Manager. In this scenario the immutable static data ought to be packaged in the image.

questions.explanation_pt:
A escolha certa é Incorporar configuração e dados estáticos imutáveis na imagem do container no momento do build.

Essa mudança remove chamadas de rede e leituras de disco da inicialização da instância, pois a configuração e os arquivos de consulta necessários já estão presentes no filesystem do container quando uma nova instância inicia. Ela reduz a latência da primeira requisição durante picos de tráfego, já que cada instância pode começar a atender imediatamente, sem buscar dados externos. Também escala de forma previsível, porque cada instância é autocontida.

Adiar processamento não crítico para tarefas em background após enviar a resposta não resolve as primeiras requisições lentas, pois o atraso ocorre antes de a primeira resposta ser enviada. O Cloud Run é orientado a requisições, e trabalho feito após o envio da resposta não é uma forma confiável de acelerar a inicialização.

Carregar configuração e dados estáticos de consulta a partir do banco de dados quando cada instância inicia ainda introduz overhead de startup por causa de chamadas de rede e I/O, que é exatamente o que causa a lentidão de cold start durante surtos.

Recuperar a configuração do Secret Manager toda vez que uma nova instância é inicializada é apropriado para valores sensíveis e dinâmicos, mas adiciona latência em cada cold start e pode aumentar a carga sobre o Secret Manager. Neste cenário, os dados estáticos imutáveis devem ser empacotados na imagem.

questions.question: You are a developer at Helios Finance who is rolling out a containerized web service to Google Kubernetes Engine and using Cloud Deploy to manage releases across Development, QA, and Production clusters. You want the process to advance on its own from the Development environment to the QA cluster when the rollout to Development completes successfully and you want to follow Google recommended practices. Which implementation should you choose?

options.text: Configure a Cloud Build trigger that subscribes to SUCCEEDED messages on the clouddeploy-operations Pub/Sub topic and runs a step that promotes the release to the QA cluster
Create a Cloud Function that listens to SUCCEEDED messages on the cloud-builds Pub/Sub topic and calls the Cloud Deploy API to promote the release to the QA cluster
Deploy a Cloud Function that subscribes to the clouddeploy-operations Pub/Sub topic and on SUCCEEDED events invokes the Cloud Deploy API to promote the release to the QA target
Build a Cloud Build pipeline with the gke-deploy builder and trigger it on SUCCEEDED messages from the cloud-builds Pub/Sub topic to deploy the application to the QA cluster

questions.correct_text: Deploy a Cloud Function that subscribes to the clouddeploy-operations Pub/Sub topic and on SUCCEEDED events invokes the Cloud Deploy API to promote the release to the QA target
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Deploy a Cloud Function that subscribes to the clouddeploy-operations Pub/Sub topic and on SUCCEEDED events invokes the Cloud Deploy API to promote the release to the QA target.

This strategy listens to Cloud Deploy operation events and reacts only when the rollout to the Development target succeeds. It, and calls the Cloud Deploy API to promote the same release to the next target which is QA. This follows Google guidance for automating promotions because Cloud Deploy emits rollout status notifications on its Pub/Sub topic and developers can attach lightweight event handlers to move the release forward without involving separate CI tooling.

Configure a Cloud Build trigger that subscribes to SUCCEEDED messages on the clouddeploy-operations Pub/Sub topic and runs a step that promotes the release to the QA cluster is not suggested because Cloud Build is a CI service and using it to react to Cloud Deploy events adds unnecessary complexity. Triggers also do not natively filter only on specific Cloud Deploy rollout states for this topic, so you would still need custom logic inside the build, which is not aligned with the intended event driven model around Cloud Deploy notifications.

Create a Cloud Function that listens to SUCCEEDED messages on the cloud-builds Pub/Sub topic and calls the Cloud Deploy API to promote the release to the QA cluster is not right because that topic carries Cloud Build events rather than Cloud Deploy rollout events. It would not fire when a rollout to Development completes in Cloud Deploy.

Build a Cloud Build pipeline with the gke-deploy builder and trigger it on SUCCEEDED messages from the cloud-builds Pub/Sub topic to deploy the app to the QA cluster is incorrect since it bypasses Cloud Deploy completely and listens to the wrong event source. If you are already managing releases and targets with Cloud Deploy then you should use Cloud Deploy’s events and API to advance the same release to QA.
