Ela então chama a Cloud Deploy API para promover o mesmo release ao próximo target, que é QA. Isso segue a orientação do Google para automatizar promoções, pois o Cloud Deploy emite notificações de status de rollout em seu tópico Pub/Sub, e os desenvolvedores podem anexar handlers de evento leves para avançar o release sem envolver ferramentas de CI separadas.

Configurar um Cloud Build trigger que se inscreve em mensagens SUCCEEDED no tópico Pub/Sub clouddeploy-operations e executa uma etapa que promove o release ao cluster de QA não é recomendado, porque o Cloud Build é um serviço de CI e usá-lo para reagir a eventos do Cloud Deploy adiciona complexidade desnecessária. Triggers também não filtram nativamente apenas por estados específicos de rollout do Cloud Deploy nesse tópico, então você ainda precisaria de lógica personalizada dentro do build, o que não está alinhado com o modelo orientado a eventos pretendido em torno das notificações do Cloud Deploy.

Criar uma Cloud Function que escuta mensagens SUCCEEDED no tópico Pub/Sub cloud-builds e chama a Cloud Deploy API para promover o release ao cluster de QA não está correto, porque esse tópico carrega eventos do Cloud Build, e não eventos de rollout do Cloud Deploy. Ele não dispararia quando um rollout para Development é concluído no Cloud Deploy.

Construir um pipeline do Cloud Build com o builder gke-deploy e acioná-lo em mensagens SUCCEEDED do tópico Pub/Sub cloud-builds para implantar o app no cluster de QA está incorreto, pois ignora o Cloud Deploy por completo e escuta a fonte de eventos errada. Se você já está gerenciando releases e targets com o Cloud Deploy, então deve usar os eventos e a API do Cloud Deploy para avançar o mesmo release até QA.

questions.question: The engineering team at mosaicapp.dev is building the backend for a cross platform mobile app and must store user profile documents and synchronize them in near real time across multiple devices. The platform should scale on its own as active users grow from 28,000 to 408,000 without complex capacity planning. Which Google Cloud product should you choose?

options.text: Cloud SQL
Cloud Firestore
Cloud Spanner
Firebase Realtime Database

questions.correct_text: Cloud Firestore
questions.explanation:
The proper option is Cloud Firestore.

It is a serverless document database that keeps user profiles synchronized across devices in near-realtime using listeners and offline caching. It on its own scales with traffic and user growth, which removes the need for complex capacity planning, and it offers flexible queries, security rules, and multi region replication that suit backend for mobile appss.

Cloud SQL is a managed relational service that needs instance sizing and connection management, and it does not supply native client listeners for near real time sync of documents. It fits traditional transactional schemas rather than mobile profile documents that need seamless synchronization.

Cloud Spanner offers horizontal scalability and strong consistency for relational schemas, yet it is designed for globally consistent relational workloads and does not provide the client side real time synchronization that mobile apps expect for document profiles. It would also be more complex and costly for this use case.

Firebase Realtime Database does provide real time synchronization, though it uses a hierarchical data model, is generally single region by default, and can be harder to scale and query for complex document data at large user counts. For new mobile backends that need rich querying and automatic scaling for document profiles, it is suboptimal.

Por conta própria, ele escala conforme o tráfego e o crescimento de usuários, o que elimina a necessidade de um planejamento de capacidade complexo, e oferece consultas flexíveis, security rules e replicação multirregional, adequadas para backends de aplicativos mobile.

O Cloud SQL é um serviço relacional gerenciado que exige dimensionamento de instância e gerenciamento de conexões, e não fornece listeners de cliente nativos para sincronização near real time de documentos. Ele se adapta a esquemas transacionais tradicionais, e não a documentos de perfil mobile que precisam de sincronização sem interrupções.

O Cloud Spanner oferece escalabilidade horizontal e forte consistência para esquemas relacionais, porém foi projetado para cargas de trabalho relacionais globalmente consistentes e não fornece a sincronização em tempo real do lado do cliente que os apps mobile esperam para perfis baseados em documentos. Também seria mais complexo e custoso para este caso de uso.

O Firebase Realtime Database de fato fornece sincronização em tempo real, embora use um modelo de dados hierárquico, seja geralmente de região única por padrão e possa ser mais difícil de escalar e consultar para dados de documentos complexos com grande número de usuários. Para novos backends mobile que precisam de consultas avançadas e escalonamento automático para perfis de documentos, ele é subótimo.

questions.question: Your analytics team at Mariner Tackle needs to export application logs from Cloud Logging into BigQuery for auditing. Before you create a log sink and choose the destination, what should you do first to prepare BigQuery for receiving the exported entries?

options.text: Select BigQuery as the sink destination in Cloud Logging
Enter a sink name in the Cloud Logging sink wizard
Create a new BigQuery dataset to store the exported logs
Create a dedicated BigQuery table for each log type in advance

questions.correct_text: Create a new BigQuery dataset to store the exported logs
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Create a new BigQuery dataset to save the exported logs. BigQuery exports from Cloud Logging require a destination dataset to exist so preparing that dataset first guarantees the sink can be created and granted the proper write access.

When exporting to BigQuery, the Log Router writes entries into a specific dataset. Once the sink begins exporting, Cloud Logging on its own builds and manages the necessary tables for the logs in that dataset, so having the dataset ready happens to be the essential prerequisite.

Select BigQuery as the sink destination in Cloud Logging is not the first preparatory step since it is part of the sink creation process rather than something you do beforehand.

Enter a sink name in the Cloud Logging sink wizard is also a step you take during the wizard and does not prepare BigQuery to receive data.

Create a dedicated BigQuery table for each log type in advance is unnecessary because Cloud Logging creates the needed tables on its own in the target dataset when the export runs.

questions.question: A logistics company runs an event-driven application on Cloud Functions that must call a backend service hosted on a Compute Engine virtual machine in a private subnet of a VPC. The virtual machine has no external IP and the traffic should use the internal address from the same region. How can you enable this connectivity without assigning a public IP to the virtual machine?

options.text: Private Google Access
Cloud NAT
Set up Serverless VPC Access connector
Private Service Connect

questions.correct_text: Set up Serverless VPC Access connector
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Set up Serverless VPC Access connector.

This strategy permits serverless to functions send traffic into your VPC using private addresses. You create a connector in the same region as the function and attach it to the function, and egress to the VPC uses the chosen subnet range so the function can call the Compute Engine VM on its internal IP. This satisfies the requirement to keep traffic private and regional while avoiding any public IP on the VM.

Private Google Access allows virtual machine instances without external IPs to reach Google APIs privately and it does not allow Cloud Functions to reach a Compute Engine instance over its internal address. It does not solve connectivity from serverless to your VM.

Cloud NAT offers outbound internet access for resources without public IPs and it does not enable connectivity from Cloud Functions to a private virtual machine inside your VPC. It is for internet egress rather than private in‑VPC access from serverless.

Private Service Connect serves to privately consume Google APIs or producer services through endpoints and load balancers and it does not directly target a single virtual machine. It is unnecessary for simple same VPC connectivity from Cloud Functions to a VM over an internal IP.

questions.question: A marketing analytics startup named Hazel Threads aggregates engagement events from mobile apps and web beacons across mosaicapp.dev and partner sites. The pipeline must ingest about 1.5 million events per minute and power dashboards within a few seconds. The team needs horizontally scalable storage that sustains very high write throughput with predictable latency. Which Google Cloud storage service should they choose to maximize performance and scalability?

options.text: Use Cloud SQL to store the interaction records and rely on relational transactions for integrity
Ingest events into BigQuery using streaming inserts to support near real time queries
Adopt Cloud Bigtable as the write path for time series event data and scale nodes horizontally
Store events in Firestore to benefit from its document model and live synchronization

questions.correct_text: Adopt Cloud Bigtable as the write path for time series event data and scale nodes horizontally
questions.explanation:
The proper option is Adopt Cloud Bigtable as the write path for time series event data and scale nodes horizontally.

The service supplies horizontally scalable write throughput with predictable low latency, which is exactly what a high velocity event stream and near-realtime dashboards require. It is built for time series and event workloads and accommodates key designs that keep writes and reads efficient. Developers can add nodes to scale throughput linearly and preserve single digit millisecond latency, and its integration with streaming ingestion tools allows dashboards to refresh within seconds.

Use Cloud SQL to save the interaction records and rely on relational transactions for integrity is unsuitable since relational instances scale mainly by increasing machine size and their write throughput is limited compared with a distributed wide column store. At the stated ingestion rate this would create bottlenecks and unpredictable latency during spikes.

Ingest events into BigQuery using streaming inserts to support near real time queries targets analytics rather than acting as a primary low latency write store. Streaming buffers, quotas, and per row costs introduce variability, and recently streamed data can have a short delay before it is dependably queryable, which makes predictable per event latency harder to guarantee.

Store events in Firestore to benefit from its document model and live synchronization is not ideal for sustained high velocity time series ingestion. Document databases face hot spotting risks and collection level limits at this scale, and they are tuned for application data access patterns and synchronization rather than massive sequential event writes with strict latency objectives.

questions.explanation_pt:
A opção correta é Adotar o Cloud Bigtable como caminho de escrita para dados de eventos de séries temporais e escalar nós horizontalmente.

O serviço fornece throughput de escrita escalável horizontalmente com baixa latência previsível, que é exatamente o que um stream de eventos de alta velocidade e dashboards em near-realtime exigem. Ele foi construído para cargas de trabalho de séries temporais e de eventos e acomoda designs de chave que mantêm escritas e leituras eficientes. Os desenvolvedores podem adicionar nós para escalar o throughput linearmente e preservar latência de um dígito em milissegundos, e sua integração com ferramentas de ingestão de streaming permite que os dashboards atualizem em segundos.

Usar o Cloud SQL para salvar os registros de interação e contar com transações relacionais para a integridade é inadequado, pois instâncias relacionais escalam principalmente aumentando o tamanho da máquina e seu throughput de escrita é limitado em comparação com um wide column store distribuído. Na taxa de ingestão indicada, isso criaria gargalos e latência imprevisível durante picos.

Ingerir eventos no BigQuery usando streaming inserts para suportar consultas near real time tem como foco análises em vez de atuar como um armazenamento primário de escrita de baixa latência. Buffers de streaming, cotas e custos por linha introduzem variabilidade, e dados recém-transmitidos podem ter um curto atraso antes de serem consultáveis de forma confiável, o que dificulta garantir uma latência previsível por evento.

Armazenar eventos no Firestore para se beneficiar de seu modelo de documentos e sincronização ao vivo não é ideal para ingestão sustentada de séries temporais de alta velocidade. Bancos de documentos enfrentam riscos de hot spotting e limites em nível de coleção nessa escala, e são ajustados para padrões de acesso a dados de aplicações e sincronização, em vez de escritas sequenciais massivas de eventos com objetivos rigorosos de latência.

questions.question: Within Aldermark Press, a Compute Engine VM hosts three internal services and stores sensitive configuration values in its instance metadata. You need to ensure that only one authorized service on the VM can read those metadata values whereas the other processes on the same machine cannot. Which approach should you take?

options.text: Enable Shielded VM on the instance to isolate metadata from unauthorized processes
Create a VPC Service Controls perimeter around the project to block metadata access by other applications
Attach and use a dedicated service account with minimal IAM and have only the intended service fetch configuration using that identity
Mark the metadata entry as private by setting a hidden flag on the instance metadata

questions.correct_text: Attach and use a dedicated service account with minimal IAM and have only the intended service fetch configuration using that identity
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Attach and use a dedicated service account with minimal IAM and have only the intended service fetch configuration using that identity.

Metadata on a Compute Engine VM is accessible to any process that can reach the metadata server, which means you cannot enforce per process restrictions there. The secure model is to stop storing secrets in instance metadata and instead put them in Secret Manager, and grant only the minimal needed permissions to a dedicated service account. Run the authorized service with that identity and have it retrieve the configuration so other processes do not have the IAM permissions or credentials to access the secret.

Enable Shielded VM on the instance to isolate metadata from unauthorized processes is not right because Shielded VM protects boot integrity and helps defend against firmware and kernel tampering, yet it does not supply process level isolation or restrict access to the metadata server inside the guest.

Create a VPC Service Controls perimeter around the project to block metadata access by other apps is incorrect because VPC Service Controls govern access to Google APIs and services at the perimeter and do not apply to the instance metadata server, which is a link local endpoint available inside the VM.

Mark the metadata entry as private by setting a hidden flag on the instance metadata is incorrect because there is no hidden flag or per key access control for instance metadata, and any process on the VM can query metadata if it can reach the endpoint.

O modelo seguro é parar de armazenar segredos nos metadados da instância e, em vez disso, colocá-los no Secret Manager, concedendo apenas as permissões mínimas necessárias a uma service account dedicada. Execute o serviço autorizado com essa identidade e faça com que ele recupere a configuração, de modo que outros processos não tenham as permissões de IAM ou as credenciais para acessar o segredo.

Habilitar a Shielded VM na instância para isolar os metadados de processos não autorizados não está correto, pois a Shielded VM protege a integridade de boot e ajuda a defender contra adulteração de firmware e kernel, porém não fornece isolamento em nível de processo nem restringe o acesso ao servidor de metadados dentro do guest.

Criar um perímetro do VPC Service Controls em torno do projeto para bloquear o acesso aos metadados por outros apps está incorreto, pois o VPC Service Controls governa o acesso às APIs e serviços do Google no perímetro e não se aplica ao servidor de metadados da instância, que é um endpoint link local disponível dentro da VM.

questions.question: Mistral Networks at loomwright.io is preparing a worldwide launch of its core service and needs the database to achieve 99.999% availability whereas keeping read latency very low for users across all continents. Which actions should the team prioritize to meet these goals?

options.text: Build a Cloud Dataflow pipeline that replicates data into multiple different databases
Provision a multi-regional Cloud Spanner instance configured as "nam-eur-asia1"
Create a single-node Cloud Spanner instance to minimize cost
Run two independent Cloud Spanner instances in different regions each with one node and route reads from the application
Scale the Cloud Spanner instance to at least 3 nodes
Use a multi-regional Cloud Spanner instance with the "nam3" configuration

questions.correct_text: Provision a multi-regional Cloud Spanner instance configured as "nam-eur-asia1"
questions.explanation:
The correct choices are Provision a multi-regional Cloud Spanner instance configured as "nam-eur-asia1" and Scale the Cloud Spanner instance to at least 3 nodes.

A multi-region configuration supplies a five nines availability SLA and places replicas across continents so reads are served close to users whereas writes remain strongly consistent through quorum replication. The configuration that spans North America, Europe, and Asia keeps read latency low for a global user base and offers automatic failover without operational complexity.

Increasing the node count supplies more compute and serving capacity for your splits which improves throughput and helps reduce tail latency during peak traffic and maintenance events. A larger fleet spreads leaders more evenly which lowers the risk of hotspots and accommodates consistent low latency for a worldwide launch.

Build a Cloud Dataflow pipeline that replicates data into several different databases introduces unnecessary replication and consistency challenges and it does not provide globally consistent reads or a five nines availability guarantee.

Create a single-node Cloud Spanner instance to minimize cost reduces resiliency and performance and concentrates load on a single compute resource which can increase tail latency and risk during maintenance. This does not meet the availability and latency goals.

Run two independent Cloud Spanner instances in different regions each with one node and route reads from the app builds separate databases with no synchronous replication or global consistency. Application-level routing adds complexity and still fails to supply a single highly available store.

Use a multi-regional Cloud Spanner instance with the "nam3" configuration is limited to North America so users in Europe and Asia would experience higher read latency. This does not satisfy the requirement for very low latency across all continents.

As escolhas corretas são Provisionar uma instância multirregional do Cloud Spanner configurada como "nam-eur-asia1" e Escalar a instância do Cloud Spanner para pelo menos 3 nós.

Uma configuração multirregião fornece um SLA de disponibilidade de cinco noves e posiciona réplicas em diferentes continentes, de modo que as leituras são atendidas próximas dos usuários enquanto as gravações permanecem fortemente consistentes por meio de replicação por quórum. A configuração que abrange América do Norte, Europa e Ásia mantém a latência de leitura baixa para uma base de usuários global e oferece failover automático sem complexidade operacional.

Aumentar a contagem de nós fornece mais capacidade de computação e de atendimento para seus splits, o que melhora o throughput e ajuda a reduzir a latência de cauda durante picos de tráfego e eventos de manutenção. Uma frota maior distribui os líderes de forma mais uniforme, o que reduz o risco de hotspots e acomoda uma latência baixa e consistente para um lançamento mundial.

Construir um pipeline do Cloud Dataflow que replica dados para vários bancos de dados diferentes introduz replicação desnecessária e desafios de consistência, e não fornece leituras globalmente consistentes nem uma garantia de disponibilidade de cinco noves.

Criar uma instância de nó único do Cloud Spanner para minimizar custo reduz a resiliência e o desempenho e concentra a carga em um único recurso de computação, o que pode aumentar a latência de cauda e o risco durante a manutenção. Isso não atende às metas de disponibilidade e latência.

Executar duas instâncias independentes do Cloud Spanner em regiões diferentes, cada uma com um nó, e rotear as leituras a partir do app cria bancos de dados separados sem replicação síncrona ou consistência global. O roteamento em nível de aplicação adiciona complexidade e ainda assim não consegue fornecer um único armazenamento altamente disponível.

Usar uma instância multirregional do Cloud Spanner com a configuração "nam3" está limitada à América do Norte, então usuários na Europa e na Ásia teriam latência de leitura mais alta. Isso não satisfaz o requisito de latência muito baixa em todos os continentes.

questions.question: A claims processing tool at Trailhead Outdoors Finance runs on Compute Engine and keeps state in memory whereas handling jobs. When the instance is stopped or deleted the service must be able to complete the current task instead of being cut off abruptly. What should you implement to let the VM shut down gracefully?

options.text: Resize the instance to a larger machine type to speed up processing
Configure an instance shutdown script that runs when the VM receives a termination signal
Disable automatic deletion of the boot disk by setting the autoDelete flag to false
Run the workload on a preemptible VM to take advantage of the preemption notice

questions.correct_text: Configure an instance shutdown script that runs when the VM receives a termination signal
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Configure an instance shutdown script that runs when the VM receives a termination signal.

In Compute Engine a shutdown script runs when the instance is stopped, deleted, or preempted. This permits your to application handle the termination signal, finish the job in progress, flush or checkpoint state to durable storage, and exit cleanly. Compute Engine waits for the shutdown script to complete within a grace period, which allows your service to wrap up work instead of being cut off.

Resize the instance to a larger machine type to speed up processing is wrong because more CPU or memory might make some tasks finish faster but it does not supply a mechanism for a controlled shutdown when the VM is stopped or deleted.

Disable automatic deletion of the boot disk by setting the autoDelete flag to false is not correct because keeping the boot disk after deletion preserves data on disk only and it does not help an in memory process finish its current task before termination.

Run the service on a preemptible VM to take advantage of the preemption notice is not correct because preemptible instances can be terminated at any time and only receive a brief notice. This increases the chance of interruption and still needs a shutdown script to handle termination gracefully.

Executar o serviço em uma VM preemptível para aproveitar o aviso de preempção não está correto porque instâncias preemptíveis podem ser terminadas a qualquer momento e recebem apenas um aviso breve. Isso aumenta a chance de interrupção e ainda assim requer um script de desligamento para tratar o término de forma graciosa.

questions.question: You manage a Cloud Build continuous integration pipeline for a monorepo at Halcyon Foods, and the workflow has 9 steps that include linting, unit tests, building two container images, and scanning artifacts. The team wants to shorten the overall build wall time without reducing test coverage or skipping quality checks. What should you change in the Cloud Build setup to reduce the total execution time?

options.text: Enable Docker layer caching for image builds in Cloud Build
Use a larger memory machine type for the build workers
Configure independent steps to run concurrently by setting proper waitFor values
Run only a fraction of the tests on each commit and defer the rest to a nightly job

questions.correct_text: Configure independent steps to run concurrently by setting proper waitFor values
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Configure independent steps to run concurrently by setting proper waitFor values.

Cloud Build permits you to run build steps in parallel when there are no dependencies between them. By setting waitFor so that linting, unit tests, container image builds, and artifact scans that do not depend on one another start at the same time, the pipeline shortens the critical path and reduces overall wall time while preserving full test coverage and all quality checks.

Enable Docker layer caching for image builds in Cloud Build is not the right change because there is no single toggle that guarantees persistent Docker layer cache across builds on ephemeral workers. Even when you configure caching techniques, they only speed the image build portion and do not shorten the rest of the pipeline including tests and scans, so the overall wall time may not improve enough.

Use a larger memory machine type for the build workers does not inherently reduce total duration if steps are still executed sequentially. More memory helps only if the service is memory constrained. Without parallelization the critical path remains largely the same and costs may increase without meaningful time savings.

Run only a fraction of the tests on each commit and defer the rest to a nightly job violates the requirement to keep test coverage and quality checks intact. This strategy reduces verification on each change and increases risk, which the scenario specifically disallows.

Mais memória só ajuda se o serviço estiver limitado por memória. Sem paralelização, o caminho crítico permanece praticamente o mesmo e os custos podem aumentar sem economia de tempo significativa.

Executar apenas uma fração dos testes em cada commit e adiar o restante para um job noturno viola o requisito de manter a cobertura de testes e as verificações de qualidade intactas. Essa estratégia reduz a verificação em cada mudança e aumenta o risco, o que o cenário especificamente não permite.

questions.question: Almanac Books is rolling out continuous integration with Cloud Build for a service hosted in a Git repository on mosaicapp.dev. You need unit tests to run on its own after every push to the main branch and the build must stop if any test fails. How should you configure Cloud Build to accomplish this?

options.text: Schedule unit tests with Cloud Scheduler to run every 30 minutes
Add a test step to the cloudbuild.yaml that runs the unit test command and causes the build to fail on test errors
Set up a dedicated private worker pool in Cloud Build to execute tests separately from other builds
Create a Cloud Function that listens for repository push events and triggers the test workflow

questions.correct_text: Add a test step to the cloudbuild.yaml that runs the unit test command and causes the build to fail on test errors
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Add a test step to the cloudbuild.yaml that runs the unit test command and causes the build to fail on test errors.

This strategy keeps testing inside the CI pipeline and guarantees that a nonzero exit code from the test command fails the step which immediately stops the build. Configure a Cloud Build trigger on the repository to run on pushes to the main branch and point it to cloudbuild.yaml, and the test step in cloudbuild.yaml will enforce that failures halt the pipeline.

Schedule unit tests with Cloud Scheduler to run every 38 minutes is not right since it is time based rather than event driven and it would not guarantee tests after every push or stop the associated build on failure.

Set up a dedicated private worker pool in Cloud Build to execute tests separately from other builds is incorrect because worker pools supply isolation and networking control but they do not address running tests on each push or failing a build when tests fail.

Create a Cloud Function that listens for repository push events and triggers the test workflow is incorrect because Cloud Build already offers native repository triggers and adding a function adds unnecessary complexity without improving how test failures stop the build.

questions.question: Foxglove Botanicals operates a Go microservice that handles high volume reads and writes against Cloud Spanner for order processing, and the team wants to boost throughput and lower latency whereas following Google recommended guidance for client access. Which approach should they use to connect the service to Cloud Spanner?

options.text: Adopt a third party HTTP client to perform writes to Cloud Spanner
Use Google API Client Libraries to call the Spanner REST API
Use the Cloud Client Libraries for Spanner in Go
Implement a custom gRPC client over the Spanner API

questions.correct_text: Use the Cloud Client Libraries for Spanner in Go
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Use the Cloud Client Libraries for Spanner in Go.

This strategy happens to be the Google suggested way to access Cloud Spanner from Go for high throughput and low latency. It uses gRPC under the hood, manages sessions and connection pools for you, applies automatic retries with backoff, and offers efficient streaming along with strong transactional semantics. These features help maximize throughput and minimize latency while following supported best practices.

Adopt a third party HTTP client to perform writes to Cloud Spanner is a poor match because you would be bypassing the optimized and supported client behavior including session pooling and streaming. Hand crafting HTTP calls increases complexity and generally reduces performance for data plane operations.

Use Google API Client Libraries to call the Spanner REST API is not ideal for high performance data access. The general Google API libraries target broad REST usage and do not supply the Spanner specific optimizations such as gRPC streaming and built in session management that the Cloud Client Libraries offer.

Implement a custom gRPC client over the Spanner API is unnecessary and risky. You would have to build and preserve complex pieces like session and connection pooling, retries, and transaction handling yourself, which the official library already supplies and keeps aligned with service changes.

questions.question:
You need to deploy an internet-facing microservices application to GKE. You want to validate new features using the A/B testing method. You have the following requirements for deploying new container image releases:
1. There is no downtime when new container images are deployed.
2. New production releases are tested and verified using a subset of production users.
Which approach should you take?

options.text: A. 1. Configure your CI/CD pipeline to update the Deployment manifest file by replacing the container version with the latest version. 2. Recreate the Pods in your cluster by applying the Deployment manifest file. 3. Validate the application’s performance by comparing its functionality with the previous release version, and roll back if an issue arises.

B. 1. Install Cloud Service Mesh on your GKE cluster. 2. Create two Deployments on the GKE cluster, and label them with different version names. 3. Configure a weight-based traffic splitting action to send a small percentage of traffic to the Deployment that references the new version of the application.

C. 1. Create a second namespace on GKE for the new release version. 2. Create a Deployment configuration for the second namespace with the desired number of Pods. 3. Deploy new container versions in the second namespace. 4. Update the Ingress configuration to route traffic to the namespace with the new container versions.

D. 1. Implement a rolling update pattern by replacing the Pods gradually with the new release version. 2. Validate the application’s performance for the new subset of users during the rollout, and roll back if an issue arises.

questions.correct_text: B. 1. Install Cloud Service Mesh on your GKE cluster. 2. Create two Deployments on the GKE cluster, and label them with different version names. 3. Configure a weight-based traffic splitting action to send a small percentage of traffic to the Deployment that references the new version of the application.
questions.explanation: A/B testing requires running two versions simultaneously and splitting a controlled percentage of live traffic to the new one with zero downtime - Cloud Service Mesh weight-based traffic splitting does exactly this. A (replace image and recreate Pods) causes downtime and offers no traffic subset testing. C (separate namespace + Ingress switch) is an all-or-nothing cutover, not a percentage split to a subset of users. D (rolling update) gradually replaces all Pods toward 100% new version and cannot reliably hold a fixed subset for A/B comparison.

questions.question: You are building a Java Web Server that needs to interact with the Cloud Storage API on your users’ behalf. Users should be able to authenticate to the Cloud Storage API using their Google identities. Which workflow should you implement in your web application?

options.text: A. 1. When a user arrives at your application, prompt them for their Google username and password. 2. Store an SHA password hash in your application’s database along with the user’s username. 3. The application authenticates to the Cloud Storage API using HTTPs requests with the user’s username and password hash in the Authorization request header.

B. 1. When a user arrives at your application, prompt them for their Google username and password. 2. Forward the user’s username and password in an HTTPS request to the Google authorization server, and request an access token. 3. The Google server validates the user’s credentials and returns an access token to the application. 4. The application uses the access token to call the Cloud Storage API.

C. 1. When a user arrives at your application, route them to an Oauth consent screen with a list of requested permissions that prompts the user to sign in with SSO to their Google Account. 2. After the user signs in and provides consent, your application receives an authorization code from a Google server. 3. The Google server returns the authorization code to the user, which is stored in the browser’s cookies. 4. The user authenticates to the Cloud Storage API using the authorization code in the cookie.

D. 1. When a user arrives at your application, route them to an Oauth consent screen with a list of requested permissions that prompts the user to sign in with SSO to their Google Account. 2. After the user signs in and provides consent, your application receives an authorization code from a Google server. 3. The application requests a Google Server to exchange the authorization code with an access token. 4. The Google server responds with the access token that is used by the application to call the Cloud Storage API.

questions.correct_text: D. 1. When a user arrives at your application, route them to an Oauth consent screen with a list of requested permissions that prompts the user to sign in with SSO to their Google Account. 2. After the user signs in and provides consent, your application receives an authorization code from a Google server. 3. The application requests a Google Server to exchange the authorization code with an access token. 4. The Google server responds with the access token that is used by the application to call the Cloud Storage API.
questions.explanation: This is the correct OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow for a server-side web app acting on a user's behalf: redirect to the consent screen, receive an authorization code, then the server securely exchanges that code for an access token to call the API. A and B require collecting and handling the user's actual Google password, which is forbidden and insecure - Google never exposes credentials to your app. C is wrong because the authorization code itself is not used to call the API; it must be exchanged server-side for an access token, and storing it in cookies is incorrect.

questions.question: You have an application running on GKE. The application is currently using a logging library and is outputting to standard output. You need to export the logs to Cloud Logging, and you need the logs to include metadata about each request. You want to use the simplest method to accomplish this. Which approach should you take?

options.text: A. Update your application to output logs in JSON format, and add the necessary metadata to the JSON.
B. Change your application’s logging library to the Cloud Logging library, and configure your application to export logs to Cloud Logging.
C. Install the Fluent Bit agent on each of your GKE nodes, and have the agent export all logs from /var/log.
D. Update your application to output logs in CSV format, and add the necessary metadata to the CSV.

questions.correct_text: A. Update your application to output logs in JSON format, and add the necessary metadata to the JSON.
questions.explanation: On GKE the Cloud Logging agent automatically collects stdout/stderr; emitting structured JSON lets Cloud Logging parse fields (including custom metadata) into the structured payload with no extra agents or library changes - the simplest method since the app already writes to stdout. B (switching to the Cloud Logging client library) is more code/effort and unnecessary on GKE where stdout is already captured. C (manually installing Fluent Bit) duplicates GKE's built-in logging agent and adds operational overhead. D (CSV) is not natively parsed into structured fields by Cloud Logging the way JSON is.

questions.question: You are a developer at a financial institution. You leverage Cloud Shell to interact with Google Cloud services. User data is at present kept on an ephemeral disk; though, a new corporate policy requires that you can cease storing sensitive data on an ephemeral disk. You must set up a new storage approach for your user data. You'd like to reduce code changes. To what location should you store your user data?

options.text: A. Store user data on a Cloud Shell home disk, and log in at least every 120 days to prevent its deletion.
B. Store user data on a persistent disk in a Compute Engine instance.
C. Store user data in a Cloud Storage bucket.
D. Store user data in BigQuery tables.

questions.correct_text: C. Store user data in a Cloud Storage bucket.
questions.explanation: Cloud Storage is durable, persistent (not ephemeral), and accessible from Cloud Shell with minimal code changes via gsutil/client libraries, satisfying the policy to stop storing sensitive data on ephemeral disk. A (Cloud Shell home disk) is still tied to Cloud Shell's lifecycle, gets deleted after inactivity, and isn't appropriate durable storage for sensitive corporate data. B (Compute Engine persistent disk) requires provisioning and managing a VM, far more effort and code/access changes. D (BigQuery) is an analytics warehouse for structured query workloads, not a general-purpose store for arbitrary user data with minimal changes.

questions.question: Your team is developing an event-driven workload and has already created a Pub/Sub topic for incoming messages. You want each message processed in near real time, you want the runtime to stand alone from any other system, and you only want compute charges when new messages actually arrive. Which architecture is the simplest and most cost-effective?

options.text: A. Deploy your code on Cloud Run functions and configure a Pub/Sub trigger so the function fires on every new message in the topic.
B. Deploy your code on Cloud Run functions and configure a Pub/Sub trigger to invoke it. Then use the Pub/Sub API to create a pull subscription on the same topic and read messages from it.
C. Run the application on Compute Engine and set up a Pub/Sub push subscription that forwards each new message to it.
D. Run the application on GKE and use the Pub/Sub API to create a pull subscription on the topic, fetching messages from there.

questions.correct_text: A. Deploy your code on Cloud Run functions and configure a Pub/Sub trigger so the function fires on every new message in the topic.
questions.explanation: Cloud Run functions with a Pub/Sub trigger process each message in near real time, run as a standalone managed runtime, and bill only when invocations occur (scale to zero) - the simplest, most cost-effective event-driven design. B adds a redundant manual pull subscription on top of the trigger, causing duplicate/conflicting consumption and extra complexity. C (Compute Engine) runs continuously and bills even when idle, so it isn't cost-effective and adds VM management. D (GKE pull subscription) keeps a cluster running with idle cost and management overhead, not scale-to-zero.

questions.question: Your group has built an application running in a single GKE cluster. The workload is broken into two separate Deployments, each exposed by its own Service and reached through a different HTTP path. A legacy client running on-premises needs to access the application through Cloud Interconnect using a single IP address. How should you expose the application? (Choose 2)

options.text: A. Provision a Gateway using the gke-l7-rilb Gateway Class Name specification.
B. Add the networking.gke.io/load-balancer-type: "Internal" annotation to a Service.
C. Create a Service of type LoadBalancer.
D. Create a Service of type NodePort.
E. Create a single Service whose selector matches both Deployments.
F. Define an HTTPRoute that targets both Services.

questions.correct_text: A. Provision a Gateway using the gke-l7-rilb Gateway Class Name specification. | F. Define an HTTPRoute that targets both Services.
questions.explanation: An on-prem client reaching the app over Cloud Interconnect needs an internal (private) entry point, and routing by HTTP path to two different Services requires L7 path-based routing through a single IP. The gke-l7-rilb Gateway class provisions an internal regional L7 load balancer (single internal IP), and an HTTPRoute maps each HTTP path to its respective Service. B (Internal LoadBalancer annotation) is an L4 internal load balancer and can't do HTTP path-based routing to two Services. C (LoadBalancer) creates an external L4 endpoint, wrong for private interconnect access and no path routing. D (NodePort) exposes per-node ports, not a single stable IP with L7 routing. E (one Service selecting both Deployments) can't route by path and would blend unrelated pods.

questions.question: You are building an application from several microservices that must stay private to the cluster. You want each microservice to have its own configurable replica count, and you want every microservice to find the others using a stable name even after pods are rescheduled. What should you do?

options.text: A. Deploy every microservice as a Deployment. Expose the Deployment inside the cluster with a Service, and have other microservices reach it through the Service's DNS name.
B. Deploy every microservice as a Deployment. Expose the Deployment inside the cluster with an Ingress, and have other microservices reach it through the Ingress IP address.
C. Deploy every microservice as a Pod. Expose the Pod inside the cluster with a Service, and have other microservices reach it through the Service's DNS name.
D. Deploy every microservice as a Pod. Expose the Pod inside the cluster with an Ingress, and have other microservices reach it through the Ingress IP address.

questions.correct_text: A. Deploy every microservice as a Deployment. Expose the Deployment inside the cluster with a Service, and have other microservices reach it through the Service's DNS name.
questions.explanation: A Deployment manages a configurable replica count and self-healing for stateless microservices, while a ClusterIP Service provides a stable in-cluster DNS name that keeps working even after pods are rescheduled to new IPs - meeting all requirements with cluster-private access. B and D use Ingress, which exposes services externally and provides no internal stable-name discovery between microservices (and an IP isn't a stable name). C deploys bare Pods, which lack replica management and self-healing that Deployments provide.

questions.question: Your application runs as a container inside a GKE cluster, and you must inject a secret while preventing the secret value from ever being exposed through Kubernetes API calls or in the deployment manifest. Which approach should you choose?

options.text: A. Define a Kubernetes Secret and surface its value to the container as an environment variable.
B. Turn on GKE Application-layer Secrets Encryption for the cluster, using a key from Cloud Key Management Service (KMS).

C. Place the secret inside Cloud KMS. Create a Google service account that can read it, export the service account credentials, and provide them to the container as an environment variable so the application can fetch the secret from Cloud KMS.

D. Place the secret inside Secret Manager. Create a Google service account that can read it, link that service account to a Kubernetes service account through Workload Identity, and have the pod retrieve the secret from Secret Manager at runtime.

questions.correct_text: D. Place the secret inside Secret Manager. Create a Google service account that can read it, link that service account to a Kubernetes service account through Workload Identity, and have the pod retrieve the secret from Secret Manager at runtime.
questions.explanation: Storing the secret in Secret Manager and accessing it at runtime via Workload Identity keeps the value out of the deployment manifest and out of the Kubernetes API entirely, with no exported keys - the recommended secure pattern. A (Kubernetes Secret as env var) stores the value in etcd and exposes it via the Kubernetes API and manifests (base64, not encrypted). B (application-layer encryption) protects Kubernetes Secrets at rest but the value is still retrievable through the Kubernetes API. C requires exporting service account credentials into the container, a discouraged long-lived key practice.

questions.question: You operate a microservices stack on GKE that uses Istio. Service-to-service communication is governed by an Istio AuthorizationPolicy, a Kubernetes NetworkPolicy, and an Istio PeerAuthentication that enables mTLS in STRICT mode. After deployment, certain HTTP requests between pods are dropped. Which configuration is the most plausible root cause?

options.text: A. A Kubernetes NetworkPolicy resource is blocking HTTP traffic between the Pods.
B. The pod making the HTTP call is targeting the wrong TCP port on the destination pod.
C. Your cluster's AuthorizationPolicy is denying HTTP requests for certain paths in the application.
D. The cluster has mTLS in permissive mode, but the sidecar proxy on the calling pod is emitting plaintext traffic.

questions.correct_text: A. A Kubernetes NetworkPolicy resource is blocking HTTP traffic between the Pods.
questions.explanation: NetworkPolicy operates at L3/L4 on the pod network and is enforced independently of Istio; a misconfigured NetworkPolicy will silently drop pod-to-pod packets regardless of correct mesh config, making it the most plausible cause of dropped HTTP requests. B (wrong TCP port) would typically cause connection refused/errors for all calls to that service rather than the selective drops described, and is a coding mistake rather than a policy interaction. C (AuthorizationPolicy denying paths) returns HTTP 403 responses rather than dropping/blocking traffic. D contradicts the scenario, which states mTLS is in STRICT mode, not permissive.

questions.question: You are building a microservices-based application that will be deployed to GKE. Several of the services must call various Google Cloud APIs. How should you set up authentication for these workloads while staying aligned with Google Cloud security guidance? (Choose 2)

options.text: A. Use the service account attached to the GKE node.
B. Turn on Workload Identity for the cluster.
C. Pull the Google service account key from Secret Manager when needed.
D. Store the Google service account key in Secret Manager.
E. Use gcloud to link Google service accounts to Kubernetes service accounts with the roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser role.

questions.correct_text: B. Turn on Workload Identity for the cluster. | E. Use gcloud to link Google service accounts to Kubernetes service accounts with the roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser role.
questions.explanation: Google-recommended GKE workload auth is Workload Identity: enable it on the cluster (B) and bind Kubernetes service accounts to Google service accounts via the roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser role (E), so workloads obtain short-lived credentials with no exported keys. A (node service account) grants the same broad permissions to all pods on the node, violating least privilege. C and D (storing/pulling service account keys from Secret Manager) rely on long-lived exported keys, which Google explicitly discourages.

questions.question: Your team is building an ecommerce website. Shoppers sign in to the site and add products to their cart; they are signed out automatically after 30 minutes of inactivity. The cart contents must persist across sessions and devices. Which combination of Google Cloud services should you select for session state and cart storage?

options.text: A. Keep session and cart data in the instance's local memory and turn on cookie-based session affinity in a global HTTP(S) load balancer.
B. Save the cart as a Cloud Storage object whose name matches the session identifier.
C. Persist both session and cart data in BigQuery.
D. Hold session state in Memorystore for Redis and store the cart contents in Firestore.

questions.correct_text: D. Hold session state in Memorystore for Redis and store the cart contents in Firestore.
questions.explanation: Memorystore for Redis is ideal for fast, ephemeral session state with TTLs (e.g., 30-minute inactivity expiry), while Firestore durably persists cart contents and syncs across sessions and devices. A (in-memory + session affinity) loses data on instance failure and doesn't persist carts across devices. B (one Cloud Storage object per session) ties the cart to a transient session ID, so it won't persist across sessions/devices and is awkward for frequent reads/writes. C (BigQuery) is an analytics warehouse, not a low-latency transactional store for session/cart operations.

questions.question: You recently built a web application that uploads log files to a Cloud Storage bucket every day. Authenticated users routinely inspect logs from the past two weeks looking for critical events. After that, logs are reviewed once a year by an external auditor. Data must be stored for at least 7 years. You want a storage solution that meets these requirements and minimizes cost. What should you do? (Choose 2)

options.text: A. Use Bucket Lock to set the retention policy on the data.
B. Run a scheduled job that switches objects older than 14 days to Coldline storage.
C. Issue a JSON Web Token (JWT) to users that need access to the Coldline buckets.
D. Define a lifecycle management policy that transitions objects older than 14 days to Coldline storage.
E. Define a lifecycle management policy that transitions objects older than 14 days to Nearline storage.

questions.correct_text: A. Use Bucket Lock to set the retention policy on the data. | D. Define a lifecycle management policy that transitions objects older than 14 days to Coldline storage.
questions.explanation: Data must be retained for at least 7 years (compliance), so Bucket Lock with a retention policy (A) prevents deletion/overwriting for the required period. After the first two weeks objects are accessed at most once a year (auditor), which matches the Coldline access pattern (designed for data accessed less than once per quarter), so a managed lifecycle rule transitioning objects older than 14 days to Coldline (D) minimizes cost. E is wrong because Nearline targets data accessed about once a month, which is more expensive than Coldline for annual access. B is wrong because running a scheduled job duplicates what built-in lifecycle management does for free, adding operational overhead. C is wrong because JWTs are an authentication mechanism, not a storage/retention solution, and do not address cost or the 7-year requirement.

questions.question: You are building a web application that will run on Google Cloud. Incoming traffic is highly unpredictable, with no users on most days and large surges on others. You need the application to automatically scale up and down, and you want to minimize the cost of running the application. Which architecture should you pick?

B. Build the application with Firestore as the database and deploy it on a GKE Standard cluster.
C. Build the application with Cloud SQL as the database and deploy it on a GKE Autopilot cluster.
D. Build the application with Firestore as the database and deploy it on a Compute Engine managed instance group.

questions.question: You are building an ecommerce web app on Cloud Run that uses Memorystore for Redis. When a shopper signs in, the application caches their session, name, address, and preferences in Redis so checkout is fast. During testing, the Cloud Run service cannot connect to the Memorystore instance. Which configuration is most likely the cause?

options.text: A. The Memorystore for Redis instance was provisioned without a public IP address.
B. The Serverless VPC Access connector was created in a different region than the Cloud Run service.
C. The firewall rule that allowed Cloud Run to reach Memorystore was deleted by the DevOps team during a routine update.
D. Your application uses a Serverless VPC Access connector that sits on a different subnet in a different region than your Cloud Run service.

questions.correct_text: B. The Serverless VPC Access connector was created in a different region than the Cloud Run service.
questions.explanation: Cloud Run reaches Memorystore (which only has private/internal IPs) through a Serverless VPC Access connector, and the connector must be in the same region as the Cloud Run service. A is not a cause: Memorystore for Redis intentionally has no public IP, which is normal. C is wrong: Memorystore access does not depend on a manually created firewall rule that DevOps would delete; connectivity is via the connector. D conflates two issues and is less precise; the canonical sample-form answer is the region mismatch of the connector (B).

questions.question: Your organization has recently launched an effort to replatform its legacy applications onto GKE. You need to decompose a monolithic application into microservices. Several instances will read from and write to a shared configuration file that currently lives on a shared file system. You want to keep the changes required to the application minimal. What should you do?

options.text: A. Create a Cloud Storage bucket and mount it inside the container with FUSE.
B. Provision a new persistent disk and mount the volume as a shared PersistentVolume.
C. Provision a Filestore instance and mount the volume as an nfs PersistentVolume.
D. Create a ConfigMap and volumeMount that hold the contents of the configuration file.

questions.correct_text: C. Provision a Filestore instance and mount the volume as an nfs PersistentVolume.
questions.explanation: Multiple pod instances must concurrently read and write a shared file on a shared filesystem with minimal code change. Filestore provides managed NFS that supports ReadWriteMany, mountable as an NFS PersistentVolume so all instances share the same files. A (Cloud Storage FUSE) is object storage that does not behave like a true POSIX shared filesystem for concurrent read/write and would likely require app changes. B (a persistent disk PersistentVolume) supports ReadWriteOnce for read/write from a single node, not concurrent shared writes across instances. D (ConfigMap) is read-only from the pod's perspective and not suitable for an application that writes to the shared config file.

B. Create one Pub/Sub topic and create one pull subscription per audit service instance.
C. Create one Pub/Sub topic and create a single push subscription.
D. Create one Pub/Sub topic per authentication service instance, each with one pull subscription.

questions.question: You are building an application in a brand-new programming language that has no Cloud Client Libraries available. The application sends REST calls to Google Cloud services. It runs on Cloud Run with an attached service account, and you want to configure it so that it can authenticate to Google Cloud while requiring as little operational maintenance as possible. What should you do?

options.text: A. Bundle an API key with the application and place its value in the Authorization header.
B. Fetch the access token from the metadata server and place it in the Authorization header.
C. Use an API key for the service account as the value of the GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS environment variable.
D. At startup, save the output of gcloud auth application-default print-access-token to a file referenced by the GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS environment variable.

questions.correct_text: B. Fetch the access token from the metadata server and place it in the Authorization header.
questions.explanation: With no client library and an attached service account, the app can query the Cloud Run metadata server to obtain a short-lived OAuth access token for the service account and put it in the Authorization: Bearer header. questions.question: Your team has built a mobile web application where users around the world vote on trending topics. For every topic, you anticipate a very high volume of votes during each 30-minute voting period. You must capture and tally the votes for every topic in each 30-minute window and also store the raw votes for later analysis. Which architecture should you choose?

options.text: A. Save the votes in Memorystore and use Cloud Run functions to push the totals into BigQuery. Display the results in Google Data Studio.
B. Publish the votes to Pub/Sub and use a Dataflow pipeline to write both the totals and the raw votes to BigQuery. Display the results in Google Data Studio.
C. Publish the votes to Pub/Sub and use Cloud Run functions to write the totals and raw votes to Cloud Storage. Display the results in Google Data Studio.
D. Authenticate mobile users through Firebase and publish votes directly into Firestore. Export the votes to a CSV file and import it into Sheets for reporting.

questions.correct_text: B. Publish the votes to Pub/Sub and use a Dataflow pipeline to write both the totals and the raw votes to BigQuery. Display the results in Google Data Studio.
questions.explanation: You need to ingest a very high, bursty volume of votes globally, tally per-topic counts within fixed 30-minute windows, and keep the raw votes for analysis. Pub/Sub absorbs the global high-throughput ingest and decouples producers; Dataflow performs windowed aggregation (the 30-minute tumbling windows) and writes both the aggregated totals and the raw events to BigQuery for storage and later analysis; Data Studio visualizes. A relies on Memorystore plus functions, which does not natively do windowed stream aggregation at this scale and risks data loss. C writes to Cloud Storage and uses functions, lacking proper windowed tallying and easy analytics. D (Firebase/Firestore then CSV export to Sheets) does not scale to very high write volumes or support windowed stream tallying and analytics.

questions.question: You have written a Node.js Cloud Run function whose source code is stored in a Git repository. You want any committed change to be tested automatically. You author a Cloud Build configuration that pushes the source to a uniquely named Cloud Run function, invokes the function, and then deletes the function before reporting status. You need to ensure the build still records whether the test passed or failed. What should you do?

options.text: A. Reorder the steps so the Cloud Run function is deleted before the test step runs.
B. Add a waitFor entry on the Cloud Build step that deletes the Cloud Run function, listing the test step as a required predecessor.
C. Have the Cloud Build step write the Cloud Run function output to a file and return 0. Add a step after the Cloud Run function deletion that reads the file and fails the build if the test failed.

D. Have the Cloud Build test step set its outcome in an environment variable called result and return 0. Add a final step after the Cloud Run function deletion that fails the build if result is not OK.

questions.correct_text: C. Have the Cloud Build step write the Cloud Run function output to a file and return 0. Add a step after the Cloud Run function deletion that reads the file and fails the build if the test failed.
questions.explanation: The cleanup (delete) step must always run so test resources aren't left behind, which means the test step cannot fail the build directly (a non-zero exit would stop the pipeline before deletion). Persisting the test result to a file in the shared /workspace, returning 0 so cleanup proceeds, and then adding a final step that reads the file and fails the build (C) correctly records pass/fail while guaranteeing cleanup. A (delete before testing) destroys the function before you can invoke it. B (waitFor only orders steps) does not by itself capture and propagate the test result to the build status. D relies on an environment variable to persist across separate Cloud Build steps, but env vars do not persist between steps the way files in /workspace do, so it would not work reliably.

questions.question: You are recording significant audit activity to Cloud Logging. You need to read that data from Cloud Logging to perform near real-time analysis, with multiple consumer processes each running a different type of analysis. What should you do?

options.text: A. Write a program that pulls logs directly from the Cloud Logging API.
B. Configure a Cloud Logging sink to Pub/Sub and have each consumer read from its own Pub/Sub subscription.
C. Write a Cloud Function endpoint that polls the Cloud Logging API and copies the logs to Dataproc.
D. Configure a Cloud Logging sink to Cloud Storage and have consumers read the data from a Cloud Storage bucket.

questions.correct_text: B. Configure a Cloud Logging sink to Pub/Sub and have each consumer read from its own Pub/Sub subscription.
questions.explanation: You need near real-time, multi-consumer fan-out where each consumer runs different analysis. A Cloud Logging sink to a Pub/Sub topic streams logs in near real time, and giving each consumer its own subscription means every consumer receives a full independent copy of the messages, enabling parallel different analyses. A (polling the Logging API) is not real-time and doesn't fan out cleanly to multiple consumers. C (Cloud Function copying to Dataproc) is convoluted, adds overhead, and isn't the standard real-time fan-out pattern. D (sink to Cloud Storage) is batch/file-based, not near real-time, and is poorly suited to streaming multi-consumer analysis.

questions.question: Birchwood Retail has a new build of a containerized service that has passed functional tests and is ready to run on Google Kubernetes Engine. Because staging could not reproduce full production load, you want to limit the risk of performance regressions as the rollout goes live, and the deployment must be automated. Which strategy should you choose?

options.text: Use a continuous delivery pipeline to deploy a canary on GKE and only widen traffic when Cloud Monitoring metrics stay healthy
Run a blue-green release through your pipeline and cut over all traffic once Cloud Monitoring shows stable performance
Configure Cloud Load Balancing with weighted backends to gradually shift traffic between two GKE versions while watching latency and errors in Cloud Monitoring
Roll out with kubectl using a RollingUpdate strategy and reverse it with kubectl rollout undo if Cloud Monitoring shows problems

questions.correct_text: Use a continuous delivery pipeline to deploy a canary on GKE and only widen traffic when Cloud Monitoring metrics stay healthy
questions.explanation: Because staging could not reproduce production load, you must validate against real production traffic gradually. A canary deployment driven by a CD pipeline (e.g., Cloud Deploy) sends a small slice of live traffic to the new version and only widens it when Cloud Monitoring metrics stay healthy, limiting the blast radius of any performance regression while keeping it automated. B (blue-green) cuts over all traffic at once after staging-style validation, exposing 100% of users immediately to any unseen regression. C (LB weighted backends) is a manual/infra-centric approach that lacks the automated canary analysis and gating the question requires. D (RollingUpdate + manual rollout undo) replaces pods broadly and depends on manual intervention to revert, offering weaker risk control than an automated canary.

questions.question: At MetroHail you are building a dispatch platform on Cloud Run that keeps short-lived session data in Memorystore for Redis. You created a Serverless VPC Access connector so the service can reach the Redis instance inside your VPC. During integration testing, requests that read sessions from Redis fail almost every time. Which configuration is the most likely cause?

options.text: The Memorystore for Redis instance is not reachable from the public internet
The VPC that hosts the Redis instance has an incorrect network route
The Cloud Run service uses a Serverless VPC Access connector in a different region
The Serverless VPC Access connector is attached to a different VPC network than the Redis instance

questions.correct_text: The Serverless VPC Access connector is attached to a different VPC network than the Redis instance
questions.explanation: For Cloud Run to reach a Memorystore for Redis instance through Serverless VPC Access, the connector must be in the same VPC network (and compatible region) as the Redis instance. If the connector is attached to a different VPC, traffic cannot route to the private Redis IP and reads fail almost every time. A is wrong: Memorystore is private by design and not being internet-reachable is expected, not a fault. B (incorrect route) is possible but less likely than a misconfigured connector/VPC mismatch and is vaguer. C (different region) can cause connectivity issues too, but the connector being attached to a different VPC entirely is the most direct cause of consistent failure for private VPC resource access.

questions.question: RhythmReach is launching a podcast discovery app where users sign in and get episode recommendations tailored to their interests. A listener's preferences must persist durably and stay available across all devices. The app must also sign users out after 25 minutes of inactivity. Following Google Cloud best practices, which storage combination should the team choose?

options.text: Keep session data in Memorystore for Memcached and store user preferences in Cloud SQL
Record session data in BigQuery and save user preferences in Cloud Storage
Maintain session data in Memorystore for Redis and store user preferences in Firestore
Write session data to Firestore and keep user preferences on the VM's local filesystem

questions.correct_text: Maintain session data in Memorystore for Redis and store user preferences in Firestore
questions.explanation: Short-lived session data with an inactivity timeout fits Memorystore for Redis, which offers fast in-memory access and TTL/expiry for the 25-minute idle sign-out. Durable user preferences that must persist and be available across all devices fit Firestore (durable, replicated, cross-device sync). A is weaker: Memcached lacks Redis's richer features (and per-key TTL semantics are simpler in Redis), and Cloud SQL is fine for preferences but Firestore is the Google-favored choice for cross-device app data. B is wrong: BigQuery is an analytics warehouse, not a session store, and Cloud Storage is object storage, poor for structured preference queries. D is wrong: storing preferences on a VM's local filesystem is not durable or cross-device available.

questions.question: You are responsible for planning the migration to Google Cloud of an important application that runs on Oracle Database. The new platform must be a horizontally scalable, globally available SQL database. Which service should you use, and what type of schema migration is recommended?

questions.correct_text: Cloud Spanner with sequential primary keys migration
questions.explanation: The requirements point to a globally distributed SQL database with synchronized replicas and shards across multiple servers, which is Cloud Spanner. You need to be careful about hotspotting since Cloud Spanner splits data among servers by key ranges; if you insert records with a monotonically increasing integer as the key, every insert lands at the end of the key space and bottlenecks on one server. You should plan a schema migration that avoids sequential primary keys.

questions.question: You have this SQL statement in BigQuery: SELECT ANY_VALUE(fruit) as any_value FROM UNNEST(['apple', 'banana', 'pear']) as fruit; What is the result of this query?

options.text: A table with 3 rows
Apple
Banana
Pear
One of the values, randomly

questions.correct_text: One of the values, randomly
questions.explanation: The interesting elements of this query are: UNNEST, which takes an ARRAY and returns a table (and can also be used outside the FROM clause with the IN operator); and analytic functions, which compute aggregate values over a group of rows. ANY_VALUE returns a random value from the input or NULL if there are no input rows. Starting from a table built on the fly from an array, the query can return any value each time it is executed.

Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL with the default configuration
Cloud Storage with lifecycle management
Cloud Datastore with transactional commits

questions.correct_text: Cloud Datastore with transactional commits
questions.explanation: Cloud Datastore (Firestore in Datastore mode) is a low-cost, serverless NoSQL service that offers strong consistency, ACID atomic transactions, and serializable isolation, and it stores semi-structured (schemaless/partially structured) entities, matching all stated requirements. A/B (Cloud SQL MySQL/PostgreSQL default) are relational with rigid schemas (not partially structured) and incur always-on instance cost, less aligned with 'low-cost' serverless and 'partially structured.' C (Cloud Storage) is object storage with no transactions, atomicity, or serializable isolation.

questions.question: You have been asked to design an application that lets users upload images and documents to Cloud Storage. The files must be processed, classified, and remain available for one month. After that, they must be archived. You want to create a simple and effective solution. Which of the following is the best choice?

Use Google Cloud Storage triggers and call a function that classifies the files; configure the bucket with a lifecycle rule that changes the storage class of objects to Coldline Storage.
Create a Linux cron job on a VM that performs all the requested tasks.
Use Cloud Scheduler and set up an App Engine application.

questions.correct_text: Use Google Cloud Storage triggers and call a function that classifies the files; configure the bucket with a lifecycle rule that changes the storage class of objects to Coldline Storage.
questions.explanation: A Cloud Storage trigger invoking a Cloud Function on upload handles processing/classification event-driven, and an Object Lifecycle Management rule automatically transitions objects to a colder/archival class after the retention period, which is the simplest, fully managed solution. (Coldline is the offered archival-tier option and fits 'archived after a month.') A is weaker: 'a function that performs all the tasks' including archiving manually is more code and reinvents lifecycle management. C (VM cron job) is operationally heavy and not serverless. D (Cloud Scheduler + App Engine) adds unneeded components for what triggers and lifecycle rules do automatically.

questions.question: You want to upload files from an on-premises virtual machine to Google Cloud Storage as part of a data migration. These files will be consumed by CloudDataProc Hadoop cluster in a GCP environment.Which command should you use?

options.text: gsutil cp [LOCAL_OBJECT] gs://[DESTINATION_BUCKET_NAME]/
gcloud cp [LOCAL_OBJECT] gs://[DESTINATION_BUCKET_NAME]/
hadoop fs cp [LOCAL_OBJECT] gs://[DESTINATION_BUCKET_NAME]/
gcloud dataproc cp [LOCAL_OBJECT] gs://[DESTINATION_BUCKET_NAME]/

questions.correct_text: gsutil cp [LOCAL_OBJECT] gs://[DESTINATION_BUCKET_NAME]/
questions.explanation: The gsutil command-line tool is the dedicated utility for interacting with Cloud Storage, and 'gsutil cp [LOCAL_OBJECT] gs://[DESTINATION_BUCKET_NAME]/' correctly uploads local files from the on-premises VM into a bucket where Dataproc can later read them. Option B is invalid because gcloud has no 'cp' command for Cloud Storage objects. Option C ('hadoop fs cp') would require an already-running Hadoop cluster with the GCS connector and is not the correct way to perform the initial on-premises-to-cloud upload. Option D is not a real gcloud dataproc subcommand. Therefore gsutil cp is the right choice for staging migration data in Cloud Storage.
