questions.explanation_pt: O Private Google Access permite que instâncias de VM que possuem apenas endereços IP internos alcancem as APIs e serviços do Google, como a API do Cloud Storage, pela rede interna do Google sem exigir IPs externos. Ele é habilitado por sub-rede e é a solução padrão para instâncias sem endereços IP públicos. O VPC Network Peering conecta duas redes VPC entre si, mas por si só não concede acesso às APIs do Google. O Shared VPC compartilha recursos de rede entre projetos, e o Carrier Peering é para conectividade on-premises com os serviços do Google; nenhum dos dois resolve diretamente o requisito de acesso às APIs sem IP público.

questions.question: You are a developer working with the CI/CD team to troubleshoot a new feature that your team introduced. The CI/CD team used HashiCorp Packer to create a new Compute Engine image from your development branch. The image was successfully built, but is not booting up. You need to investigate the issue with the CI/CD team. What should you do?

options.text: Create a new feature branch, and ask the build team to rebuild the image.
Shut down the deployed virtual machine, export the disk, and then mount the disk locally to access the boot logs.
Install Packer locally, build the Compute Engine image locally, and then run it in your personal Google Cloud project.
Check Compute Engine OS logs using the serial port, and check the Cloud Logging logs to confirm access to the serial port.

questions.correct_text: Check Compute Engine OS logs using the serial port, and check the Cloud Logging logs to confirm access to the serial port.
questions.explanation: When a Compute Engine image builds successfully but the resulting VM fails to boot, the serial console (serial port) output contains the OS-level boot logs that reveal where startup stalls or fails. Checking the serial port output, and confirming via Cloud Logging that serial port access is enabled and captured, lets you diagnose the boot problem directly. Rebuilding from a new branch or building locally (options A and C) does not investigate the actual failure and may not reproduce it. Shutting down and mounting the disk locally (option B) is far more cumbersome and unnecessary when serial console logs are readily available.

topics.exam_domain_name: Construir e testar aplicações

questions.explanation_pt: Quando uma imagem do Compute Engine é construída com sucesso, mas a VM resultante não consegue inicializar, a saída do console serial (porta serial) contém os logs de boot no nível do SO que revelam onde a inicialização trava ou falha. Verificar a saída da porta serial e confirmar via Cloud Logging que o acesso à porta serial está habilitado e sendo capturado permite diagnosticar o problema de boot diretamente. Reconstruir a partir de um novo branch ou construir localmente (opções A e C) não investiga a falha real e pode não reproduzi-la. Desligar e montar o disco localmente (opção B) é muito mais trabalhoso e desnecessário quando os logs do console serial estão prontamente disponíveis.

questions.question: You manage an application that runs in a Compute Engine instance. You also have multiple backend services executing in stand-alone Docker containers running in Compute Engine instances. The Compute Engine instances supporting the backend services are scaled by managed instance groups in multiple regions. You want your calling application to be loosely coupled. You need to be able to invoke distinct service implementations that are chosen based on the value of an HTTP header found in the request. Which Google Cloud feature should you use to invoke the backend services?

options.text: Traffic Director
Service Directory
Anthos Service Mesh
Internal HTTP(S) Load Balancing

questions.correct_text: Traffic Director
questions.explanation: Traffic Director is Google Cloud's managed service mesh control plane that supports advanced request routing, including selecting distinct backend services based on HTTP header values, while keeping the calling application loosely coupled across multi-region managed instance groups. It programs the data plane (proxies/xDS clients) to perform header-based routing without coupling the client to specific service instances. Internal HTTP(S) Load Balancing alone offers more limited routing and is regional, not the full mesh-style traffic management needed here. Service Directory is a service registry for discovery, not a traffic router, and Anthos Service Mesh is oriented toward GKE/Anthos environments rather than these stand-alone Docker-on-Compute-Engine backends.

topics.exam_domain_name: Projetar apps cloud-native escaláveis, seguras e confiáveis

questions.explanation_pt: O Traffic Director é o control plane de service mesh gerenciado do Google Cloud, que oferece suporte a roteamento avançado de requisições, incluindo a seleção de backend services distintos com base em valores de cabeçalhos HTTP, mantendo a aplicação chamadora fracamente acoplada em managed instance groups multirregionais. Ele programa o data plane (proxies/clientes xDS) para realizar o roteamento baseado em cabeçalhos sem acoplar o cliente a instâncias específicas de serviço. O Internal HTTP(S) Load Balancing isoladamente oferece roteamento mais limitado e é regional, não o gerenciamento de tráfego completo no estilo mesh necessário aqui. O Service Directory é um registro de serviços para descoberta, não um roteador de tráfego, e o Anthos Service Mesh é voltado para ambientes GKE/Anthos, em vez desses backends independentes baseados em Docker sobre o Compute Engine.

questions.question: Your team is developing an ecommerce platform for your company. Users will log in to the website and add items to their shopping cart. Users will be automatically logged out after 30 minutes of inactivity. When users log back in, their shopping cart should be saved. How should you store users' session and shopping cart information while following Google-recommended best practices?

options.text: Store the session information in Pub/Sub, and store the shopping cart information in Cloud SQL.
Store the shopping cart information in a file on Cloud Storage where the filename is the SESSION ID.
Store the session and shopping cart information in a MySQL database running on multiple Compute Engine instances.
Store the session information in Memorystore for Redis or Memorystore for Memcached, and store the shopping cart information in Firestore.

questions.correct_text: Store the session information in Memorystore for Redis or Memorystore for Memcached, and store the shopping cart information in Firestore.
questions.explanation: Memorystore (Redis or Memcached) is the Google-recommended in-memory store for fast, low-latency session state, while Firestore is a managed NoSQL database well suited to persisting structured shopping cart data that must survive logouts and be retrieved when the user returns. This combination separates ephemeral session lookups from durable cart storage, both using fully managed services that scale automatically. Option A misuses Pub/Sub, which is a messaging service, not a session store. Option B abuses Cloud Storage object files keyed by session ID, which is inefficient and not designed for transactional cart updates. Option C requires self-managing MySQL on Compute Engine instances, adding operational overhead and not following managed-service best practices.

topics.exam_domain_name: Projetar apps cloud-native escaláveis, seguras e confiáveis

questions.explanation_pt: O Memorystore (Redis ou Memcached) é o armazenamento em memória recomendado pelo Google para estado de sessão rápido e de baixa latência, enquanto o Firestore é um banco de dados NoSQL gerenciado bem adequado para persistir dados estruturados de carrinho de compras que precisam sobreviver a logouts e ser recuperados quando o usuário retornar. Essa combinação separa as consultas efêmeras de sessão do armazenamento durável do carrinho, ambos usando serviços totalmente gerenciados que escalam automaticamente. A opção A usa indevidamente o Pub/Sub, que é um serviço de mensageria, não um armazenamento de sessão. A opção B abusa de arquivos de objetos do Cloud Storage indexados por session ID, o que é ineficiente e não foi projetado para atualizações transacionais de carrinho. A opção C exige autogerenciar MySQL em instâncias do Compute Engine, adicionando sobrecarga operacional e não seguindo as práticas recomendadas de serviços gerenciados.

questions.question: You are designing a resource-sharing policy for applications used by different teams in a Google Kubernetes Engine cluster. You need to ensure that all applications can access the resources needed to run. What should you do? (Choose two.)

options.text: Specify the resource limits and requests in the object specifications.
Create a namespace for each team, and attach resource quotas to each namespace.
Create a LimitRange to specify the default compute resource requirements for each namespace.
Create a Kubernetes service account (KSA) for each application, and assign each KSA to the namespace.
Use the Anthos Policy Controller to enforce label annotations on all namespaces. Use taints and tolerations to allow resource sharing for namespaces.

questions.correct_text: Create a namespace for each team, and attach resource quotas to each namespace. | Create a LimitRange to specify the default compute resource requirements for each namespace.
questions.explanation: Creating a namespace per team with ResourceQuotas (B) bounds the aggregate CPU, memory, and object counts each team can consume, preventing one team from starving others while guaranteeing fair access. A LimitRange (C) sets default and per-object compute requests and limits within a namespace, ensuring Pods that omit explicit resource settings still get sensible defaults so the scheduler can place them. Together they enforce a workable resource-sharing policy. Option A (per-object limits/requests) helps individual workloads but does not establish a team-level sharing policy on its own. Option D concerns identity/access via service accounts, not resource sharing, and Option E mixes policy label enforcement with taints/tolerations, which control scheduling affinity rather than resource quotas.

topics.exam_domain_name: Configurar aplicações cloud-native para deployment

questions.explanation_pt: Criar um namespace por equipe com ResourceQuotas (B) limita o total agregado de CPU, memória e contagem de objetos que cada equipe pode consumir, evitando que uma equipe prive as outras de recursos e garantindo acesso justo. Um LimitRange (C) define requests e limits de computação padrão e por objeto dentro de um namespace, garantindo que Pods que omitam configurações explícitas de recursos ainda recebam padrões sensatos para que o scheduler possa alocá-los. Juntos, eles aplicam uma política viável de compartilhamento de recursos. A opção A (limits/requests por objeto) ajuda cargas de trabalho individuais, mas não estabelece por si só uma política de compartilhamento em nível de equipe. A opção D diz respeito a identidade/acesso via service accounts, não a compartilhamento de recursos, e a opção E mistura aplicação de políticas por labels com taints/tolerations, que controlam afinidade de agendamento em vez de cotas de recursos.

questions.question: You are developing a new application that has the following design requirements:✑ Creation and changes to the application infrastructure are versioned and auditable.✑ The application and deployment infrastructure uses Google-managed services as much as possible.✑ The application runs on a serverless compute platform.How should you design the application's architecture?

options.text: 1. Store the application and infrastructure source code in a Git repository. 2. Use Cloud Build to deploy the application infrastructure with Terraform. 3. Deploy the application to a Cloud Function as a pipeline step.

1. Deploy Jenkins from the Google Cloud Marketplace, and define a continuous integration pipeline in Jenkins. 2. Configure a pipeline step to pull the application source code from a Git repository. 3. Deploy the application source code to App Engine as a pipeline step.

1. Create a continuous integration pipeline on Cloud Build, and configure the pipeline to deploy the application infrastructure using Deployment Manager templates. 2. Configure a pipeline step to create a container with the latest application source code. 3. Deploy the container to a Compute Engine instance as a pipeline step.

1. Deploy the application infrastructure using gcloud commands. 2. Use Cloud Build to define a continuous integration pipeline for changes to the application source code. 3. Configure a pipeline step to pull the application source code from a Git repository, and create a containerized application. 4. Deploy the new container on Cloud Run as a pipeline step.

questions.correct_text: 1. Store the application and infrastructure source code in a Git repository. 2. Use Cloud Build to deploy the application infrastructure with Terraform. 3. Deploy the application to a Cloud Function as a pipeline step.
questions.explanation: Storing both application and infrastructure code in Git makes all infrastructure changes versioned and auditable, Cloud Build with Terraform provisions the infrastructure declaratively, and Cloud Functions provides a true serverless compute platform, satisfying all three requirements with Google-managed services. Option B relies on self-managed Jenkins from the Marketplace, which is not a Google-managed service. Option C deploys to a Compute Engine instance, which is not serverless. Option D provisions infrastructure with imperative gcloud commands, so changes are not declaratively versioned or fully auditable as infrastructure-as-code, even though Cloud Run is serverless.

topics.exam_domain_name: Configurar aplicações cloud-native para deployment

questions.explanation_pt: Armazenar tanto o código da aplicação quanto o de infraestrutura no Git torna todas as mudanças de infraestrutura versionadas e auditáveis, o Cloud Build com Terraform provisiona a infraestrutura de forma declarativa, e o Cloud Functions oferece uma plataforma de computação verdadeiramente serverless, atendendo aos três requisitos com serviços gerenciados pelo Google. A opção B depende de um Jenkins autogerenciado do Marketplace, que não é um serviço gerenciado pelo Google. A opção C implanta em uma instância do Compute Engine, que não é serverless. A opção D provisiona a infraestrutura com comandos imperativos do gcloud, de modo que as mudanças não são versionadas de forma declarativa nem totalmente auditáveis como infraestrutura como código, embora o Cloud Run seja serverless.

questions.question: You are creating and running containers across different projects in Google Cloud. The application you are developing needs to access Google Cloud services from within Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). What should you do?

options.text: Assign a Google service account to the GKE nodes.
Use a Google service account to run the Pod with Workload Identity.
Store the Google service account credentials as a Kubernetes Secret.
Use a Google service account with GKE role-based access control (RBAC).

questions.correct_text: Use a Google service account to run the Pod with Workload Identity.
questions.explanation: Workload Identity is the Google-recommended way for GKE workloads to access Google Cloud services: it binds a Kubernetes service account to a Google service account, letting Pods authenticate securely without managing or distributing static credentials, and it works cleanly across projects. Option A grants the node's service account to every Pod on that node, violating least privilege and giving coarse, shared access. Option C stores long-lived service account key files as Kubernetes Secrets, which is discouraged due to credential leakage and rotation burden. Option D conflates RBAC, which controls access to the Kubernetes API, with Google Cloud IAM authentication, so it does not enable Pods to call Google Cloud services.

topics.exam_domain_name: Integrar aplicações com serviços do Google Cloud

questions.explanation_pt: O Workload Identity é a forma recomendada pelo Google para que cargas de trabalho do GKE acessem serviços do Google Cloud: ele vincula uma Kubernetes service account a uma Google service account, permitindo que os Pods se autentiquem com segurança sem gerenciar ou distribuir credenciais estáticas, e funciona de forma limpa entre projetos. A opção A concede a service account do nó a todos os Pods naquele nó, violando o princípio do menor privilégio e dando acesso amplo e compartilhado. A opção C armazena arquivos de chave de service account de longa duração como Kubernetes Secrets, o que é desencorajado devido ao vazamento de credenciais e à carga de rotação. A opção D confunde RBAC, que controla o acesso à API do Kubernetes, com a autenticação IAM do Google Cloud, portanto não habilita os Pods a chamar serviços do Google Cloud.

questions.question: You have containerized a legacy application that stores its configuration on an NFS share. You need to deploy this application to Google Kubernetes Engine(GKE) and do not want the application serving traffic until after the configuration has been retrieved. What should you do?

options.text: Use the gsutil utility to copy files from within the Docker container at startup, and start the service using an ENTRYPOINT script.
Create a PersistentVolumeClaim on the GKE cluster. Access the configuration files from the volume, and start the service using an ENTRYPOINT script.
Use the COPY statement in the Dockerfile to load the configuration into the container image. Verify that the configuration is available, and start the service using an ENTRYPOINT script.
Add a startup script to the GKE instance group to mount the NFS share at node startup. Copy the configuration files into the container, and start the service using an ENTRYPOINT script.

questions.correct_text: Create a PersistentVolumeClaim on the GKE cluster. Access the configuration files from the volume, and start the service using an ENTRYPOINT script.
questions.explanation: A PersistentVolumeClaim lets the Pod mount the NFS-backed storage and read the configuration at runtime, and using an ENTRYPOINT script that retrieves the configuration before launching the service ensures the application does not serve traffic until configuration is loaded. This keeps configuration external and mutable rather than baked into the image. Option A using gsutil targets Cloud Storage, not the existing NFS share. Option C bakes configuration into the image with COPY, which defeats externalized configuration and requires a rebuild for every change. Option D adds node-level startup scripts to mount NFS and copy files, which is fragile, node-coupled, and not the Kubernetes-native pattern for volumes.

topics.exam_domain_name: Configurar aplicações cloud-native para deployment

questions.explanation_pt: Um PersistentVolumeClaim permite que o Pod monte o armazenamento baseado em NFS e leia a configuração em tempo de execução, e usar um script de ENTRYPOINT que recupera a configuração antes de iniciar o serviço garante que a aplicação não atenda tráfego até que a configuração seja carregada. Isso mantém a configuração externa e mutável, em vez de embutida na imagem. A opção A, usando gsutil, tem como alvo o Cloud Storage, não o compartilhamento NFS existente. A opção C embute a configuração na imagem com COPY, o que anula a configuração externalizada e exige um rebuild a cada mudança. A opção D adiciona scripts de inicialização no nível do node para montar NFS e copiar arquivos, o que é frágil, acoplado ao node e não é o padrão nativo do Kubernetes para volumes.

questions.question: Your team is developing a new application using a PostgreSQL database and Cloud Run. You are responsible for ensuring that all traffic is kept private on GoogleCloud. You want to use managed services and follow Google-recommended best practices. What should you do?

options.text: 1. Enable Cloud SQL and Cloud Run in the same project. 2. Configure a private IP address for Cloud SQL. Enable private services access. 3. Create a Serverless VPC Access connector. 4. Configure Cloud Run to use the connector to connect to Cloud SQL.

1. Install PostgreSQL on a Compute Engine virtual machine (VM), and enable Cloud Run in the same project. 2. Configure a private IP address for the VM. Enable private services access. 3. Create a Serverless VPC Access connector. 4. Configure Cloud Run to use the connector to connect to the VM hosting PostgreSQL.

1. Use Cloud SQL and Cloud Run in different projects. 2. Configure a private IP address for Cloud SQL. Enable private services access. 3. Create a Serverless VPC Access connector. 4. Set up a VPN connection between the two projects. Configure Cloud Run to use the connector to connect to Cloud SQL.

1. Install PostgreSQL on a Compute Engine VM, and enable Cloud Run in different projects. 2. Configure a private IP address for the VM. Enable private services access. 3. Create a Serverless VPC Access connector. 4. Set up a VPN connection between the two projects. Configure Cloud Run to use the connector to access the VM hosting PostgreSQL

questions.correct_text: 1. Enable Cloud SQL and Cloud Run in the same project. 2. Configure a private IP address for Cloud SQL. Enable private services access. 3. Create a Serverless VPC Access connector. 4. Configure Cloud Run to use the connector to connect to Cloud SQL.
questions.explanation: Option A is the Google-recommended pattern for connecting Cloud Run to a PostgreSQL database entirely over private networking using managed services. Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL is the managed database, configured with a private IP via private services access (a peered VPC range), and a Serverless VPC Access connector lets the serverless Cloud Run service reach that private IP inside the VPC. Options B and D rely on self-managed PostgreSQL on a Compute Engine VM, which is not a managed service and adds operational overhead, so they violate the requirement to use managed services. Option C unnecessarily splits resources across projects and adds a VPN, which is not needed since VPC peering and a connector already provide private connectivity within a single VPC.

topics.exam_domain_name: Integrar aplicações com serviços do Google Cloud

questions.explanation_pt: A opção A é o padrão recomendado pelo Google para conectar o Cloud Run a um banco de dados PostgreSQL inteiramente por meio de rede privada, usando serviços gerenciados. O Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL é o banco de dados gerenciado, configurado com um IP privado via private services access (uma faixa de VPC com peering), e um Serverless VPC Access connector permite que o serviço serverless do Cloud Run alcance esse IP privado dentro da VPC. As opções B e D dependem de PostgreSQL autogerenciado em uma VM do Compute Engine, que não é um serviço gerenciado e adiciona sobrecarga operacional, violando assim o requisito de usar serviços gerenciados. A opção C divide recursos entre projetos desnecessariamente e adiciona uma VPN, o que não é necessário, já que o VPC peering e um connector já fornecem conectividade privada dentro de uma única VPC.

questions.question: You are developing an application that will allow clients to download a file from your website for a specific period of time. How should you design the application to complete this task while following Google-recommended best practices?

options.text: Configure the application to send the file to the client as an email attachment.
Generate and assign a Cloud Storage-signed URL for the file. Make the URL available for the client to download.
Create a temporary Cloud Storage bucket with time expiration specified, and give download permissions to the bucket. Copy the file, and send it to the client.
Generate the HTTP cookies with time expiration specified. If the time is valid, copy the file from the Cloud Storage bucket, and make the file available for the client to download.

questions.correct_text: Generate and assign a Cloud Storage-signed URL for the file. Make the URL available for the client to download.
questions.explanation: A Cloud Storage signed URL is the recommended way to grant temporary, time-limited access to a specific object without exposing credentials or making the object public. The signed URL embeds an expiration time, so the client can download the file directly from Cloud Storage only during the valid window. Sending the file as an email attachment (A) is unreliable for large files and provides no controlled expiration. Creating a temporary bucket with broad download permissions (C) is heavy-handed and risks exposing other data. Using HTTP cookies (D) requires building custom server-side validation and copying logic instead of leveraging the built-in, secure signed URL mechanism.

topics.exam_domain_name: Integrar aplicações com serviços do Google Cloud

questions.explanation_pt: Uma signed URL do Cloud Storage é a forma recomendada de conceder acesso temporário e por tempo limitado a um objeto específico, sem expor credenciais nem tornar o objeto público. A signed URL embute um tempo de expiração, de modo que o cliente pode baixar o arquivo diretamente do Cloud Storage apenas durante a janela válida. Enviar o arquivo como anexo de e-mail (A) não é confiável para arquivos grandes e não oferece expiração controlada. Criar um bucket temporário com permissões amplas de download (C) é uma abordagem exagerada e arrisca expor outros dados. Usar cookies HTTP (D) exige construir validação personalizada no lado do servidor e lógica de cópia, em vez de aproveitar o mecanismo de signed URL, que é seguro e integrado.

questions.question: Your development team has been asked to refactor an existing monolithic application into a set of composable microservices. Which design aspects should you implement for the new application? (Choose two.)

options.text: Develop the microservice code in the same programming language used by the microservice caller.
Create an API contract agreement between the microservice implementation and microservice caller.
Require asynchronous communications between all microservice implementations and microservice callers.
Ensure that sufficient instances of the microservice are running to accommodate the performance requirements.
Implement a versioning scheme to permit future changes that could be incompatible with the current interface.

questions.correct_text: Create an API contract agreement between the microservice implementation and microservice caller. | Implement a versioning scheme to permit future changes that could be incompatible with the current interface.
questions.explanation: Well-designed microservices communicate through clearly defined, technology-agnostic interfaces, so establishing an API contract between a service and its callers (B) is essential to keep services loosely coupled. A versioning scheme (E) is equally important so the interface can evolve without breaking existing consumers, allowing backward-incompatible changes to be introduced safely. Requiring the same programming language (A) defeats a core benefit of microservices, which is technology independence. Mandating asynchronous communication for all calls (C) is too prescriptive, as many interactions are appropriately synchronous. Ensuring sufficient instances for performance (D) is an operational scaling concern rather than a design aspect of composability.

topics.exam_domain_name: Projetar apps cloud-native escaláveis, seguras e confiáveis

questions.explanation_pt: Microsserviços bem projetados se comunicam por meio de interfaces claramente definidas e independentes de tecnologia, portanto estabelecer um contrato de API entre um serviço e seus chamadores (B) é essencial para manter os serviços fracamente acoplados. Um esquema de versionamento (E) é igualmente importante para que a interface possa evoluir sem quebrar os consumidores existentes, permitindo que mudanças incompatíveis com versões anteriores sejam introduzidas com segurança. Exigir a mesma linguagem de programação (A) anula um benefício central dos microsserviços, que é a independência de tecnologia. Tornar obrigatória a comunicação assíncrona para todas as chamadas (C) é prescritivo demais, já que muitas interações são apropriadamente síncronas. Garantir instâncias suficientes para desempenho (D) é uma preocupação operacional de escalabilidade, e não um aspecto de design da componibilidade.

questions.question: You deployed a new application to Google Kubernetes Engine and are experiencing some performance degradation. Your logs are being written to CloudLogging, and you are using a Prometheus sidecar model for capturing metrics. You need to correlate the metrics and data from the logs to troubleshoot the performance issue and send real-time alerts while minimizing costs. What should you do?

options.text: Create custom metrics from the Cloud Logging logs, and use Prometheus to import the results using the Cloud Monitoring REST API.
Export the Cloud Logging logs and the Prometheus metrics to Cloud Bigtable. Run a query to join the results, and analyze in Google Data Studio.
Export the Cloud Logging logs and stream the Prometheus metrics to BigQuery. Run a recurring query to join the results, and send notifications using Cloud Tasks.

Export the Prometheus metrics and use Cloud Monitoring to view them as external metrics. Configure Cloud Monitoring to create log-based metrics from the logs, and correlate them with the Prometheus data.

questions.correct_text: Export the Prometheus metrics and use Cloud Monitoring to view them as external metrics. Configure Cloud Monitoring to create log-based metrics from the logs, and correlate them with the Prometheus data.
questions.explanation: Cloud Monitoring can ingest Prometheus metrics (via Managed Service for Prometheus or as external metrics) and create log-based metrics from Cloud Logging entries, allowing both data sources to be correlated and alerted on within a single managed platform, which minimizes cost and complexity. Option D leverages these native capabilities for real-time alerting without building custom pipelines. Option A inverts the flow by importing into Prometheus and adds unnecessary custom work. Option B uses Bigtable and Data Studio for batch analysis, which cannot deliver real-time alerts. Option C streams to BigQuery with recurring queries and Cloud Tasks, an expensive and non-real-time approach that misuses Cloud Tasks for alerting.

topics.exam_domain_name: Integrar aplicações com serviços do Google Cloud

questions.explanation_pt: O Cloud Monitoring pode ingerir métricas do Prometheus (via Managed Service for Prometheus ou como métricas externas) e criar log-based metrics a partir de entradas do Cloud Logging, permitindo correlacionar e gerar alertas sobre ambas as fontes de dados dentro de uma única plataforma gerenciada, o que minimiza custo e complexidade. A opção D aproveita essas capacidades nativas para alertas em tempo real sem construir pipelines personalizados. A opção A inverte o fluxo ao importar para o Prometheus e adiciona trabalho personalizado desnecessário. A opção B usa Bigtable e Data Studio para análise em lote, o que não consegue entregar alertas em tempo real. A opção C transmite para o BigQuery com consultas recorrentes e Cloud Tasks, uma abordagem cara e não em tempo real que usa o Cloud Tasks de forma inadequada para alertas.

questions.question: You have been tasked with planning the migration of your company's application from on-premises to Google Cloud. Your company's monolithic application is an ecommerce website. The application will be migrated to microservices deployed on Google Cloud in stages. The majority of your company's revenue is generated through online sales, so it is important to minimize risk during the migration. You need to prioritize features and select the first functionality to migrate. What should you do?

options.text: Migrate the Product catalog, which has integrations to the frontend and product database.
Migrate Payment processing, which has integrations to the frontend, order database, and third-party payment vendor.
Migrate Order fulfillment, which has integrations to the order database, inventory system, and third-party shipping vendor.
Migrate the Shopping cart, which has integrations to the frontend, cart database, inventory system, and payment processing system.

questions.correct_text: Migrate the Product catalog, which has integrations to the frontend and product database.
questions.explanation: To minimize risk during a staged strangler-fig migration, you should begin with the component that has the fewest and least critical integrations, so any issues have limited blast radius on revenue. The product catalog (A) integrates only with the frontend and product database and is largely read-oriented, making it the lowest-risk first candidate. Payment processing (B) and order fulfillment (C) touch money movement, third-party vendors, and core transactional systems, so failures there directly threaten revenue. The shopping cart (D) has many dependencies including inventory and payment processing, making it complex and risky to migrate first.

topics.exam_domain_name: Projetar apps cloud-native escaláveis, seguras e confiáveis

questions.explanation_pt: Para minimizar o risco durante uma migração escalonada com o padrão strangler-fig, você deve começar pelo componente que tem as integrações em menor número e menos críticas, de modo que qualquer problema tenha um raio de impacto limitado sobre a receita. O catálogo de produtos (A) integra-se apenas com o frontend e o banco de dados de produtos e é majoritariamente orientado a leitura, o que o torna o primeiro candidato de menor risco. O processamento de pagamentos (B) e o atendimento de pedidos (C) envolvem movimentação de dinheiro, fornecedores terceirizados e sistemas transacionais centrais, então falhas nesses pontos ameaçam diretamente a receita. O carrinho de compras (D) tem muitas dependências, incluindo inventário e processamento de pagamentos, o que torna sua migração complexa e arriscada como primeiro passo.

questions.question: Your team develops services that run on Google Kubernetes Engine. Your team's code is stored in Cloud Source Repositories. You need to quickly identify bugs in the code before it is deployed to production. You want to invest in automation to improve developer feedback and make the process as efficient as possible.What should you do?

options.text: Use Spinnaker to automate building container images from code based on Git tags.
Use Cloud Build to automate building container images from code based on Git tags.
Use Spinnaker to automate deploying container images to the production environment.
Use Cloud Build to automate building container images from code based on forked versions.

questions.correct_text: Use Cloud Build to automate building container images from code based on Git tags.
questions.explanation: Cloud Build is Google Cloud's native CI service that can automatically build container images from source in Cloud Source Repositories, triggered by events such as Git tags or branch pushes. Triggering builds on tags lets the team run automated tests and quickly surface bugs before promotion, giving fast developer feedback efficiently. Spinnaker is a continuous delivery tool focused on deploying artifacts, not building images for early bug detection, so options A and C miss the build/test feedback goal. Building from forked versions (D) does not match the team's tag-based workflow and adds unnecessary complexity.

topics.exam_domain_name: Construir e testar aplicações

questions.explanation_pt: O Cloud Build é o serviço de CI nativo do Google Cloud que pode construir imagens de contêiner automaticamente a partir do código-fonte no Cloud Source Repositories, acionado por eventos como tags Git ou pushes em branches. Acionar builds em tags permite que a equipe execute testes automatizados e identifique bugs rapidamente antes da promoção, oferecendo feedback rápido e eficiente aos desenvolvedores. O Spinnaker é uma ferramenta de entrega contínua focada em implantar artefatos, não em construir imagens para detecção precoce de bugs, então as opções A e C não atendem ao objetivo de feedback de build/teste. Construir a partir de versões com fork (D) não corresponde ao fluxo de trabalho baseado em tags da equipe e adiciona complexidade desnecessária.

questions.question: Your team is developing an application in Google Cloud that executes with user identities maintained by Cloud Identity. Each of your application's users will have an associated Pub/Sub topic to which messages are published, and a Pub/Sub subscription where the same user will retrieve published messages. You need to ensure that only authorized users can publish and subscribe to their own specific Pub/Sub topic and subscription. What should you do?

options.text: Bind the user identity to the pubsub.publisher and pubsub.subscriber roles at the resource level.
Grant the user identity the pubsub.publisher and pubsub.subscriber roles at the project level.
Grant the user identity a custom role that contains the pubsub.topics.create and pubsub.subscriptions.create permissions.
Configure the application to run as a service account that has the pubsub.publisher and pubsub.subscriber roles.

questions.correct_text: Bind the user identity to the pubsub.publisher and pubsub.subscriber roles at the resource level.
questions.explanation: Pub/Sub supports IAM policies at the individual resource level (per topic and per subscription), so binding each user identity to the pubsub.publisher and pubsub.subscriber roles on their specific topic and subscription enforces least privilege and ensures users can only access their own resources. Granting these roles at the project level (B) would let every user publish and subscribe to all topics, violating isolation. A custom role with create permissions (C) lets users create resources but does not restrict publish/subscribe access to their own resource. Running the application as a single shared service account (D) does not authorize per-user access based on individual Cloud Identity users.

topics.exam_domain_name: Integrar aplicações com serviços do Google Cloud

questions.explanation_pt: O Pub/Sub oferece suporte a políticas de IAM no nível de cada recurso individual (por tópico e por subscription), então associar cada identidade de usuário aos papéis pubsub.publisher e pubsub.subscriber em seu tópico e subscription específicos impõe o privilégio mínimo e garante que os usuários só possam acessar seus próprios recursos. Conceder esses papéis no nível do projeto (B) permitiria que todos os usuários publicassem e se inscrevessem em todos os tópicos, violando o isolamento. Um papel personalizado com permissões de criação (C) permite que os usuários criem recursos, mas não restringe o acesso de publicação/inscrição ao seu próprio recurso. Executar a aplicação como uma única service account compartilhada (D) não autoriza o acesso por usuário com base nos usuários individuais do Cloud Identity.

questions.question: You are evaluating developer tools to help drive Google Kubernetes Engine adoption and integration with your development environment, which includes VS Code and IntelliJ. What should you do?

options.text: Use Cloud Code to develop applications.
Use the Cloud Shell integrated Code Editor to edit code and configuration files.
Use a Cloud Notebook instance to ingest and process data and deploy models.
Use Cloud Shell to manage your infrastructure and applications from the command line.

questions.correct_text: Use Cloud Code to develop applications.
questions.explanation: Cloud Code is the Google plugin for VS Code and IntelliJ that provides integrated tooling for developing, debugging, and deploying applications to GKE directly from the IDE, making it the best fit for driving GKE adoption within those editors. The Cloud Shell Code Editor (B) is browser-based and not the local VS Code/IntelliJ environment described. A Cloud Notebook (C) targets data science and ML workflows, not general GKE application development. Cloud Shell (D) is a command-line environment, not an IDE integration that improves the developer experience in VS Code and IntelliJ.

topics.exam_domain_name: Construir e testar aplicações

questions.explanation_pt: O Cloud Code é o plugin do Google para VS Code e IntelliJ que fornece ferramentas integradas para desenvolver, depurar e implantar aplicações no GKE diretamente a partir da IDE, tornando-o a melhor opção para impulsionar a adoção do GKE nesses editores. O Cloud Shell Code Editor (B) é baseado em navegador e não é o ambiente local de VS Code/IntelliJ descrito. Um Cloud Notebook (C) é voltado para fluxos de trabalho de data science e ML, não para o desenvolvimento geral de aplicações no GKE. O Cloud Shell (D) é um ambiente de linha de comando, não uma integração de IDE que melhora a experiência do desenvolvedor no VS Code e IntelliJ.

questions.question: You are developing an ecommerce web application that uses App Engine standard environment and Memorystore for Redis. When a user logs into the app, the application caches the user's information (e.g., session, name, address, preferences), which is stored for quick retrieval during checkout.While testing your application in a browser, you get a 502 Bad Gateway error. You have determined that the application is not connecting to Memorystore. What is the reason for this error?

options.text: Your Memorystore for Redis instance was deployed without a public IP address.
You configured your Serverless VPC Access connector in a different region than your App Engine instance.
The firewall rule allowing a connection between App Engine and Memorystore was removed during an infrastructure update by the DevOps team.
You configured your application to use a Serverless VPC Access connector on a different subnet in a different availability zone than your App Engine instance.

questions.correct_text: You configured your Serverless VPC Access connector in a different region than your App Engine instance.
questions.explanation: App Engine standard connects to Memorystore over a private IP using a Serverless VPC Access connector, and that connector must be created in the same region as the App Engine application; a region mismatch breaks connectivity and produces a 502 Bad Gateway. Memorystore for Redis only exposes a private IP and is not meant to be reached via a public IP, so option A misstates how it works. There are no user-managed firewall rules required between App Engine and Memorystore through the connector, so C is incorrect. Memorystore is a regional service and the connector requirement is region-based, not zone/subnet-based as D claims.

topics.exam_domain_name: Integrar aplicações com serviços do Google Cloud

questions.explanation_pt: O App Engine standard se conecta ao Memorystore por um IP privado usando um conector Serverless VPC Access, e esse conector deve ser criado na mesma região que a aplicação do App Engine; uma incompatibilidade de região quebra a conectividade e produz um erro 502 Bad Gateway. O Memorystore for Redis expõe apenas um IP privado e não foi projetado para ser acessado por um IP público, então a opção A descreve incorretamente seu funcionamento. Não são necessárias regras de firewall gerenciadas pelo usuário entre o App Engine e o Memorystore através do conector, então C está incorreta. O Memorystore é um serviço regional e o requisito do conector é baseado em região, não em zona/sub-rede como afirma a opção D.

questions.question: Your team develops services that run on Google Cloud. You need to build a data processing service and will use Cloud Functions. The data to be processed by the function is sensitive. You need to ensure that invocations can only happen from authorized services and follow Google-recommended best practices for securing functions. What should you do?

options.text: Enable Identity-Aware Proxy in your project. Secure function access using its permissions.
Create a service account with the Cloud Functions Viewer role. Use that service account to invoke the function.
Create a service account with the Cloud Functions Invoker role. Use that service account to invoke the function.
Create an OAuth 2.0 client ID for your calling service in the same project as the function you want to secure. Use those credentials to invoke the function.

questions.correct_text: Create a service account with the Cloud Functions Invoker role. Use that service account to invoke the function.
questions.explanation: The Google-recommended way to restrict Cloud Functions invocation to authorized callers is service-to-service authentication: create a service account, grant it the Cloud Functions Invoker (roles/cloudfunctions.invoker) role, and have the calling service authenticate as that account with an identity token. The Cloud Functions Viewer role (B) only grants read access to function metadata and cannot invoke the function. Identity-Aware Proxy (A) secures user-facing HTTPS apps behind a load balancer and is not the standard mechanism for service-to-service function invocation. Manually creating an OAuth 2.0 client ID (D) is unnecessary and not the recommended pattern, since invocation authorization is controlled through IAM roles on a service account.

topics.exam_domain_name: Projetar apps cloud-native escaláveis, seguras e confiáveis

questions.explanation_pt: A forma recomendada pelo Google para restringir a invocação de Cloud Functions a chamadores autorizados é a autenticação service-to-service: crie uma service account, conceda a ela o papel Cloud Functions Invoker (roles/cloudfunctions.invoker) e faça com que o serviço chamador se autentique como essa conta usando um identity token. O papel Cloud Functions Viewer (B) concede apenas acesso de leitura aos metadados da função e não pode invocá-la. O Identity-Aware Proxy (A) protege aplicações HTTPS voltadas ao usuário por trás de um load balancer e não é o mecanismo padrão para invocação service-to-service de funções. Criar manualmente um OAuth 2.0 client ID (D) é desnecessário e não é o padrão recomendado, já que a autorização de invocação é controlada por papéis IAM em uma service account.

questions.question: You are deploying your applications on Compute Engine. One of your Compute Engine instances failed to launch. What should you do? (Choose two.)

options.text: Determine whether your file system is corrupted.
Access Compute Engine as a different SSH user.
Troubleshoot firewall rules or routes on an instance.
Check whether your instance boot disk is completely full.
Check whether network traffic to or from your instance is being dropped.

questions.correct_text: Determine whether your file system is corrupted. | Check whether your instance boot disk is completely full.
questions.explanation: When a Compute Engine instance fails to launch, the most common boot-time causes are a corrupted file system or a boot disk that is completely full, both of which prevent the OS from starting successfully; you can inspect these via the serial console output and by mounting the disk. Therefore checking for file system corruption (A) and a full boot disk (D) are the correct troubleshooting steps for a launch failure. SSH user changes (B), firewall rules/routes (C), and dropped network traffic (E) are all connectivity-related issues that only matter once the instance has already booted and is running, so they do not explain a failure to launch.

topics.exam_domain_name: Configurar aplicações cloud-native para deployment

questions.explanation_pt: Quando uma instância do Compute Engine falha ao iniciar, as causas mais comuns no momento do boot são um sistema de arquivos corrompido ou um boot disk completamente cheio, ambos os quais impedem o SO de iniciar com sucesso; você pode inspecionar isso através da saída do serial console e montando o disco. Portanto, verificar a corrupção do sistema de arquivos (A) e um boot disk cheio (D) são os passos corretos de troubleshooting para uma falha de inicialização. Alterações de usuário SSH (B), firewall rules/routes (C) e tráfego de rede descartado (E) são todos problemas relacionados à conectividade que só importam depois que a instância já passou pelo boot e está em execução, então não explicam uma falha ao iniciar.

questions.question: Your web application is deployed to the corporate intranet. You need to migrate the web application to Google Cloud. The web application must be available only to company employees and accessible to employees as they travel. You need to ensure the security and accessibility of the web application while minimizing application changes. What should you do?

options.text: Configure the application to check authentication credentials for each HTTP(S) request to the application.
Configure Identity-Aware Proxy to allow employees to access the application through its public IP address.

Configure a Compute Engine instance that requests users to log in to their corporate account. Change the web application DNS to point to the proxy Compute Engine instance. After authenticating, the Compute Engine instance forwards requests to and from the web application.

Configure a Compute Engine instance that requests users to log in to their corporate account. Change the web application DNS to point to the proxy Compute Engine instance. After authenticating, the Compute Engine issues an HTTP redirect to a public IP address hosting the web application.

questions.correct_text: Configure Identity-Aware Proxy to allow employees to access the application through its public IP address.
questions.explanation: Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) provides a central authorization layer for applications accessed over HTTPS, enforcing Google identity-based access control without requiring code changes to the application itself. By placing the app behind a load balancer with IAP enabled, only authenticated company employees can reach it from anywhere they travel, satisfying both security and accessibility while minimizing application changes (B). Building authentication into the application code (A) requires significant changes. The custom proxy Compute Engine approaches (C and D) reinvent functionality IAP already provides, are harder to secure and maintain, and option D's HTTP redirect to a public IP would bypass authentication entirely, exposing the app.

topics.exam_domain_name: Projetar apps cloud-native escaláveis, seguras e confiáveis

questions.explanation_pt: O Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) fornece uma camada central de autorização para aplicações acessadas via HTTPS, impondo controle de acesso baseado em identidade Google sem exigir mudanças no código da própria aplicação. Ao colocar a app por trás de um load balancer com o IAP habilitado, apenas funcionários autenticados da empresa conseguem acessá-la de qualquer lugar para onde viajem, atendendo tanto à segurança quanto à acessibilidade ao mesmo tempo em que minimiza alterações na aplicação (B). Embutir autenticação no código da aplicação (A) exige mudanças significativas. As abordagens de proxy customizado no Compute Engine (C e D) reinventam funcionalidades que o IAP já fornece, são mais difíceis de proteger e manter, e o redirecionamento HTTP para um IP público da opção D ignoraria completamente a autenticação, expondo a app.

questions.question: You have an application that uses an HTTP Cloud Function to process user activity from both desktop browser and mobile application clients. This function will serve as the endpoint for all metric submissions using HTTP POST.Due to legacy restrictions, the function must be mapped to a domain that is separate from the domain requested by users on web or mobile sessions. The domain for the Cloud Function is https://fn.example.com. Desktop and mobile clients use the domain https://www.example.com. You need to add a header to the function'sHTTP response so that only those browser and mobile sessions can submit metrics to the Cloud Function. Which response header should you add?

options.text: Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://*.example.com
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://fn.example.com
Access-Control-Allow-origin: https://www.example.com

questions.correct_text: Access-Control-Allow-origin: https://www.example.com
questions.explanation: This is a cross-origin resource sharing (CORS) scenario: the function on fn.example.com must accept requests originating from the www.example.com domain. The Access-Control-Allow-Origin header must specify the exact origin allowed to call the resource, so https://www.example.com is correct (D). A wildcard value (A) would allow any origin to submit metrics, defeating the requirement to restrict to browser/mobile sessions. The CORS spec does not support wildcard subdomain patterns like https://*.example.com (B), so that value is invalid. Setting the header to https://fn.example.com (C) names the function's own domain rather than the requesting origin, which would not authorize the www client.

topics.exam_domain_name: Integrar aplicações com serviços do Google Cloud

questions.explanation_pt: Este é um cenário de cross-origin resource sharing (CORS): a função em fn.example.com deve aceitar requisições originadas do domínio www.example.com. O header Access-Control-Allow-Origin deve especificar a origem exata autorizada a chamar o recurso, então https://www.example.com é o correto (D). Um valor curinga (A) permitiria que qualquer origem enviasse métricas, anulando o requisito de restringir às sessões de navegador/mobile. A especificação CORS não suporta padrões de subdomínio com curinga como https://*.example.com (B), então esse valor é inválido. Definir o header como https://fn.example.com (C) nomeia o próprio domínio da função em vez da origem que faz a requisição, o que não autorizaria o cliente www.

questions.question: You have an HTTP Cloud Function that is called via POST. Each submission's request body has a flat, unnested JSON structure containing numeric and text data. After the Cloud Function completes, the collected data should be immediately available for ongoing and complex analytics by many users in parallel. How should you persist the submissions?

options.text: Directly persist each POST request's JSON data into Datastore.
Transform the POST request's JSON data, and stream it into BigQuery.
Transform the POST request's JSON data, and store it in a regional Cloud SQL cluster.
Persist each POST request's JSON data as an individual file within Cloud Storage, with the file name containing the request identifier.

questions.correct_text: Transform the POST request's JSON data, and stream it into BigQuery.
questions.explanation: The data is flat, structured JSON with numeric and text fields that must be immediately queryable for ongoing and complex analytics by many concurrent users, which is exactly the workload BigQuery is designed for; streaming inserts make the data available for query within seconds (B). Datastore/Firestore (A) is a NoSQL document store optimized for transactional lookups, not complex analytical queries at scale. Cloud SQL (C) is a relational OLTP database that does not scale well for large-scale parallel analytics. Storing each request as an individual Cloud Storage file (D) makes immediate, complex querying impractical since you would need to parse and aggregate many objects.

topics.exam_domain_name: Integrar aplicações com serviços do Google Cloud

questions.explanation_pt: Os dados são JSON plano e estruturado com campos numéricos e de texto que precisam estar imediatamente consultáveis para analytics contínuos e complexos por muitos usuários concorrentes, que é exatamente o tipo de carga de trabalho para o qual o BigQuery foi projetado; streaming inserts tornam os dados disponíveis para consulta em segundos (B). O Datastore/Firestore (A) é um document store NoSQL otimizado para lookups transacionais, não para consultas analíticas complexas em escala. O Cloud SQL (C) é um banco de dados relacional OLTP que não escala bem para analytics paralelos em larga escala. Armazenar cada requisição como um arquivo individual no Cloud Storage (D) torna a consulta imediata e complexa impraticável, já que seria necessário fazer parse e agregar muitos objetos.

questions.question: Your security team is auditing all deployed applications running in Google Kubernetes Engine. After completing the audit, your team discovers that some of the applications send traffic within the cluster in clear text. You need to ensure that all application traffic is encrypted as quickly as possible while minimizing changes to your applications and maintaining support from Google. What should you do?

options.text: Use Network Policies to block traffic between applications.
Install Istio, enable proxy injection on your application namespace, and then enable mTLS.
Define Trusted Network ranges within the application, and configure the applications to allow traffic only from those networks.
Use an automated process to request SSL Certificates for your applications from Let's Encrypt and add them to your applications.

questions.correct_text: Install Istio, enable proxy injection on your application namespace, and then enable mTLS.
questions.explanation: Installing Istio (Anthos Service Mesh), enabling sidecar proxy injection on the application namespace, and turning on mutual TLS (mTLS) transparently encrypts all service-to-service traffic in the cluster without modifying application code, and it is a Google-supported solution (B). Network Policies (A) control which pods can communicate but do not encrypt traffic. Trusted Network ranges (C) restrict source IPs but leave traffic in clear text and require application changes. Manually requesting Let's Encrypt certificates and adding them to each application (D) requires significant per-application changes and ongoing certificate management, and is slower and harder to maintain than a service mesh with automatic mTLS.

topics.exam_domain_name: Projetar apps cloud-native escaláveis, seguras e confiáveis

questions.explanation_pt: Instalar o Istio (Anthos Service Mesh), habilitar a injeção de sidecar proxy no namespace da aplicação e ativar o mutual TLS (mTLS) criptografa de forma transparente todo o tráfego service-to-service no cluster sem modificar o código da aplicação, além de ser uma solução com suporte do Google (B). As Network Policies (A) controlam quais pods podem se comunicar, mas não criptografam o tráfego. Os Trusted Network ranges (C) restringem os IPs de origem, mas deixam o tráfego em texto claro e exigem alterações na aplicação. Solicitar manualmente certificados Let's Encrypt e adicioná-los a cada aplicação (D) requer alterações significativas por aplicação e gerenciamento contínuo de certificados, sendo mais lento e mais difícil de manter do que um service mesh com mTLS automático.

questions.question: You migrated some of your applications to Google Cloud. You are using a legacy monitoring platform deployed on-premises for both on-premises and cloud- deployed applications. You discover that your notification system is responding slowly to time-critical problems in the cloud applications. What should you do?

options.text: Replace your monitoring platform with Cloud Monitoring.
Install the Cloud Monitoring agent on your Compute Engine instances.
Migrate some traffic back to your old platform. Perform A/B testing on the two platforms concurrently.
Use Cloud Logging and Cloud Monitoring to capture logs, monitor, and send alerts. Send them to your existing platform.

questions.correct_text: Use Cloud Logging and Cloud Monitoring to capture logs, monitor, and send alerts. Send them to your existing platform.
questions.explanation: Cloud Logging and Cloud Monitoring run natively within Google Cloud, so they can capture logs, monitor metrics, and trigger alerts on cloud-deployed applications with minimal latency, and the resulting alerts can be forwarded to your existing on-premises platform via notification channels or webhooks. This solves the slow notification problem for time-critical cloud issues while preserving your investment in the legacy platform for on-premises apps. Option A (fully replacing the platform) is unnecessarily disruptive and ignores the on-premises systems still served by the legacy tool. Option B only installs an agent for metrics collection but does not address the alerting/notification latency or integrate with the existing platform. Option C (A/B testing monitoring platforms by shifting traffic) is not a valid way to fix notification speed and adds operational complexity.

topics.exam_domain_name: Integrar aplicações com serviços do Google Cloud

questions.explanation_pt: O Cloud Logging e o Cloud Monitoring rodam nativamente dentro do Google Cloud, de modo que podem capturar logs, monitorar métricas e disparar alertas em aplicações implantadas na nuvem com latência mínima, e os alertas resultantes podem ser encaminhados para sua plataforma on-premises existente por meio de notification channels ou webhooks. Isso resolve o problema de notificações lentas para questões críticas de tempo na nuvem, ao mesmo tempo em que preserva seu investimento na plataforma legada para aplicações on-premises. A opção A (substituir completamente a plataforma) é desnecessariamente disruptiva e ignora os sistemas on-premises ainda atendidos pela ferramenta legada. A opção B apenas instala um agent para coleta de métricas, mas não resolve a latência de alerta/notificação nem se integra à plataforma existente. A opção C (testes A/B de plataformas de monitoramento desviando tráfego) não é uma forma válida de corrigir a velocidade das notificações e adiciona complexidade operacional.

questions.question: You recently deployed your application in Google Kubernetes Engine, and now need to release a new version of your application. You need the ability to instantly roll back to the previous version in case there are issues with the new version. Which deployment model should you use?

options.text: Perform a rolling deployment, and test your new application after the deployment is complete.
Perform A/B testing, and test your application periodically after the new tests are implemented.
Perform a blue/green deployment, and test your new application after the deployment is. complete.
Perform a canary deployment, and test your new application periodically after the new version is deployed.

questions.correct_text: Perform a blue/green deployment, and test your new application after the deployment is. complete.
questions.explanation: A blue/green deployment runs two complete environments side by side: the current (blue) version keeps serving traffic while the new (green) version is fully deployed and tested, then traffic is switched over. If issues appear, you can instantly roll back by routing traffic back to the still-running blue environment, satisfying the requirement for immediate rollback. A rolling deployment (A) gradually replaces pods, so rollback requires redeploying the old version and is not instantaneous. Canary (D) exposes the new version to a subset of users incrementally and also lacks an instant full rollback switch. A/B testing (B) is for comparing feature variants for business metrics, not for safe release with instant rollback.

topics.exam_domain_name: Configurar aplicações cloud-native para deployment

questions.explanation_pt: Um deployment blue/green executa dois ambientes completos lado a lado: a versão atual (blue) continua atendendo o tráfego enquanto a nova versão (green) é totalmente implantada e testada, e então o tráfego é redirecionado. Se surgirem problemas, é possível fazer rollback instantaneamente roteando o tráfego de volta para o ambiente blue ainda em execução, atendendo ao requisito de rollback imediato. Um rolling deployment (A) substitui os pods gradualmente, de modo que o rollback exige reimplantar a versão antiga e não é instantâneo. O canary (D) expõe a nova versão a um subconjunto de usuários de forma incremental e também não oferece uma troca de rollback completo instantâneo. O teste A/B (B) serve para comparar variantes de funcionalidades por métricas de negócio, não para lançamento seguro com rollback instantâneo.

questions.question: You developed a JavaScript web application that needs to access Google Drive's API and obtain permission from users to store files in their Google Drives. You need to select an authorization approach for your application. What should you do?

options.text: Create an API key.
Create a SAML token.
Create a service account.
Create an OAuth Client ID.

questions.correct_text: Create an OAuth Client ID.
questions.explanation: Accessing user-owned data such as files in a user's Google Drive requires the user's consent, which is exactly what OAuth 2.0 provides through a consent flow; creating an OAuth Client ID lets your JavaScript application request authorization and act on behalf of the signed-in user. An API key (A) only identifies the calling project and cannot authorize access to private user data or obtain user consent. A service account (C) represents an application identity, not the end user, so it cannot store files in an arbitrary user's personal Drive without domain-wide delegation, which is not the right approach here. A SAML token (B) is used for enterprise SSO/federation, not for delegated authorization to Google APIs.

topics.exam_domain_name: Integrar aplicações com serviços do Google Cloud

questions.explanation_pt: Acessar dados pertencentes ao usuário, como arquivos no Google Drive de um usuário, requer o consentimento do usuário, que é exatamente o que o OAuth 2.0 fornece por meio de um fluxo de consentimento; criar um OAuth Client ID permite que sua aplicação JavaScript solicite autorização e atue em nome do usuário autenticado. Uma API key (A) apenas identifica o projeto que faz a chamada e não pode autorizar acesso a dados privados do usuário nem obter o consentimento dele. Uma service account (C) representa a identidade de uma aplicação, não a do usuário final, então ela não pode armazenar arquivos no Drive pessoal de um usuário arbitrário sem domain-wide delegation, o que não é a abordagem correta aqui. Um token SAML (B) é usado para SSO/federação corporativa, não para autorização delegada às APIs do Google.

questions.question: You manage an ecommerce application that processes purchases from customers who can subsequently cancel or change those purchases. You discover that order volumes are highly variable and the backend order-processing system can only process one request at a time. You want to ensure seamless performance for customers regardless of usage volume. It is crucial that customers' order update requests are performed in the sequence in which they were generated. What should you do?

options.text: Send the purchase and change requests over WebSockets to the backend.
Send the purchase and change requests as REST requests to the backend.
Use a Pub/Sub subscriber in pull mode and use a data store to manage ordering.
Use a Pub/Sub subscriber in push mode and use a data store to manage ordering.

questions.correct_text: Use a Pub/Sub subscriber in pull mode and use a data store to manage ordering.
questions.explanation: Pub/Sub decouples the variable, bursty incoming request volume from the single-threaded backend, buffering messages so the backend can process them at its own pace without dropping requests. Using a pull subscriber lets the backend control its consumption rate (processing one at a time), and combining it with a data store to track and enforce ordering ensures each customer's update requests are applied in the sequence they were generated, since Pub/Sub does not guarantee strict global ordering by default without ordering keys. Push mode (D) would have Pub/Sub deliver messages to the backend at its own rate, which can overwhelm a single-threaded processor and offers less control over pacing. Sending requests directly over WebSockets (A) or REST (B) provides no buffering, so spikes would overload the backend and there is no mechanism to smooth load or preserve sequencing.

topics.exam_domain_name: Projetar apps cloud-native escaláveis, seguras e confiáveis

questions.explanation_pt: O Pub/Sub desacopla o volume variável e de picos das requisições recebidas do backend single-threaded, fazendo buffer das mensagens para que o backend possa processá-las em seu próprio ritmo sem descartar requisições. Usar um pull subscriber permite que o backend controle sua taxa de consumo (processando uma de cada vez), e combiná-lo com um data store para rastrear e impor a ordenação garante que as requisições de atualização de cada cliente sejam aplicadas na sequência em que foram geradas, já que o Pub/Sub não garante ordenação global estrita por padrão sem ordering keys. O modo push (D) faria o Pub/Sub entregar mensagens ao backend em seu próprio ritmo, o que pode sobrecarregar um processador single-threaded e oferece menos controle sobre o ritmo. Enviar requisições diretamente por WebSockets (A) ou REST (B) não fornece buffer, então os picos sobrecarregariam o backend e não haveria mecanismo para suavizar a carga ou preservar a sequência.

questions.question: Your company needs a database solution that stores customer purchase history and meets the following requirements:✑ Customers can query their purchase immediately after submission.✑ Purchases can be sorted on a variety of fields.✑ Distinct record formats can be stored at the same time.Which storage option satisfies these requirements?

options.text: Firestore in Native mode
Cloud Storage using an object read
Cloud SQL using a SQL SELECT statement
Firestore in Datastore mode using a global query

questions.correct_text: Firestore in Native mode
questions.explanation: Firestore in Native mode is a document database that offers strong consistency (so customers can query a purchase immediately after submission), supports indexing and sorting/filtering on multiple fields, and stores schema-flexible documents, allowing distinct record formats side by side. Cloud SQL (C) enforces a fixed relational schema, so storing distinct record formats simultaneously is awkward and violates the requirement. Cloud Storage (B) is object storage with no query, sort, or structured field capabilities. Firestore in Datastore mode (D) is intended for server-side workloads and does not support the real-time client query experience and feature set the way Native mode does, making Native mode the best fit for this customer-facing application.

topics.exam_domain_name: Projetar apps cloud-native escaláveis, seguras e confiáveis

questions.explanation_pt: O Firestore in Native mode é um banco de dados de documentos que oferece consistência forte (portanto os clientes podem consultar uma compra imediatamente após o envio), suporta indexação e ordenação/filtragem em múltiplos campos e armazena documentos com schema flexível, permitindo formatos de registro distintos lado a lado. O Cloud SQL (C) impõe um schema relacional fixo, então armazenar formatos de registro distintos simultaneamente é trabalhoso e viola o requisito. O Cloud Storage (B) é armazenamento de objetos sem capacidade de consulta, ordenação ou campos estruturados. O Firestore in Datastore mode (D) é destinado a cargas de trabalho do lado do servidor e não suporta a experiência de consulta em tempo real do cliente nem o conjunto de recursos da forma que o Native mode suporta, tornando o Native mode a melhor escolha para esta aplicação voltada ao cliente.

questions.question: You recently developed a new service on Cloud Run. The new service authenticates using a custom service and then writes transactional information to a CloudSpanner database. You need to verify that your application can support up to 5,000 read and 1,000 write transactions per second while identifying any bottlenecks that occur. Your test infrastructure must be able to autoscale. What should you do?

options.text: Build a test harness to generate requests and deploy it to Cloud Run. Analyze the VPC Flow Logs using Cloud Logging.
Create a Google Kubernetes Engine cluster running the Locust or JMeter images to dynamically generate load tests. Analyze the results using Cloud Trace.
Create a Cloud Task to generate a test load. Use Cloud Scheduler to run 60,000 Cloud Task transactions per minute for 10 minutes. Analyze the results using Cloud Monitoring.
Create a Compute Engine instance that uses a LAMP stack image from the Marketplace, and use Apache Bench to generate load tests against the service. Analyze the results using Cloud Trace.

questions.correct_text: Create a Google Kubernetes Engine cluster running the Locust or JMeter images to dynamically generate load tests. Analyze the results using Cloud Trace.
questions.explanation: Running Locust or JMeter on a GKE cluster lets you generate large, distributed, autoscaling load (thousands of read/write transactions per second) against the Cloud Run service, and Cloud Trace surfaces latency breakdowns to identify bottlenecks across the request path including the Spanner writes. Option A is wrong because deploying a test harness to Cloud Run does not give you a proper load-testing framework, and VPC Flow Logs only show network-level traffic, not application latency or bottlenecks. Option C misuses Cloud Tasks/Cloud Scheduler, which are for asynchronous job dispatch and cron scheduling rather than sustained, measurable load generation, and it cannot reliably sustain precise per-second transaction rates. Option D relies on a single Compute Engine VM with Apache Bench, which neither autoscales nor reliably produces 5,000+ TPS, failing the autoscaling requirement.

questions.explanation_pt: Executar o Locust ou o JMeter em um cluster GKE permite gerar carga grande, distribuída e com autoscaling (milhares de transações de leitura/escrita por segundo) contra o serviço do Cloud Run, e o Cloud Trace mostra a divisão de latência para identificar gargalos ao longo do caminho da requisição, incluindo as escritas no Spanner. A opção A está errada porque implantar um harness de teste no Cloud Run não fornece um framework adequado de teste de carga, e os VPC Flow Logs mostram apenas tráfego no nível de rede, não a latência ou os gargalos da aplicação. A opção C usa indevidamente o Cloud Tasks/Cloud Scheduler, que servem para despacho assíncrono de jobs e agendamento de cron, em vez de geração de carga sustentada e mensurável, e não consegue sustentar de forma confiável taxas precisas de transações por segundo. A opção D depende de uma única VM do Compute Engine com o Apache Bench, que não faz autoscaling nem produz de forma confiável mais de 5.000 TPS, falhando no requisito de autoscaling.

questions.question: You are using Cloud Build for your CI/CD pipeline to complete several tasks, including copying certain files to Compute Engine virtual machines. Your pipeline requires a flat file that is generated in one builder in the pipeline to be accessible by subsequent builders in the same pipeline. How should you store the file so that all the builders in the pipeline can access it?

options.text: Store and retrieve the file contents using Compute Engine instance metadata.
Output the file contents to a file in /workspace. Read from the same /workspace file in the subsequent build step.
Use gsutil to output the file contents to a Cloud Storage object. Read from the same object in the subsequent build step.
Add a build argument that runs an HTTP POST via curl to a separate web server to persist the value in one builder. Use an HTTP GET via curl from the subsequent build step to read the value.

questions.correct_text: Output the file contents to a file in /workspace. Read from the same /workspace file in the subsequent build step.
questions.explanation: In Cloud Build, the /workspace directory is a persistent volume that is mounted into every build step in the same pipeline, so a file written to /workspace by one builder is automatically available to all subsequent builders. Option C using Cloud Storage would work but adds unnecessary latency, cost, and complexity for sharing a simple intermediate file within a single build. Option A misuses Compute Engine instance metadata, which is for VM configuration and is not a mechanism for passing files between build steps. Option D, persisting the value via curl to a separate web server, is fragile, requires extra infrastructure, and introduces security and reliability concerns when a built-in shared volume already exists.

topics.exam_domain_name: Construir e testar aplicações

questions.explanation_pt: No Cloud Build, o diretório /workspace é um volume persistente que é montado em cada etapa de build no mesmo pipeline, então um arquivo escrito em /workspace por um builder fica automaticamente disponível para todos os builders subsequentes. A opção C, usando o Cloud Storage, funcionaria, mas adiciona latência, custo e complexidade desnecessários para compartilhar um simples arquivo intermediário dentro de um único build. A opção A usa indevidamente o metadata de instância do Compute Engine, que serve para configuração de VMs e não é um mecanismo para passar arquivos entre etapas de build. A opção D, persistir o valor via curl para um servidor web separado, é frágil, requer infraestrutura extra e introduz preocupações de segurança e confiabilidade quando já existe um volume compartilhado embutido.

questions.question: Your company’s development teams want to use various open source operating systems in their Docker builds. When images are created in published containers in your company’s environment, you need to scan them for Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs). The scanning process must not impact software development agility. You want to use managed services where possible. What should you do?

options.text: Enable the Vulnerability scanning setting in the Container Registry.
Create a Cloud Function that is triggered on a code check-in and scan the code for CVEs.
Disallow the use of non-commercially supported base images in your development environment.
Use Cloud Monitoring to review the output of Cloud Build to determine whether a vulnerable version has been used.

questions.correct_text: Enable the Vulnerability scanning setting in the Container Registry.
questions.explanation: Enabling the Vulnerability scanning (Container Analysis) setting in Container Registry is a fully managed feature that automatically scans pushed images for CVEs across many open source operating systems without adding manual steps, so it does not slow down development agility. Option B scans source code on check-in via a Cloud Function, but CVE scanning targets the built container layers and OS packages, not raw source, and building this is not a managed service. Option C, disallowing non-commercially supported base images, restricts the teams' freedom to use open source operating systems, which is contrary to the requirement. Option D, parsing Cloud Build output in Cloud Monitoring, is an unreliable, manual approach that does not perform actual vulnerability scanning of published images.
