Com ordering keys configuradas, o emulador se comporta como o serviço real, de modo que você pode verificar que o subscriber processa as mensagens em ordem. Um framework de mocking apenas simula as expectativas do seu próprio código e não reproduziria fielmente a entrega e a semântica de ordenação do Pub/Sub. Criar um topic e uma subscription por testador usa recursos de nuvem reais (cobráveis) e adiciona sobrecarga de gerenciamento, e os filtros de subscription selecionam mensagens por atributo, em vez de garantir ou testar a ordenação.

questions.question: You have an application deployed in Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) that reads and processes Pub/Sub messages. Each Pod handles a fixed number of messages per minute. The rate at which messages are published to the Pub/Sub topic varies considerably throughout the day and week, including occasional large batches of messages published at a single moment.You want to scale your GKE Deployment to be able to process messages in a timely manner. What GKE feature should you use to automatically adapt your workload?

options.text: Vertical Pod Autoscaler in Auto mode
Vertical Pod Autoscaler in Recommendation mode
Horizontal Pod Autoscaler based on an external metric
Horizontal Pod Autoscaler based on resources utilization

questions.correct_text: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler based on an external metric
questions.explanation: Because each Pod processes a fixed number of messages per minute and the workload should scale with the number of pending messages, you need to add or remove Pods based on the Pub/Sub backlog. The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler can scale on an external metric such as the Pub/Sub subscription's num_undelivered_messages, which directly reflects demand and handles bursty traffic. HPA based on resource utilization (CPU/memory) does not track the message backlog and would react poorly to sudden batches. The Vertical Pod Autoscaler only resizes a Pod's CPU/memory requests rather than changing replica count, so it cannot increase throughput by adding Pods, and recommendation mode merely suggests values without applying them.

topics.exam_domain_name: Projetar apps cloud-native escaláveis, seguras e confiáveis

questions.explanation_pt: Como cada Pod processa um número fixo de mensagens por minuto e a carga de trabalho deve escalar com o número de mensagens pendentes, você precisa adicionar ou remover Pods com base no backlog do Pub/Sub. O Horizontal Pod Autoscaler pode escalar com base em uma métrica externa, como o num_undelivered_messages da subscription do Pub/Sub, que reflete diretamente a demanda e lida com tráfego em rajadas. O HPA baseado em utilização de recursos (CPU/memória) não acompanha o backlog de mensagens e reagiria mal a lotes repentinos. O Vertical Pod Autoscaler apenas redimensiona as solicitações de CPU/memória de um Pod, em vez de alterar a contagem de réplicas, então não pode aumentar a throughput adicionando Pods, e o modo de recomendação apenas sugere valores sem aplicá-los.

questions.question: You are using Cloud Run to host a web application. You need to securely obtain the application project ID and region where the application is running and display this information to users. You want to use the most performant approach. What should you do?

options.text: Use HTTP requests to query the available metadata server at the http://metadata.google.internal/ endpoint with the Metadata-Flavor: Google header.

In the Google Cloud console, navigate to the Project Dashboard and gather configuration details. Navigate to the Cloud Run “Variables & Secrets” tab, and add the desired environment variables in Key:Value format.
In the Google Cloud console, navigate to the Project Dashboard and gather configuration details. Write the application configuration information to Cloud Run's in-memory container filesystem.
Make an API call to the Cloud Asset Inventory API from the application and format the request to include instance metadata.

questions.correct_text: Use HTTP requests to query the available metadata server at the http://metadata.google.internal/ endpoint with the Metadata-Flavor: Google header.
questions.explanation: On Cloud Run the metadata server at http://metadata.google.internal/ exposes runtime details such as the project ID and region, and querying it with the required Metadata-Flavor: Google header is the most performant and secure way to obtain this information at runtime without hardcoding it. Manually copying values into environment variables or the in-memory filesystem is error-prone and not portable across projects or regions, requiring redeployment when values change. Calling the Cloud Asset Inventory API adds latency, extra permissions, and unnecessary complexity for data the metadata server already provides locally.

questions.question: You need to deploy resources from your laptop to Google Cloud using Terraform. Resources in your Google Cloud environment must be created using a service account. Your Cloud Identity has the roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator Identity and Access Management (IAM) role and the necessary permissions to deploy the resources using Terraform. You want to set up your development environment to deploy the desired resources following Google-recommended best practices. What should you do?

options.text: 1. Download the service account’s key file in JSON format, and store it locally on your laptop.2. Set the GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS environment variable to the path of your downloaded key file.

1. Run the following command from a command line: gcloud config set auth/impersonate_service_account [email protected].2. Set the GOOGLE_OAUTH_ACCESS_TOKEN environment variable to the value that is returned by the gcloud auth print-access-token command.
1. Run the following command from a command line: gcloud auth application-default login.2. In the browser window that opens, authenticate using your personal credentials.

1. Store the service account's key file in JSON format in Hashicorp Vault.2. Integrate Terraform with Vault to retrieve the key file dynamically, and authenticate to Vault using a short-lived access token.

questions.correct_text: 1. Run the following command from a command line: gcloud config set auth/impersonate_service_account [email protected].2. Set the GOOGLE_OAUTH_ACCESS_TOKEN environment variable to the value that is returned by the gcloud auth print-access-token command.
questions.explanation: Service account impersonation is the Google-recommended best practice because it avoids creating and storing long-lived service account key files, which are a security risk. Since your user identity holds roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator, you can have gcloud impersonate the service account and Terraform can authenticate using the resulting short-lived access token (via GOOGLE_OAUTH_ACCESS_TOKEN or the impersonate_service_account setting). Downloading a JSON key file (option A) is explicitly discouraged because the key can be leaked and never expires. Authenticating with personal credentials via application-default login (option C) does not deploy as the required service account, and storing the key in Vault (option D) still relies on a persistent exportable key rather than eliminating it.

topics.exam_domain_name: Configurar aplicações cloud-native para deployment

questions.explanation_pt: A impersonation de service account é a prática recomendada pelo Google porque evita criar e armazenar arquivos de chave de service account de longa duração, que representam um risco de segurança. Como sua identidade de usuário possui a role roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator, você pode fazer o gcloud impersonar a service account e o Terraform pode se autenticar usando o token de acesso de curta duração resultante (via GOOGLE_OAUTH_ACCESS_TOKEN ou a configuração impersonate_service_account). Baixar um arquivo de chave JSON (opção A) é explicitamente desencorajado porque a chave pode vazar e nunca expira. Autenticar com credenciais pessoais via application-default login (opção C) não implanta como a service account exigida, e armazenar a chave no Vault (opção D) ainda depende de uma chave exportável persistente, em vez de eliminá-la.

questions.question: Your company uses Cloud Logging to manage large volumes of log data. You need to build a real-time log analysis architecture that pushes logs to a third-party application for processing. What should you do?

options.text: Create a Cloud Logging log export to Pub/Sub.
Create a Cloud Logging log export to BigQuery.
Create a Cloud Logging log export to Cloud Storage.
Create a Cloud Function to read Cloud Logging log entries and send them to the third-party application.

questions.correct_text: Create a Cloud Logging log export to Pub/Sub.
questions.explanation: For real-time streaming of logs to an external system, a Cloud Logging sink (log export) to Pub/Sub is the correct choice because Pub/Sub delivers log entries with low latency and lets a third-party application subscribe and process them as they arrive. Exporting to BigQuery is suited to analytical queries on stored logs, not real-time push to an external app, and exporting to Cloud Storage produces batched files written periodically, which is not real-time. Writing a Cloud Function to poll Cloud Logging is custom, less reliable, and Cloud Logging is not designed to be read in a push, real-time manner that way; the Pub/Sub sink is the native, scalable solution.

topics.exam_domain_name: Integrar aplicações com serviços do Google Cloud

questions.explanation_pt: Para streaming em tempo real de logs para um sistema externo, um sink do Cloud Logging (exportação de logs) para o Pub/Sub é a escolha correta, porque o Pub/Sub entrega entradas de log com baixa latência e permite que um aplicativo de terceiros faça a assinatura e os processe à medida que chegam. Exportar para o BigQuery é adequado para consultas analíticas em logs armazenados, não para envio em tempo real a um app externo, e exportar para o Cloud Storage produz arquivos em lote gravados periodicamente, o que não é tempo real. Escrever uma Cloud Function para fazer polling do Cloud Logging é uma solução personalizada, menos confiável, e o Cloud Logging não foi projetado para ser lido dessa forma por push em tempo real; o sink do Pub/Sub é a solução nativa e escalável.

questions.question: You are developing a new public-facing application that needs to retrieve specific properties in the metadata of users’ objects in their respective Cloud Storage buckets. Due to privacy and data residency requirements, you must retrieve only the metadata and not the object data. You want to maximize the performance of the retrieval process. How should you retrieve the metadata?

options.text: Use the patch method.
Use the compose method.
Use the copy method.
Use the fields request parameter.

questions.correct_text: Use the fields request parameter.
questions.explanation: The Cloud Storage JSON API supports a partial response mechanism via the fields request parameter, which lets you request only specific properties (such as metadata fields) and excludes the object payload, minimizing the amount of data transferred and maximizing retrieval performance. This satisfies the requirement to retrieve only metadata without downloading object data. The patch method (A) is used to update an object's metadata, not to read it efficiently. The compose method (B) concatenates multiple objects into one, and the copy method (C) duplicates objects; neither is for selectively reading metadata.

topics.exam_domain_name: Integrar aplicações com serviços do Google Cloud

questions.explanation_pt: A JSON API do Cloud Storage oferece suporte a um mecanismo de resposta parcial por meio do parâmetro de requisição fields, que permite solicitar apenas propriedades específicas (como campos de metadados) e exclui o payload do objeto, minimizando a quantidade de dados transferidos e maximizando o desempenho da recuperação. Isso atende ao requisito de recuperar apenas os metadados sem baixar os dados do objeto. O método patch (A) é usado para atualizar os metadados de um objeto, não para lê-los de forma eficiente. O método compose (B) concatena vários objetos em um só, e o método copy (C) duplica objetos; nenhum deles serve para ler metadados seletivamente.

questions.question: You are deploying a microservices application to Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) that will broadcast livestreams. You expect unpredictable traffic patterns and large variations in the number of concurrent users. Your application must meet the following requirements:• Scales automatically during popular events and maintains high availability• Is resilient in the event of hardware failuresHow should you configure the deployment parameters? (Choose two.)

options.text: Distribute your workload evenly using a multi-zonal node pool.
Distribute your workload evenly using multiple zonal node pools.
Use cluster autoscaler to resize the number of nodes in the node pool, and use a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler to scale the workload.
Create a managed instance group for Compute Engine with the cluster nodes. Configure autoscaling rules for the managed instance group.

Create alerting policies in Cloud Monitoring based on GKE CPU and memory utilization. Ask an on-duty engineer to scale the workload by executing a script when CPU and memory usage exceed predefined thresholds.

questions.correct_text: Distribute your workload evenly using a multi-zonal node pool. | Use cluster autoscaler to resize the number of nodes in the node pool, and use a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler to scale the workload.
questions.explanation: A multi-zonal (regional) node pool distributes nodes across multiple zones in a region, providing resilience against zonal hardware failures and high availability (A). Combining the cluster autoscaler, which adds or removes nodes based on pending pods, with a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler, which scales replicas based on observed metrics, automatically handles unpredictable and bursty traffic (C). Option B (multiple separate zonal node pools) and option D (manually managing a Compute Engine MIG) do not provide the integrated, automatic GKE scaling and HA expected here. Option E relies on manual human intervention, which cannot react quickly enough for unpredictable livestream spikes and is not truly automatic.

topics.exam_domain_name: Projetar apps cloud-native escaláveis, seguras e confiáveis

questions.explanation_pt: Um node pool multizonal (regional) distribui os nós por várias zonas de uma região, proporcionando resiliência contra falhas de hardware zonais e alta disponibilidade (A). Combinar o cluster autoscaler, que adiciona ou remove nós com base em pods pendentes, com um Horizontal Pod Autoscaler, que escala réplicas com base em métricas observadas, lida automaticamente com tráfego imprevisível e em rajadas (C). A opção B (vários node pools zonais separados) e a opção D (gerenciar manualmente um MIG do Compute Engine) não fornecem o escalonamento e a HA do GKE integrados e automáticos esperados aqui. A opção E depende de intervenção humana manual, que não consegue reagir com rapidez suficiente para picos imprevisíveis de livestream e não é verdadeiramente automática.

questions.question: You work at a rapidly growing financial technology startup. You manage the payment processing application written in Go and hosted on Cloud Run in the Singapore region (asia-southeast1). The payment processing application processes data stored in a Cloud Storage bucket that is also located in the Singapore region.The startup plans to expand further into the Asia Pacific region. You plan to deploy the Payment Gateway in Jakarta, Hong Kong, and Taiwan over the next six months. Each location has data residency requirements that require customer data to reside in the country where the transaction was made. You want to minimize the cost of these deployments. What should you do?

options.text: Create a Cloud Storage bucket in each region, and create a Cloud Run service of the payment processing application in each region.
Create a Cloud Storage bucket in each region, and create three Cloud Run services of the payment processing application in the Singapore region.
Create three Cloud Storage buckets in the Asia multi-region, and create three Cloud Run services of the payment processing application in the Singapore region.
Create three Cloud Storage buckets in the Asia multi-region, and create three Cloud Run revisions of the payment processing application in the Singapore region.

questions.correct_text: Create a Cloud Storage bucket in each region, and create a Cloud Run service of the payment processing application in each region.
questions.explanation: Data residency requirements mandate that customer data stay in the country where the transaction occurred, so you must place a regional Cloud Storage bucket in each country and run the payment processing service in that same region so data never leaves the jurisdiction (A). Multi-region buckets in the Asia multi-region (C and D) spread data across multiple countries, violating residency requirements. Running all services only in Singapore (B and D) would route processing of other countries' data through Singapore and adds cross-region latency and egress cost, and Cloud Run revisions (D) are just versions of one service, not separate regional deployments. Option A keeps data local while avoiding unnecessary cross-region traffic, minimizing cost and satisfying compliance.

topics.exam_domain_name: Projetar apps cloud-native escaláveis, seguras e confiáveis

questions.explanation_pt: Os requisitos de residência de dados exigem que os dados do cliente permaneçam no país onde a transação ocorreu, portanto você deve colocar um bucket regional do Cloud Storage em cada país e executar o serviço de processamento de pagamentos nessa mesma região para que os dados nunca saiam da jurisdição (A). Buckets multirregionais na multirregião Ásia (C e D) espalham os dados por vários países, violando os requisitos de residência. Executar todos os serviços apenas em Singapura (B e D) rotearia o processamento dos dados de outros países por Singapura e adiciona latência e custo de egress entre regiões, e as revisões do Cloud Run (D) são apenas versões de um único serviço, não implantações regionais separadas. A opção A mantém os dados locais, evitando tráfego desnecessário entre regiões, minimizando custos e satisfazendo a conformidade.

questions.question: You recently joined a new team that has a Cloud Spanner database instance running in production. Your manager has asked you to optimize the Spanner instance to reduce cost while maintaining high reliability and availability of the database. What should you do?

options.text: Use Cloud Logging to check for error logs, and reduce Spanner processing units by small increments until you find the minimum capacity required.
Use Cloud Trace to monitor the requests per sec of incoming requests to Spanner, and reduce Spanner processing units by small increments until you find the minimum capacity required.
Use Cloud Monitoring to monitor the CPU utilization, and reduce Spanner processing units by small increments until you find the minimum capacity required.
Use Snapshot Debugger to check for application errors, and reduce Spanner processing units by small increments until you find the minimum capacity required.

questions.correct_text: Use Cloud Monitoring to monitor the CPU utilization, and reduce Spanner processing units by small increments until you find the minimum capacity required.
questions.explanation: Cloud Spanner capacity is sized primarily by CPU utilization, and Google recommends keeping CPU below a target threshold for reliability; using Cloud Monitoring to watch CPU utilization while incrementally lowering processing units lets you find the minimum capacity that maintains availability (C). Cloud Logging error logs (A) and Snapshot Debugger (D) surface application errors, not the utilization signal that drives Spanner sizing. Cloud Trace (B) measures request latency and traces, not the CPU-based capacity metric Spanner scaling is based on, so it is not the right tool for right-sizing processing units.

topics.exam_domain_name: Projetar apps cloud-native escaláveis, seguras e confiáveis

questions.explanation_pt: A capacidade do Cloud Spanner é dimensionada principalmente pela utilização de CPU, e o Google recomenda manter a CPU abaixo de um limite-alvo para garantir confiabilidade; usar o Cloud Monitoring para observar a utilização de CPU enquanto reduz gradualmente as processing units permite encontrar a capacidade mínima que mantém a disponibilidade (C). Os logs de erro do Cloud Logging (A) e o Snapshot Debugger (D) expõem erros de aplicação, não o sinal de utilização que orienta o dimensionamento do Spanner. O Cloud Trace (B) mede latência de requisições e traces, não a métrica de capacidade baseada em CPU na qual o escalonamento do Spanner se baseia, por isso não é a ferramenta certa para o right-sizing das processing units.

questions.question: You have recently instrumented a new application with OpenTelemetry, and you want to check the latency of your application requests in Trace. You want to ensure that a specific request is always traced. What should you do?

options.text: Wait 10 minutes, then verify that Trace captures those types of requests automatically.
Write a custom script that sends this type of request repeatedly from your dev project.
Use the Trace API to apply custom attributes to the trace.
Add the X-Cloud-Trace-Context header to the request with the appropriate parameters.

questions.correct_text: Add the X-Cloud-Trace-Context header to the request with the appropriate parameters.
questions.explanation: Cloud Trace samples requests automatically and does not capture every request, so to force a particular request to always be traced you set the trace context explicitly. Adding the X-Cloud-Trace-Context header with the trace ID and the trace-enabled (sampling) flag set instructs the tracing system to record that specific request. Waiting and verifying automatic capture (A) relies on sampling and gives no guarantee a given request is traced. Repeatedly sending the request (B) just generates more sampled traffic without guaranteeing the specific request is captured. Applying custom attributes via the Trace API (C) annotates existing spans but does not control whether the request is sampled/traced in the first place.

topics.exam_domain_name: Integrar aplicações com serviços do Google Cloud

questions.explanation_pt: O Cloud Trace amostra requisições automaticamente e não captura todas as requisições, então, para forçar que uma requisição específica seja sempre rastreada, você define o contexto de trace explicitamente. Adicionar o cabeçalho X-Cloud-Trace-Context com o trace ID e a flag de trace habilitado (sampling) definida instrui o sistema de tracing a registrar aquela requisição específica. Esperar e verificar a captura automática (A) depende da amostragem e não dá nenhuma garantia de que uma dada requisição seja rastreada. Enviar a requisição repetidamente (B) apenas gera mais tráfego amostrado sem garantir que a requisição específica seja capturada. Aplicar atributos personalizados via Trace API (C) anota spans existentes, mas não controla se a requisição é amostrada/rastreada em primeiro lugar.

questions.question: You are trying to connect to your Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster using kubectl from Cloud Shell. You have deployed your GKE cluster with a public endpoint. From Cloud Shell, you run the following command:You notice that the kubectl commands time out without returning an error message. What is the most likely cause of this issue?

options.text: Your user account does not have privileges to interact with the cluster using kubectl.
Your Cloud Shell external IP address is not part of the authorized networks of the cluster.
The Cloud Shell is not part of the same VPC as the GKE cluster.
A VPC firewall is blocking access to the cluster’s endpoint.

questions.correct_text: Your Cloud Shell external IP address is not part of the authorized networks of the cluster.
questions.explanation: When a GKE cluster has master authorized networks enabled, only the listed CIDR ranges may reach the public control plane endpoint, and connections from other sources silently time out rather than returning an auth error. Because Cloud Shell uses ephemeral external IP addresses that change, those IPs are typically not in the authorized networks list, so kubectl hangs and times out. An IAM/RBAC permission problem (A) would return a clear forbidden/authorization error, not a timeout. Cloud Shell does not need to be in the same VPC for a public endpoint cluster (C), since access is over the public IP. A VPC firewall (D) governs traffic to your VPC resources, not access to the Google-managed public control plane endpoint.

topics.exam_domain_name: Configurar aplicações cloud-native para deployment

questions.explanation_pt: Quando um cluster GKE tem os master authorized networks habilitados, apenas os ranges de CIDR listados podem alcançar o endpoint público do control plane, e as conexões de outras origens expiram silenciosamente em vez de retornar um erro de autenticação. Como o Cloud Shell usa endereços IP externos efêmeros que mudam, esses IPs normalmente não estão na lista de authorized networks, então o kubectl trava e expira. Um problema de permissão de IAM/RBAC (A) retornaria um erro claro de forbidden/autorização, não um timeout. O Cloud Shell não precisa estar na mesma VPC para um cluster com endpoint público (C), já que o acesso é feito pelo IP público. Um firewall de VPC (D) controla o tráfego para os recursos da sua VPC, não o acesso ao endpoint público do control plane gerenciado pelo Google.

questions.question: You are developing a web application that contains private images and videos stored in a Cloud Storage bucket. Your users are anonymous and do not have Google Accounts. You want to use your application-specific logic to control access to the images and videos. How should you configure access?

options.text: Cache each web application user's IP address to create a named IP table using Google Cloud Armor. Create a Google Cloud Armor security policy that allows users to access the backend bucket.
Grant the Storage Object Viewer IAM role to allUsers. Allow users to access the bucket after authenticating through your web application.
Configure Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) to authenticate users into the web application. Allow users to access the bucket after authenticating through IAP.
Generate a signed URL that grants read access to the bucket. Allow users to access the URL after authenticating through your web application.

questions.correct_text: Generate a signed URL that grants read access to the bucket. Allow users to access the URL after authenticating through your web application.
questions.explanation: Signed URLs grant time-limited access to specific Cloud Storage objects without requiring the requester to have a Google Account, which exactly fits anonymous users whose access is governed by your application's own logic. Your app authenticates the user with its own logic and then generates a signed URL so the user can read the private object directly. Granting Storage Object Viewer to allUsers (B) makes the objects fully public to everyone, defeating private access control. IAP (C) protects HTTPS/web resources behind it and is oriented to Google identities, not anonymous access to bucket objects. Cloud Armor IP allowlisting (A) is a coarse network control, not per-user application-driven object access.

questions.explanation_pt: As Signed URLs concedem acesso por tempo limitado a objetos específicos do Cloud Storage sem exigir que o solicitante tenha uma Conta Google, o que se encaixa exatamente para usuários anônimos cujo acesso é regido pela lógica da sua própria aplicação. Sua aplicação autentica o usuário com sua própria lógica e então gera uma signed URL para que o usuário possa ler o objeto privado diretamente. Conceder Storage Object Viewer para allUsers (B) torna os objetos totalmente públicos para todos, anulando o controle de acesso privado. O IAP (C) protege recursos HTTPS/web por trás dele e é orientado a identidades do Google, não a acesso anônimo a objetos de bucket. O allowlisting de IP do Cloud Armor (A) é um controle de rede grosseiro, não um acesso a objetos por usuário, orientado pela aplicação.

questions.question: You need to configure a Deployment on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). You want to include a check that verifies that the containers can connect to the database. If the Pod is failing to connect, you want a script on the container to run to complete a graceful shutdown. How should you configure the Deployment?

options.text: Create two jobs: one that checks whether the container can connect to the database, and another that runs the shutdown script if the Pod is failing.

Create the Deployment with a livenessProbe for the container that will fail if the container can't connect to the database. Configure a Prestop lifecycle handler that runs the shutdown script if the container is failing.
Create the Deployment with a PostStart lifecycle handler that checks the service availability. Configure a PreStop lifecycle handler that runs the shutdown script if the container is failing.
Create the Deployment with an initContainer that checks the service availability. Configure a Prestop lifecycle handler that runs the shutdown script if the Pod is failing.

questions.correct_text: Create the Deployment with a livenessProbe for the container that will fail if the container can't connect to the database. Configure a Prestop lifecycle handler that runs the shutdown script if the container is failing.
questions.explanation: A livenessProbe is the correct mechanism to continuously verify the container's health, such as its ability to connect to the database, and failing the probe signals Kubernetes that the container is unhealthy. The PreStop lifecycle handler runs just before the container is terminated, making it the right place to execute a graceful shutdown script. Using separate Jobs (A) cannot manage the lifecycle of the running Pod's container. A PostStart handler (C) runs only once right after the container starts, so it cannot continuously monitor connectivity over time. An initContainer (D) only runs to completion before the main container starts and cannot detect ongoing connection failures during runtime.

topics.exam_domain_name: Configurar aplicações cloud-native para deployment

questions.explanation_pt: Uma livenessProbe é o mecanismo correto para verificar continuamente a saúde do contêiner, como sua capacidade de se conectar ao banco de dados, e a falha da probe sinaliza ao Kubernetes que o contêiner está não saudável. O lifecycle handler PreStop é executado logo antes de o contêiner ser encerrado, sendo o lugar certo para executar um script de shutdown gracioso. Usar Jobs separados (A) não consegue gerenciar o ciclo de vida do contêiner do Pod em execução. Um handler PostStart (C) é executado apenas uma vez logo após o contêiner iniciar, então não consegue monitorar continuamente a conectividade ao longo do tempo. Um initContainer (D) só é executado até a conclusão antes do contêiner principal iniciar e não consegue detectar falhas de conexão contínuas durante a execução.

questions.question: You are responsible for deploying a new API. That API will have three different URL paths:• https://yourcompany.com/students• https://yourcompany.com/teachers• https://yourcompany.com/classesYou need to configure each API URL path to invoke a different function in your code. What should you do?

options.text: Create one Cloud Function as a backend service exposed using an HTTPS load balancer.
Create three Cloud Functions exposed directly.
Create one Cloud Function exposed directly.
Create three Cloud Functions as three backend services exposed using an HTTPS load balancer.

questions.correct_text: Create three Cloud Functions as three backend services exposed using an HTTPS load balancer.
questions.explanation: Routing distinct URL paths to distinct functions requires URL path-based routing, which an external HTTPS load balancer provides through URL maps that match paths to different backend services. Creating three Cloud Functions, each fronted as a backend service behind the HTTPS load balancer, lets you map /students, /teachers, and /classes to the appropriate function. A single function (A or C) cannot natively split traffic by path to different code units in this design. Exposing three functions directly (B) gives each its own separate URL rather than a unified domain with shared path-based routing, so it does not satisfy the requirement of one host with multiple paths.

questions.explanation_pt: Rotear caminhos de URL distintos para funções distintas exige roteamento baseado em caminho de URL, que um external HTTPS load balancer fornece por meio de URL maps que correspondem caminhos a diferentes backend services. Criar três Cloud Functions, cada uma exposta como um backend service por trás do HTTPS load balancer, permite mapear /students, /teachers e /classes para a função apropriada. Uma única função (A ou C) não consegue, nativamente, dividir o tráfego por caminho para diferentes unidades de código nesse design. Expor as três funções diretamente (B) dá a cada uma sua própria URL separada em vez de um domínio unificado com roteamento compartilhado baseado em caminho, então não satisfaz o requisito de um host com múltiplos caminhos.

questions.question: You are deploying a microservices application to Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). The application will receive daily updates. You expect to deploy a large number of distinct containers that will run on the Linux operating system (OS). You want to be alerted to any known OS vulnerabilities in the new containers. You want to follow Google-recommended best practices. What should you do?

options.text: Use the gcloud CLI to call Container Analysis to scan new container images. Review the vulnerability results before each deployment.
Enable Container Analysis, and upload new container images to Artifact Registry. Review the vulnerability results before each deployment.
Enable Container Analysis, and upload new container images to Artifact Registry. Review the critical vulnerability results before each deployment.
Use the Container Analysis REST API to call Container Analysis to scan new container images. Review the vulnerability results before each deployment.

questions.correct_text: Enable Container Analysis, and upload new container images to Artifact Registry. Review the vulnerability results before each deployment.
questions.explanation: The Google-recommended approach is to enable Container Analysis and store images in Artifact Registry, which automatically scans images on push and continuously rescans for newly discovered OS vulnerabilities, then review the results before deploying. Because new OS vulnerabilities can surface at any time, you must review all known vulnerability results, not just critical ones, so option C is too narrow and could let high or medium severity issues through. Options A and D rely on manually invoking Container Analysis via the gcloud CLI or REST API, which is not the recommended automated pattern and is harder to maintain at scale with a large number of frequently updated images. Integrating scanning natively with Artifact Registry provides automatic, ongoing vulnerability detection without custom tooling.

topics.exam_domain_name: Projetar apps cloud-native escaláveis, seguras e confiáveis

questions.explanation_pt: A abordagem recomendada pelo Google é habilitar o Container Analysis e armazenar as imagens no Artifact Registry, que escaneia automaticamente as imagens no push e faz reescaneamentos contínuos em busca de vulnerabilidades de SO recém-descobertas, e então revisar os resultados antes de fazer o deploy. Como novas vulnerabilidades de SO podem surgir a qualquer momento, você precisa revisar todos os resultados de vulnerabilidades conhecidas, não apenas as críticas, então a opção C é restrita demais e poderia deixar passar problemas de severidade alta ou média. As opções A e D dependem de invocar manualmente o Container Analysis via gcloud CLI ou REST API, o que não é o padrão automatizado recomendado e é mais difícil de manter em escala com um grande número de imagens atualizadas com frequência. Integrar o escaneamento nativamente com o Artifact Registry oferece detecção de vulnerabilidades automática e contínua, sem ferramentas personalizadas.

questions.question: You are a developer at a large organization. You have an application written in Go running in a production Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster. You need to add a new feature that requires access to BigQuery. You want to grant BigQuery access to your GKE cluster following Google-recommended best practices. What should you do?

options.text: Create a Google service account with BigQuery access. Add the JSON key to Secret Manager, and use the Go client library to access the JSON key.
Create a Google service account with BigQuery access. Add the Google service account JSON key as a Kubernetes secret, and configure the application to use this secret.
Create a Google service account with BigQuery access. Add the Google service account JSON key to Secret Manager, and use an init container to access the secret for the application to use.
Create a Google service account and a Kubernetes service account. Configure Workload Identity on the GKE cluster, and reference the Kubernetes service account on the application Deployment.

questions.correct_text: Create a Google service account and a Kubernetes service account. Configure Workload Identity on the GKE cluster, and reference the Kubernetes service account on the application Deployment.
questions.explanation: Workload Identity is the Google-recommended best practice for granting GKE workloads access to Google Cloud APIs such as BigQuery, because it binds a Kubernetes service account to a Google service account without managing or distributing long-lived JSON key files. You create both service accounts, enable Workload Identity on the cluster, establish the IAM binding, and reference the Kubernetes service account in the Deployment so pods automatically obtain short-lived credentials. Options A, B, and C all rely on exported JSON service account keys, which are a security liability that Google explicitly discourages, regardless of whether they are stored in Secret Manager, a Kubernetes secret, or accessed via an init container. Avoiding static keys reduces the risk of credential leakage and eliminates manual rotation overhead.

questions.explanation_pt: O Workload Identity é a prática recomendada pelo Google para conceder a workloads do GKE acesso a APIs do Google Cloud, como o BigQuery, porque ele vincula uma service account do Kubernetes a uma service account do Google sem gerenciar ou distribuir arquivos de chave JSON de longa duração. Você cria as duas service accounts, habilita o Workload Identity no cluster, estabelece o binding de IAM e referencia a service account do Kubernetes no Deployment, de modo que os pods obtêm automaticamente credenciais de curta duração. As opções A, B e C dependem todas de chaves JSON de service account exportadas, que são um risco de segurança que o Google desencoraja explicitamente, independentemente de estarem armazenadas no Secret Manager, em um secret do Kubernetes ou acessadas por um init container. Evitar chaves estáticas reduz o risco de vazamento de credenciais e elimina o trabalho de rotação manual.

questions.question: You have an application written in Python running in production on Cloud Run. Your application needs to read/write data stored in a Cloud Storage bucket in the same project. You want to grant access to your application following the principle of least privilege. What should you do?

options.text: Create a user-managed service account with a custom Identity and Access Management (IAM) role.
Create a user-managed service account with the Storage Admin Identity and Access Management (IAM) role.
Create a user-managed service account with the Project Editor Identity and Access Management (IAM) role.
Use the default service account linked to the Cloud Run revision in production.

questions.correct_text: Create a user-managed service account with a custom Identity and Access Management (IAM) role.
questions.explanation: Following the principle of least privilege means creating a dedicated user-managed service account and granting it only the specific permissions needed to read and write objects in the one bucket, which a custom IAM role (or narrowly scoped predefined roles) accomplishes. The Storage Admin role grants far broader permissions, including bucket management and deletion, exceeding what the application requires. The Project Editor role is even more excessive, granting wide access across the entire project, and the default service account also typically carries broad permissions and is shared, making it unsuitable for least-privilege design. A custom role tailored to the exact storage object operations gives the tightest possible scope.

topics.exam_domain_name: Projetar apps cloud-native escaláveis, seguras e confiáveis

questions.explanation_pt: Seguir o princípio do menor privilégio significa criar uma service account dedicada gerenciada pelo usuário e conceder a ela apenas as permissões específicas necessárias para ler e gravar objetos no único bucket, o que é alcançado por uma role de IAM personalizada (ou roles predefinidas de escopo restrito). A role Storage Admin concede permissões muito mais amplas, incluindo gerenciamento e exclusão de buckets, excedendo o que a aplicação requer. A role Project Editor é ainda mais excessiva, concedendo acesso amplo a todo o projeto, e a service account padrão também costuma ter permissões amplas e é compartilhada, tornando-a inadequada para um design de menor privilégio. Uma role personalizada adaptada às operações exatas de objetos de storage oferece o escopo mais restrito possível.

questions.question: Your team is developing unit tests for Cloud Function code. The code is stored in a Cloud Source Repositories repository. You are responsible for implementing the tests. Only a specific service account has the necessary permissions to deploy the code to Cloud Functions. You want to ensure that the code cannot be deployed without first passing the tests. How should you configure the unit testing process?

options.text: Configure Cloud Build to deploy the Cloud Function. If the code passes the tests, a deployment approval is sent to you.
Configure Cloud Build to deploy the Cloud Function, using the specific service account as the build agent. Run the unit tests after successful deployment.
Configure Cloud Build to run the unit tests. If the code passes the tests, the developer deploys the Cloud Function.
Configure Cloud Build to run the unit tests, using the specific service account as the build agent. If the code passes the tests, Cloud Build deploys the Cloud Function.

questions.correct_text: Configure Cloud Build to run the unit tests, using the specific service account as the build agent. If the code passes the tests, Cloud Build deploys the Cloud Function.
questions.explanation: The correct approach is to configure Cloud Build to run the unit tests first and only deploy the Cloud Function if the tests pass, using the privileged service account as the build identity so that deployment can only ever happen through the gated pipeline. This guarantees the code cannot be deployed without passing the tests, because the developer no longer holds direct deploy permissions and the build halts on test failure. Options A and B deploy before or independently of test success, which defeats the gate, and option B even runs tests after deployment. Option C lets the developer deploy manually after tests, which does not technically prevent an untested deployment since the deploy step is outside the automated pipeline.

questions.question: Your team detected a spike of errors in an application running on Cloud Run in your production project. The application is configured to read messages from Pub/Sub topic A, process the messages, and write the messages to topic B. You want to conduct tests to identify the cause of the errors. You can use a set of mock messages for testing. What should you do?

options.text: Deploy the Pub/Sub and Cloud Run emulators on your local machine. Deploy the application locally, and change the logging level in the application to DEBUG or INFO. Write mock messages to topic A, and then analyze the logs.
Use the gcloud CLI to write mock messages to topic A. Change the logging level in the application to DEBUG or INFO, and then analyze the logs.
Deploy the Pub/Sub emulator on your local machine. Point the production application to your local Pub/Sub topics. Write mock messages to topic A, and then analyze the logs.
Use the Google Cloud console to write mock messages to topic A. Change the logging level in the application to DEBUG or INFO, and then analyze the logs.

questions.correct_text: Deploy the Pub/Sub and Cloud Run emulators on your local machine. Deploy the application locally, and change the logging level in the application to DEBUG or INFO. Write mock messages to topic A, and then analyze the logs.
questions.explanation: The safest and most effective way to reproduce and debug the error is to run everything locally using the Pub/Sub and Cloud Run emulators, deploy the application locally, raise the logging verbosity to DEBUG or INFO, publish mock messages to topic A, and analyze the resulting logs. This isolates testing entirely from production so that mock messages and verbose logging do not affect live data or real subscribers. Options B and D write mock test messages directly to the production topic A and change logging on the production application, which contaminates production and risks side effects. Option C points the production application at local topics, which is fragile, mixes production and local environments, and does not properly isolate the test.

questions.explanation_pt: A forma mais segura e eficaz de reproduzir e depurar o erro é executar tudo localmente usando os emuladores do Pub/Sub e do Cloud Run, fazer o deploy da aplicação localmente, aumentar o nível de verbosidade do logging para DEBUG ou INFO, publicar mensagens de teste (mock) no tópico A e analisar os logs resultantes. Isso isola completamente o teste da produção, de modo que as mensagens de teste e o logging verboso não afetem dados em produção nem assinantes reais. As opções B e D gravam mensagens de teste diretamente no tópico A de produção e alteram o logging da aplicação em produção, o que contamina a produção e arrisca efeitos colaterais. A opção C aponta a aplicação de produção para tópicos locais, o que é frágil, mistura os ambientes de produção e local e não isola adequadamente o teste.

questions.question: You are developing a Java Web Server that needs to interact with Google Cloud services via the Google Cloud API on the user's behalf. Users should be able to authenticate to the Google Cloud API using their Google Cloud identities. Which workflow should you implement in your web application?

options.text: 1. When a user arrives at your application, prompt them for their Google username and password.2. Store an SHA password hash in your application's database along with the user's username.3. The application authenticates to the Google Cloud API using HTTPs requests with the user's username and password hash in the Authorization request header.

1. When a user arrives at your application, prompt them for their Google username and password.2. Forward the user's username and password in an HTTPS request to the Google Cloud authorization server, and request an access token.3. The Google server validates the user's credentials and returns an access token to the application.4. The application uses the access token to call the Google Cloud API.

1. When a user arrives at your application, route them to a Google Cloud consent screen with a list of requested permissions that prompts the user to sign in with SSO to their Google Account.2. After the user signs in and provides consent, your application receives an authorization code from a Google server.3. The Google server returns the authorization code to the user, which is stored in the browser's cookies.4. The user authenticates to the Google Cloud API using the authorization code in the cookie.

1. When a user arrives at your application, route them to a Google Cloud consent screen with a list of requested permissions that prompts the user to sign in with SSO to their Google Account.2. After the user signs in and provides consent, your application receives an authorization code from a Google server.3. The application requests a Google Server to exchange the authorization code with an access token.4. The Google server responds with the access token that is used by the application to call the Google Cloud API.

questions.correct_text: 1. When a user arrives at your application, route them to a Google Cloud consent screen with a list of requested permissions that prompts the user to sign in with SSO to their Google Account.2. After the user signs in and provides consent, your application receives an authorization code from a Google server.3. The application requests a Google Server to exchange the authorization code with an access token.4. The Google server responds with the access token that is used by the application to call the Google Cloud API.
questions.explanation: Option D describes the standard OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow, which is the correct way to let users authenticate with their Google identities and authorize your app to call Google Cloud APIs on their behalf. The user is redirected to a Google consent screen, signs in via SSO, and the app receives a short-lived authorization code that it securely exchanges (server-side, with its client secret) for an access token used to call the API. Options A and B are wrong because they require the application to handle the user's actual Google password, which violates OAuth principles and exposes credentials; Google's authorization server does not accept passwords from third-party apps. Option C is wrong because the raw authorization code should never be stored in a browser cookie or used directly to call the API; it must first be exchanged for an access token over a secure back channel.

topics.exam_domain_name: Integrar aplicações com serviços do Google Cloud

questions.explanation_pt: A opção D descreve o fluxo padrão de authorization code do OAuth 2.0, que é a forma correta de permitir que usuários se autentiquem com suas identidades Google e autorizem seu aplicativo a chamar APIs do Google Cloud em nome deles. O usuário é redirecionado para uma tela de consentimento do Google, faz login via SSO, e o aplicativo recebe um authorization code de curta duração que ele troca com segurança (no lado do servidor, com seu client secret) por um access token usado para chamar a API. As opções A e B estão erradas porque exigem que o aplicativo manipule a senha real do Google do usuário, o que viola os princípios do OAuth e expõe credenciais; o servidor de autorização do Google não aceita senhas de aplicativos de terceiros. A opção C está errada porque o authorization code bruto nunca deve ser armazenado em um cookie de navegador nem usado diretamente para chamar a API; ele precisa primeiro ser trocado por um access token através de um canal seguro de back channel.

questions.question: You recently developed a new application. You want to deploy the application on Cloud Run without a Dockerfile. Your organization requires that all container images are pushed to a centrally managed container repository. How should you build your container using Google Cloud services? (Choose two.)

options.text: Push your source code to Artifact Registry.
Submit a Cloud Build job to push the image.
Use the pack build command with pack CLI.
Include the --source flag with the gcloud run deploy CLI command.
Include the --platform=kubernetes flag with the gcloud run deploy CLI command.

questions.correct_text: Use the pack build command with pack CLI. | Include the --source flag with the gcloud run deploy CLI command.
questions.explanation: To deploy to Cloud Run without writing a Dockerfile while pushing images to a central repository, you use Cloud Native Buildpacks. Option C, the 'pack build' command with the pack CLI, builds an OCI image directly from source using buildpacks without requiring a Dockerfile. Option D, 'gcloud run deploy --source', also leverages Buildpacks (via Cloud Build) to build the image from source and push it to Artifact Registry automatically, then deploy it. Option A is wrong because Artifact Registry stores built container images, not raw source code. Option B (a generic Cloud Build job to 'push the image') presumes an already-built image and typically implies a Dockerfile, and Option E is invalid because '--platform=kubernetes' is not how managed Cloud Run builds containers from source.

topics.exam_domain_name: Configurar aplicações cloud-native para deployment

questions.explanation_pt: Para fazer deploy no Cloud Run sem escrever um Dockerfile, enviando imagens para um repositório central, você usa Cloud Native Buildpacks. A opção C, o comando 'pack build' com a CLI pack, constrói uma imagem OCI diretamente a partir do código-fonte usando buildpacks, sem exigir um Dockerfile. A opção D, 'gcloud run deploy --source', também utiliza Buildpacks (via Cloud Build) para construir a imagem a partir do código-fonte e enviá-la automaticamente para o Artifact Registry, então fazer o deploy. A opção A está errada porque o Artifact Registry armazena imagens de contêiner já construídas, não código-fonte bruto. A opção B (um job genérico do Cloud Build para 'enviar a imagem') pressupõe uma imagem já construída e normalmente implica um Dockerfile, e a opção E é inválida porque '--platform=kubernetes' não é a forma como o Cloud Run gerenciado constrói contêineres a partir do código-fonte.

questions.question: You work for an organization that manages an online ecommerce website. Your company plans to expand across the world; however, the estore currently serves one specific region. You need to select a SQL database and configure a schema that will scale as your organization grows. You want to create a table that stores all customer transactions and ensure that the customer (CustomerId) and the transaction (TransactionId) are unique. What should you do?

options.text: Create a Cloud SQL table that has TransactionId and CustomerId configured as primary keys. Use an incremental number for the TransactionId.
Create a Cloud SQL table that has TransactionId and CustomerId configured as primary keys. Use a random string (UUID) for the Transactionid.
Create a Cloud Spanner table that has TransactionId and CustomerId configured as primary keys. Use a random string (UUID) for the TransactionId.
Create a Cloud Spanner table that has TransactionId and CustomerId configured as primary keys. Use an incremental number for the TransactionId.

questions.correct_text: Create a Cloud Spanner table that has TransactionId and CustomerId configured as primary keys. Use a random string (UUID) for the TransactionId.
questions.explanation: Cloud Spanner is the right choice because it is a horizontally scalable, globally distributed relational SQL database that supports strong consistency and can grow as the company expands worldwide, unlike Cloud SQL which is a regional, vertically scaled service. This rules out options A and B. Between the two Spanner options, using a random UUID (option C) for the primary key is the recommended practice to avoid hotspotting. Spanner shards data by primary key range, so monotonically incremental keys (option D) concentrate all new writes on the last shard, creating a write hotspot that limits throughput and scalability. A UUID distributes writes evenly across the key space.

topics.exam_domain_name: Projetar apps cloud-native escaláveis, seguras e confiáveis

questions.explanation_pt: O Cloud Spanner é a escolha certa porque é um banco de dados relacional SQL horizontalmente escalável e distribuído globalmente, que oferece consistência forte (strong consistency) e pode crescer à medida que a empresa se expande mundialmente, diferentemente do Cloud SQL, que é um serviço regional e escalado verticalmente. Isso elimina as opções A e B. Entre as duas opções de Spanner, usar um UUID aleatório (opção C) para a chave primária é a prática recomendada para evitar hotspotting. O Spanner faz o sharding dos dados por intervalo de chave primária, então chaves monotonicamente incrementais (opção D) concentram todas as novas escritas no último shard, criando um hotspot de escrita que limita a taxa de transferência (throughput) e a escalabilidade. Um UUID distribui as escritas uniformemente por todo o espaço de chaves.

questions.question: You are monitoring a web application that is written in Go and deployed in Google Kubernetes Engine. You notice an increase in CPU and memory utilization. You need to determine which source code is consuming the most CPU and memory resources. What should you do?

options.text: Download, install, and start the Snapshot Debugger agent in your VM. Take debug snapshots of the functions that take the longest time. Review the call stack frame, and identify the local variables at that level in the stack.
Import the Cloud Profiler package into your application, and initialize the Profiler agent. Review the generated flame graph in the Google Cloud console to identify time-intensive functions.

Import OpenTelemetry and Trace export packages into your application, and create the trace provider.Review the latency data for your application on the Trace overview page, and identify where bottlenecks are occurring.

Create a Cloud Logging query that gathers the web application's logs. Write a Python script that calculates the difference between the timestamps from the beginning and the end of the application's longest functions to identity time-intensive functions.

questions.correct_text: Import the Cloud Profiler package into your application, and initialize the Profiler agent. Review the generated flame graph in the Google Cloud console to identify time-intensive functions.
questions.explanation: Cloud Profiler is purpose-built to identify which parts of your source code consume the most CPU and memory with low overhead in production. Option B is correct because you import the Profiler package, initialize the agent, and review the resulting flame graphs in the console to pinpoint the most resource-intensive functions. Option A (Snapshot Debugger) inspects variable state at a point in execution but does not aggregate CPU or memory consumption by function. Option C (Cloud Trace via OpenTelemetry) measures request latency and distributed-call bottlenecks, not code-level CPU/memory usage. Option D is a fragile, manual approach using log timestamps that measures elapsed time only and cannot attribute CPU or memory consumption to specific code.

questions.explanation_pt: O Cloud Profiler foi criado especificamente para identificar quais partes do seu código-fonte consomem mais CPU e memória, com baixo overhead em produção. A opção B está correta porque você importa o pacote do Profiler, inicializa o agente e analisa os flame graphs resultantes no console para identificar as funções que mais consomem recursos. questions.question: You have a container deployed on Google Kubernetes Engine. The container can sometimes be slow to launch, so you have implemented a liveness probe. You notice that the liveness probe occasionally fails on launch. What should you do?

options.text: Add a startup probe.
Increase the initial delay for the liveness probe.
Increase the CPU limit for the container.
Add a readiness probe.

questions.correct_text: Add a startup probe.
questions.explanation: A startup probe (option A) is the correct solution for containers that are slow to launch. It disables the liveness and readiness checks until the application has finished starting up, preventing the liveness probe from killing a container that simply needs more time to initialize. Option B (increasing the liveness initial delay) is a less robust workaround because it forces a fixed wait for every container and either delays detection of real failures or still fails if startup time varies. Option C (increasing the CPU limit) may not address the underlying slow-startup behavior and wastes resources. Option D (readiness probe) only controls whether traffic is routed to the pod and does not prevent the liveness probe from restarting a slow-starting container.

topics.exam_domain_name: Configurar aplicações cloud-native para deployment

questions.explanation_pt: Um startup probe (opção A) é a solução correta para contêineres que demoram a iniciar. Ele desabilita as verificações de liveness e readiness até que o aplicativo termine de inicializar, evitando que o liveness probe encerre um contêiner que simplesmente precisa de mais tempo para inicializar. A opção B (aumentar o delay inicial do liveness) é uma solução alternativa menos robusta, pois força uma espera fixa para todo contêiner e ou atrasa a detecção de falhas reais ou ainda falha se o tempo de inicialização variar. A opção C (aumentar o limite de CPU) pode não resolver o comportamento subjacente de inicialização lenta e desperdiça recursos. A opção D (readiness probe) apenas controla se o tráfego é roteado para o pod e não impede que o liveness probe reinicie um contêiner de inicialização lenta.

questions.question: You work for an organization that manages an ecommerce site. Your application is deployed behind a global HTTP(S) load balancer. You need to test a new product recommendation algorithm. You plan to use A/B testing to determine the new algorithm’s effect on sales in a randomized way. How should you test this feature?

options.text: Split traffic between versions using weights.
Enable the new recommendation feature flag on a single instance.
Mirror traffic to the new version of your application.
Use HTTP header-based routing.

questions.correct_text: Split traffic between versions using weights.
questions.explanation: A/B testing for a randomized experiment requires sending a fixed percentage of users to each version, which is exactly what weight-based traffic splitting on a global HTTP(S) load balancer provides. By assigning weights (for example 90/10) across backend services or versions, you randomly distribute users and can measure the new algorithm's effect on sales. Header-based routing (D) routes deterministically based on request attributes, so it segments users rather than randomizing them, which is suited to feature targeting, not statistical A/B tests. Mirroring traffic (C) sends shadow copies to the new version but the responses are discarded, so users never actually receive the new recommendations and sales cannot be measured. Enabling a flag on a single instance (B) does not give a controlled, randomized split of production users.

topics.exam_domain_name: Configurar aplicações cloud-native para deployment

questions.explanation_pt: Teste A/B para um experimento randomizado exige enviar uma porcentagem fixa de usuários para cada versão, que é exatamente o que a divisão de tráfego baseada em pesos (weight-based) em um global HTTP(S) load balancer oferece. Ao atribuir pesos (por exemplo 90/10) entre backend services ou versões, você distribui os usuários aleatoriamente e pode medir o efeito do novo algoritmo nas vendas. O roteamento baseado em headers (D) roteia de forma determinística com base nos atributos da requisição, então ele segmenta os usuários em vez de randomizá-los, o que é adequado para direcionamento de funcionalidades (feature targeting), não para testes A/B estatísticos. O espelhamento de tráfego (mirroring) (C) envia cópias sombra (shadow copies) para a nova versão, mas as respostas são descartadas, então os usuários nunca recebem de fato as novas recomendações e as vendas não podem ser medidas. Habilitar uma flag em uma única instância (B) não fornece uma divisão controlada e randomizada dos usuários em produção.

questions.question: You plan to deploy a new application revision with a Deployment resource to Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) in production. The container might not work correctly. You want to minimize risk in case there are issues after deploying the revision. You want to follow Google-recommended best practices. What should you do?

options.text: Perform a rolling update with a PodDisruptionBudget of 80%.
Perform a rolling update with a HorizontalPodAutoscaler scale-down policy value of 0.
Convert the Deployment to a StatefulSet, and perform a rolling update with a PodDisruptionBudget of 80%.
Convert the Deployment to a StatefulSet, and perform a rolling update with a HorizontalPodAutoscaler scale-down policy value of 0.

questions.correct_text: Perform a rolling update with a PodDisruptionBudget of 80%.
questions.explanation: A GKE Deployment performs a rolling update by default, gradually replacing old Pods with new ones, and a PodDisruptionBudget helps keep enough Pods available during the rollout. If the new container fails its readiness/liveness probes, the rollout stalls and you can quickly roll back to the previous ReplicaSet, minimizing risk. A HorizontalPodAutoscaler scale-down policy (B, D) controls autoscaling behavior, not the safety of a revision rollout, so it does not address bad-revision risk. Converting the Deployment to a StatefulSet (C, D) is unnecessary and adds complexity, since StatefulSets are for stateful workloads with stable identities and ordered updates, not for a standard application revision. Therefore the simplest Google-recommended approach is a rolling update protected by a PodDisruptionBudget.

topics.exam_domain_name: Configurar aplicações cloud-native para deployment

questions.explanation_pt: Um Deployment do GKE realiza um rolling update por padrão, substituindo gradualmente os Pods antigos pelos novos, e um PodDisruptionBudget ajuda a manter Pods suficientes disponíveis durante o lançamento. Se o novo container falhar nos readiness/liveness probes, o rollout trava e você pode fazer rollback rapidamente para o ReplicaSet anterior, minimizando o risco. Uma política de scale-down do HorizontalPodAutoscaler (B, D) controla o comportamento de autoscaling, não a segurança do lançamento de uma revisão, então não trata o risco de uma revisão ruim. Converter o Deployment em um StatefulSet (C, D) é desnecessário e adiciona complexidade, já que StatefulSets são para workloads stateful com identidades estáveis e atualizações ordenadas, não para uma revisão de aplicação padrão. Portanto, a abordagem mais simples recomendada pelo Google é um rolling update protegido por um PodDisruptionBudget.

questions.question: Before promoting your new application code to production, you want to conduct testing across a variety of different users. Although this plan is risky, you want to test the new version of the application with production users and you want to control which users are forwarded to the new version of the application based on their operating system. If bugs are discovered in the new version, you want to roll back the newly deployed version of the application as quickly as possible.What should you do?

options.text: Deploy your application on Cloud Run. Use traffic splitting to direct a subset of user traffic to the new version based on the revision tag.
Deploy your application on Google Kubernetes Engine with Anthos Service Mesh. Use traffic splitting to direct a subset of user traffic to the new version based on the user-agent header.
Deploy your application on App Engine. Use traffic splitting to direct a subset of user traffic to the new version based on the IP address.
Deploy your application on Compute Engine. Use Traffic Director to direct a subset of user traffic to the new version based on predefined weights.

questions.correct_text: Deploy your application on Google Kubernetes Engine with Anthos Service Mesh. Use traffic splitting to direct a subset of user traffic to the new version based on the user-agent header.
questions.explanation: Routing users based on their operating system requires matching on the user-agent HTTP header, and Anthos Service Mesh (Cloud Service Mesh) on GKE supports advanced traffic management with header-based traffic splitting, allowing fast rollback by shifting weights back to the stable version. Cloud Run traffic splitting (A) splits by percentage/revision tag and cannot route based on arbitrary request headers like user-agent. App Engine traffic splitting (C) supports splitting by IP or cookie, not by user-agent/OS. Traffic Director with predefined weights on Compute Engine (D) does weighted splitting but the question specifically needs OS-based routing, which weights alone do not provide. Thus the service mesh user-agent routing approach is the correct fit.

questions.question: Your team is writing a backend application to implement the business logic for an interactive voice response (IVR) system that will support a payroll application. The IVR system has the following technical characteristics:• Each customer phone call is associated with a unique IVR session.• The IVR system creates a separate persistent gRPC connection to the backend for each session.• If the connection is interrupted, the IVR system establishes a new connection, causing a slight latency for that call.You need to determine which compute environment should be used to deploy the backend application. Using current call data, you determine that:• Call duration ranges from 1 to 30 minutes.• Calls are typically made during business hours.• There are significant spikes of calls around certain known dates (e.g., pay days), or when large payroll changes occur.You want to minimize cost, effort, and operational overhead. Where should you deploy the backend application?

options.text: Compute Engine
Google Kubernetes Engine cluster in Standard mode
Cloud Functions
Cloud Run

questions.correct_text: Cloud Run
questions.explanation: Cloud Run supports persistent gRPC connections (including streaming) with configurable request timeouts up to long durations covering the 1-to-30-minute calls, and it scales automatically to handle the spiky business-hours and pay-day traffic, scaling to zero when idle to minimize cost and operational overhead. Cloud Functions (C) is poorly suited for long-lived persistent gRPC sessions and bidirectional streaming connections. Compute Engine (A) and GKE Standard (B) can handle the workload but require significant capacity planning, autoscaling configuration, and operational management, increasing effort and cost rather than minimizing them. Cloud Run delivers the serverless autoscaling and managed operations the requirements call for while supporting the needed connection model.
