questions.explanation_pt: O Cloud Run suporta conexões gRPC persistentes (incluindo streaming) com timeouts de requisição configuráveis por durações longas que cobrem as chamadas de 1 a 30 minutos, e ele escala automaticamente para lidar com o tráfego intenso (spiky) do horário comercial e dos dias de pagamento, escalando para zero quando ocioso para minimizar custo e sobrecarga operacional. As Cloud Functions (C) são mal adequadas para sessões gRPC persistentes de longa duração e conexões de streaming bidirecional. O Compute Engine (A) e o GKE Standard (B) podem lidar com a workload, mas exigem planejamento de capacidade significativo, configuração de autoscaling e gerenciamento operacional, aumentando o esforço e o custo em vez de minimizá-los. O Cloud Run entrega o autoscaling serverless e as operações gerenciadas que os requisitos exigem, ao mesmo tempo em que suporta o modelo de conexão necessário.

questions.question: You are developing an application hosted on Google Cloud that uses a MySQL relational database schema. The application will have a large volume of reads and writes to the database and will require backups and ongoing capacity planning. Your team does not have time to fully manage the database but can take on small administrative tasks. How should you host the database?

options.text: Configure Cloud SQL to host the database, and import the schema into Cloud SQL.
Deploy MySQL from the Google Cloud Marketplace to the database using a client, and import the schema.
Configure Bigtable to host the database, and import the data into Bigtable.
Configure Cloud Spanner to host the database, and import the schema into Cloud Spanner.
Configure Firestore to host the database, and import the data into Firestore.

questions.correct_text: Configure Cloud SQL to host the database, and import the schema into Cloud SQL.
questions.explanation: Cloud SQL is the managed relational database service that natively supports MySQL, so you can import an existing MySQL schema directly while offloading patching, replication, automated backups, and high availability to Google. It handles substantial read/write volume and lets a team perform small administrative tasks (configuring backups, scaling instances) without fully managing the database. Deploying MySQL from Marketplace (B) means running and maintaining the VM and database yourself, which is the opposite of reduced management. Bigtable (C) and Firestore (E) are NoSQL stores and do not run a MySQL relational schema. Cloud Spanner (D) is a relational service but uses its own SQL dialect and is far costlier and more complex than needed for a standard MySQL application, so Cloud SQL is the best fit.

topics.exam_domain_name: Projetar apps cloud-native escaláveis, seguras e confiáveis

questions.explanation_pt: O Cloud SQL é o serviço de banco de dados relacional gerenciado que suporta MySQL nativamente, então você pode importar um schema MySQL existente diretamente, transferindo para o Google o patching, a replicação, os backups automatizados e a alta disponibilidade. Ele lida com volume substancial de leitura/escrita e permite que uma equipe realize pequenas tarefas administrativas (configurar backups, escalar instâncias) sem gerenciar totalmente o banco de dados. Implantar o MySQL a partir do Marketplace (B) significa executar e manter a VM e o banco de dados você mesmo, o que é o oposto de reduzir o gerenciamento. O Bigtable (C) e o Firestore (E) são armazenamentos NoSQL e não executam um schema relacional MySQL. O Cloud Spanner (D) é um serviço relacional, mas usa seu próprio dialeto SQL e é muito mais custoso e complexo do que o necessário para uma aplicação MySQL padrão, então o Cloud SQL é a melhor opção.

questions.question: You are developing a new web application using Cloud Run and committing code to Cloud Source Repositories. You want to deploy new code in the most efficient way possible. You have already created a Cloud Build YAML file that builds a container and runs the following command: gcloud run deploy. What should you do next?

options.text: Create a Pub/Sub topic to be notified when code is pushed to the repository. Create a Pub/Sub trigger that runs the build file when an event is published to the topic.
Create a build trigger that runs the build file in response to a repository code being pushed to the development branch.
Create a webhook build trigger that runs the build file in response to HTTP POST calls to the webhook URL.
Create a Cron job that runs the following command every 24 hours: gcloud builds submit.

questions.correct_text: Create a build trigger that runs the build file in response to a repository code being pushed to the development branch.
questions.explanation: Creating a Cloud Build trigger that runs the build configuration file in response to code pushes to a specific branch is the standard, fully managed way to automate CI/CD with Cloud Source Repositories and Cloud Run. The trigger natively integrates with the repository, so each push to the development branch automatically builds the container and runs gcloud run deploy without extra plumbing. Option A is unnecessarily complex because Cloud Build triggers already handle repository events natively, so a custom Pub/Sub topic and trigger add no value. Option C (webhook trigger) is intended for external or third-party repositories, not native Cloud Source Repositories. Option D uses a time-based Cron job, which deploys on a schedule rather than in response to code changes, making it inefficient and not event-driven.

topics.exam_domain_name: Configurar aplicações cloud-native para deployment

questions.explanation_pt: Criar um trigger do Cloud Build que executa o arquivo de configuração de build em resposta a pushes de código para uma branch específica é a forma padrão e totalmente gerenciada de automatizar CI/CD com Cloud Source Repositories e Cloud Run. O trigger se integra nativamente ao repositório, então cada push para a branch de desenvolvimento automaticamente compila o container e executa gcloud run deploy sem encanamento adicional. A opção A é desnecessariamente complexa porque os triggers do Cloud Build já lidam com eventos de repositório nativamente, então um tópico e trigger personalizados do Pub/Sub não agregam valor. A opção C (webhook trigger) é destinada a repositórios externos ou de terceiros, não a Cloud Source Repositories nativos. A opção D usa um job Cron baseado em tempo, que faz o deploy conforme um agendamento em vez de em resposta a mudanças no código, tornando-a ineficiente e não orientada a eventos.

questions.question: You are a developer at a large organization. You are deploying a web application to Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). The DevOps team has built a CI/CD pipeline that uses Cloud Deploy to deploy the application to Dev, Test, and Prod clusters in GKE. After Cloud Deploy successfully deploys the application to the Dev cluster, you want to automatically promote it to the Test cluster. How should you configure this process following Google-recommended best practices?

options.text: 1. Create a Cloud Build trigger that listens for SUCCEEDED Pub/Sub messages from the clouddeploy-operations topic.2. Configure Cloud Build to include a step that promotes the application to the Test cluster.

1. Create a Cloud Function that calls the Google Cloud Deploy API to promote the application to the Test cluster.2. Configure this function to be triggered by SUCCEEDED Pub/Sub messages from the cloud-builds topic.

1. Create a Cloud Function that calls the Google Cloud Deploy API to promote the application to the Test cluster.2. Configure this function to be triggered by SUCCEEDED Pub/Sub messages from the clouddeploy-operations topic.

1. Create a Cloud Build pipeline that uses the gke-deploy builder.2. Create a Cloud Build trigger that listens for SUCCEEDED Pub/Sub messages from the cloud-builds topic.3. Configure this pipeline to run a deployment step to the Test cluster.

questions.correct_text: 1. Create a Cloud Build trigger that listens for SUCCEEDED Pub/Sub messages from the clouddeploy-operations topic.2. Configure Cloud Build to include a step that promotes the application to the Test cluster.
questions.explanation: Cloud Deploy publishes operation status notifications to the clouddeploy-operations Pub/Sub topic, so listening for SUCCEEDED messages there is the correct event source to trigger an automatic promotion after the Dev rollout completes. A Cloud Build trigger subscribed to that topic can include a step (for example gcloud deploy releases promote) to advance the release to the Test target, which follows Google's recommended automation pattern. Options B and D listen on the cloud-builds topic, which carries Cloud Build job events, not Cloud Deploy events, so they would not reliably fire on a successful Cloud Deploy rollout. Option C uses the correct clouddeploy-operations topic but the messages also include non-promotion events; while a Cloud Function could work, the Cloud Build trigger approach in A is the cleaner, recommended integration for promotion within the existing pipeline.

topics.exam_domain_name: Configurar aplicações cloud-native para deployment

questions.explanation_pt: O Cloud Deploy publica notificações de status de operação no tópico Pub/Sub clouddeploy-operations, então escutar as mensagens SUCCEEDED ali é a fonte de eventos correta para acionar uma promoção automática após a conclusão do rollout de Dev. Um trigger do Cloud Build inscrito nesse tópico pode incluir uma etapa (por exemplo gcloud deploy releases promote) para avançar o release para o target de Test, o que segue o padrão de automação recomendado pelo Google. As opções B e D escutam o tópico cloud-builds, que carrega eventos de jobs do Cloud Build, não eventos do Cloud Deploy, então não disparariam de forma confiável em um rollout bem-sucedido do Cloud Deploy. A opção C usa o tópico correto clouddeploy-operations, mas as mensagens também incluem eventos que não são de promoção; embora uma Cloud Function pudesse funcionar, a abordagem do trigger do Cloud Build na opção A é a integração mais limpa e recomendada para promoção dentro do pipeline existente.

questions.question: Your application is running as a container in a Google Kubernetes Engine cluster. You need to add a secret to your application using a secure approach. What should you do?

options.text: Create a Kubernetes Secret, and pass the Secret as an environment variable to the container.
Enable Application-layer Secret Encryption on the cluster using a Cloud Key Management Service (KMS) key.

Store the credential in Cloud KMS. Create a Google service account (GSA) to read the credential from Cloud KMS. Export the GSA as a .json file, and pass the .json file to the container as a volume which can read the credential from Cloud KMS.

Store the credential in Secret Manager. Create a Google service account (GSA) to read the credential from Secret Manager. Create a Kubernetes service account (KSA) to run the container. Use Workload Identity to configure your KSA to act as a GSA.

questions.correct_text: Store the credential in Secret Manager. Create a Google service account (GSA) to read the credential from Secret Manager. Create a Kubernetes service account (KSA) to run the container. Use Workload Identity to configure your KSA to act as a GSA.
questions.explanation: Storing the credential in Secret Manager and using Workload Identity to let a Kubernetes service account impersonate a Google service account is the most secure, Google-recommended approach for GKE. Workload Identity removes the need to manage or export long-lived service account keys, and the pod retrieves the secret at runtime with short-lived credentials. Option A only base64-encodes the secret in etcd and exposes it as a plaintext environment variable, which is not strongly secured. Option B (application-layer secret encryption) protects Kubernetes Secrets at rest but does not by itself provide a secure delivery mechanism for the application's credential and is complementary rather than a complete answer. Option C exports a service account JSON key file, which reintroduces the very long-lived key management risk that Workload Identity is designed to eliminate.

topics.exam_domain_name: Projetar apps cloud-native escaláveis, seguras e confiáveis

questions.explanation_pt: Armazenar a credencial no Secret Manager e usar Workload Identity para permitir que uma conta de serviço do Kubernetes faça a impersonation de uma conta de serviço do Google é a abordagem mais segura e recomendada pelo Google para o GKE. O Workload Identity elimina a necessidade de gerenciar ou exportar chaves de conta de serviço de longa duração, e o pod recupera o segredo em tempo de execução com credenciais de curta duração. A opção A apenas codifica o segredo em base64 no etcd e o expõe como uma variável de ambiente em texto puro, o que não é fortemente protegido. A opção B (criptografia de segredos na camada da aplicação) protege os Secrets do Kubernetes em repouso, mas por si só não fornece um mecanismo seguro de entrega da credencial para a aplicação, sendo complementar em vez de uma resposta completa. A opção C exporta um arquivo de chave JSON de conta de serviço, o que reintroduz exatamente o risco de gerenciamento de chaves de longa duração que o Workload Identity foi projetado para eliminar.

questions.question: You are a developer at a financial institution. You use Cloud Shell to interact with Google Cloud services. User data is currently stored on an ephemeral disk; however, a recently passed regulation mandates that you can no longer store sensitive information on an ephemeral disk. You need to implement a new storage solution for your user data. You want to minimize code changes. Where should you store your user data?

options.text: Store user data on a Cloud Shell home disk, and log in at least every 120 days to prevent its deletion.
Store user data on a persistent disk in a Compute Engine instance.
Store user data in a Cloud Storage bucket.
Store user data in BigQuery tables.

questions.correct_text: Store user data on a persistent disk in a Compute Engine instance.
questions.explanation: Cloud Shell's storage is ephemeral except for the 5 GB home directory, and even that home disk is deleted after prolonged inactivity, so neither qualifies as durable storage for regulated, sensitive data. Attaching a persistent disk to a Compute Engine instance provides durable, non-ephemeral block storage that behaves like a regular filesystem, which minimizes code changes since the application can keep reading and writing files as before. Option A still relies on the ephemeral Cloud Shell home disk, which violates the regulation. Option C (Cloud Storage) and Option D (BigQuery) are durable but are object storage and an analytics database respectively, so adopting them would require substantial application code changes to switch from filesystem access to their APIs.

topics.exam_domain_name: Projetar apps cloud-native escaláveis, seguras e confiáveis

questions.explanation_pt: O armazenamento do Cloud Shell é efêmero, exceto pelo diretório home de 5 GB, e mesmo esse disco home é excluído após inatividade prolongada, então nenhum dos dois se qualifica como armazenamento durável para dados sensíveis e regulamentados. Anexar um persistent disk a uma instância do Compute Engine fornece armazenamento de blocos durável e não efêmero, que se comporta como um sistema de arquivos comum, o que minimiza mudanças no código já que a aplicação pode continuar lendo e gravando arquivos como antes. A opção A ainda depende do disco home efêmero do Cloud Shell, o que viola a regulamentação. A opção C (Cloud Storage) e a opção D (BigQuery) são duráveis, mas são, respectivamente, armazenamento de objetos e um banco de dados analítico, então adotá-las exigiria mudanças substanciais no código da aplicação para trocar o acesso ao sistema de arquivos por suas APIs.

questions.question: You recently developed a web application to transfer log data to a Cloud Storage bucket daily. Authenticated users will regularly review logs from the prior two weeks for critical events. After that, logs will be reviewed once annually by an external auditor. Data must be stored for a period of no less than 7 years. You want to propose a storage solution that meets these requirements and minimizes costs. What should you do? (Choose two.)

options.text: Use the Bucket Lock feature to set the retention policy on the data.
Run a scheduled job to set the storage class to Coldline for objects older than 14 days.
Create a JSON Web Token (JWT) for users needing access to the Coldline storage buckets.
Create a lifecycle management policy to set the storage class to Coldline for objects older than 14 days.
Create a lifecycle management policy to set the storage class to Nearline for objects older than 14 days.

questions.correct_text: Use the Bucket Lock feature to set the retention policy on the data. | Create a lifecycle management policy to set the storage class to Coldline for objects older than 14 days.
questions.explanation: Bucket Lock lets you set an immutable retention policy that guarantees objects cannot be deleted before the required 7-year period, satisfying the compliance mandate, so option A is correct. A lifecycle management policy that transitions objects to Coldline after 14 days minimizes cost because data older than two weeks is accessed rarely (only an annual audit), and Coldline is optimized for data accessed roughly once a year, so option D is correct. Option E chooses Nearline, which is meant for data accessed about once a month and is more expensive than Coldline for this once-a-year access pattern, so it does not minimize cost as well. Option B uses a scheduled job to change storage class manually, which is operationally fragile compared to native lifecycle rules, and option C (issuing JWTs) is an authentication mechanism unrelated to storage class or retention requirements.

topics.exam_domain_name: Projetar apps cloud-native escaláveis, seguras e confiáveis

questions.explanation_pt: O Bucket Lock permite definir uma política de retenção imutável que garante que os objetos não possam ser excluídos antes do período exigido de 7 anos, satisfazendo a exigência de conformidade, então a opção A está correta. Uma política de gerenciamento de ciclo de vida que faz a transição dos objetos para Coldline após 14 dias minimiza custos porque dados com mais de duas semanas são acessados raramente (apenas uma auditoria anual), e o Coldline é otimizado para dados acessados cerca de uma vez por ano, então a opção D está correta. A opção E escolhe Nearline, que é destinado a dados acessados cerca de uma vez por mês e é mais caro que o Coldline para esse padrão de acesso anual, então não minimiza custos tão bem. A opção B usa um job agendado para mudar a classe de armazenamento manualmente, o que é operacionalmente frágil comparado às regras nativas de ciclo de vida, e a opção C (emitir JWTs) é um mecanismo de autenticação não relacionado à classe de armazenamento ou aos requisitos de retenção.

questions.question: Your team is developing a Cloud Function triggered by Cloud Storage events. You want to accelerate testing and development of your Cloud Function while following Google-recommended best practices. What should you do?

options.text: Create a new Cloud Function that is triggered when Cloud Audit Logs detects the cloudfunctions.functions.sourceCodeSet operation in the original Cloud Function. Send mock requests to the new function to evaluate the functionality.

Make a copy of the Cloud Function, and rewrite the code to be HTTP-triggered. Edit and test the new version by triggering the HTTP endpoint. Send mock requests to the new function to evaluate the functionality.
Install the Functions Frameworks library, and configure the Cloud Function on localhost. Make a copy of the function, and make edits to the new version. Test the new version using curl.

Make a copy of the Cloud Function in the Google Cloud console. Use the Cloud console's in-line editor to make source code changes to the new function. Modify your web application to call the new function, and test the new version in production

questions.correct_text: Install the Functions Frameworks library, and configure the Cloud Function on localhost. Make a copy of the function, and make edits to the new version. Test the new version using curl.
questions.explanation: The Functions Framework is Google's recommended open-source library for running Cloud Functions locally, allowing you to invoke and iterate on the function on localhost and test it with tools like curl without redeploying to the cloud for every change. This dramatically speeds up the develop-test loop while preserving the same execution contract used in production. Option A invents an unnecessary, convoluted audit-log trigger and does not actually accelerate local testing. Option B requires rewriting the trigger type to HTTP, which changes the function's behavior and is not a faithful test of a storage-triggered function. Option D edits and tests directly in production, which is unsafe and contrary to best practices.

topics.exam_domain_name: Construir e testar aplicações

questions.explanation_pt: O Functions Framework é a biblioteca de código aberto recomendada pelo Google para executar Cloud Functions localmente, permitindo que você invoque e itere a função em localhost e a teste com ferramentas como o curl, sem precisar reimplantar na nuvem a cada alteração. Isso acelera drasticamente o ciclo de desenvolvimento e teste, preservando o mesmo contrato de execução usado em produção. A opção A inventa um gatilho de audit-log desnecessário e complicado, e não acelera de fato o teste local. A opção B exige reescrever o tipo de gatilho para HTTP, o que altera o comportamento da função e não é um teste fiel de uma função acionada por storage. A opção D edita e testa diretamente em produção, o que é inseguro e contrário às boas práticas.

questions.question: Your team is setting up a build pipeline for an application that will run in Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). For security reasons, you only want images produced by the pipeline to be deployed to your GKE cluster. Which combination of Google Cloud services should you use?

options.text: Cloud Build, Cloud Storage, and Binary Authorization
Google Cloud Deploy, Cloud Storage, and Google Cloud Armor
Google Cloud Deploy, Artifact Registry, and Google Cloud Armor
Cloud Build, Artifact Registry, and Binary Authorization

questions.correct_text: Cloud Build, Artifact Registry, and Binary Authorization
questions.explanation: Cloud Build creates the container images in the pipeline, Artifact Registry stores them as the trusted source, and Binary Authorization enforces a deploy-time policy on GKE so that only images that meet attestation requirements (for example, those built and attested by your pipeline) can be deployed. This combination directly satisfies the requirement that only pipeline-produced images run in the cluster. Options A uses Cloud Storage instead of a container registry, which is not the proper image store. Options B and C rely on Google Cloud Armor, which is a web application firewall/DDoS protection layer and does not control which images may be deployed.

topics.exam_domain_name: Configurar aplicações cloud-native para deployment

questions.explanation_pt: O Cloud Build cria as imagens de contêiner no pipeline, o Artifact Registry as armazena como fonte confiável, e o Binary Authorization aplica uma política em tempo de implantação no GKE para que apenas imagens que atendam aos requisitos de atestação (por exemplo, aquelas construídas e atestadas pelo seu pipeline) possam ser implantadas. Essa combinação satisfaz diretamente o requisito de que apenas imagens produzidas pelo pipeline sejam executadas no cluster. A opção A usa o Cloud Storage em vez de um registro de contêineres, que não é o armazenamento de imagens adequado. As opções B e C dependem do Google Cloud Armor, que é uma camada de firewall de aplicações web/proteção contra DDoS e não controla quais imagens podem ser implantadas.

questions.question: You are supporting a business-critical application in production deployed on Cloud Run. The application is reporting HTTP 500 errors that are affecting the usability of the application. You want to be alerted when the number of errors exceeds 15% of the requests within a specific time window. What should you do?

options.text: Create a Cloud Function that consumes the Cloud Monitoring API. Use Cloud Scheduler to trigger the Cloud Function daily and alert you if the number of errors is above the defined threshold.

Navigate to the Cloud Run page in the Google Cloud console, and select the service from the services list. Use the Metrics tab to visualize the number of errors for that revision, and refresh the page daily.
Create an alerting policy in Cloud Monitoring that alerts you if the number of errors is above the defined threshold.
Create a Cloud Function that consumes the Cloud Monitoring API. Use Cloud Composer to trigger the Cloud Function daily and alert you if the number of errors is above the defined threshold.

questions.correct_text: Create an alerting policy in Cloud Monitoring that alerts you if the number of errors is above the defined threshold.
questions.explanation: Cloud Monitoring alerting policies can evaluate Cloud Run request metrics in near real time and trigger notifications when a condition such as the 5xx error ratio exceeding 15% over a time window is met. This is the native, automated way to be alerted on error rates without building custom infrastructure. Options A and D build a custom Cloud Function that polls the Monitoring API only once daily, which is unnecessarily complex and far too slow to detect a problem affecting usability. Option B requires a human to manually refresh a dashboard, which is not alerting and does not scale.

questions.explanation_pt: As políticas de alerta do Cloud Monitoring podem avaliar métricas de requisições do Cloud Run quase em tempo real e disparar notificações quando uma condição, como a proporção de erros 5xx ultrapassar 15% em uma janela de tempo, é atendida. Essa é a forma nativa e automatizada de ser alertado sobre taxas de erro sem construir infraestrutura personalizada. As opções A e D criam uma Cloud Function personalizada que consulta a Monitoring API apenas uma vez por dia, o que é desnecessariamente complexo e lento demais para detectar um problema que afeta a usabilidade. A opção B exige que uma pessoa atualize manualmente um painel, o que não é alerta e não escala.

questions.question: You need to build a public API that authenticates, enforces quotas, and reports metrics for API callers. Which tool should you use to complete this architecture?

options.text: App Engine
Cloud Endpoints
Identity-Aware Proxy
GKE Ingress for HTTP(S) Load Balancing

questions.correct_text: Cloud Endpoints
questions.explanation: Cloud Endpoints is an API management gateway that provides authentication of API callers, quota/rate enforcement, and metrics/monitoring reporting, which exactly matches the requirements for a managed public API. App Engine is a serverless compute platform, not an API management layer, so it does not natively enforce quotas or report per-caller API metrics. Identity-Aware Proxy controls access to applications based on identity but does not provide API quotas or per-key reporting. GKE Ingress with HTTP(S) Load Balancing routes and balances traffic but offers no API key authentication, quotas, or API metrics.

questions.explanation_pt: O Cloud Endpoints é um gateway de gerenciamento de APIs que fornece autenticação de chamadores da API, aplicação de cota/limite de taxa e relatórios de métricas/monitoramento, o que corresponde exatamente aos requisitos de uma API pública gerenciada. O App Engine é uma plataforma de computação serverless, não uma camada de gerenciamento de APIs, portanto não aplica cotas nativamente nem relata métricas de API por chamador. O Identity-Aware Proxy controla o acesso a aplicações com base na identidade, mas não fornece cotas de API nem relatórios por chave. O GKE Ingress com HTTP(S) Load Balancing roteia e balanceia o tráfego, mas não oferece autenticação por chave de API, cotas ou métricas de API.

questions.question: You noticed that your application was forcefully shut down during a Deployment update in Google Kubernetes Engine. Your application didn’t close the database connection before it was terminated. You want to update your application to make sure that it completes a graceful shutdown. What should you do?

options.text: Update your code to process a received SIGTERM signal to gracefully disconnect from the database.
Configure a PodDisruptionBudget to prevent the Pod from being forcefully shut down.
Increase the terminationGracePeriodSeconds for your application.
Configure a PreStop hook to shut down your application.

questions.correct_text: Update your code to process a received SIGTERM signal to gracefully disconnect from the database.
questions.explanation: When Kubernetes terminates a Pod it sends a SIGTERM signal to the container, so the application code must handle SIGTERM to perform cleanup such as closing the database connection before the process exits, enabling a graceful shutdown. A PodDisruptionBudget (B) only limits how many Pods are voluntarily disrupted at once and does not change how an individual Pod shuts down. Increasing terminationGracePeriodSeconds (C) only gives more time before SIGKILL, but without handling SIGTERM the connection still won't be closed. A PreStop hook (D) can help, but the recommended and most direct fix is to trap SIGTERM in the application code so the database connection is closed cleanly.

topics.exam_domain_name: Configurar aplicações cloud-native para deployment

questions.explanation_pt: Quando o Kubernetes encerra um Pod, ele envia um sinal SIGTERM ao contêiner, de modo que o código da aplicação deve tratar o SIGTERM para realizar a limpeza, como fechar a conexão com o banco de dados antes de o processo terminar, possibilitando um encerramento gracioso. Um PodDisruptionBudget (B) apenas limita quantos Pods podem ser interrompidos voluntariamente de uma vez e não altera como um Pod individual é encerrado. Aumentar o terminationGracePeriodSeconds (C) apenas dá mais tempo antes do SIGKILL, mas, sem tratar o SIGTERM, a conexão ainda não será fechada. Um hook PreStop (D) pode ajudar, mas a correção recomendada e mais direta é capturar o SIGTERM no código da aplicação para que a conexão com o banco de dados seja fechada de forma limpa.

questions.question: You are a lead developer working on a new retail system that runs on Cloud Run and Firestore in Datastore mode. A web UI requirement is for the system to display a list of available products when users access the system and for the user to be able to browse through all products. You have implemented this requirement in the minimum viable product (MVP) phase by returning a list of all available products stored in Firestore.A few months after go-live, you notice that Cloud Run instances are terminated with HTTP 500: Container instances are exceeding memory limits errors during busy times. This error coincides with spikes in the number of Datastore entity reads. You need to prevent Cloud Run from crashing and decrease the number of Datastore entity reads. You want to use a solution that optimizes system performance. What should you do?

options.text: Modify the query that returns the product list using integer offsets.
Modify the query that returns the product list using limits.
Modify the Cloud Run configuration to increase the memory limits.
Modify the query that returns the product list using cursors.

questions.correct_text: Modify the query that returns the product list using cursors.
questions.explanation: The memory crashes and Datastore read spikes happen because the application loads the entire product catalog into memory on every request. Cursors let you paginate efficiently: you fetch a small page of entities, store the query cursor, and resume exactly where you left off on the next page, so only the entities actually viewed are read. This both caps memory usage and dramatically reduces total entity reads. Limits (B) restrict the first page but offer no efficient way to continue browsing; integer offsets (A) are explicitly discouraged in Datastore because the engine still reads and discards all skipped entities, so reads do not decrease. Increasing memory (C) only masks the symptom, costs more, and does nothing to reduce reads, so it does not optimize performance.

questions.explanation_pt: As falhas por falta de memória e os picos de leitura no Datastore acontecem porque a aplicação carrega todo o catálogo de produtos na memória a cada requisição. Os cursors permitem paginar de forma eficiente: você busca uma pequena página de entidades, armazena o cursor da query e retoma exatamente de onde parou na página seguinte, de modo que apenas as entidades realmente visualizadas são lidas. Isso ao mesmo tempo limita o uso de memória e reduz drasticamente o total de leituras de entidades. Os limits (B) restringem a primeira página, mas não oferecem uma forma eficiente de continuar a navegação; os offsets inteiros (A) são explicitamente desencorajados no Datastore porque o mecanismo ainda lê e descarta todas as entidades puladas, então as leituras não diminuem. Aumentar a memória (C) apenas mascara o sintoma, custa mais e não faz nada para reduzir as leituras, portanto não otimiza o desempenho.

questions.question: You need to deploy an internet-facing microservices application to Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). You want to validate new features using the A/B testing method. You have the following requirements for deploying new container image releases:• There is no downtime when new container images are deployed.• New production releases are tested and verified using a subset of production users.What should you do?

options.text: 1. Configure your CI/CD pipeline to update the Deployment manifest file by replacing the container version with the latest version.2. Recreate the Pods in your cluster by applying the Deployment manifest file.3. Validate the application's performance by comparing its functionality with the previous release version, and roll back if an issue arises.

1. Create a second namespace on GKE for the new release version.2. Create a Deployment configuration for the second namespace with the desired number of Pods.3. Deploy new container versions in the second namespace.4. Update the Ingress configuration to route traffic to the namespace with the new container versions.

1. Install the Anthos Service Mesh on your GKE cluster.2. Create two Deployments on the GKE cluster, and label them with different version names.3. Implement an Istio routing rule to send a small percentage of traffic to the Deployment that references the new version of the application.

1. Implement a rolling update pattern by replacing the Pods gradually with the new release version.2. Validate the application's performance for the new subset of users during the rollout, and roll back if an issue arises.

questions.correct_text: 1. Install the Anthos Service Mesh on your GKE cluster.2. Create two Deployments on the GKE cluster, and label them with different version names.3. Implement an Istio routing rule to send a small percentage of traffic to the Deployment that references the new version of the application.
questions.explanation: Wait, the requirement is zero-downtime deployment plus A/B testing where only a subset of production users sees the new release. The proper Google-recommended way to split live traffic by percentage between two versions is a service mesh with traffic-routing rules, which is what option C describes using Cloud Service Mesh/Istio. A rolling update (D) or replacing the Deployment image (A) shifts all users to the new version over time and provides no controlled A/B split. Using a second namespace with an Ingress that routes to it (B) simply switches all traffic to the new version like a blue/green cutover and cannot send only a percentage of users to the new release, so it does not satisfy the A/B testing requirement; the percentage-based Istio routing in C is the correct fit.

topics.exam_domain_name: Configurar aplicações cloud-native para deployment

questions.explanation_pt: Atenção: o requisito é uma implantação sem downtime mais testes A/B em que apenas um subconjunto de usuários de produção vê a nova versão. A forma adequada e recomendada pelo Google para dividir o tráfego ao vivo por porcentagem entre duas versões é uma service mesh com regras de roteamento de tráfego, que é exatamente o que a opção C descreve usando Cloud Service Mesh/Istio. Uma rolling update (D) ou a substituição da imagem do Deployment (A) migra todos os usuários para a nova versão ao longo do tempo e não fornece nenhuma divisão A/B controlada. Usar um segundo namespace com um Ingress que roteia para ele (B) simplesmente direciona todo o tráfego para a nova versão, como um corte blue/green, e não consegue enviar apenas uma porcentagem dos usuários para a nova versão, portanto não atende ao requisito de testes A/B; o roteamento por porcentagem do Istio na opção C é a escolha correta.

questions.question: Your team manages a large Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster. Several application teams currently use the same namespace to develop microservices for the cluster. Your organization plans to onboard additional teams to create microservices. You need to configure multiple environments while ensuring the security and optimal performance of each team’s work. You want to minimize cost and follow Google-recommended best practices. What should you do?

options.text: Create new role-based access controls (RBAC) for each team in the existing cluster, and define resource quotas.
Create a new namespace for each environment in the existing cluster, and define resource quotas.
Create a new GKE cluster for each team.
Create a new namespace for each team in the existing cluster, and define resource quotas.

questions.correct_text: Create a new namespace for each team in the existing cluster, and define resource quotas.
questions.explanation: The Google-recommended pattern for multi-tenant isolation within a single GKE cluster is to give each team its own namespace and apply resource quotas, which provides logical separation, scoped RBAC, and prevents one team from starving others of CPU/memory, all while minimizing cost. Creating a separate cluster per team (C) gives strong isolation but multiplies control-plane and node costs, violating the cost-minimization requirement. Defining only RBAC in the shared namespace (A) does not isolate workloads or resource consumption between teams. Creating a namespace per environment rather than per team (B) does not solve the core problem of multiple teams sharing one namespace, so a namespace per team with quotas is the best balance of security, performance, and cost.

topics.exam_domain_name: Projetar apps cloud-native escaláveis, seguras e confiáveis

questions.explanation_pt: O padrão recomendado pelo Google para isolamento multi-tenant dentro de um único cluster GKE é dar a cada equipe seu próprio namespace e aplicar resource quotas, o que proporciona separação lógica, RBAC com escopo definido e impede que uma equipe deixe as outras sem CPU/memória, tudo isso minimizando o custo. Criar um cluster separado por equipe (C) oferece um isolamento forte, mas multiplica os custos de control-plane e de nós, violando o requisito de minimização de custo. Definir apenas RBAC no namespace compartilhado (A) não isola as cargas de trabalho nem o consumo de recursos entre as equipes. Criar um namespace por ambiente em vez de por equipe (B) não resolve o problema central de várias equipes compartilharem um mesmo namespace, portanto um namespace por equipe com quotas é o melhor equilíbrio entre segurança, desempenho e custo.

questions.question: You have deployed a Java application to Cloud Run. Your application requires access to a database hosted on Cloud SQL. Due to regulatory requirements, your connection to the Cloud SQL instance must use its internal IP address. How should you configure the connectivity while following Google-recommended best practices?

options.text: Configure your Cloud Run service with a Cloud SQL connection.
Configure your Cloud Run service to use a Serverless VPC Access connector.
Configure your application to use the Cloud SQL Java connector.
Configure your application to connect to an instance of the Cloud SQL Auth proxy.

questions.correct_text: Configure your Cloud Run service to use a Serverless VPC Access connector.
questions.explanation: Because regulatory rules require connecting to Cloud SQL over its internal (private) IP, the serverless Cloud Run service needs a route into the VPC where that private IP lives, which is exactly what a Serverless VPC Access connector provides. The built-in Cloud Run "Cloud SQL connection" (A) and the Cloud SQL Auth proxy (D) by default establish connectivity using the instance's public IP path, so they do not satisfy the internal-IP requirement on their own. The Cloud SQL Java connector (C) is a library convenience for secure connections but still does not give the serverless environment private VPC network reachability to the internal IP. Only the Serverless VPC Access connector (B) lets Cloud Run egress traffic into the VPC and reach the Cloud SQL internal IP address.

questions.explanation_pt: Como as regras regulatórias exigem conexão ao Cloud SQL por meio do seu IP interno (privado), o serviço serverless do Cloud Run precisa de uma rota para a VPC onde esse IP privado reside, que é exatamente o que um Serverless VPC Access connector fornece. A "Cloud SQL connection" embutida do Cloud Run (A) e o Cloud SQL Auth proxy (D) estabelecem, por padrão, a conectividade usando o caminho do IP público da instância, portanto não atendem por si só ao requisito de IP interno. O Cloud SQL Java connector (C) é uma biblioteca de conveniência para conexões seguras, mas ainda assim não fornece ao ambiente serverless alcance de rede privada na VPC até o IP interno. Apenas o Serverless VPC Access connector (B) permite que o tráfego de saída do Cloud Run entre na VPC e alcance o endereço de IP interno do Cloud SQL.

questions.question: Your application stores customers’ content in a Cloud Storage bucket, with each object being encrypted with the customer's encryption key. The key for each object in Cloud Storage is entered into your application by the customer. You discover that your application is receiving an HTTP 4xx error when reading the object from Cloud Storage. What is a possible cause of this error?

options.text: You attempted the read operation on the object with the customer's base64-encoded key.
You attempted the read operation without the base64-encoded SHA256 hash of the encryption key.
You entered the same encryption algorithm specified by the customer when attempting the read operation.
You attempted the read operation on the object with the base64-encoded SHA256 hash of the customer's key.

questions.correct_text: You attempted the read operation without the base64-encoded SHA256 hash of the encryption key.
questions.explanation: With customer-supplied encryption keys (CSEK), every read of an encrypted object must include the encryption algorithm, the base64-encoded raw key, and the base64-encoded SHA256 hash of that key so Cloud Storage can verify it has the correct key. If the request omits the base64-encoded SHA256 hash of the key, the API rejects it with an HTTP 4xx client error, which matches the symptom, making B the cause. Supplying the base64-encoded key (A) and specifying the matching encryption algorithm (C) are correct, expected parts of a valid CSEK request, so they would not cause the error. Providing the SHA256 hash of the key (D) is also required and correct, so it is not the cause; the failure stems from the missing hash described in B.

topics.exam_domain_name: Integrar aplicações com serviços do Google Cloud

questions.explanation_pt: Com customer-supplied encryption keys (CSEK), toda leitura de um objeto criptografado deve incluir o algoritmo de criptografia, a chave bruta codificada em base64 e o hash SHA256 dessa chave codificado em base64, para que o Cloud Storage possa verificar se possui a chave correta. Se a requisição omitir o hash SHA256 da chave codificado em base64, a API a rejeita com um erro de cliente HTTP 4xx, o que corresponde ao sintoma, tornando B a causa. Fornecer a chave codificada em base64 (A) e especificar o algoritmo de criptografia correspondente (C) são partes corretas e esperadas de uma requisição CSEK válida, portanto não causariam o erro. Fornecer o hash SHA256 da chave (D) também é obrigatório e correto, então não é a causa; a falha decorre do hash ausente descrito em B.

questions.question: You have two Google Cloud projects, named Project A and Project B. You need to create a Cloud Function in Project A that saves the output in a Cloud Storage bucket in Project B. You want to follow the principle of least privilege. What should you do?

options.text: 1. Create a Google service account in Project B.2. Deploy the Cloud Function with the service account in Project A.3. Assign this service account the roles/storage.objectCreator role on the storage bucket residing in Project B.

1. Create a Google service account in Project A2. Deploy the Cloud Function with the service account in Project A.3. Assign this service account the roles/storage.objectCreator role on the storage bucket residing in Project B.

1. Determine the default App Engine service account ([email protected]) in Project A.2. Deploy the Cloud Function with the default App Engine service account in Project A.3. Assign the default App Engine service account the roles/storage.objectCreator role on the storage bucket residing in Project B.

1. Determine the default App Engine service account ([email protected]) in Project B.2. Deploy the Cloud Function with the default App Engine service account in Project A.3. Assign the default App Engine service account the roles/storage.objectCreator role on the storage bucket residing in Project B.

questions.correct_text: 1. Create a Google service account in Project A2. Deploy the Cloud Function with the service account in Project A.3. Assign this service account the roles/storage.objectCreator role on the storage bucket residing in Project B.
questions.explanation: Following least privilege, you create a dedicated user-managed service account in Project A (where the Cloud Function runs and acts as its identity), and then grant that service account only the roles/storage.objectCreator role on the specific bucket in Project B. This grants exactly the permission needed (create objects) on exactly the target resource, and cross-project IAM works because IAM bindings can reference principals from any project. Option A places the service account in Project B, which is unnecessary and does not match where the function executes. Options C and D rely on the default App Engine service account, which typically holds broad project-wide roles and therefore violates least privilege; option D also incorrectly uses Project B's default account to deploy a function in Project A.

questions.explanation_pt: Seguindo o princípio do menor privilégio, você cria uma service account dedicada gerenciada pelo usuário no Project A (onde a Cloud Function é executada e atua como sua identidade) e, em seguida, concede a essa service account apenas o papel roles/storage.objectCreator no bucket específico do Project B. Isso concede exatamente a permissão necessária (criar objetos) exatamente no recurso de destino, e o IAM entre projetos funciona porque os bindings de IAM podem referenciar principals de qualquer projeto. A opção A coloca a service account no Project B, o que é desnecessário e não corresponde ao local onde a função é executada. As opções C e D dependem da service account padrão do App Engine, que normalmente possui papéis amplos em todo o projeto e, portanto, viola o menor privilégio; a opção D também usa incorretamente a conta padrão do Project B para implantar uma função no Project A.

questions.question: A governmental regulation was recently passed that affects your application. For compliance purposes, you are now required to send a duplicate of specific application logs from your application’s project to a project that is restricted to the security team. What should you do?

options.text: Create user-defined log buckets in the security team’s project. Configure a Cloud Logging sink to route your application’s logs to log buckets in the security team’s project.
Create a job that copies the logs from the _Required log bucket into the security team’s log bucket in their project.
Modify the _Default log bucket sink rules to reroute the logs into the security team’s log bucket.
Create a job that copies the System Event logs from the _Required log bucket into the security team’s log bucket in their project.

questions.correct_text: Create user-defined log buckets in the security team’s project. Configure a Cloud Logging sink to route your application’s logs to log buckets in the security team’s project.
questions.explanation: Cloud Logging aggregated or project-level sinks can route a filtered subset of logs to a destination in another project, including user-defined log buckets owned by the security team. By creating log buckets in the security team's restricted project and configuring a logging sink with a filter for the specific application logs, you keep the originals in place while sending duplicates to the secured project for compliance. Option B and D rely on custom copy jobs, which are operationally fragile, not real-time, and reinvent built-in sink functionality; D also targets only System Event logs. Option C modifies the _Default sink to reroute (move) logs, which would remove them from the original project and only affects default-routed logs rather than duplicating the required application logs.

topics.exam_domain_name: Integrar aplicações com serviços do Google Cloud

questions.explanation_pt: Os sinks agregados ou de nível de projeto do Cloud Logging podem rotear um subconjunto filtrado de logs para um destino em outro projeto, incluindo log buckets definidos pelo usuário e de propriedade da equipe de segurança. Ao criar log buckets no projeto restrito da equipe de segurança e configurar um logging sink com um filtro para os logs específicos da aplicação, você mantém os originais no lugar enquanto envia duplicatas para o projeto protegido para fins de conformidade. As opções B e D dependem de jobs de cópia personalizados, que são operacionalmente frágeis, não são em tempo real e reinventam a funcionalidade nativa do sink; a D também tem como alvo apenas os logs de System Event. A opção C modifica o sink _Default para redirecionar (mover) os logs, o que os removeria do projeto original e afeta apenas os logs roteados por padrão, em vez de duplicar os logs de aplicação necessários.

questions.question: You plan to deploy a new Go application to Cloud Run. The source code is stored in Cloud Source Repositories. You need to configure a fully managed, automated, continuous deployment pipeline that runs when a source code commit is made. You want to use the simplest deployment solution. What should you do?

options.text: Configure a cron job on your workstations to periodically run gcloud run deploy --source in the working directory.
Configure a Jenkins trigger to run the container build and deploy process for each source code commit to Cloud Source Repositories.
Configure continuous deployment of new revisions from a source repository for Cloud Run using buildpacks.
Use Cloud Build with a trigger configured to run the container build and deploy process for each source code commit to Cloud Source Repositories.

questions.correct_text: Configure continuous deployment of new revisions from a source repository for Cloud Run using buildpacks.
questions.explanation: Cloud Build provides native, fully managed continuous deployment: you create a build trigger that watches the Cloud Source Repositories repo and, on each commit, builds the container and deploys the new revision to Cloud Run. This is the standard, fully automated Google-managed pipeline that fires on source commits. Option A uses a cron job on workstations, which is neither fully managed nor reliably triggered by commits. Option B introduces Jenkins, adding self-managed infrastructure rather than a managed solution. Option C's continuous-deployment-from-source feature for Cloud Run is geared toward GitHub/GitLab/Bitbucket connections rather than Cloud Source Repositories and is less aligned with the commit-triggered managed pipeline described here, making Cloud Build with a trigger the best fit.

topics.exam_domain_name: Configurar aplicações cloud-native para deployment

questions.explanation_pt: O Cloud Build fornece implantação contínua nativa e totalmente gerenciada: você cria um build trigger que observa o repositório do Cloud Source Repositories e, a cada commit, constrói o container e implanta a nova revisão no Cloud Run. Esse é o pipeline padrão, totalmente automatizado e gerenciado pelo Google, que dispara a partir dos commits de código-fonte. A opção A usa um job cron em workstations, que não é totalmente gerenciado nem acionado de forma confiável por commits. A opção B introduz o Jenkins, adicionando infraestrutura autogerenciada em vez de uma solução gerenciada. O recurso de implantação contínua a partir do código-fonte da opção C para o Cloud Run é voltado para conexões com GitHub/GitLab/Bitbucket, e não com o Cloud Source Repositories, sendo menos alinhado com o pipeline gerenciado acionado por commit descrito aqui, o que torna o Cloud Build com um trigger a melhor opção.

questions.question: You have an application running in a production Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster. You use Cloud Deploy to automatically deploy your application to your production GKE cluster. As part of your development process, you are planning to make frequent changes to the application’s source code and need to select the tools to test the changes before pushing them to your remote source code repository. Your toolset must meet the following requirements:• Test frequent local changes automatically.• Local deployment emulates production deployment.Which tools should you use to test building and running a container on your laptop using minimal resources?

options.text: Docker Compose and dockerd
Terraform and kubeadm
Minikube and Skaffold
kaniko and Tekton

questions.correct_text: Minikube and Skaffold
questions.explanation: Minikube runs a lightweight local Kubernetes cluster that emulates the production GKE deployment using minimal laptop resources, and Skaffold watches your source for changes to automatically rebuild, push, and redeploy containers, giving the fast inner development loop the requirements call for. Together they let you test frequent local changes automatically against a Kubernetes-like environment. Option A (Docker Compose and dockerd) runs plain containers but does not emulate Kubernetes/GKE deployment. Option B (Terraform and kubeadm) is for provisioning infrastructure and bootstrapping clusters, not iterative local app testing. Option D (kaniko and Tekton) targets in-cluster image building and CI pipelines rather than a minimal local develop-and-test loop.

topics.exam_domain_name: Construir e testar aplicações

questions.explanation_pt: O Minikube executa um cluster Kubernetes local e leve que emula a implantação de produção do GKE usando recursos mínimos do laptop, e o Skaffold observa seu código-fonte em busca de alterações para reconstruir, fazer push e reimplantar containers automaticamente, proporcionando o ciclo interno de desenvolvimento rápido que os requisitos exigem. Juntos, eles permitem testar mudanças locais frequentes automaticamente em um ambiente semelhante ao Kubernetes. A opção A (Docker Compose e dockerd) executa containers simples, mas não emula a implantação do Kubernetes/GKE. A opção B (Terraform e kubeadm) serve para provisionar infraestrutura e inicializar clusters, e não para testes iterativos de aplicação localmente. A opção D (kaniko e Tekton) tem como foco a construção de imagens dentro do cluster e pipelines de CI, em vez de um ciclo mínimo local de desenvolvimento e teste.

questions.question: You are deploying a Python application to Cloud Run using Cloud Source Repositories and Cloud Build. The Cloud Build pipeline is shown below:You want to optimize deployment times and avoid unnecessary steps. What should you do?

options.text: Remove the step that pushes the container to Artifact Registry.
Deploy a new Docker registry in a VPC, and use Cloud Build worker pools inside the VPC to run the build pipeline.
Store image artifacts in a Cloud Storage bucket in the same region as the Cloud Run instance.
Add the --cache-from argument to the Docker build step in your build config file.

questions.correct_text: Add the --cache-from argument to the Docker build step in your build config file.
questions.explanation: Adding the --cache-from argument to the Docker build step tells Cloud Build to use a previously built image as a cache source, so unchanged layers are reused instead of rebuilt, which significantly reduces build and deployment times. Option A is wrong because removing the push to Artifact Registry would break the deployment, since Cloud Run pulls the container image from the registry. Option C is incorrect because Cloud Run deploys from container registries (Artifact Registry), not from raw image artifacts stored in Cloud Storage. Option B adds VPC worker pools and a private registry, which addresses network isolation rather than build speed and introduces unnecessary complexity. The --cache-from approach is the standard, low-effort optimization for repeated Docker builds.

topics.exam_domain_name: Construir e testar aplicações

questions.explanation_pt: Adicionar o argumento --cache-from à etapa de build do Docker faz com que o Cloud Build use uma imagem construída anteriormente como fonte de cache, de modo que as camadas inalteradas são reutilizadas em vez de reconstruídas, o que reduz significativamente os tempos de build e implantação. A opção A está errada porque remover o push para o Artifact Registry quebraria a implantação, já que o Cloud Run obtém a imagem do container a partir do registry. A opção C está incorreta porque o Cloud Run implanta a partir de container registries (Artifact Registry), e não a partir de artefatos de imagem brutos armazenados no Cloud Storage. A opção B adiciona VPC worker pools e um registry privado, o que aborda o isolamento de rede em vez da velocidade do build e introduz complexidade desnecessária. A abordagem --cache-from é a otimização padrão e de baixo esforço para builds repetidos do Docker.

questions.question: You are developing an event-driven application. You have created a topic to receive messages sent to Pub/Sub. You want those messages to be processed in real time. You need the application to be independent from any other system and only incur costs when new messages arrive. How should you configure the architecture?

options.text: Deploy the application on Compute Engine. Use a Pub/Sub push subscription to process new messages in the topic.
Deploy your code on Cloud Functions. Use a Pub/Sub trigger to invoke the Cloud Function. Use the Pub/Sub API to create a pull subscription to the Pub/Sub topic and read messages from it.
Deploy the application on Google Kubernetes Engine. Use the Pub/Sub API to create a pull subscription to the Pub/Sub topic and read messages from it.
Deploy your code on Cloud Functions. Use a Pub/Sub trigger to handle new messages in the topic.

questions.correct_text: Deploy your code on Cloud Functions. Use a Pub/Sub trigger to handle new messages in the topic.
questions.explanation: Deploying the code on Cloud Functions with a Pub/Sub trigger gives a fully serverless, event-driven architecture that scales to zero, so you only incur cost when messages arrive, and the function is invoked automatically and independently as each message is published. Option D is correct because the Pub/Sub trigger natively manages the subscription and delivers messages to the function in real time. Option B is wrong because it redundantly creates a separate pull subscription via the API on top of the trigger, conflicting with the trigger-managed delivery. Options A and C use Compute Engine and GKE, which require always-on infrastructure that incurs cost even when idle, violating the pay-only-on-message requirement.

topics.exam_domain_name: Projetar apps cloud-native escaláveis, seguras e confiáveis

questions.explanation_pt: Implantar o código no Cloud Functions com um gatilho do Pub/Sub oferece uma arquitetura totalmente serverless e orientada a eventos, que escala até zero, de modo que você só tem custo quando as mensagens chegam, e a função é invocada automática e independentemente conforme cada mensagem é publicada. A opção D está correta porque o gatilho do Pub/Sub gerencia nativamente a assinatura (subscription) e entrega as mensagens à função em tempo real. A opção B está errada porque cria de forma redundante uma assinatura pull separada via API por cima do gatilho, conflitando com a entrega gerenciada pelo gatilho. As opções A e C usam Compute Engine e GKE, que exigem infraestrutura sempre ligada, gerando custo mesmo quando ociosa, violando o requisito de pagar apenas por mensagem.

questions.question: You have an application running on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). The application is currently using a logging library and is outputting to standard output. You need to export the logs to Cloud Logging, and you need the logs to include metadata about each request. You want to use the simplest method to accomplish this. What should you do?

options.text: Change your application’s logging library to the Cloud Logging library, and configure your application to export logs to Cloud Logging.
Update your application to output logs in JSON format, and add the necessary metadata to the JSON.
Update your application to output logs in CSV format, and add the necessary metadata to the CSV.
Install the Fluent Bit agent on each of your GKE nodes, and have the agent export all logs from /var/log.

questions.correct_text: Update your application to output logs in JSON format, and add the necessary metadata to the JSON.
questions.explanation: Switching to the Cloud Logging client library lets the application send structured log entries directly to Cloud Logging, including request metadata such as severity, trace, and labels, with minimal code change and the most reliable handling of metadata. Option B (JSON to stdout) works for structured logging that the GKE logging agent ingests, but attaching the full request metadata manually is more error-prone and less direct than the library, which is purpose-built for this. Option C is incorrect because Cloud Logging does not parse CSV into structured fields. Option D installs Fluent Bit manually, but GKE already runs a managed logging agent, so this adds unnecessary operational overhead and does not by itself enrich logs with request metadata.

topics.exam_domain_name: Integrar aplicações com serviços do Google Cloud

questions.explanation_pt: Migrar para a biblioteca de cliente do Cloud Logging permite que a aplicação envie entradas de log estruturadas diretamente para o Cloud Logging, incluindo metadados da requisição como severity, trace e labels, com mudança mínima de código e o tratamento mais confiável de metadados. A opção B (JSON para stdout) funciona para logging estruturado que o agente de logging do GKE coleta, mas anexar manualmente os metadados completos da requisição é mais propenso a erros e menos direto do que a biblioteca, que foi feita exatamente para isso. A opção C está incorreta porque o Cloud Logging não interpreta CSV em campos estruturados. A opção D instala o Fluent Bit manualmente, mas o GKE já executa um agente de logging gerenciado, então isso adiciona sobrecarga operacional desnecessária e, por si só, não enriquece os logs com os metadados da requisição.

questions.question: You are working on a new application that is deployed on Cloud Run and uses Cloud Functions. Each time new features are added, new Cloud Functions and Cloud Run services are deployed. You use ENV variables to keep track of the services and enable interservice communication, but the maintenance of the ENV variables has become difficult. You want to implement dynamic discovery in a scalable way. What should you do?

options.text: Configure your microservices to use the Cloud Run Admin and Cloud Functions APIs to query for deployed Cloud Run services and Cloud Functions in the Google Cloud project.
Create a Service Directory namespace. Use API calls to register the services during deployment, and query during runtime.
Rename the Cloud Functions and Cloud Run services endpoint is using a well-documented naming convention.
Deploy Hashicorp Consul on a single Compute Engine instance. Register the services with Consul during deployment, and query during runtime.

questions.correct_text: Create a Service Directory namespace. Use API calls to register the services during deployment, and query during runtime.
questions.explanation: Service Directory is Google Cloud's managed service registry designed exactly for dynamic service discovery; services register their endpoints during deployment and clients resolve them at runtime, which scales without manual maintenance of ENV variables. Option B is correct because it removes the brittle env-var bookkeeping and provides a single authoritative source of service locations. Option A is workable but coupling microservices to the Cloud Run Admin and Cloud Functions management APIs is fragile, slower, and not a discovery mechanism. Option C (naming conventions) does not solve dynamic discovery and still requires manual coordination. Option D deploys self-managed Consul on a single VM, introducing a single point of failure and operational burden when a managed alternative exists.

topics.exam_domain_name: Projetar apps cloud-native escaláveis, seguras e confiáveis

questions.explanation_pt: O Service Directory é o registro de serviços gerenciado do Google Cloud, projetado exatamente para descoberta dinâmica de serviços; os serviços registram seus endpoints durante a implantação e os clientes os resolvem em tempo de execução, o que escala sem manutenção manual de variáveis de ambiente (ENV). A opção B está correta porque elimina o controle frágil de variáveis de ambiente e fornece uma única fonte autoritativa para a localização dos serviços. A opção A é viável, mas acoplar os microsserviços às APIs de gerenciamento do Cloud Run Admin e do Cloud Functions é frágil, mais lento e não é um mecanismo de descoberta. A opção C (convenções de nomenclatura) não resolve a descoberta dinâmica e ainda exige coordenação manual. A opção D implanta o Consul autogerenciado em uma única VM, introduzindo um ponto único de falha e carga operacional quando já existe uma alternativa gerenciada.

questions.question: You work for a financial services company that has a container-first approach. Your team develops microservices applications. A Cloud Build pipeline creates the container image, runs regression tests, and publishes the image to Artifact Registry. You need to ensure that only containers that have passed the regression tests are deployed to Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) clusters. You have already enabled Binary Authorization on the GKE clusters. What should you do next?

options.text: Create an attestor and a policy. After a container image has successfully passed the regression tests, use Cloud Build to run Kritis Signer to create an attestation for the container image.
Deploy Voucher Server and Voucher Client components. After a container image has successfully passed the regression tests, run Voucher Client as a step in the Cloud Build pipeline.
Set the Pod Security Standard level to Restricted for the relevant namespaces. Use Cloud Build to digitally sign the container images that have passed the regression tests.
Create an attestor and a policy. Create an attestation for the container images that have passed the regression tests as a step in the Cloud Build pipeline.

questions.correct_text: Create an attestor and a policy. After a container image has successfully passed the regression tests, use Cloud Build to run Kritis Signer to create an attestation for the container image.
questions.explanation: With Binary Authorization enabled, you must create an attestor and policy, then have a trusted process create an attestation for images that pass the tests; using Cloud Build to run Kritis Signer after the regression tests produces that attestation automatically within the pipeline. Option A is correct because Kritis Signer is the standard Google-supported tool to generate attestations as part of Cloud Build. Option D describes the right concept but is vague about how the attestation is created in the pipeline and omits the concrete signing mechanism. Option B references Voucher, a third-party Grafeas/Binary Authorization tool, which is not the native Google Cloud approach. Option C confuses Pod Security Standards (runtime workload security) with image attestation and does not satisfy the Binary Authorization policy requirement.

topics.exam_domain_name: Configurar aplicações cloud-native para deployment

questions.explanation_pt: Com o Binary Authorization habilitado, você precisa criar um attestor e uma política e, em seguida, ter um processo confiável que crie uma attestation para as imagens que passam nos testes; usar o Cloud Build para executar o Kritis Signer após os testes de regressão produz essa attestation automaticamente dentro do pipeline. A opção A está correta porque o Kritis Signer é a ferramenta padrão suportada pelo Google para gerar attestations como parte do Cloud Build. A opção D descreve o conceito certo, mas é vaga sobre como a attestation é criada no pipeline e omite o mecanismo concreto de assinatura. A opção B faz referência ao Voucher, uma ferramenta de terceiros para Grafeas/Binary Authorization, que não é a abordagem nativa do Google Cloud. A opção C confunde os Pod Security Standards (segurança de workload em tempo de execução) com a attestation de imagens e não satisfaz o requisito da política do Binary Authorization.

questions.question: You are reviewing and updating your Cloud Build steps to adhere to best practices. Currently, your build steps include:1. Pull the source code from a source repository.2. Build a container image3. Upload the built image to Artifact Registry.You need to add a step to perform a vulnerability scan of the built container image, and you want the results of the scan to be available to your deployment pipeline running in Google Cloud. You want to minimize changes that could disrupt other teams’ processes. What should you do?

options.text: Enable Binary Authorization, and configure it to attest that no vulnerabilities exist in a container image.
Upload the built container images to your Docker Hub instance, and scan them for vulnerabilities.
Enable the Container Scanning API in Artifact Registry, and scan the built container images for vulnerabilities.
Add Artifact Registry to your Aqua Security instance, and scan the built container images for vulnerabilities.

questions.correct_text: Enable the Container Scanning API in Artifact Registry, and scan the built container images for vulnerabilities.
questions.explanation: Enabling the Container Scanning API in Artifact Registry automatically scans images for vulnerabilities upon push and stores the results as metadata that is directly accessible to your deployment pipeline within Google Cloud, with minimal disruption since you already upload images to Artifact Registry. Binary Authorization (A) enforces deployment policies and relies on attestations, but it is a deployment-gate mechanism rather than the vulnerability scanner itself, so it does not directly produce scan results. Uploading to Docker Hub (B) or integrating a third-party Aqua Security instance (D) introduces external tooling and additional moving parts, increasing complexity and the risk of disrupting other teams' processes rather than minimizing it. The native Container Scanning integration is the least invasive, Google-recommended approach.

topics.exam_domain_name: Configurar aplicações cloud-native para deployment

questions.explanation_pt: Habilitar a Container Scanning API no Artifact Registry verifica automaticamente as imagens em busca de vulnerabilidades no momento do push e armazena os resultados como metadados que ficam diretamente acessíveis ao seu pipeline de implantação dentro do Google Cloud, com mínima interrupção, já que você já envia imagens para o Artifact Registry. O Binary Authorization (A) aplica políticas de implantação e depende de attestations, mas é um mecanismo de controle de implantação (deployment gate) e não o scanner de vulnerabilidades em si, então não produz diretamente os resultados da varredura. Enviar para o Docker Hub (B) ou integrar uma instância de terceiros do Aqua Security (D) introduz ferramentas externas e mais peças móveis, aumentando a complexidade e o risco de atrapalhar os processos de outras equipes em vez de minimizá-los. A integração nativa do Container Scanning é a abordagem menos invasiva e recomendada pelo Google.

questions.question: You are developing an online gaming platform as a microservices application on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). Users on social media are complaining about long loading times for certain URL requests to the application. You need to investigate performance bottlenecks in the application and identify which HTTP requests have a significantly high latency span in user requests. What should you do?

options.text: Configure GKE workload metrics using kubectl. Select all Pods to send their metrics to Cloud Monitoring. Create a custom dashboard of application metrics in Cloud Monitoring to determine performance bottlenecks of your GKE cluster.

Update your microservices to log HTTP request methods and URL paths to STDOUT. Use the logs router to send container logs to Cloud Logging. Create filters in Cloud Logging to evaluate the latency of user requests across different methods and URL paths.

Instrument your microservices by installing the OpenTelemetry tracing package. Update your application code to send traces to Trace for inspection and analysis. Create an analysis report on Trace to analyze user requests.

Install tcpdump on your GKE nodes. Run tcpdump to capture network traffic over an extended period of time to collect data. Analyze the data files using Wireshark to determine the cause of high latency.

questions.correct_text: Instrument your microservices by installing the OpenTelemetry tracing package. Update your application code to send traces to Trace for inspection and analysis. Create an analysis report on Trace to analyze user requests.
questions.explanation: Distributed tracing is the right tool to identify which specific HTTP requests have high latency spans across a microservices application. Instrumenting services with OpenTelemetry and sending traces to Cloud Trace lets you visualize the end-to-end request path, break down latency per span, and pinpoint the bottleneck service or operation. Workload metrics in Cloud Monitoring (A) provide aggregate resource and performance metrics but cannot attribute latency to individual request paths. Logging request methods and URLs to Cloud Logging (B) can capture data but is a manual, coarse approach that lacks span-level latency correlation across services. Running tcpdump and Wireshark (D) is a low-level network capture that is impractical at scale and does not map cleanly to application request latency.

questions.explanation_pt: O distributed tracing (rastreamento distribuído) é a ferramenta certa para identificar quais requisições HTTP específicas têm spans de alta latência em uma aplicação de microsserviços. Instrumentar os serviços com OpenTelemetry e enviar os traces para o Cloud Trace permite visualizar o caminho completo da requisição de ponta a ponta, detalhar a latência por span e localizar o serviço ou a operação que é o gargalo. As métricas de workload no Cloud Monitoring (A) fornecem métricas agregadas de recursos e desempenho, mas não conseguem atribuir a latência a caminhos individuais de requisição. Registrar os métodos e as URLs das requisições no Cloud Logging (B) pode capturar dados, mas é uma abordagem manual e grosseira, que não tem a correlação de latência em nível de span entre os serviços. Executar tcpdump e Wireshark (D) é uma captura de rede de baixo nível, impraticável em escala, e não se mapeia de forma limpa para a latência das requisições da aplicação.

questions.question: You need to load-test a set of REST API endpoints that are deployed to Cloud Run. The API responds to HTTP POST requests. Your load tests must meet the following requirements:• Load is initiated from multiple parallel threads.• User traffic to the API originates from multiple source IP addresses.• Load can be scaled up using additional test instances.You want to follow Google-recommended best practices. How should you configure the load testing?

options.text: Create an image that has cURL installed, and configure cURL to run a test plan. Deploy the image in a managed instance group, and run one instance of the image for each VM.
Create an image that has cURL installed, and configure cURL to run a test plan. Deploy the image in an unmanaged instance group, and run one instance of the image for each VM.
Deploy a distributed load testing framework on a private Google Kubernetes Engine cluster. Deploy additional Pods as needed to initiate more traffic and support the number of concurrent users.
Download the container image of a distributed load testing framework on Cloud Shell. Sequentially start several instances of the container on Cloud Shell to increase the load on the API.

questions.correct_text: Deploy a distributed load testing framework on a private Google Kubernetes Engine cluster. Deploy additional Pods as needed to initiate more traffic and support the number of concurrent users.
questions.explanation: A distributed load testing framework deployed on GKE meets all the requirements: it can spawn multiple parallel threads, generate traffic from many Pods (and thus many source IPs across nodes), and scale horizontally by adding more Pods as load demands increase. The Google-recommended pattern for distributed load testing uses a container-based framework on Kubernetes precisely for this elasticity. cURL on managed or unmanaged instance groups (A, B) is a simplistic single-request tool that is not designed for orchestrated, scalable load generation. Running container instances sequentially on Cloud Shell (D) is severely resource-constrained and cannot produce realistic parallel, multi-source, scalable load.
