A regra deve ser aplicada à política do projeto de produção (não ao projeto de UAT), porque o objetivo é bloquear imagens não atestadas especificamente em produção. As opções A e B armazenam a chave de forma insegura como um secret do Kubernetes, e a C aplica a regra ao projeto de UAT, o que não protegeria a produção.

questions.question: You work for a company that operates an ecommerce website. You are developing a new integration that will manage all order fulfillment steps after orders are placed. You have created multiple Cloud Functions to process each order. You need to orchestrate the execution of the functions, using the output of each function to determine the flow. You want to minimize the latency of this process. What should you do?

options.text: Use Workflows to call the functions, and use callbacks to handle the execution logic.
Use Workflows to call the functions, and use conditional jumps to handle the execution logic.
Use Cloud Composer to call the functions, and use an Apache Airflow HTTP operator to handle the execution logic.
Use Cloud Composer to call the functions, and use an Apache Airflow operator to handle the execution logic.

questions.correct_text: Use Workflows to call the functions, and use conditional jumps to handle the execution logic.
questions.explanation: Workflows is the right serverless orchestrator for sequencing Cloud Functions where each step's output drives the next decision, and conditional jumps (switch/next steps) let you branch the flow based on function results with very low latency. Callbacks (A) are designed for pausing a workflow to wait for an external event or human approval, which adds latency rather than minimizing it and does not fit pure function-to-function branching. Cloud Composer (C and D) runs Apache Airflow, which is built for scheduled batch data pipelines and carries higher latency and operational overhead from its always-on environment, making it unsuitable for a low-latency, event-driven order fulfillment flow.

questions.explanation_pt: O Workflows é o orquestrador serverless correto para sequenciar Cloud Functions onde a saída de cada etapa direciona a próxima decisão, e os saltos condicionais (etapas switch/next) permitem ramificar o fluxo com base nos resultados das funções com latência muito baixa. Callbacks (A) são projetados para pausar um workflow à espera de um evento externo ou de aprovação humana, o que adiciona latência em vez de minimizá-la e não se adequa à ramificação pura de função para função. O Cloud Composer (C e D) executa o Apache Airflow, que é feito para pipelines de dados em lote agendados e carrega maior latência e sobrecarga operacional devido ao seu ambiente sempre ativo, tornando-o inadequado para um fluxo de processamento de pedidos de baixa latência e orientado a eventos.

questions.question: You are currently pushing container images to Artifact Registry and deploying a containerized microservices application to GKE. After deploying the application, you notice that the services do not behave as expected. You use the kubectl get pods command to inspect the state of the application Pods, and discover that one of the Pods has a state of CrashLoopBackoff. How should you troubleshoot the Pod?

options.text: Connect to the problematic Pod by running the kubectl exec -it POD_NAME - /bin/bash command where the POD_NAME parameter is the name of the problematic Pod. Inspect the logs in the /var/log/messages folder to determine the root cause.

Execute the gcloud projects get-iam-policy PROJECT_ID command where the PROJECT_ID parameter is the name of the project where your Artifact Registry resides. Inspect the IAM bindings of the node pool s service account. Validate if the service account has the roles/artifactregistry.reader role.

Run the kubectl logs POD_NAME command where the POD_NAME parameter is the name of the problematic Pod. Analyze the logs of the Pod from previous runs to determine the root cause of failed start attempts of the Pod.

In the Google Cloud console, navigate to Cloud Logging in the project of the cluster’s VPC. Enter a filter to show denied egress traffic to the Private Google Access CIDR range. Validate if egress traffic is denied from your GKE cluster to the Private Google Access CIDR range.

questions.correct_text: Run the kubectl logs POD_NAME command where the POD_NAME parameter is the name of the problematic Pod. Analyze the logs of the Pod from previous runs to determine the root cause of failed start attempts of the Pod.
questions.explanation: A CrashLoopBackOff means the container starts and then repeatedly exits, so the correct first step is to read the application's own output with kubectl logs POD_NAME, including logs from the previous (crashed) instance via the --previous flag, to find why startup fails. Using kubectl exec (A) typically fails on a crashing Pod because no container is running to attach to, and /var/log/messages is not where containerized apps write their stdout/stderr. Checking the node pool service account's Artifact Registry IAM (B) would relate to ImagePullBackOff, not a container that successfully starts and then crashes. Investigating denied egress to the Private Google Access range (D) addresses network connectivity, which is not the indicated symptom.

topics.exam_domain_name: Configurar aplicações cloud-native para deployment

questions.explanation_pt: Um CrashLoopBackOff significa que o container inicia e depois sai repetidamente, então o primeiro passo correto é ler a própria saída da aplicação com kubectl logs POD_NAME, incluindo os logs da instância anterior (que falhou) por meio da flag --previous, para descobrir por que a inicialização falha. Usar kubectl exec (A) normalmente falha em um Pod que está travando, porque não há container em execução para se conectar, e /var/log/messages não é onde as aplicações em container gravam seu stdout/stderr. Verificar o IAM do Artifact Registry da conta de serviço do node pool (B) estaria relacionado a um ImagePullBackOff, não a um container que inicia com sucesso e depois trava. Investigar egress negado para o intervalo do Private Google Access (D) trata de conectividade de rede, que não é o sintoma indicado.

questions.question: You use Cloud Build to build and test container images prior to deploying them to Cloud Run. Your images are stored in Artifact Registry. You need to ensure that only container images that have passed testing are deployed. You want to minimize operational overhead. What should you do?

options.text: Deploy a new revision to a Cloud Run service. Assign a tag that allows access to the revision at a specific URL without serving traffic. Test that revision again. Migrate the traffic to the Cloud Run service after you confirm that the new revision is performing as expected.

Enable Binary Authorization on your Cloud Run service. Create an attestation if the container image has passed all tests. Configure Binary Authorization to allow only images with appropriate attestation to be deployed to the Cloud Run service.
Create a GKE cluster. Verify that all tests have passed, and then deploy the image to the GKE cluster.
Configure build provenance on your Cloud Build pipeline. Verify that all the tests have passed, and then deploy the image to a Cloud Run service.

questions.correct_text: Enable Binary Authorization on your Cloud Run service. Create an attestation if the container image has passed all tests. Configure Binary Authorization to allow only images with appropriate attestation to be deployed to the Cloud Run service.
questions.explanation: Cloud Run supports Binary Authorization, so enabling it and creating an attestation only for images that pass testing lets you enforce a policy that allows only attested images to be deployed, with minimal operational overhead. This automatically blocks any untested image at deploy time. Tagging a revision without serving traffic (A) is a controlled rollout technique but does not actually prevent untested images from being deployed. Switching to GKE (C) adds unnecessary complexity for a Cloud Run workload. Build provenance (D) records how an image was built but does not by itself enforce that only tested images can be deployed, so it provides no deployment-time gate.

topics.exam_domain_name: Configurar aplicações cloud-native para deployment

questions.explanation_pt: O Cloud Run oferece suporte ao Binary Authorization, então habilitá-lo e criar uma atestação apenas para imagens que passam nos testes permite aplicar uma política que autoriza somente imagens atestadas a serem implantadas, com sobrecarga operacional mínima. Isso bloqueia automaticamente qualquer imagem não testada no momento da implantação. Marcar uma revisão sem servir tráfego (A) é uma técnica de rollout controlado, mas não impede de fato que imagens não testadas sejam implantadas. Migrar para o GKE (C) adiciona complexidade desnecessária para uma carga de trabalho do Cloud Run. A proveniência de build (D) registra como uma imagem foi construída, mas por si só não garante que apenas imagens testadas possam ser implantadas, portanto não fornece um controle no momento da implantação.

questions.question: You are developing a scalable web application for internal users. Your organization uses Google Workspace. You need to set up authentication to the application for the users, and then deploy the application on Google Cloud. You plan to use cloud-native features, and you want to minimize infrastructure management effort. What should you do? (Choose two.)

options.text: Create a Compute Engine VM, configure a web server, and deploy the application in a VPC.
Containerize the application, and deploy it as a Cloud Run service.
Configure Cloud SQL database with a table containing the users and password hashes. Add an authentication screen to ensure that only internal users can access the application.
Configure Identity Aware Proxy, and grant the roles/iap.httpsResourceAccessor IAM role to the users that need to access the application.
Configure Identity Aware Proxy, and grant the roles/iap.tunnelResourceAccessor IAM role to the users that need to access the application.

questions.correct_text: Containerize the application, and deploy it as a Cloud Run service. | Configure Identity Aware Proxy, and grant the roles/iap.httpsResourceAccessor IAM role to the users that need to access the application.
questions.explanation: Cloud Run (B) is a fully managed, cloud-native platform that runs containers without requiring you to manage servers, so it minimizes infrastructure effort and scales automatically. Identity-Aware Proxy (D) provides centralized authentication for web applications and integrates with Google Workspace identities; granting roles/iap.httpsResourceAccessor authorizes users to reach the application over HTTPS through IAP. A Compute Engine VM (A) requires you to manage the OS, web server, and patching, which contradicts the goal of minimal infrastructure management. Building a custom Cloud SQL password table with a homegrown auth screen (C) reinvents authentication insecurely instead of using Workspace identities. The roles/iap.tunnelResourceAccessor role (E) is for TCP forwarding/SSH tunnels, not for granting access to an HTTPS web application.

topics.exam_domain_name: Projetar apps cloud-native escaláveis, seguras e confiáveis

questions.explanation_pt: O Cloud Run (B) é uma plataforma totalmente gerenciada e nativa da nuvem que executa containers sem exigir que você gerencie servidores, minimizando o esforço de infraestrutura e escalando automaticamente. O Identity-Aware Proxy (D) fornece autenticação centralizada para aplicações web e integra-se às identidades do Google Workspace; conceder o papel roles/iap.httpsResourceAccessor autoriza os usuários a acessar a aplicação por HTTPS através do IAP. Uma VM do Compute Engine (A) exige que você gerencie o SO, o servidor web e a aplicação de patches, o que contraria o objetivo de mínimo gerenciamento de infraestrutura. Construir uma tabela personalizada de senhas no Cloud SQL com uma tela de autenticação caseira (C) reinventa a autenticação de forma insegura, em vez de usar as identidades do Workspace. O papel roles/iap.tunnelResourceAccessor (E) é para encaminhamento TCP/túneis SSH, não para conceder acesso a uma aplicação web HTTPS.

questions.question: You work for an ecommerce company, and you are responsible for deploying and managing multiple APIs. The operations team wants to review the traffic patterns in the orders-prod and users-prod environments. These are the only environments in the store-prod environment group. You want to follow Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: Assign the Apigee Analytics Viewer IAM role to the operations team for both environments. Use Cloud Monitoring to review traffic patterns.
Assign the Apigee Analytics Viewer IAM role to the operations team for both environments. Use Apigee API Analytics to review traffic patterns.
Assign the Apigee API Reader IAM role to each user of the operations team for both environments. Use Cloud Monitoring to review traffic patterns.
Assign the Apigee API Reader IAM role to each user of the operations team for both environments. Use Apigee API Analytics to review traffic patterns.

questions.correct_text: Assign the Apigee Analytics Viewer IAM role to the operations team for both environments. Use Apigee API Analytics to review traffic patterns.
questions.explanation: The Apigee Analytics Viewer role grants read access to API analytics data, which is exactly what the operations team needs to review traffic patterns, and Apigee API Analytics is the purpose-built tool for visualizing proxy traffic, latency, and error trends per environment. Options C and D use the Apigee API Reader role, which is intended for viewing API proxy configuration and runtime resources rather than analytics dashboards, so it does not align with the least-privilege need to view traffic data. Cloud Monitoring (A and C) surfaces general infrastructure and custom metrics but is not the recommended tool for analyzing Apigee API traffic patterns, which are richer in Apigee API Analytics. Therefore assigning Analytics Viewer plus using Apigee API Analytics (B) follows Google-recommended practice.

topics.exam_domain_name: Integrar aplicações com serviços do Google Cloud

questions.explanation_pt: A role Apigee Analytics Viewer concede acesso de leitura aos dados de analytics de APIs, que é exatamente o que a equipe de operações precisa para revisar padrões de tráfego, e o Apigee API Analytics é a ferramenta criada especificamente para visualizar tráfego de proxy, latência e tendências de erros por ambiente. As opções C e D usam a role Apigee API Reader, que se destina a visualizar a configuração de proxies de API e recursos de runtime, e não os dashboards de analytics, portanto não atende à necessidade de privilégio mínimo para visualizar dados de tráfego. O Cloud Monitoring (A e C) expõe métricas gerais de infraestrutura e métricas personalizadas, mas não é a ferramenta recomendada para analisar padrões de tráfego de APIs do Apigee, que são mais ricos no Apigee API Analytics. Portanto, atribuir a role Analytics Viewer e usar o Apigee API Analytics (B) segue a prática recomendada pelo Google.

questions.question: You are migrating a containerized application to Cloud Run. You plan to use Cloud Build to build your container image and push it to Artifact Registry, and you plan to use Cloud Deploy to deploy the image to production. You need to ensure that only secure images are deployed to production. What should you do?

options.text: Use Cloud Armor in front of Cloud Run to protect the container image from threats.
Use Artifact Analysis to scan the image for vulnerabilities. Use Cloud Key Management Service to encrypt the image to be deployed to production.
Use Secret Manager to store the encrypted image. Deploy this image to production.
Use Binary Authorization to enforce a policy that only allows images that have been signed with a trusted key to be deployed to production.

questions.correct_text: Use Binary Authorization to enforce a policy that only allows images that have been signed with a trusted key to be deployed to production.
questions.explanation: Binary Authorization (D) is a deploy-time security control that enforces policies requiring container images to be signed by trusted attestors before they can run, ensuring only verified, secure images reach production. This directly satisfies the requirement to gate deployments to known-good images built through your pipeline. Cloud Armor (A) protects running services against network and web attacks but does nothing to validate image provenance or integrity. Cloud KMS encrypting an image (B) and Secret Manager storing an encrypted image (C) do not enforce deployment policy; Artifact Analysis scanning is useful for finding vulnerabilities but on its own does not block unsigned or untrusted images from being deployed, and Secret Manager is not designed to store container images at all.

topics.exam_domain_name: Configurar aplicações cloud-native para deployment

questions.explanation_pt: O Binary Authorization (D) é um controle de segurança em tempo de implantação que aplica políticas exigindo que as imagens de contêiner sejam assinadas por atestadores confiáveis antes que possam ser executadas, garantindo que apenas imagens verificadas e seguras cheguem à produção. Isso atende diretamente ao requisito de restringir as implantações a imagens conhecidas e confiáveis criadas pelo seu pipeline. O Cloud Armor (A) protege serviços em execução contra ataques de rede e web, mas não faz nada para validar a procedência ou integridade da imagem. O Cloud KMS criptografando uma imagem (B) e o Secret Manager armazenando uma imagem criptografada (C) não aplicam política de implantação; a varredura do Artifact Analysis é útil para encontrar vulnerabilidades, mas por si só não bloqueia a implantação de imagens não assinadas ou não confiáveis, e o Secret Manager não foi projetado para armazenar imagens de contêiner.

questions.question: Your team uses Cloud Storage for a video and image application that was recently migrated to Google Cloud. Following a viral surge, users are reporting application instability, coinciding with a 10x increase in HTTP 429 error codes from Cloud Storage APIs. You need to resolve the errors and establish a long-term solution. You want to ensure that the application remains stable if the load increases again in the future. What should you do?

options.text: Optimize the application code to reduce unnecessary calls to Cloud Storage APIs to prevent HTTP 429 errors.

Compress the video and images files to reduce their size, and minimize storage costs and bandwidth usage. Implement a custom throttling mechanism in the application that limits the number of concurrent API calls.
Migrate all image and video data to Firestore. Replace the Cloud Storage APIs in the application code with the new Firestore database.
Implement a retry strategy with exponential backoff for requests that encounter HTTP 429 errors.

questions.correct_text: Implement a retry strategy with exponential backoff for requests that encounter HTTP 429 errors.
questions.explanation: HTTP 429 (Too Many Requests) from Cloud Storage indicates rate limiting, and the Google-recommended way to handle these transient throttling responses is to retry with exponential backoff (D), which spreads retries over increasing intervals so the application stays stable as Cloud Storage automatically scales request capacity over time. Simply optimizing code to reduce calls (A) may help marginally but does not provide a robust mechanism to absorb future load spikes and does not properly handle the 429 responses that still occur. Compressing files plus a custom throttling mechanism (B) addresses cost and concurrency but does not correctly respond to 429 errors and limits legitimate throughput. Migrating media to Firestore (C) is inappropriate because Firestore is a document database, not object storage for large video and image binaries, and would be costly and unsuitable.

topics.exam_domain_name: Projetar apps cloud-native escaláveis, seguras e confiáveis

questions.explanation_pt: O HTTP 429 (Too Many Requests) do Cloud Storage indica limitação de taxa (rate limiting), e a maneira recomendada pelo Google de lidar com essas respostas transitórias de throttling é tentar novamente com exponential backoff (D), que distribui as novas tentativas em intervalos crescentes para que a aplicação permaneça estável enquanto o Cloud Storage escala automaticamente a capacidade de requisições ao longo do tempo. Simplesmente otimizar o código para reduzir as chamadas (A) pode ajudar marginalmente, mas não fornece um mecanismo robusto para absorver futuros picos de carga e não trata adequadamente as respostas 429 que ainda ocorrem. Comprimir arquivos e usar um mecanismo de throttling personalizado (B) aborda custo e concorrência, mas não responde corretamente aos erros 429 e limita a vazão legítima. Migrar a mídia para o Firestore (C) é inadequado porque o Firestore é um banco de dados de documentos, não um armazenamento de objetos para grandes binários de vídeo e imagem, e seria caro e inadequado.

questions.question: You are developing a container build pipeline for an application hosted on GKE. You have the following requirements:• Only images that are created using your build pipeline should be deployed on your GKE cluster.• All code and build artifacts should remain within your environment and protected from data exfiltration.How should you build the pipeline?

options.text: 1. Create a build pipeline by using Cloud Build with the default worker pool.2. Deploy container images to a private container registry in your VPC.3. Create a VPC firewall policy in your project that denies all egress and ingress traffic to public networks.

1. Create a build pipeline by using Cloud Build with a private worker pool.2. Use VPC Service Controls to place all components and services in your CI/CD pipeline inside a security perimeter.3. Configure your GKE cluster to only allow container images signed by Binary Authorization.

1. Create a build pipeline by using Cloud Build with a private worker pool.2. Configure the CI/CD pipeline to build container images and store them in Artifact Registry.3. Configure Artifact Registry to encrypt container images by using customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK).

1. Create a build pipeline by using Cloud Build with the default worker pool.2. Configure the CI/CD pipeline to build container images and store them in Artifact Registry.3. Configure your GKE cluster to only allow container images signed by Binary Authorization.

questions.correct_text: 1. Create a build pipeline by using Cloud Build with a private worker pool.2. Use VPC Service Controls to place all components and services in your CI/CD pipeline inside a security perimeter.3. Configure your GKE cluster to only allow container images signed by Binary Authorization.
questions.explanation: A Cloud Build private worker pool runs builds inside your VPC so build traffic and artifacts stay within your environment, VPC Service Controls create a security perimeter around the CI/CD services to prevent data exfiltration, and Binary Authorization ensures the GKE cluster only deploys images that were signed by your pipeline (B). This combination satisfies both requirements: provenance enforcement and exfiltration protection. Options A and D use the default worker pool, which runs in a Google-managed tenant project rather than your VPC, so it does not keep all build activity within your environment. Option A relies only on a firewall policy and lacks any mechanism to guarantee that only pipeline-built images are deployed. Option C uses a private worker pool but relies on CMEK encryption, which protects data at rest but does not enforce that only authorized images are deployed nor establish a perimeter against exfiltration.

topics.exam_domain_name: Configurar aplicações cloud-native para deployment

questions.explanation_pt: Um private worker pool do Cloud Build executa as builds dentro da sua VPC, de modo que o tráfego e os artefatos da build permanecem no seu ambiente; o VPC Service Controls cria um perímetro de segurança em torno dos serviços de CI/CD para evitar a exfiltração de dados; e o Binary Authorization garante que o cluster GKE só implante imagens que foram assinadas pelo seu pipeline (B). Essa combinação atende a ambos os requisitos: aplicação da procedência e proteção contra exfiltração. As opções A e D usam o worker pool padrão, que é executado em um projeto de tenant gerenciado pelo Google em vez da sua VPC, portanto não mantém toda a atividade de build dentro do seu ambiente. A opção A depende apenas de uma política de firewall e não tem nenhum mecanismo para garantir que apenas imagens criadas pelo pipeline sejam implantadas. A opção C usa um private worker pool, mas depende da criptografia CMEK, que protege os dados em repouso, mas não impõe que apenas imagens autorizadas sejam implantadas nem estabelece um perímetro contra exfiltração.

questions.question: You are a developer at a company that operates an ecommerce website. The website stores the customer order data in a Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL database. Data scientists on the marketing team access this data to run their reports. Every time they run these reports, the website's performance is negatively affected. You want to provide access to up-to-date customer order datasets without affecting your website. What should you do?

options.text: Configure Cloud Scheduler to run an hourly Cloud Function that exports the data from the Cloud SQL database into CSV format and sends the data to a Cloud Storage bucket.
Set up a Bigtable table for the data science team. Configure the application to perform dual writes to both Cloud SQL and Bigtable simultaneously.
Set up a BigQuery dataset for the data science team. Configure Datastream to replicate the relevant Cloud SQL tables in BigQuery.
Create a clone of the PostgreSQL database instance for the data science team. Schedule a job to create a new clone every 15 minutes.

questions.correct_text: Set up a BigQuery dataset for the data science team. Configure Datastream to replicate the relevant Cloud SQL tables in BigQuery.
questions.explanation: Datastream provides serverless change data capture (CDC) that continuously replicates changes from Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL into BigQuery in near real time, giving the data scientists up-to-date data in an analytics-optimized warehouse without their queries touching the operational database. This isolates the heavy reporting workload from the production website, eliminating the performance impact. The hourly CSV export to Cloud Storage (A) is batch, stale by up to an hour, and still loads the source database during export, and CSV in a bucket is not a query-friendly dataset. Dual writes to Bigtable (B) add application complexity, are error-prone for consistency, and Bigtable is a NoSQL wide-column store unsuited to relational reporting. Cloning the instance every 15 minutes (D) is operationally expensive, not up to date between clones, and the clone operation itself strains the source.

topics.exam_domain_name: Integrar aplicações com serviços do Google Cloud

questions.explanation_pt: O Datastream fornece change data capture (CDC) serverless que replica continuamente as alterações do Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL para o BigQuery em near real time, oferecendo aos cientistas de dados dados atualizados em um data warehouse otimizado para analytics, sem que suas consultas toquem o banco de dados operacional. Isso isola a pesada carga de relatórios do site de produção, eliminando o impacto no desempenho. A exportação CSV horária para o Cloud Storage (A) é em batch, fica desatualizada em até uma hora e ainda carrega o banco de dados de origem durante a exportação, além de um CSV em um bucket não ser um dataset amigável para consultas. As gravações duplicadas (dual writes) no Bigtable (B) adicionam complexidade à aplicação, são propensas a erros de consistência, e o Bigtable é um armazenamento NoSQL wide-column inadequado para relatórios relacionais. Clonar a instância a cada 15 minutos (D) é operacionalmente caro, não fica atualizado entre os clones, e a própria operação de clonagem sobrecarrega a origem.

questions.question: You are developing a web application by using Cloud Run and Cloud Storage. You are notified of a production issue that you need to troubleshoot immediately. You need to implement a workaround that requires you to execute a script on a Git repository. Your corporate laptop is unavailable but you have your personal computer. You can use your corporate credentials to access the required Git repository and Google Cloud resources. You want to fix the issue as quickly and efficiently as possible while minimizing additional cost. What should you do?

options.text: Create and launch a workstation with Cloud Workstations on your personal computer. Authenticate and set up API access in the workstation. Clone the Git repository and execute the workaround script. Ensure that the issue has been fixed.

Install VS Code and the extension Cloud Code for VS Code on your personal computer. Check the Cloud Run logs in Cloud Code to confirm the error. Execute the workaround script. Ensure that the issue has been fixed.
Connect to the Google Cloud console and open Cloud Shell on your personal computer. Clone the Git repository and execute the workaround script. Ensure that the issue has been fixed.
Download and install the gcloud CLI on your personal computer. Authenticate and set up API access. Clone the Git repository and execute the workaround script. Ensure that the issue has been fixed.

questions.correct_text: Connect to the Google Cloud console and open Cloud Shell on your personal computer. Clone the Git repository and execute the workaround script. Ensure that the issue has been fixed.
questions.explanation: Cloud Shell is a browser-based environment accessible from any computer via the Google Cloud console; it comes pre-authenticated with your corporate credentials, includes the gcloud CLI and git, and requires no local installation or additional cost, making it the fastest way to clone the repo and run the workaround script from a personal machine. Creating a Cloud Workstation (A) provisions a managed VM that incurs cost and setup time, which is unnecessary for a quick fix. Installing VS Code with Cloud Code (B) requires local installation and authentication setup and does not by itself give you a place to execute the script efficiently. Installing the gcloud CLI locally (D) also requires download, install, and manual authentication, which is slower and puts corporate credentials on a personal device unnecessarily.

topics.exam_domain_name: Construir e testar aplicações

questions.explanation_pt: O Cloud Shell é um ambiente baseado em navegador, acessível de qualquer computador por meio do console do Google Cloud; ele já vem pré-autenticado com suas credenciais corporativas, inclui a gcloud CLI e o git, e não exige instalação local nem custo adicional, sendo a forma mais rápida de clonar o repositório e executar o script de contorno a partir de uma máquina pessoal. Criar um Cloud Workstation (A) provisiona uma VM gerenciada que gera custo e tempo de configuração, o que é desnecessário para uma correção rápida. Instalar o VS Code com o Cloud Code (B) exige instalação local e configuração de autenticação, e por si só não oferece um lugar para executar o script de forma eficiente. Instalar a gcloud CLI localmente (D) também exige download, instalação e autenticação manual, o que é mais lento e coloca credenciais corporativas em um dispositivo pessoal sem necessidade.

questions.question: You are using App Engine and Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL to develop an application. You want to test your application code locally before deploying new application versions to the development environment that is shared with other developers. You need to set up your App Engine local development environment to test your application while keeping all traffic to Cloud SQL instances encrypted and authenticated to Cloud IAM and PostgreSQL. What should you do before starting the local development server?

options.text: Install PostgreSQL on your local workstation. Run a local PostgreSQL database on your workstation. Configure the application to connect to a PostgreSQL instance on localhost.

Download and install the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy to your local development environment. Configure the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy to connect to the Cloud SQL instance and run the proxy. Configure the application to connect to a PostgreSQL instance on localhost.

Deploy a Compute Engine instance, and install HAProxy on the instance. Configure Cloud SQL Auth Proxy on the instance, and use the instance’s service account to authenticate to Cloud SQL. Configure the application to connect to the Compute Engine instance's IP address.

Configure your local development server to connect to the private IP address of the Cloud SQL instance. Encrypt database entries with a cryptographic library before submitting them to the database. Store the decryption key as an environment variable in App Engine.

questions.correct_text: Download and install the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy to your local development environment. Configure the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy to connect to the Cloud SQL instance and run the proxy. Configure the application to connect to a PostgreSQL instance on localhost.
questions.explanation: The Cloud SQL Auth Proxy is the recommended way to connect to a Cloud SQL instance from a local development environment; it establishes a secure, encrypted (TLS) tunnel and authenticates using IAM, then exposes the database on localhost so the application connects as if to a local PostgreSQL instance while still using IAM and PostgreSQL authentication. Running a local PostgreSQL database (A) does not test against the actual shared Cloud SQL data and provides no IAM-authenticated encrypted connection to Cloud SQL. Deploying a Compute Engine instance with HAProxy (C) is overly complex, adds cost, and is unnecessary for local testing. Connecting directly to the private IP (D) is generally not reachable from a local workstation, and rolling your own encryption with a key stored in App Engine does not meet the requirement of IAM-authenticated, transport-encrypted connections to Cloud SQL.

topics.exam_domain_name: Construir e testar aplicações

questions.explanation_pt: O Cloud SQL Auth Proxy é a maneira recomendada de se conectar a uma instância do Cloud SQL a partir de um ambiente de desenvolvimento local; ele estabelece um túnel seguro e criptografado (TLS) e autentica usando IAM, expondo então o banco de dados no localhost para que a aplicação se conecte como se fosse a uma instância local do PostgreSQL, ainda usando autenticação IAM e do PostgreSQL. Executar um banco de dados PostgreSQL local (A) não testa contra os dados reais compartilhados no Cloud SQL e não oferece uma conexão criptografada autenticada por IAM ao Cloud SQL. Implantar uma instância do Compute Engine com HAProxy (C) é excessivamente complexo, adiciona custo e é desnecessário para testes locais. Conectar-se diretamente ao IP privado (D) geralmente não é alcançável a partir de uma estação de trabalho local, e criar sua própria criptografia com uma chave armazenada no App Engine não atende ao requisito de conexões autenticadas por IAM e criptografadas em trânsito ao Cloud SQL.

questions.question: You are developing a public web application on Cloud Run. You expose the Cloud Run service directly with its public IP address. You are now running a load test to ensure that your application is resilient against high traffic loads. You notice that your application performs as expected when you initiate light traffic. However, when you generate high loads, your web server runs slowly and returns error messages. How should you troubleshoot this issue?

options.text: Check the network traffic to Cloud Run in Cloud Monitoring to validate whether a traffic spike occurred. If necessary, enable traffic splitting on the Cloud Run instance to route some of the traffic to a previous instance revision.
Check the min-instances value for your Cloud Run service. If necessary, increase the min-instances value to match the maximum number of virtual users in your load test.

Check whether Cloud Armor is detecting distributed denial of service (DDoS) attacks and is blocking traffic before the traffic is routed to your Cloud Run service. If necessary, disable any Cloud Armor policies in your project.
Check whether the Cloud Run service has scaled to a number of instances that equals the max-instances value. If necessary, increase the max-instances value.

questions.correct_text: Check whether the Cloud Run service has scaled to a number of instances that equals the max-instances value. If necessary, increase the max-instances value.
questions.explanation: Cloud Run scales out by creating container instances up to the configured max-instances limit; under high load the service can hit that ceiling, after which additional requests queue, slow down, and eventually fail, which matches the symptom of slow responses and errors only under heavy traffic. Verifying the instance count against max-instances and raising the limit directly addresses the bottleneck. Traffic splitting to a previous revision (A) is for gradual rollouts, not capacity, and does not add throughput. Increasing min-instances (B) only reduces cold-start latency by keeping idle instances warm; it does not raise the scaling ceiling. Disabling Cloud Armor (C) is speculative and would remove security protection, and the scenario describes a direct public IP with no indication that Cloud Armor is blocking legitimate load-test traffic.

topics.exam_domain_name: Projetar apps cloud-native escaláveis, seguras e confiáveis

questions.explanation_pt: O Cloud Run escala criando instâncias de contêiner até o limite configurado de max-instances; sob carga alta, o serviço pode atingir esse teto, após o qual requisições adicionais ficam na fila, ficam mais lentas e acabam falhando, o que corresponde ao sintoma de respostas lentas e erros apenas sob tráfego intenso. Verificar a contagem de instâncias em relação ao max-instances e aumentar o limite resolve diretamente o gargalo. A divisão de tráfego para uma revisão anterior (A) serve para implantações graduais, não para capacidade, e não adiciona throughput. Aumentar o min-instances (B) apenas reduz a latência de cold start ao manter instâncias ociosas aquecidas; não eleva o teto de escalonamento. Desativar o Cloud Armor (C) é especulativo e removeria a proteção de segurança, e o cenário descreve um IP público direto sem indicação de que o Cloud Armor esteja bloqueando o tráfego legítimo do teste de carga.

questions.question: You are developing a new image processing application that needs to handle various tasks, such as resizing, cropping, and watermarking images. You also need to monitor the workflow and ensure that it scales efficiently when there are large volumes of images. You want to automate the image processing tasks and workflow monitoring with the least effort. What should you do?

options.text: Employ Cloud Composer to manage the image processing workflows. Use Dataproc for workflow monitoring and analytics.
Use Cloud Run to deploy the image processing functions. Use Apigee to expose the API. Use Cloud Logging for workflow monitoring.
Implement Workflows to orchestrate the image processing tasks. Use Cloud Logging for workflow monitoring.
Use Cloud Build to trigger Cloud Functions for the image processing tasks. Use Cloud Monitoring for workflow monitoring.

questions.correct_text: Implement Workflows to orchestrate the image processing tasks. Use Cloud Logging for workflow monitoring.
questions.explanation: Workflows is a serverless orchestration service that chains together steps such as resizing, cropping, and watermarking by calling other services, scales automatically with the volume of images, and requires minimal operational effort, while Cloud Logging captures execution logs for monitoring the workflow. Cloud Composer with Dataproc (A) is heavier-weight, requires managing an Airflow environment and Spark/Hadoop clusters, and is overkill for lightweight image task orchestration. Cloud Run plus Apigee (B) introduces API management overhead that is unnecessary for an internal processing workflow and does not provide built-in orchestration. Cloud Build triggering Cloud Functions (D) repurposes a CI/CD tool for runtime task execution, which is not its intended use and offers no real workflow orchestration or monitoring of the task sequence.

topics.exam_domain_name: Integrar aplicações com serviços do Google Cloud

questions.explanation_pt: O Workflows é um serviço de orquestração serverless que encadeia etapas como redimensionar, recortar e aplicar marca d'água chamando outros serviços, escala automaticamente conforme o volume de imagens e exige esforço operacional mínimo, enquanto o Cloud Logging captura logs de execução para monitorar o fluxo de trabalho. O Cloud Composer com Dataproc (A) é mais pesado, exige gerenciar um ambiente Airflow e clusters Spark/Hadoop, e é exagerado para orquestrar tarefas leves de imagem. O Cloud Run mais Apigee (B) introduz sobrecarga de gerenciamento de API que é desnecessária para um fluxo de processamento interno e não fornece orquestração integrada. O Cloud Build acionando Cloud Functions (D) reaproveita uma ferramenta de CI/CD para execução de tarefas em runtime, o que não é seu uso pretendido e não oferece orquestração de fluxo de trabalho real nem monitoramento da sequência de tarefas.

questions.question: You are developing a web application that will be deployed to production on Cloud Run. The application consists of multiple microservices, some of which will be publicly accessible and others that will only be accessible after authentication by Google identities. You need to ensure that only authenticated users can access the restricted services, while allowing unrestricted access to the public services of the application. You want to use the most secure approach while minimizing management overhead and complexity. How should you configure access?

options.text: Enable Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) for all microservices. Develop a new microservice that checks the authentication requirements for each application and controls access to the respective services.
Enable Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) for all microservices. Manage access control lists (ACLs) for the restricted services, and configure allAuthenticatedUsers access to the public services.
Use Cloud Endpoints with Firebase Authentication for all microservices. Configure Firebase rules to manage access control lists (ACLs) for each service, allowing access to the public services.

Configure separate Cloud Run services for the public and restricted microservices. Enable Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) only for the restricted services, and configure the Cloud Run ingress settings to ‘Internal and Cloud Load Balancing’.

questions.correct_text: Configure separate Cloud Run services for the public and restricted microservices. Enable Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) only for the restricted services, and configure the Cloud Run ingress settings to ‘Internal and Cloud Load Balancing’.
questions.explanation: Separating public and restricted microservices into distinct Cloud Run services lets you apply IAP only where authentication is required, while leaving public services open, which is the cleanest and most secure design with minimal overhead. IAP requires traffic to come through an external HTTPS load balancer, so setting the restricted services' ingress to 'Internal and Cloud Load Balancing' ensures users cannot bypass IAP by hitting the run.app URL directly. Option A reinvents IAM with a custom auth microservice, adding unnecessary complexity and risk. Option B applies IAP to every service (including ones that should be public) and uses ACL/allAuthenticatedUsers in a way that contradicts the public-access requirement. Option C with Cloud Endpoints and Firebase rules is heavier to manage and not the recommended pattern for Google-identity-gated Cloud Run access.

topics.exam_domain_name: Projetar apps cloud-native escaláveis, seguras e confiáveis

questions.explanation_pt: Separar microsserviços públicos e restritos em serviços distintos do Cloud Run permite aplicar o IAP apenas onde a autenticação é necessária, deixando os serviços públicos abertos, o que é o design mais limpo e seguro com sobrecarga mínima. O IAP exige que o tráfego passe por um balanceador de carga HTTPS externo, então definir o ingress dos serviços restritos como 'Internal and Cloud Load Balancing' garante que os usuários não possam contornar o IAP acessando a URL run.app diretamente. A opção A reinventa o IAM com um microsserviço de autenticação personalizado, adicionando complexidade e risco desnecessários. A opção B aplica o IAP a todos os serviços (inclusive aos que deveriam ser públicos) e usa ACL/allAuthenticatedUsers de uma forma que contradiz o requisito de acesso público. A opção C com Cloud Endpoints e regras do Firebase é mais difícil de gerenciar e não é o padrão recomendado para acesso ao Cloud Run protegido por identidade Google.

questions.question: You are the lead developer for a company that provides a financial risk calculation API. The API is built on Cloud Run and has a gRPC interface. You frequently develop optimizations to the risk calculators. You want to enable these optimizations for select customers who registered to try out the optimizations prior to rolling out the optimization to all customers. Your CI/CD pipeline has built a new image and stored it in the Artifact Registry.Which rollout strategy should you use?

options.text: Migrate the traffic to the new service by setting Cloud Run’s traffic split based on the percentage of registered customers.
Migrate the traffic to the new service by using a blue/green deployment approach.
Migrate the traffic to the new service by using a feature flag for registered customers.
Migrate the traffic to the new service and enable session affinity for Cloud Run.

questions.correct_text: Migrate the traffic to the new service by using a feature flag for registered customers.
questions.explanation: Cloud Run's built-in traffic splitting and blue/green capabilities route traffic by percentage or by revision, but they cannot target a specific, identifiable set of registered customers. To enable an optimization only for select opted-in customers, a feature flag evaluated per request based on the customer's identity is the correct mechanism, giving precise, user-level control. Option A splits by percentage and would hit random users, not the registered ones. Option B blue/green is an all-or-nothing cutover, not selective enablement. Option D session affinity only keeps a client pinned to an instance and does nothing to select which customers receive the new optimization.

topics.exam_domain_name: Configurar aplicações cloud-native para deployment

questions.explanation_pt: Os recursos nativos de divisão de tráfego e blue/green do Cloud Run roteiam o tráfego por porcentagem ou por revisão, mas não conseguem direcioná-lo a um conjunto específico e identificável de clientes registrados. Para habilitar uma otimização apenas para clientes selecionados que optaram por participar, uma feature flag avaliada por requisição com base na identidade do cliente é o mecanismo correto, oferecendo controle preciso no nível do usuário. A opção A divide por porcentagem e atingiria usuários aleatórios, não os registrados. A opção B (blue/green) é uma transição do tipo tudo ou nada, e não uma ativação seletiva. A opção D (session affinity) apenas mantém um cliente fixado em uma instância e não faz nada para selecionar quais clientes recebem a nova otimização.

questions.question: Your ecommerce application has a rapidly growing user base, and it is experiencing performance issues due to excessive requests to your backend API. Your team develops and manages this API. The Cloud SQL backend database is struggling to handle the high demand, leading to latency and timeouts. You need to implement a solution that optimizes API performance and improves user experience. What should you do?

options.text: Use Apigee to expose your API. Use Memorystore for Redis to cache frequently accessed data. Implement exponential backoff in the application to retry failed requests.
Use Apigee to expose your API. Implement rate limiting and access control policies in Apigee to control API traffic. Use Pub/Sub to queue requests to prevent database overload.
Use Cloud Load Balancing to expose your API. Use Cloud CDN in front of the load balancer to cache responses. Implement exponential backoff to retry failed requests.

Use Cloud Load Balancing to expose your API. Increase the memory for the database instances to handle more concurrent requests. Implement a custom rate-limiting mechanism in your application code to control API requests.

questions.correct_text: Use Apigee to expose your API. Use Memorystore for Redis to cache frequently accessed data. Implement exponential backoff in the application to retry failed requests.
questions.explanation: The core problem is too many requests reaching an overloaded Cloud SQL backend, so the best fix combines an API management layer (Apigee) with a cache (Memorystore for Redis) to serve frequently accessed data without hitting the database, plus exponential backoff to handle transient failures gracefully. This directly reduces database load and improves latency. Option B's Pub/Sub queue is suited to asynchronous workloads and would not work for synchronous read-heavy API requests, and it does not address caching reads. Option C's Cloud CDN only caches cacheable HTTP responses at the edge and is poorly suited to dynamic, per-user API data backed by Cloud SQL. Option D simply scaling up database memory is a costly, limited stopgap that does not address the root cause of excessive repeated queries.

topics.exam_domain_name: Projetar apps cloud-native escaláveis, seguras e confiáveis

questions.explanation_pt: O problema central é o excesso de requisições chegando a um backend Cloud SQL sobrecarregado, então a melhor solução combina uma camada de gerenciamento de API (Apigee) com um cache (Memorystore for Redis) para servir dados acessados com frequência sem atingir o banco de dados, além de exponential backoff para lidar de forma elegante com falhas transitórias. Isso reduz diretamente a carga no banco de dados e melhora a latência. A fila de Pub/Sub da opção B é adequada para cargas de trabalho assíncronas e não funcionaria para requisições de API síncronas com muitas leituras, além de não tratar do cache de leituras. O Cloud CDN da opção C apenas armazena em cache respostas HTTP cacheáveis na borda e é pouco adequado para dados de API dinâmicos e por usuário sustentados pelo Cloud SQL. A opção D, simplesmente aumentar a memória do banco de dados, é uma medida paliativa cara e limitada que não trata da causa raiz das consultas repetidas excessivas.

questions.question: You need to deploy a new feature into production on Cloud Run. Your company’s SRE team mandates gradual deployments to avoid large downtimes caused by code change errors. You want to configure this deployment with minimal effort. What should you do?

options.text: Configure the application’s frontend load balancer to toggle between the new and old revisions.
Configure the application code to send a small percentage of users to the newly deployed revision.

Deploy the feature with “Serve this revision immediately” unchecked, and configure the new revision to serve a small percentage of traffic. Check for errors, and increase traffic to the revision as appropriate.

Deploy the feature with “Serve this revision immediately” checked. Check for errors, roll back to the previous revision, and repeat the process until you have verified that the deployment is bug-free.

questions.correct_text: Deploy the feature with “Serve this revision immediately” unchecked, and configure the new revision to serve a small percentage of traffic. Check for errors, and increase traffic to the revision as appropriate.
questions.explanation: Cloud Run natively supports gradual (canary) rollouts through revision-based traffic management. Deploying the new revision without serving it immediately means the new revision receives no traffic by default; you then assign it a small percentage of traffic, monitor for errors, and progressively increase it, which is the minimal-effort, Google-recommended approach. Options A and B push the rollout logic into the load balancer or application code, adding effort and duplicating functionality Cloud Run already provides. Option D serves the revision immediately to all users and relies on repeated rollbacks, which causes exactly the downtime and disruption the SRE team wants to avoid.

topics.exam_domain_name: Configurar aplicações cloud-native para deployment

questions.explanation_pt: O Cloud Run oferece suporte nativo a lançamentos graduais (canary) por meio do gerenciamento de tráfego baseado em revisões. Implantar a nova revisão sem servi-la imediatamente significa que, por padrão, ela não recebe tráfego; em seguida, você atribui a ela uma pequena porcentagem de tráfego, monitora a ocorrência de erros e a aumenta progressivamente, o que é a abordagem de menor esforço e recomendada pelo Google. As opções A e B empurram a lógica de lançamento para o load balancer ou para o código da aplicação, aumentando o esforço e duplicando funcionalidades que o Cloud Run já fornece. A opção D serve a revisão imediatamente a todos os usuários e depende de rollbacks repetidos, o que causa exatamente a indisponibilidade e a disrupção que a equipe de SRE quer evitar.

questions.question: You are developing an external-facing application on GKE that provides a streaming API to users. You want to offer two subscription tiers, “basic" and “premium", to users based on the number of API requests that each client application is allowed to make each day. You want to design the application architecture to provide subscription tiers to users while following Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: 1. Configure the service on GKE as a backend to an Apigee proxy.2. Provide API keys to users to identify client applications.3. Configure a Quota policy in Apigee for API keys based on the subscription tier.

1. Configure the service on GKE as a backend to an Apigee proxy.2. Provide API keys to users to identify client applications.3. Configure a SpikeArrest policy in Apigee for API keys based on the subscription tier.

1. Configure the service on GKE as a backend to two new projects, each with a separate Application Load Balancer.2. Configure the quota "Queries per second (QPS) per region per network” for each project individually.3. Provide users with API endpoints based on the subscription tier.

1. Deploy the application to two GKE clusters, one for each subscription tier. Configure each cluster to have a separate Ingress.2. Configure each cluster as a backend to an Apigee proxy.3. Provide API keys to users to identify client applications.4. Configure separate rate limits for client applications based on the subscription tier.

questions.correct_text: 1. Configure the service on GKE as a backend to an Apigee proxy.2. Provide API keys to users to identify client applications.3. Configure a Quota policy in Apigee for API keys based on the subscription tier.
questions.explanation: Fronting the GKE service with an Apigee proxy and issuing API keys to identify client applications, then applying a Quota policy keyed to the subscription tier, is the Google-recommended way to enforce a daily request allowance per tier. The Quota policy is designed to count and cap requests over a time window such as per day, which exactly matches the requirement. Option B's SpikeArrest smooths short-term traffic spikes (per second/minute) and does not enforce daily totals. Option C relies on per-project regional QPS quotas and separate load balancers, which is operationally complex and not designed for per-client daily limits. Option D duplicates infrastructure with two clusters and is far more complex than configuring tier-based quotas in a single Apigee proxy.

topics.exam_domain_name: Integrar aplicações com serviços do Google Cloud

questions.explanation_pt: Colocar um proxy do Apigee na frente do serviço do GKE e emitir API keys para identificar as aplicações cliente, aplicando então uma Quota policy vinculada ao nível de assinatura, é a forma recomendada pelo Google de impor um limite diário de requisições por nível. A Quota policy foi projetada para contar e limitar requisições ao longo de uma janela de tempo, como por dia, o que corresponde exatamente ao requisito. O SpikeArrest da opção B suaviza picos de tráfego de curto prazo (por segundo/minuto) e não impõe totais diários. A opção C depende de cotas de QPS regionais por projeto e de load balancers separados, o que é operacionalmente complexo e não foi projetado para limites diários por cliente. A opção D duplica a infraestrutura com dois clusters e é muito mais complexa do que configurar cotas baseadas em nível em um único proxy do Apigee.

questions.question: Your organization has users and groups configured in an external identity provider (IdP). You want to leverage the same external IdP to allow Google Cloud console access to all employees. You also want to personalize the sign-in experience by displaying the user's name and photo when users access the Google Cloud console. What should you do?

options.text: Configure workforce identity federation with the external IdP, and set up attribute mapping.
Configure a service account for each individual by using the user name and photo, and grant permissions for each user to impersonate their respective service accounts.
Configure workload identity federation to get the external IdP tokens, and use these tokens to sign in to the Google Cloud console.
Create a Google group that includes organization email IDs for all users. Ask users to use the same name, work email ID, and password to register and sign in.

questions.correct_text: Configure workforce identity federation with the external IdP, and set up attribute mapping.
questions.explanation: Workforce identity federation lets you grant employees access to Google Cloud (including the console) using identities from an external IdP, without provisioning Google accounts. By configuring SAML/OIDC federation and attribute mapping, you can map IdP attributes such as the user's name and photo into the federated session, personalizing the sign-in experience. Option C is wrong because workload identity federation is designed for non-human workloads (applications/services), not interactive human console access. Option B is impractical and misuses service accounts, which are not meant to represent individual humans for console sign-in. Option D abandons the external IdP entirely and requires duplicate credentials, defeating the goal of leveraging the existing IdP.

topics.exam_domain_name: Projetar apps cloud-native escaláveis, seguras e confiáveis

questions.explanation_pt: A workforce identity federation permite conceder aos funcionários acesso ao Google Cloud (incluindo o console) usando identidades de um IdP externo, sem provisionar contas Google. Ao configurar a federação SAML/OIDC e o mapeamento de atributos, você pode mapear atributos do IdP, como o nome e a foto do usuário, para a sessão federada, personalizando a experiência de login. A opção C está errada porque a workload identity federation foi projetada para cargas de trabalho não humanas (aplicações/serviços), e não para acesso interativo de humanos ao console. A opção B é impraticável e usa indevidamente service accounts, que não foram feitas para representar humanos individuais no login do console. A opção D abandona completamente o IdP externo e exige credenciais duplicadas, frustrando o objetivo de aproveitar o IdP existente.

questions.question: You are developing a new API that creates requests on an asynchronous message service. Requests will be consumed by different services. You need to expose the API by using a gRPC interface while minimizing infrastructure management overhead. How should you deploy the API?

options.text: Deploy your API to App Engine. Create a Pub/Sub topic, and configure your API to push messages to the topic.
Deploy your API as a Cloud Run service. Create a Pub/Sub topic, and configure your API to push messages to the topic.
Deploy your API to a GKE cluster. Create a Kafka cluster, and configure your API to write messages to the cluster.
Deploy your API on a Compute Engine instance. Create a Kafka cluster, and configure your API to write messages to the cluster.

questions.correct_text: Deploy your API as a Cloud Run service. Create a Pub/Sub topic, and configure your API to push messages to the topic.
questions.explanation: Cloud Run is a fully managed serverless platform that natively supports gRPC (including unary and streaming) and minimizes infrastructure management overhead, satisfying both requirements. Pairing it with a Pub/Sub topic provides a managed asynchronous message service whose messages can be consumed by multiple different subscribers/services. App Engine standard does not support arbitrary gRPC endpoints as cleanly, making option A weaker for a gRPC API. Options C and D rely on self-managed Kafka clusters on GKE or Compute Engine, which significantly increase operational overhead and contradict the requirement to minimize infrastructure management.

topics.exam_domain_name: Projetar apps cloud-native escaláveis, seguras e confiáveis

questions.explanation_pt: O Cloud Run é uma plataforma serverless totalmente gerenciada que oferece suporte nativo a gRPC (incluindo unário e streaming) e minimiza a sobrecarga de gerenciamento de infraestrutura, atendendo a ambos os requisitos. Combiná-lo com um tópico do Pub/Sub fornece um serviço de mensagens assíncrono gerenciado, cujas mensagens podem ser consumidas por vários assinantes/serviços diferentes. O App Engine standard não oferece suporte a endpoints gRPC arbitrários de forma tão limpa, o que torna a opção A mais fraca para uma API gRPC. As opções C e D dependem de clusters Kafka autogerenciados no GKE ou no Compute Engine, o que aumenta significativamente a sobrecarga operacional e contradiz o requisito de minimizar o gerenciamento de infraestrutura.

questions.question: You are about to deploy an application hosted on a Compute Engine instance with Windows OS and Cloud SQL. You plan to use the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy for connectivity to the Cloud SQL instance. You plan to follow Google-recommended practices and the principle of least privilege. You have already created a custom service account. What should you do next?

options.text: Create and assign a custom role with the cloudsql.instances.connect permission to the custom service account. Adjust the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy start command to specify your instance connection name.
Grant the custom service account the roles/cloudsql.client role. Adjust the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy start command to use the --unix-socket CLI option.
Grant the custom service account the roles/cloudsql.editor role.
Grant the custom service account the roles/cloudsql.viewer role. Adjust the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy start command to specify your instance connection name.

questions.correct_text: Create and assign a custom role with the cloudsql.instances.connect permission to the custom service account. Adjust the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy start command to specify your instance connection name.
questions.explanation: Following least privilege, the service account only needs the single permission cloudsql.instances.connect, which a custom role grants without the extra permissions bundled into predefined roles. The Cloud SQL Auth Proxy must also be started with the instance connection name so it can establish the secure connection. Option B grants roles/cloudsql.client, which works but includes more than the minimal permission and is less aligned with strict least privilege when a custom role is the stated goal; additionally --unix-socket is not the typical pattern on Windows. Options C and D grant editor/viewer roles, which are either over-privileged or lack the connect permission entirely, so they do not properly support the proxy connection.

topics.exam_domain_name: Integrar aplicações com serviços do Google Cloud

questions.explanation_pt: Seguindo o princípio do menor privilégio, a service account precisa apenas da única permissão cloudsql.instances.connect, que um custom role concede sem as permissões extras agrupadas nos predefined roles. O Cloud SQL Auth Proxy também precisa ser iniciado com o instance connection name para que possa estabelecer a conexão segura. A opção B concede roles/cloudsql.client, que funciona, mas inclui mais do que a permissão mínima e está menos alinhada com o menor privilégio estrito quando o objetivo declarado é um custom role; além disso, --unix-socket não é o padrão típico no Windows. As opções C e D concedem os roles editor/viewer, que são ou superprivilegiados ou não têm a permissão connect, portanto não dão suporte adequado à conexão do proxy.

questions.question: You are developing a secure document sharing platform. The platform allows users to share documents with other users who may be external to their organization. Access to these documents should be revoked after a configurable time period. The documents are stored in Cloud Storage. How should you configure Cloud Storage to support this functionality?

options.text: Create signed policy documents on the Cloud Storage bucket.
Apply access control list (ACL) permissions to the Cloud Storage bucket.
Generate a signed URL for each document the user wants to share.
Grant the Storage Object Viewer IAM role to all authenticated users.

questions.correct_text: Generate a signed URL for each document the user wants to share.
questions.explanation: A signed URL grants time-limited access to a specific Cloud Storage object using a cryptographically signed link, so it works for users external to the organization and automatically expires after the configured period, effectively revoking access. This matches the requirement to share individual documents with anyone and have access expire after a configurable time. Signed policy documents (option A) govern form-based uploads, not per-document time-limited read sharing. ACLs (option B) require the recipient to have a recognizable identity and do not provide automatic time-based expiry. Granting Storage Object Viewer to all authenticated users (option D) is overly broad, insecure, and provides no expiration or per-document scoping.

topics.exam_domain_name: Integrar aplicações com serviços do Google Cloud

questions.explanation_pt: Uma signed URL concede acesso por tempo limitado a um objeto específico do Cloud Storage usando um link assinado criptograficamente, então funciona para usuários externos à organização e expira automaticamente após o período configurado, revogando o acesso de forma efetiva. Isso atende ao requisito de compartilhar documentos individuais com qualquer pessoa e fazer com que o acesso expire após um tempo configurável. Os signed policy documents (opção A) regem uploads baseados em formulário, e não o compartilhamento de leitura por documento e por tempo limitado. As ACLs (opção B) exigem que o destinatário tenha uma identidade reconhecível e não fornecem expiração automática por tempo. Conceder o Storage Object Viewer a todos os usuários autenticados (opção D) é excessivamente amplo, inseguro e não oferece expiração nem escopo por documento.

questions.question: You work for an environmental agency in a large city. You are developing a new monitoring platform that will capture air quality readings from thousands of locations in the city. You want the air quality reading devices to send and receive their data payload to the newly created RESTful backend systems every minute by using a curl command. The backend systems are running in a single cloud region and are using Premium Tier networking. You need to connect the devices to the backend while minimizing the daily average latency, measured by using Time to First Byte (TTFB). How should you build this service?

options.text: 1. Run the air quality devices’ backends on Compute Engine VMs.2. Create a weighted round robin routing policy on Cloud DNS.3. Configure the air quality devices to connect by using this DNS.

1. Run the air quality devices’ backends on Compute Engine VMs.2. Create a round robin routing policy on Cloud DNS for these Compute Engine VMs.3. Configure the air quality devices to connect by using this DNS.

1. Run the air quality devices' backends in a managed instance group.2. Create an external passthrough Network Load Balancer to connect to the managed instance group.3. Configure a connection between the air quality devices and the Network Load Balancer.

1 Run the air quality devices' backends in a managed instance group.2. Create an external Application Load Balancer, and connect it to the managed instance group.3. Configure a connection between the air quality devices and the Application Load Balancer.

questions.correct_text: 1 Run the air quality devices' backends in a managed instance group.2. Create an external Application Load Balancer, and connect it to the managed instance group.3. Configure a connection between the air quality devices and the Application Load Balancer.
questions.explanation: Because devices use curl to send and receive RESTful (HTTP) payloads, the external Application Load Balancer is the correct choice: it is a global HTTP(S) load balancer that leverages Premium Tier networking and Google's edge to terminate connections close to clients, minimizing Time to First Byte. Backing it with a managed instance group provides scalable, health-checked backends. The external passthrough Network Load Balancer (option C) operates at L4 and is regional, so it does not optimize HTTP TTFB or use the global edge as effectively. Cloud DNS round robin or weighted policies (options A and B) only distribute DNS responses and do not provide load balancing intelligence or edge proximity to reduce latency, leaving clients to connect directly to VMs.

topics.exam_domain_name: Projetar apps cloud-native escaláveis, seguras e confiáveis

questions.explanation_pt: Como os dispositivos usam curl para enviar e receber payloads RESTful (HTTP), o external Application Load Balancer é a escolha correta: é um load balancer HTTP(S) global que aproveita a rede do Premium Tier e a edge do Google para terminar conexões próximo aos clientes, minimizando o Time to First Byte. Apoiá-lo com um managed instance group fornece backends escaláveis e com verificação de integridade. O external passthrough Network Load Balancer (opção C) opera na camada L4 e é regional, portanto não otimiza o TTFB de HTTP nem usa a edge global de forma tão eficaz. As políticas de round robin ou ponderadas do Cloud DNS (opções A e B) apenas distribuem respostas de DNS e não fornecem inteligência de load balancing nem proximidade de edge para reduzir a latência, deixando os clientes conectarem-se diretamente às VMs.

questions.question: Your infrastructure team is responsible for creating and managing Compute Engine VMs. Your team uses the Google Cloud console and gcloud CLI to provision resources for the development environment. You need to ensure that all Compute Engine VMs are labeled correctly for compliance reasons. In case of missing labels, you need to implement corrective actions so the labels are configured accordingly without changing the current deployment process. You want to use the most scalable approach. What should you do?

options.text: Use a Cloud Audit Logs trigger to invoke a Cloud Function when a Compute Engine VM is created. Check for missing labels and assign them if necessary.
Deploy resources with Terraform. Use the gcloud terraform vet command with a policy to ensure that every Compute Engine VM that is provisioned by Terraform has labels set.
Write a script to check all Compute Engine VMs for missing labels regularly by using Cloud Scheduler. Use the script to assign the labels.
Check all Compute Engine VMs for missing labels regularly. Use the console to assign the labels.

questions.correct_text: Use a Cloud Audit Logs trigger to invoke a Cloud Function when a Compute Engine VM is created. Check for missing labels and assign them if necessary.
questions.explanation: An event-driven approach using a Cloud Audit Logs trigger to invoke a Cloud Function whenever a Compute Engine VM is created scales automatically and reacts in near real time, applying corrective labels without changing how the team provisions resources via console or gcloud. Because the team uses both the console and gcloud (not only IaC), option B with gcloud terraform vet would not cover resources created outside of Terraform and does not match the stated workflow. Options C and D rely on periodic polling, which is less timely, more error-prone, and (in D) entirely manual, so neither is the most scalable corrective mechanism. The audit-log-triggered function intercepts every creation event regardless of the tool used, making it the best fit.

topics.exam_domain_name: Integrar aplicações com serviços do Google Cloud

questions.explanation_pt: Uma abordagem orientada a eventos usando um trigger do Cloud Audit Logs para invocar uma Cloud Function sempre que uma VM do Compute Engine é criada escala automaticamente e reage em tempo quase real, aplicando labels corretivas sem mudar a forma como a equipe provisiona recursos via console ou gcloud. Como a equipe usa tanto o console quanto o gcloud (e não apenas IaC), a opção B com gcloud terraform vet não cobriria recursos criados fora do Terraform e não corresponde ao fluxo de trabalho descrito. As opções C e D dependem de polling periódico, que é menos oportuno, mais propenso a erros e (na D) totalmente manual, portanto nenhuma é o mecanismo corretivo mais escalável. A função acionada por audit log intercepta cada evento de criação independentemente da ferramenta usada, tornando-a a melhor opção.

questions.question: You are developing a discussion portal that is built on Cloud Run. Incoming external requests are routed through a set of microservices before a response is sent. Some of these microservices connect to databases. You need to run a load test to identify any bottlenecks in the application when it is under load. You want to follow Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: Modify the response to include a time series that shows elapsed time per service. Use Log Analytics in Cloud Logging to create a heatmap that exposes any service that could be a bottleneck.
Configure Cloud Trace to capture the requests from the load testing clients. Review the timings in Cloud Trace.
Expose the latency metrics per service for each request. Configure Google Cloud Managed Service for Prometheus, and use it to scrape and analyze the metrics.
Add log statements that capture elapsed time. Analyze the logs and metrics by using BigQuery.

questions.correct_text: Configure Cloud Trace to capture the requests from the load testing clients. Review the timings in Cloud Trace.
questions.explanation: Cloud Trace captures distributed traces that show the latency contribution of each microservice as a request flows through the chain, making it the recommended way to pinpoint bottlenecks across services and database calls during a load test. Configuring Cloud Trace to capture requests from the load-testing clients lets you review per-hop timings and identify the slow component directly. Embedding timing in the response (A) or in logs analyzed by BigQuery (D) is custom, brittle instrumentation that lacks the automatic span correlation tracing provides. Prometheus metrics (C) give aggregate per-service latency but not the per-request, end-to-end breakdown needed to trace a single slow path through the microservices.

topics.exam_domain_name: Integrar aplicações com serviços do Google Cloud

questions.explanation_pt: O Cloud Trace captura rastreamentos distribuídos que mostram a contribuição de latência de cada microsserviço à medida que uma requisição percorre a cadeia, tornando-o a forma recomendada de identificar gargalos entre serviços e chamadas de banco de dados durante um teste de carga. Configurar o Cloud Trace para capturar requisições dos clientes de teste de carga permite revisar os tempos de cada salto (per-hop) e identificar diretamente o componente lento. Embutir a medição de tempo na resposta (A) ou em logs analisados pelo BigQuery (D) é uma instrumentação personalizada e frágil, que não possui a correlação automática de spans que o tracing fornece. As métricas do Prometheus (C) fornecem a latência agregada por serviço, mas não o detalhamento por requisição, de ponta a ponta, necessário para rastrear um único caminho lento através dos microsserviços.

questions.question: Your team currently uses Bigtable as their database backend. In your application's app profile, you notice that the connection to the Bigtable cluster is specified as single-cluster routing, and the cluster’s connection logic is configured to conduct manual failover when the cluster is unavailable. You want to optimize the application code to have more efficient and highly available Bigtable connectivity. What should you do?

options.text: Set up Memcached so that queries hit the cache layer first and automatically get data from Bigtable in the event of a cache miss.
Increase the Bigtable client’s connection pool size.
Configure a Dataflow template, and use a Beam connector to stream data changes.
Configure the app profile to use multi-cluster routing.

questions.correct_text: Configure the app profile to use multi-cluster routing.
questions.explanation: Configuring the app profile to use multi-cluster routing lets the Bigtable client automatically route requests to the nearest available cluster and fail over transparently if one becomes unavailable, providing higher availability than single-cluster routing with manual failover. This removes the custom manual-failover logic and improves resiliency without application-side intervention. Adding a Memcached cache layer (A) addresses read latency but not connection availability or failover. Increasing the connection pool size (B) can help throughput but does nothing for cross-cluster high availability, and a Dataflow/Beam streaming pipeline (C) is for change data capture, not application connectivity.

topics.exam_domain_name: Projetar apps cloud-native escaláveis, seguras e confiáveis

questions.explanation_pt: Configurar o app profile para usar multi-cluster routing permite que o cliente do Bigtable roteie automaticamente as requisições para o cluster mais próximo disponível e faça failover de forma transparente caso um deles fique indisponível, oferecendo maior disponibilidade do que o single-cluster routing com failover manual. Isso elimina a lógica personalizada de failover manual e melhora a resiliência sem intervenção do lado da aplicação. Adicionar uma camada de cache com Memcached (A) trata a latência de leitura, mas não a disponibilidade de conexão nem o failover.
