Aumentar o tamanho do connection pool (B) pode ajudar na vazão (throughput), mas não faz nada pela alta disponibilidade entre clusters, e um pipeline de streaming com Dataflow/Beam (C) serve para change data capture, não para a conectividade da aplicação.

questions.question: You work for an ecommerce company. Your company is migrating multiple applications to Google Cloud, and you are assisting with the migration of one of the applications. The application is currently deployed on a VM without any OS dependencies. You have created a Dockerfile and used it to upload a new image to Artifact Registry. You want to minimize the infrastructure and operational complexity. What should you do?

options.text: Deploy the image to Cloud Run.
Deploy the image to a GKE Autopilot cluster.
Deploy the image to a GKE Standard cluster.
Deploy the image to a Compute Engine instance.

questions.correct_text: Deploy the image to Cloud Run.
questions.explanation: Because the application is a stateless containerized workload with no OS dependencies and the goal is to minimize infrastructure and operational complexity, Cloud Run is the best target: it is fully managed, serverless, scales to zero, and requires no cluster or node management. Deploying to a GKE Autopilot cluster (B) reduces some node management but still involves Kubernetes concepts and cluster overhead. A GKE Standard cluster (C) requires managing nodes and the control plane configuration, and a Compute Engine instance (D) reintroduces VM and OS-level operational burden, the opposite of the stated goal. Cloud Run directly runs the Artifact Registry image with the least operational effort.

topics.exam_domain_name: Configurar aplicações cloud-native para deployment

questions.explanation_pt: Como a aplicação é uma carga de trabalho stateless em contêiner, sem dependências de SO, e o objetivo é minimizar a infraestrutura e a complexidade operacional, o Cloud Run é o melhor destino: é totalmente gerenciado, serverless, escala até zero e não exige gerenciamento de cluster ou de nós. Implantar em um cluster GKE Autopilot (B) reduz parte do gerenciamento de nós, mas ainda envolve conceitos de Kubernetes e o overhead de cluster. Um cluster GKE Standard (C) exige gerenciar os nós e a configuração do control plane, e uma instância do Compute Engine (D) reintroduz a carga operacional de VM e de nível de SO, o oposto do objetivo declarado. O Cloud Run executa diretamente a imagem do Artifact Registry com o menor esforço operacional.

questions.question: You recently deployed an Apigee API proxy to your organization across two regions. Both regions are configured with a separate backend that is hosting the API. You need to configure Apigee to route traffic to the appropriate local region backend. What should you do?

options.text: Create a TargetEndpoint with a weighted load balancing algorithm. Configure the API proxy to use the same weights for each region's backend.

Configure a regional internal Application Load Balancer in each region, and use health checks to verify that each backend is active. Create a DNS A record that contains the IP addresses of both regions' load balancers. Configure a Targetserver for each region that uses this DNS name.

Configure a global external Application Load Balancer and configure each region’s backend with a different regional backend service. Each region communicates to this single global external Application Load Balancer as its TargetServer.
Configure a TargetServer for each region's backend host names. Configure the API proxy to choose the TargetServer based on the system.region.name flow variable.

questions.correct_text: Configure a TargetServer for each region's backend host names. Configure the API proxy to choose the TargetServer based on the system.region.name flow variable.
questions.explanation: In Apigee you define a TargetServer for each region's backend host and then reference the appropriate TargetServer dynamically in the TargetEndpoint based on the deployment's region. Using the system.region.name flow variable lets each regional Apigee instance select its local backend's TargetServer, achieving region-local routing. A weighted TargetEndpoint with equal weights (A) would distribute traffic across both regions rather than keeping it local. Building internal or global load balancers fronted by DNS (B and C) adds unnecessary infrastructure and does not give Apigee per-region awareness as cleanly as resolving the TargetServer by the runtime region variable.

topics.exam_domain_name: Integrar aplicações com serviços do Google Cloud

questions.explanation_pt: No Apigee você define um TargetServer para o host de backend de cada região e então referencia o TargetServer apropriado dinamicamente no TargetEndpoint com base na região da implantação. Usar a variável de fluxo system.region.name permite que cada instância regional do Apigee selecione o TargetServer de seu backend local, alcançando o roteamento local por região. Um TargetEndpoint ponderado com pesos iguais (A) distribuiria o tráfego entre ambas as regiões em vez de mantê-lo local. Construir load balancers internos ou globais por trás de DNS (B e C) adiciona infraestrutura desnecessária e não dá ao Apigee a percepção por região de forma tão limpa quanto resolver o TargetServer pela variável de região em runtime.

questions.question: You are a developer that works for a local concert venue. Customers use your company’s website to purchase tickets for events. You need to provide customers with immediate confirmation when a selected seat has been reserved. How should you design the ticket ordering process?

options.text: Add the seat reservation to a Cloud Tasks queue, which triggers Workflows to process the seat reservation.
Publish the seat reservation to a Pub/Sub topic. Configure the backend service to use Eventarc to process the seat reservation on GKE.
Upload the seat reservation to a Cloud Storage bucket, which triggers an event to a Cloud Run service that processes the orders.

Submit the seat reservation in an HTTP POST request to an Application Load Balancer. Configure the Application Load Balancer to distribute the request to a Compute Engine managed instance group that processes the reservation.

questions.correct_text: Submit the seat reservation in an HTTP POST request to an Application Load Balancer. Configure the Application Load Balancer to distribute the request to a Compute Engine managed instance group that processes the reservation.
questions.explanation: The requirement is an immediate, synchronous confirmation that a seat has been reserved, which means the client must receive the result within the same request/response cycle. Submitting an HTTP POST to an Application Load Balancer that routes to a Compute Engine managed instance group lets the backend process the reservation and return success or failure directly to the customer in real time. Options A, B, and C all rely on asynchronous, decoupled patterns (Cloud Tasks queues, Pub/Sub with Eventarc, and Cloud Storage triggers), which process the reservation in the background and cannot guarantee an immediate confirmation to the user. These event-driven designs introduce latency and eventual consistency, making them unsuitable for synchronous seat confirmation.

topics.exam_domain_name: Projetar apps cloud-native escaláveis, seguras e confiáveis

questions.explanation_pt: O requisito é uma confirmação imediata e síncrona de que um assento foi reservado, o que significa que o cliente deve receber o resultado dentro do mesmo ciclo de requisição/resposta. Enviar um HTTP POST para um Application Load Balancer que roteia para um managed instance group do Compute Engine permite que o backend processe a reserva e retorne sucesso ou falha diretamente ao cliente em tempo real. As opções A, B e C dependem todas de padrões assíncronos e desacoplados (filas do Cloud Tasks, Pub/Sub com Eventarc e gatilhos do Cloud Storage), que processam a reserva em segundo plano e não podem garantir uma confirmação imediata ao usuário. Esses designs orientados a eventos introduzem latência e consistência eventual, tornando-os inadequados para a confirmação síncrona de assento.

questions.question: You have an application running in production on Cloud Run. Your team needs to change one of the application’s services to return a new field. You want to test the new revision on 10% of your clients using the least amount of effort. You also need to keep your service backward compatible.What should you do?

options.text: Replace the current service with the new revision. Deploy the new revision with no traffic allocated. After the deployment, split the traffic between the previous service and the new revision.
Update the current service with the new changes. Deploy the new revision. After the deployment, split the traffic between the current service and the new revision.
Update the current service with the new changes. Deploy the new revision with no traffic allocated. Split the traffic between the current service and the new revision.
Replace the current service with the new revision. Deploy the new revision. Create a load balancer to split the traffic between the previous service and the new revision.

questions.correct_text: Update the current service with the new changes. Deploy the new revision with no traffic allocated. Split the traffic between the current service and the new revision.
questions.explanation: Cloud Run supports multiple revisions of the same service with traffic splitting, which is the lowest-effort way to canary-test a change on a subset of clients. You update the existing service with the new code and deploy a new revision with no traffic allocated (using --no-traffic), then split traffic so that 10% goes to the new revision while keeping backward compatibility. Replacing the service (options A and D) is unnecessary and would discard the revision history that enables built-in traffic splitting. Option B deploys the new revision and immediately serves traffic on it before the split, which is not the controlled approach, and option D adds an external load balancer that is redundant since Cloud Run handles traffic splitting natively.

topics.exam_domain_name: Configurar aplicações cloud-native para deployment

questions.explanation_pt: O Cloud Run oferece suporte a múltiplas revisões do mesmo serviço com divisão de tráfego (traffic splitting), que é a forma de menor esforço para fazer um teste canário de uma mudança em um subconjunto de clientes. Você atualiza o serviço existente com o novo código e implanta uma nova revisão sem tráfego alocado (usando --no-traffic) e, em seguida, divide o tráfego de modo que 10% vá para a nova revisão, mantendo a compatibilidade com versões anteriores. Substituir o serviço (opções A e D) é desnecessário e descartaria o histórico de revisões que possibilita a divisão de tráfego nativa. A opção B implanta a nova revisão e imediatamente direciona tráfego para ela antes da divisão, o que não é a abordagem controlada, e a opção D adiciona um load balancer externo que é redundante, já que o Cloud Run lida com a divisão de tráfego de forma nativa.

questions.question: Your team plans to use AlloyDB as their database backend for an upcoming application release. Your application is currently hosted in a different project and network than the AlloyDB instances. You need to securely connect your application to the AlloyDB instance while keeping the projects isolated. You want to minimize additional operations and follow Google-recommended practices. How should you configure the network for database connectivity?

options.text: Provision a Shared VPC project where both the application project and the AlloyDB project are service projects.
Use AlloyDB Auth Proxy and configure the application project’s firewall to allow connections to port 5433.
Provision a service account from the AlloyDB project. Use this service account’s JSON key file as the --credentials-file to connect to the AlloyDB instance.
Ask the database team to provision AlloyDB databases in the same project and network as the application.

questions.correct_text: Use AlloyDB Auth Proxy and configure the application project’s firewall to allow connections to port 5433.
questions.explanation: The AlloyDB Auth Proxy provides secure, IAM-based connectivity to an AlloyDB instance using automatic TLS encryption and identity verification, without requiring the projects to share a VPC or expose the instance broadly. It connects on AlloyDB's default port 5433, so allowing that port through the application project's firewall lets the app connect securely while keeping the projects isolated and minimizing operational overhead. Option A (Shared VPC) and option D (co-locating databases) break the isolation requirement or add significant restructuring. Option C distributes a long-lived service account JSON key, which is a security anti-pattern and is not the recommended way to establish network connectivity.

topics.exam_domain_name: Integrar aplicações com serviços do Google Cloud

questions.explanation_pt: O AlloyDB Auth Proxy fornece conectividade segura e baseada em IAM a uma instância do AlloyDB usando criptografia TLS automática e verificação de identidade, sem exigir que os projetos compartilhem uma VPC ou exponham a instância de forma ampla. Ele se conecta na porta padrão 5433 do AlloyDB, então permitir essa porta no firewall do projeto da aplicação deixa o app se conectar com segurança, mantendo os projetos isolados e minimizando a sobrecarga operacional. A opção A (Shared VPC) e a opção D (co-localizar os bancos de dados) quebram o requisito de isolamento ou adicionam reestruturação significativa. A opção C distribui uma chave JSON de service account de longa duração, o que é um anti-padrão de segurança e não é a forma recomendada de estabelecer conectividade de rede.

questions.question: You have an on-premises containerized service written in the current stable version of Python 3 that is available only to users in the United States. The service has high traffic during the day and no traffic at night. You need to migrate this application to Google Cloud and track error logs after the migration in Error Reporting. You want to minimize the cost and effort of these tasks. What should you do?

options.text: Deploy the code on Cloud Run. Configure your code to write errors to standard error.
Deploy the code on Cloud Run. Configure your code to stream errors to a Cloud Storage bucket.
Deploy the code on a GKE Autopilot cluster. Configure your code to write error logs to standard error.
Deploy the code on a GKE Autopilot cluster. Configure your code to write error logs to a Cloud Storage bucket.

questions.correct_text: Deploy the code on Cloud Run. Configure your code to write errors to standard error.
questions.explanation: Cloud Run is the lowest-cost, lowest-effort target for a containerized stateless service with spiky daytime traffic and zero traffic at night because it scales to zero, so you pay nothing when idle. Cloud Run automatically captures application logs written to standard output and standard error, and writing errors to standard error lets Error Reporting automatically detect and group them with no extra configuration. Options C and D use GKE Autopilot, which still incurs more management overhead and cost than Cloud Run for this bursty workload. Options B and D route errors to a Cloud Storage bucket, which does not feed Error Reporting automatically and adds unnecessary complexity.

topics.exam_domain_name: Integrar aplicações com serviços do Google Cloud

questions.explanation_pt: O Cloud Run é o destino de menor custo e menor esforço para um serviço stateless em contêiner com tráfego instável durante o dia e tráfego zero à noite, porque ele escala até zero, então você não paga nada quando está ocioso. O Cloud Run captura automaticamente os logs da aplicação escritos no standard output e no standard error, e escrever erros no standard error permite que o Error Reporting os detecte e agrupe automaticamente, sem configuração extra. As opções C e D usam o GKE Autopilot, que ainda gera mais sobrecarga de gerenciamento e custo do que o Cloud Run para essa carga de trabalho em rajadas. As opções B e D direcionam os erros para um bucket do Cloud Storage, que não alimenta o Error Reporting automaticamente e adiciona complexidade desnecessária.

questions.question: You have an application running on a GKE cluster. Your application has a stateless web frontend, and has a high-availability requirement. Your cluster is set to automatically upgrade, and some of your nodes need to be drained. You need to ensure that the application has a serving capacity of 10% of the Pods prior to the drain. What should you do?

options.text: Configure a Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA) to increase the memory and CPU by 10% and set the updateMode to Auto.
Configure the Pod replica count to be 10% more than the current replica count.
Configure a Pod Disruption Budget (PDB) value to have a minAvailable value of 10%.
Configure the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) maxReplicas value to 10% more than the current replica count.

questions.correct_text: Configure a Pod Disruption Budget (PDB) value to have a minAvailable value of 10%.
questions.explanation: A Pod Disruption Budget (PDB) limits voluntary disruptions such as node drains during automatic upgrades, ensuring a minimum number or percentage of Pods remain available. Setting minAvailable to 10% guarantees at least that fraction of the application's Pods stays running before the eviction proceeds, satisfying the high-availability requirement during drains. A Vertical Pod Autoscaler only adjusts CPU and memory of Pods and does not protect availability during evictions. Simply increasing the replica count or raising the HPA maxReplicas does not stop the drain from evicting Pods all at once, so they do not guarantee serving capacity during the disruption.

topics.exam_domain_name: Projetar apps cloud-native escaláveis, seguras e confiáveis

questions.explanation_pt: Um Pod Disruption Budget (PDB) limita interrupções voluntárias, como drenagens de nós (node drains) durante upgrades automáticos, garantindo que um número ou percentual mínimo de Pods permaneça disponível. Definir minAvailable como 10% garante que pelo menos essa fração dos Pods da aplicação continue em execução antes que a evicção prossiga, atendendo ao requisito de alta disponibilidade durante as drenagens. Um Vertical Pod Autoscaler apenas ajusta a CPU e a memória dos Pods e não protege a disponibilidade durante as evicções. Simplesmente aumentar o número de réplicas ou elevar o maxReplicas do HPA não impede que a drenagem evicte todos os Pods de uma vez, então isso não garante a capacidade de atendimento durante a interrupção.

questions.question: You have developed a Python application that you want to containerize and deploy to Cloud Run. You have developed a Cloud Build pipeline with the following steps:After triggering the pipeline, you notice in the Cloud Build logs that the final step of the pipeline fails and the container is unable to be deployed to Cloud Run. What is the cause of this issue, and how should you resolve it?

options.text: The final step uses a Cloud Run instance name that does not match the container name. Update the deployment step so that the Cloud Run instance name matches the container name, and rerun the pipeline.
The Docker container image has not been pushed to Artifact Registry. Add a step to the pipeline to push the application container image to Artifact Registry, and rerun the pipeline.
Cloud Run does not allow unauthenticated invocations. Remove the --allow-unauthenticated parameter to enforce authentication on the application, and rerun the pipeline.
Unit tests in the pipeline are failing. Update the application code so that all unit tests pass, and rerun the pipeline.

questions.correct_text: The Docker container image has not been pushed to Artifact Registry. Add a step to the pipeline to push the application container image to Artifact Registry, and rerun the pipeline.
questions.explanation: Cloud Run deploys container images that must be stored in a registry such as Artifact Registry, so the deploy step fails if the built image was never pushed there. Adding a build step that pushes the image to Artifact Registry before the deploy step resolves the failure, since gcloud run deploy references an image URI in the registry. Mismatched instance and container names do not cause deployment failures because the service name and image are independent. The --allow-unauthenticated flag controls invocation access, not deployment success, and failing unit tests would surface in an earlier test step rather than the final deploy step.

topics.exam_domain_name: Configurar aplicações cloud-native para deployment

questions.explanation_pt: O Cloud Run implanta imagens de contêiner que precisam estar armazenadas em um registry como o Artifact Registry, então a etapa de implantação falha se a imagem construída nunca foi enviada para lá. Adicionar uma etapa de build que envia (push) a imagem para o Artifact Registry antes da etapa de implantação resolve a falha, já que o gcloud run deploy faz referência a uma URI de imagem no registry. Nomes incompatíveis de instância e contêiner não causam falhas de implantação, porque o nome do serviço e a imagem são independentes. A flag --allow-unauthenticated controla o acesso de invocação, não o sucesso da implantação, e testes unitários com falha apareceriam em uma etapa de teste anterior, e não na etapa final de implantação.

questions.question: Your infrastructure team uses Terraform Cloud and manages Google Cloud resources by using Terraform configuration files. You want to configure an infrastructure as code pipeline that authenticates to Google Cloud APIs. You want to use the most secure approach and minimize changes to the configuration. How should you configure the authentication?

options.text: Use Terraform on GKE. Create a Kubernetes service account to execute the Terraform code. Use workload identity federation to authenticate as the Google service account.
Install Terraform on a Compute Engine VM. Configure the VM by using a service account that has the required permissions to manage the Google Cloud resources.
Configure Terraform Cloud to use workload identity federation to authenticate to the Google Cloud APIs.

Create a service account that has the required permissions to manage the Google Cloud resources, and import the service account key to Terraform Cloud. Use this service account to authenticate to the Google Cloud APIs.

questions.correct_text: Configure Terraform Cloud to use workload identity federation to authenticate to the Google Cloud APIs.
questions.explanation: Workload identity federation lets external systems like Terraform Cloud obtain short-lived Google Cloud credentials by exchanging their own identity tokens, eliminating long-lived service account keys. Configuring Terraform Cloud directly with workload identity federation is the most secure approach and requires minimal configuration changes since it works with the existing Terraform Cloud setup. Running Terraform on GKE or a Compute Engine VM adds unnecessary infrastructure and migration effort away from Terraform Cloud. Importing a service account key creates a long-lived credential that can be leaked, which is the least secure option.

topics.exam_domain_name: Configurar aplicações cloud-native para deployment

questions.explanation_pt: A workload identity federation permite que sistemas externos como o Terraform Cloud obtenham credenciais de curta duração do Google Cloud trocando seus próprios tokens de identidade, eliminando chaves de service account de longa duração. Configurar o Terraform Cloud diretamente com workload identity federation é a abordagem mais segura e exige mudanças mínimas de configuração, já que funciona com a configuração existente do Terraform Cloud. Executar o Terraform no GKE ou em uma VM do Compute Engine adiciona infraestrutura desnecessária e esforço de migração para fora do Terraform Cloud. Importar uma chave de service account cria uma credencial de longa duração que pode vazar, o que é a opção menos segura.

questions.question: Your team has created an application that is hosted on a GKE cluster. You need to connect the application to a REST service that is deployed in two GKE clusters in two different regions. How should you set up the connection and health checks? (Choose two.)

options.text: Use Cloud Service Mesh with sidecar proxies to connect the application to the REST service.
Use Cloud Service Mesh with proxyless gRPC to connect the application to the REST service.
Configure the REST service's firewall to allow health checks originating from the GKE service’s IP ranges.
Configure the REST service's firewall to allow health checks originating from the GKE control plane’s IP ranges.
Configure the REST service's firewall to allow health checks originating from the GKE check probe’s IP ranges.

questions.correct_text: Use Cloud Service Mesh with sidecar proxies to connect the application to the REST service. | Configure the REST service's firewall to allow health checks originating from the GKE check probe’s IP ranges.
questions.explanation: Cloud Service Mesh with sidecar proxies (Envoy) connects the application to a multi-region REST service, handling traffic routing and load balancing across the clusters in different regions. Google Cloud health check probes originate from well-known Google IP ranges (such as 35.191.0.0/16 and 130.211.0.0/22), so the REST service firewall must allow traffic from those health check probe IP ranges for the checks to succeed. Proxyless gRPC is intended for gRPC services rather than a REST service. Allowing the GKE service IP ranges or the GKE control plane IP ranges does not cover the Google-managed health checker source ranges, so those firewall rules would not permit the health probes.

topics.exam_domain_name: Integrar aplicações com serviços do Google Cloud

questions.explanation_pt: O Cloud Service Mesh com sidecar proxies (Envoy) conecta a aplicação a um serviço REST multirregião, lidando com o roteamento de tráfego e o balanceamento de carga entre os clusters em diferentes regiões. As sondagens de health check do Google Cloud se originam de faixas de IP bem conhecidas do Google (como 35.191.0.0/16 e 130.211.0.0/22), então o firewall do serviço REST precisa permitir o tráfego dessas faixas de IP das sondagens de health check para que as verificações sejam bem-sucedidas. O proxyless gRPC é destinado a serviços gRPC, e não a um serviço REST. Permitir as faixas de IP do service do GKE ou as faixas de IP do control plane do GKE não cobre as faixas de origem do verificador de saúde gerenciado pelo Google, então essas regras de firewall não permitiriam as sondagens de health check.

questions.question: You are using the latest stable version of Python 3 to develop an API that stores data in a Cloud SQL database. You need to perform CRUD operations on the production database securely and reliably with minimal effort. What should you do?

options.text: 1. Use Cloud Composer to manage the connection to the Cloud SQL database from your Python application.2. Grant an IAM role to the service account that includes the composer.worker permission.
1. Use the Cloud SQL API to connect to the Cloud SQL database from your Python application.2. Grant an IAM role to the service account that includes the cloudsql.instances.login permission.

1. Use the Cloud SQL connector library for Python to connect to the Cloud SQL database through a Cloud SQL Auth Proxy.2. Grant an IAM role to the service account that includes the cloudsql.instances.connect permission.
1. Use the Cloud SQL emulator to connect to the Cloud SQL database from Cloud Shell2. Grant an IAM role to the user that includes the cloudsql.instances.login permission.

questions.correct_text: 1. Use the Cloud SQL connector library for Python to connect to the Cloud SQL database through a Cloud SQL Auth Proxy.2. Grant an IAM role to the service account that includes the cloudsql.instances.connect permission.
questions.explanation: The Cloud SQL Python Connector library establishes a secure, encrypted connection to Cloud SQL through the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy, handling IAM-based authentication and TLS automatically with minimal effort. The service account needs the cloudsql.instances.connect permission (part of the Cloud SQL Client role) to open these connections. The cloudsql.instances.login permission is only for IAM database authentication of users, not for establishing the connection itself, and using the raw Cloud SQL Admin API is for instance management rather than CRUD data operations. Cloud Composer is an orchestration service that adds unnecessary overhead, and the Cloud SQL emulator is meant for local development, not for operating on a production database.

topics.exam_domain_name: Integrar aplicações com serviços do Google Cloud

questions.explanation_pt: A biblioteca Cloud SQL Python Connector estabelece uma conexão segura e criptografada com o Cloud SQL por meio do Cloud SQL Auth Proxy, lidando automaticamente com a autenticação baseada em IAM e o TLS com esforço mínimo. A service account precisa da permissão cloudsql.instances.connect (parte da função Cloud SQL Client) para abrir essas conexões. A permissão cloudsql.instances.login é apenas para a autenticação de banco de dados via IAM de usuários, e não para estabelecer a conexão em si, e usar a Cloud SQL Admin API diretamente serve para o gerenciamento de instâncias, e não para operações CRUD de dados. O Cloud Composer é um serviço de orquestração que adiciona sobrecarga desnecessária, e o emulador do Cloud SQL é destinado ao desenvolvimento local, e não para operar em um banco de dados de produção.

questions.question: Your company manages an application that captures stock data in an internal database. You need to create an API that provides real-time stock data to users. You want to return stock data to users as quickly as possible, and you want your solution to be highly scalable. What should you do?

options.text: Create a BigQuery dataset and table to act as the internal database. Query the table when user requests are received.
Create a Memorystore for Redis instance to store all stock market data. Query this database when user requests are received.
Create a Bigtable instance. Query the table when user requests are received. Configure a Pub/Sub topic to queue user requests that your API will respond to.

Create a Memorystore for Redis instance, and use this database to store the most accessed stock data. Query this instance first when user requests are received, and fall back to the internal database.

questions.correct_text: Create a Memorystore for Redis instance, and use this database to store the most accessed stock data. Query this instance first when user requests are received, and fall back to the internal database.
questions.explanation: Option D is correct because it combines a fast in-memory cache (Memorystore for Redis) for the most frequently accessed stock data with a fallback to the authoritative internal database, providing sub-millisecond reads for hot data while keeping the source of truth intact and scalable. Option B stores all stock market data in Redis, which is costly and unnecessary since most queries hit a small subset of popular symbols, and Redis is not intended to be the system of record. Option A querying BigQuery per request introduces analytical-query latency that is unsuitable for real-time, low-latency API responses. Option C adds Bigtable plus Pub/Sub queuing, but queuing requests through Pub/Sub adds latency and complexity rather than returning data as quickly as possible.

topics.exam_domain_name: Projetar apps cloud-native escaláveis, seguras e confiáveis

questions.explanation_pt: A opção D está correta porque combina um cache rápido em memória (Memorystore for Redis) para os dados de ações acessados com mais frequência com um fallback para o banco de dados interno autoritativo, fornecendo leituras em submilissegundos para os dados quentes (hot data) enquanto mantém a fonte da verdade intacta e escalável. A opção B armazena todos os dados do mercado de ações no Redis, o que é caro e desnecessário, já que a maioria das consultas atinge um pequeno subconjunto de símbolos populares, e o Redis não é destinado a ser o sistema de registro (system of record). A opção A, ao consultar o BigQuery a cada requisição, introduz latência de consulta analítica, que é inadequada para respostas de API em tempo real e de baixa latência. A opção C adiciona o Bigtable mais o enfileiramento via Pub/Sub, mas enfileirar requisições pelo Pub/Sub adiciona latência e complexidade em vez de retornar os dados o mais rápido possível.

questions.question: You are designing a microservices architecture for a new application that will be deployed on Cloud Run. The application requires high-throughput communication between the internal microservices. You want to use the most effective, lowest latency communication protocol for this application. What should you do?

options.text: Configure the Cloud Run service to use HTTP/2. Implement gRPC for communication between the microservices. Use streaming gRPCs when a large amount of data has to be sent.
Implement the microservices with the REST API communication protocol. Use Apigee with rate-limiting to provide the best QoS for high-priority services.
Use SOAP to build the microservices API, and use XML as the data format for communication across the microservices. Define SOAP data contracts for each microservice.
Use HTTP REST to communicate across the microservices. Implement pagination and add indexing to your database.

questions.correct_text: Configure the Cloud Run service to use HTTP/2. Implement gRPC for communication between the microservices. Use streaming gRPCs when a large amount of data has to be sent.
questions.explanation: Option A is correct because gRPC over HTTP/2 provides the lowest-latency, highest-throughput communication for internal microservices through binary Protocol Buffers serialization and multiplexed connections, and Cloud Run supports HTTP/2 and gRPC including streaming for large payloads. Option B uses REST with Apigee rate-limiting, which is a management/gateway concern and does not deliver the lowest-latency internal protocol. Option C uses SOAP with verbose XML, which is heavyweight and far slower than gRPC. Option D uses HTTP REST with pagination and indexing, which are general optimizations but still rely on text-based JSON over HTTP/1.1-style semantics and do not match gRPC's efficiency.

topics.exam_domain_name: Projetar apps cloud-native escaláveis, seguras e confiáveis

questions.explanation_pt: A opção A está correta porque o gRPC sobre HTTP/2 fornece a comunicação de menor latência e maior throughput para microserviços internos, por meio da serialização binária com Protocol Buffers e conexões multiplexadas, e o Cloud Run oferece suporte a HTTP/2 e gRPC, incluindo streaming para payloads grandes. A opção B usa REST com rate-limiting do Apigee, o que é uma questão de gerenciamento/gateway e não entrega o protocolo interno de menor latência. A opção C usa SOAP com XML verboso, que é pesado e muito mais lento que o gRPC. A opção D usa HTTP REST com paginação e indexação, que são otimizações gerais, mas ainda dependem de JSON baseado em texto sobre semântica no estilo HTTP/1.1 e não se equiparam à eficiência do gRPC.

questions.question: Your company recently modernized their monolith ecommerce site to a microservices application in GKE. Your team uses Google Cloud's operations suite for monitoring and logging. You want to improve the logging indexing and searchabilty in Cloud Logging across your microservices with the least amount of effort. What should you do?

options.text: Ask the SRE team to enable Managed Service for Prometheus on your GKE cluster.
Reconfigure your applications to write logs to an emptyDir volume. Configure a sidecar agent to read the logs and send them to the Cloud Logging API.
Update your microservices code to emit logs in JSON format.
Instrument your microservices code with OpenTelemetry libraries.

questions.correct_text: Update your microservices code to emit logs in JSON format.
questions.explanation: Option C is correct because emitting structured logs in JSON format lets the Cloud Logging agent on GKE automatically parse fields into the jsonPayload, making logs indexed and searchable by individual fields with minimal effort. Option A enabling Managed Service for Prometheus addresses metrics, not log indexing and searchability. Option B introduces an emptyDir volume and a sidecar logging agent, which adds significant operational overhead compared to simply changing the log format. Option D instrumenting with OpenTelemetry primarily improves traces and metrics and requires substantial code changes, so it is not the least-effort way to improve log searchability.

topics.exam_domain_name: Integrar aplicações com serviços do Google Cloud

questions.explanation_pt: A opção C está correta porque emitir logs estruturados em formato JSON permite que o agente do Cloud Logging no GKE faça o parsing automático dos campos para o jsonPayload, tornando os logs indexados e pesquisáveis por campos individuais com esforço mínimo. A opção A, habilitar o Managed Service for Prometheus, trata de métricas, não da indexação e pesquisabilidade de logs. A opção B introduz um volume emptyDir e um sidecar com agente de logging, o que adiciona uma sobrecarga operacional significativa em comparação a simplesmente alterar o formato do log. A opção D, instrumentar com OpenTelemetry, melhora principalmente traces e métricas e exige mudanças substanciais no código, portanto não é a forma de menor esforço para melhorar a pesquisabilidade dos logs.

questions.question: You recently developed an application that will be hosted on Cloud Run. You need to conduct a load test. You want to analyze the load test logs second by second to understand your Cloud Run service's response to rapid traffic spikes. You want to minimize effort. How should you analyze the logs?

options.text: Use estimation to extrapolate performance from summary monitoring charts.
Analyze the log data in BigQuery by configuring a BigQuery log sink with the appropriate inclusion filter for your application.
Use Cloud Monitoring’s default log console for analysis.
Analyze the log data in Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL by pushing logs to a Pub/Sub topic. Use Dataflow to process and ingest the logs.

questions.correct_text: Analyze the log data in BigQuery by configuring a BigQuery log sink with the appropriate inclusion filter for your application.
questions.explanation: Option B is correct because routing Cloud Run logs to BigQuery via a log sink with an inclusion filter lets you run SQL queries to aggregate and analyze log entries at second-by-second granularity with minimal effort and high scalability. Option A relying on summary monitoring charts cannot provide precise per-second log-level analysis of traffic spikes. Option C the Cloud Monitoring/Logs console is fine for ad hoc viewing but is not well suited to detailed time-series aggregation of load-test logs. Option D pushing logs to Pub/Sub, processing with Dataflow, and loading into Cloud SQL is a far more complex pipeline that contradicts the requirement to minimize effort.

topics.exam_domain_name: Integrar aplicações com serviços do Google Cloud

questions.explanation_pt: A opção B está correta porque rotear os logs do Cloud Run para o BigQuery por meio de um log sink com um filtro de inclusão permite executar consultas SQL para agregar e analisar as entradas de log em granularidade de segundo a segundo, com esforço mínimo e alta escalabilidade. A opção A, depender de gráficos de monitoramento resumidos, não consegue fornecer análise precisa de logs por segundo dos picos de tráfego. A opção C, o console do Cloud Monitoring/Logs, é adequado para visualização ad hoc, mas não é bem indicado para a agregação detalhada de séries temporais dos logs de teste de carga. A opção D, enviar os logs para o Pub/Sub, processar com Dataflow e carregar no Cloud SQL, é um pipeline muito mais complexo que contraria o requisito de minimizar o esforço.

questions.question: You are deploying a microservices application to GKE. One microservice needs to download files from a Cloud Storage bucket. You have an IAM service account with the Storage Object Viewer role on the project with the bucket. You need to configure your application to access the Cloud Storage bucket while following Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: Assign the IAM service account to the cluster’s node pool. Configure the application to authenticate to the bucket by using Application Default Credentials.

Assign the IAM service account to the cluster’s node pool. Encrypt the IAM service account key file by using a symmetric block cipher, and store the encrypted file on a persistent volume. Store the encryption key in Secret Manager.

Create a Kubernetes service account. Create a Kubernetes secret with a base64-encoded IAM service account key file. Annotate the Kubernetes secret with the Kubernetes service account. Assign the Kubernetes ServiceAccount to the Pods that need to access the bucket.

Create a Kubernetes service account. Use an IAM policy to bind the IAM service account to a Kubernetes service account. Annotate the Kubernetes ServiceAccount object with the name of the bound IAM service account. Assign the Kubernetes ServiceAccount to the Pods that need to access the bucket.

questions.correct_text: Create a Kubernetes service account. Use an IAM policy to bind the IAM service account to a Kubernetes service account. Annotate the Kubernetes ServiceAccount object with the name of the bound IAM service account. Assign the Kubernetes ServiceAccount to the Pods that need to access the bucket.
questions.explanation: Option D is correct because it describes Workload Identity, the Google-recommended way for GKE workloads to access Google Cloud services: you bind the Kubernetes service account to the IAM service account via an IAM policy and annotate the KSA, so Pods obtain short-lived credentials without managing key files. Option A assigning the service account to the node pool grants the permissions to every workload on those nodes, violating least privilege. Options B and C rely on exporting and storing long-lived IAM service account keys, which Google discourages because key files are a security risk and an operational burden, regardless of encryption or base64 encoding.

topics.exam_domain_name: Projetar apps cloud-native escaláveis, seguras e confiáveis

questions.explanation_pt: A opção D está correta porque descreve o Workload Identity, a forma recomendada pelo Google para que cargas de trabalho do GKE acessem serviços do Google Cloud: você vincula a conta de serviço do Kubernetes à conta de serviço do IAM por meio de uma política do IAM e adiciona a anotação na KSA, de modo que os Pods obtêm credenciais de curta duração sem gerenciar arquivos de chave. A opção A, atribuir a conta de serviço ao node pool, concede as permissões a todas as cargas de trabalho nesses nós, violando o privilégio mínimo. As opções B e C dependem de exportar e armazenar chaves de longa duração da conta de serviço do IAM, o que o Google desencoraja porque arquivos de chave são um risco de segurança e um ônus operacional, independentemente de criptografia ou codificação em base64.

questions.question: You are developing a new ecommerce website for your company. You want customers to receive a customized email notification when they place an order. You need to configure this email service while minimizing deployment effort. What should you do?

options.text: Create a Cloud Function that is triggered by a create type event in Firestore,
Create an email-sending application hosted on Compute Engine that is invoked by an HTTP request.
Create an email notification channel, and set up an alerting policy that is based on log metrics from a create type event.
Use Pub/Sub to send an email when the orders/ API returns an HTTP response of 200 OK.

questions.correct_text: Create a Cloud Function that is triggered by a create type event in Firestore,
questions.explanation: A Cloud Function triggered by a Firestore 'create' event is the lowest-effort, fully serverless way to react to new orders and send a customized email, since the function fires automatically whenever a new order document is written. This event-driven approach requires no servers to provision or manage. Option B requires building and maintaining a Compute Engine VM plus an HTTP invocation mechanism, which is far more operational overhead. Option C uses Cloud Monitoring alerting/log-based metrics, which is intended for operational alerts to administrators, not transactional customer notifications, and cannot easily customize per-order content. Option D misuses Pub/Sub, which is a messaging service and does not natively send emails or trigger on API HTTP responses.

topics.exam_domain_name: Integrar aplicações com serviços do Google Cloud

questions.explanation_pt: Uma Cloud Function acionada por um evento 'create' do Firestore é a forma de menor esforço e totalmente serverless de reagir a novos pedidos e enviar um e-mail personalizado, já que a função é disparada automaticamente sempre que um novo documento de pedido é gravado. Essa abordagem orientada a eventos não exige provisionar nem gerenciar servidores. A opção B exige construir e manter uma VM do Compute Engine além de um mecanismo de invocação HTTP, o que representa uma sobrecarga operacional muito maior. A opção C usa alertas do Cloud Monitoring/métricas baseadas em logs, que se destinam a alertas operacionais para administradores, não a notificações transacionais para clientes, e não consegue personalizar facilmente o conteúdo por pedido. A opção D usa o Pub/Sub de forma indevida, pois ele é um serviço de mensageria e não envia e-mails nativamente nem é acionado por respostas HTTP de API.

questions.question: You are developing an online chat application where users can upload profile pictures. Uploaded profile pictures must comply with content policies. You need to detect inappropriate images and label those images automatically when they are uploaded. In the future, this process will need to be expanded to include additional processing tasks such as watermarking and image compression.You want to simplify orchestration and minimize operational overhead of the image scanning and labeling steps while also ensuring that additional steps can be added and removed easily later on. What should you do?

options.text: Save user-uploaded images to a temporary Cloud Storage bucket. Implement code on the backend server to retrieve the image content and call the Vision API to process each new uploaded image.

Save user-uploaded images to a Cloud Storage bucket. Configure a Cloud Function that is triggered when a new image is uploaded and calls one or more Cloud Run services. Create additional Cloud Run services that call the Vision API to process each new uploaded image.

Save user-uploaded images to a Cloud Storage bucket. Configure a Cloud Function that is triggered when a new image is uploaded and publishes a message to a Pub/Sub topic. Deploy microservices in GKE that subscribe to the Pub/Sub topic and call the Vision API to process each new uploaded image.

Save user-uploaded images to a Cloud Storage bucket. Create an Eventarc trigger that connects the bucket to the Workflows event receiver when a new image is uploaded. Create a workflow in Workflows with multiple Cloud Functions that call the Vision API to process each new uploaded image.

questions.correct_text: Save user-uploaded images to a Cloud Storage bucket. Create an Eventarc trigger that connects the bucket to the Workflows event receiver when a new image is uploaded. Create a workflow in Workflows with multiple Cloud Functions that call the Vision API to process each new uploaded image.
questions.explanation: Using an Eventarc trigger to connect the Cloud Storage bucket to a Workflows event receiver, and defining a workflow that orchestrates multiple Cloud Functions (Vision API scanning/labeling, and later watermarking and compression), best satisfies the requirement to simplify orchestration and make steps easy to add or remove. Workflows provides a managed, declarative pipeline where individual steps can be inserted or deleted without rewiring custom code, minimizing operational overhead. Option A relies on backend server polling/retrieval rather than event-driven orchestration and does not address easy step addition. Option B chains Cloud Run services from a function but lacks a central orchestrator, making the multi-step flow harder to manage. Option C introduces GKE microservices and Pub/Sub fan-out, which adds significant operational overhead and is the opposite of minimizing management.

topics.exam_domain_name: Integrar aplicações com serviços do Google Cloud

questions.explanation_pt: Usar um gatilho do Eventarc para conectar o bucket do Cloud Storage a um receptor de eventos do Workflows, e definir um workflow que orquestra múltiplas Cloud Functions (escaneamento/rotulagem com a Vision API e, posteriormente, marca d'água e compressão), atende melhor ao requisito de simplificar a orquestração e tornar as etapas fáceis de adicionar ou remover. O Workflows fornece um pipeline gerenciado e declarativo onde etapas individuais podem ser inseridas ou excluídas sem reescrever código personalizado, minimizando a sobrecarga operacional. A opção A depende de polling/recuperação por um servidor backend em vez de orquestração orientada a eventos e não trata da facilidade de adicionar etapas. A opção B encadeia serviços do Cloud Run a partir de uma função, mas carece de um orquestrador central, tornando o fluxo de múltiplas etapas mais difícil de gerenciar. A opção C introduz microsserviços no GKE e fan-out com Pub/Sub, o que adiciona uma sobrecarga operacional significativa e é o oposto de minimizar o gerenciamento.

questions.question: You are responsible for improving the security of your Cloud Run services to protect these services against supply chain threats. You need to ensure that there are adequate security controls such as SLSA Level 3 builds for container images and non-falsifiable provenance for container images by using Google Cloud tools. What should you do?

options.text: Ask developers to build container images locally and ensure strict version controls by using Container Registry.
Use Cloud Build to build container images. Configure a Binary Authorization policy on the Cloud Run job.
Use Cloud Deploy to generate authenticated and non-falsifiable build provenance for container images.
Use Cloud Build to build container images. Use Cloud Scheduler to automate delivery of your applications to a series of target environments in a defined sequence.

questions.correct_text: Use Cloud Build to build container images. Configure a Binary Authorization policy on the Cloud Run job.
questions.explanation: Cloud Deploy (working with Cloud Build) generates authenticated, non-falsifiable build provenance and supports SLSA Level 3 build assurances, directly addressing supply chain protection for container images. The cryptographically signed provenance attests how and where the image was built, which is the core requirement. Option A has developers build locally, which produces no trusted, non-falsifiable provenance and weakens the supply chain. Option B's Binary Authorization enforces deployment policy (only allowing approved images) but does not itself generate the non-falsifiable provenance the question requires. Option D adds Cloud Scheduler for delivery automation, which is unrelated to producing build provenance.

topics.exam_domain_name: Configurar aplicações cloud-native para deployment

questions.explanation_pt: O Cloud Deploy (funcionando junto com o Cloud Build) gera proveniência de build autenticada e não falsificável e oferece suporte às garantias de build SLSA Nível 3, atendendo diretamente à proteção da cadeia de suprimentos para imagens de contêiner. A proveniência assinada criptograficamente atesta como e onde a imagem foi construída, que é o requisito central. A opção A faz os desenvolvedores construírem localmente, o que não produz uma proveniência confiável e não falsificável e enfraquece a cadeia de suprimentos. O Binary Authorization da opção B aplica a política de implantação (permitindo apenas imagens aprovadas), mas por si só não gera a proveniência não falsificável que a questão exige. A opção D adiciona o Cloud Scheduler para automação de entrega, o que não tem relação com a produção de proveniência de build.

questions.question: You are designing a microservices application on GKE that will expose a public API to users. Users will interact with the application by using OAuth 2.0, and illegitimate requests should receive a 403 response code. You need the API to be resilient against distributed denial of service (DDoS) attacks and critical security risks such as SQL injection (SQL) and cross-site scripting (XSS).You want to design the application's architecture while following Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: Install Service Mesh in your GKE cluster. Configure Service Mesh user authentication to integrate the service hosted on GKE by using an OpenID Connect-compliant identity provider. Expose the application externally by using an Istio Ingress Gateway. Use VPC firewall rules to restrict Ingress traffic to the Ingress gateway.
Run an Apache HTTP server on Cloud Run to expose a service with a public IP address. Configure the Apache HTTP server as a reverse proxy to only forward valid requests to the API hosted on GKE.
Use an external Application Load Balancer with Cloud Armor. Integrate Cloud Armor with reCAPTCHA Enterprise. Configure the load balancer to forward traffic to the application hosted on GKE.

Use an external Application Load Balancer with Cloud Armor, and configure the load balancer to forward requests to Apigee to check the validity of the API requests. Configure GKE as the application's backend.

questions.correct_text: Use an external Application Load Balancer with Cloud Armor. Integrate Cloud Armor with reCAPTCHA Enterprise. Configure the load balancer to forward traffic to the application hosted on GKE.
questions.explanation: An external Application Load Balancer with Cloud Armor is the Google-recommended way to protect a public GKE-backed API: Cloud Armor provides DDoS mitigation and preconfigured WAF rules for SQL injection and XSS, and integrating reCAPTCHA Enterprise helps distinguish legitimate from illegitimate (bot) traffic so bad requests can be denied with a 403. This places defenses at the edge before traffic reaches the application. Option A (Service Mesh with Istio Ingress and VPC firewall rules) handles authentication and east-west security but does not provide managed DDoS protection or a WAF for SQLi/XSS. Option B's Apache reverse proxy on Cloud Run is a custom, unmanaged solution that does not meet the resilience and managed WAF requirements. Option D adds Apigee for API request validation but is more complex than needed for the stated DDoS and OWASP-risk protection, which Cloud Armor handles directly.

topics.exam_domain_name: Projetar apps cloud-native escaláveis, seguras e confiáveis

questions.explanation_pt: Um external Application Load Balancer com Cloud Armor é a forma recomendada pelo Google para proteger uma API pública baseada em GKE: o Cloud Armor fornece mitigação de DDoS e regras de WAF pré-configuradas para SQL injection e XSS, e a integração com o reCAPTCHA Enterprise ajuda a distinguir tráfego legítimo de ilegítimo (bots), de modo que requisições maliciosas possam ser negadas com um 403. Isso posiciona as defesas na borda (edge), antes que o tráfego chegue à aplicação. A opção A (Service Mesh com Istio Ingress e regras de firewall da VPC) trata de autenticação e segurança east-west, mas não fornece proteção gerenciada contra DDoS nem um WAF para SQLi/XSS. A opção B, um reverse proxy Apache no Cloud Run, é uma solução customizada e não gerenciada que não atende aos requisitos de resiliência e de WAF gerenciado. A opção D adiciona o Apigee para validação de requisições de API, mas é mais complexa do que o necessário para a proteção contra DDoS e riscos OWASP descrita, que o Cloud Armor trata diretamente.

questions.question: You are compiling a compliance report on vulnerability metadata for a specific set of images identified by Artifact Analysis. Metadata from images scanned more than 30 days ago are missing from the compliance report. You need to access the vulnerability metadata for these older images. What should you do?

options.text: Create a Pub/Sub subscription to pull from Artifact Analysis topics.
Check Artifact Analysis storage buckets in Cloud Storage.
Push or pull the images from Artifact Registry.
Check Cloud Trace logs for Artifact Analysis findings.

questions.correct_text: Push or pull the images from Artifact Registry.
questions.explanation: Artifact Analysis retains vulnerability occurrence metadata for a limited time (occurrences for images not pushed/pulled are removed after about 30 days), but the underlying note and exported metadata are accessible via the Artifact Analysis storage buckets in Cloud Storage, which is where you can retrieve metadata for older scanned images. Checking those Cloud Storage buckets lets you build the compliance report for images scanned more than 30 days ago. Option A's Pub/Sub subscription only delivers new scan notifications going forward and cannot recover already-aged metadata. Option C (pushing/pulling images from Artifact Registry) would trigger rescanning rather than retrieve the historical metadata you need. Option D is incorrect because Cloud Trace handles latency tracing, not vulnerability findings.

topics.exam_domain_name: Configurar aplicações cloud-native para deployment

questions.explanation_pt: O Artifact Analysis retém os metadados de ocorrências de vulnerabilidades por um tempo limitado (as ocorrências de imagens que não são enviadas/baixadas (push/pull) são removidas após cerca de 30 dias), mas a note subjacente e os metadados exportados ficam acessíveis por meio dos buckets de armazenamento do Artifact Analysis no Cloud Storage, que é onde você pode recuperar os metadados de imagens escaneadas mais antigas. Verificar esses buckets do Cloud Storage permite montar o relatório de conformidade para imagens escaneadas há mais de 30 dias. A subscription do Pub/Sub da opção A entrega apenas notificações de novos scans daqui para frente e não consegue recuperar metadados que já expiraram. A opção C (fazer push/pull de imagens do Artifact Registry) acionaria um novo escaneamento em vez de recuperar os metadados históricos de que você precisa. A opção D está incorreta porque o Cloud Trace trata de rastreamento de latência, não de descobertas de vulnerabilidades.

questions.question: Your team runs a Python job that reads millions of customer record files stored in a Cloud Storage bucket. To comply with regulatory requirements, you need to ensure that customer data is immediately deleted once the job is completed. You want to minimize the time required to complete this task. What should you do?

options.text: Add a final step in the job that deletes all the objects in the bucket in bulk by using batch requests to the Cloud Storage API.
Configure Object Lifecycle Management on the Cloud Storage bucket that deletes all the objects in the bucket at the end of the job execution.
Remove the bucket from the Google Cloud console when the job is completed
Use the gcloud CLI to execute the gcloud storage rm --recursive gs://BUCKET_NAME/ command.

questions.correct_text: Add a final step in the job that deletes all the objects in the bucket in bulk by using batch requests to the Cloud Storage API.
questions.explanation: Because deletion must happen immediately when the job finishes and time-to-completion must be minimized, the most efficient programmatic approach is to add a final step in the job that deletes all objects using batch requests to the Cloud Storage API, which deletes many objects in parallel with minimal overhead. Object Lifecycle Management (B) is wrong because lifecycle rules run asynchronously at most once per day and cannot be triggered to fire 'at the end of a job', so deletion would not be immediate. Removing the bucket from the console (C) is a manual step that does not satisfy automated, immediate, programmatic deletion and is error-prone. Using gcloud storage rm --recursive (D) works but invokes the CLI sequentially from an external process and is slower and less integrated than issuing batched API deletes directly within the already-running job.

topics.exam_domain_name: Integrar aplicações com serviços do Google Cloud

questions.explanation_pt: Como a exclusão deve ocorrer imediatamente quando o job termina e o tempo até a conclusão deve ser minimizado, a abordagem programática mais eficiente é adicionar um passo final no job que exclui todos os objetos usando batch requests para a Cloud Storage API, o que exclui muitos objetos em paralelo com o mínimo de overhead. O Object Lifecycle Management (B) está errado porque as regras de ciclo de vida são executadas de forma assíncrona no máximo uma vez por dia e não podem ser acionadas para disparar 'ao final de um job', de modo que a exclusão não seria imediata. Remover o bucket pelo console (C) é um passo manual que não atende à exclusão programática, automatizada e imediata, além de ser propenso a erros. Usar gcloud storage rm --recursive (D) funciona, mas invoca a CLI de forma sequencial a partir de um processo externo, sendo mais lento e menos integrado do que emitir exclusões em batch via API diretamente dentro do job que já está em execução.

questions.question: You have a Cloud Run service that needs to connect to a Cloud SQL instance in a different project. You provisioned the Cloud Run service account with the Cloud SQL Client IAM role on the project that is hosting Cloud SQL. However, when you test the connection, the connection fails. You want to fix the connection failure while following Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: Add the cloudsql.instances.connect IAM permission to the Cloud Run service account.
Request additional API quota for Cloud SQL Auth Proxy,
Enable the Cloud SQL Admin API in both projects.
Migrate the Cloud SQL instance into the same project as the Cloud Run service.

questions.correct_text: Enable the Cloud SQL Admin API in both projects.
questions.explanation: When Cloud Run connects to Cloud SQL across projects, the Cloud SQL Admin API must be enabled in both the Cloud Run project (so the client/connector can call the API) and the Cloud SQL host project, so enabling the Cloud SQL Admin API in both projects fixes the connection failure. Adding the cloudsql.instances.connect permission (A) is unnecessary because the Cloud SQL Client role already grants the required connect permissions, so the IAM side is correct. Requesting more API quota (B) addresses throttling, not a hard connection failure. Migrating the instance into the same project (D) is a heavy, unnecessary change that violates the goal of a minimal, recommended fix and is not required for cross-project connectivity.

topics.exam_domain_name: Integrar aplicações com serviços do Google Cloud

questions.explanation_pt: Quando o Cloud Run se conecta ao Cloud SQL entre projetos, a Cloud SQL Admin API precisa estar habilitada tanto no projeto do Cloud Run (para que o cliente/conector possa chamar a API) quanto no projeto que hospeda o Cloud SQL, portanto habilitar a Cloud SQL Admin API em ambos os projetos corrige a falha de conexão. Adicionar a permissão cloudsql.instances.connect (A) é desnecessário porque a role Cloud SQL Client já concede as permissões de conexão necessárias, então o lado do IAM está correto. Solicitar mais cota de API (B) resolve throttling, não uma falha total de conexão. Migrar a instância para o mesmo projeto (D) é uma mudança pesada e desnecessária que viola o objetivo de uma correção mínima e recomendada, além de não ser necessária para conectividade entre projetos.

questions.question: You developed a Python script that retrieves information from files that are uploaded to Cloud Storage and writes the information to Bigtable. You have completed testing on your local environment and created the python-script service account with the Bigtable User IAM role. You want to deploy the code with the appropriate authentication while following Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: 1. Deploy your code to Cloud Functions. Create a Cloud Storage trigger.2. Configure IAM binding for authentication.
1. Deploy your code to Cloud Functions. Create a Cloud Storage trigger.2. Create a service account key for authentication
1. Deploy your image to Cloud Run. Create a trigger in Cloud Scheduler that triggers the service every minute.2. Configure IAM binding for authentication.
1. Deploy your image to Cloud Run. Create a trigger in Cloud Scheduler that triggers the service every minute.2. Create a service account key for authentication.

questions.correct_text: 1. Deploy your code to Cloud Functions. Create a Cloud Storage trigger.2. Configure IAM binding for authentication.
questions.explanation: The workload is event-driven (it should run when a file is uploaded to Cloud Storage), so deploying to Cloud Functions with a Cloud Storage trigger is the correct, efficient fit, and authentication should use IAM bindings that attach the python-script service account to the function rather than embedded keys. Option B is wrong because creating and managing service account keys is discouraged; attaching a service account and relying on Application Default Credentials is the recommended, more secure practice. Options C and D use Cloud Run polled by Cloud Scheduler every minute, which is an inefficient polling pattern for an event that should trigger only on upload, and D additionally uses a service account key, compounding the security issue.

topics.exam_domain_name: Integrar aplicações com serviços do Google Cloud

questions.explanation_pt: A carga de trabalho é orientada a eventos (deve ser executada quando um arquivo é enviado para o Cloud Storage), então fazer o deploy em Cloud Functions com um gatilho do Cloud Storage é a escolha correta e eficiente, e a autenticação deve usar bindings de IAM que vinculam a service account python-script à função, em vez de chaves embutidas. A opção B está errada porque criar e gerenciar chaves de service account é desencorajado; vincular uma service account e depender do Application Default Credentials é a prática recomendada e mais segura. As opções C e D usam Cloud Run consultado pelo Cloud Scheduler a cada minuto, o que é um padrão de polling ineficiente para um evento que deveria ser disparado apenas no upload, e a D ainda usa uma chave de service account, agravando o problema de segurança.

questions.question: You work for an ecommerce company. You are developing a new application with the following requirements:• The application must have access to the most up-to-date data at all times.• Due to company policy, data older than 30 days must be automatically deleted.You need to determine which service should host the database, and how to configure the data deletion. You want to use the most efficient solution. What should you do?

options.text: Configure Spanner to host the database. Use Data Catalog to delete data older than 30 days.
Configure Spanner to host the database. Create a time-to-live policy that deletes data older than 30 days.
Configure Bigtable to host the database. Create a time-to-live policy that deletes data older than 30 days.
Configure Bigtable to host the database. Create a garbage collection policy in Bigtable that deletes data older than 30 days.

questions.correct_text: Configure Spanner to host the database. Create a time-to-live policy that deletes data older than 30 days.
questions.explanation: The requirement for always-current, strongly consistent data plus automatic age-based deletion is met by Cloud Spanner, which provides strong external consistency, combined with a native time-to-live (TTL) policy that automatically deletes rows older than a defined retention period, matching option B. Option A is wrong because Data Catalog is a metadata and data discovery service and cannot delete table rows. Bigtable options (C and D) are weaker fits: Bigtable does not offer Spanner's relational strong-consistency guarantees in the same way, and although Bigtable uses garbage collection policies for cell/version expiration, option C invents a non-existent 'time-to-live policy' for Bigtable, while D's garbage collection works at the cell-version level rather than cleanly enforcing a 30-day record-deletion requirement as efficiently as Spanner TTL.

topics.exam_domain_name: Projetar apps cloud-native escaláveis, seguras e confiáveis

questions.explanation_pt: O requisito de dados sempre atualizados e fortemente consistentes, somado à exclusão automática baseada na idade, é atendido pelo Cloud Spanner, que oferece consistência externa forte, combinado com uma política nativa de time-to-live (TTL) que exclui automaticamente linhas mais antigas que um período de retenção definido, correspondendo à opção B. A opção A está errada porque o Data Catalog é um serviço de metadados e descoberta de dados e não pode excluir linhas de tabelas. As opções do Bigtable (C e D) são menos adequadas: o Bigtable não oferece as garantias relacionais de consistência forte do Spanner da mesma maneira, e embora o Bigtable use políticas de garbage collection para expiração de células/versões, a opção C inventa uma 'política de time-to-live' inexistente para o Bigtable, enquanto o garbage collection da D atua no nível de versão de célula em vez de impor de forma limpa um requisito de exclusão de registros em 30 dias com a mesma eficiência do TTL do Spanner.

questions.question: You are a developer at an ecommerce company. You are tasked with developing a globally consistent shopping cart for logged-in users across both mobile and desktop clients. You need to configure how the items that are added to users’ carts are stored. How should you configure this cart service?

options.text: Store the carts in a separate Memorystore for Redis instance, and configure each user's IP address as the key.
Store the carts in a separate Firestore document, and configure each user ID as the document's key.
Insert the carts in a separate Spanner table, and configure each user's encrypted password as the primary key.
Create and store the carts in the shopping-cart HTTP cookie.

questions.correct_text: Store the carts in a separate Firestore document, and configure each user ID as the document's key.
questions.explanation: Firestore is a fully managed, globally available NoSQL document database that offers strong consistency and supports both mobile and web client SDKs, making it ideal for a shopping cart keyed by user ID so the same logged-in user sees a consistent cart across devices. Storing each cart as a document keyed by user ID lets the application read and write the cart directly and reliably. Option A (Memorystore for Redis keyed by IP address) is wrong because Redis is an in-memory cache without durable global consistency, and IP addresses change and are not a stable per-user identifier. Option C is wrong because using an encrypted password as a primary key is a serious security anti-pattern and Spanner is overkill here. Option D (HTTP cookies) cannot deliver a consistent cart across separate mobile and desktop clients since cookies are per browser/device and have size limits.

topics.exam_domain_name: Projetar apps cloud-native escaláveis, seguras e confiáveis

questions.explanation_pt: O Firestore é um banco de dados de documentos NoSQL totalmente gerenciado e disponível globalmente que oferece consistência forte e dá suporte a SDKs para clientes mobile e web, tornando-o ideal para um carrinho de compras indexado por user ID, de modo que o mesmo usuário logado veja um carrinho consistente entre dispositivos. Armazenar cada carrinho como um documento indexado por user ID permite que a aplicação leia e escreva o carrinho de forma direta e confiável. A opção A (Memorystore for Redis indexado por endereço IP) está errada porque o Redis é um cache em memória sem consistência global durável, e endereços IP mudam e não são um identificador estável por usuário. A opção C está errada porque usar uma senha criptografada como chave primária é um sério antipadrão de segurança, e o Spanner é exagerado aqui. A opção D (cookies HTTP) não consegue entregar um carrinho consistente entre clientes mobile e desktop separados, já que cookies são por navegador/dispositivo e têm limites de tamanho.

questions.question: You are deploying a containerized application to GKE. You have set up a build pipeline by using Cloud Build that builds a Java application and pushes the application container image to Artifact Registry. Your build pipeline executes multiple sequential steps that reference Docker container images with the same layers.You notice that the Cloud Build pipeline runs are taking longer than expected to complete. How should you optimize the Docker image build process?

options.text: Add the --squash parameter to the Docker build steps to combine newly built layers into a single layer.
Configure Cloud Build to use a private pool in your VPC for pipeline executions.
Specify the cached image by adding the --cache-from argument in your build config file with the image as a cache source.
Store container artifacts on Cloud Storage. Configure Cloud CDN on the Cloud Storage bucket to enable caching on edge locations.

questions.correct_text: Specify the cached image by adding the --cache-from argument in your build config file with the image as a cache source.
questions.explanation: When sequential build steps reuse Docker images that share the same layers, Cloud Build can be sped up by reusing previously built layers via the Docker layer cache. Specifying a previously built image with the --cache-from argument in the build config tells Docker to pull that image and reuse its matching layers instead of rebuilding them, which directly reduces build time. Option A (--squash) collapses layers into one, which actually defeats layer caching and reuse. Option B (private pool) changes where builds run for networking/isolation reasons but does not address redundant layer rebuilds. Option D (Cloud Storage with Cloud CDN) is for serving static content at the edge and has nothing to do with accelerating Docker image builds.

topics.exam_domain_name: Construir e testar aplicações

questions.explanation_pt: Quando etapas de build sequenciais reutilizam imagens Docker que compartilham as mesmas camadas, o Cloud Build pode ser acelerado reutilizando camadas previamente construídas por meio do cache de camadas do Docker. Especificar uma imagem previamente construída com o argumento --cache-from na configuração do build instrui o Docker a baixar essa imagem e reutilizar suas camadas correspondentes em vez de reconstruí-las, o que reduz diretamente o tempo de build. A opção A (--squash) colapsa as camadas em uma só, o que na verdade anula o cache e a reutilização de camadas. A opção B (private pool) muda onde os builds são executados por motivos de rede/isolamento, mas não resolve a reconstrução redundante de camadas. A opção D (Cloud Storage com Cloud CDN) serve para entregar conteúdo estático na borda e não tem nada a ver com acelerar builds de imagens Docker.

questions.question: You are developing a dashboard that aggregates temperature readings from thousands of IoT devices monitoring a city's ambient temperature. You expect a large amount of viewing traffic resulting in a large amount of data egress once the dashboard is live. The dashboard temperature display data doesn't need to be real-time and can tolerate a few seconds of lag. You decide to deploy Memorystore for Redis as the storage backend. You want to ensure that the dashboard will be highly available. How should you configure the service in Memorystore for Redis?

options.text: Update Memorystore for Redis to the latest version.
Configure Memorystore to use read replicas.
Use Private Service Access to enable low-latency network throughput.
Set up Serverless VPC Access to avoid receiving traffic over the internet.

questions.correct_text: Configure Memorystore to use read replicas.
questions.explanation: Memorystore for Redis provides high availability through the Standard tier with replication, and enabling read replicas adds capacity to serve heavy read traffic while improving availability, which fits a read-heavy dashboard that tolerates a few seconds of lag. Read replicas let the many concurrent dashboard viewers be served from replica nodes, scaling read throughput and providing redundancy. Option A (updating to the latest version) does not by itself make the instance highly available. Options C (Private Service Access) and D (Serverless VPC Access) address network connectivity and routing, not availability or read scalability of the Redis service itself.

topics.exam_domain_name: Projetar apps cloud-native escaláveis, seguras e confiáveis

questions.explanation_pt: O Memorystore for Redis oferece alta disponibilidade por meio do tier Standard com replicação, e habilitar read replicas adiciona capacidade para atender tráfego intenso de leitura ao mesmo tempo em que melhora a disponibilidade, o que se encaixa em um dashboard com muitas leituras que tolera alguns segundos de atraso. As read replicas permitem que os muitos visualizadores simultâneos do dashboard sejam atendidos por nós replica, escalando a taxa de leitura e fornecendo redundância. A opção A (atualizar para a versão mais recente) não torna, por si só, a instância altamente disponível. As opções C (Private Service Access) e D (Serverless VPC Access) tratam de conectividade e roteamento de rede, não da disponibilidade ou da escalabilidade de leitura do próprio serviço Redis.

questions.question: You are responsible for developing a new ecommerce application that is running on Cloud Run. You need to connect your application to a Cloud SQL database that is in a separate project. This project is on an isolated network dedicated to multiple databases without a public IP. You need to connect your application to this database. What should you do?

options.text: Create a Private Service Connect endpoint on your network. Create a Serverless VPC Access connector on your project. Use Cloud SQL Language Connectors to create an internal connection.
Configure VPC Network Peering between both networks. In Cloud Run, create a Cloud SQL connection that uses the internal IP. Use Cloud SQL Language Connectors to interact with the database.
Configure private services access on your project. In Cloud Run, create a Cloud SQL connection. Use Cloud SQL Language Connectors to interact with the database.

Create a subnet on your VPC. Create a Serverless VPC Access connector on your project using the new subnet. In Cloud Run, create a Cloud SQL connection. Use Cloud SQL Language Connectors to interact with the database.
