questions.correct_text: Create a Private Service Connect endpoint on your network. Create a Serverless VPC Access connector on your project. Use Cloud SQL Language Connectors to create an internal connection.
questions.explanation: Cloud Run needs to reach a Cloud SQL instance that has only a private IP in a separate project on an isolated network, so the application must route traffic through the VPC. Creating a subnet and a Serverless VPC Access connector on that subnet gives Cloud Run a path into the VPC, and the Cloud SQL connection plus the Cloud SQL connectors then reach the private IP through that connectivity. Option A misuses Private Service Connect with redundant components for this scenario. Option B relies on VPC Network Peering between the two networks, which is more operationally complex and not required if the connector and proper private connectivity are configured. Option C configures private services access alone but provides no Serverless VPC Access connector, so Cloud Run still has no route into the VPC to reach the private IP.

topics.exam_domain_name: Integrar aplicações com serviços do Google Cloud

questions.explanation_pt: O Cloud Run precisa alcançar uma instância do Cloud SQL que tem apenas um IP privado em um projeto separado em uma rede isolada, então o aplicativo deve rotear o tráfego através da VPC. Criar uma sub-rede e um conector Serverless VPC Access nessa sub-rede dá ao Cloud Run um caminho para dentro da VPC, e a conexão do Cloud SQL mais os conectores do Cloud SQL então alcançam o IP privado através dessa conectividade. A opção A usa indevidamente o Private Service Connect com componentes redundantes para este cenário. A opção B depende do VPC Network Peering entre as duas redes, o que é operacionalmente mais complexo e não é necessário se o conector e a conectividade privada adequada estiverem configurados. A opção C configura apenas o private services access, mas não fornece nenhum conector Serverless VPC Access, então o Cloud Run ainda não tem rota para dentro da VPC para alcançar o IP privado.

questions.question: You are deploying new workloads on a GKE Autopilot mode cluster. You need to ensure that the Pods are scheduled on nodes that use Arm architecture CPUs. The cluster currently has no Arm-based CPUs. You want to minimize cluster operations. How should you ensure that the workloads on the GKE cluster will use Arm-based CPU nodes?

options.text: Apply Pod tolerations to request GKE to avoid scheduling Pods on nodes that do not have Arm-based CPUs.
Apply node taints on node pools to tell GKE to only schedule your workloads on Arm-based CPU nodes.
Deploy a new cluster in GKE Standard mode, and set up a node pool with Arm-based CPU nodes. Use nodeSelector in your manifest to ensure that Pods are scheduled in this node pool.
Request the Scale-out compute class and the arm64 architecture in your manifest.

questions.correct_text: Request the Scale-out compute class and the arm64 architecture in your manifest.
questions.explanation: In GKE Autopilot you do not manage node pools directly; instead you request hardware by selecting a compute class and CPU architecture in the workload manifest. Requesting the Scale-out compute class together with the arm64 architecture tells Autopilot to provision and schedule the Pods on Arm-based nodes automatically, which minimizes cluster operations. Options A and B describe manual taints and tolerations on node pools, which is the Standard-mode model and is not how you select Arm nodes in Autopilot. Option C abandons Autopilot to build a Standard cluster with a manually managed Arm node pool, contradicting the goal of minimizing cluster operations.

topics.exam_domain_name: Configurar aplicações cloud-native para deployment

questions.explanation_pt: No GKE Autopilot você não gerencia node pools diretamente; em vez disso, você solicita hardware selecionando uma compute class e uma arquitetura de CPU no manifesto da workload. Solicitar a compute class Scale-out junto com a arquitetura arm64 diz ao Autopilot para provisionar e agendar os Pods em nós baseados em Arm automaticamente, o que minimiza as operações de cluster. As opções A e B descrevem taints e tolerations manuais em node pools, o que é o modelo do modo Standard e não é como você seleciona nós Arm no Autopilot. A opção C abandona o Autopilot para construir um cluster Standard com um node pool Arm gerenciado manualmente, contradizendo o objetivo de minimizar as operações de cluster.

questions.question: You are developing a new Python 3 API that needs to be deployed to Cloud Run. Your Cloud Run service sits behind an Apigee proxy. You need to ensure that the Cloud Run service is running with the already deployed Apigee proxy. You want to conduct this testing as quickly as possible. What should you do?

options.text: Store the service code as a zip file in a Cloud Storage bucket. Deploy your application by using the gcloud run deploy --source command, and test the integration by pointing Apigee to Cloud Run.
Use the Cloud Run emulator to test your application locally. Test the integration by pointing Apigee to your local Cloud Run emulator.
Build a container image locally, and push the image to Artifact Registry. Deploy the Image to Cloud Run, and test the integration by pointing Apigee to Cloud Run.
Deploy your application directly from the current directory by using the gcloud run deploy --source command, and test the integration by pointing Apigee to Cloud Run.

questions.correct_text: Deploy your application directly from the current directory by using the gcloud run deploy --source command, and test the integration by pointing Apigee to Cloud Run.
questions.explanation: The fastest way to deploy a Cloud Run service from your source is to run gcloud run deploy --source from the current working directory, which uses Cloud Build/buildpacks to build the container and deploy it in a single step without needing to manually build or push images. You can then point the already-deployed Apigee proxy at the resulting Cloud Run URL to validate the integration. Option C requires manually building a container image and pushing it to Artifact Registry, adding extra steps that slow down the iteration. Option A needlessly stages the code as a zip in Cloud Storage, which is not how --source deploys work. Option B is wrong because the Cloud Run emulator runs locally and cannot be reached by the Apigee proxy running in Google Cloud, so the integration cannot be tested that way.

topics.exam_domain_name: Configurar aplicações cloud-native para deployment

questions.explanation_pt: A maneira mais rápida de implantar um serviço do Cloud Run a partir do seu código-fonte é executar gcloud run deploy --source a partir do diretório de trabalho atual, o que usa o Cloud Build/buildpacks para construir o contêiner e implantá-lo em uma única etapa, sem precisar construir ou enviar imagens manualmente. Você pode então apontar o proxy Apigee já implantado para a URL resultante do Cloud Run para validar a integração. A opção C exige construir manualmente uma imagem de contêiner e enviá-la para o Artifact Registry, adicionando etapas extras que tornam a iteração mais lenta. A opção A desnecessariamente prepara o código como um zip no Cloud Storage, o que não é como as implantações com --source funcionam. A opção B está errada porque o emulador do Cloud Run roda localmente e não pode ser alcançado pelo proxy Apigee rodando no Google Cloud, então a integração não pode ser testada dessa forma.

questions.question: Your company is planning a global event. You need to configure an event registration portal for the event. You have decided to deploy the registration service by using Cloud Run. Your company’s marketing team does not want to advertise the Cloud Run service URL. They want the registration portal to be accessed by using a personalized hostname or path in your custom domain URL pattern, for example, .example.com. How should you configure access to the service while following Google-recommended practices?

options.text: Configure Cloud Armor to block traffic on the Cloud Run service URL and allow reroutes from only the custom domain URL pattern.
Set up an HAProxy on Compute Engine, and add routing rules for a custom domain to the Cloud Run service URL.
Add a global external Application Load Balancer in front of the service, and configure a DNS record that points to the load balancer’s IP address.
Create a CNAME record that points to the Cloud Run service URL.

questions.correct_text: Add a global external Application Load Balancer in front of the service, and configure a DNS record that points to the load balancer’s IP address.
questions.explanation: The Google-recommended way to serve a Cloud Run service under a custom domain and hide the default run.app URL is to place a global external Application Load Balancer in front of the service using a serverless network endpoint group, then create a DNS record pointing your custom domain to the load balancer's static IP. This gives full control over hostnames, paths, TLS certificates, and lets you restrict ingress so the run.app URL is not used directly. Option D (a CNAME to the run.app URL) still exposes the service URL and does not give the desired routing control. Option B (HAProxy on Compute Engine) is an unmanaged, undifferentiated solution that Google does not recommend. Option A misuses Cloud Armor, which filters traffic but does not provide custom-domain hostname/path mapping for Cloud Run.

topics.exam_domain_name: Projetar apps cloud-native escaláveis, seguras e confiáveis

questions.explanation_pt: A maneira recomendada pelo Google para servir um serviço do Cloud Run sob um domínio personalizado e ocultar a URL padrão run.app é colocar um global external Application Load Balancer na frente do serviço usando um serverless network endpoint group, e então criar um registro DNS apontando seu domínio personalizado para o IP estático do load balancer. Isso dá controle total sobre hostnames, paths, certificados TLS e permite restringir o ingress para que a URL run.app não seja usada diretamente. A opção D (um CNAME para a URL run.app) ainda expõe a URL do serviço e não dá o controle de roteamento desejado. A opção B (HAProxy no Compute Engine) é uma solução não gerenciada e indiferenciada que o Google não recomenda. A opção A usa indevidamente o Cloud Armor, que filtra o tráfego mas não fornece mapeamento de hostname/path de domínio personalizado para o Cloud Run.

questions.question: You are building a Workflow to process complex data analytics for your application. You plan to use the Workflow to execute a Cloud Run job while following Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: Create a Pub/Sub topic, and subscribe the Cloud Run job to the topic.
Configure an Eventarc trigger to invoke the Cloud Run job, and include the trigger in a step of the Workflow.
Use the Cloud Run Admin API connector to execute the Cloud Run job within the Workflow.
Determine the entry point of the Cloud Run job, and send an HTTP request from the Workflow.

questions.correct_text: Use the Cloud Run Admin API connector to execute the Cloud Run job within the Workflow.
questions.explanation: To execute a Cloud Run job from within a Workflow following Google-recommended practices, you use the built-in Cloud Run Admin API connector, which calls the jobs.run method, handles authentication, polls the operation, and waits for completion before continuing. This native connector integration is simpler and more reliable than crafting raw HTTP requests. Option D (sending a manual HTTP request to a job entry point) is incorrect because Cloud Run jobs are not invoked by direct HTTP entry points like services; they are started via the Admin API. Option B uses Eventarc, which is for event-driven triggering rather than imperative invocation inside a workflow step. Option A is wrong because Cloud Run jobs cannot subscribe to a Pub/Sub topic.

topics.exam_domain_name: Integrar aplicações com serviços do Google Cloud

questions.explanation_pt: Para executar um Cloud Run job de dentro de um Workflow seguindo as práticas recomendadas pelo Google, você usa o conector integrado da Cloud Run Admin API, que chama o método jobs.run, lida com a autenticação, faz polling da operação e aguarda a conclusão antes de continuar. Essa integração nativa do conector é mais simples e confiável do que criar requisições HTTP brutas. A opção D (enviar uma requisição HTTP manual para um ponto de entrada do job) está incorreta porque os Cloud Run jobs não são invocados por pontos de entrada HTTP diretos como os serviços; eles são iniciados via Admin API. A opção B usa o Eventarc, que serve para acionamento orientado a eventos em vez de invocação imperativa dentro de uma etapa do workflow. A opção A está errada porque os Cloud Run jobs não podem se inscrever em um tópico do Pub/Sub.

questions.question: You are developing an application that needs to connect to a Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL database by using the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy. The Cloud SQL Auth Proxy is hosted in a different Google Cloud VPC network. The Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instance has public and private IP addresses. You are required to use the private IP for security reasons. When testing the connection to the Cloud SQL instance, you can connect by using the public IP address, but you are unable to connect by using the private IP address. How should you fix this issue?

options.text: Run the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy as a background service.
Add the --private-ip option when starting the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy.
Set up VPC Network Peering between your VPC and the VPC where the Cloud SQL instance is deployed.
Grant yourself the IAM role that provides access to the Cloud SQL instance.

questions.correct_text: Add the --private-ip option when starting the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy.
questions.explanation: By default the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy connects to the instance using its public IP address, which is why your public connection works but the private one fails. To force the proxy to use the instance's private IP, you must start it with the --private-ip flag (or the equivalent IP type setting), so it routes over the private network path. Option C (VPC Network Peering) is not what enables private IP for the proxy; private IP connectivity to Cloud SQL is provided through Private Service Access, and the question is specifically about the proxy ignoring the private IP. Option A (running the proxy as a background service) only affects process management, not which IP is used. Option D (granting an IAM role) addresses authorization, but the public connection already works, so credentials are not the problem.

topics.exam_domain_name: Integrar aplicações com serviços do Google Cloud

questions.explanation_pt: Por padrão, o Cloud SQL Auth Proxy se conecta à instância usando seu endereço de IP público, e é por isso que sua conexão pública funciona, mas a privada falha. Para forçar o proxy a usar o IP privado da instância, você deve iniciá-lo com a flag --private-ip (ou a configuração equivalente de tipo de IP), para que ele roteie pelo caminho de rede privada. A opção C (VPC Network Peering) não é o que habilita o IP privado para o proxy; a conectividade por IP privado ao Cloud SQL é fornecida por meio do Private Service Access, e a questão é especificamente sobre o proxy ignorar o IP privado. A opção A (executar o proxy como um serviço em segundo plano) afeta apenas o gerenciamento de processos, não qual IP é usado. A opção D (conceder um papel IAM) trata de autorização, mas a conexão pública já funciona, então as credenciais não são o problema.

questions.question: You are developing a custom job scheduler that must have a persistent cache containing entries of all Compute Engine VMs that are in a running state (not deleted, stopped, or suspended). The job scheduler checks this cache and only sends jobs to the available Compute Engine VMs in the cache. You need to ensure that the available Compute Engine instance cache is not stale. What should you do?

options.text: Set up an organization-level Cloud Storage log sink with a filter to capture the audit log events for Compute Engine. Configure an Eventarc trigger that executes when the Cloud Storage bucket is updated and sends these events to the application to update the cache.

Set up a Cloud Asset Inventory real-time feed of insert and delete events with the asset types filter set to compute.googleapis.com/Instance. Configure an Eventarc trigger that sends these events to the application to update the cache.

Set up an organization-level Pub/Sub log sink with a filter to capture the audit log events for Compute Engine. Configure an Eventarc trigger that sends these events to the application to update the cache.
Set up an organization-level BigQuery log sink. Configure the application to query this BigQuery table every minute to retrieve the last minute’s events and update the cache.

questions.correct_text: Set up a Cloud Asset Inventory real-time feed of insert and delete events with the asset types filter set to compute.googleapis.com/Instance. Configure an Eventarc trigger that sends these events to the application to update the cache.
questions.explanation: Cloud Asset Inventory provides a real-time feed that publishes resource change notifications to Pub/Sub whenever assets are created, updated, or deleted, so configuring a feed filtered to compute.googleapis.com/Instance lets you capture VM insert and delete events and update the cache via an Eventarc trigger as state changes. This keeps the cache fresh and accurate without polling. Option C relies on audit log sinks, which capture API call events but are less directly tied to actual asset state and require more parsing to determine running state. Option D polls a BigQuery table every minute, introducing latency and staleness rather than real-time updates. Option A routes change data through a Cloud Storage bucket sink, which is an indirect, batch-oriented path that delays cache updates.

topics.exam_domain_name: Integrar aplicações com serviços do Google Cloud

questions.explanation_pt: O Cloud Asset Inventory fornece um feed em tempo real que publica notificações de alteração de recursos no Pub/Sub sempre que ativos são criados, atualizados ou excluídos. Assim, configurar um feed filtrado para compute.googleapis.com/Instance permite capturar eventos de criação e exclusão de VMs e atualizar o cache por meio de um trigger do Eventarc conforme o estado muda. Isso mantém o cache atualizado e preciso sem fazer polling. A opção C depende de sinks de audit logs, que capturam eventos de chamadas de API, mas estão menos diretamente ligados ao estado real dos ativos e exigem mais parsing para determinar o estado de execução. A opção D faz polling de uma tabela do BigQuery a cada minuto, introduzindo latência e dados desatualizados em vez de atualizações em tempo real. A opção A roteia os dados de alteração por um sink de bucket do Cloud Storage, que é um caminho indireto e orientado a batch que atrasa as atualizações do cache.

questions.question: You have a Cloud Run service that connects to a Cloud SQL Enterprise edition database instance using the default Cloud SQL connection. You need to enable more than 100 connections per Cloud Run instance. What should you do?

options.text: Increase the queries per minute quota limit of the Cloud SQL Admin API.
Increase the max_connection flag in Cloud SQL for PostgresSQL.
Upgrade to Cloud SQL Enterprise Plus edition.
Use Cloud SQL Auth Proxy in a sidecar.

questions.correct_text: Upgrade to Cloud SQL Enterprise Plus edition.
questions.explanation: Cloud SQL Enterprise edition imposes a hard ceiling on the number of connections (the max_connections value is capped based on the instance's memory and edition), and the default connection path limits how many connections a single Cloud Run instance can sustain. Upgrading to Cloud SQL Enterprise Plus edition raises these limits substantially, allowing more than 100 connections per instance, so C is correct. Increasing the Cloud SQL Admin API quota (A) only affects administrative API calls, not data-plane database connections. Raising max_connections (B) cannot exceed the edition's enforced maximum, so it will not get you past the Enterprise limit. Running the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy as a sidecar (D) changes the connection mechanism for security but does not increase the maximum number of allowed connections.

topics.exam_domain_name: Projetar apps cloud-native escaláveis, seguras e confiáveis

questions.explanation_pt: A edição Cloud SQL Enterprise impõe um teto rígido ao número de conexões (o valor de max_connections é limitado com base na memória e na edição da instância), e o caminho de conexão padrão limita quantas conexões uma única instância do Cloud Run consegue sustentar. Fazer upgrade para a edição Cloud SQL Enterprise Plus eleva esses limites substancialmente, permitindo mais de 100 conexões por instância, portanto C está correta. Aumentar a cota da API Cloud SQL Admin (A) afeta apenas chamadas administrativas de API, não as conexões de banco de dados do data plane. Aumentar max_connections (B) não pode exceder o máximo imposto pela edição, então não permitirá ultrapassar o limite do Enterprise. Executar o Cloud SQL Auth Proxy como sidecar (D) altera o mecanismo de conexão por segurança, mas não aumenta o número máximo de conexões permitidas.

questions.question: You are developing a new mobile game that will be deployed on GKE and Cloud Run as a set of microservices. Currently, there are no projections for the game’s user volume.You need to store the following data types:• Data type 1: leaderboard data• Data type 2: player profiles, chats, and news feed• Data type 3: player clickstream data for BIYou need to identify a data storage solution that is easy to use, cost-effective, scalable, and supports offline caching on the user’s device. Which data storage option should you choose for the different data types?

options.text: • Data type 1: Memorystore• Data type 2: Firestore• Data type 3: BigQuery
• Data type 1: Memorystore• Data type 2: Spanner• Data type 3: Bigtable
• Data type 1: Firestore• Data type 2: Cloud SQL• Data type 3: BigQuery
• Data type 1: Firestore• Data type 2: Firestore• Data type 3: BigQuery

questions.correct_text: • Data type 1: Memorystore• Data type 2: Firestore• Data type 3: BigQuery
questions.explanation: Leaderboard data (type 1) needs extremely fast reads and writes for ranking, so Memorystore (in-memory Redis with sorted sets) is the ideal low-latency choice. Player profiles, chats, and news feed (type 2) are semi-structured, scale unpredictably, and must support offline caching and real-time sync on the user's device, which is exactly what Firestore offers through its mobile SDKs. Clickstream data for BI (type 3) is high-volume analytical data best served by BigQuery's serverless data warehouse. Option A matches all three correctly. The other options misassign at least one type: B uses Spanner (overkill and costly with no projections) and Bigtable for BI; C places leaderboards in Firestore and profiles in Cloud SQL (no offline device caching); D loses the in-memory speed needed for leaderboards.

topics.exam_domain_name: Projetar apps cloud-native escaláveis, seguras e confiáveis

questions.explanation_pt: Os dados de leaderboard (tipo 1) precisam de leituras e gravações extremamente rápidas para o ranqueamento, então o Memorystore (Redis em memória com sorted sets) é a escolha ideal de baixa latência. Perfis de jogadores, chats e feed de notícias (tipo 2) são semiestruturados, escalam de forma imprevisível e devem suportar cache offline e sincronização em tempo real no dispositivo do usuário, que é exatamente o que o Firestore oferece por meio de seus SDKs mobile. Dados de clickstream para BI (tipo 3) são dados analíticos de alto volume, mais bem atendidos pelo data warehouse serverless do BigQuery. A opção A associa os três corretamente. As outras opções atribuem incorretamente pelo menos um tipo: B usa Spanner (excessivo e caro, sem projeções) e Bigtable para BI; C coloca os leaderboards no Firestore e os perfis no Cloud SQL (sem cache offline no dispositivo); D perde a velocidade em memória necessária para os leaderboards.

questions.question: Your team developed a web-based game that has many simultaneous players. Recently, users have started to complain that the leaderboard tallies the top scores too slowly. You investigated the issue and discovered that the application stack is currently using Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL. You want to improve the leaderboard performance as much as possible to provide a better user experience. What should you do?

options.text: Re-implement the leaderboard data to be stored in Memorystore for Redis.
Optimize the SQL queries to minimize slow-running queries.
Migrate the database and store the data in AlloyDB.
Update Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL to the latest version.

questions.correct_text: Re-implement the leaderboard data to be stored in Memorystore for Redis.
questions.explanation: Leaderboard tallying of top scores for many simultaneous players is a read/write-heavy, latency-sensitive workload that relational engines handle poorly under high concurrency. Re-implementing the leaderboard in Memorystore for Redis (A) provides sub-millisecond in-memory operations and native sorted sets that compute rankings instantly, giving the largest possible performance improvement. Optimizing SQL queries (B) helps marginally but is still bound by disk-backed relational processing. Migrating to AlloyDB (C) improves PostgreSQL performance but remains a relational database, not the optimal structure for real-time ranking. Updating Cloud SQL to the latest version (D) yields negligible gains for this access pattern.

topics.exam_domain_name: Projetar apps cloud-native escaláveis, seguras e confiáveis

questions.explanation_pt: A contabilização das maiores pontuações do leaderboard para muitos jogadores simultâneos é uma carga de trabalho intensiva em leitura/gravação e sensível à latência, que motores relacionais lidam mal sob alta concorrência. Reimplementar o leaderboard no Memorystore for Redis (A) fornece operações em memória de sub-milissegundo e sorted sets nativos que calculam rankings instantaneamente, oferecendo a maior melhoria de desempenho possível. Otimizar as consultas SQL (B) ajuda marginalmente, mas ainda está limitado pelo processamento relacional baseado em disco. Migrar para o AlloyDB (C) melhora o desempenho do PostgreSQL, mas continua sendo um banco de dados relacional, não a estrutura ideal para ranqueamento em tempo real. Atualizar o Cloud SQL para a versão mais recente (D) traz ganhos insignificantes para esse padrão de acesso.

questions.question: You are a developer at a large corporation. You manage three GKE clusters. Your team’s developers need to switch from one cluster to another regularly on the same workstation. You want to configure individual access to these multiple clusters securely while following Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: Ask the developers to use Cloud Shell and run the gcloud container clusters get-credentials command to switch to another cluster.
Ask the developers to open three terminals on their workstation and use the kubectl config set command to configure access to each cluster.
Ask the developers to install the gcloud CLI on their workstation and run the gcloud container clusters get-credentials command to switch to another cluster.
In a text file, define the clusters, users, and contexts. Email the file to the developers and ask them to use the kubectl config set command to add cluster, user, and context details to the file.

questions.correct_text: Ask the developers to install the gcloud CLI on their workstation and run the gcloud container clusters get-credentials command to switch to another cluster.
questions.explanation: The Google-recommended approach for accessing GKE clusters from a workstation is to install the gcloud CLI locally and run gcloud container clusters get-credentials, which automatically writes the correct cluster endpoint, certificate, user, and context entries into kubeconfig and uses the gke-gcloud-auth-plugin for secure, IAM-backed authentication. This lets developers switch contexts safely without manual credential editing, so C is correct. Cloud Shell (A) works but is ephemeral and not a per-workstation setup for regular local switching. Manually configuring with kubectl config set across three terminals (B) is error-prone and not recommended. Emailing a text file of clusters, users, and contexts (D) exposes sensitive configuration insecurely and is a poor practice.

topics.exam_domain_name: Configurar aplicações cloud-native para deployment

questions.explanation_pt: A abordagem recomendada pelo Google para acessar clusters GKE a partir de uma estação de trabalho é instalar a gcloud CLI localmente e executar gcloud container clusters get-credentials, que grava automaticamente o endpoint correto do cluster, o certificado, o usuário e as entradas de contexto no kubeconfig e usa o gke-gcloud-auth-plugin para autenticação segura e respaldada por IAM. Isso permite que os desenvolvedores troquem de contexto com segurança, sem edição manual de credenciais, portanto C está correta. O Cloud Shell (A) funciona, mas é efêmero e não é uma configuração por estação de trabalho para troca local regular. Configurar manualmente com kubectl config set em três terminais (B) é propenso a erros e não é recomendado. Enviar por e-mail um arquivo de texto com clusters, usuários e contextos (D) expõe configurações sensíveis de forma insegura e é uma prática ruim.

questions.question: You are tasked with using C++ to build and deploy a microservice for an application hosted on Google Cloud. The code needs to be containerized and use several custom software libraries that your team has built. You want to minimize maintenance of the application’s underlying infrastructure. How should you deploy the microservice?

options.text: Use Cloud Run functions to deploy the microservice.
Use Cloud Build to create the container, and deploy it on Cloud Run.
Use Cloud Shell to containerize your microservice, and deploy it on GKE Standard.
Use Cloud Shell to containerize your microservice, and deploy it on a Container-Optimized OS Compute Engine instance.

questions.correct_text: Use Cloud Build to create the container, and deploy it on Cloud Run.
questions.explanation: The microservice is written in C++ with custom libraries and must be containerized while minimizing infrastructure maintenance. Using Cloud Build to build the container image and deploying it to Cloud Run (B) lets you package any language and dependencies into a container while Cloud Run fully manages the serverless runtime, so it is correct. Cloud Run functions (A) target supported runtime languages and event-driven snippets, not arbitrary C++ with bundled custom libraries. GKE Standard (C) requires you to manage nodes and cluster infrastructure, increasing maintenance. A Container-Optimized OS Compute Engine instance (D) still requires you to manage and patch the VM, which is the most operational overhead.

topics.exam_domain_name: Configurar aplicações cloud-native para deployment

questions.explanation_pt: O microsserviço é escrito em C++ com bibliotecas personalizadas e precisa ser containerizado minimizando a manutenção da infraestrutura. Usar o Cloud Build para construir a imagem do contêiner e implantá-la no Cloud Run (B) permite empacotar qualquer linguagem e dependências em um contêiner, enquanto o Cloud Run gerencia totalmente o runtime serverless, portanto está correta. As Cloud Run functions (A) têm como alvo linguagens de runtime suportadas e trechos orientados a eventos, não C++ arbitrário com bibliotecas personalizadas empacotadas. O GKE Standard (C) exige que você gerencie nós e a infraestrutura do cluster, aumentando a manutenção. Uma instância do Compute Engine com Container-Optimized OS (D) ainda exige que você gerencie e aplique patches na VM, o que representa a maior sobrecarga operacional.

questions.question: Your team is trying to reduce their cloud spend, and you want to evaluate your GKE Autopilot cluster costs. When reviewing the manifests, you see that resource requests are currently not specified. Your application is stateless and fault-tolerant, and there are no specific hardware or memory requirements on nodes. You want to modify the cluster to be scalable and cost-effective as quickly as possible while maintaining a cluster with sufficient computing resources. What should you do?

options.text: Request that your Pods run as Spot Pods, and use the cloud.google.com/gke-spot=true label in your YAML manifest.
Request the Balanced compute class in your YAML manifest.
In the YAML deployment configuration manifest, request and set the maximum CPU to 5 vCPU.
Set up Cloud Trace and Cloud Monitoring, identify the maximum memory used in the past 30 days, and set the YAML manifest to request that amount of memory.

questions.correct_text: Request that your Pods run as Spot Pods, and use the cloud.google.com/gke-spot=true label in your YAML manifest.
questions.explanation: Because the application is stateless and fault-tolerant with no special hardware needs, running its Pods as Spot Pods is the fastest way to cut cost while keeping the cluster scalable, since Autopilot Spot Pods are billed at heavily discounted rates and the workload can tolerate the occasional preemption. You select them with the cloud.google.com/gke-spot=true node selector/label in the manifest. The Balanced compute class changes the CPU/memory platform but does not deliver the same cost savings as Spot. Hard-capping CPU to 5 vCPU or sizing memory from 30 days of Cloud Monitoring data addresses right-sizing requests, not the quick, large cost reduction Spot provides, and Cloud Trace is for latency analysis, not memory sizing.

topics.exam_domain_name: Configurar aplicações cloud-native para deployment

questions.explanation_pt: Como a aplicação é stateless e tolerante a falhas, sem necessidades de hardware especial, executar seus Pods como Spot Pods é a forma mais rápida de reduzir custos mantendo o cluster escalável, já que os Spot Pods do Autopilot são cobrados a taxas com fortes descontos e a carga de trabalho pode tolerar a preempção ocasional. Você os seleciona com o node selector/label cloud.google.com/gke-spot=true no manifesto. A compute class Balanced altera a plataforma de CPU/memória, mas não oferece a mesma economia de custos que o Spot. Limitar a CPU em 5 vCPU ou dimensionar a memória a partir de 30 dias de dados do Cloud Monitoring trata do right-sizing das requests, não da redução de custos rápida e expressiva que o Spot proporciona, e o Cloud Trace serve para análise de latência, não para dimensionamento de memória.

questions.question: You are building an application that will store frequently accessed data in a Memorystore for Redis Cluster instance. You would like to make the application resilient to network issues. You need to ensure that the application handles client disconnections from a Redis instance gracefully to minimize disruption and ensure stability of the application. What should you do?

options.text: Immediately terminate the application instance upon detecting a Redis disconnection to force a restart, and wait for clients to reconnect to the cache as soon as the application becomes available.
Configure the Redis client to reconnect after a fixed delay of 60 seconds.
Use Memorystore’s automatic failover mechanisms to make the Redis cache available in a secondary zone.
Implement exponential backoff with a jitter when reconnecting after a disconnection. Configure client-side caching to serve data during brief outages.

questions.correct_text: Implement exponential backoff with a jitter when reconnecting after a disconnection. Configure client-side caching to serve data during brief outages.
questions.explanation: To handle Redis client disconnections gracefully, the client should implement exponential backoff with jitter when reconnecting, which avoids thundering-herd reconnection storms and spreads retries out to let the instance recover, while client-side caching can serve data during brief outages to minimize disruption. Immediately terminating and restarting the application is disruptive and does nothing to make reconnection resilient. A fixed 60-second reconnect delay is both slow and prone to synchronized retries across many clients. Memorystore's automatic failover improves backend availability but does not address how the client gracefully tolerates and recovers from transient disconnections, which is what the question asks.

topics.exam_domain_name: Projetar apps cloud-native escaláveis, seguras e confiáveis

questions.explanation_pt: Para lidar com desconexões do cliente Redis de forma elegante, o cliente deve implementar exponential backoff com jitter ao reconectar, o que evita tempestades de reconexão do tipo thundering-herd e distribui as novas tentativas para permitir que a instância se recupere, enquanto o caching no lado do cliente pode servir dados durante interrupções breves para minimizar a disrupção. Encerrar e reiniciar imediatamente a aplicação é disruptivo e não torna a reconexão resiliente. Um atraso fixo de reconexão de 60 segundos é lento e propenso a novas tentativas sincronizadas entre muitos clientes. O failover automático do Memorystore melhora a disponibilidade do backend, mas não trata de como o cliente tolera e se recupera de forma elegante de desconexões transitórias, que é o que a questão pergunta.
